Phlogopite is a layered monoclinic mica used in insulation, construction, coatings, reinforcement, radiation applications, and atomic-track dating. This study modeled its response to irradiation using XTANT-3, which combines transport Monte Carlo, Boltzmann collision integrals, and tight-binding molecular dynamics to capture nonequilibrium electronic and atomic dynamics, electron–phonon coupling, and nonthermal bond changes. Simulations used a 396-atom cell and a 10 fs, 92 eV laser pulse.

The valence band is dominated by oxygen p states, while K, Mg, Si, and Al contribute to the conduction band. The calculated bandgap is 7.5 eV in the ideal structure and about 6.5 eV at room temperature.

At approximately 0.17 eV/atom and an electronic temperature of 11,000 K, hydrogen first detaches, diffuses, and crosses the Mg layer, while the remaining lattice stays stable. This threshold agrees with the reported experimental value of 1000 kGy, equivalent to roughly 0.2 eV/atom. Electron–phonon coupling raises the threshold compared with a Born–Oppenheimer simulation because electronic cooling suppresses nonthermal Mg and Si displacement.

Near 0.4 eV/atom, Mg becomes liquid-like while other sublattices remain solid, producing a superionic state with two liquid subsystems. Above about 0.5 eV/atom, the full lattice disorders. At roughly 0.9 eV/atom, the bandgap collapses and the material becomes metallic. At 2 eV/atom, nonthermal heating rapidly accelerates oxygen first, followed by potassium and other elements, leading to complete disorder within a few hundred femtoseconds. Incident-photon fluence thresholds were also estimated under specified absorption and transport assumptions. Overall, irradiation dose can generate superionic, semimetallic, and metallic transient states in phlogopite.

The lecture evaluates major green-building projects by examining stakeholder interests, market evidence, costs, risks, and adoption of innovation.

Winthrop Center was developed in Boston between 2016 and 2018 as a large Passive House project. Market comparisons, including the 2019 sale of 100 Summer Street at a four-percent capitalization rate, suggested that buyers were not assigning a premium to its green features. Winthrop Center also lost State Street as a potential anchor tenant because the competing property had a more usable floor plate, a stronger office entrance, and lower rent. Winthrop’s owner retained its rent premium because long leases made lowering rent financially difficult. In response to questions, the case was described as having no preleasing before construction, although participants disagreed about wording elsewhere in the case.

The project faced additional disruptions when COVID-19 caused HSBC to withdraw from a planned January 2020 loan syndication, pausing construction for nearly three months. A Kuwait-based sovereign wealth fund later financed the $700 million loan. Cornell Tech was an important risk-reduction precedent for Winthrop: its 250,000-square-foot Passive House building, developed with Hudson and Cornell, included Cornell’s equity participation and affordable student housing. Hudson had previously withdrawn from an earlier market-rate project because first-time development risks, likely construction premiums, uncertain rents, and unproven operating savings made the economics unattractive.

Passive House studies cited a construction-cost premium ranging from 1% to 8%, depending on experience and knowledge. Winthrop Center’s premium was said to have reached only 1% because of an experienced developer, consultants, and construction team. Triple-glazed windows and thermal-bridge treatment were identified as major cost components. The case’s larger beneficiaries were expected to be tenants and public authorities: the building provided lower operating costs, while Massachusetts building codes and Boston’s regulatory process helped spread Passive House practices. Boston subsequently became home to large projects including Winthrop Center, Bunker Hill Redevelopment, and Northland Newton Development.

The lecture describes a diffusion pathway for sustainable design: scientific and design communities establish the concept; corporate real-estate and MUSH projects—municipal governments, universities, schools, and hospitals—serve as lower-risk pilots; broader commercial development follows; and regulation ultimately drives mass adoption. As information spreads, experience reduces cost and risk premiums, market rents begin rewarding performance, and new practices become standard. Massachusetts’s forthcoming net-zero stretch code was presented as a possible route toward wider Passive House adoption.

The second case concerns L&L Development’s planned $1 billion 425 Park Avenue project, conceived in 2012 with 670,000 square feet of office space and 18,000 square feet of retail. The project faced a cash-consuming ground lease, financing uncertainty after Lehman Brothers’ failure, zoning requirements to retain 25% of an existing structure, and an estimated 8% cost premium from the difficult structural work. Its Park Avenue location, proximity to Central Park, large floor plates, and proximity to Midtown’s financial tenants were major advantages over competitors such as One World Trade Center and Hudson Yard.

L&L’s strategy was to create a “healthiest building” in New York in response to interest in indoor environmental quality, sick-building syndrome, employee health, and productivity. Options included upgraded ventilation and MERV 15 filtration, WELL certification, the less stringent and less expensive Fitwell system, CDC certification, and a LEED-based baseline. The proposed ventilation and filtration system represented a $12.3 million initial cost and a $3.9 million annual operating increase; overall health-related costs were estimated at roughly 2% to 6% above the baseline. Potential tenant benefits included lower health-insurance costs, improved productivity, reduced turnover and absenteeism, and better employee retention. The lecture stressed that many projected benefits depended on assumptions rather than demonstrated results for the proposed tenants.

Adoption was discussed through the law of diffusion of innovation, with roughly 15% to 18% adoption identified as a tipping point, and through Geoffrey Moore’s “chasm” model, which warns that many new products fail when moving from enthusiasts to the mainstream. Because most occupants require quantitative evidence, L&L needed enough early adopters to generate credible performance data. The likely target was sophisticated financial tenants, particularly hedge funds or financial firms able to lease entire floors and value both health benefits and office prestige. Participants also emphasized that leasing decisions involve multiple parties: a general partner may choose the office, limited partners pay, and facilities, human-resources, and finance executives may value different benefits.

The outcome was mixed. WELL adoption accelerated, and Citadel reportedly leased about 200,000 square feet, later extending toward 300,000 square feet in a record New York office transaction. Nevertheless, much of the building remained unleased. Structural difficulties delayed the project by more than a year, cost roughly $100 million, and contributed to financial distress and the loss of equity by 2020; the lecture attributed these problems to project risk rather than the healthy-building strategy. More broadly, data presented for five U.S. central business districts showed demand rising by 7 million square feet for ultra-healthy, high-quality offices while demand for lower-quality buildings fell by 25 million square feet, supporting the broader “flight to quality” trend.

The lecture examines utility from beliefs, motivated optimism, and deviations from Bayesian learning. Anticipatory utility can encourage information seeking and shape beliefs about the future. When belief utility is concave, people are information-averse; when it is convex, they are information-loving. If beliefs are manipulable and future outcomes cannot be changed, people may prefer optimistic beliefs because these improve current happiness. Optimal expectations balance this benefit against distorted decisions and possible future disappointment.

Evidence from Weinstein and other studies indicates widespread overoptimism about future events, including marriage, business success, health, travel, income, and longevity. People also tend to overestimate their abilities and traits. MIT students appear comparatively underconfident, especially female students, possibly because frequent feedback limits overconfidence, negative expectations can be self-motivating, and reduced overconfidence lowers the risk of disappointment.

Related research on ego utility argues that positive illusions can support happiness, productivity, care for others, coping with negative feedback, and mental health. “Depressive realism” may therefore be harmful. Positive biases are stronger for personally important matters, perceived control, and ambiguous feedback, but weaker when reliable, objective feedback is available.

Laboratory studies show asymmetric belief updating: people generally update appropriately after positive feedback but discount negative information. They also pay more for information expected to be favorable. Motivated memory may reinforce these beliefs because positive signals are remembered better over time. Real-world evidence links overconfidence to excessive trading, investment losses, managerial hubris, and value-destroying mergers.

Although Bayesian learning provides a mathematically grounded method for updating probabilities, it is cognitively demanding. People generally recognize whether evidence should raise or lower an estimate but often determine the magnitude of adjustment poorly. They therefore rely on heuristics that enable quick decisions but generate systematic errors.

Three major biases are discussed. The gambler’s fallacy treats an absent outcome as more likely after a long streak, as illustrated by coin-flip experiments and potentially by judges’ or loan officers’ decisions. The hot-hand fallacy assumes recent successful performances will continue, causing people to overinfer underlying skill from small samples. Both reflect the mistaken “law of small numbers.” Base-rate neglect causes people to focus on test accuracy while ignoring disease prevalence; in the lecture’s HIV example, the correct probability after a positive 99%-accurate test is 50%, not 99%. Base-rate neglect can also distort judgments of highly accurate tests when prevalence is low.

Other heuristics include representativeness, illustrated by the Linda problem, in which similarity judgments override the conjunction law, and availability, in which vivid events are judged more frequent than they are. Research on online information suggests that people may fail to evaluate source accuracy unless attention is drawn to it, with inattention potentially mattering more than partisanship.

The lecture concludes that misinformation can arise from limited attention, incorrect theories, motivated beliefs, or difficulty learning probabilistically. These causes have different policy implications: salience and labeling may help when people overlook information or hold incorrect theories, but correcting deliberately maintained beliefs may reduce well-being and provoke resistance. Providing better information is more clearly beneficial when systematic learning errors, rather than motivated rejection of truth, cause poor decisions.

The passage explains how defect-resistant topological surface states can be adapted to lasers. Conventional lasers are sensitive to dust, mirror misalignment, and other defects, and at higher power their color and beam profile can destabilize as unwanted wavelengths appear. In some electronic insulators, surface states conduct while the interior does not. Because reversing an electron’s direction requires flipping its spin and losing energy, these surface electrons can conduct with minimal scattering from defects.

To reproduce this behavior with light, a two-dimensional lattice of coupled optical waveguide rings replaces the electronic crystal. Carefully selecting which rings are excited confines amplified light to the edge, while phase-shifting connections cause unprotected light to be scattered out unless its color changes. The surviving protected mode is amplified and dominates the output.

Accurate modeling and precise fabrication were essential. Experiments comparing protected and unprotected designs showed that protected lasing continued after rings were removed, was more efficient, and did not develop unwanted colors as power increased. Such stable, single-wavelength lasers could support applications including 5G networks and space-based interferometers.

In Phase 1, a few participants had temporary decreases in lymphocyte counts 1–3 days after the first dose of BNT162b1 or BNT162b2; counts returned to normal by 6–8 days after Dose 1. The 10-, 20-, and 30-µg doses were generally well tolerated, but the 100-µg BNT162b1 dose was stopped after Dose 1 because of injection-site reactions or systemic events. No participants left Phase 1 because of medical problems, and no single medical problem occurred in more than two participants in any dose group. BNT162b2 at 30 µg was selected for Phase 2/3.

Injection-site reactions and systemic events after BNT162b1 or BNT162b2 were well tolerated, resolved quickly, and were generally mild or moderate. Injection-site pain was the most common injection-site reaction, while tiredness and headache were the most common systemic events. Results were similar in Phase 2/3 and among booster groups.

In Phase 2/3, 30-µg BNT162b2 was well tolerated. Few participants left the blinded phase because of medical problems: 32 of 21,926 in the BNT162b2 group and 36 of 21,921 in the placebo group. Most medical problems were mild or moderate, and most among BNT162b2 recipients involved injection-site reactions or systemic events. No single medical problem occurred in more than 1% of participants aged 12–15 years.

Serious medical problems were rare, with no single serious problem reaching 1% in the reported groups. Researchers generally did not consider them vaccine-related, although a small number following BNT162b2 or a booster were considered possibly related. Four of 324 BNT162b2SA recipients in Phase 3 had serious problems, none considered vaccine-related.

No participant died in Phase 1. During Phase 2/3, 85 of 23,141 initial BNT162b2 recipients, 62 of 21,371 initial placebo recipients later given BNT162b2, and 23 of 23,141 placebo-only recipients died from different causes; researchers did not believe BNT162b2 caused the deaths. No deaths occurred in the reported Phase 3 BNT162b2SA group.

The lecture presents neutral-particle diagnostics for indirectly measuring the core ion distribution in magnetic-confinement plasmas. Because core ions are fully ionized and well confined, diagnostics based on electrons or laser-accessible atoms cannot directly provide their distribution. The proposed approach is to convert some core ions into neutrals, which can escape and carry information about the original ion population.

Neutrals can be produced through charge exchange with edge neutrals or an injected neutral beam; radiative recombination is negligible because reionization is rapid. Their escape is limited by electron-impact ionization, ion-impact ionization, and further charge exchange. Charge exchange generally dominates, so neutral diagnostics require relatively low-density plasmas to provide sufficiently long neutral mean free paths.

A passive diagnostic uses escaping neutrals, a stripping cell to convert them into ions, magnetic analysis, and energy-resolved detection to infer the core ion distribution and fast-ion tails. It is line-integrated and can include signals from cold edge neutrals. An active diagnostic intersects a neutral beam with the core to localize the measurement. Charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy can determine impurity density, flow, and temperature, while beam-modulation techniques separate the diagnostic signal from background radiation. Beam-emission spectroscopy measures localized electron-density fluctuations, although detailed atomic modeling and beam attenuation are required. Finally, the motional Stark effect uses magnetic-field-induced splitting of neutral-beam emission to determine the magnetic-field magnitude and orientation, helping reconstruct the tokamak’s poloidal field and current distribution.

This educational case describes Toyota’s escalating quality crisis with ChassisCo’s Athens, Georgia plant, which made rear-suspension cradles for the 2003 Suprima crossover. By late 2004, after 14 months of production, output was barely 60% of target, many parts and cradles were nonconforming, and problem tracking was inadequate. ChassisCo had doubled automation and value-added work, expanded quality staffing from 18 to 90, assumed responsibility for 85 parts, and operated 12-hour days, seven days a week, but Toyota considered these efforts insufficient.

The case explains the Toyota Production System as an integrated system based on jidoka, just-in-time production, waste and variability reduction, problem solving, continuous improvement, and respect for people. Toyota develops suppliers as long-term partners through training, collaboration, communication, and early escalation of problems. ChassisCo’s first Suprima launch in 1997 benefited from Japanese-made stamped parts, Toyota-designed plant and equipment, and extensive Japanese support; ChassisCo eventually controlled its quality problems and received an award in 2002. A successful 1999 Responsa launch at a new St. Louis plant, including increased automation and local sourcing, led Toyota to give ChassisCo broader project-management and sourcing responsibilities for the more complex 2003 Suprima.

Toyota and ChassisCo underestimated the resulting capability gaps. ChassisCo lacked effective part tracking, stage-gate and executive-review processes, supplier-management resources, familiarity with Toyota’s Technical Instruction Sheets and tuning practices, and the capacity to meet stringent individual-part requirements. Decentralization had dispersed lessons from earlier launches, while concurrent projects stretched its engineering resources. The program had 102 tool sets to qualify but only two tool-and-die engineers, lacked a supplier-management group and materials manager, and encountered resistance to adding prelaunch staff. Aggressive Toyota cost targets and a riveted design increased complexity, while ChassisCo accepted low-cost suppliers, selected an inexperienced supplier, underestimated logistics costs, and failed to tell Toyota that the target price was unrealistic.

Toyota also initially addressed supplier problems too late. ChassisCo had not adequately audited its second-tier suppliers or developed staff capable of doing so. When Bernstein visited suppliers in 2003, he found severe quality and production deficiencies, including problems at the Tulsa plant that threatened startup rates. ChassisCo lacked defined processes for quickly correcting these issues.

The Suprima launched on time in September 2003 despite Athens failing the required high-volume production trial three times in August. Production remained below target, suppliers also missed output requirements, and ChassisCo lacked standardized work, defect-feedback systems, and second-tier inspection processes. Automated welding eliminated the real-time visual feedback available in manual welding, increasing inspection, rework, and root-cause analysis needs. Scrap, downtime, poor part quality, inventory inspection, overtime, and cost overruns followed. Toyota audits in 2004 found assembly-critical weld nonconformances; Athens scored only 13% in a November arc-welding audit, and external defects rose from 565 per week in July 2003 to 2,845 per week in July 2004.

By late 2004, Bernstein was visiting Athens at least twice weekly, prioritizing problems, and creating activity checklists, but progress remained elusive. The plant averaged four hours of daily overtime plus Saturday work, prompting concerns about burnout and a downward spiral. Its weak quality-information system and lack of defect-flowout control made it difficult to determine whether known-defective cradles had reached TMMGA. ChassisCo’s plant manager said the facility was losing money and requested a price increase; Bernstein insisted that quality, not merely cost, required immediate corrective action. The case ends by asking participants to identify ChassisCo’s and Toyota’s respective responsibilities and options for resolving the crisis, including whether TPS or a different approach was needed.

Radiotheranostics uses agents that bind to biological targets for both diagnostic imaging and radiopharmaceutical therapy. Although approved agents such as [¹⁷⁷Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 support personalized cancer treatment, standardized dosing and intervals overlook variability in pharmacokinetics, tumor burden, and radiobiological sensitivity, affecting efficacy and toxicity.

Computational nuclear oncology and theranostic digital twins (TDTs) offer model-informed personalization. Physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models incorporate patient physiology and drug properties to predict radiopharmaceutical activity, absorbed doses, and treatment responses. They comprise computational, anatomical-physiological, and radiopharmaceutical frameworks and may be developed bottom-up, top-down, or through a middle-out combination of mechanistic knowledge and patient-data calibration.

Clinical adoption depends on model verification, validation, and uncertainty quantification (VVUQ). Verification checks conceptual and computational implementation through physiology review, mass-balance and unit checks, simulation testing, and visual inspection. Internal validation assesses goodness of fit, model selection, and parameter sensitivity using graphical, statistical, Bayesian, and resampling methods. External validation evaluates generalizability through independent data or data splitting, while uncertainty quantification propagates parameter uncertainty and evaluates output precision, bias, and accuracy.

TDTs extend PBPK models through bidirectional feedback between patients and virtual representations, integrating evolving imaging, laboratory, and clinical data to support personalized treatment decisions. Their continuous updates, noisy inputs, and sparse datasets require iterative VVUQ. Fit-for-purpose radiopharmaceutical standards remain underdeveloped, limiting regulatory translation and consistent clinical implementation.

McGill University researchers developed DOLPHIN, an AI tool that analyzes exon and junction information to reveal previously hidden disease markers and variation within single cells that gene-level methods obscure. In pancreatic cancer data, DOLPHIN identified more than 800 markers missed by conventional tools and distinguished high-risk, aggressive cancers from less severe cases, potentially enabling earlier detection and better treatment selection. The tool also produces detailed single-cell profiles for digital cell models and simulations of disease and drug responses before laboratory or clinical trials. Researchers plan to expand it from several datasets to millions of cells to improve virtual cell models.

The paper proposes a scalable, theory-driven framework for evaluating and training the persuasive capabilities of large language models (LLMs), grounded in Bayesian persuasion. It defines LLM persuasion as a sender’s strategic disclosure of information that shifts a receiver’s beliefs in the sender’s favor. The framework formalizes signaling, Bayesian belief updates, receiver best responses, Bayes plausibility, and the “concavification” of the sender’s payoff, explaining why partial transparency can be more effective than complete disclosure or opacity.

The authors repurpose existing human-persuasion datasets to create opinion-change environments in which both sender and receiver are LLMs. They measure persuasive benefit through persuasion gains and strategic disclosure through the conditional mutual information between messages and underlying states. A human study with 45 participants supports the plausibility of these environments.

Experiments show that stronger frontier models, including DeepSeek-R1, achieve greater persuasion gains and exhibit theoretically predicted behaviors such as adaptive information revelation. Reinforcement learning is used to train sender LLMs against receiver LLMs; even the small Llama3.2-3B-Instruct model can reach persuasive performance comparable to larger models. Reinforcement-learned improvements produce significantly higher gains and transfer across different receiver architectures, suggesting that LLMs can learn effective information-design strategies.

The Clock is a simple, versatile zone offense based on a 1-3-1 free-lance passing attack, basic rotations, and sharp, crisp ball movement. It creates outside shots, basket cuts, and post-roll opportunities and can be used against person-to-person, 1-3-1, and 1-2-2 defenses.

Corner-pass options have wings cut to the basket for return passes while corners can feed an open post. When defenses prevent open shots, the ball is quickly reversed to attack the weak side. Wings may also dribble toward the corner, causing the corner player to backcut while the wing becomes the baseline cutter. Clock continuity maintains these rotations and passing options.

Against a 1-3-1 zone, the offense exploits baseline weaknesses through cuts, post entries, and reversals. Against a 1-2-2 zone, it attacks vulnerabilities in the middle and corners. Basic rules include rolling the post after baseline-corner passes and having baseline corners backcut when the ball enters the middle.

When a trap or double team occurs, the “Cat” counter immediately shifts to a 2-1-2 alignment and moves the ball with sharp, accurate passes without dribbling. If passing lanes are completely denied, the offense passes the ball out of the trap.

Two “Crunch Time” specials are included. “Vegas” uses a weakside double screen and return skip pass for a shot, with options to feed a rolling post or make an “X” pass. “Back” uses a weakside lob, with positioning, passing, and screening options before returning to basic Clock action if the lob is unavailable.

Two State Department circulars address passport issuance. Such citizens should retain full protection until they effectively abandon U.S. residence and domicile.

NVIDIA’s Turing GPU architecture combines rasterization, real-time ray tracing, AI, and simulation. The TU102, its highest-performing model, contains six GPCs, 36 TPCs, and 72 SMs, providing 6,144 CUDA cores, 576 Tensor Cores, 72 RT Cores, 96 ROP units, 6 MB of L2 cache, and a 384-bit GDDR6 interface. Each SM has 64 CUDA cores, eight Tensor Cores, one RT Core, a 256 KB register file, four texture units, and 96 KB of configurable L1/shared memory. Its SMs support concurrent FP32 and INT32 execution, independent thread scheduling, and unified L1, shared-memory, and texture caching.

The TU104 scales the same architecture to six GPCs and 48 SMs, with 3,072 CUDA cores, 368 Tensor Cores, and 48 RT Cores. The TU106 has three GPCs and 36 SMs, with 2,304 CUDA cores, 288 Tensor Cores, and 36 RT Cores. TU102 and TU104 support second-generation NVLink; TU106 supports neither NVLink nor SLI. The Tesla T4 uses a reduced TU104 configuration and is aimed at data-center, enterprise, and edge inference.

Turing Tensor Cores support FP16, INT8, and INT4 operations and accelerate neural-network training and inference. NVIDIA NGX uses these cores for client-side AI features including Deep Learning Super Sampling (DLSS), AI Inpainting, AI Super Rez, and AI Slow-Mo. DLSS uses neural networks trained against 64-times-supersampled references to produce target-resolution images from lower-cost inputs. AI InPainting synthesizes replacement content, AI Slow-Mo generates interpolated video frames, and AI Super Rez creates enlarged images and video.

Turing’s memory subsystem uses redesigned GDDR6 signaling at 14 Gbps, offering a stated 20% power-efficiency improvement over GDDR5X. Improved memory compression and larger caches raise effective bandwidth by approximately 50% relative to Pascal in the cited TU102/RTX 2080 Ti comparison.

The display engine supports DisplayPort 1.4a, 8K output at 60 Hz, DSC 1.2, HDR, and tone mapping. The enhanced NVENC encoder supports H.265 8K encoding at 30 fps and provides bitrate savings for H.265 and H.264, while NVDEC adds HEVC 4:4:4 and VP9 high-bit-depth formats. USB Type-C and VirtualLink consolidate VR display, power, and data connections through one connector.

Turing also introduces Mesh Shading, Variable Rate Shading (VRS), Texture Space Shading (TSS), and Multi-View Rendering. Mesh shading uses task and mesh shaders to process large object lists cooperatively and reduce CPU draw-call bottlenecks. VRS independently assigns shading rates to 16-by-16 screen regions, supporting content-adaptive, motion-adaptive, and foveated rendering. TSS computes and caches shading in texture space, allowing visibility and appearance sampling to use independent grids and rates and enabling reuse between stereo views. Multi-View Rendering supports up to four hardware views per pass and up to 32 API-level views, improving VR, stereo, shadow-map, and instanced rendering.

Dedicated RT Cores accelerate bounding-volume-hierarchy traversal and ray-triangle intersection testing, freeing SMs for other work. NVIDIA describes Turing as delivering more than 10 Giga Rays per second and roughly tenfold faster software ray tracing than Pascal. A hybrid rendering model uses rasterization where effective and ray tracing for effects such as reflections, refractions, shadows, and ambient occlusion, with denoising reducing the rays required.

The final sections explain ray casting, BVH construction and refitting, denoising, ray-traced shadows, ambient occlusion, and reflections. They position these technologies together as enabling real-time ray tracing on a single GPU.

Baker & McKenzie’s October 15, 2001 Global Employment Law Alert summarizes recent labor, employment, employee-benefit, discrimination, immigration, privacy, union, and legislative developments worldwide through country and regional briefs linked to detailed sources. Other developments include efforts to end child labor in West African cocoa production, allegations of “virtual slave” labor involving South Korean companies abroad, and reports of worsening trade-union rights violations, particularly in Africa. The September 11 attacks feature prominently, with job cuts and production reductions reported at General Motors, Fiat, airlines, and other businesses; Boeing’s forecast of a prolonged airline downturn; renewed privacy-policy reviews; and growing concern about cyberterrorism. DLSS 4 Multi Frame Generation, introduced with Blackwell, can generate up to three additional frames for every traditionally rendered frame. Its AI model is described as 40% faster and using 30% less VRAM than the previous frame-generation method, while an AI-based optical-flow model reduces computational cost. Enhanced Flip Metering moves pacing logic to the display engine for more precise timing, and the Blackwell display engine doubles pixel-processing capability.

DLSS 4 also introduces transformer-based neural networks, replacing the CNN architecture used since DLSS 2. Transformers use self-attention to identify longer-range patterns across larger pixel windows and support models with twice as many parameters. New transformer models for DLSS Super Resolution, Ray Reconstruction, and Deep Learning Anti-Aliasing are intended to improve temporal stability, motion detail, lighting, antialiasing, and denoiser artifacts. Super Resolution reconstructs higher-resolution images from lower-resolution inputs; Ray Reconstruction generates additional pixels for ray-traced scenes; and DLAA applies Super Resolution technology at native resolution.

Blackwell is also designed to advance neural shaders, which use trained AI models to approximate complex rendering algorithms. New Cooperative Vectors APIs for DirectX 12 and Vulkan, combined with Slang features, allow graphics shaders to access Tensor Cores. Potential applications include neural texture compression, neural materials, radiance caching, subsurface-scattering skin, and generative facial rendering.

RTX Neural Texture Compression uses neural networks to compress and decompress textures more efficiently than traditional methods. The cited Neural Materials demo reduces memory use for its materials from 1,110 MB to 333 MB. Stochastic Texture Filtering adds randomized sampling to reduce aliasing and moiré patterns, with Blackwell providing a doubled point-sampled texture-filtering rate. Neural Radiance Cache traces an initial ray segment and uses live-trained neural networks to infer additional lighting bounces, reducing GPU work while improving indirect lighting. RTX Skin applies ray-traced subsurface scattering to translucent materials. RTX Neural Faces uses a TensorRT-optimized generative model to infer realistic faces from rasterized geometry and 3D pose data, with training based on offline images covering angles, lighting, emotion, and occlusion.

The Blackwell GPU family includes GB202, with 92.2 billion transistors, 192 SMs, 24,576 CUDA Cores, 192 RT Cores, 768 Tensor Cores, and 768 Texture Units; it powers the GeForce RTX 5090. GB203 has 45.6 billion transistors, 84 SMs, 10,752 CUDA Cores, 84 RT Cores, and 336 Tensor Cores; it powers the RTX 5080 and RTX 5070 Ti. GB205 has 31 billion transistors, 50 SMs, 6,400 CUDA Cores, 50 RT Cores, and 200 Tensor Cores; it powers the RTX 5070.

It disclaims warranties, limits liability under its sales terms, excludes suitability for medical, military, aircraft, space, and life-support applications, and provides design materials and third-party information without implied licenses or warranties.

The application, which claims priority to U.S. Ser. No. 16/985,649 filed August 5, 2020, discloses systems, methods, and computer-readable media for a variable multiplexer that provides vehicle communication-bus compatibility. Vehicle manufacturers may use standardized multi-pin data link connectors while assigning different functions to individual pins, requiring vehicle-specific cables. An external device can electronically configure a variable multiplexer to map connector pins to corresponding external-device pins, enabling use of one cable across vehicles with different pinout configurations.

The external device may include a variable multiplexer, network gateway, connection detector, pinout-determination component, pinout-modification component, and storage. Upon connection to a vehicle communication bus, the device detects the connection, determines the connector’s pinout configuration, and reconfigures the multiplexer accordingly. The pinout may be identified by sending a vehicle identifier such as a VIN to a remote system maintaining a vehicle-to-pinout index. Alternatively, the device can monitor bus traffic, identify enabled and disabled pins, compare observations with known configurations, and use transmitted checksum values to verify the matching configuration. The described methods may be implemented through processor-executable instructions, including distributed or cloud-based implementations.

Equality is presented as a moral and social ideal based on equal value, nondiscrimination, and equal opportunity. Education is identified as a principal means of achieving it by providing accessible resources and opportunities. Formal equality of opportunity requires all social groups to have comparable chances to attain advantageous positions through their knowledge and talents rather than their origin or caste.

Education is described as a continuous, socially shaped process that develops individuals, perfects human nature, and supports social order and socialization. Equality of opportunity in education, associated historically with compulsory schooling and James S. Coleman’s research, means enabling everyone to develop their talents and benefit from education without discrimination or unfair advantage. It includes equal educational conditions regardless of family or economic origin and requires accessible, appropriate provision that responds to different abilities and needs.

Five categories affect equality of opportunity: economic, geographical, political, individual, and social factors. Economic conditions are identified as primary, while state policies are expected to address disadvantages arising from economic, social, regional, and biological differences. Individual abilities and social customs, including gender roles, can also limit access and success.

In Turkey, the Ministry of National Education shapes policy, while National Education Councils advise on reforms. Major concerns include inadequate schools, economic difficulties, insufficiently equipped learning environments, and students’ lack of motivation. Recommendations include early and independent assessment of children’s abilities, improved access and educational quality, reduced regional and school-type achievement gaps, stronger teacher training and recruitment, equal qualification of schools, expanded high-quality preschool education, and scientifically planned school locations and classroom capacity.

The article examines the political controversy surrounding Bad Bunny’s selection to headline the Super Bowl LX halftime show. The NFL’s announcement drew backlash from MAGA influencers and right-wing commentators who highlighted that he predominantly sings in Spanish and has criticized Donald Trump and ICE. It also reports DHS adviser Corey Lewandowski’s warning that undocumented immigrants attending the event could be detained and deported.

The article frames the dispute as a culture war, arguing that opposition targets Bad Bunny’s activism rather than his music. His decision to avoid touring the continental U.S. over fears of ICE raids, criticism of Puerto Rico’s territorial status and the Trump administration, and support for LGBTQ+ rights are central to the controversy. The NFL’s choice is also presented as a business strategy for attracting younger and global audiences, drawing on Roc Nation’s involvement, Bad Bunny’s international popularity, and Kendrick Lamar’s politically charged 2024 performance. Bad Bunny says the show is for his people, culture, and history, while the article describes the Super Bowl as a referendum on American identity and political divisions.

The passage describes patterns as a way to create reusable components, standardize shared implementations, improve code quality through repeated use, and make distributed-system design more systematic. It introduces single-node container patterns that tightly couple containers on one machine, often within a Kubernetes pod sharing resources such as volumes, network or process namespaces, and localhost.

The sidecar pattern adds a companion container that augments an application without requiring changes to it. Examples include adding HTTPS termination to a legacy HTTP service, synchronizing dynamic configuration, monitoring resource usage through a shared process namespace, and synchronizing source code from Git to support a simple PaaS. Reusable sidecars should be parameterized, expose stable APIs, and be documented in their Dockerfiles through exposed ports, environment-variable defaults, and standard metadata labels.

The ambassador pattern separates an application’s external interactions into a companion container. An ambassador can route requests among storage shards, perform environment-specific service discovery and brokering, or split production and experimental traffic. The application connects to the ambassador on localhost, while the ambassador handles external networking. This pattern can either accompany individual application pods or operate as a shared routing service, trading deployment simplicity for additional network overhead.

The adapter pattern converts an application’s interface into a standard expected by shared infrastructure. It can translate heterogeneous monitoring protocols, normalize and redirect logs, capture slow queries, or provide rich database health checks. Using an adapter avoids patching and maintaining third-party or precompiled images while allowing standardized tools to be reused across applications.

Microservices divide an application into focused components that communicate through formal APIs. This supports independent team ownership, deployment, iteration, and scaling, but makes debugging and architecture more difficult because failures span multiple services and machines. Shared patterns can reduce these difficulties by documenting proven designs and reusable solutions.

For distributed systems, a replicated load-balanced service uses identical instances to provide redundancy and horizontal scaling. Readiness probes distinguish running instances from those ready to accept traffic. Session tracking can route a user consistently to one replica using IP affinity, cookies, or consistent hashing. A caching tier can improve latency and request capacity, while reverse proxies can provide rate limiting and denial-of-service protection. A separate replicated nginx tier can terminate SSL before traffic passes through a Varnish cache to application servers.

Sharded services divide state among shards, each responsible for a subset of requests, with a root selecting the appropriate shard. Sharding allows services to handle state too large for one machine and uses memory more efficiently than independent replicated caches. Because each request maps to a fixed shard, shard failures can cause repeated misses, making cache hit rate and failure tolerance important considerations. Replicating each shard improves resilience, supports independent shard scaling, and permits “hot sharding,” though it adds complexity. Traffic can be routed through per-pod ambassadors or a shared routing service. Sharding functions typically use a deterministic, uniformly distributed hash modulo the shard count, and their keys must distinguish only request attributes that affect the response.

The passage outlines NVIDIA’s RTX Blackwell architecture and RTX 50 Series technologies. Blackwell unifies FP32 and INT32 cores, doubling throughput for many integer instructions, though each core operates as only one type per clock cycle. Texture units increase from 512 in the RTX 4090 to 680 in the RTX 5090, with bilinear-filtered throughput rising from 1,290.2 to 1,636.76 gigatexels/sec and point-sampling performance doubling.

GDDR7 memory uses PAM3 signaling to improve signal-to-noise ratio, channel density, bandwidth, and energy efficiency. The RTX 5090 provides 28 Gbps memory and 1.792 TB/sec peak bandwidth, while the RTX 5080 provides 30 Gbps and 960 GB/sec. GDDR7 includes always-enabled built-in ECC with single-bit correction, plus EDR support.

Fifth-generation Tensor Cores support FP16, BF16, TF32, INT8, FP8, and new FP4 and FP6 operations. FP4 can reduce model memory to less than half that of FP16 while providing more than twice the prior-generation performance; the cited FLUX.dev example falls from over 23 GB to under 10 GB of VRAM.

Fourth-generation RT Cores double ray-triangle intersection throughput. Mega Geometry adds cluster-level acceleration structures, batched GPU-driven APIs, and partitioned top-level acceleration structures to support detailed level-of-detail geometry and reduce BVH-management overhead. It is supported through DirectX 12, Vulkan, and OptiX 9.0 across RTX GPUs from Turing onward. Linear Swept Spheres provide hardware-accelerated hair and strand rendering, delivering roughly twice the speed and requiring about one-fifth the VRAM of Disjoint Orthogonal Triangle Strips.

SER 2.0 improves shader execution reordering with twice-efficient reorder logic and greater precision, while the programmable AI Management Processor uses a dedicated RISC-V processor to schedule GPU contexts with lower latency and reduced CPU involvement.

Blackwell adds 4:2:2 video encoding and decoding, a ninth-generation NVENC with improved AV1 and HEVC quality, and a sixth-generation NVDEC with twice the H.264 decoding speed. It also supports DisplayPort 2.1b at up to 80 Gbps, including 8K 165 Hz and 4K 480 Hz operation with DSC.

Max-Q improvements include finer-grained clock, power, and voltage-rail gating, clock adjustments up to 1,000 times faster, and sleep entry ten times faster than Ada. These changes can produce up to 50% power savings in small-language-model inference scenarios.

DLSS 4 introduces Multi Frame Generation, which can create up to three additional frames per traditionally rendered frame using a model that is 40% faster and uses 30% less VRAM. New transformer-based models improve Super Resolution, Ray Reconstruction, and Deep Learning Anti-Aliasing, with greater temporal stability, reduced ghosting, and improved detail in motion.

Blackwell also enables neural shaders through Cooperative Vectors and Slang. Applications include RTX Neural Materials, Neural Texture Compression with up to seven-to-one VRAM compression, Stochastic Texture Filtering, Neural Radiance Cache, RTX Skin for real-time subsurface scattering, and RTX Neural Faces for generative real-time facial rendering.

The passage identifies GB202 as the flagship chip, with 192 SMs, 24,576 CUDA cores, 192 RT Cores, and 768 Tensor Cores; GB203 with 84 SMs and 10,752 CUDA cores; and GB205 with 50 SMs and 6,400 CUDA cores. The RTX 5090 uses GB202, the RTX 5080 and 5070 Ti use GB203, and the RTX 5070 uses GB205. The specifications are presented as reliable only as of the stated date and are subject to NVIDIA’s corrections, standard sales terms, and usage-risk disclaimers.

A gifted player is shooting more than passing and keeping the puck away from his body. The team is struggling against a strong, hard-working opponent that plays differently, has speed throughout its four lines, activates its defensemen and creates breaks through effort. The speaker says the team’s work comes in spurts and urges players to focus on each minute, follow the game plan and rely collectively rather than play as individuals or worry about outcomes. The next game is a major test, and the opponent’s greater hunger mirrors last year, when the speaker’s team was hungrier.

NVIDIA has developed the GPU into a leading parallel-processing engine for gaming, content creation, high-performance and datacenter computing, and AI. Its Turing architecture introduces major efficiency and performance advances through new streaming multiprocessor and GDDR6 memory designs, while hardware accelerators and hybrid rendering combine rasterization, real-time ray tracing, AI, and simulation to improve game realism, neural-network effects, and interactive 3D workflows. Tensor Cores also support new deep-learning neural services for games and professional graphics.

An Oct. 24, 2001 compilation of news clippings centered on Enron’s financial and disclosure controversies. Enron shares closed at $19.79, down $0.86 for the day and more than 40% over the preceding week, after trading above $80 earlier in the year. The company reported a $618 million third-quarter loss, including $1.01 billion in write-offs, and a $1.2 billion reduction in shareholder equity related to terminating transactions involving a partnership managed by CFO Andrew Fastow. The SEC opened an informal inquiry into Enron’s dealings with LJM Cayman and LJM2 Co-Investment, partnerships involved in complex financing and hedging arrangements. Internal LJM2 documents cited in The Wall Street Journal said Fastow and possibly several other Enron officials earned millions through management fees and capital increases, while billions of dollars in Enron assets and stock were involved.

During an investor call, Chairman and CEO Kenneth Lay defended Fastow, acknowledged the inherent conflict of interest, said Enron had safeguards and adequate liquidity, and declined to answer detailed questions about the partnerships because of the SEC inquiry and shareholder lawsuits. Fastow also declined to answer questions. Analysts, including Goldman Sachs’ David Fleischer, said Enron’s limited disclosure and difficult-to-understand transactions were severely undermining the company’s credibility; Lay said the company was trying to be transparent.

Treasurer Ben Glisan said Enron might need several hundred million dollars over 20 months to cover potential shortfalls tied to about $3.3 billion in notes sold by Marlin and Osprey investment vehicles and guaranteed by Enron. Asset sales were expected to raise at least $2.2 billion by the end of 2002, including $1.55 billion from the planned sale of Portland General Electric. If proceeds were insufficient, Enron could issue equity—up to $1 billion in a worst-case scenario—diluting holders of about 850 million shares. Enron cited $3.35 billion in bank credit lines, including $1.75 billion expiring the following May if not renewed, and $1.85 billion in commercial paper; it also sought a $750 million loan arrangement with Citigroup. Lay said Arthur Andersen had determined that no Marlin write-down was required despite nearly $1 billion of guaranteed debt. Enron also said the Whitewing and Atlantic Water Trust financing vehicles could lead to dilution if it lost its investment-grade rating.

Other reports covered Enron’s elevated option volatility, a law firm’s investigation of potential shareholder claims, and a CNNfn panelist’s advice that prospective investors pause purchases of the stock. Other clippings said the Dow fell 0.39% and the Nasdaq 0.21% amid mixed earnings; AES sought help from India’s prime minister to resolve disputes with the Orissa government; analysts warned LNG project delays could create tanker oversupply as the fleet grew by about 37% by 2004; British Gas offered Brazilian assets to ONGC for operating rights to Indian fields purchased from Enron; and a House stimulus proposal would give Enron a $254 million tax refund while Senate Democrats presented a $70 billion alternative.

Pete Newell introduced and used the Reverse Action offense in the late 1950s. Its basic guard-around continuity is simple but difficult to defend because successful execution depends on precise footwork, timing, communication, and coordinated play by the passer, screener, and receiver. The offense primarily features a weakside wing rub cut off a post screen, while also supporting post-ups, two-player guard-around isolation, and counters against defensive overplays.

Entries can begin from either side through passes or dribbles, with wing, post, back-cut, back-door, and lob-pass options. The continuation relies on reversals, guard-around cuts, and additional screens based on defensive deployment. Guard-around reads include driving when a defender chases over, driving and kicking when weakside defenders sag, pulling up when the defender goes under, driving opposite when the defender cheats over, rolling when the defense switches, and slipping against show-and-recover defense.

The sideline triangle creates post isolation and includes lob-pass, high-post-feed, post-split, down-screen, high-post-split, and post-isolation options. Post counters vary by defensive positioning: a high-side defender yields a power layup, a baseline-side defender a baby hook, a defender playing behind permits a turn-and-face triple threat, a full front can be countered with a lob, and a double team can be answered by releasing to the elbow or short corner. Ball reversal, corner feeds, and point feeds can improve passing angles.

Reverse Action’s spacing also creates immediate back-cut opportunities against overplays and pass denials. Late-clock or timeout options include weakside screen-and-roll, double screens, and a back-screen lob.

Tesla Motors, Inc. filed an 8-K disclosing that CFO Deepak Ahuja intends to retire after seven years, remaining to help select a successor and ensure an effective transition, with Musk and Ahuja's comments attached as Exhibit 99.1. At the June 9, 2015 annual meeting, Antonio J. Gracias and Kimbal Musk were elected Class II directors, PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP was ratified as auditor, and stockholder proposals by Mark Peters and Elizabeth Farrell Peters were not approved.

A soccer defensive wall consists of defenders standing shoulder-to-shoulder, usually 10 yards from a free kick, to block the near side of the goal and give the goalkeeper more time and space to cover the remaining angle. Wall building becomes important as players develop accurate free-kick shooting, generally around age 12. The goalkeeper alone decides whether to build a wall, based on the ball’s location and the goalkeeper’s training, experience, and confidence. Wall size increases when the ball is closer to the goal or more central; walls may range from two players to as many as eight. All defenders should anticipate a wall and promptly retreat to build it, mark attackers, or prepare a counterattack.

Defenders must comply with the Laws of the Game, particularly Law 13. The ball is placed where the foul or violation occurred, subject to penalty-kick and indirect-free-kick exceptions. Until the kick is taken, defenders must remain at least 10 yards from the ball unless positioned on their own goal line. Faking a kick is permitted. When three or more defenders form a wall, attackers must remain at least one yard away until the ball is in play.

The referee is not required to give defenders time to form a wall. An immediate restart is a quick free kick, and play may continue even if defenders are still organizing or are improperly positioned unless a defender is delaying the restart. If attackers choose a ceremonial free kick and request that an improperly placed wall be moved, they must wait while the referee corrects it. The referee may mark the ball and restraining line with vanishing spray. Blocking the restart is unsporting conduct and warrants an immediate yellow card.

In the traditional method, the goalkeeper serves as wall setter. The first defender, called the Anchor or Post-man, moves to an imaginary line from the near post to the ball and 10 yards from the ball. From the near post, the goalkeeper directs the Anchor left or right by a defined number of steps, then says “Hold.” The remaining players arrive facing the ball and fill in shoulder-to-shoulder beside the Anchor, commonly from tallest to shortest, shifting as the Anchor is adjusted. The wall must block direct shots, prevent gaps, and make other shots as difficult as possible. Players may protect certain body parts, jump, and absorb the shot, but may not move their hands toward the ball, create gaps, rush the kick, or jump so high that the ball can pass underneath.

An alternative uses a designated Wall Setter, usually a forward or lead midfielder, positioned beyond the ball. The Wall Setter positions the Anchor using the same calls and signals, allowing the goalkeeper to maintain visibility, respond to quick kicks, and protect the far side of the goal while the Anchor faces the ball throughout.

In the rare case of an indirect free kick less than 10 yards from goal, defenders must immediately form a wall on the goal line between the posts. The coach and goalkeeper determine the approach, which may include a designated “bullet player” who sprints at the ball as soon as it moves. Because the kick is indirect, defenders may avoid a straight shot if the ball touches no one.

Coaching guidance includes using a rope to demonstrate wall angles, keeping wall size appropriate, positioning goalkeepers centrally rather than cheating toward an expected shot side, testing for gaps, training the goalkeeper against shots around the wall, and warning players not to use delaying tactics or reposition the ball illegally.

Indian press clippings from November 14–18, 2001 focused on efforts to resolve the crisis surrounding Maharashtra’s Dabhol Power Company (DPC). IDBI-led financial institutions, facing roughly Rs 6,100 crore in exposure, set a $700 million reserve price for DPC’s 85 percent stake, comprising Enron’s 65 percent and Bechtel’s and General Electric’s 10 percent each. BSES and Tata Power began due diligence but reportedly offered no more than $400 million. Enron was reportedly willing to accept a 30 percent reduction from its original $1.2 billion valuation, while the bidders sought larger discounts.

DPC’s 740 MW first phase was mothballed, while the 1,444 MW second phase was about 90 percent complete but had halted construction. Lenders, DPC, BSES and Tata Power discussed concessions needed to revive the project, including a Rs 2.70 tariff, reductions in equity values and interest rates, minimum alternate tax exemption, mega-power status, conversion of foreign debt into rupees, a 15-year-or-longer moratorium, payment security, and separation of the LNG facility from the power project. Tata Power and BSES sought a distribution zone for up to 1,500 MW and the ability to sell electricity directly, but the Maharashtra State Electricity Board (MSEB) said it could not surrender financially important distribution areas.

Enron’s proposed acquisition by Dynegy was not expected immediately to affect DPC, and negotiations over the sale of Enron’s stake continued. DPC’s arbitration tribunal was scheduled to meet in London on November 24 concerning the Maharashtra government’s nonpayment of a Rs 102 crore December power bill, although the Supreme Court had restrained DPC from pursuing arbitration until the jurisdiction of the Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission was resolved.

MSEB asked DPC to postpone its November 19 board meeting in Houston because the Bombay High Court had restrained DPC from issuing a final termination notice until further orders, with the next hearing set for December 3. The Maharashtra government declined permission for its representatives to attend, and MSEB subsequently said it would not participate because DPC had ignored its rebate claim and sought to rescind the power purchase agreement. DPC also faced a Rs 57 crore default on interest and guarantee fees, while the halted second phase and future debt servicing remained concerns.

The Bombay High Court also restrained the central government, customs authorities and State Bank of India from encashing DPC-related customs guarantees. The dispute concerned a Rs 245 crore duty notice and a Rs 45 crore penalty, which customs said brought DPC’s liability to Rs 290 crore.

State-owned Shipping Corporation of India took possession of the LNG tanker “LNG Laxmi” after the Oman government helped reorganize financing for the $220 million Greenfield Shipping venture and replaced DPC’s planned 20-year charter with a 20-year charter at over $70,000 per day. SCI retained 20 percent of Greenfield and also secured a 34.21 percent stake in a Rs 130 crore Petronet LNG venture involving two additional tankers.

Commentary also questioned how Arthur Andersen audited Enron after the company disclosed that it had overstated profits by about one-fifth over four years, drawing parallels with earlier audit failures. Another commentary argued that a lasting DPC solution would require separating generation assets from port, gas-terminal and regasification infrastructure and valuing the two project phases differently.

A reverse play deceives defenders by moving the ball in one direction before transferring it to a player moving the opposite way. In a traditional reverse, a quarterback hands or tosses the ball to a moving RB or WR, who tosses it back to another receiver crossing in the opposite direction. Offensive linemen help by releasing their blocks to form a “seal” around the ball carrier. Carolina’s 2018 play used DJ Moore and Curtis Samuel, with blockers shielding Samuel as he gained 15 yards and cut across for a touchdown. A fake reverse uses multiple handoffs and route motion to mislead defenders, as Kyler Murray did before running behind favorable blocking. In a reverse screen, the ball returns to the quarterback for a downfield pass while blockers form a protective screen; Purdue used this variation for a touchdown. A reverse pass also gives the quarterback a running option, allowing him to receive the ball back in stride for a touchdown. When executed and disguised properly, reverse plays can produce large gains, but errors can cause major yardage losses.

Packers coach Mike McCarthy says cornerback Damarious Randall has had an outstanding offseason and stood out during OTAs and minicamp. Randall is rebounding from an injury-plagued, inconsistent season and embracing a starting nickel role after Sam Shields’ injury. With Davon House, Kevin King and LaDarius Gunter on the perimeter, Randall could excel at slot, though early offseason hype may not carry into September.

The IDC report examines technology trends supporting industrial development and manufacturing, emphasizing visualization, digital twins, and high-performance computing (HPC). Cloud-based engineering workstations can provide teams with shared, scalable access to current data and common databases, while AR/VR may reshape collaborative and virtual development processes. Digital twins digitally map data, processes, plants, and products for continuous monitoring, problem detection, scenario simulation, and collaboration, supporting new services and business models such as “Product as a Service” and outcome-based services.

Industrial simulation, modeling, and analysis increasingly require complex calculations, creating trade-offs between calculation time and accuracy amid inadequate legacy infrastructure and high computing costs. Forty-two percent of respondents reported that their simulations were outdated or inaccurate, and half said calculations and iterations took too long. Demand for HPC is expected to rise from 8% of respondents currently identifying high demand to nearly half within two years. About 81% regard HPC as a game changer for product and process innovation because it enables complex calculations, faster and higher-quality simulations, new industrial use cases, and greater innovation and agility.

Most surveyed enterprises currently lack in-house HPC, and external infrastructure is the preferred or planned option. IDC expects public-cloud HPC to become the leading architecture, followed by hybrid-cloud systems and prebuilt standard systems. HPC as a Service (HPCaaS) offers elastic performance, operational flexibility, cost optimization, modern hardware, and reduced upfront investment, but requires trained personnel to operate virtual clusters, program calculations, and interpret results. Major challenges include security and intellectual-property risks, energy consumption, high ownership and licensing costs, insufficient expertise, computing-capacity limits, infrastructure complexity, availability, and limited scalability.

IDC recommends virtual product and manufacturing development, a holistic data strategy built around a single source of truth, careful selection among on-premises, HPCaaS, and hybrid operating models, attention to scalability, security, and energy efficiency, and use of external expertise where necessary. The findings come from a December 2021 survey of 200 technology-related decision-makers at industrial enterprises with more than 500 employees in Germany, Austria, and Switzerland.

The court affirmed summary judgment for Farmway Credit Union, which was permitted to repossess and sell Melvin Douglas’s collateral and apply the proceeds to his outstanding debt of $111,290.17. Douglas and his wife had granted security interests and agreed before his death that Farmway could sell the collateral; his heirs continued cooperating after his death. The estate administrator later sought possession of the sold property but had taken no steps to stop the sales or seek injunctive relief, and the claim against the Secretary of Revenue was not part of the appeal. The court held that an administrator’s statutory rights to possess and marshal a decedent’s property are not absolute and do not override a secured creditor’s contractual right to exhaust its security. It declined to decide whether self-help repossession is permitted without a specific agreement. Summary judgment was not premature because the security agreement and pre-death sale agreement were uncontroverted, leaving only a question of law.

Counter is a football run play that fakes Power in one direction, then uses blocks—including a pulling guard kicking out an edge defender and a fullback inserting—to send the runner the opposite way. It exploits aggressive defenses that overpursue Power, leaving linebackers at bad angles and often giving the offense more bodies at the point of attack. Its main weaknesses are slower development than plays such as power or trap, vulnerability in the open B gap, and defensive responses that spill the pulling guard and force the runner laterally toward reinforcements.

Counter Trey assignments are detailed for odd 3-4 and even 4-3 fronts. In both, the left tackle and center maintain B-gap integrity, the left guard pulls and kicks out the playside edge defender, the fullback follows into the lane to block a linebacker, and the quarterback opens left, swings right, and hands off to the tailback. Receivers push the near safeties.

Variations include Singleback GT Counter, where the backside tackle replaces the fullback as the insert blocker and the fullback secures the edge defender, and Gun Split GT Counter, which adds triple-option reads of the edge defender as the dive key and the alley defender as the pitch key.

After Virgin America’s final revenue flights between San Francisco and Los Angeles, Alaska Airlines will replace the Virgin America brand across 29 shared U.S. and Mexican airports. The transition includes removing Virgin signage, kiosks, counters and gates, moving employees onto Alaska’s systems and consolidating websites, apps, check-in kiosks and call centers. Alaska acquired Virgin America for $2.6 billion two years earlier and expects the changeover to be smooth after extensive planning and testing. Fans and frequent fliers planned celebrations for the final flight, while industry analyst Henry Harteveldt cited Virgin America’s innovations, including fleetwide Wi-Fi, in-seat power, at-seat ordering and a spending-based frequent-flier program. Some Virgin America aircraft interiors will remain until the end of 2019 despite updated Alaska livery.

China criticized a U.S. nuclear strategy report portraying Beijing as a potential adversary, urged Washington to reduce its larger arsenal, and called for joint regional stability efforts. China’s Defense Ministry called its 300-warhead arsenal the minimum needed for security and pledged never to initiate nuclear use. The report sought to prevent China from viewing even limited nuclear use as acceptable, supported New START, and was criticized by arms-control groups. Trump’s doctrine reversed Obama’s push to reduce nuclear weapons’ military role.

Texas quarterback Arch Manning’s first four games as the Longhorns’ full-time starter yielded two strong performances and two struggles: a 61.3% completion rate, 888 yards, nine touchdowns and three interceptions. This followed his nearly perfect 2024 emergency start against Mississippi State, amid high expectations and questions about a possible injury as his Heisman Trophy odds faded.

Digital twins can improve industrial efficiency, accuracy, flexibility, and sustainability by digitally mapping products, processes, data, and plants for continuous monitoring, problem detection, and scenario simulation. In tire development, virtual environments can reduce development time by up to 50%, while lowering raw-material use, CO₂ emissions, and time to market. IDC expects digital twins to enable new services and business models, including product- and outcome-based services.

Data visualization and cloud-based engineering workstations can improve collaboration by giving development teams access to shared, current information. Digital twins can also combine data from producers, operators, customers, and partners, while AR/VR can support redesigned collaborative development processes.

High-performance computing is presented as a major driver of industrial innovation and agility. It enables complex simulations, modeling, statistical analysis, and optimization; accelerates calculations and iterations; unlocks previously impractical use cases; and helps integrate advanced analysis into product and process development. Four out of five industry decision-makers surveyed consider HPC a game changer, rising to 96% among enterprises already using it. Demand is expected to grow substantially: while only 8% currently report high demand, nearly half are expected to do so within two years. More than a quarter of enterprises already use professional HPC infrastructure, and another 39% are planning or piloting it.

Most surveyed HPC users favor external infrastructure, including cloud providers and colocation datacenters, because this provides greater flexibility and avoids major upfront investment and operating costs. Only 6% currently operate on-premises HPC, although 28% plan to do so. Major challenges include security and intellectual-property risks, hardware and licensing expenses, energy consumption, insufficient capacity, system complexity, availability, scalability, and shortages of HPC expertise. Security is a leading concern for 72%, while 58% cite energy consumption and sustainability.

Cloud-based architectures are expected to become dominant, followed by hybrid and prebuilt systems. Public cloud can replace costly capital expenditure with flexible operating expenditure, expand performance during demand peaks, and provide access to current hardware and analysis methods. Hybrid architectures can retain sensitive work on-premises while offloading noncritical workloads. HPC-as-a-Service is also viewed as a foundation for collaborative digital development, new data-based services, and HPC-enabled business models; 81% of enterprises already implementing HPC intend to develop such models. Its benefits depend on retaining trained personnel to configure, operate, program, and interpret HPC calculations. Cloud HPC may also improve energy efficiency, although continued modernization and appropriate operating models remain necessary.

Paradox Interactive apologized for regional price increases of up to 40% in June 2017, saying currency shifts had prompted an effort to equalize prices. The backlash led CEO Fredrik Wester to promise refunds, before offering free DLC when refunds were deemed impractical. Despite the controversy, Paradox had a successful year, opening a mobile studio in Sweden, acquiring Triumph Studios, hiring Civilization V designer Jon Shafer, and continuing its console publishing work. The company is focused on cross-platform concepts for PlayStation and Xbox, particularly deep strategy games, but remains cautious about the Nintendo Switch.

Paradox is also preparing to bring established strategy properties to mobile through its new studio. It plans to retain its focus on deep, complex, long-playing experiences while adapting them for smartphones, without distracting from PC. Sjöberg described mobile as a major growth opportunity but said Paradox would approach the competitive market carefully and expand gradually into new platforms and genres.

The paper develops a mathematical framework for analyzing cubic-to-tetragonal phase coexistence in ferroelectrics using high-resolution X-ray diffraction and 3D reciprocal-space mapping. Extending adaptive-state and WLR concepts, it models a cubic–tetragonal interface through the macroscopic averaging of periodically arranged tetragonal domains, without necessarily requiring miniaturized domains.

Three tetragonal variants and six permissible domain walls are considered. The framework derives mismatch-free habit-plane conditions, interface indices, real- and reciprocal-space orientation relationships, and Bragg-peak separations for 24 adaptive-state/cubic connection variants. For the representative Ta(110)Tb assemblage, coexistence requires specific domain volume ratios, and the model predicts three-component peak splitting from two tetragonal domains, the adaptive average, and the cubic phase.

Applied to PMN-35PT near its cubic–tetragonal transition around 435 K, the predicted peak separations strongly agree with 3D reciprocal-space measurements at 437 K, supporting the adaptive-state orientation relationships. Peak-width analysis indicates domains of several hundred nanometers while not excluding miniaturization closer to the transition.

Chewable probiotics are supplements containing live microorganisms that confer health benefits, balance intestinal microflora, and support digestive and immune health. This preprint examined antibody escape by SARS-CoV-2 BA.2.86 (Pirola) and its descendant JN.1. BA.2.86 has 33 spike mutations relative to BA.2, distributed across the NTD, RBD, and S1/S2–S2 regions. Using spike pseudoviruses and sera from 30 healthcare workers before and after BNT162b2 XBB.1.5 vaccination, the researchers found that pre-XBB.1.5 vaccination sera neutralized BA.2.86 and JN.1 approximately 40-fold and 80-fold less efficiently than ancestral Wuhan-Hu-01, respectively. The XBB.1.5 vaccine substantially improved neutralization of both variants, eliminated the JN.1–BA.2.86 difference, and reduced titers to 11- and 12-fold below ancestral levels.

Reverse mutational scanning of 33 BA.2.86 mutants, each reverting one mutation to the BA.2 sequence, identified the 16MPLF insertion and K356T, N460K, V483Δ, A484K, F486P, and P621S/P621S mutations as contributors to immune escape. Removing the MPLF insertion or restoring Y144 produced BA.2-like neutralization after XBB.1.5 vaccination.

Limitations include reliance on pseudoviruses, incomplete information on prior infections and hybrid immunity, a healthcare-worker cohort that may not represent elderly or immunocompromised populations, and testing of single rather than combined mutations.

The design combines a 16-bit ADS8681W SAR ADC with an eight-channel MUX36D08 differential multiplexer. It supports fast voltage, current, or temperature sensing, uses three digital lines to select inputs, and communicates with the controller through enhanced SPI.

The Washington Supreme Court affirmed the confirmation of South Bend’s local improvement assessment roll for filling low and tide lands. The city initially estimated the project’s cost at $9,500, relying on anticipated government dredging material. When all material was deposited within a 1,500-foot area, the fill there increased from 18 to 36 inches, and the city hired private contractors to complete work outside that area. The actual cost borne by benefited property was $89,199.92.

The court held that the preliminary cost estimate was intended only to guide the city council in deciding whether to initiate the improvement. Under the applicable statute, an assessment could be increased after notice and hearing when the actual bona fide cost exceeded the estimate, with the additional amount apportioned among benefited parcels. The substantial increase was valid because it reflected changed conditions and the project’s actual cost.

The court also rejected the claim that the improvement ordinance was indefinite or lacked required specifications, finding that it complied with the governing statute. Evidence strongly supported the benefit assessed, and the remaining procedural attacks revealed no irregularity.
