The lecture reviews Porter’s argument that companies should move beyond corporate social responsibility toward corporate social integration by embedding selected social and environmental priorities into core strategy. It criticizes CSR approaches driven by external rankings, excessive stakeholder demands, morality, license to operate, vague long-term sustainability goals, or reputation. These motivations are presented as incomplete because they are difficult to measure, may ignore competitive capabilities, can postpone action, or lack clear evidence of business value.

Porter’s framework distinguishes generic social impacts, value-chain impacts, and social dimensions of the competitive context. It spans reactive “good citizenship” and risk mitigation at one end and strategic CSR at the other. Under strategic CSR, companies deliberately reject some issues while selecting others that can create competitive advantage or reinforce existing capabilities. Examples include Whole Foods, Siemens, GE, and Toyota creating new market positions, and Nestlé and UPS integrating sustainability into core operations. Sustainability initiatives should become part of the company’s “DNA.”

The lecture emphasizes a life-cycle view of products and services because many environmental and social impacts occur outside company facilities, especially in suppliers and customer use. Priorities should therefore reflect where impacts are greatest. For automobiles, roughly 70% of life-cycle emissions occur during use, making product efficiency more significant than deep supply-chain intervention. Conversely, fragmented agricultural supply chains may justify deeper supplier engagement, as illustrated by Starbucks, Unilever, and Nestlé. Waste, packaging, and transportation are accessible starting points because they are measurable and directly affect costs, but they are not automatically the most strategic priorities.

Implementation requires life-cycle assessment, credible operational measurements, ambitious targets, and incentives or penalties tied to reliable metrics. Suppliers may first be asked to report environmental data before sustainability measures are incorporated into procurement and contracts. The lecture closes by asking teams to compare company sustainability practices and assess whether rankings such as the Carbon Disclosure Project reflect genuine strategic performance.

Erik Demaine introduces a course on the mathematics and algorithms of folding and unfolding. He frames the field around three geometric structures: linkages with rigid bars and hinges, paper that may be creased but not stretched, torn, or cut, and polyhedra that may be folded from flat sheets or unfolded into nonoverlapping nets. Applications include robotics, computer graphics, mechanical linkages, manufacturing, nanotechnology, optics, medical devices and drug delivery, aerospace deployment, protein folding, sculpture, and reconfigurable architecture.

The course distinguishes foldability questions, which ask whether a given structure can fold, from design questions, which seek a folding structure that achieves a target shape or property. Results are categorized as universality results that construct foldings, decision algorithms that determine foldability, or hardness results showing that some problems are computationally intractable. The course includes lectures, a few problem sets, a project and presentation for credit, and an optional weekly open-problem session.

For linkages, Demaine reviews historical mechanisms converting circular motion into straight-line motion, universal linkages that can trace curves, and rigidity and reconfiguration problems. Rigidity is algorithmically manageable in two dimensions but remains open in three dimensions. General nonintersecting reconfiguration is intractable, although special chains and trees admit useful results and examples of locked configurations.

For paper, determining which crease patterns fold flat is NP-hard, though single-vertex patterns are understood. Mountain-and-valley assignment for maps remains open in important cases. Computational origami design has universal constructions for shapes and two-color patterns. The Origamizer can fold arbitrary polyhedral surfaces with practical crease layouts, while optimal use of paper through the tree method is NP-complete. Additional topics include one-cut constructions, curved creases, self-folding and programmable matter, and the unresolved effects of material thickness.

For polyhedra, whether every convex polyhedron has a nonoverlapping edge unfolding remains unknown, while some nonconvex polyhedra do not. General unfoldings always exist for convex and orthogonal polyhedra, but not for all nonconvex forms. Hinged-dissection results show that any finite collection of equal-area polygons can be realized from one hinged chain without collisions, with a three-dimensional version requiring an additional condition.

Tamil Nadu’s sugar output is forecast to fall by more than one-third to 600,000 tonnes in the 2017/18 season, down from about 1 million tonnes, due to the state’s century-worst drought. Drought and debt have hit farmers and producers, prompting protests in New Delhi. India expects 20.3 million tonnes of sugar for 2016/17, while back-to-back droughts have damaged Maharashtra’s cane crop. Tamil Nadu’s cotton production is also projected to fall 21%.

A Yale-led team compiled an urban population dataset extending to 3700 B.C. by digitizing, geocoding, and standardizing past research. Metrocosm’s animation visualizes city growth and recorded populations, though the dataset is incomplete and unevenly represents regions and cities.

The paper presents a bound-preserving adaptive coupling of cell-centered finite volume (CCFV) and discontinuous Galerkin (DG) methods for steady convection–diffusion problems. Convection-dominated flows create steep layers that can cause oscillations in DG approximations. The proposed approach monitors DG cell averages and replaces the approximation with CCFV near cells violating prescribed bounds, without manipulating cell averages or modifying the underlying schemes. Conservative slope limiters can then ensure bound preservation throughout the solution, and the procedure is compatible with hp-adaptivity.

The model problem includes diffusion, convection, reaction, source terms, Dirichlet conditions, and homogeneous Neumann conditions on a bounded polyhedral domain. The domain is partitioned into FV and DG regions with matching interfaces, polynomial DG approximations, and piecewise-constant FV approximations. FV meshes must satisfy two-point-flux admissibility, including cell-center orthogonality, while shape-regularity conditions ensure suitable facet geometry and transmissibilities. The paper also reviews oscillation-control methods, noting trade-offs among cost, conservation, accuracy, and bound preservation.

The instructor outlines a paper-driven computer security course focused on building secure systems, understanding why systems fail, and examining security mechanisms. Students must read assigned research papers and submit questions before each lecture. Laboratory assignments use a web server to explore vulnerabilities and defenses in several languages, including C, Assembly, Python, and JavaScript. Lectures will be recorded, online discussion will use Piazza, and students must follow MIT rules for security research. There will be two quizzes and no final exam.

Security is defined as achieving a goal despite adversaries. The analysis framework has three parts: a policy specifying what should be enforced, often involving confidentiality, integrity, or availability; a threat model stating assumptions about an attacker’s capabilities; and mechanisms implementing the policy. Security design is iterative because threat models and mechanisms may be wrong, systems contain bugs, and attackers reveal weaknesses. Although every system has a breaking point, this does not make it useless; identifying limitations helps determine when designs are appropriate. Security mechanisms can also enable new capabilities, illustrated by Google’s Native Client, which safely runs native x86 code in browsers.

The lecture presents failures in each part of the framework. Weak policies include Yahoo account-recovery questions, which broadened password authentication and enabled access to Sarah Palin’s account using publicly available information. Mat Honan’s account was compromised through a chain of individually reasonable recovery mechanisms involving Gmail, an Apple email service, and Amazon, demonstrating the difficulty of reasoning about interacting systems. Flawed threat models often assume users choose strong passwords, avoid phishing sites, or trust hardware and certificate authorities; examples show that human behavior changes, 56-bit Kerberos encryption became practical to break, compromised hardware can undermine software protections, and trusting hundreds of certificate authorities creates a weak link. Secure operating-system prototypes were also compromised through an insecure source-code server.

Mechanism failures include iCloud’s “Find My iPhone” interface omitting password-guessing limits, a Citibank URL that may have exposed other customers’ accounts, and an Android SecureRandom initialization bug that produced predictable Bitcoin keys. Reusing a Bitcoin signature nonce is a related but distinct weakness. Edge-case testing is therefore essential. An SSL certificate encoding mismatch illustrates the danger: a length-prefixed certificate name containing a null byte was interpreted by C software as a different, shorter hostname.

A detailed C demonstration shows how an unbounded input function can overflow a 128-byte stack buffer, overwrite the return address, and redirect execution. Carefully constructed input can inject shellcode and run arbitrary shell commands. Reversing the direction of stack growth does not eliminate the problem because nested calls place return addresses near buffers. Non-executable stacks block injected stack code but can be bypassed with return-to-libc techniques. The preferred remedy is to avoid unsafe functions and correct the source code, while broader defenses include minimizing the trusted computing base so that only a small number of components enforce security policy.

**Filing overview.** Tesla, Inc. (Delaware; Palo Alto, CA; File No. 001-34756) filed a Form 10-Q for the quarterly period ended June 30, 2018. As of July 27, 2018, 170,593,144 common shares were outstanding. Tesla is a large accelerated filer and not a shell company. The filing includes a forward-looking statements caution.

**Results (unaudited).** Q2 2018 total revenues were $4,002.2 million vs. $2,789.6 million a year earlier; six-month revenues were $7,411.0 million vs. $5,485.8 million. Q2 revenue comprised automotive sales of $3,117.9 million, automotive leasing of $239.8 million, energy generation and storage of $374.4 million, and services and other of $270.1 million. Gross profit was $618.9 million vs. $666.6 million; operating expenses were $1,240.3 million vs. $907.5 million, including $103.4 million of restructuring and other charges; loss from operations was $(621.4) million vs. $(240.9) million. Net loss was $(742.7) million vs. $(401.4) million (six months: $(1,527.3) million vs. $(798.6) million); loss attributable to common stockholders was $(717.5) million, or $(4.22) per share vs. $(2.04) (six months: $(8.42)). Comprehensive loss was $(781.9) million, including a $(64.4) million currency translation adjustment.

**Balance sheet and cash flow.** At June 30, 2018 total assets were $27,910.0 million (vs. $28,655.4 million at December 31, 2017), including cash and equivalents of $2,236.4 million (vs. $3,367.9 million), inventory of $3,324.6 million (vs. $2,263.5 million), operating lease vehicles of $2,282.0 million (vs. $4,116.6 million), solar energy systems leased and to be leased of $6,340.0 million, and property, plant and equipment of $10,969.3 million. Total liabilities were $22,642.9 million; stockholders' equity $3,906.4 million, including a $5,768.8 million accumulated deficit; customer deposits were $942.1 million. For the six months, operating activities used $528.0 million of cash, investing used $1,411.5 million, financing provided $770.3 million, and cash plus restricted cash ended at $2,783.2 million.

**Accounting policies.** Tesla designs, manufactures and sells electric vehicles and solar energy generation and storage products, operating in two reportable segments. It adopted ASC 606 on January 1, 2018 using the modified retrospective method, recording a $623.2 million decrease to beginning accumulated deficit. Certain vehicle sales with resale value guarantees moved from operating lease accounting to sales with a right of return; prepayments were reclassified from deferred revenue to customer deposits; investment tax credit deferred revenue was reclassified; and collateralized lease borrowings decreased $210.3 million. Without adoption, Q2 net loss would have been $(796.6) million and six-month net loss $(1,617.6) million.

**Revenue recognition.** Automotive sales revenue is recognized on delivery, with connectivity, Supercharger access and over-the-air updates recognized over time and Autopilot/full self-driving revenue on delivery; regulatory credit (ZEV/GHG) revenue is recognized on transfer with no related deferred revenue. The direct leasing program offers terms up to 48 months ($94.5 million Q2 and $169.3 million six-month leasing revenue). Buyback sales to leasing partners remain interest-bearing collateralized borrowings under ASC 840, with a maximum potential repurchase of $776.4 million ($534.9 million within 12 months), $915.4 million recorded in resale value guarantees and $148.4 million in deferred revenue, generating $84.7 million Q2 and $167.2 million six-month revenue, with no material losses to date. Certain international programs where exercise is probable remain operating leases ($139.3 million exercisable within 12 months; $60.6 million and $76.7 million revenue). Energy segment sales use installation-based recognition for residential/small commercial and percentage-of-completion for large commercial/utility projects; deferred revenue was $152.3 million for customer payments and $221.5 million for leases; unsatisfied obligations under contracts over one year totaled $135.7 million, of which $38.8 million is expected within 12 months and the remainder over up to 30 years. Energy leasing revenue was $139.8 million for Q2 and $251.9 million for six months.

**Other notes.** Gross unrecognized tax benefits were $236.8 million; the July 2018 Altera decision and pending Tax Cuts and Jobs Act measurement-period adjustments are not expected to materially affect the financial statements. Anti-dilutive shares excluded from diluted EPS included 9.93 million stock-based awards, 1.50 million convertible senior notes and 0.27 million warrants (Q2). No entity represented 10% or more of accounts receivable; the company is dependent on largely single-source suppliers. Accrued warranty was $524.0 million at quarter end after a $118.7 million quarterly provision and $37.1 million from revenue standard adoption. Net intangible assets were $300.4 million, including $47.0 million of SolarCity in-process R&D (a $13.3 million abandonment loss and $26.5 million placed into production in Q2). Fair value measurements include $1,235.7 million of Level I money market funds and $12.4 million of Level II interest rate swaps (notional $313.97 million). Inventory write-downs were $24.6 million in Q2 and $41.9 million for six months. Construction in progress of $1,333.6 million includes $540.4 million (Gigafactory 1) and $649.5 million (Gigafactory 2) transferred to land and buildings; capitalized interest was $34.5 million for six months; $955.4 million of Panasonic production equipment and $4.14 billion total Gigafactory 1 costs have been capitalized. The club wants to settle but disputes the amount; how the dogs entered is unknown, and Eyes To Heaven is expected to recover and continue racing.

Hugh Bowman is seeking reductions to two riding suspensions so he can ride Winx in the Apollo Stakes on February 17. Trainer Michael Tubman celebrated his 70th birthday when Bye See won the Freshmark Handicap at Rosehill. Broadcaster Gary Harley and trainer Evan Holland were knocked down by Allez Rev after a Gosford race but escaped injury.

Brad Widdup, who left Godolphin to train independently, has 35 horses in work and aims to expand his stable to 60. Corey Brown explained to stewards that he followed Gary Portelli’s instructions by taking Exceltic outside eventual winner Performer.

Gerald Ryan’s Menari is being prepared for The Galaxy, while Joe Pride plans a limited campaign for Terravista, beginning in the Lightning Stakes. Kinky Boom’s Golden Slipper price firmed from $101 to $35, and Tony McEvoy also holds Slipper favourite Sunlight.

The passage disputes Yale Law School professor Keith Whittington’s claim that professors should exercise discretion and avoid offensive remarks after Charlie Kirk’s assassination to preserve academic freedom. It argues that classroom speech standards requiring relevance and competence do not justify punishing professors for isolated off-topic or incorrect comments. It also cites investigations of only a small number of professors critical of Kirk as evidence of viewpoint discrimination. The passage emphasizes that academic freedom supports intellectual honesty and truth and should protect even objectionable speech, regardless of political viewpoint. It characterizes the AAUP’s 1940 Statement of Principles as a moral guide rather than an enforceable rule and notes that its 1970 Interpretive Comments called controversy central to free academic inquiry. Ultimately, it argues that self-censorship and discretion, especially when motivated by fear, undermine academic freedom rather than defend it.

Microsoft Corporation’s Form 10-Q reports financial results for the three and nine months ended March 31, 2016. For the quarter, revenue was $20.531 billion, compared with $21.729 billion a year earlier; gross margin was $12.809 billion; operating income was $5.283 billion; and net income was $3.756 billion, or $0.47 per diluted share. For the nine months, revenue was $64.706 billion, operating income was $17.102 billion, and net income was $13.676 billion, or $1.70 per diluted share, compared with $71.400 billion, $20.214 billion, and $15.388 billion, respectively, in the prior-year periods.

At March 31, 2016, Microsoft reported $181.869 billion in assets, $107.063 billion in liabilities, and $74.806 billion in stockholders’ equity. Cash and equivalents totaled $7.170 billion, short-term investments were $98.382 billion, and short- and long-term debt totaled $46.394 billion. Net cash from operations was $10.367 billion for the quarter and $24.861 billion for the nine months. During the nine months, Microsoft spent $5.688 billion on property and equipment, repurchased $12.292 billion of common stock, and paid $8.185 billion in dividends.

Segment results were mixed. Productivity and Business Processes reported quarterly revenue of $6.522 billion and operating income of $2.994 billion. Intelligent Cloud reported revenue of $6.096 billion and operating income of $2.188 billion. More Personal Computing reported revenue of $9.458 billion and operating income of $1.645 billion, compared with $1.049 billion a year earlier. Corporate and Other reported a quarterly operating loss of $1.544 billion, primarily reflecting $1.6 billion of net Windows 10 revenue deferrals. For the nine months, Windows 10-related deferrals totaled $4.6 billion.

Microsoft adopted new accounting guidance on share-based payments in the third quarter of fiscal 2016 and retrospectively adjusted prior-quarter results. Revenue recognition, financial-instrument, and lease standards issued by the FASB were not yet adopted and were expected to take effect between 2018 and 2019. Microsoft also recast prior-period segment information to reflect its Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, and More Personal Computing reporting structure, without affecting consolidated net income or cash flows.

Third-quarter operating highlights included a commercial-cloud annualized run rate exceeding $10 billion, 22.2 million Office 365 Consumer subscribers, 110% growth in Azure revenue, more than doubled Dynamics CRM Online seat additions, and more than doubled Enterprise Mobility customers, reaching 27,000. Windows 10 was active on more than 270 million devices, while Xbox Live monthly active users increased 26% to 46 million.

Microsoft used derivatives to manage foreign-currency, equity-price, interest-rate, credit, and commodity risks. It reported $373 million of unrealized investment losses at March 31, 2016 and stated that management did not believe the remaining losses represented other-than-temporary impairments.

Microsoft completed 14 acquisitions during the nine months for $1.3 billion in cash consideration, in addition to its earlier $2.5 billion acquisition of Mojang. Goodwill increased to $17.948 billion. A phone-business restructuring plan was expected to eliminate up to 7,800 positions in fiscal 2016, with $780 million of charges incurred to date.

The filing disclosed continuing intellectual-property, antitrust, regulatory, tax, and product-related litigation, including patent disputes involving IPCom and InterDigital, a Chinese regulatory investigation, and cell-phone health-effect claims. Microsoft had accrued $530 million of legal liabilities and estimated that reasonably possible adverse outcomes beyond recorded amounts could reach approximately $1.6 billion. Deloitte & Touche reviewed the interim statements, found no material modifications necessary, and reported that the review was narrower than an audit.

Microsoft Corporation reported that at its November 28, 2018 annual shareholders meeting, 6,722,310,265 of 7,677,511,729 voting shares were represented. Shareholders re-elected all 14 director nominees, approved executive compensation on an advisory basis with 96.0% support, and ratified Deloitte & Touche LLP as Microsoft’s independent auditor for fiscal 2019 with 97.6% support.

Molecular-dynamics simulations using a first-principles-parameterized effective Hamiltonian, benchmarked against DFT, investigated ferroelectric topological textures in Zr-substituted BaTiO₃ (BZT). In an ordered 12.5% Zr superlattice with a chemically doubled unit cell along [111], nanodomains hosted an alternating sequence of Q=−2 antiskyrmions composed of six −1/3 topological quarks and Q=+4 skyrmions composed of six +2/3 quarks. Both shared the same six-vortex geometry, with each vortex’s charge shifting by an integer between the two chemically distinct halves. A complementary field-theoretic interpretation attributes the alternation to a sign-changing chemical background and associated layer-dependent anisotropy, although the microscopic charge-transfer mechanism remains unresolved.

Random Zr substitution from 0% to 12.5% preserved nanodomains and recognizable nontrivial textures at 1 K, but quenched disorder distorted and pinned vortex lines, redistributed fractional charges, and produced fluctuating plane-resolved charges. These randomly substituted systems exhibited a “skyrmion-glass”-like patchwork rather than a uniform −2 or +4 texture.

Thermal ramping showed that Zr generally reduced intrinsic stability relative to pure BaTiO₃. Critical temperatures dropped at low Zr concentration, reached a minimum near 6–8%, and partially recovered by 12.5% because disorder-assisted pinning counterbalanced ferroelectric softening. Nontrivial textures remained stable over broad cryogenic ranges, in some cases approaching 100 K, while larger domains were generally more robust. Higher Zr contents could instead fragment into multidomain states during heating.

The ordered 12.5% superlattice remained rhombohedral above room temperature, with transitions near 320 K on cooling and 345 K on heating. At 293 K, reversed domains could not persist without bias, but a local [111]-directed electric field of about 350 kV/cm wrote and maintained cylindrical domains with uniform Q=+4 textures while the field remained applied. Random 12.5% BZT instead developed multidomain states under the same field. The study identifies epitaxial strain, compositional patterning, and electrostatic engineering as possible routes to improved room-temperature retention and highlights BZT as a platform for fractionalized ferroelectric topology and potential multistate memory applications.

Using first-principles LDA, QSGW, and QSGŴ calculations, the study examines WSe₂/CrI₃ bilayers and ferromagnetically or antiferromagnetically coupled trilayers. Density-functional calculations find a strained C1 stacking with a 3.53 Å interlayer distance. LDA predicts a 0.77 eV type-II band alignment, whereas QSGW and QSGŴ predict type-I alignment with both band edges dominated by WSe₂ W-d states, giving gaps of 2.33 and 2.21 eV, respectively.

The calculations reproduce the WSe₂ A and B Wannier–Mott excitons and the localized CrI₃ Frenkel excitons at 1.45, 1.85, and 2.1 eV. They also predict novel interlayer excitons near 1.84 eV that consistently appear between the A and B excitons across all configurations. These states combine delocalized, bright WSe₂ optical character with magnetic CrI₃ character, have binding energies around 400 meV, and possess oscillator strengths nearly twenty times those of intralayer CrI₃ excitons, though roughly two orders of magnitude below the A exciton. Their optical polarization differs from that of the nearby A₂s exciton, which may aid experimental identification.

Proximity-induced magnetic fields split the A and B excitons. Splittings range from tens to roughly 100 GHz in bilayer and antiferromagnetic trilayer structures and reach about 1000 GHz in the ferromagnetic trilayer. Their magnitudes are highly sensitive to Cr-d/W-d band alignment, interlayer spacing, strain, and interface effects. The interlayer excitons remain robust across configurations and are presented as promising controllable states for photonic and spintronic applications. Radiative and nonradiative lifetimes could not be calculated because the present approach omits dynamical vertex effects and exciton–phonon coupling. Exploratory comparisons indicate that CrBr₃ may produce brighter interlayer excitons but smaller A- and B-exciton splittings than CrI₃.

Maharashtra’s effort to renegotiate its power-purchase agreement with Enron-promoted Dabhol Power Company was disrupted when committee chairman Madhav Godbole resigned after former chief minister Sharad Pawar criticized the panel’s “negative approach.” A DPC meeting was cancelled, but Godbole withdrew his resignation after the state cabinet backed him and Chief Minister Vilasrao Deshmukh appealed for his continued involvement. The next meeting was set for May 29. Pawar said his comments were personal, while three other committee members had also resigned.

Godbole called the original Dabhol agreement an “inexcusable failure of governance” and supported a judicial inquiry into alleged favoritism, misrepresentation and the contract’s validity. He said Phase I utilization averaged only 30–40 percent and Maharashtra required only a marginal portion of its output. He also planned to complete a report on Phase II and restructuring the Maharashtra State Electricity Board.

The central government said it would facilitate negotiations and consider worthwhile Godbole committee recommendations acceptable to both DPC and MSEB, but would not intervene before Maharashtra reached a final decision. It rejected expectations that NTPC would rescue the project and considered involving the Power Trading Corporation to sell surplus power in deficit states. Maharashtra separately referred the dispute to the Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission, involving DPC’s preliminary termination notice, force majeure and rebate claims.

Lenders had suspended further Phase II disbursements while awaiting a government meeting, although domestic lenders expressed confidence in a settlement. The Godbole committee’s report also questioned Dabhol’s base-load design, demand assumptions and alternatives, while financial exercises indicated that absorbing Phase II would require substantial tariff increases, reduced losses and much higher consumption. Separately, MSEB was found not to have fully provided confidential records to the NGO Prayas as ordered by MERC.

Michael Liersch, head of goals-based advice and strategy at JPMorgan, told Business Insider that most investors can succeed with a plan, perspective, and patience. His five tips: (1) Make a plan — create a budget to see where your money goes, then decide how much to invest and save; (2) Reframe decisions — focus on future goals such as a house or retirement instead of current spending, and see market declines as buying opportunities rather than reasons to panic sell; (3) Stay the course — returns are a long game, so match the investment timeline to your goals, be patient, and don't try to time the market; (4) Don't go alone — get a second opinion from someone with a different mindset, such as a spouse, parent, child, or adviser; (5) Take small steps — begin by paying down a credit card or adding a few dollars to an IRA, and automate contributions to build momentum.

Asian-Pacific stocks rose as senior U.S. officials downplayed North Korea conflict risks, while U.S. stocks logged their largest weekly loss in months on disappointing earnings and escalating threats. Japan’s economy grew faster than expected in the April–June quarter, driven by household spending, marking a sixth straight quarter of growth under Prime Minister Shinzo Abe. U.S. inflation remained subdued, the weaker dollar supported the sluggish economy, and Dallas Fed President Robert Kaplan said rates were appropriate absent clear signs of higher inflation.

The paper argues that the reproduction number R, a widely used measure of how fast a pathogen spreads, has a major shortcoming: it does not account for the time-varying number of tests (diagnostics) performed, even though empirical estimates of R are themselves time-varying and cases become visible only through testing. The authors relate R to the "acceleration index" ε introduced in earlier work by Baunez et al., an elasticity measuring the proportional responsiveness of cases to tests. The index equals the ratio of the daily positivity rate to the average positivity rate, and can be interpreted as the ratio of current to average viral speed; ε above one signals acceleration, below one deceleration.

Theoretically, the ratio of ε to R decomposes into an infectivity intensity (current infectious potential relative to its historical average) over a test intensity (current tests relative to their historical average). The two measures coincide only when the infectivity function is specified so as to account for calendar-time test variation; otherwise ε is more general, and R is a special case. Consequently, R overestimates viral acceleration when test intensity exceeds infectivity intensity and underestimates it when the reverse holds. Under deterministic exponential growth with tests also growing exponentially, R stays constant while ε varies, rising to a plateau equal to the ratio of growth rates. A two-period schematic example (constant cases, with tests halved or doubled) shows R remaining at one while ε moves to 1.5 (accelerating) or 0.75 (decelerating). Unreported SIR simulations with time-varying tests and observed only among the tested indicated the acceleration index captures peaks and deceleration better than an unadjusted R.

Empirically, using French data from May 13, 2020 to October 26, 2022 (spanning pre- and post-vaccination periods), R substantially underestimates viral spread relative to ε, with the discrepancy most severe during the autumn 2022 Omicron wave. The two measures diverge from around August 5, 2020: as R fell from about 1.5 to 1 by late September, ε rose to roughly 1.9 and plateaued, indicating worsening rather than improvement. The October 30, 2020 lock-down coincided with a sharp reduction in testing, so R fell below one while ε still indicated acceleration. In 2022, infectivity intensity consistently exceeded test intensity, so R underestimated viral acceleration. Department-level maps showed ε declining everywhere during the second lock-down, while R suggested widespread deceleration; three weeks later ε still showed an acceleration regime in nearly all départements. A similar analysis for five other countries (Appendix C) found R may under- or overestimate viral acceleration depending on country and period; in South Korea and Argentina, test intensity tracked infectivity intensity closely, narrowing the gap. Whenever ε exceeds one, the authors suggest diagnostic effort should accelerate.

The authors conclude that the acceleration index is a sufficient, unit-free statistic of viral spread and a test-adjusted reproduction number, recommended for real-time dashboards and policy guidance; tracking R together with test and infectivity intensities is formally equivalent but less parsimonious. Limitations noted include uncounted and asymptomatic cases, the dependence of accuracy on test volume, and the cost of testing policies.

Pershing Square’s U.S. long portfolio rose slightly from $5.96 billion to $6.01 billion in Q2 2017, remaining at seven positions and heavily concentrated in Restaurant Brands International (~41%), Chipotle Mexican Grill (~20%) and Mondelēz International (10.41%), which together represented 71.06% of 13F value. Changes included establishing a roughly 3% ADP stake at a $97.30 cost basis; selling the remaining roughly 5% APD 13F stake near $145; increasing HHC by one-third through warrant conversions; and reducing MDLZ by about 37%. QSR and CMG were unchanged, while PAH was trimmed roughly 5% at $8.78. NOMD remained a roughly 19%-owned position. Pershing Square also held just under 10% each of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac through 13D disclosures, though these were not 13F securities. Its only publicly known short was Herbalife, allocated 9% of capital; regulatory rules do not require disclosure of other shorts.

Poland Local Board of Education dissolved teacher Cassandra Kibler’s contract following an allegation of an inappropriate relationship with a student; her Ohio teaching license was revoked, and she had been on unpaid leave since April 2017. The board also reviewed two proposals to reduce district operating costs through school consolidation and repurposing Dobbins for athletics, but took no action.

A May 2001 compilation of energy-industry reports focused primarily on Enron. A Washington Post analysis said California’s electricity crisis resulted from an inept deregulation system that required utilities to rely on volatile short-term power markets while capping retail rates. Generators and traders posted large profits while consumers faced higher costs, several utilities incurred losses and Pacific Gas & Electric entered bankruptcy. Enron reported a 75% increase in wholesale-services profits, though it said little came from California.

A federal appeals court ruled that Enron could fulfill its contracts to supply California universities by purchasing power from investor-owned utilities rather than the costly spot market. The ruling could save Enron up to $12 million monthly while shifting costs to the state. California had spent $5 billion since January buying electricity for customers of three troubled utilities, recovering only $1 billion, and said it would seek reconsideration of the ruling.

Enron was considering bids for U.K. power stations, including Fiddler’s Ferry and Ferrybridge, to profit from price volatility, meet supply obligations and expand risk-management services. It already owned 50% of Teesside Power Station. Prices in the U.K. balancing mechanism ranged from £1,036 to negative £434 per megawatt-hour because of severe supply swings.

Scottish Power planned to reorganize into three divisions focused on generation, power supply, infrastructure and overseas expansion after adjusted pretax profit fell 15% and adjusted earnings per share declined 26%. It was considering selling Southern Water, retained its remaining stake in the loss-making Thus telecommunications venture, and considered buying Enron’s Portland General unit.

In India, lenders to Enron’s Dabhol Power Company were seeking to resolve a dispute over the Maharashtra State Electricity Board’s refusal to buy all power at the contracted price and its failure to pay disputed bills. Lenders holding nearly $2 billion in loans offered to lower interest rates to prevent default but threatened legal action against DPC, MSEB and the governments. Bombay customs also blocked about ₹300 crore of DPC imports over a dispute between concessional and normal duty rates. Enron agreed to meet a Maharashtra negotiating committee on May 11 without making proposals; possible subjects included lowering the tariff, selling excess power and restructuring ownership.

Northern Border Partners completed its $100 million acquisition of the 350-mile Midwestern Gas Transmission system from El Paso after Federal Trade Commission approval. Enron and Williams owned the partnership’s general-partner interests.

BP Amoco was also studying a roughly $200 million liquefied-natural-gas terminal at the Port of Tampa. The project would require at least four years of regulatory approvals and aimed to supply gas-fired utilities in Florida, where demand was projected to grow rapidly.

Microsoft Corporation’s Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2017 describes its strategy, operations, segments, and principal risks. Microsoft’s mission is to empower every person and organization, with a strategy centered on intelligent cloud and edge technologies infused with artificial intelligence. Its three connected ambitions are to reinvent productivity and business processes, build the intelligent cloud platform, and create more personal computing.

Microsoft operates in more than 190 countries and reports through three segments:

- **Productivity and Business Processes:** Includes commercial and consumer Office offerings, Office 365, LinkedIn, Dynamics 365, and related on-premises products. Microsoft completed its $27.0 billion LinkedIn acquisition in December 2016.
- **Intelligent Cloud:** Includes Azure, SQL Server, Windows Server, Visual Studio, System Center, enterprise support, and consulting services. Azure supports public, private, and hybrid cloud deployments.
- **More Personal Computing:** Includes Windows, Surface and other devices, Xbox hardware, games and services, and search advertising.

Microsoft develops most products internally through business-specific engineering groups, including Office, Artificial Intelligence and Research, Cloud and Enterprise, Windows and Devices, and LinkedIn. Fiscal 2017 research and development expense was $13.0 billion, or 14% of revenue. The company held more than 66,000 issued patents and over 35,000 pending patents. Products are distributed through OEMs, direct sales, distributors, resellers, online portals, marketplaces, and retail stores.

As of June 30, 2017, Microsoft employed approximately 124,000 people, including 73,000 in the United States and 51,000 internationally. No individual customer accounted for more than 10% of revenue in fiscal 2017, 2016, or 2015.

The filing identifies risks including intense competition, execution and margin pressures in cloud and subscription businesses, uncertain returns on investments in new products, acquisition integration and impairment risks, intellectual-property protection and infringement claims, cybersecurity threats, outages and data loss, competition-law scrutiny, global regulatory compliance, difficulty attracting and retaining employees, litigation, tax liabilities, and hardware quality or supply-chain problems. It also cautions that forward-looking statements are subject to risks and uncertainties and that Microsoft undertakes no obligation to update them.
Simone Askew, a 20-year-old West Point cadet, became the first Black woman to lead its Corps of Cadets, the highest cadet leadership position.

Syrian rebels faced a Wednesday deadline to accept Russian-backed surrender terms or face renewed military operations in Daraa and Quneitra. More than 30 towns had already returned to government control. Russia rejected rebels’ proposals for a ceasefire, army withdrawal and safe passage, insisting the army return to pre-2011 positions and local police oversee surrendered towns. Air strikes paused during negotiations. The offensive displaced 270,000–330,000 people, while Jordan and Israel kept their borders closed; more than 140 civilians were reportedly killed. Governments and rights groups criticized the offensive, and the UN Security Council scheduled an emergency meeting. Moscow said it hoped rebels would surrender their weapons, while Jordan’s foreign minister called for a ceasefire.

The commissioner expressed confidence that Las Vegas would become a successful NHL market despite building, ownership and economic hurdles. The expansion schedule was in the team’s hands, unrelated to Seattle and had not negatively affected the season. Fan enthusiasm validated the market, while the team’s success was portrayed as positive for hockey rather than criticism of other clubs. Scientists found insufficient evidence to establish a referenced link, and the franchise was praised for expanding its fan base.

NVIDIA reported unaudited results for the second quarter of fiscal 2020, ended July 28, 2019. Quarterly revenue was $2.579 billion, down 17% year over year but up 16% sequentially. Gross margin was 59.8%, operating income was $571 million, net income was $552 million, and diluted earnings per share were $0.90. For the first half, revenue was $4.799 billion, net income was $947 million, and diluted earnings per share were $1.54.

GPU revenue declined 21% year over year to $2.104 billion, while Tegra Processor revenue increased 2% to $475 million. By market, gaming revenue fell 27% to $1.313 billion, professional visualization rose 4% to $291 million, data center declined 14% to $655 million, automotive increased 30% to $209 million, and OEM and other revenue fell 4% to $111 million. Gross margin decreased due primarily to lower gaming and data center margins, while operating expenses rose 19%, primarily because of employee additions, compensation, infrastructure, and stock-based compensation.

Cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities totaled $8.475 billion at July 28, 2019, compared with $7.422 billion at fiscal year-end. First-half operating cash flow was $1.656 billion. NVIDIA paid $195 million in dividends and intended to return the remaining $2.11 billion of its planned $3 billion fiscal 2020 capital return through dividends and repurchases, with repurchases potentially extending into fiscal 2021.

NVIDIA also entered into an agreement to acquire Mellanox Technologies for $125 per share in cash, representing an enterprise value of approximately $6.9 billion. Mellanox shareholders approved the transaction, and U.S. and Mexican regulatory approvals had been received, while European and Chinese reviews remained underway. A $350 million termination fee could apply in specified circumstances.

The company adopted a new lease accounting standard, recognizing $470 million of operating lease assets and $500 million of liabilities. Consolidated securities and derivative lawsuits concerning statements about channel inventory and cryptocurrency mining remained pending, and no related contingency was accrued because losses were not considered probable. Management concluded disclosure controls were effective, with no material changes in internal controls or previously disclosed risk factors.

The study examines curriculum differentiation (CD) in Ethiopian secondary education, focusing on the intentions of national policy documents and how school principals and teachers conceptualize CD. It distinguishes CD through tracking among school types, fields of study, streams, ability groups, and geographic settings from classroom-level differentiation of content, instruction, assessment, and learning environments within inclusive classrooms. It notes that tracking can create unequal access, hierarchy, and exclusion when students are categorized by factors unrelated to their needs and abilities.

The study analyzed three national documents—the 2023 Education and Training Policy, the 2020 General Education Curriculum Framework, and the 2012 Guidelines for Curriculum Differentiation and Individualized Educational Programs—using a qualitative case study of two government secondary schools in Addis Ababa. One school was a regular institution serving mixed-ability students and offering science and social-science streams plus limited language-subject differentiation. The other was a special day school for selected high academic achievers that differentiated curriculum components. Two principals and 17 subject teachers were interviewed.

The 2023 policy and 2020 framework emphasize student placement in tracks, streams, fields of study, and special schools, as well as options for talented students and students with disabilities. By contrast, the 2012 guidelines emphasize a common curriculum in inclusive classrooms, with teachers adapting content, instructional processes, assessments, and learning environments to students’ needs, interests, and readiness. The documents share a broad commitment to diverse learners but differ in their strategies, creating some policy inconsistency.

Participants’ conceptualizations fell into five themes: CD as gifted programs; placement into subjects, streams, and schools; special curricula for groups; identification and accommodation of talents; and curricular planning or teaching strategies. Views ranged from limited awareness and divergence from policy to alignment with policy. Respondents frequently focused on gifted or high-achieving students, sometimes supported segregated school placement, and often conflated gifted students with high academic achievers. The study attributes this diversity partly to incoherent policy guidance and limited engagement by principals and teachers with reform ideas.

The study concludes that policy coherence and clearer operational guidance are needed, while recognizing continuing debate over tracking and inclusion. It recommends clearer identification and support for gifted students, flexible subject difficulty and pathways, opportunities in arts, music, and vocational areas, and corresponding flexibility in assessment and examinations. It also recommends further research with larger samples because the study covered only two schools and 19 participants.

Former FBI Deputy Director Andrew McCabe was fired March 16, two days before his planned early retirement at 50, following an Inspector General investigation into unauthorized disclosures related to the bureau’s Hillary Clinton email probe. Under FERS, he was eligible for an estimated $60,000 annual pension at a special enhanced rate, but his firing may prevent him from receiving payments until age 57 and eight months and may also end health insurance coverage for his family. It remains unclear how much, if any, pension he will receive before then. Lawmakers are offering temporary Capitol Hill jobs because McCabe fell days short of the federal service required for early retirement eligibility, but former officials dispute whether such work would preserve his pension. McCabe can appeal, and no criminal charges are expected.

The St. Louis Blues have nine core players under contract through at least three seasons for a combined $47.425 million cap cost. The group includes Vladimir Tarasenko, Alexander Steen, Jaden Schwartz, Patrik Berglund, Vladimir Sobotka, Alex Pietrangelo, Colton Parayko and Jake Allen. Several deals appear strong, particularly Pietrangelo’s, while Parayko could become the team’s best defenseman. Potential concerns include Steen’s age and the limited production of Sobotka and Berglund.

Defensemen Jay Bouwmeester, Carl Gunnarsson, Robert Bortuzzo and Nate Prosser have two years remaining, while Joel Edmundson is slated to become a restricted free agent. The Blues also face decisions involving Paul Stastny and Robby Fabbri. Despite lacking a surplus scorer and having allowed David Backes and Troy Brouwer to leave, the club’s salary structure and several favorable contracts leave it in a strong position.

NVIDIA Corporation filed a Form 8-K on February 24, 2021, announcing results for the quarter and fiscal year ended January 31, 2021. Exhibit 99.1 contains the results press release, and Exhibit 99.2 contains CFO Colette M. Kress’s commentary. The materials were furnished—not deemed filed—under specified securities laws.
The CBI began probing the alleged 2017 SSC CGL Tier II paper leak. The Supreme Court said court monitoring was unnecessary but allowed petitioners to return if dissatisfied.

- **Basel II:** The revised capital adequacy rules were nearing completion and were targeted for implementation in 2004. Reporting described them as more closely tying capital to individual credit risk, but potentially difficult and costly to implement. Australia’s APRA warned that proposed mortgage-capital rules could create competitive inequalities and sought a 20% standardized housing risk weighting or greater national discretion. Southeast Asian central banks said limited infrastructure and regulatory capacity could impede timely adoption. Large banks considered the rules overly conservative, while smaller and developing-market banks warned of higher capital costs and wider disparities between countries. The Institute of International Finance estimated implementation costs of $2.25 trillion over five years for 30,000 banks. External credit-rating requirements and the 2004 deadline also drew criticism, with some countries advocating a longer phase-in.

- **Derivatives regulation:** Derivatives industry officials expected Basel II’s internal-ratings calibration to be revised but continued to oppose the 15% “W” charge applied when credit derivatives are used for credit-risk mitigation. ISDA also criticized rigid capital floors and arbitrary charges. The report highlighted European implementation delays, possible divergence between U.S. and European systems, and uncertainty over whether the “W” factor would be eliminated.

- **Credit-derivatives documentation:** An ISDA working group was nearing a preliminary proposal for standardized documentation covering swaps based on convertible bonds and zero-coupon convertible securities, intended to facilitate stripping and improve liquidity. A new ISDA subcommittee was addressing how swaps should treat successor entities following mergers, demergers, or restructurings, with AT&T’s planned separation and unresolved National Power contracts adding urgency.

- **Argentina debt exchange:** Deutsche Bank and ABN Amro withdrew from managing Argentina’s debt swap because lawyers raised concerns about possible U.S. securities-law violations involving research conducted before the transaction. Banco de Galicia was also reported to be excluding itself from the U.S. offering.

- **California electricity regulation:** California’s Independent System Operator faced federal scrutiny over its independence after the state replaced its governing board and obtained extensive access and influence. The ISO maintained that state support did not make California a market participant, while critics argued that its governance had violated federal independence requirements.

- **Structured products:** The report described capital-protected notes, equity-linked notes, knock-in and knock-out options, and warrants as flexible investment products traded on exchanges such as the CBOE. It noted that lower returns on Indian savings products could increase demand for structured products offering a balance between capital protection and potentially higher returns.

The S&P 500 closed Friday at its lowest level since early July after falling 2.36% last week, despite a 1.5% gain the prior week. Using 2013–2014 China Education Panel Survey data covering students in grades seven and nine, the study examines how parental education relates to children’s cognitive ability. After handling missing data, the sample included 13,981 students from 438 classes in 112 schools across 28 county-level regions in China. Multiple linear regression assessed the effects of parental education, controlling for child, family, and school characteristics and testing mediation through educational expectations and parent-child interaction. Findings show a significant positive association: a one-year increase in either parent’s maximum education corresponds to a 0.019-point increase in children’s cognitive ability. Educational expectations and parent-child companionship exert significant partial mediating effects. Parental education has greater effects on girls than boys and greater effects in urban than rural families. Its impact also declines as children’s cognitive ability rises. The findings are intended to inform policies addressing educational disparities and the “Matthew effect.”

The lecture shifts sustainable real estate finance from the asset and building levels to portfolio-level public-market financing. The portfolio framework connects institutional investors, including pension funds and insurers, with equity and debt vehicles. The main vehicles discussed are REITs and green bonds, alongside benchmarking, disclosure, and data needed to evaluate sustainability.

REITs are publicly traded companies that primarily invest in income-generating commercial real estate. They can raise capital through share issuance, bank loans, and corporate bonds. Rental income generates revenue, and U.S. REITs receive a pass-through tax advantage provided they invest at least 75% of their assets in real estate and distribute at least 90% of annual income. Compared with direct property investment, REIT shares offer greater diversification, lower capital requirements, pooled risk, tax advantages, and liquidity because they can be sold on a stock exchange. Disadvantages include less control and limited knowledge of the underlying properties. The United States has roughly 250–260 REITs.

Participants described varied national models. Colombia’s PEY, founded in 2008, adapted the U.S. REIT model to local tax laws and trades on the BVC. Mexico, South Korea, and Thailand also developed REIT markets, with Thailand introducing them after the Asian financial crisis to restore market liquidity. China did not establish REITs despite discussion and research beginning around 2002. During the pandemic recession, when cities faced declining land-sale revenue, the government launched infrastructure-focused REITs through listed quasi-government corporations. Unlike U.S. REITs, these vehicles generally lacked the same tax advantage and initially financed infrastructure rather than commercial property; expansion toward commercial real estate was under consideration.

Research presented on green REITs found that many REITs have adopted net-zero and other ESG targets. Interviews with institutional investors suggested that capital providers, particularly pro-ESG institutions in Western and Northern Europe, are pressuring REIT managers to improve portfolio sustainability to attract capital. Findings were described as preliminary, with Middle Eastern institutions showing the least interest in the sample. Earlier research associated REITs with larger shares of LEED-certified and Energy Star properties with higher returns, better performance, and lower beta. However, reverse causality remains possible because stronger-performing REITs may have more resources for green investments. A current project uses 2010–2019 data for 178 REITs to compare “green talking,” measured through pledges and disclosures, with “green doing,” measured through actual investment, and to test their effects on stock returns, alpha, beta, return on assets, and return on equity.

Green bonds are fixed-income securities issued by governments, municipalities, or companies that promise to use proceeds for environmentally beneficial investments such as renewable energy and climate resilience. Their green designation is primarily based on the use of proceeds rather than a general tax exemption, although related incentives or lower market yields may apply. Issuers are encouraged to follow green-bond principles and provide evidence that promised projects were implemented. Research cited in the lecture found that green REITs can obtain lower bond spreads and financing costs on average. Fannie Mae’s model includes issuing bonds backed by pools of mortgages on energy-efficient buildings. Smaller developers may find it difficult to issue these securities because investors require stable, established companies and credible repayment prospects.

The lecture also examined municipal green financing. Municipal bonds can fund infrastructure and public services and be repaid through property-tax revenue. Where cities lack property-tax systems or adequate revenue, state-owned infrastructure companies may issue bonds on their behalf and rely on land-sale proceeds for repayment, creating substantial risk when real-estate markets decline.

Finally, the lecture emphasized data, measurement, assurance, and benchmarking as necessary to prevent greenwashing. Building-level utility data can be collected through the EPA’s Portfolio Manager and modeled for portfolio owners. ESG data firms aggregate information from utilities and properties, while third parties such as DNV provide carbon assurance. Scope 3 embodied-carbon measurement remains especially difficult. CRREM applies carbon limits to portfolios, while GRESB serves as a portfolio-level counterpart to building certifications such as LEED. GRESB scores participating REITs, private-equity funds, pension funds, and asset managers across ESG categories, enabling peer comparisons, trend analysis, and identification of weaknesses. Studies cited found associations between higher GRESB scores, stronger performance, and lower borrowing costs, although these were average relationships rather than guarantees. The broader ESG-rating system remains inconsistent and noisy, prompting MIT’s ESG Confusion project to develop methods for deriving more reliable measures, including for the real-estate sector.

The stack-enable procedure initializes the processor and cache system with a pre-memory stack, allocates stack space among processor cores, maps it into global address space, configures x86-64 MTRRs, and creates a `UEFI_SEC_PEI_HAND_OFF` structure. It must run on all cores. Protected-mode SS is unchanged; real mode uses a 16-bit segment:offset stack. It returns success, warns and resets an already active stack, or reports an unknown processor family. AARCH64 systems with a PSP use the PSP to initialize DRAM instead.

A corresponding teardown procedure, invoked only by the BSP after memory becomes available, disables the pre-memory stack and CAR mode without changing MTRRs. It flushes all cache lines, leaving the BSP’s cache enabled and its contents invalidated without write-back.

`AmdCreateStruct` allocates and pre-initializes an AGESA structure using pre-memory heap, post-memory DRAM, or host-provided storage. With host allocation, the host must ensure sufficient space. Successful initialization overlays the original parameters with the new structure; insufficient space returns an error and preserves the parameters.

NVIDIA’s whitepaper introduces the GA10x class of Ampere GPUs, including the GA102 and GA104 architectures. GA10x builds on Turing and targets improved graphics, AI, ray tracing, rendering, data-center, and storage workloads. The document claims up to 1.7× faster raster performance, up to 2× faster ray tracing, and up to 1.9× better power efficiency than Turing.

GA102 is fabricated using Samsung’s 8nm process and contains 28.3 billion transistors. A full GA102 has seven graphics processing clusters, 42 texture processing clusters, 84 streaming multiprocessors, 10,752 CUDA cores, 84 second-generation RT cores, and 336 third-generation Tensor cores. Its SMs provide dual-datapath FP32 processing, larger unified L1 cache and shared memory, and concurrent execution of ray tracing with graphics or compute.

The second-generation RT cores double ray/triangle intersection throughput and add an Interpolate Triangle Position unit for hardware-accelerated motion blur. NVIDIA states that this can make ray-traced motion blur up to eight times faster than on Turing, with measured motion-blur rendering up to five times faster on an RTX 3080 than an RTX 2080 Super.

Third-generation Tensor cores support structured sparsity, TF32, BF16, FP16, INT8, and INT4 operations. Sparsity uses a 2-out-of-4 pattern to double throughput and halve weight storage, while TF32 provides up to five times the prior-generation training throughput. The RTX 3080 is stated to deliver 2.7× the dense FP16 throughput of an RTX 2080 Super when sparsity is enabled. Ampere GPUs also enhance DLSS with 9× upscaling, enabling many games to run at 8K/60 on the RTX 3090.

GA10x supports GDDR6X memory using PAM4 signaling, with rates up to 19.5 Gbps and peak bandwidth up to 936 GB/sec. Third-generation NVLink provides 112.5 GB/sec aggregate bandwidth between two supported GPUs, while PCIe 4.0 offers up to 64 GB/sec of host bandwidth. RTX IO, working with Microsoft’s DirectStorage API, moves asset decompression onto the GPU and is claimed to provide up to 100× storage throughput and 20× lower CPU utilization compared with traditional approaches.

The GeForce RTX 3090 uses GA102 with 10,496 CUDA cores and 24 GB of GDDR6X for 8K HDR gaming. The RTX 3080 provides up to twice the RTX 2080’s performance and 1.5× its memory bandwidth. The GA104-based RTX 3070 offers performance comparable to the RTX 2080 Ti but lacks NVLink and uses GDDR6 rather than GDDR6X.

The workstation RTX A6000 and data-center A40 have 10,752 CUDA cores, 84 RT cores, 336 Tensor cores, and 48 GB of GDDR6 memory; NVLink can combine two GPUs for 96 GB. The A40 supports virtual workstations and is claimed to provide up to twice the FP32 and ray-tracing throughput and five times the AI throughput of a Quadro RTX 6000, or ten times with sparsity.

GA10x also supports DisplayPort 1.4a and HDMI 2.1, including 8K at 60 Hz and 4K at 120 Hz. Fifth-generation NVDEC provides hardware decoding for MPEG-2, VC-1, H.264, H.265, VP8, VP9, and AV1, including AV1 playback up to 8K60 HDR with low CPU usage. Seventh-generation NVENC supports hardware encoding up to 4K H.264 and 8K HEVC. New GDDR6X Error Detection and Replay technology detects transmission errors and retries failed memory transactions.

The instructor outlines the course: Carroll’s general relativity textbook is semi-required, with Schutz, Misner–Thorne–Wheeler, and Wald recommended as references. Grading consists entirely of 11 problem sets—ten worth 9% and one worth 10%—with no final exam. The first half of the semester covers mathematical foundations and aims to derive Einstein’s field equations; the second examines cosmology, black holes, dense stars, gravitational waves, neutron stars, and related applications.

Special relativity is introduced geometrically to establish the mathematical tools needed for general relativity. Spacetime is defined as a manifold of events endowed with a metric. A manifold organizes events and their connectivity; an event represents something happening at a particular place and time and exists independently of coordinate labels; and the metric defines distances between events. The lecture emphasizes that the metric ultimately encodes gravity.

An inertial reference frame is represented by a lattice of synchronized clocks and measuring rods. The rods are orthogonal and uniformly marked, while the clocks tick uniformly. Einstein synchronization uses the invariant speed of light: a reflected light pulse must return at the midpoint between its emission and reception times. The lecture notes that gravity alters light propagation, complicating this clock-synchronization procedure in strong gravitational fields. Units are chosen so the speed of light equals one, making velocities dimensionless.

Finally, displacement vectors between events are introduced. Although their components depend on the observer, the underlying geometric objects remain unchanged. Lorentz transformations relate different observers’ components, with Einstein summation notation used for repeated indices. A spacetime vector is defined as a quartet of components that transforms between inertial frames according to the Lorentz transformation law and obeys the usual linearity properties of a vector space.

The study investigates whether automated mammographic-density predictions from low-dose mammography, at approximately 10% of the standard radiation dose, can support breast-cancer risk assessment in younger women. It focuses on variability between standard- and low-dose predictions and factors that may reduce confidence in low-dose estimates.

The independent ALDRAM test dataset contains paired standard- and low-dose mammograms from 147 women aged 31–45 with previous unilateral breast cancer. Models were trained using 15,290 standard-dose PROCAS mammograms with averaged radiologist density labels and corresponding simulated low-dose images. Preprocessed images were analyzed with ResNet-18 models trained separately on standard and simulated low-dose data. Models were selected for agreement between dose conditions, and possible sources of variation were examined.

On the PROCAS test set, the selected standard- and low-dose models had similarly high accuracy against radiologist labels. On ALDRAM, low-dose predictions differed slightly more from standard-dose predictions than standard-dose predictions differed from one another, although this difference was not statistically significant. Variation between craniocaudal and mediolateral oblique views at the same dose was at least as large, and possibly larger, than variation between doses for the same view. Averaging both views and predictions from multiple models significantly improved agreement; combined models achieved a rank correlation of 0.990 and RMSE of 1.92.

Age and actual dose ratio were not associated with prediction differences. Performance worsened at higher mammographic densities, with low-dose models generally predicting lower densities. Performance also worsened for smaller breasts, where low-dose predictions were substantially lower; differences between image sizes were attributed mainly to their different breast-area distributions. Large discrepancies between views or between separately trained models were associated with larger standard-versus-low-dose differences. No notable outliers were identified. Overall, the findings indicate that low-dose density prediction is feasible and can closely match standard-dose prediction, particularly after averaging views and models, but corrections may be needed for denser and smaller breasts and for systematic low-dose underestimation.

The study applies a machine-learning Food Processing Score (FPro) to GroceryDB, an open-source database of more than 50,000 foods and beverages collected in May 2021 from Walmart, Target, and Whole Foods online stores. FoodProX uses 12 nutrition-label nutrients standardized per 100 grams and was trained using NOVA classifications, producing a continuous score from 0 for unprocessed foods to 1 for ultra-processed foods. Ingredient lists were also organized as hierarchical trees, and the new Ingredient Processing Score (IgFPro) ranks ingredients by their contribution to processing.

Processing-score distributions were similar across the three stores, with most products falling in the ultra-processed range. Whole Foods offered more minimally processed and fewer ultra-processed products, while Target had a particularly high share of highly processed items. Processing varied substantially within categories such as cereals, milk alternatives, pasta, and snack bars, but little within jerky, popcorn, chips, bread, biscuits, and macaroni and cheese. GroceryDB’s score distribution resembled FNDDS and followed similar trends to the much larger USDA Branded Food Products Database, although only 44% of its products appeared in that database and fewer than 30% appeared in Open Food Facts.

Across categories, a 10% increase in FPro was associated with an 8.7% decrease in price per calorie, although the relationship varied by category: the decrease was 24.3% for soups and stews but 1.2% for cereals, while price increased with processing for milk and milk substitutes. Whole Foods provided a wider range of cereal processing levels, used less sugar and fewer natural flavors, and rarely contained corn syrup, whereas Walmart and Target cereals were generally more processed. Whole Foods also offered less-processed soups, yogurt, and milk alternatives; pizza, macaroni and cheese, and popcorn were highly processed in all stores.

More complex ingredient trees were associated with greater processing. IgFPro identified some additives and commodity oils as stronger markers of ultra-processing than ingredients such as xanthan gum, guar gum, locust bean gum, and salt. The authors state that the association between processing and cheaper calories may contribute to nutritional disparities, while emphasizing that effects vary by food group.

GroceryDB is presented as a resource for consumer decision-making, public-health interventions, supermarket layout design, and ingredient reformulation. Limitations include reliance on limited nutrition-label data and partial dependence on manual classification systems; processing methods that leave similar nutrient profiles, such as frying, puffing, or extrusion, may not be distinguished. Comprehensive ingredient and processing data are proposed as a path toward a less subjective, potentially unsupervised scoring system.

Tecomaria capensis (Cape honeysuckle), in the Bignoniaceae family, is a popular garden and hedging plant that is deciduous in cold areas. It is a scrambling shrub or small tree up to 6 m, with opposite compound leaves, trumpet-shaped orange-red or pale-orange flowers throughout the year, and flattened fruit. It occurs in thicket and on forest margins in southern and eastern South Africa and tropical Africa. SANBI automatically classified it as Least Concern. Sunbirds, butterflies and honey bees visit it; game browse it, and the larvae of two hawkmoths eat its leaves. It is used traditionally for fever, pain, sleeplessness, chest ailments, dysentery, and stimulating milk flow in nursing mothers. Its wood is carved into isixhoxho necklets worn by mothers as protective symbols and indicators of social status. It grows in well-drained soil with compost and fertiliser; it should be mulched, watered regularly until established, and pruned in late winter to encourage new growth and flowering.

The passage outlines NVIDIA’s Turing GPU architecture and its associated rendering, AI, connectivity, and compute technologies. VirtualLink provides power, display, and data over a single USB-C connector, allowing VR use on thin devices that cannot accommodate multiple connectors. For SLI configurations, Turing TU102 and TU104 use second-generation NVLink rather than MIO and PCIe: TU102 has two x8 links and TU104 one, with two-way SLI supported but three- and four-way configurations unavailable.

Turing introduces hybrid rendering, combining rasterization with ray tracing and AI. Dedicated RT Cores in each Streaming Multiprocessor accelerate bounding-volume-hierarchy traversal and ray-triangle intersection testing, freeing the SM for other graphics and compute work. Combined with denoising, this makes single-GPU real-time ray tracing practical and is described as roughly ten times faster than software ray tracing on Pascal. Turing ray-traced shadows, ambient occlusion, and reflections provide more physically accurate results than conventional shadow maps, screen-space ambient occlusion, and screen-space or cubemap reflections. The technology supports NVIDIA RTX, OptiX, Microsoft DXR, and a forthcoming Vulkan ray-tracing API.

NVIDIA NGX is a deep-learning technology stack within RTX that uses Turing Tensor Cores for AI-based graphics and application features. Its pretrained models are distributed through GeForce Experience or Quadro Experience and can interface with CUDA 10, DirectX, Vulkan, and TensorRT. Deep Learning Super-Sampling (DLSS) learns from 64-times-supersampled reference images to reconstruct high-quality frames from fewer samples, reducing shading work while maintaining quality similar to temporal antialiasing. DLSS 2X produces output approaching 64-times supersampling. Other NGX features include AI inpainting, which synthesizes replacement image content; AI Slow-Mo, which inserts interpolated frames for smooth slow motion; and AI Super Rez, which enlarges images or video by 2, 4, or 8 times using newly generated pixels.

Mesh shading adds Task and Mesh shader stages. Task shaders process object lists in parallel and launch cooperative mesh shaders, reducing CPU draw-call bottlenecks and allowing hundreds of thousands of objects to be rendered in real time. They can also select appropriate levels of detail and perform positional geometry operations such as dynamic spherical cutaways.

Variable Rate Shading (VRS) permits independent shading rates for each 16-by-16-pixel region while leaving visibility rates unchanged. Supported algorithms include Content Adaptive Shading for low-detail or slowly changing regions, Motion Adaptive Shading for moving objects, and Foveated Rendering for peripheral vision. VRS can also raise shading rates when using multisample antialiasing.

Texture Space Shading decouples visibility sampling from appearance sampling by computing and storing shading values in texture space. Previously shaded texels can be reused within or across frames, improving temporal stability, VR and AR performance, and rendering efficiency. Multi-View Rendering lets Turing fetch and shade geometry once for multiple viewpoints or character instances, supporting up to four views per hardware pass and 32 at the API level. It expands Pascal’s simultaneous multi-projection capabilities and supports stereoscopic VR, canted wide-field-of-view displays, multiple instances, and cascaded shadow maps.

Turing also extends DirectX 12 resource binding with bindless constant-buffer and unordered-access views, permits different resource types to share heaps, and supports Tier 2 resource heaps. Its VR features include VirtualLink, Multi-View Rendering, foveated rendering, and expanded VRWorks Audio using RT Cores for ray-traced sound.

The full TU104 contains six graphics processing clusters, 48 SMs, 3,072 CUDA Cores, 368 Tensor Cores, 48 RT Cores, 256-bit memory, and 13.6 billion transistors; it is used in products including the GeForce RTX 2080, Tesla T4, and Quadro RTX 5000. The Tesla T4 uses a reduced TU104 configuration with 40 SMs, 2,560 CUDA Cores, 320 Tensor Cores, and 320 GB/s memory bandwidth, targeting data-center inference. TU106, used in the GeForce RTX 2070, has 36 SMs, 2,304 CUDA Cores, 288 Tensor Cores, and 36 RT Cores but supports neither NVLink nor SLI.

The passage introduces RTX-OPS as a workload-based metric for hybrid rendering. It weights tensor operations at 20%, FP32 operations at 80%, RT operations at 40%, and INT32 operations at 28% of a representative frame. It also explains ray casting, ray intersections, BVH construction and refitting, and denoising as complementary techniques for reducing computational cost and visual noise.

The document concludes with accuracy and liability disclaimers, restrictions concerning product suitability and intellectual-property licensing, trademark notices, and a 2018 NVIDIA copyright statement.
Headphone views are shown; broken-line environmental features are excluded from the claimed design.
