The paper examines how the COVID-19 pandemic affected global education and how Comparative and International Education might help rebuild education systems while advancing the UN Sustainable Development Goals, particularly Goal 4 on inclusive, equitable, quality education and lifelong learning. Adopted in 2015, the 17 SDGs establish humanity’s collective vision for 2030; the Incheon Declaration expands Goal 4 into the global vision for education.

Despite decades of educational expansion, major shortfalls remained by 2020 in participation, quality, and equality. Before COVID-19, 258 million school-age children were not attending school. Education quality was deficient in inputs, teaching and learning processes, student outcomes, and post-school effects, while inequalities persisted by socioeconomic status, gender, race or ethnicity, and across education access, completion, certification, and employment. COVID-19 intensified these problems: school closures affected about 91% of students and the shift to distance learning reduced opportunities and quality, disproportionately harming disadvantaged learners and widening educational inequalities. South African survey findings illustrated losses of contact with teachers, inability to collect school fees, and failure to distribute homework.

At the same time, the pandemic accelerated the adoption of educational technology and presented an opportunity to pursue more equitable, inclusive, lifelong education. The paper argues that Comparative and International Education should assess technological responses in their system-specific and societal contexts and develop recommendations for using technology toward the 2030 education goals.

The field must also address its own weaknesses: unresponsiveness to new developments, the “black box syndrome,” limited indigenous theory, marginalization in universities, Northern Hegemony, and insufficient demonstrated influence on scholarship, classroom practice, system reform, or education policy. Using pandemic experiences, the field can help restore education, surpass pre-pandemic provision, and build stronger systems aligned with the 2030 agenda.

Closson sued to foreclose a materialman’s lien for $863.35 in lumber used to construct a residence on Marie Billman’s property. Contractor Levi Worley failed to pay for the lumber, and Closson signed a $1,500 bond with Worley conditioned on completing the residence according to their building contract.

The court held that the contract and bond must be construed together. Worley was required to furnish and pay for the necessary materials and deliver the residence free of materialman’s liens; therefore, his failure to pay for the lumber breached the bond despite completion of the house according to plans and specifications. Closson was a guarantor rather than a surety because his undertaking assured Worley’s performance of the principal contract. The answer stated a prima facie claim against Closson and was sufficient to avoid circuity of action. Because the guaranty was part of the original transaction, acceptance was unnecessary. Closson bore the burden of pleading and proving failure to receive notice of default and resulting damage. The judgment was affirmed.

Mesh shading moves object-list processing from the CPU to parallel GPU programs. VRS supports shading from once per 16 pixels to eight times per pixel, reducing unnecessary work and improving frame rate. Texture-space shading caches and reuses results, while MVR extends single-pass stereo to render multiple differently positioned or directed views in one pass.

Texas Tech officials briefly posted a written FAQ on new directives prohibiting faculty from speaking or teaching about transgender identity, then removed it after three days without explanation. The FAQ said “noncompliant language” meant outdated or inaccurate syllabus content, did not define gender identity, and omitted “transgender” from its answers. It stated that the directives did not affect independent research but applied to teaching.

Faculty could teach content relevant to students’ programs and career paths and facilitate discussion of the state’s position on gender alongside other views, but could not advocate for a viewpoint. Officials discouraged personal statements of LGBTQ allyship or student support and advised omitting personal-pronoun language, while allowing preferred-name policies on syllabi.

The guidance applied only to Texas Tech’s flagship campus. At other system campuses, faculty reported conflicting verbal instructions and were told to avoid terms including “transgender,” “gender-affirming care,” “diversity, equity and inclusion,” and “affirmative action.” Health-care faculty raised concern that students might not be prepared for transgender-patient care included in certification exams. The Texas AAUP opposed the policies, arguing that universities should protect faculty’s constitutional rights to teach and research without censorship and develop free-speech policies with faculty participation.

This continuation application describes map-based route planning for vehicles, particularly automated guided vehicles (AGVs). A scheduling system obtains a target vehicle’s start location and destination, a map containing nodes and node information, and motion-status information for other vehicles in the region. Vehicle motion status may be classified as static when its location remains unchanged over a period and moving when its location changes.

The system modifies map-node information to account for other vehicles. For static vehicles, nodes in a preset region around each vehicle may receive high weights, disabled turning, or impassable/barrier status. For moving vehicles, nodes along portions of their planned routes that remain ahead may also be assigned high weights. The resulting candidate or target map is used to select available start and destination nodes and calculate a route through node-based total costs.

Disclosed route-planning methods use open and closed node sets, binary-heap selection of minimum-cost nodes, and iterative expansion of reachable adjacent nodes. Costs can include node weight, distance, and turning cost, with a Manhattan-distance estimate to the destination; other algorithms identified include A-star, modified A-star, Dijkstra, Floyd-Warshall, Bellman-Ford, and RRT. One process first plans around static vehicles and, if the route overlaps a moving vehicle’s route, modifies the map further and replans. The disclosure also describes a route-planning system containing a server, network, vehicles, terminal devices, storage, and processing modules for obtaining locations and maps, monitoring motion status, and determining routes, with potential task allocation to idle AGVs.

The passage sets out U.S. policy toward the Soviet Union for 1983. It urges firm arms-control standards—real reductions, military equality, verifiability, stability, and warheads as the principal START unit of account—and identifies the USSR as impeding progress. On regional issues, the U.S. should test Soviet intentions on Afghanistan, expand U.S.-PRC dialogue, seek a Kampuchean settlement, press for Cuban withdrawal in Namibia/Angola, warn against unacceptable actions such as MiG deliveries to Nicaragua, and avoid Middle East dialogue that could restore Moscow’s role. It should pursue Soviet human-rights improvements through private diplomacy while promoting democracy in Poland and the CSCE. Economic steps must not strengthen Soviet military power, subsidize the Soviet economy, or undermine broader strategy; a Joint Commercial Commission session could address trade pressures. Reciprocal bilateral steps, including a possible umbrella cultural agreement, could broaden access to Soviet society. Dialogue should proceed through summitry, ministerial meetings, ambassadorial contacts, and specialist talks between the State Department and Soviet MFA. The overall aim is to protect U.S. security interests and encourage Soviet concessions while holding Moscow responsible for continued tensions if it refuses the stated criteria.

W. T. Hay was discharged from debts after bankruptcy. Before bankruptcy, he conveyed real estate to his brother, who then conveyed an interest to Hay’s wife, Matilda M. Hay. Deposit National Bank later executed a judgment against Hay and levied on that property, alleging that the conveyance was made to hinder creditors. Hay sought a stay of the execution, but the lower court declined to stay it as to the levied property. The Supreme Court affirmed and dismissed Hay’s appeal because he had no ownership interest in or claim to the property, had not listed it among his bankruptcy assets, and was not aggrieved by the sale. If the conveyance was fraudulent, the property would belong to the bankruptcy trustee; otherwise, title remained in Matilda Hay. Questions concerning the bank’s enforcement rights and the effect of the sale could be raised by her, not Hay.

The case examines the National Women’s Soccer League’s development, Lisa Baird’s first year as commissioner, and the league’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic. It traces the NWSL’s creation after the WUSA folded in 2003 after losing $90 million and the financially unstable Women’s Professional Soccer League ceased operations in 2012. Founded in 2013, the NWSL adopted a single-entity structure inspired by Major League Soccer. U.S. Soccer initially financed its operations, front office, and the salaries of national-team players allocated to NWSL clubs, while investors accepted that the league would lose money before becoming sustainable.

The case also describes unequal compensation between the U.S. women’s and men’s national teams. A 2017 collective bargaining agreement improved conditions for the USWNT, but players still filed a 2019 lawsuit alleging institutionalized gender discrimination and pay disparities. The dispute drew national attention to equal-pay issues in sports. Meanwhile, the NWSL faced limited media coverage, uneven attendance, and fan-engagement challenges. Its most committed supporters were highly active online, organized in team supporter groups, and quick to challenge the lack of recognition given to women’s sports.

Baird’s career included brand management at Procter & Gamble, leadership roles at General Motors, IBM, the NFL, and the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee, where she generated more than $1 billion in sponsorship and media agreements, and a position at New York Public Radio. She became NWSL commissioner on March 10, 2020. During her job interview, she emphasized developing sponsorships, media, licensing, and other revenue streams, building a larger staff, and establishing a distinct model for women’s professional sports.

Two days after the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic, Baird canceled the NWSL preseason. Concerned that losing an entire season could threaten the league’s stability, she organized workstreams covering medical protocols, financing, competition formats, host locations, players, childcare, and social justice. A federal Paycheck Protection Program loan helped the league pay non-allocated players and continue health insurance. The league also secured Google, Verizon, and P&G/Secret as sponsors. Medical criteria established a phased progression from individual training to small-group and then full-team training.

The resulting Challenge Cup was held near Salt Lake City from June 27 to July 26, 2020, making the NWSL the first U.S. professional sports league to resume play. Eight teams participated after Orlando Pride withdrew because of COVID-19 cases, and players could opt out. More than 500 players, coaches, and staff were tested three times weekly under strict operating, travel, and sanitization protocols. The tournament produced no positive tests among more than 2,000 tests and cost $1.8 million. CBS broadcast the games with virtual fan representations, and the opener drew a then-record 572,000 viewers; the final, won 2–0 by the Houston Dash for its first championship, attracted more than 650,000 viewers. Players also used the platform to support racial justice, including allowing Black Lives Matter messaging and collective demonstrations during the national anthem.

Baird subsequently used CBS programming opportunities created by the Mountain West Conference’s postponement of its football season to arrange a Fall Series. The 18-game competition ran from September 5 to October 17, with the nine teams divided into three regional pods and continuing the medical protocols established for the Challenge Cup. Players associated with local businesses competed for the Verizon Community Shield, and grants went to Portland’s Mimi’s Fresh Tees, the Houston chapter of the NAACP, and DC SCORES. Despite concerns about another outbreak, several players opted out, while some USWNT and non-allocated players went to European clubs.

Entering 2021, Baird’s priorities included expanding and engaging the fan base, adding Racing Louisville and Kansas City for 2021 and Angel City FC and Sacramento for 2022, developing a rebrand for the league’s tenth anniversary, and defining its relationship with U.S. Soccer following the league’s December 2020 separation. The league increased allocation money to $400,000, and Portland signed USWNT players Lindsey Horan and Crystal Dunn directly, demonstrating the tradeoffs between player security and salary controls. Another Challenge Cup was held from April 9 to May 8 before the regular season began May 15. In 2020, television viewership rose 493% from 2019, social-media mentions increased 152%, and traditional-media mentions rose 55%. The league ended Baird’s first year with higher ratings, new sponsors, expansion plans, greater social-justice visibility, and negotiations to begin with the NWSL Players Association for a long-term collective bargaining agreement aimed at attracting and retaining elite players while ensuring league sustainability.

Cu-doped NiO thin films were fabricated on ITO-coated glass by 1.5-minute spray pyrolysis at 450 °C using a 7 wt% copper chloride precursor, alongside undoped NiO. XRD, FESEM, UV–Vis, Raman, photoluminescence, and electrical measurements assessed their properties and LPG sensing. Cu incorporation retained the cubic NiO (111) structure, increased lattice parameters from 4.18 to 4.20 Å, and reduced crystallite size from 21 to 20 nm. Raman peak shifts, PL quenching and broadening, and enhanced visible absorption indicated structural disorder and additional defect states. The direct optical bandgap narrowed from 3.70 to 3.65 eV. Under approximately 1 vol% LPG, Cu-doped films showed a larger current increase and lower resistance than undoped NiO. At 5 V, gas sensitivity increased from 1.3 for NiO to 1.8 for NiO:Cu. The results indicate that Cu doping improves charge transport, surface reactivity, and LPG sensing performance through structural and electronic modifications.

This passage is an excerpt from AMD AGESA/AGESATM BIOS core software documentation describing PEI/DXE components, build integration, host-environment services, entry procedures, and required call-outs.

**PPIs and PEIM/DXE components:** `AMD_PEI_INIT_EARLY_PPI` is published after `AmdInitEarly` returns and early processor core initialization completes, usable as a callback trigger or dependency. `AMD_PEI_INIT_POST_PPI` is published after `AmdInitPost` completes, and an `AMD_MEMORY_INFO_HOB` is published at that time for boot modes other than `BOOT_ON_S3_RESUME`, reporting available system memory through memory range descriptors. `AMD_MEM_INIT_PPI` signals that main memory initialization completed and is used internally to notify `AmdProcessorInitPeim` to perform post-memory clean-up; system memory is not generally usable until the standard `EfiMemory` PPI is posted. One PEIM performs post-reset initialization, calling AGESATM core entry points to initialize memory subcomponents and publishing `AmdInitPostPPI` on success. Another PEIM coordinates reset requests from the northbridge, southbridge, and processor PEIMs, issuing a warm reset if any requested one or otherwise publishing the reset-is-complete PPI. The `AmdCpuDxe` driver performs late initialization, calling `AmdInitLate` to generate data tables used by other drivers and publishing `AgesaDxeProtocol` (from `AmdCpuDxeDriverInit`) so other drivers can access and update tables during POST. `AmdGpuVgaControlDxe` monitors `PciIo` protocol requests and enables VGA decoding for the processor iGPU only when the host requests it.

**Build and integration:** The `\Addendum` directory contains reference files (`Cpcar32.asm`, `<Plat>Options.c`, `<Plat>RecoveryOptions.c`) that are not intended to be included in builds; the Options/RecoveryOptions files are copied into the platform tip build directory, which is also the target of `vcproj` build output. UEFI control files under `\UEFI` include `AgesaPei0Libs.inf`, `AgesaPei1Libs.inf`, and `AgesaDxe0Libs.inf`. The AGESA build requires environment variables `AGESA_ROOT` (full path to the directory containing `AGESA.h`, including trailing `\`) and `AGESA_OptsDir` (full path to the platform tip build directory). Integration steps include copying `<plat>Options.c`, creating `OptionsIds.h` with the desired IDS support, setting the environment variables, generating the doxygen documentation (`arch2008.chm`), and enabling CAR before `AmdInitReset` using the "ByHost" allocation method. The host must not modify SS or ESP while CAR is enabled and must not modify cache controls (MTRRs) from reset through final return from `AmdInitPost`. Two build methods are described: Binary Modules (AMD-distributed source and control files, "indirect," routed through a common entry point) and Source Integration (host integrates source and builds a ROM with its own tool set). Platform solutions are identified by code names such as "Danube" and "Maranello," with build customizations set through `<plat>Options.c` and build configuration elements.

**Stack (CAR) procedures:** Native assembler, "stackless" macros using a register-passing model apply to x86-64 APUs; AArch64 APUs with the Platform Security Processor (PSP) do not use the stack and very early macros because the PSP initializes DRAM. `AMD_ENABLE_STACK` initializes the processor and cache, allocates pre-memory stack space per core, maps it to global address space, sets MTRRs, and creates a `UEFI_SEC_PEI_HAND_OFF` instance in the stack frame; EBX is preserved for use as a stackless return address, and it returns `AGESA_SUCCESS`, `AGESA_WARNING` (stack re-entry), or `AGESA_FATAL` (unknown processor family). `AMD_DISABLE_STACK` is executed once by the BSP when main memory becomes available, flushing caches and disabling CAR mode. The very early macro must precede `AMD_ENABLE_STACK` and entry into 32-bit mode.

**Service functions:** `AmdCreateStruct`/`AmdReleaseStruct` allocate and release storage for AGESA parameter blocks using `PreMemHeap`, `PostMemDram`, or `ByHost` allocation (the host must pre-allocate and ensure sufficient space, with `StdHeader` used as the base). Other services include `AmdReadSpd`, `AmdGetDataEye` (bitmap of 31 elements of 32 bits, normalized to the 1D trained center), `AmdGetApicAddress` (x86-64 only), `AmdGetPciAddress` (per-die base PCI address), `AmdGetExeSize` (pre-memory execution cache size), `AmdIdentifyCore` (socket/die/core), `AmdGetFruAddress` (maps an address to DIMM, chip select, bank, row, column for FRU identification), `AmdMergeMmioRange`, and `AmdReadEventLog` (reads the oldest entry from a circular buffer).

**Entry procedures:** `AmdInitReset` performs minimal processor initialization; the BSP initializes the primary non-coherent HyperTransport link and returns for a recovery-mode test, while APs wait for BSP commands, and up to three execution cache regions are allocated under rules including 32-KByte alignment, no spanning the 1-MByte or 4-GByte boundaries, and at most two regions above 1 MByte. `AmdInitEarly` performs full processor initialization (BSP: full coherent and non-coherent HyperTransport init, power management configuration, warm-reset request if needed; APs: power management configuration). `AmdInitPost` locates, initializes, and brings system memory online; the BSP transfers HOBs and artifact data out of pre-memory cache into a main-memory buffer and disables the pre-memory stack, while APs perform directed memory initialization, halt, set MTRRs, clear execution-cache MTRRs, disable processor cache, and set Top-of-Memory. Later procedures allocate permanent buffer space for UEFI HOBs and artifact data and move that data into host-controlled memory, perform display/graphics configuration after PCI enumeration but before the video BIOS call, and `AmdInitLate` generates OS-facing informational tables (DMI, ACPI IVRS, PState, WHEA-MCE, WHEA-CMC, ACPI ASL library, CRAT, CDIT), with the BSP ensuring a known-good power state and APs setting final registers and PState. Suspend/resume entry points save critical registers to the SMM save area at Ready-To-Boot, re-initialize silicon and memory from `NvStorage` on resume, restore processor state from `VolatileStorage` after PCI control structures are re-established, and perform a final re-initialization just before OS handoff.

**Required host-environment call-outs:** `AgesaAllocateBuffer` allocates post-memory buffers (checking `HeapStatus` for `HEAP_RUNTIME_SYSTEM_MEM`, mappable to `EfiACPIMemoryNVS` or `EfiRuntimeServicesData`), `AgesaDeallocateBuffer` releases them, `AgesaReset` performs cold or warm reset (the `BiosRstDet[2:0]` bits are reserved for AGESA), `AgesaLocateBuffer` returns a handle's address and length, `AgesaReadSpd` reads DIMM SPD data over SMBus with block read recommended (not used by newer Family 17h/21h APUs with PSP), and `AgesaRunApTask` runs code on a specific AP by APIC ID or on all APs, tied to `AmdLateRunApTask`. Status codes include `AGESA_SUCCESS`, `WARNING`, `ERROR`, `FATAL`, `ALERT`, `UNSUPPORTED`, and `BOUNDS_CHK`.

Best Buy is offering $220 off the Lenovo Legion 7i Gen 10, reducing its price to $1,650. It features a color-accurate 2,560 × 1,600 OLED screen, a 165-Hz refresh rate, and a 115-watt RTX 5060. While the keyboard and trackpad are excellent, battery life falls below five hours.

The Jerusalem Post requests $5 monthly support to remain accessible without a paywall, offering an ad-light experience, Premium content, a Hebrew-learning magazine, the Jerusalem Report, and an ePaper.

Amazon.com, Inc. submitted a Form 8-K dated February 1, 2018, announcing its fourth-quarter 2017 and year-ended December 31, 2017 financial results. The filing includes a press release announcing the results (Exhibit 99.1) and information about non-GAAP measures in Amazon’s public disclosures (Exhibit 99.2). It was signed by Brian T. Olsavsky, Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer.

Toronto van attack suspect Alek Minassian, 25, appeared in court and was charged with 10 counts of first-degree murder after driving a rental van into pedestrians, killing 10 and injuring 15. Authorities said the attack did not change Canada’s threat level or security preparations for the June G7 summit. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau urged Canadians to remain united and keep each other safe.

U.S. airlines recorded their lowest cancellation, mishandled-baggage and passenger-bumping rates in decades last year; cancellations fell to 1.17%, while on-time arrivals rose to 81.4%. Complaints declined 11.3%, and Hawaiian ranked first for on-time flights among 12 major carriers.

Improving farmers’ conditions requires broad, practical education, training in executive abilities and the dignity of labor, and cooperation through organizations such as the Grange. Voluntary action should lead, but government should assist through farmers’ associations and coordinate federal, state, and educational agricultural efforts. Institutes and dairy, breeders’, and horticultural associations have advanced farmers, while federal cooperation has organized responses to the boll weevil and cattle fever tick. Irrigation and forest preservation benefit the Rocky Mountains and Great Plains, while White Mountain and Southern Appalachian forests also require state and national action.

The passage supports constructing a memorial amphitheater at Arlington for Memorial Day observances and honoring soldiers and sailors buried there. It also favors placing marriage and divorce under national authority to address conflicting state laws and abuses, and urges federal authority to prohibit polygamy.

Oregon Health & Science University researchers reported limited progress toward creating functional human eggs using somatic cell nuclear transfer. Their technique produced three healthy mice from eggs containing adult skin-cell DNA in 2022, but has mostly failed with human cells. The team developed “mitomeiosis,” a process for reducing chromosome number, but substantial refinement is needed before clinical testing. Researchers see potential applications in infertility treatment, preventing heritable diseases and enabling same-sex couples to have genetically related children.

A study of 19 mothers and their babies, aged four months to two years, found that mothers released more dopamine while watching videos of their own children. Higher dopamine release was associated with sensitive, responsive caregiving and adjusting behavior to infants’ needs, while less-responsive mothers showed lower dopamine responses.

Researchers said dopamine may motivate caregiving, continue influencing mother-child bonds as children grow, and support nurturing relationships generally. They also said responsive caregiving is important to infant brain development.

The findings build on rodent research and earlier work linking mother-infant bonding to oxytocin. Published online in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the study was small and could not determine whether strong maternal bonding predates childbirth. Similar effects in fathers and other non-biological caregivers require further research.

This paper reviews the effects of trauma and adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) on postsecondary students and examines trauma-informed care (TIC) in health professions education, particularly occupational therapy (OT). Trauma may affect attendance, concentration, memory, communication, emotional regulation, social relationships, academic performance, and school persistence. Studies of OT students found that many had experienced trauma before or during OT education, and 93% of participants reported effects on sleep, social participation, and education. Fear of stigma often prevented students from disclosing their experiences to educators.

The literature search covered peer-reviewed studies and reports published mainly from 2015 onward, using PubMed, Google Scholar, and the American Journal of Occupational Therapy. The review describes SAMHSA’s six TIC principles—safety, trustworthiness and transparency, peer support, collaboration and mutuality, empowerment, voice and choice, and recognition of cultural, historical, and gender-specific issues—and its ten implementation domains. These include leadership, workforce development, collaboration, financing, physical environment, engagement, screening and referral, quality assurance, policy, and evaluation.

The paper identifies gaps in OT curricula, noting that few programs include trauma education and that TIC content remains limited. Simulation-based training through the PATH model improved students’ trauma knowledge and self-efficacy, while health and wellness coaching was presented as a possible way to strengthen coping and resilience. Recommended educational practices include faculty training, predictable and flexible instruction, advance notice of potentially triggering content, classroom check-ins, clear communication, peer support, self-care instruction, positive feedback, culturally responsive and inclusive teaching, universal design, and simulation-based learning. The paper concludes that TIC may help OT educators create safer, more supportive learning environments and improve student well-being, engagement, retention, and academic success.

The June 8, 2001 issue of National Journal’s CongressDailyAM reports:

- House appropriators proposed FY2002 allocations largely aligned with President Bush’s budget but exceeding his requests for Labor-HHS, VA-HUD, and Energy and Water. House leaders said they would support Bush’s nearly $7 billion FY2001 supplemental request, despite demands for additional defense spending, and warned that the president might veto a larger bill.
- House Republicans said Democratic control of the Senate would have limited effect on House politics. They planned to pursue energy, prescription drug, campaign finance, tax, patients’ rights, and trade legislation before the August recess. Gephardt and other Democrats maintained that Republican leaders continued to reject meaningful bipartisan cooperation.
- Republican Rep. Steve Largent announced plans to resign his Oklahoma House seat in November to run for governor and asked state officials to schedule an early special election. His departure will create the seventh House special election of the year.
- Rep. Asa Hutchinson’s expected departure for the Drug Enforcement Administration left his business-liability legislation without its chief House sponsor. Its prospects were further complicated by the Senate’s shifted balance, though bipartisan support for small-business reforms could still help.
- Labor Secretary Elaine Chao scheduled ergonomics forums and a September policy decision. Republicans praised the effort, while Democrats urged Chao to issue a new workplace rule.
- FDA officials warned that about two million mailed parcels containing regulated products enter the United States annually, overwhelming inspection capacity. They cited risks of contaminated, ineffective, or counterfeit drugs and called for tighter controls on reimportation.
- The House Energy and Commerce Committee remained open to generic-drug patent reforms in a Medicare drug bill, despite opposition from brand-name manufacturers and concerns from Rep. Henry Waxman.
- European officials expressed concern that Bush’s steel-import investigation could disrupt the upcoming U.S.-EU summit. They also opposed U.S. “unilateralism,” defended continued Kyoto Protocol negotiations, and said an announcement on a new trade round would be premature.
- Senate Republicans and Democrats continued negotiating an organizing resolution and assurances for rapid consideration of Bush’s nominees. Republicans dropped filibuster threats and hoped to finish the agreement by Tuesday.
- Bush nominated Jo Anne Barnhart for Social Security commissioner. Republican members of the Census Monitoring Board also released a report supporting the 2000 census’s accuracy and questioning statistical sampling.
- Airlines announced voluntary customer-service commitments intended to become contractual, while Rep. John Mica scheduled a hearing to evaluate their progress. House Republicans introduced the National Monument Fairness Act, requiring public and state input on large presidential monument designations and congressional approval within two years.
- The issue also listed congressional floor actions, hearings, markups, and events for the week, covering energy policy, pharmaceuticals, the District government, military and environmental appropriations, nominations, death-penalty disparities, census oversight, science legislation, aviation, campaign finance, fisheries, and other matters.

AMC Entertainment Holdings (AMC) faces management proposals to double authorized shares to 1.1 billion, risking further shareholder dilution. Despite recent debt refinancings, net debt remains above $3 billion, with weak Q3 box office revenue, ongoing losses, negative equity, and persistent cash burn leaving AMC trading at a steep discount to peer CNK. The pandemic severely hurt the theater business as attendance plunged and releases were delayed. The article is written by a part-time trader and Seeking Alpha contributor educated at Lehigh University (Finance and Accounting), focused on long/short equities, and includes standard disclaimers stating the author holds no positions, receives no compensation beyond Seeking Alpha, and that content is general information rather than investment advice. The remaining material consists of unrelated Seeking Alpha article headlines, charts of a stock price ranging roughly 2.80–2.99 over October 6–10, 2025, and box office headlines noting Taylor Swift's album release party topping the domestic weekend with $33M and 'One Battle After Another' debuting at $22.4M, along with a Swift–AMC promotional film distribution tie-up.

The passage argues that BBC Panorama’s “Saving Syria’s Children” may be fabricated, citing disputed injuries, inconsistent victim counts, and widely varying times for the alleged attack. It questions the BBC team’s chronology and the political connections of the medical personnel shown, notes that professional simulations can create more convincing injuries, and calls the evidence for fakery undeniable. It also raises broader concerns about possible BBC-medical collusion in narratives supporting Western intervention.

Malaria rapid diagnostic tests commonly detect Plasmodium falciparum through PfHRP2 and PfHRP3. Deletions in the pfhrp2/3 genes can produce false-negative results, with reported false-negative rates reaching 80% in heavily affected settings. By 2023, WHO maps documented these deletions in 40 of 47 surveyed countries. Non-HRP2-based tests offer alternatives but generally have lower sensitivity, and no WHO-prequalified Pf-pLDH combination test is available for countries that must distinguish P. falciparum from P. vivax.

This study used an individual-based P. falciparum transmission model to assess the selection and spread of pfhrp2 deletions. It incorporated malaria prevalence, microscopy use, treatment seeking, diagnostic testing, adherence to RDT results, RDT brands, HRP3 cross-reactivity and parasite fitness costs. WHO Malaria Threat Maps data were used to estimate linkage between pfhrp2 and pfhrp3 deletions, while Bayesian fitting to Eritrean and Ethiopian surveys jointly estimated fitness and cross-reactivity parameters. An ensemble machine-learning model derived from transmission simulations was used to predict selection rates in other settings.

Two risk measures were developed. The Innate Risk Score estimates how quickly deletions would spread once established, assuming reliance on HRP2-based RDTs; it classifies regions by the time needed for misdiagnosed clinically relevant infections to rise from 1% to 5%. The Prospective Risk Score incorporates current deletion prevalence, current RDT use and assumed geographic spread from neighboring regions. Simulations assumed that deletion prevalence and treatment conditions would remain constant.

Analysis of WHO data found that 63.5% of pfhrp2-deleted samples globally also had pfhrp3 deletions; the African estimate was 61.2%, with a normalized linkage disequilibrium coefficient of 0.762. Model fitting estimated relative fitness of 96.4% for pfhrp2-deleted parasites and a 29.0% probability that infections containing only pfhrp2-deleted parasites would still test positive because of HRP3 cross-reactivity. Malaria prevalence was the strongest determinant of selection, particularly below 20% prevalence.

Under the Innate scenario, at least one first administrative region in 73 of 106 modeled countries was predicted to reach 5% misdiagnosis within 20 years. Twenty countries had a majority of their regions classified as high risk; all but Solomon Islands, Papua New Guinea and Guyana were in Africa. Eritrea, Ethiopia, Zambia and Tanzania contained regions consistently classified as high risk, whereas many high-transmission regions in Central and West Africa were predicted to have low or marginal risk. Very-low-transmission regions appeared most susceptible but also had highly uncertain, stochastic trajectories that could include strain fade-out.

Under the Prospective scenario, 29 of 49 modeled African countries had at least one region predicted to reach or already exceed 5% misdiagnosis within 20 years. If HRP2-based RDTs remained dominant, deletions were predicted to spread south from the Horn of Africa through East Africa and increase in West Africa, particularly Senegal and Mali. Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Senegal, South Sudan, Sudan, Kenya, Tanzania, Zimbabwe and Zambia had majority shares of regions classified as high prospective risk.

The findings indicate a substantial threat to HRP2-based malaria diagnosis and support prioritizing molecular surveillance, particularly in Senegal, Zambia and Kenya, and considering alternative or combination RDTs. The authors caution that results are constrained by uncertain prevalence estimates, limited and inconsistent surveillance, uncertain fitness estimates, simplified parasite-movement assumptions, constant future transmission and treatment conditions, and an equilibrium assumption for pfhrp2/pfhrp3 linkage. More longitudinal data are needed to refine predictions and clarify non-RDT-mediated evolutionary pressures.

Researchers combined somatic cell nuclear transfer, fertilization, and the molecule roscovitine to produce human eggs from adult skin cells. Some developed into early embryos after the cells began shedding excess chromosomes, but none had correct chromosome sets or were viable. The team is working to improve chromosome division; the technique remains inefficient and risky, requires donor eggs, and may take at least a decade to reach clinical trials. It could eventually help women with infertility and possibly allow same-sex male couples to have children genetically related to both partners.

The lecture models a protein backbone as a mechanical linkage with fixed edge lengths and fixed bond angles, allowing portions of the chain to rotate about edges. It distinguishes the protein-folding problem—determining the three-dimensional shape of a given chain—from protein design, which seeks a chain that folds into a specified shape.

Four linkage problems are introduced: span, the maximum and minimum distance between endpoints; flattening, the existence of a non-self-intersecting planar configuration; flat-state connectivity, whether all planar configurations are mutually reachable; and locked chains, which cannot escape some configurations.

Minimum and maximum span restricted to flat configurations are NP-hard through reductions from partition. The corresponding unrestricted three-dimensional problems remain open, although orthogonal chains admit a linear-time maximum-span algorithm. Determining whether a fixed-angle chain has a flat, non-self-intersecting state is also NP-hard. Flat-state connectivity is known for orthogonal and obtuse chains and for chains with equal acute angles, but remains open for arbitrary open chains and fixed-angle trees. Locked examples exist for chains with equal edge lengths and angles, but the combined equilateral, equiangular, and obtuse case remains open.

The lecture then presents a ribosome-inspired model of producible protein chains. A chain is produced link by link from a cone representing the ribosome; outside the cone it may not self-intersect or penetrate the cone. A canonical configuration is defined that places the chain within a narrower cone. By canonicalizing configurations and reversing the production process, the lecture proves algorithmically that all producible configurations lie in one connected component. Flat states are also producible, so producible chains are flat-state connected, and motions can be found between states. This is proposed as a possible mechanical model for efficient protein folding, while the actual biological folding mechanism and several related questions remain unresolved.

A July 31, 2001 IEP News email assembled reports on California’s electricity crisis, long-term power contracts, financial conflicts among Gov. Gray Davis’s energy advisers, utility bankruptcies, public-power proposals, electricity refunds, and deregulation developments in other states.

A Los Angeles Times commentary by State Controller Kathleen Connell and economist Peter Navarro argued that the Davis administration’s $43 billion in long-term power contracts would burden California with billions in unnecessary costs and debt. It attributed the state’s $8 billion in short-term purchases to a flawed deregulated market and contracts negotiated at peak prices. It said cooler weather, conservation, reduced demand and federal price caps—not the contracts—had improved conditions, and called for public review of major energy decisions and preservation of the Public Utilities Commission’s rate-setting authority.

The Los Angeles Times reported that the SEC had begun a preliminary inquiry into whether Davis’s energy consultants used inside information to trade in power-company stocks, following a request from Republican Secretary of State Bill Jones. Five advisers had been fired over possible conflicts; four owned Calpine stock and one owned Enron shares. Davis spokesman Steve Maviglio also disclosed a $12,000 Calpine investment and ownership of Enron stock, while legal-affairs secretary Barry Goode disclosed that he had recently held Williams stock. Separately, consultants Chris Lehane and Mark Fabiani agreed under a lawsuit settlement to forgo state compensation and leave Davis’s administration.

Salon reported that Davis was trying to arrange a state bailout for insolvent Southern California Edison, which claimed nearly $4 billion in debt. An August 15 legislative deadline was approaching while the Assembly remained in recess, and efforts to reconvene for a vote failed. Competing bills differed over state acquisition of transmission lines, Edison’s responsibility for losses and the state’s financial role. The article highlighted Davis’s ties to Edison, which had contributed more than $350,000 to his campaign and over 35% of the $1 million he had raised from utilities and energy companies. Critics included consumer advocates, legislators and Republicans who preferred bankruptcy or opposed a bailout. It also noted criticism that the state’s long-term contracts favored fossil-fuel generation over renewables.

Two November ballot measures would give San Francisco voters a role in replacing PG&E with public power, either through a municipal utility district covering San Francisco and Brisbane or a city-run water and power agency. PG&E spent more than $200,000 opposing the proposals. Supporters cited blackouts, rate increases, PG&E’s bankruptcy and state-budget pressures; a Public Policy Institute of California poll found nearly two-thirds of Californians supported replacing private utilities with local public authorities. Opponents argued the measures would not solve supply shortages and could raise costs.

Federal regulators limited California’s potential electricity refunds to just under $4 billion, less than the roughly $9 billion sought by the state. FERC’s order covered purchases made only since October 2000 and excluded power bought directly by the Department of Water Resources. Davis planned to appeal, and an evidentiary hearing was ordered to determine the final amount.

Reports described high wholesale prices, demand, transmission problems, limited Northwestern hydroelectric power and aging-plant maintenance as factors in the crisis. Southern California Edison and PG&E said they had lost nearly $14 billion since June 2000. PG&E filed for bankruptcy protection on April 6, prompting the state to begin buying power for nearly nine million customers and later for San Diego Gas & Electric. Approved average residential increases were 37 percent for the heaviest users and 38 percent for commercial customers, with increases of up to 49 percent for industrial customers and 15–20 percent for agricultural customers. California and natural-gas companies also accused El Paso Corp. of restricting gas deliveries to raise California prices.

Other reports said Maryland regulators were reviewing Constellation Energy Group’s proposed separation of Baltimore Gas and Electric because BGE would carry $2.4 billion in debt while rates remained frozen through 2006. Texas was beginning a deregulation pilot in which up to 5 percent of customers could choose new providers, ahead of statewide deregulation scheduled for January 1.

Gas colic results from gas produced during hindgut fermentation failing to pass through the large colon, causing distension and pain. Although common, it can lead to complications including displacement or twisting of the colon. Contributing factors include inadequate forage, stall confinement, reduced hindgut motility, stress, ulcers, intestinal inflammation, dehydration, insufficient exercise, and abrupt feed changes.

The passage emphasizes constant access to forage, as horses are grazing animals, and recommends pasture turnout or other outdoor activity to promote motility and reduce stress. Slow feeders can keep hay available and encourage calm, self-regulated eating. Feed changes should be gradual: hay transitions take about a week, while new commercial feeds may require two to three weeks. Prebiotics may support microbial adjustment, and unfamiliar bran should not be fed only occasionally. Suggested supplements include B vitamins, yeast or yeast culture, and colostrum. The article also recommends limiting inflammatory ingredients such as sugar and soy and noting that many fortified feeds contain both.

Newark police seek help locating nine suspects in seven unsolved crimes dating to June 2016. Guillermo Borges is wanted for shooting and wounding a man on Broad Street; three men are suspected of an armed grocery robbery. Other cases include taxi-driver and other armed robberies and a shooting. Tips may be submitted through Crime Stopper lines, NewarkPD.org, or the police app; they are confidential and may earn rewards.

Asus launched the Zenfone 5Z in India at ₹29,999 (6/64GB), ₹32,999 (6/128GB), and ₹36,999 (8/256GB), available exclusively through Flipkart from July 15. It features a 6.2-inch notched FHD+ display, Snapdragon 845, Android Oreo, rear fingerprint sensor, dual rear cameras, and a 3,300mAh battery with fast and AI charging. Offers include ICICI card discounts, no-cost EMI, Flipkart protection, and Jio cashback and data benefits.

In *People v Helzer*, the Michigan Supreme Court held that sexual delinquency is an alternate sentencing provision, not an element or penalty enhancement of the principal offense. Conviction on the principal charge may occur without proving sexual delinquency, but a sexual-delinquency conviction requires a separate hearing with proof beyond a reasonable doubt.

Unless the defendant waives a jury trial, a second, separately empaneled jury must decide sexual delinquency after conviction on the principal charge. Because that charge carries a possible life sentence, the defendant is entitled to 20 peremptory challenges for the second jury; the initial jury receives only the challenges appropriate for the principal charge. The sexual-delinquency charge must be included in the original indictment or information, although pre-trial amendments are permitted. After the principal trial begins, the prosecution waives the right to charge sexual delinquency. The principal jury must not be informed of the charge, and leakage of the charge requires a mistrial or reversal.

The court found no error in Helzer’s gross-indecency trial and affirmed those convictions, but remanded for a separate-jury hearing on sexual delinquency if the prosecution pursued the charge, with 20 peremptory challenges. It declined to address the defendant’s constitutional claims at that stage. Chief Justice Kavanagh dissented, concluding that the sexual-delinquency statute was unconstitutional because it was vague.

Tesla reported that underwriters exercised their full option to purchase $127.5 million of additional 2.375% Convertible Senior Notes due March 15, 2022. Tesla issued the option notes on March 30, 2017 under a supplemental indenture. It also entered into additional note hedge transactions, paying approximately $26.6 million, intended generally to reduce dilution and offset potential conversion-related cash payments above the notes’ principal. Tesla issued additional warrants permitting purchase of approximately 0.8 million common shares at $655 per share, subject to adjustment, and received approximately $6.9 million from their sale. The warrants are separate from the notes, may be cash-settled at Tesla’s election, and confer no rights on noteholders.

NVIDIA’s Turing GPU architecture introduces GDDR6 memory, real-time ray tracing, AI acceleration, and new rendering and display technologies. Turing was the first architecture to use GDDR6, operating at 14 Gbps with 20% better power efficiency than Pascal’s GDDR5X. Its redesigned interfaces, signal training, clock gating, package design, and board-level signal-integrity work reduced crosstalk by 40%. TU102 includes 6 MB of L2 cache, twice GP102’s 3 MB, while improved memory compression and higher raw bandwidth produce roughly 50% greater effective bandwidth on TU102-based RTX 2080 Ti than on GP102-based 1080 Ti.

Turing’s display engine supports DisplayPort 1.4a, 8K at 60 Hz, DSC 1.2, USB-C, native HDR processing, and BT.2100 tone mapping. It can drive two 8K displays at 60 Hz. Its enhanced NVENC unit supports 8K H.265 encoding at 30 fps and provides up to 25% HEVC and 15% H.264 bitrate savings, while NVDEC adds HEVC 4:4:4 8/10/12-bit and VP9 10/12-bit HDR decoding. Turing also supports VirtualLink, allowing VR headsets to receive power, display data, and tracking data through one USB-C connector.

For SLI, TU102 and TU104 use second-generation NVLink instead of MIO or PCIe links. TU102 has two x8 links and TU104 one, each providing 25 GB/s per direction; TU102 supports two-way SLI but not three- or four-way configurations.

Dedicated RT Cores accelerate bounding-volume-hierarchy traversal and ray-triangle intersection testing, freeing streaming multiprocessors for other graphics and compute work. Turing supports hybrid rendering, using rasterization for visibility and ray tracing for selected reflections, refractions, shadows, and other effects. Combined with denoising and efficient BVH structures, RT Cores deliver more than 10 Giga Rays per second and about ten times Pascal’s software-based ray-tracing performance. Ray-traced shadows, ambient occlusion, and reflections can replace conventional shadow maps, screen-space ambient occlusion, and screen-space or cubemap reflection techniques.

NVIDIA RTX also includes NGX, a Tensor-Core-accelerated deep-learning stack with pre-trained services for games and applications. Deep Learning Super-Sampling (DLSS) reconstructs high-quality target-resolution images from lower-resolution rendering, providing quality similar to temporal anti-aliasing with roughly half the shading work; DLSS 2X approaches 64-times-supersampled quality. Combined with Tensor Cores, DLSS enables the RTX 2080 Ti to achieve twice the performance of the GTX 1080 Ti. Other NGX features include AI Inpainting, AI Slow-Mo, and AI Super Rez, which can enlarge images or video by 2x, 4x, or 8x and perform real-time 1080p-to-4K upscaling.

Mesh shading adds cooperative task and mesh shader stages, allowing many objects to be processed without individual CPU draw calls. This can increase real-time object counts by more than an order of magnitude and supports dynamic level-of-detail selection and geometric cutaways. Variable Rate Shading controls shading independently of visibility in 16×16-pixel regions, enabling content-adaptive, motion-adaptive, and foveated rendering. Texture Space Shading decouples appearance sampling from visibility, stores results in texture space, and reuses them across frames, pixels, or stereo views. Multi-View Rendering supports up to four hardware views per pass and up to 32 views through the API, enabling efficient stereo, shadow, character, and multi-view rendering. Turing also adds bindless constant-buffer and unordered-access views and Tier 2 resource heaps.

Turing further improves VR through VirtualLink, Multi-View Rendering, Variable Rate Shading, and RT-accelerated audio. The TU104 GPU contains 3,072 CUDA Cores, 368 Tensor Cores, and 48 RT Cores, with one x8 NVLink link. TU106 lacks NVLink and SLI and contains 2,304 CUDA Cores, 288 Tensor Cores, and 36 RT Cores. The Tesla T4 uses a reduced TU104 configuration with 2,560 CUDA Cores, 320 Tensor Cores, a 256-bit memory interface, and 320 GB/s bandwidth.

RTX-OPS is presented as a workload-based metric combining tensor, FP32, RT-core, and INT32 operations according to their expected utilization: 20%, 80%, 40%, and 28%, respectively. The RTX 2080 Ti example produces a total of 78 RTX-OPS.

The American Cancer Society recommends regular colorectal cancer screening for average-risk adults beginning at age 45, using either a high-sensitivity stool-based test or a structural exam based on preference and availability. The qualified recommendation reflects limited direct evidence in ages 45–49; screening at age 50 and older remains a strong recommendation. Options include annual FIT or HSgFOBT, mt-sDNA every three years, colonoscopy every 10 years, CT colonography every five years, and flexible sigmoidoscopy every five years, with no option prioritized. Positive non-colonoscopy tests require timely colonoscopy follow-up.

The change is supported by increasing colorectal cancer incidence among younger adults, microsimulation models, and evidence that younger cohorts will retain elevated risk as they age. Average-risk adults in good health with life expectancy over 10 years should continue screening through age 75; decisions should be individualized from ages 76–85, and screening should be discouraged after age 85.

European wholesale prompt power prices fell as stronger wind supply and easing demand curbed trading, while forward contracts tracked lower coal prices. German and French baseload prices declined 16% and 20%, respectively; gas and oil prices rose.

The University of Manchester Students’ Union launched Earth Week with a panel featuring Friends of the Earth campaigner Asad Rehman and Campaign Against Climate Change’s Martin Empson. Rehman linked climate change’s disproportionate impact on poorer countries with migration, arguing that climate refugees deserve legal protection and that richer nations share responsibility for emissions and injustice. Empson urged support for environmental and migration campaigns through protests, petitions, contacting MPs, donations, and cooperation to strengthen their voices and create hope.

American Girl will release its first male doll, Logan Everett, Thursday as part of a new contemporary series. The drummer character sells for $115, or about $140 with accessories and a book. American Girl will also revive Felicity Merriman and release filmmaker Z Yang and World War II-era Hawaii doll Nanea in 2017.

Canada’s Privacy Commissioner opened a formal investigation into Uber’s 2016 breach, which exposed data from more than 57 million riders and drivers. Uber reports no evidence of misuse but has not disclosed how many Canadians were affected. The commissioner cannot fine companies but may seek Federal Court orders requiring compliance.

Quantum spin relaxation in radical-pair systems is relevant to quantum computing, spintronics, quantum biophysics, molecular qubits, organic semiconductors, and avian magnetoreception. Modeling two electron spins coupled to many nuclear spins is challenging because initial room-temperature nuclear configurations require ensemble averaging, Hilbert and Liouville spaces grow exponentially, and nanosecond-to-microsecond relaxation requires stable long-time propagation. Monte Carlo sampling addresses configuration averaging, while classical nuclear-spin treatments can approximate high-field or many-nucleus systems but may be inaccurate for significant non-Markovian hyperfine relaxation.

The work introduces tensor-network methods to spin chemistry, presents the radical-pair problem and its computational challenges, and showcases avian magnetoreception. The radical-pair Hamiltonian includes Zeeman, hyperfine, exchange, dipolar, and Haberkorn singlet/triplet relaxation terms, while electronic-state populations are calculated from ensemble-averaged evolved states.

A stochastic matrix product state representation uses spin-coherent sampling and an automatically constructed matrix product operator, reducing wavefunction storage from exponential \(O(d^N)\) to \(O(Ndm^2)\). Deterministic matrix product density operators avoid large stochastic ensembles and can be implemented through direct vectorization or locally purified tensor networks. Density-operator scaling is reduced from \(O(d^{2N})\) to \(O(Nd^2\chi^2)\), although Liouville-space growth and specialized superoperator techniques remain challenging.

A cave rescue expert described the Thai rescue of 12 boys and their soccer coach, missing for nine days in the flooded Tham Luang Nang Non cave, as among the toughest he has seen. The team was found alive about 1.2 miles inside the cave but weak from nine days without food, with water and a doctor and nurse available.

The expert said rescuers must often wait before acting because the trapped people may be alive and safe, while unnecessary risks could endanger rescuers. During flooding, teams can monitor water and weather, divert or pump water, search for alternative entrances, and in some cases use divers to make contact or supplies.

Three main escape options were considered: teaching the boys to dive through tight, dark passages; drilling an entrance; or waiting for monsoon floodwaters to recede. Each carries major difficulties, including novice diving, difficult drilling and mapping, and potentially weeks of flooding. If the group’s location remains safe and they can receive food and care, they may need to remain underground until conditions improve.

Terry Rozier scored a career-high 31 points with seven rebounds as the injury-shortened Boston Celtics beat the Atlanta Hawks 119-110. Jayson Tatum added 27 points, Jaylen Brown scored 19, and Al Horford had 17 points and seven assists. Boston turned a one-point halftime deficit into a 19-point third-quarter lead. Taruean Prince led Atlanta with 31 points and eight rebounds, while Dennis Schroder scored 25.

Kyrie Irving missed his second straight game with a right quad contusion and will reclaim his starting spot when available. Boston had only 10 players suited up, while Atlanta lost DeAndre’ Bembry to injury. Prince was selected for the Rising Stars game, and Boston’s reported signing of Greg Monroe remains unannounced.

President-elect Donald Trump drew attention after criticizing the cover photo of CNN’s book *Unprecedented*, calling it the worst photo of himself while saying he hoped the book did well. CNN promoted a different commemorative 2017 edition. The episode followed other widely noticed Twitter activity, including his brief follow of “Emergency Kittens,” his claim that Hillary Clinton’s campaign knew it would lose after canceling election-night fireworks, and his retweet of a New Year’s montage featuring Ivanka Trump. Users responded with awkward Trump images and comments mocking his concern as vain and distracting from presidential matters. The featured image shows Trump speaking at a Las Vegas rally in January 2016.

Bank of Japan sources say policymakers are unlikely to tighten policy quickly because low inflation persists and a sharp yen appreciation could weaken Japan’s export-driven recovery. The bank’s money printing has depreciated the yen, and officials fear yen spikes could follow signals of normalization. Meanwhile, the Fed, ECB and Bank of England are leaving easing cycles, leaving the BOJ further behind with limited tools to counter recession. Despite strong growth, high job availability and pressure from financial institutions, the BOJ may modestly raise yield targets next year without launching a full rate-hike cycle. Some policymakers want inflation above 1%, while Kuroda’s April succession and Prime Minister Abe’s priorities add uncertainty. The bank is slowing bond and ETF purchases but could deepen negative rates or bankroll government debt if economic shocks emerge.

The Arizona Supreme Court held that A.R.S. § 13-4033(B) prohibits a defendant in a noncapital case from directly appealing a contested post-judgment restitution order entered pursuant to a plea agreement that provided for restitution up to a specified cap. Such defendants must seek review through Rule 32 post-conviction relief proceedings.

Frank Hoffman pleaded no contest to DUI and agreed to pay restitution up to $53,653.45. After a contested hearing, the court ordered $40,933.45 in restitution. The superior court dismissed his direct appeal, and the court of appeals declined special action relief. The Supreme Court affirmed.

The Court concluded that a post-judgment restitution order is part of the “sentence” for purposes of § 13-4033(B). This interpretation advances the legislature’s goal of limiting direct appeals after plea agreements, avoids a bifurcated system of appellate review, and accords with restitution’s statutory and customary role in sentencing. Although § 13-4033(A)(3) generally permits appeals of post-judgment orders affecting substantial rights, subsection (B) is an exception for orders entered pursuant to plea agreements. Hoffman’s challenge to the amount did not remove the order from the agreement because the amount remained within the agreed cap. Rule 32 proceedings provide the constitutionally required route for appellate review. The Court disapproved two appellate decisions to the extent they conflicted with this interpretation.

This medRxiv preprint describes a blood-based test for detecting primary glial malignancies (GLI-M) and differentiating them from benign brain tumors, epithelial cancers with brain metastases, and nonglial CNS malignancies. The test enriches viable circulating glial cells from peripheral blood using a proprietary medium and identifies them by multiplexed immunocytochemistry based on GFAP and OLIG2 expression.

Analytical validation showed a detection limit of 1 cell per 5 mL, an overall quantification limit of 6 cells per 5 mL, marker-specific sensitivities of 92.5% for GFAP and 95.0% for OLIG2, and 100% specificity. Samples could be stored at 2–8°C for up to 48 hours with no more than 15% cell loss.

In blinded case-control and prospective studies, the test generally achieved 100% sensitivity and specificity, although one of 31 cases in a prospective cohort was missed, yielding 92.9% sensitivity. Across all cases, the authors reported sensitivity above 99% and 100% specificity. FISH testing of matched blood and tumor samples from 44 patients showed 100% concordance for EGFR status. The assay does not detect rarer tumors such as CNS lymphoma or gliosarcoma and is not intended to determine tumor subtype or grade. The study was funded entirely by Datar Cancer Genetics; several authors were company employees and one was its founder.

Apple Inc.’s Form 10-Q for the fiscal quarter ended December 25, 2021 reported net sales of $123.945 billion, up 11% from $111.439 billion a year earlier. Product sales were $104.429 billion and services sales were $19.516 billion. Gross margin increased to $54.243 billion, or 43.8% of sales, and operating income rose to $41.488 billion. Net income was $34.630 billion, with diluted earnings per share of $2.10.

Revenue increased for iPhone, Mac, Wearables, Home and Accessories, and Services, led by Mac at 25%, Services at 24%, Wearables at 13%, and iPhone at 9%. iPad sales declined 14%. By geography, net sales rose in the Americas, Europe, Greater China, and Rest of Asia Pacific, while declining in Japan.

At December 25, 2021, Apple reported $381.191 billion of assets, $309.259 billion of liabilities, and $71.932 billion of shareholders’ equity. Cash and cash equivalents totaled $37.119 billion, and marketable securities totaled $165.477 billion. Operating activities generated $46.966 billion of cash, investing activities used $16.106 billion, and financing activities used $28.159 billion.

Apple repurchased $20.4 billion of common stock and paid $3.7 billion in dividends and dividend equivalents during the quarter. It had $40.5 billion remaining under its $315 billion repurchase authorization and declared a quarterly dividend of $0.22 per share. Manufacturing purchase obligations totaled $47.6 billion, primarily noncancelable.

The company reported continued pandemic-related operational effects, including supply shortages, while stating that available cash, operating cash flow, and debt-market access should meet its requirements over the next 12 months and beyond. It also disclosed the Epic Games antitrust litigation, effective disclosure controls, no material changes in risk factors or market risk, and no changes in internal financial reporting controls that materially affected or were reasonably likely to materially affect them.

U.S. stock futures edged higher before the Federal Reserve’s interest-rate decision and Janet Yellen’s statement, with economists widely expecting a 1-to-1.25-point rate increase. Dow, Nasdaq-100 and S&P 500 futures gained 0.12%, 0.16% and 0.06%, respectively, amid average options volume. Apple CEO Tim Cook confirmed the company’s autonomous-vehicle plans. Tesla options volume rose after reports about a five-star Model X crash rating and a call for its stock to reach $1,000. Micron recovered following a bullish Macquarie Research note.

Carleton University in Ottawa is hiring an Allan Slaight Chair to establish a research and teaching program on magic, perception and deception, including why people are gullible to fake news and political persuasion. The five-year renewable post, potentially leading to tenure, is backed by a $2 million matching grant from the Slaight Family Foundation for the salary, graduate hires, travel to magic archives and a digital archive linking worldwide information on magic. About 80 applicants have applied, and an announcement is expected that summer. In a University of London experiment, 120 participants were shown a card trick; 87% detected its duplicate-card mechanism when there was no feigned swipe, compared with 60% after seeing an empty hand. Researchers said people who construct an explanation may become locked into it and rationalize tricks they cannot immediately explain.

Apple Inc. filed a Form 8-K on July 31, 2018, reporting its financial results for the third fiscal quarter ended June 30, 2018. The filing attached Apple’s press release as Exhibit 99.1 and related data sheet as Exhibit 99.2, and was signed by CFO Luca Maestri.

Adam Henrique and Travis Zajac described the Kings as a deep, fast, physical team that cycles pucks, controls play, rolls all four lines, and features puck-moving defensemen and strong goaltending. Their own team started nervously and tentatively, gave away too many pucks, and struggled to forecheck, but improved later by playing more aggressively. Zajac said they must get pucks behind the Kings’ defense, generate traffic and shots, retain possession, and improve execution. Henrique expected the physical play to intensify during the finals and said his return after missing most of the year has added leadership and depth.

A hockey player credits his father, Patrick Kane, and supportive coaches for his development. Playing for Buffalo’s strong OHL team is exciting; he enjoys both setting up and scoring goals, can play either wing or center, and will do whatever benefits the team. After choosing the OHL over college, he remained in contact with Don Harkins, a great supporter and fan. Playing for Buffalo would be special, especially with the hope of bringing the city its first cup.

U.S. stocks rallied after President Trump’s November election on expectations of tax cuts, infrastructure spending and deregulation, but gains in several “Trump trades” slowed after his inauguration.

- **Hospital stocks:** Fell 7.1% from election to inauguration, then recovered 4.1%. Fears of immediate repeal of the Affordable Care Act drove the initial decline; difficulties passing healthcare legislation prompted the recovery.
- **Infrastructure stocks:** Rose 13% before inauguration and 2.4% afterward. Trump’s proposed $1 trillion infrastructure package and regulatory reforms supported the sector, but no package has materialized and implementation may be difficult.
- **Banks:** Gained 20.8% before inauguration and 3.1% afterward. Expectations of deregulation, economic growth, inflation and higher interest rates fueled the rally, while slowing loan growth and doubts about congressional action tempered gains.
- **Small-cap stocks:** Rose 12.6% before inauguration and 5.3% afterward. Broad tax cuts, including a proposed 15% corporate rate, continued to support the Russell 2000, though doubts about Trump’s legislative prospects and concerns that foreign-policy involvement could distract from his domestic agenda weighed on performance.

Former U.S. senator and former Anchorage mayor Mark Begich entered Alaska’s governor race as the lone Democratic candidate, prompting fears that he and independent incumbent Bill Walker could split the vote and help Republicans win. Begich said he would not run unless he thought he could win, while the Democratic Party insists it can prevail in a three-way race.

Walker and running mate Byron Mallott will bypass the primary and gather signatures, preserving their 2014 unity-ticket arrangement. The ticket followed Walker’s departure from the Republican Party and alliance with Democratic nominee Mallott.

Republican state Sen. Mike Dunleavy, an early favorite in the Aug. 21 primary, supports deeper deficit cuts, school choice and full oil-wealth fund dividends. Libertarian William “Billy” Toien is also running. Begich criticized Walker and lawmakers for focusing on budget details rather than a broader vision for Alaska and supports constitutional protection for the dividend formula. Voter reactions were mixed, with some praising Walker’s political courage, others backing Begich because of dissatisfaction with Walker, and others remaining undecided.

The Sixth Circuit affirmed Dr. Howard W. Ellzey’s convictions for conspiracy and eleven substantive counts of illegally distributing controlled substances. Evidence showed that Ellzey prescribed amphetamines to brief “diet” visits, allowed individuals to obtain duplicate prescriptions through two offices, and wrote 29,000 of the 39,000 Schedule II prescriptions surveyed in Memphis, nearly all for amphetamine-type drugs. The court found substantial evidence supporting the convictions and rejected Ellzey’s challenges to the admission of his prescriptions, jury instructions, and use of “distributing” rather than “dispensing.” His sentence included concurrent three-year terms, probation on one count, and $18,000 in fines.

The Nov. 23, 2001 Energy Central Direct daily edition presents 85 selected electric-power articles and gas-industry headlines. Lead stories cover federal restrictions on Southern Co.’s wholesale rates, E.ON’s planned U.S. acquisitions, FERC efforts to expedite hydro relicensing, and Los Angeles retaining its stake in a Nevada power plant.

Much of the issue focuses on Enron’s financial collapse and California’s electricity crisis. Enron reported progress on debt repayment but lost a quarter of its value for a second consecutive day as FERC expressed concern, traders reduced dealings, and Dynegy sought to accelerate its acquisition. California developments included rulings against preferential treatment of electricity buyers, adequate supply despite a worsening budget crisis, consumer concerns over a potential $84 million CARE cut, and the PG&E bankruptcy.

Other coverage addresses power prices, regulation, transmission, generation projects, mergers, nuclear and environmental issues, renewables, workforce concerns, and international energy developments. The edition also includes Restructuring Today coverage, a CAL ISO load forecast, advertisements, and subscription information.
