Natural zircon single crystals from Australia’s Mud Tank deposit were shock-compressed near [100] to 13.6 and 51.3 GPa and analyzed using X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, Raman and infrared spectroscopy, cathodoluminescence, and photoluminescence. Simulations estimated residual heating of 21°C and 182°C, respectively, although temperatures were likely overestimated because the zircon–reidite transition was omitted from calculations.

At 13.6 GPa, the sample was strongly fractured but retained crystalline zircon, with no definitive evidence of a bulk phase transformation; minor reidite domains could not be excluded. Reddish, lower-intensity cathodoluminescent patches near fractures indicated increased structural defects, possibly associated with shock damage or partial transformation through an intermediate phase.

At 51.3 GPa, zircon transformed predominantly into textured, mosaic reidite, with weak residual zircon concentrated near fractures. The observed orientation relation was (112)reidite ∥ (200)zircon. Cathodoluminescence became about six times weaker and shifted toward blue emission near 430 nm. Rare-earth-element lines became stronger relative to broad-band emission, and splitting of Dy³⁺ lines indicated at least two local ionic environments. Bright yellow, 2–10 μm speckles, commonly associated with crystallographic planes, were attributed to rare-earth ions segregated on dislocations and planar defects.

The rapid segregation occurred without prolonged annealing and may result from reconstructive transformation-induced charge imbalance and release of trace ions into interstitial positions. Vacancy-assisted transport or movement along defects and boundaries may contribute, but the mechanism remains unresolved. No ZrO₂ phases were detected. The transformation may therefore alter trace-element distributions while leaving zircon and reidite isotopic characteristics and trace-element ratios approximately similar, and extensive fracturing may facilitate later release of segregated elements upon interaction with fluids or melts.

The patent application is a continuation in a series of related ladar transmitter patents and incorporates several prior disclosures by reference. It describes a ladar transmitter and receiver in which a laser source, optics, beam scanner, and transmission optics direct pulses toward selected range points, while the receiver processes reflections to determine range, intensity, and spatial position. Shot lists, environmental sensing, and pre-scan compression can reduce bandwidth demands.

The disclosure addresses the cost, size, weight, power, bandwidth, eye-safety, noise, and limited-range shortcomings of conventional ladar systems. It introduces an optical field splitter/inverter that divides and inverts a scan field so that fast scan regions move toward the field edges and slower regions toward the center, thereby increasing dwell time, revisit frequency, and capacity for interline skips in desired areas. Embodiments include W-shaped reflectors, a triangular prism, paired scanning mirrors, overlapping fields, adjustable hinges, and ray-traced reflective regions.

For resonant Lissajous scans, which conventionally revisit field edges more densely than the center, the disclosure adds a slowly induced periodic phase drift to one or both mirrors. The drift can be selected using total least squares and singular value decomposition to reduce gaps in a designated gaze region without reducing the base scan’s revisit rate.

The disclosure also presents an ellipsoidal conjugate reflector positioned between two scan mirrors. By optically reimaging the beam between mirrors located near the ellipsoid’s foci, the design permits smaller, similarly sized mirrors, a more compact scanner, and potentially greater scan speed, tilt angle, and field of view. A coplanar-angle design constraint produces a planar reflected ray fan and limits scan-field distortion.

A June 5, 2001 email compilation detailed California’s electricity and natural-gas crisis, citing high demand, rising wholesale prices, transmission bottlenecks, scarce hydroelectric power, and maintenance and equipment failures at aging plants. PG&E and Southern California Edison had lost nearly $14 billion since June 2000 and could not pass those costs to consumers under deregulation. After PG&E filed for bankruptcy on April 6, California began purchasing power for PG&E, Edison, and San Diego Gas & Electric, with rate increases approved to finance those purchases.

President Bush opposed federal wholesale electricity price caps, while Democratic politicians and consumer advocates argued that temporary cost-based limits were needed because California’s market lacked effective competition. Rep. Doug Ose proposed extending a FERC emergency pricing order across the 13-state West, pegging spot prices to the cost of the least efficient generating plant; Democrats warned this could facilitate price manipulation. Ten economists said price restraints could prevent withholding and encourage supply, and a Washington Post-ABC poll found 56% of respondents favored limits. A state Senate committee received approval to subpoena eight power companies—including Enron, Dynegy, Williams, Duke, Mirant, AES, NRG, and Reliant—about bidding and pricing, while also considering demands for information from state agencies.

Electricity production was expected to improve as plants returned from spring maintenance, with all existing facilities scheduled to operate by mid-June. Nevertheless, observers said inadequate generation and expected peak demand of more than 45,000 megawatts meant blackouts remained likely. Planned outages had fallen from 9,800 megawatts to about 4,144 megawatts, in addition to roughly 2,673 megawatts of forced outages. San Onofre Unit 3 returned to operation with 1,120 megawatts of capacity, while repairs at AES’s Huntington Beach plant faced delays. Californian consumers reduced electricity use 11% overall and about 10% during peak hours in May, and the state began rebates for customers cutting consumption by at least 20%. GWF Energy also signed a 10-year contract to supply up to 430 megawatts, with initial deliveries planned from a 90-megawatt plant in September.

Political disagreement over the crisis intensified as Gov. Gray Davis and the Bush administration blamed each other, with commentary describing “victims and villains” stereotypes portraying Texans as greedy and Californians as careless. Experts said the crisis had roots across both parties and that most California generators were not Texas-based oil companies. Bush assigned FERC member Patrick Wood III to investigate, and FERC faced criticism for insufficient staffing, data gathering, and enforcement of “just and reasonable” prices.

PG&E creditors approved $17.5 million in management bonuses contingent on filing a reorganization plan by January. PG&E separately sued, claiming regulators’ allocation of consumer revenue shortchanged it by $2.2 billion and could require additional rate increases. Southern California Edison mounted a $3 million shareholder lobbying campaign for a bailout under which the state would purchase its transmission lines for $2.7 billion, prompting objections from legislators. San Diego Gas & Electric sought $915 million in rate recoveries, with the largest increases applying to heavy electricity users.

Other companies and projects faced scrutiny or policy disputes. Chevron warned that its Richmond and El Segundo refineries would reduce gasoline production if they were not exempted from rotating blackouts, potentially raising fuel prices. Critics said San Jose’s proposed support for Calpine’s 600-megawatt Metcalf plant was too generous because the city would finance most of a $50 million pipeline extension while Calpine would reimburse only $10 million. Supporters cited new monitoring, park funding, and reduced freshwater use.

Natural-gas constraints also contributed to electricity prices. About 85% of California’s gas arrived from outside the state, pipeline capacity was constrained, and gas-fired plants generated nearly half the state’s electricity. Regulators scrutinized alleged market manipulation by El Paso and Southern California Gas, disputed claims about storage and trading, and considered disclosure requirements and renewed price limits. The “Frontline” documentary “Blackout” portrayed the crisis as a national deregulatory experiment and highlighted Enron’s role as an intermediary earning billions in daily trading volume.

The White House blocked congressionally approved funding for the Council of Inspectors General on Integrity and Efficiency, effectively shutting down the federal oversight office after midnight Tuesday. The move was separate from the broader congressional funding dispute and prompted condemnation from Senate Republicans urging its reversal.

- The Dec. 31, 2001 collection examines Enron’s collapse and related corporate, regulatory, investment and energy issues. Enron’s failure was widely viewed as a consequence of pressure to meet lofty earnings expectations, expansion into unfamiliar markets, misleading information to Wall Street and questionable partnerships. Its $68 billion peak valuation in August 2001 implied 91% annual free-cash-flow growth for six years. Nortel experienced a similar cycle, spending more than $32 billion on 19 acquisitions as its stock rose and then fell more than 99%. Fuller and Jensen argue that companies should resist earnings “guidance,” disclose strategies, value drivers and auditable metrics, and address stock overvaluation openly.

- Bandwidth trading largely collapsed with Enron and the telecommunications downturn. Excess fiber-optic capacity, slower Internet growth and telecommunications companies’ reluctance to trade a core product left little liquidity. Enron-inspired expansions by El Paso, Williams and Dynegy were threatened by the market’s disappearance, and a recovery in bandwidth prices appeared distant.

- Large write-offs can signal deteriorating finances and should not automatically be dismissed as one-time events. Bethlehem Steel took a $1 billion deferred-tax write-off and filed for bankruptcy three months later. S&P 500 companies reported more than $165 billion in unusual charges in 2001, while public-company bankruptcy filings through mid-December reached 241, compared with 176 for all of 2000. A six-year study found stocks with the largest charges relative to sales had a median 9.4% decline over the following 90 days, versus a 1.48% gain for stocks with the smallest charges. The use of adjusted “pro forma” earnings instead of GAAP figures drew criticism for obscuring warnings. At Home and Lucent posted large charges that preceded serious financial trouble, while Providian’s legal charge preceded falling revenue, rising credit losses and severe stock declines.

- Enron became a test of SEC Chairman Harvey Pitt, whose less confrontational enforcement approach differed from that of Arthur Levitt. Pitt assigned roughly six attorneys and accountants to the investigation and described it as a priority for “real time” enforcement. The case could force him to recuse himself because Arthur Andersen, Enron’s auditor, was also under investigation and had been a client of his law firm. Congressional hearings and investigations were expected, while Pitt’s policy of considering corporate cooperation when deciding penalties drew criticism.

- Warning signs of corporate distress included rising credit-default-swap costs, declining bond prices, withdrawal of bank credit lines, breaches of debt-to-earnings covenants, large debt payments approaching and the hiring of bankruptcy counsel or restructuring advisers. Enron’s credit-default spreads rose well before its share price collapsed; bonds trading below 40 cents on the dollar were described as a strong indication that filing was imminent.

- A Vanguard survey of 500 401(k) participants found muted near-term stock-return expectations but unrealistically optimistic long-term forecasts. Investors expected an average 7% annual stock return over one or two years, yet the median long-term forecast was 15%, compared with historical annual returns of 10.7% since 1926. Respondents also underestimated company-stock risk, and financial planners cited in the article generally advised limiting employer-stock holdings to 5% of a 401(k).

- Polaroid sought bankruptcy-court approval for retention payments to 45 executives, including a potential bonus for Chief Executive Gary DiCamillo of up to twice his nearly $850,000 prior-year compensation. The plan was defended as necessary to retain personnel needed to wind down the company and repay creditors, but it angered former employees who lost jobs, benefits and retirement money. Such bonuses had become common in Chapter 11 cases.

- Energy producers including Mirant, NRG and Dynegy delayed or reduced plant spending after Enron’s collapse and credit-rating downgrades. One forecast of new U.S. generating capacity was cut from 320,000 megawatts to 150,000–200,000 megawatts, while the Department of Energy estimated that at least 185,000 megawatts would be needed by 2010. Some industry participants expected further construction if demand materialized, while others viewed transmission shortages as a greater threat than insufficient generation.

- Commentary by Peter Navarro argued that the University of California’s portfolio managers should have sold Enron before its decline rather than holding the stock, and recommended broad index funds, sale of sharply declining individual holdings and use of any court-awarded damages to compensate Enron employees whose retirement savings were lost.

- American Electric Power acquired Enron Wind’s 160-megawatt Indian Mesa Wind Power Project in Texas for $175 million, assumed related long-term power-supply arrangements and retained Enron Wind for operations and maintenance. Separately, Credit Suisse First Boston resigned after one meeting of Enron’s 15-member unsecured creditors committee, citing the time burden and limited benefit of its $70.66 million exposure; Westdeutsche Landesbank replaced it. The committee proposed information barriers allowing members to trade Enron securities without improperly using nonpublic information.

- California Public Utilities Commission President Loretta Lynch said the state’s 1996 electricity deregulation plan lacked safeguards to halt a market meltdown and that document disputes delayed investigations into alleged manipulation by generators and traders. She described Enron as benefiting from a volatile market with little regulation.

- Year-end stock-award commentary recognized Enron and Providian as major losers, citing their collapses, while noting strong gains among retailers, security-software companies, REITs newly admitted to the S&P 500, and video-rental chains benefiting from DVD demand. Ford and Hewlett-Packard received a family-affair award, Philip Morris’s proposed Altria name change received a name-related award, and asbestos-exposed companies were noted for continued bankruptcy filings.

NASA researchers have proposed a theoretical plan to prevent asteroid Bennu from striking Earth on September 22, 2135, although the estimated impact probability is about 1 in 2,700. The Hypervelocity Asteroid Mitigation Mission for Emergency Response, or HAMMER, could use a nearly nine-tonne impactor to push Bennu from Earth’s path or a nuclear device to nudge it away. Although no such mission is being built, NASA engineer Brent Barbee says design studies could improve preparedness for threatening objects.

Past impacts show that even moderate space debris can injure people and damage property. The 1908 Tunguska event flattened 80 million trees, while a 2013 meteor injured 1,100 people. NASA’s Planetary Defense Coordination Office detects about 1,000 new objects annually and develops plans to deflect or destroy them.

Bennu offers scientists a well-studied test target. NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft is approaching Bennu to map it, determine its composition, collect a 2.1-ounce sample, and potentially gather data for developing a larger response craft.

The Citi Simplicity® Card offers a 0% introductory APR for 21 months on balance transfers and 12 months on purchases, followed by a variable APR of 17.99%–28.74% based on creditworthiness. It has no annual fee, late fees, or penalty APR and allows flexible payment dates for automatic payments. Balance transfers must occur within four months of account opening; the fee is 3% (minimum $5) during that period and 5% afterward. The recommended credit score is 670–850, though approval is not guaranteed. The card is aimed primarily at consumers seeking a lengthy interest-free period to pay down debt. Motley Fool discloses that it may receive compensation from partners and that Citi is an advertising partner, but says compensation does not influence its product ratings.

Party-list Rep. Lito Atienza filed House Bill 4758 to replace the MMDA with a Metropolitan Manila government headed by an elected governor. The proposed government would include a governor, vice governor and Metro Manila Council, elected by residents of Metro Manila’s 16 cities and Pateros, with council members representing congressional districts. Atienza said the appointed-chair structure lacks accountability and has been ineffective in addressing traffic, flooding, peace and order, and garbage problems, necessitating a permanent body and master development plan.

Manchester City overcame Burnley despite Fernandinho’s late first-half red card. Gael Clichy scored after the break, and substitute Sergio Aguero added the second from a tight angle; Burnley failed to equalize. The victory moved City to third, within two points of Liverpool, and renewed optimism in their title challenge. Fernandinho received a four-match ban, while City’s seven red cards in 30 matches under Pep Guardiola highlighted continuing disciplinary problems.

Eric Fung, 37, grew up in New York, studied advertising and public relations, then moved to Silicon Valley at 24 after rejecting corporate life. He joined a startup, co-founded a company in 2019, and later opened three restaurants while hiring managers to run them. Frustrated by California’s cost of living and what he saw as the fading Bay Area “magic,” he moved to Japan in 2024 for a fresh start.

In Tokyo, Fung founded Colega AI, a US-registered, remote-first company with seven staff, including three in Tokyo. He chose Japan’s large base of small businesses as a test market and works with a local partner to navigate language and cultural barriers. Adjusting to long hours and seniority hierarchies while fostering a flexible startup culture has been challenging. He and his wife Shana have also faced difficulty making friends, but they enjoy Tokyo’s safety, convenience, and lower housing costs, renting a Shibuya studio for about $1,350.

The Consumer Mortgage Coalition urged Treasury to let lenders use the National Directory of New Hires for income verification to avoid IRS-related mortgage processing delays. The proposal requires consumer consent and encrypted transmission to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac; the group also seeks congressional funding to modernize IVES.

CompareCards highlights changing credit-card offers featuring 0% introductory APRs lasting 12–21 months, which can reduce interest on balances or large purchases. It notes that consumers who pay balances in full and on time generally benefit, and lists cards from Discover, Bank of America, Citi, and Capital One. Featured benefits include rotating or selected-category cash back, first-year cash-back matching, statement-credit rewards, points, up to 5% travel rewards, flexible redemption, contactless cards, virtual cards, sign-up bonuses, and no annual fees on several products. Most cards charge variable APRs after the introductory period, while some impose balance-transfer fees, promotional limits, or category caps. The page also explains fixed versus variable APRs, notes that low-interest offers may provide substantial savings when normal APRs are high, and states that CompareCards objectively evaluates more than 100 cards from over 50 issuers. It discloses that the site receives compensation from listed companies but says this does not affect its ratings or reviews.
ESPN highlights the Cubs’ “Korean corn dog,” previews the Savannah Bananas’ 2026 selection show, and quotes Stephen A. Smith urging the Yankees to keep up in Game 4.

Sirius XM’s satellite cuts are projected to boost free cash flow ~20% by 2026, while cheap-share retirements improve per-share value and ROIC. The stock trades at ~7.6× EV/EBITDA versus 15× historically; an unlevered DCF suggests 2–3× upside, with 11–12% ROIC versus ~6% WACC.

NVIDIA’s GA10x Ampere architecture delivers up to 2× improvements in programmable shading, ray tracing, and AI over Turing while being up to 1.9× more power efficient. Its GA10x streaming multiprocessors feature dual-datapath FP32 processing, larger unified L1 and shared memory, four third-generation Tensor Cores, and one second-generation RT Core per SM. The full GA102 contains seven GPCs, 84 SMs, 112 ROPs, 384-bit memory, and 6,144 KB of L2 cache. Moving ROPs into GPCs improves raster, multisample antialiasing, pixel fillrate, and blending performance.

Second-generation RT Cores double ray/triangle intersection performance over Turing and support hardware-accelerated motion blur, including moving and deforming geometry. They can operate concurrently with graphics or compute workloads. Ray-traced motion blur can render up to eight times faster than on Turing, while an RTX 3080 measured up to five times faster than an RTX 2080 Super in a Blender Cycles test.

Third-generation Tensor Cores support FP16, INT8, INT4, TF32, and BF16, along with 2-out-of-4 fine-grained structured sparsity. Sparsity can double tensor throughput by skipping zero-valued elements, and TF32 provides up to five times the prior generation’s AI training throughput. Tensor Cores accelerate AI denoising, DLSS with up to 8K support, NVIDIA Broadcast, Canvas, and other AI applications.

GA10x GPUs introduce GDDR6X memory using PAM4 signaling, supporting rates up to 19.5 Gbps and peak bandwidth of 936 GB/sec. GDDR6X also adds Error Detection and Replay, which detects failed memory transmissions and retries them. The RTX A6000 and A40 each have 48 GB of GDDR6 memory and can scale to 96 GB using two GPUs connected with third-generation NVLink. NVLink provides four x4 links totaling 112.5 GB/sec between two GPUs.

PCIe Gen 4 doubles PCIe 3.0 bandwidth, offering up to 16 GT/s and 64 GB/sec peak bandwidth on a x16 slot. GA10x GPUs also support simultaneous compute and graphics operations.

NVIDIA RTX IO uses GPU-based lossless decompression and Microsoft DirectStorage to move compressed assets directly from NVMe SSDs to GPUs. It is described as accelerating I/O by up to 100 times versus hard drives and traditional storage APIs, reducing CPU utilization, shortening game loading times, reducing stutter and pop-in, and supporting high-rate texture streaming.

The NVIDIA A40 targets data-center visual computing, providing up to 2× FP32 throughput, 2× ray-tracing throughput, and 5× or 10× with sparsity for AI training and data science compared with the Quadro RTX 6000. It supports virtualization, Quadro Sync, NVIDIA EGX, and 48-to-96 GB memory scaling.

Ampere GPUs support 4K at 120 Hz and 8K at 60 Hz through DisplayPort 1.4a and HDMI 2.1. Fifth-generation NVDEC provides hardware decoding for MPEG-2, VC-1, H.264, H.265, VP8, VP9, and AV1, including 8K60 HDR AV1 playback with low CPU usage. Seventh-generation NVENC provides hardware encoding for H.264 through 4K and HEVC through 8K while reducing CPU load.

The GeForce RTX 3090 includes 24 GB of GDDR6X memory, 82 SMs, and 10,496 CUDA cores and is 1.5 times faster than the TITAN RTX. The RTX 3070 uses GA104, supports GDDR6X architecture but uses GDDR6 memory, lacks NVLink, and is described as faster than the previous-generation RTX 2080 Ti. The RTX A6000 includes 10,752 CUDA Cores, 84 second-generation RT Cores, and 48 GB of GDDR6 memory, with support for 96 GB through dual-GPU NVLink.

A computer-model analysis of the 2014–2016 West African Ebola epidemic found that about 3% of patients, termed “superspreaders,” caused roughly 61% of secondary infections, while the average patient infected 2.39 people. Transmission was limited in hospitals but substantial among people treated at home, where symptoms were often mistaken for other diseases and traditional funeral handling of infectious bodies spread the virus. Age also predicted superspreading, as caregivers of infants and older adults were especially exposed. Similar patterns occurred during SARS and MERS outbreaks. Ebola was ultimately stopped through safe burials and prompt hospitalization rather than vaccines or drugs.

The global automated fare collection (AFC) system market was valued at $4.81 billion in 2016 and is projected to reach $12.81 billion by 2024, with a 13.3% CAGR from 2017 to 2024. AFC automates public-transport ticketing, commonly through contactless smart cards, enabling faster transactions, shorter queues, easier revenue collection, and use of one card across transit modes. Growth drivers include technology adoption, new AFC applications, operational efficiency, accuracy, transaction security, and government investment; limited awareness and smart-card use are restraints. The market is segmented by component, application, technology platform, and geography. Major players include Advanced Card Systems, Atos, Cubic, LG CNS, NXP, Omron, Samsung SDS, Scheidt & Bachmann, Thales, and LECIP.

Bayhorse Silver Inc. increased its TSX-V-approved non-brokered private placement from up to 1.5 million to 3 million units at C$0.10 each, for gross proceeds of C$300,000. Each unit includes one common share and half a warrant exercisable at C$0.15 for 24 months. Existing shareholders may participate; proceeds will fund equipment, Bayhorse Mine operations, working capital and administrative costs.

The application describes non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) mechanisms for transmitting small uplink data in new radio while a user equipment (UE) is in RRC idle or inactive states, reducing state-transition overhead, latency, power consumption, and multiuser sequence collisions.

In conventional LTE, sending data from an idle UE requires a scheduling request, random access, authentication, access-stratum security establishment, and RRC reconfiguration. Control-plane small-data transmission can carry packets in NAS messages for MME security checks and forwarding, while user-plane transmission can preserve and later resume the RRC context. The passage also discusses LTE downlink multi-user superposition transmission and notes that Rel-14 did not address uplink NOMA.

For NR, a gNB may configure contention-based physical uplink shared channel resources as a configured-grant PUSCH (CFG-PUSCH) and broadcast their configuration through remaining system information. The broadcast information may specify resource allocations and NOMA parameters such as DMRS ports, multiple-access signatures, and interleavers. An idle UE may transmit small data through CFG-PUSCH while remaining idle or briefly entering connected mode, using an established NAS security context without AS security activation, bearer establishment beyond SRB1, or RRC reconfiguration. Procedures may include random-access preambles, contention resolution, timing advance, and CFG-PUSCH payloads containing UE identity, small-data and last-packet indicators, or NAS PDUs. An AMF may authenticate and forward the data to a gateway. An inactive UE may transmit immediately through configured-grant resources using its stored AS security context, without connecting, while transmitting an I-RNTI, requested cause, and data; random access may be used if uplink timing alignment must be restored.

To address collisions caused by random selection of preambles, DMRS ports, or multiple-access signatures, the application proposes UE-specific reference bits generated from low-correlation M-sequences, Gold sequences, or sparse sequences initialized using UE-specific and optional multiple-access identifiers. The reference bits and information bits may be jointly encoded with a systematic LDPC encoder. Reference bits can then be extracted and transmitted as a front-loaded preamble or DMRS, while information and parity bits undergo UE-specific interleaving, rate matching, modulation, optional spreading, and resource-element mapping. This arrangement supports UE-activity detection and channel estimation, can improve decoding, and avoids performance degradation caused by indistinguishable colliding preamble or DMRS transmissions.

Configured-grant NOMA may use spreading-, codebook-, or interleaver-based signatures, including sparse subcarrier-activation patterns, cell-specific signature pools, and mappings between DMRS ports and signatures. Multiple CFG-PUSCH resources may be configured for different payloads or transmission periods. DMRS length and port extensions, extended cyclic prefixes, guard periods, and reserved edge subcarriers may address multiplexing and asynchronous interference. NOMA may also be applied to PUSCH during random access, allowing UEs sharing preamble-associated resources to use different signatures and reducing contention. Receivers monitor CFG-RNTI-scrambled responses, retransmit after a negative acknowledgment or missed response, and may be directed to enter connected mode for retransmission. The disclosure further describes DRX paging, configured-grant activation in idle mode, and embodiments within 3GPP NR radio-access and core-network architectures.

Massachusetts lawmakers passed a supplemental budget with $15 million for schools serving students displaced by Hurricane Maria. More than 2,300 students from Puerto Rico have arrived since September, and funding will use the existing aid formula.

After passing an online “Jeopardy!” contestant test despite lacking trivia expertise, the author reflects on the unresolved biological basis of memory. The passage contrasts Lashley’s evidence for distributed memory storage with Penfield’s findings linking specific memories to localized brain regions. It also recounts UCLA experiments suggesting memory can be transferred by RNA in snails and earlier planarian experiments the author unsuccessfully tried to replicate. The author emphasizes that scientific questions can remain unsettled, particularly concerning learning, memory, and age-related memory loss.

The Tax Court reviewed an IRS determination allowing collection by levy of Robert Poindexter’s unpaid 1994 and 1996 income taxes. Poindexter, a songwriter, requested a collection due process hearing, claimed his returns were inaccurate because of a dispute over royalties, and asked the IRS to subpoena record companies, but he offered no alternative to collection and declined to file amended returns.

The Court rejected the IRS’s argument that a taxpayer may challenge underlying tax liabilities under section 6330(c)(2)(B) only when the IRS assesses an amount different from the amount reported. However, it granted summary judgment for the IRS because Poindexter’s petition failed to comply with Tax Court Rule 331 and raised no justiciable facts. He did not identify the disputed income, deductions, credits, or computations, provide evidence concerning royalties or copyright violations, or substantiate his claims of procedural errors and improper levies. No levies had yet been made. Thus, despite the Appeals officer’s error in refusing to consider the assessments’ accuracy, Poindexter had not established grounds to overturn the determination.

Acting CDC Director Jim O’Neill approved updated Covid-19 vaccine recommendations, allowing people older than six months to receive an updated shot after discussing risks and benefits with a provider. Insurance coverage remains, but the recommendation leaves prescription requirements unclear. Approval also lets states order updated vaccines for low-income children through the Vaccines for Children program; a delayed sign-off had left roughly 50% of participating children without access. O’Neill also approved separate MMR and chickenpox shots for children under four, replacing the combined vaccine.

Agent Mutual, owner of OnTheMarket.com, plans to float the third-largest UK property portal on AIM, raising £50 million to boost marketing, sales, customer relations and technology in its challenge to Rightmove and Zoopla. It has abandoned mutual status and signed long-term listing agreements with several agencies, while analysts said reaching the necessary scale remains a significant challenge.

Police seek witnesses to an alleged unprovoked assault on a father in Coed Bach Park, Pontarddulais, on 29 June. He was spat at, punched and kicked while his children watched. The two men were described as bare-chested and wearing a blue vest.

The court reviewed whether the insured’s records complied with burglary policies requiring records sufficient for insurers to determine accurately the amount of loss. The insured kept cash and payroll checks in a safe and recorded only their combined total of $2,922 on a scratch pad, without separately identifying the checks. Conflicting testimony about the notation was resolved in the insured’s favor when considering a directed verdict.

The court held that substantial, rather than absolute, compliance is required, but written records must permit determination of liability without supplying essential details from an interested party’s memory. Records for stolen cash need not be as extensive as those for merchandise, yet a mere total on an envelope was insufficient. Because the stolen funds included negotiable checks, records needed to identify each check sufficiently to permit claims against its drawer. The insured’s ability to recover $182 only by remembering two checks demonstrated the inadequacy of his records. The court therefore held that he breached the policy condition and reversed the judgment, directing dismissal of the complaint.

The Ninth Circuit affirmed the Tax Court’s judgment that Pacific Basin Manufacturing & Trade Co. owed income tax deficiencies for 1975 and 1976. The Delaware corporation manufactured jewelry in American Samoa and excluded sales to its Hawaii parent under 26 U.S.C. § 931(a). The IRS agreed the corporation qualified for the exclusion but ruled that § 931(b) made the proceeds taxable because they were received in the United States. The court held that “received” has its ordinary meaning and that receipt occurred when the parent’s checks were deposited in the corporation’s Honolulu bank account, when the corporation gained custody and control of the funds. It rejected the corporation’s argument that receipt should depend on its primary physical presence in American Samoa, as that interpretation would largely nullify § 931(b).

The study evaluates steady-state global variance reduction techniques (VRTs) and their interactions with population control techniques (PCTs) in time-dependent Monte Carlo neutron transport simulations. It examines implicit capture, Cooper–Larsen weight windows, CADIS, and FW-CADIS, alongside uniform and weight-based combing. These methods adjust particle counts and weights to improve statistical efficiency, but incompatible combinations can increase computational costs, exhaust memory, or reduce accuracy.

Two computational approaches were used. Shift, coupled with the deterministic DENOVO code, was tested on a pulsed iron slab; its time-dependent implementation supported spatial weight windows and mandatory weight-based combing. MC/DC, designed for scalable time-dependent transport, was tested on the supercritical and subcritical AZURV1 benchmarks and the moving-geometry 1D SCRAM problem. It supported delayed neutrons, moving geometries, dynamic weight windows, and both combing methods, but lacked deterministic coupling, so Cooper–Larsen windows were derived from preliminary Monte Carlo simulations. Performance was evaluated on the Lassen supercomputer using a figure of merit based on variance and runtime, with helper-simulation and compilation costs included.

In the Shift pulsed-slab test, FW-CADIS achieved the best average figure of merit among the tested VRTs, although its deterministic preprocessing costs limited the improvement; CADIS performed worse than analog simulation for the global tally. Static weight windows and mandatory weight-based combing may also have interfered with performance.

For supercritical AZURV1, Cooper–Larsen windows combined with uniform combing dramatically improved efficiency, and time-dependent windows performed better than static windows. Combining Cooper–Larsen windows with weight-based combing exhausted memory because resetting particle weights at census produced excessive splitting at the pulse edge. Implicit capture also performed poorly with uniform combing in both supercritical and subcritical tests.

In 1D SCRAM, population control greatly improved runtime and efficiency by stabilizing particle populations across time steps. Cooper–Larsen windows with uniform combing performed best, while implicit capture with uniform combing underperformed and Cooper–Larsen windows with weight-based combing again caused memory overload. Overall, the results show that properly matched VRTs and PCTs can make time-dependent simulations substantially more efficient, whereas incompatible combinations can severely degrade performance.

The article argues that language education should emphasize its central purpose: “language connects.” Low enrollment and program cuts, especially in German and French, highlight the need to reconnect language learning with this purpose and support recruitment, retention, and program viability. It proposes fostering “imagined communities,” in which students imagine themselves interacting authentically with target-language speakers, cultures, materials, and everyday situations.

The approach uses task-based instruction and requires instructor-created, plausible scenarios tailored to students and curriculum. Examples include planning a move abroad by finding an apartment, shopping for furnishings, navigating transit, finding food, and preparing for work or study. Activities, assignments, and assessments should be authentic, provide student autonomy, and include just-in-time vocabulary, grammar, cultural guidance, and scaffolding.

A yearlong study in two eighth-grade German classrooms reported deeper cultural and language learning, new ways of examining cultures, increased connection and community membership, and continued study beyond required years. Sustainability requires documentation, collaboration among instructors, and continual revision based on student needs and reflections. With planning, the approach can be adapted across K–16 settings, languages, and proficiency levels.

The National Endowment for the Humanities and First Nations Development Institute will each contribute about $2 million to competitive grants for tribal Native-language education, prioritizing effective immersion and language retention or restoration efforts. An advisory committee will guide outreach and proposal selection, with about 15 programs expected to be funded annually.

The May 3, 2001 Enron news digest covered:

- **Pompano Beach, Florida:** A public meeting was scheduled on Enron’s proposed power plant, while the City Commission was expected to vote on a zoning variance.
- **California electricity crisis:** A proposal would authorize the state to stop buying electricity above specified prices despite the risk of more blackouts. Proponents argued the boycott could pressure wholesalers and reduce costs, but economists said it was unlikely to succeed because prolonged blackouts would impose substantial economic losses. California was spending as much as $90 million daily on electricity, and officials estimated summer spending could exceed $1 billion weekly.
- **India’s Dabhol project:** Indian lenders asked the government to help resolve the dispute between Enron’s 65%-owned Dabhol Power Co. and the Maharashtra State Electricity Board over power pricing and unpaid bills. MSEB owed roughly $48 million, and Dabhol’s board had authorized management to stop selling power if no resolution was reached. A government panel formed to renegotiate the $2.9 billion project postponed its meeting with Dabhol until May 11 at the company’s request. DPC maintained that attending did not constitute an offer to renegotiate the contract.
- **Bush energy policy:** The Democratic National Committee accused oil and gas interests of influencing the administration’s energy agenda, citing donor contributions, regulatory rollbacks, proposed drilling, reduced conservation funding and the composition of Bush’s energy transition team. It maintained that the policy prioritized energy-industry interests and a clean environment.
- **European power trading:** British utility Innogy began wholesale trading between France and Italy and was preparing to enter Germany. France emerged as a potentially central market, while Innogy planned to emphasize trading services rather than acquiring physical assets.
- **Mosaic Group:** Mosaic reported first-quarter revenue of $171.8 million, up 89%, and a 29% increase in diluted cash earnings per share. Its Paradigm unit also expanded its customer-acquisition contract with Enron’s New Power.
- **European telecommunications:** Investors’ views of British Telecom, Deutsche Telekom and Royal KPN improved as asset sales and debt-reduction plans narrowed bond spreads and lowered bankruptcy-swap costs.
- **Corporate credit derivatives:** European corporations were increasingly using credit default swaps to hedge debtor default risk. Market participants said the instruments could be cheaper and more flexible than traditional alternatives, though documentation and complexity remained obstacles.
- **Allegheny Energy purchase:** Allegheny completed its acquisition of 1,710 megawatts of gas-fired generating capacity in Tennessee, Indiana and Illinois from Enron North America. The transaction, financed with debt and equity, was expected to increase 2001 earnings and expand Allegheny’s planned capacity to more than 14,000 megawatts by 2005.
- **Power-profit outlook:** Salomon Smith Barney sharply reduced its forecast for gas-fired generation profitability in 2002 and beyond because projected electricity prices were falling faster than natural-gas prices. It nevertheless expected energy traders such as Enron to benefit from greater trading volumes and volatility outside summer.
- **Northern Border Partners:** Fitch affirmed the partnership’s BBB+ senior-debt rating and its pipeline affiliate’s A- rating, changing both outlooks to stable after reviewing acquisitions and financing plans.
- **Wind power:** EnergieKontor signed a framework agreement for Enron Wind to supply 200 megawatts of turbines for projects in Germany and Spain. EnergieKontor was also pursuing authorization for up to 15 Spanish wind farms totaling 700 megawatts.
- **Scottish Power:** Scottish Power reported lower annual profits and adjusted earnings and was restructuring into three divisions centered on generation, power supply and infrastructure. It was considering selling Southern Water while retaining its remaining stake in loss-making Thus, and U.S. expansion was central to its strategy.

This disclosure describes methods, geranyl pyrophosphate:olivetolic acid geranyltransferase (GOT) polypeptides, encoding nucleic acids, vectors, and genetically modified host cells for producing cannabinoids, precursors, and derivatives in vivo or in cell-free systems. Central to the disclosure is CsPT4, a novel GOT polypeptide that converts geranyl pyrophosphate (GPP) and olivetolic acid into cannabigerolic acid (CBGA) in an amount at least ten times higher than the previously described CsPT1 polypeptide (SEQ ID NO:82). Its truncated CsPT4t form (SEQ ID NO:100), lacking N-terminal residues 1–76, retains activity comparable to full-length CsPT4, unlike longer truncations. These polypeptides are readily reconstituted in recombinant cells and have broad substrate specificity that enables production of non-naturally occurring cannabinoids and precursors.

The disclosed pathway combines hexanoyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA through tetraketide synthase to form olivetolic acid, which GOT combines with GPP to produce CBGA. Synthase enzymes can then convert CBGA into compounds such as tetrahydrocannabinolic acid and cannabidiolic acid. Engineered cells may also express enzymes that generate GPP, malonyl-CoA, or acyl-CoA compounds, including GPPS, ACC1, acyl-activating enzymes, fatty acyl-CoA synthetases or ligases, and mevalonate-pathway enzymes. Suitable hosts include yeast, plant, and prokaryotic cells; heterologous nucleic acids may be chromosomally integrated, extrachromosomal, vector-borne, and promoter-controlled. Cultures may use sugars, carboxylic acids, olivetolic acid or its derivatives as feedstocks, followed by product recovery. Drawings describe biosynthetic pathways, expression constructs, strains, and LC-MS detection of CBGA, CBDA, and THCA. The application is a continuation of prior patent filings, includes an XML sequence listing, and was supported by National Science Foundation grants.

Rep. Garret Graves said the shooting of Rep. Steve Scalise and three others reflects divisive political rhetoric, while criticizing misinformation and sensationalism. Scalise remains in critical condition after James T. Hodgkinson shot him; police have not stated a motive. Bernie Sanders condemned the violence, Republicans cited increased threats, and President Trump called for unity.

Amazon.com, Inc.’s unaudited Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2019 reported Q3 net sales of $69.981 billion, up 24%, comprising $39.726 billion of product sales and $30.255 billion of service sales. Operating income declined to $3.157 billion from $3.724 billion, while net income fell to $2.134 billion from $2.883 billion and diluted earnings per share decreased to $4.23 from $5.75. For the first nine months, sales rose 20% to $193.086 billion, operating income increased to $10.662 billion from $8.635 billion, net income rose to $8.320 billion from $7.046 billion, and diluted earnings per share increased to $16.53 from $14.10.

Q3 segment sales grew 24% in North America to $42.638 billion, 18% internationally to $18.348 billion, and 35% for AWS to $8.995 billion. North American operating income declined to $1.282 billion because of higher shipping and marketing costs. International operating loss was $386 million, compared with $385 million, primarily reflecting higher marketing expense. AWS operating income rose to $2.261 billion from $2.077 billion due to increased customer usage and productivity, partly offset by price reductions and higher infrastructure and payroll spending.

Nine-month operating cash flow increased to $18.855 billion from $14.246 billion. Investing cash outflow widened to $20.745 billion from $8.797 billion, primarily reflecting purchases, sales, and maturities of marketable securities and investments in property and equipment. Financing cash outflow was $6.495 billion. Net cash capital expenditures for the nine months were $8.7 billion, primarily supporting fulfillment capacity and technology infrastructure, largely for AWS. At September 30, 2019, cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities had a fair value of $43.4 billion, total assets were $199.099 billion, and stockholders’ equity was $56.508 billion.

The company adopted new lease accounting guidance on January 1, 2019 without retrospectively adjusting prior periods, recognizing approximately $21 billion of operating lease assets and liabilities. It also adopted guidance requiring capitalization of substantially all episodic television production costs, resulting in approximately $631 million of incremental capitalized film costs during the first nine months of 2019. Lease liabilities totaled $49.278 billion at quarter-end. The filing also reported $24.3 billion of unsecured senior notes, no borrowings under the $7 billion commercial paper program or $7 billion unsecured credit agreement, and $603 million outstanding under a separate secured credit facility. Total contractual commitments were $137.299 billion.

Cost of sales increased primarily because of higher product and shipping costs; shipping costs were $9.6 billion in Q3 versus $6.6 billion a year earlier. Fulfillment costs rose with sales volume, inventory levels, and expansion of fulfillment and physical-store networks, while marketing expenses increased due to online channels and related payroll. Foreign currency changes reduced Q3 sales by $500 million and nine-month sales by $2.4 billion. Management stated that operating cash flows, cash and marketable securities, and borrowing arrangements were sufficient to meet anticipated operating cash needs for at least the next twelve months.

Nine-month stock-based compensation was $5.024 billion, no common shares were repurchased under the $5 billion authorization, and $9.4 billion of unrecognized compensation cost remained for unvested awards. Tax contingencies were approximately $3.8 billion. The IRS sought approximately $1.5 billion of additional federal tax, plus interest, for 2005 and 2006 transfer-pricing adjustments, although the Ninth Circuit affirmed the Tax Court’s rejection of the IRS approach. The company was also reviewing sanctions-related orders with OFAC and BIS, appealing a South Carolina sales-tax assessment, and pursuing appeals concerning an approximately €250 million Luxembourg tax recovery. The filing cautioned that forward-looking results could differ materially due to foreign exchange, economic conditions, customer spending, competition, international expansion, legal matters, fulfillment and inventory risks, acquisitions, and other factors.

An Ilorin Magistrates’ Court remanded two herdsmen, Shehu Abubakar and Abdulkareem Maikudi, over the alleged killing of Musa Kareem following a cell-phone misunderstanding. Facing conspiracy and culpable homicide charges, they were remanded without bail pending police investigation, with the case adjourned until July 12.

The player felt energized throughout the game and credited the team’s four scoring lines and depth as key strengths. Both teams effectively killed penalties amid frequent penalties and chippy ice caused by the hot building. Maintaining composure and persistence created an opening, and the player scored with a high shot past Irbe.

A New York Times survey found widespread concern among responding federal judges about the Supreme Court’s emergency docket in Trump-related cases. Of 65 respondents, 12 said the Court used the docket appropriately, while 47 disagreed and 6 were neutral. Twelve said lower courts received sufficient guidance, compared with 48 who disagreed and five who were neutral. Of 54 judges answering, 42 said the docket harmed public perceptions, 10 saw no effect and two saw improvement. The survey may overrepresent dissatisfied judges and sympathetic districts. The newspaper reported that nearly all rulings benefited Trump, many lacked reasoning, and the orders have had broad practical effects.

Energy Central’s January 15, 2002 daily edition presents 75 electric-power industry articles, with extensive coverage of Enron’s collapse and fallout. Topics include a planned February 12 Senate hearing, scrutiny of Arthur Andersen’s document destruction, accounting warnings, political contributions, the Texas attorney general’s recusal, halted Enron shares, and effects on Spain and Britain. Other leading stories cover National Grid’s imminent $3 billion takeover of Niagara Mohawk, UBS’s acquisition of Enron’s trading business and profit-sharing arrangement, and uncertainty in the U.S. stranded-cost bond market.

Additional coverage addresses California regulatory disputes and PG&E’s bankruptcy, electricity-provider switching in Texas, Ohio deregulation, energy mergers and alliances, power-plant contracts, transmission, pricing, and international electricity markets. Renewable and nuclear stories include operational wind farms, Australian green-power plans, a Thai solar venture, the selection of Yucca Mountain for U.S. nuclear waste, and a shutdown at a Czech nuclear plant. The edition also lists utility-stock gainers and promotes forecasting, load-management, and employment resources.

Nigeria launched its National Cancer Control Plan 2018–2022 in Abuja, aiming to improve access to affordable, equitable cancer diagnostics and treatment and ensure medicine availability. At the launch, BIO Ventures for Global Health presented the Access Accelerated initiative (AAI) and its work with the Nigerian government. Led by BVGH with AORTIC, IFPMA/Access Accelerated, Pfizer, and Takeda, AAI works to expand access to cancer medicines and technologies, strengthen healthcare infrastructure, and build clinical and research capacity in Africa. Its first phase includes Nigeria, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, Kenya, and Rwanda. BVGH has completed needs assessments at eight Nigerian hospitals, with eight more underway, to guide sustainable cancer treatment access and future initiatives.

The Unemployment Insurance Appeal Board denied Michael Moss unemployment benefits because he resigned in lieu of discharge after pulling a box cutter on his supervisor. The court affirmed, finding substantial evidence of disqualifying misconduct and treating his denial of the incident as a credibility issue for the Board.

President Trump’s pardon of former Vice President Dick Cheney’s chief of staff, Scooter Libby, has renewed debate over the constitutional limits of presidential pardon power during special counsel Robert Mueller’s Russia investigation. Trump pardoned Libby, convicted in 2007 of perjury and obstruction of justice, citing his treatment by an overzealous prosecutor. Critics argued the pardon was intended to protect Trump associates, including attorney Michael Cohen, from cooperating with investigators; the White House denied that interpretation and did not rule out a future pardon for Cohen.

Legal experts agree presidents have broad pardon authority but disagree over whether corrupt motives invalidate pardons and whether a president may pardon himself. Pardons do not prevent impeachment. Historical precedents include George H.W. Bush’s Iran-Contra pardons and Bill Clinton’s pardon of Marc Rich.

Rep. Adam Schiff introduced legislation requiring disclosure of evidence when a pardon is connected to an investigation involving the president or his family. New York is also seeking to close what it calls a double-jeopardy loophole that could allow strategically timed pardons to block state prosecution. Legal analysts note that pardons do not necessarily end investigations: recipients lose protection against self-incrimination for the pardoned offense and must testify truthfully or risk prosecution for lying or obstruction.

JPMorgan downgraded Valero Energy to Neutral from Overweight but raised its adjusted target from $75 to $78. Improved returns, capital discipline and stronger free cash flow have already lifted the valuation, though further multiple gains may take time. Free cash flow should cover the dividend, but buybacks could be zero. Expected total return is 6%, versus 7% for the group.

The paper examines whether LLM agents exhibit intrinsic egoistic or altruistic tendencies when individual and collective interests conflict in a large-scale social simulation. It distinguishes altruism as an immediate sacrifice of personal utility for collective gain, rather than cooperation that may serve a long-term self-interest.

A Schelling-variant urban migration model creates the social dilemma. Nine residential blocks have a capacity of 50 agents each, and 225 agents are initially distributed randomly. Individual utility depends on block density and peaks at a density of 0.5; because the utility function is asymmetric, some individually beneficial migrations collectively prevent the system from reaching its optimal population distribution. Agents can stay or move, and can post, like, or ignore messages on a shared message board. Their observations include environmental information, guidance on strategic deliberation, personal and recent social memory, and the public message board. Experiments vary three levels of strategic deliberation and the presence or absence of the board across o1-mini, o3-mini, Qwen2.5-7B, Deepseek-V3.1, Deepseek-R1, and Gemini-2.5-pro.

The study evaluates outcomes through convergence speed, the Price of Anarchy, the Residential Gini Index, and a nine-category matrix classifying actions by their effects on individual and system utility. Gemini-2.5-pro is also used as an LLM judge for Grounded Theory-inspired open, axial, and selective coding of agent reasoning and messages.

Results identify two behavioral archetypes. “Adaptive Egoists,” including o1-mini, o3-mini, and Qwen2.5-7B, generally prioritize personal utility without communication. o1-mini and o3-mini converge to substantially sub-optimal collective welfare and unequal population distributions, while altruistic actions are nearly absent. A message board can shift these models toward prosocial behavior, most notably in o1-mini and Qwen2.5-7B, through conformity to emergent norms and public appeals for balanced densities; o3-mini shows little increase in altruistic actions. “Altruistic Optimizers,” including Gemini-2.5-pro and both Deepseek models, consistently prioritize collective welfare, achieve optimal system utility and equal population distribution with or without the board, and display reasoning centered on system-wide benefits despite personal costs.

The authors argue that selecting an LLM for social simulation also selects an underlying theory of social behavior: Adaptive Egoists may better represent bounded rationality and socially influenced, potentially sub-optimal human dynamics, whereas Altruistic Optimizers suit models of strongly prosocial collective action and common-good resource allocation. Limitations include the omission of migration costs and neighborhood heterogeneity and the use of homogeneous agents. Proposed future work includes human-participant validation and simulations incorporating heterogeneous, real-world demographic profiles.

This retrospective cohort study used MIMIC-IV data from 2011–2019 to assess associations between resting heart rate (RHR) and all-cause mortality among 1,918 adults with intracerebral hemorrhage in an ICU. Patients were grouped into four RHR quartiles, and mortality was evaluated during ICU stay and at 30 days, 90 days, and one year using survival analyses and multivariable Cox regression.

Higher RHR quartiles had greater mortality, although RHR was not significantly associated with mortality between the two lowest quartiles. When RHR exceeded 78.5 bpm, each quartile increase was associated with approximately 50%–100% higher all-cause mortality than the lowest quartile. Restricted cubic splines identified a nonlinear relationship and a 90.3-bpm threshold: RHR below 90.3 bpm may be protective, whereas RHR above 90.3 bpm was independently associated with increased mortality. RHR above 90.3 bpm showed some predictive value, with an AUC greater than 0.5.

Subgroup analyses indicated stronger associations among patients older than 60 and significant associations at 90 days and one year, but not 30 days, in patients with intraventricular hemorrhage. Age also partially mediated the relationship between RHR and mortality. Limitations included possible unmeasured blood-pressure confounding and the limited independent predictive value of RHR; randomized trials and meta-analyses were recommended. The findings support further evaluation of stratified heart-rate management for patients with ICH.

The lecture explains how hedonic pricing can quantify the benefits of green buildings and cities and support business and policy decisions. Prior studies cited indicate an average green-building rent premium of about 6% and a sale-price premium of about 7.6%.

For benefits without directly observable prices, willingness to pay can be estimated through stated preferences, such as surveys, or revealed preferences inferred from market behavior. Housing is particularly useful for revealed-preference analysis because transaction prices and rents reflect buyers’ and tenants’ valuations of property attributes, location, and neighborhood characteristics.

A hedonic model decomposes a property’s price into components such as physical space, transportation access, parks, green-building certification, and a residual representing unobserved factors. Regression estimates each component’s unit price from large datasets, such as Zillow transaction data. In a level model, coefficients represent monetary values; in a log model, they represent percentage changes in price. A dummy-variable coefficient, such as 0.06 for LEED certification, therefore indicates an estimated 6% price premium.

The central challenge is causal inference: simple comparisons between green and nongreen buildings may be “apples-to-oranges” comparisons because the buildings differ in location, age, quality, neighborhood, or other characteristics. The desired counterfactual—the same building without green features—cannot be directly observed. Endogeneity can arise through omitted variables, reverse causality, and selection bias. The lecture identifies basic regression with controls and fixed effects as a starting point, randomized controlled trials as the ideal approach, and quasi-experimental methods—including matching, regression discontinuity, instrumental variables, difference-in-differences, and propensity-score matching—for situations where experiments are impractical.

Geographic matching is presented as especially useful in real estate because it compares green buildings with nearby nongreen properties rather than buildings in different markets. This improves comparability but does not eliminate unobserved differences. The Winthrop Center example illustrates how hedonic analysis of nearby office and condominium transactions could compare the value of features such as energy efficiency and views.

The approach can also estimate premiums for schools, subway and bus service, parks, clean air, walkability, and other amenities or disamenities. Examples include an 8% school-district price premium in China and estimated subway-related premiums of 14% within 0.5 kilometers and 7.5% from 0.5 to 1 kilometer. Housing transactions thus serve as a tool for measuring otherwise unpriced urban benefits.

Finally, the lecture applies these estimates to investment decisions, including park restoration, transit development, and transit-oriented development. Improved public amenities can increase nearby property values and justify private-public partnerships, but higher prices can also produce gentrification and displacement of lower-income residents and businesses, creating a trade-off for planners and decision-makers.
Purdue ended its GEAR UP program after the Trump administration canceled a $34.9 million grant serving more than 13,000 low-income Indiana students; at least nine GEAR UP grants have been canceled.
