This continuation application describes systems and methods for dynamically overlaying replacement video on content received from a content source. A client device identifies an intermediate device, such as a set-top box, and uses video fingerprints to identify the underlying programming and select replacement content, such as a local commercial or alternate-rated version, from a replacement content server. Device-specific templates describe the position, size, cropping, transparency, blending, and playback behavior of set-top-box menus, notifications, icons, and other overlays. The client detects these elements through frame and template matching, then displays replacement video while preserving, modifying, transferring, or suppressing overlays as appropriate. Fingerprints may use Haar-like patch features, integral images, quantized indexes, fuzzy searches, and distance-based matching. Overlay masks can change over time or in response to channel and input changes, with replacement content resuming when the original source returns. Templates may be generated manually or programmatically and stored with coordinates and images for each device, model, firmware version, and overlay type.

Costa has helped fuel Britain’s coffee-shop boom and grown into the world’s second-largest coffee chain behind Starbucks. It operates more than 2,000 UK shops, with sales reaching £3.4 billion in 2016. Its new Basildon, Essex roastery was selected for its proximity to Tilbury Docks and London. The facility has quadrupled annual roasting capacity from 11,000 to 45,000 tonnes, enough to produce 2.1 billion cups, while handling 24 tonnes of beans per hour.

The sustainable roastery uses solar panels, rooftop rainwater harvesting and LED lighting. All Costa-sourced coffee is Rainforest Alliance Certified. Automated systems clean, roast, transport, measure, pack and label coffee without damaging its flavor or beans; the packing robots are expected to improve productivity by 25%.

Quality control is central to production. Every incoming bag is sampled and checked for impurities, color and moisture before tasting tests determine whether it meets Costa’s standards. About 8% of beans are typically rejected annually. Costa’s blend combines aromatic, acidic arabica beans with more bitter, robust robusta beans, sourcing from different countries when seasonal quality fluctuates.

Costa also invests heavily in staff development, training 3,000 baristas annually and promoting employees through its internal career ladder. Its “Master of Coffee,” Gennaro Pellicia, oversees coffee tasting and has his tongue insured for £10 million. With additional land at Basildon, Costa expects the roastery to remain viable for at least 30 years and could open another 6,000 shops worldwide during that period.

The session examines multi-stakeholder engagement through the palm-oil case involving Golden Aggregate Resources (GAR), a supplier whose supply chain includes smallholder and larger growers, mills, middlemen, the Indonesian government, certifying bodies, major corporations such as Nestlé and Unilever, consumers, investors, environmental groups, local and international communities, and competing producers. Because palm oil is a small, often invisible product component and commodity supply chains are opaque, companies need external expertise and collaboration to address issues beyond direct suppliers.

Students proposed three broad strategies: an activist Greenpeace-style campaign; reliance on industry self-regulation and the RSPO to reduce regulatory and investor uncertainty; and a market-driven approach in which premium certified products generate revenue for improvements to farmers and governments. Discussion addressed whether GAR should maintain higher deforestation standards, innovate to grow without deforestation, or lower standards to compete in cost-driven markets.

Participants identified certification and transparency as major challenges. Although the Indonesian ISPO standard is mandatory, the RSPO is voluntary, and only about 10 percent of palm oil is certified, with little of it sold at a premium. RSPO acceptance of mixed certified and uncertified sources can obscure actual sourcing, while certification costs and uncertain costs can burden small farmers. Suggested responses included productivity assistance, education and training, financial incentives and premium pricing, third-party audits, land-use caps, public sustainability reports, collaboration with technical NGOs, and stronger industry standards.

Stakeholder mapping and communication were also discussed. Proposed methods included celebrity endorsements, investor-focused corporate websites, dedicated sustainability staff, government incentives, stakeholder feedback, and proactive partnerships with Greenpeace and other organizations. Corporate customers were identified as influential because consumer pressure and reputational risks can prompt supply-chain changes. The difficulty of communicating sustainability commitments was noted: broad corporate claims may invite criticism, while product-level certification labels are more common, although label standards and oversight vary considerably.

The instructor described several engagement models. Greenpeace uses confrontational campaigns against prominent brands to generate media and consumer pressure, illustrated by its campaign against Nestlé and other corporate examples. The Rainforest Alliance Network used dealer sit-ins against Mitsubishi, prompting partial paper-sourcing commitments. One-on-one technical partnerships included Chiquita with the Rainforest Alliance and Dell with Goodwill for electronic-waste recycling. Walmart partnered with the Environmental Defense Fund, which co-located personnel near the company, while Starbucks used multiple specialist partners. Industry initiatives included the RSPO, Sustainability Consortium, Electronic Industry Citizenship Coalition, and Sustainable Apparel Coalition.

Effective NGO partnerships require a clearly defined objective, project design, appropriate expertise, execution support, and a company contact. NGOs differ in their willingness to work with companies: some provide technical guidance and enforce commitments, while groups such as Greenpeace primarily pressure firms. Measuring outcomes and communicating results remain difficult, and the session also noted the need for stronger regulation and consistency among sustainability labels.

The session ended with notice of a project deliverable due one week later, a planned visit from the Environmental Defense Fund, and forthcoming readings posted through the course announcements system.

The Kiss of Death is an S&P 500 sell signal triggered when the index falls from an all-time high below its monthly 21-period EMA, rebounds above it, and then breaks below the preceding low. The passage examines the S&P 500’s “first day of the month effect,” referring to the first trading day rather than the first calendar day. SPY averaged 0.24% from the previous month’s final close to the first trading day’s close, six times the 0.04% average daily gain. February and July showed the strongest monthly results. The basic strategy was unstable and unreliable, with most gains occurring before the 2008–09 financial crisis and weaker performance afterward. Adding a filter reduced trades by one-third while raising average gains to 0.35%; invested only 1.7% of the time, it reportedly returned 3% annually since 1993, with a 67% win rate, 2.5 profit factor, and 5% maximum drawdown. The paper studies repeated bilateral trade through online learning, with a broker maximizing profit while ensuring dominant-strategy incentive compatibility and individual rationality. Unlike prior work focused on economic efficiency or fixed-price mechanisms, the benchmark is the profit of the optimal mechanism in hindsight.

In the stochastic i.i.d. setting, where valuations follow a fixed unknown, possibly correlated distribution, the paper presents a polynomial-time algorithm with nearly optimal \(\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})\) regret. A matching \(\Omega(\sqrt{T})\) lower bound establishes optimality up to polylogarithmic factors. The analysis also implies that approximately \(1/\varepsilon^2\) samples are sufficient and necessary to learn an expected \(\varepsilon\)-optimal mechanism. Uniform convergence over all mechanisms is impossible, so the upper bound relies on a careful chaining analysis.

In the adversarial setting, the paper proves that no learning algorithm can achieve sublinear regret relative to a \(2/3+\varepsilon\) fraction of optimal profit, demonstrating a sharp separation from the stochastic case. Intermediate models that may permit no-regret learning remain open.

The paper also reduces an \(O(T^{3/4})\) regret bound for the joint ads problem to \(\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})\), essentially resolving an open question.

DSIC and individually rational mechanisms are represented geometrically by a monotone allocation region in the bid space and payments determined by a boundary projection. Learning remains difficult because the mechanism space is nonparametric and the profit function may be highly irregular, limiting standard discretization and convergence approaches.

Mediation analysis examines how interventions influence outcomes through intermediary variables. Valid mediators can clarify treatment mechanisms, guide refinement of interventions, and provide early indicators of success, but their causal roles require empirical validation. Structural equation modeling (SEM) accounts for latent variables and measurement error, yet conventional mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding, an assumption that is often unrealistic; omitted confounders can bias estimates.

Rank-preserving models (RPMs) offer an alternative by relying on a no-effect-modifier, or no-essential-heterogeneity, assumption, allowing omitted covariates provided they do not interact with treatment or the mediator. However, RPMs had not been extended to latent-variable models. The paper introduces the Rank-Preserving Structural Equation Model (RAPSEM), which integrates RPM with factor score regression and interaction corrections. RAPSEM treats the mediator, outcome, and covariates as latent factors and combines measurement and structural components in a formulation mathematically equivalent to standard SEM. It estimates the controlled direct effect of randomized treatment and the controlled mediation effect, while accommodating measurement error and an unobserved mediator–outcome confounder under the relaxed assumption. The paper also describes estimation, inference assumptions, simulation evaluations of robustness and power, and the method’s strengths and limitations.

A cross-sectional study in Denan district, Somali Regional State, Ethiopia, assessed visceral leishmaniasis (VL) seroprevalence, associated factors, community knowledge and practices, and sand-fly vectors from April to August 2021. Among 187 participants screened by direct agglutination test, VL seroprevalence was 9.63%. Higher positivity was associated with age 19–36, damp floors, outdoor sleeping, and sleeping near animal shelters. Knowledge and prevention practices were limited: 53.48% had heard of VL, 42% identified sand-fly bites as the transmission route, and 36% believed VL was preventable. Reported preventive practices included bed-net use (42%), insecticide spraying (32%), smoking plant material (14%), and environmental cleaning (8%). Entomological investigations collected 823 sand flies representing 12 species. Sergentomyia clydie was the most abundant species overall, while Phlebotomus orientalis was the dominant Phlebotomus species; no P. orientalis specimens were captured indoors. The authors identified Denan as a VL focus with poor community awareness and recommended further epidemiological research, improved public education, and investigation of P. orientalis bionomics and vectorial role.

The study examines whether transformers can learn transitive relations from individual training examples, a task equivalent to predicting connectivity between two nodes in a directed graph and to reasoning in simplified implicational logic. Transformers receive two node tokens as input and predict “Y” or “N” indicating whether a directed path exists. Experiments compare grid graphs, whose connectivity can be inferred through low-dimensional node embeddings, with disconnected chain graphs, which lack such simple embeddings.

Transformers learn low-dimensional grid connectivity nearly perfectly but generalize poorly on disconnected chains. Increasing model size improves grid-graph performance, while it does not improve disconnected-chain performance and may increase test loss. Scaling graph size maintains strong performance across grid sizes and improves disconnected-chain results by providing longer chains and more connected training examples.

Performance declines as grid dimensionality increases and as the number of disconnected chains grows. For higher-dimensional grids and chain graphs with many chains, increasing graph size is more beneficial than increasing model size. Overall, the results indicate that data scaling improves connectivity learning in these harder settings more than model scaling. Future work should test whether pretrained LLMs learn generalizable connectivity representations in real-world knowledge and causal graphs.

In this 1967 North Carolina case, defendant Roy Allen Whisnant withdrew his guilty plea to assault with a deadly weapon and sought a continuance to obtain witnesses from West Virginia and Florida. The court denied the request and his attorney’s request to postpone trial until the following week. He was tried the next day, convicted, and sentenced to two years’ imprisonment. The North Carolina Supreme Court ordered a new trial, finding that the immediate trial prejudiced him because the jurors likely remembered his guilty plea, counsel needed reasonable time to investigate and prepare his defense, and witnesses might have attended had the case been continued.

Accessories include custom rain covers, frame-mounted front racks, and a padded middle seat usable for pets, diaper changes, or drinks, supporting comfort, security, style, and functionality.

Jerome “Jay” Powell, a former investment banker appointed by President Donald Trump, will lead the Federal Reserve on Monday, succeeding Janet Yellen after her single term. Powell inherits low unemployment, subdued inflation, sustained growth and a gradually normalizing monetary policy. With wages and employment strong, synchronized global growth and tax cuts raising inflation concerns, he must calibrate interest-rate increases. The Fed raised rates five times under Yellen and indicated three more hikes were likely in 2018, though faster increases could unsettle markets.

The Supreme Court will hear arguments Oct. 7 in Barrett’s case, which concerns convictions under 18 U.S.C. §§ 924(c) and 924(j) arising from armed robberies and a fatal shooting. Section 924(c) punishes firearm use to advance a federal crime of violence or drug-trafficking offense; Section 924(j) applies when such a violation causes death through a firearm.

The Court must decide whether Section 924(j) creates a separate offense permitting an additional punishment for the same conduct. Under the Blockburger double-jeopardy test, separate punishments are generally permitted when each offense requires proof of an element the other does not; when one offense requires only a subset of the other’s elements, multiple punishments are barred absent clear congressional intent.

Barrett and the government argue that the statutes do not clearly authorize cumulative punishment. Court-appointed amicus McCloud argues that Section 924(c)’s requirement that sentences run consecutively to all other prison terms establishes that intent. A prior ruling held that Section 924(j), charged alone, does not inherit Section 924(c)’s mandatory minimums or consecutive-sentence requirement.

Vocational education and training assessment must address theoretical knowledge, technical skills, and workplace competencies through a comprehensive program combining written tests, skills assessments, practicum or workplace evaluations, formative and summative methods, and assessment of performance processes and products. Formative assessment requires active teacher–student participation, immediate feedback, guidance toward workplace-relevant next steps, and student self-assessment. It can deepen learning and increase motivation, although teacher preparation and student engagement are necessary.

Academic assessment tools do not always suit VET, so vocational teachers should balance academic testing with evaluations of technical skills. Competence-based education links classroom theory to industry-standard workplace performance through clearly communicated tasks, standards, and authentic practicum evaluations. Authentic assessment should reflect workplace conditions and social expectations, while reliability can be strengthened through transparent procedures, rubrics, and calibration with other vocational teachers and experts.

Assessment should span four levels of competence—knows, knows how, shows how, and does—and occur before, during, and after learning. Clear curricular outcomes, vocational competencies, performance portfolios, and workplace evaluations can promote deeper learning and student engagement.

The Second Circuit affirmed the district court’s grant of summary judgment to Reisdorf Brothers on Patrick and Linda George’s Clean Water Act and Resource Conservation and Recovery Act claims. The plaintiffs failed to establish a continuing or intermittent discharge of pollutants: the consent orders concerned a single March 2009 spill, while the evidence concerning fertilizer, pesticides, septic effluent, and molasses was insufficient or speculative to create a triable issue. The plaintiffs’ newly raised storm-water claim was not stated in the complaint, and the district court did not abuse its discretion in declining to address it.

The court also held that the RCRA claim failed because the plaintiffs neither alleged nor proved a violation of the federal regulatory criteria defining open dumping. The district court properly declined supplemental jurisdiction over the plaintiffs’ state-law adverse-possession claim, dismissing it without prejudice to renewal in state court.

Finally, the district court did not abuse its discretion by denying Reisdorf attorney’s fees. Although the plaintiffs’ federal claims failed, they had some arguable factual basis and were pursued in good faith. The judgment was affirmed, and the remaining evidentiary arguments were rejected or treated as waived.

**Summary**

This medRxiv preprint examined how kidney function status relates to new-onset heart failure (HF) using longitudinal data from the PREVEND prospective cohort in Groningen, the Netherlands.

**Background and objective:** CKD patients are at increased risk of HF, and this association is modified by age and sex and depends on whether urinary albumin excretion (UAE) or estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) is used. The study aimed to estimate age- and sex-specific transition rates between consecutive KDIGO risk stages before new-onset HF, and to estimate the age- and sex-specific association of KDIGO risk stages with new-onset HF while accounting for dynamic changes and misclassification in kidney measures.

**Methods:** A multi-state model treated three KDIGO risk stages (low; intermediate; high or very high, defined by eGFR and UAE per the 2012 KDIGO guideline) as transient states, with new-onset HF and death before HF as absorbing states, including forward, backward, and outcome transitions (except a rare backward transition). Misclassification probabilities were estimated from data; age was the time scale and sex a covariate. Kidney measures came from the first four PREVEND examinations (1997–2008), using UAE from two 24-hour urine collections and CKD-EPI eGFR from creatinine, with a sensitivity analysis using cystatin C. HF cases were adjudicated by a seven-member expert committee; follow-up ended at HF, death, or 31 December 2010. Analyses used R 3.6.3 (MSM package).

**Results:** The baseline cohort comprised 8,569 participants (6,838 low risk, 1,279 intermediate, 303 high/very high risk); higher-risk participants were older, more often men, and more often had hypertension or type 2 diabetes. Over a median 12.6 years, 4,973 (58%) completed all four visits, 373 developed new-onset HF, and 710 died before HF. Forward transition rates were below one per 100 person-years before age 50 and rose with age; low-to-intermediate rates did not differ significantly by sex (HR 1.08, 95% CI 0.87–1.33), reached ten per 100 person-years at 75, then flattened, while intermediate-to-high/very-high rates increased exponentially with age and were lower in women (HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.34–0.76). Backward intermediate-to-low rates declined with age and were higher in women. Transitions to HF increased exponentially with age and were lower in women (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.56–0.87). In a population starting at low risk at age 50, intermediate risk tripled between ages 60 and 70 and high/very high risk rose mainly after 70; by age 90, death before HF reached 58% in men and 40% in women, and HF 24% and 21%, respectively. Relative risks of HF for intermediate and high/very high versus low risk were larger in younger subjects (intermediate vs low: RR 3.4 at 60 versus 1.6 at 80; high/very high vs low: 6.1 versus 2), while absolute rate differences were larger in older subjects; no sex differences were found in RRs. Misclassification was substantial (intermediate classified as low: 18.4%; high/very high as intermediate: 15.6%) and lower with cystatin C-based eGFR. Model calibration was excellent, and cystatin C sensitivity analyses were mostly consistent.

**Discussion and limitations:** Findings extend prior single-baseline-measure studies by modelling the full disease course, handling interval censoring, and accounting for misclassification. The authors suggest slowing KDIGO stage progression could reduce HF incidence. Limitations include an UAE-enriched, predominantly Caucasian cohort and the Markov assumption.

**Conclusion:** Kidney disease progresses rapidly in middle age, more advanced KDIGO status is associated with increased new-onset HF risk, and slowing progression may reduce HF incidence. No funding or industry relationships were reported; no conflicts declared.

The Pittsburgh Penguins defeated the Washington Capitals 7-4 on Friday, winning their fourth straight and pulling within four points of the division-leading Capitals. Phil Kessel scored twice with an assist, Evgeni Malkin had two goals and two assists, and Sidney Crosby's two assists extended his NHL-longest active scoring streak to 11 games. Australian markets can be accessed through US-listed ETFs, American Depository Receipts, international brokers offering direct ASX trading, or Australian CFD brokers. The ASX provides stock and futures services, while the SSX is also available. Using EWA as a proxy, the article finds that mean-reversion strategies are less effective and consistent in Australia’s commodity-related market than in the US. Classical 200-day moving-average and Golden Cross strategies also produced no success. A seasonal strategy showed a 92% win rate since 1996 and an average gain of 2.4% per trade, but its annual return of 1.87% trailed buy-and-hold’s 7.34%.

This descriptive survey study developed a scale for assessing prospective teachers’ attitudes toward values education through distance education, a topic with limited prior research and no existing validated scale. The sample comprised 341 prospective teachers from Gazi University’s Faculty of Education, most of whom were female. A 43-item pool was created from literature, compositions by 20 prospective teachers, and expert review; pilot testing reduced it to 40 items.

Exploratory factor analysis supported a two-factor structure containing 36 items: “Necessity and Usefulness” with 21 items and “Feasibility” with 15 items. Together, the factors explained 63.286% of the total variance. The scale was not additive, so each factor should be evaluated separately. Cronbach’s alpha coefficients were .969 for Necessity and Usefulness and .961 for Feasibility, while split-half reliability coefficients were .934 and .930. Item-total correlations and subgroup comparisons indicated adequate item distinctiveness and internal consistency. Scores range from 21 to 105 for Necessity and Usefulness and from 15 to 75 for Feasibility, with higher reverse-coded scores indicating more positive attitudes.

Limitations include a predominantly female sample, participants limited to one university, and the absence of an external scale for comparison. Recommended future research includes confirmatory factor analysis with participants from multiple universities, additional validity testing, and test-retest reliability studies.

Dabhol Power Company’s board authorized management to issue a preliminary termination notice for its power-purchase agreement with the Maharashtra State Electricity Board, voting 6–1 with IDBI opposed; MSEB representatives were barred from voting as an interested party. The dispute followed MSEB’s overdue payments and its Rs 401 crore penalty against DPC. MSEB made a disputed “protest payment” of Rs 134 crore toward a Rs 146.64 crore March bill. International lenders reportedly favored ending the project and withholding Phase II funding, while Indian lenders led by IDBI urged renegotiation. Maharashtra and central governments also opposed termination and formed a committee to renegotiate the agreement, particularly its high power tariff.

Law enforcement said Stephen Paddock bought 1,000 tracer rounds for improved nighttime accuracy, though investigators did not know whether he used them during the Las Vegas attack that killed 58 and injured nearly 500. His preparations included 23 guns, some modified for automatic-style fire, cameras, and festival-viewing rooms. Post defense requires coordinated team effort: active hands and pressure on the passer, backside help, and well-executed traps. Defenders should deny entry, push off the block, face the post, and force players toward their weaker side. Disruptions include full-court pressing, adjusted 2–3 zones, and Diamond & One defense.

Amazon.com, Inc.’s unaudited Form 10-Q for the quarter ended June 30, 2017 reported Q2 net sales of $38.0 billion, up 25% from $30.4 billion a year earlier. Operating income fell from $1.29 billion to $628 million, net income declined from $857 million to $197 million, and diluted EPS fell from $1.78 to $0.40. For the first six months, net sales rose 24% to $73.7 billion, while operating income declined to $1.63 billion, net income to $921 million, and diluted EPS to $1.87.

Q2 segment sales and operating results were: North America, $22.37 billion and $436 million; International, $11.49 billion and a $724 million loss; and AWS, $4.10 billion and $916 million. For the six months, North America recorded $43.36 billion of sales and $1.03 billion of operating income, International recorded $22.55 billion and a $1.21 billion loss, and AWS recorded $7.76 billion and $1.81 billion. Expense growth reflected higher fulfillment, technology and content, marketing, payroll, and infrastructure spending.

At June 30, 2017, Amazon held $13.20 billion of cash and cash equivalents, $8.25 billion of marketable securities, $87.78 billion of total assets, and $23.21 billion of stockholders’ equity. Q2 operating cash flow was $3.83 billion, investing cash flow used $5.05 billion, and financing cash flow used $1.26 billion. Amazon acquired Souq Group for approximately $586 million and other companies for $86 million during the first six months. The company adopted inventory and stock-compensation accounting standards in Q1 2017 and planned to adopt revised revenue-recognition guidance in Q1 2018. It recorded a $600 million tax valuation allowance for Luxembourg deferred tax assets, while tax contingencies totaled $1.9 billion. Disclosed legal matters included potential sanctions issues, sales-tax claims, and patent litigation. No common shares were repurchased under Amazon’s $5 billion authorization.

This source guide documents U.S. high-level decision-making toward the Soviet Union from January 1983 to March 1985. Reagan Library White House Staff and Office Files include Executive Secretariat records (NSC and NSPG meeting files, National Security Decision Directives, Head of State File, USSR Country File), the European and Soviet Affairs Directorate's USSR files, Jack Matlock's files, those of assistants William Clark and Robert "Bud" McFarlane, and files of NSC staff John Lenczowski, Robert Linhard, Ronald Lehman, and Sven Kraemer; declassified NSDD texts are available on the Reagan Library website. Department of State records include Executive Secretariat S/S lot files, files of Lawrence Eagleburger and Kenneth Dam, Policy Planning Staff memoranda, Office of Soviet Affairs files, and the Central Foreign Policy File of embassy-Washington cables; the Historian's website lists growing online documents.

A note on covert actions explains that Truman administration concern over Soviet "psychological warfare" prompted NSC 4-A of December 1947, authorizing peacetime covert action operations, making the Director of Central Intelligence responsible and covert action an exclusively executive branch function, with the CIA chosen partly for its unvouchered funds. State and Defense objections prompted NSC 10/2 of June 18, 1948, superseding NSC 4-A and directing the CIA to conduct "covert" rather than merely "psychological" operations, defined as activities so planned that U.S. responsibility is not evident to unauthorized persons and can be plausibly disclaimed.

Parental obesity is associated with childhood obesity: a mother’s BMI at conception is closely linked to this risk, while paternal obesity also matters. Having two obese parents further increases risk. Eggs and sperm carry nutrition-responsive molecules that can influence offspring. Sperm contain non-coding RNAs that affect embryo development; in mice, RNA from obese males makes offspring fatter, and comparable changes occur in obese men. Maternal nutrition affects egg composition, while embryos from obese women show altered metabolism and defective mitochondria. Because mitochondria are maternally inherited, defects found in eggs of obese mice also appear in offspring muscle, increasing lifelong susceptibility to obesity and diabetes.

Embryos respond to their environment, meaning improved nutrition, exercise and treatment may improve egg and sperm quality. Brief anti-diabetes treatment improved eggs in obese female mice, while exercise improved reproductive cells, restored sperm non-coding RNA and prevented obesity transmission in male mice. Children conceived after maternal gastric banding were less obese than earlier-conceived siblings, but human evidence remains limited. Research is focused on interventions before conception for both parents and preventing obesity in adolescents and young adults.

Cornerbacks are defensive backs whose primary role is covering opposing wide receivers in man or zone coverage, often in one-on-one situations. They mirror receivers’ routes, react to footwork, backpedal, make sharp turns, and accelerate; mistakes can lead to large gains or touchdowns. They protect the outside thirds of the field near the boundary, giving the position its name, and teams typically deploy two, with a third sometimes used in nickel packages. Cornerbacks also contain outside runs by tackling or forcing runners inward. Their speed, agility, and ability to cover receivers without safety help make them essential to shutting down passing attacks. The passage highlights Deion Sanders, Charles Woodson, Mel Blount, Champ Bailey, Ty Law, Darrell Revis, and other notable cornerbacks, noting that 18 are in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

Defending soccer goal kicks requires strategic positioning and pressing to regain possession quickly, preferably in a dangerous area, or to prevent an opponent’s easy buildup or long kick to midfield. A goal kick is awarded when an attacking player sends the ball over the defending team’s goal line. It may be taken from anywhere in the goal area, but the ball must be stationary. Defenders are generally expected to remain outside the penalty area until the kick is taken, although the kick may proceed if they have not had time to retreat. Opponents inside the penalty area when the kick is taken or before play begins may not interfere with the ball, or the kick must be retaken. The ball is in play once it is kicked and visibly moves; opponents may then enter the penalty area. Any attacking player may take the kick, but the original kicker cannot touch the ball again.

Three main defensive tactics are described. First, defenders should use man-to-man and zone coverage to mark potential receivers throughout the field. Strikers can position themselves in front of the kicker, close-mark wing backs, or cut off short passes; midfielders can contest the ball in the air, while backs provide defensive support. Second, the team should aggressively move toward the ball, with the first striker going directly to it, other players cutting off short-pass options, and midfielders challenging aerial balls. Third, if possession is lost, the entire team should press high in the opponent’s half, while considering counterattacking and back-pass options. Teams should also recognize and defend against opponents preparing to play a flick header.

For players generally aged 10 and under, smaller fields and build-out or retreat lines are commonly used. Defenders must retreat behind the build-out line before challenging, and local rules may prohibit long kicks, requiring the team to build up from the back. Simple goal-kick plays include placing the ball at the outermost corner of the goal area and directing it to the best dribbler or to a target receiver near the sideline, with a secondary receiver positioned farther upfield. Players should keep the ball wide and upfield and never send it across their own goal. The kicker must ensure teammates and opponents are properly positioned and allow defenders time to retreat.

For players generally aged 11 and above, the kicking team can use two direct targets: one nearer the goal and one farther wide and upfield. The kick should usually go to an uncovered player; if both are covered, it can be played just short of the farther target so the player can run onto it. A supporting midfielder may become a third target when unmarked. Players must be prepared for kicks from either side of the goal area, should move forcefully toward the ball, and should account for defenders who may be added to practice. If defenders stack along the build-out line, the purpose of the rule is undermined.

At adult levels, advanced players may use nearby short passes, prearranged or deep targets, lofted balls with a low trajectory, or kicks directed to spaces where teammates can run. The goalkeeper usually takes the kick to avoid removing an outfield player from the attack. Deep kicks can create unpredictable aerial contests, so coaches may instead direct them toward specific teammates.

A goal kick is a restart, with the ball live as soon as it is touched and moves, and it is direct because a goal may be scored without another player touching it. Players should react quickly, continually track the ball, never turn their backs on it, and consider the effects of wind and field conditions. Defenders should scout opponents’ kicking tendencies and range, position midfielders to challenge for the ball, and drill against all available options.

The article backtests Larry Connors’ 3-day high/low ETF strategy from his 2009 book *High Probability ETF Trading*, using results through December 31, 2008, and updating its performance roughly 12 years later. The strategy buys an ETF after three consecutive days of lower highs and lower lows, with specified moving-average criteria, including a close above the 200-day moving average and below the 5-day moving average. Connors emphasized trading only ETFs, quantifiable rules, moving-average exits, and win ratios of at least 65%. The original tests covered the 20 most popular ETFs by volume.

A portfolio test used 25 ETFs, with a maximum of five open positions and 20% of equity allocated to each. The strategy performed well in Connors’ book and continued to show promise, although it had deteriorated somewhat; 13 of the original 20 ETFs performed worse after the original test period. The worst portfolio drawdown occurred in July 2011 during the EU debt crisis. An aggressive add-on rule was excluded from the tests.

NewMarket generates most revenue, profit, and cash flow through Afton Chemical, which makes petroleum-based fuel and lubricant additives. NewMarket is expanding in Asia through a new Singapore plant and acquired Aditivos Mexicanos for about $183 million, increasing its emerging-market presence and domestic manufacturing capacity in Mexico. The author expects emerging-market vehicle growth to support roughly 3% long-term revenue growth, with free cash flow improving after the Singapore plant is completed and potentially reaching low-double-digit margins. R&D spending of 5%–8% of sales may help develop diesel and industrial products.

Despite these opportunities, the shares appear fully valued, already reflecting high-single-digit free-cash-flow growth and trading above 12 times the author’s 2017 EBITDA estimate. The author sees insufficient undervaluation to justify a new position and believes significant growth may require diversification.

The agreement charges individuals for necessary voyage expenses connected to their misdemeanors, disabilities, attempted desertion, or disobedience. If sickness or death prevents completion, legal representatives receive the share earned for time served. Crew must account for entrusted apparel, stores, and cargo, repay losses caused by negligence, and safely handle goods. Those who properly complete the voyage and obey all duties without dishonest or unlawful acts are paid in San Francisco: whale oil at 20 cents per gallon, sperm oil at 40 cents, and whalebone at $1.25 per pound if the Pacific fleet catches over 200 whales, or $1.50 if it catches 200 or fewer. Crew must board by the ordered date and time and cannot possess or trade in distilled liquor except for medical use; violations forfeit their entire voyage share to the owners.

The paper examines how Industry 4.0, digitalization, and COVID-19 are reshaping higher education and the skills employers require. It frames Education 4.0 as a shift toward individualized, interdisciplinary, technology-enabled, lifelong, problem- and challenge-based learning, with teachers acting as mentors and greater emphasis on practical learning, digital competence, and both technical and soft skills. It reviews projected changes in employment, including demand for critical thinking, problem-solving, communication, self-management, adaptability, collaboration, and technological skills.

The study investigates how Hungarian engineering and technical management students prioritize employability skills, evaluate the benefits of studying abroad, perceive the factors affecting graduate career success, and assess higher education’s contribution to their competencies and self-awareness. It used a cross-sectional, purposive, non-probability survey conducted in 2019 and 2021. Of 165 questionnaires completed by second-year students, 147 were analyzed: 96 Mechanical and Safety Engineering students and 51 Technical Management students, all aged 19–22. Questions were informed by literature, 22 interviews with Hungarian industry representatives, and the World Economic Forum’s top 10 skills for 2050. Data were analyzed with SPSS, Excel, chi-square tests, t-tests, and CHAID decision trees.

Both faculties ranked problem-solving as the most important skill for university training, selected by 66.7% of respondents. Knowledge related to specialization was selected by 51.7% and communication skills by 29.9%. Significant differences remained: engineering students placed greater emphasis on specialization and technical and mathematical knowledge, while technical management students prioritized decision-making techniques and analytical thinking. The first hypothesis, that the groups had different skill priorities, was supported.

Studying abroad was primarily valued for improving foreign-language skills and communication, selected by 84.6%, followed by networking, selected by 53.1%, and adaptation to international norms, selected by 45.5%. Both groups similarly prioritized language development, but engineering students placed more importance on learning from foreign cultures and on new approaches to interpreting learning material, whereas technical management students emphasized networking and international adaptation. Rankings across the two faculties had a strong positive correlation.

Students in both faculties identified individual talents and skills, professional devotion, and professional networks as the leading factors in career success, with no statistically significant difference between faculties. Consequently, the hypothesis that the groups differed in the skills they considered important for future careers was not supported.

More than half of students said higher education fully contributed to knowledge of their future workplace, digital literacy, and understanding other people. Fewer than half gave fully positive ratings for writing and presenting, quantitative analysis, and teamwork. Significant faculty differences occurred for future-job knowledge, quantitative analysis, teamwork, and self-understanding, leading to partial acceptance of the hypothesis that students had different expectations of higher education. CHAID analysis identified future-job knowledge, decision-making, and approaches to interpreting learning material as important differentiating factors and classified 77.6% of students correctly.

The study concludes that universities should combine technical and IT education with communication, teamwork, creativity, critical thinking, problem-solving, self-management, international experience, and practical or project-based learning. It recommends curricular reform and multidisciplinary collaboration, while noting limitations from the small, nonrepresentative sample, reliance on one university and two faculties, and lack of prior comparable research.

Thirty-seven lawyers, including 10 incoming partners, left Cadwalader, Wickersham & Taft for Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe, joining its new Charlotte office and offices in London, Washington, D.C., and New York. Plymouth Argyle’s 2–1 League One win over Gillingham moved them off the foot of the table, leaving them level on points with the Kent club but still in the bottom four on goal difference. Goals from Joel Grant and Toumani Diagouraga proved decisive, with Ryan Taylor assisting the opener on his return from a broken ankle. Taylor’s performance restored a regular striker and strengthened hopes of survival, alongside four wins and a draw from seven matches.

However, Argyle faced a severe goalkeeping crisis, fielding a seventh goalkeeper, Kelle Roos, because three first-choice keepers were injured. About a dozen global and Asian firms, including Shell, ExxonMobil, PTTEP and Japanese companies, were approached. The sale could fund development of the capital-intensive, CO2-heavy Kasawari field, which was put on hold in 2015. The passage highlights substantial racial economic disparities in Durham and nationally. In 2014, median family income was $71,300 for whites and $43,300 for blacks, with education, age, labor-force experience, and current and past discrimination all cited as partial explanations. The wealth gap was larger: in 2015, median family wealth was $171,000 for white families and $17,600 for black families. Homeownership disparities contribute to the gap; 73% of whites versus 45% of blacks owned a primary residence.

The author favors affordable-housing policies that preserve existing housing and support ownership over policies centered on new rental units. Cited approaches include Habitat for Humanity, Rebuilding Together, Preservation Durham’s Preservation Equity Program, and property-tax circuit breakers. These measures can help low-income homeowners remain in their homes, retain or build equity, and pass assets to heirs. This conceptual survey examines slavery as an undertheorized foundation of pedagogy, using Michel Foucault’s panopticism and surveillance textualism to connect education with surveillance, extraction, textualization, capitalist imperatives, and power. Foucault describes surveillance as inherent to teaching, while racial surveillance organizes monitoring and categorization along racial lines, reproducing inequality. His panopticon framework shows how observation, examination, recordkeeping, secrecy, and discourse induce docility, normalize individuals, and automate self-regulation, though Foucault has been criticized for giving cursory attention to race and slavery.

Enslaved people served as pedagogues and guides in Ancient Greece and Rome despite their low social status, and the master–slave relationship helped shape education while teaching lessons of power. In the United States, racial chattel slavery linked education to anti-literacy laws, torture, labor monitoring, recordkeeping, and the extraction and textualization of enslaved people’s behavior and productivity. These practices supported capitalism, anticipated scientific management, and helped institutionalize practices later rearticulated through behaviorism and surveillance capitalism. Black resistance to the criminalization and destruction of Black education is described through Givens’s concept of fugitive pedagogy.

Digitalization intensifies these continuities. Data-driven pedagogy, learning analytics, learning-management systems, and platforms such as Google Classroom can extract and code experiences for monitoring, prediction, behavioral conditioning, and profit. The article proposes surveillance pedagogy: the observation and supervision of teaching and learning by actors with authority, sustained through the extraction, textualization, categorization, and differentiation of personal data. It functions simultaneously as knowledge production, organizational management, and social control. The framework invites further research into how digital technologies, artificial intelligence, platforms, educators, and corporations increasingly shape learning and control educational data, linking past systems of slavery and discipline to contemporary surveillance capitalism.

This cross-sectional study assessed lung function decline and associated factors among 302 adults with heroin use disorder receiving methadone at Muhimbili National Hospital’s Medication Assisted Therapy clinic in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. Participants were predominantly male (95.7%), with a mean age of 42.78 years. Most reported cigarette smoking, and participants reported substantial heroin smoking, prior injection, respiratory symptoms, HIV infection, or pulmonary tuberculosis.

Spirometry showed lung function decline in 28.5% of participants, with mean onset at age 44. Restrictive abnormalities were most common (13.2%), followed by obstructive abnormalities (11%) and mixed abnormalities (4.3%). Underweight participants had 4.73 times the adjusted odds of lung function decline compared with those of normal weight. HIV infection and a history of pulmonary tuberculosis were also independently associated with decline, with adjusted odds ratios of 2.61 and 2.48, respectively. Other measured sociodemographic, substance-use, and methadone-related factors were not significantly associated with decline.

The authors concluded that routine lung-function screening is needed in this population to identify undiagnosed and underdiagnosed lung disease. The study could not perform bronchodilator reversibility testing to distinguish asthma from COPD among participants with obstructive abnormalities.

Clay Williams was convicted of first-degree murder, robbery, two firearms offenses, and possession of instruments of crime after he attempted to take Mizael Velez’s cell phone at a Philadelphia Chinese store and, upon returning, shot Velez. Williams told detectives that his gun discharged during the attempted theft and that he fled. Although a shotgun cup recovered from Velez matched the type of shotgun later found in Williams’s possession, an expert could not determine that the weapon recovered had fired the fatal shot. The trial court sentenced Williams to life imprisonment without parole for murder, with concurrent terms for robbery and carrying a firearm without a license.

On appeal, the Superior Court found no waiver based solely on Williams’s late filing of his statement of matters complained of because the record did not establish proper notice. It nevertheless held that Williams waived his suppression claim because he did not explain the alleged error, and his sufficiency challenge because he did not identify any unproven elements. His claim that the court improperly admitted cumulative evidence was waived because he failed to develop the argument or cite supporting authority. Because Williams did not raise his ineffective-assistance claims in post-trial proceedings or obtain a dedicated evidentiary hearing, the court dismissed those claims without prejudice for collateral review. It denied Williams’s petition to remand for record development concerning a juror’s disclosure, finding the issue adequately developed, and affirmed the judgment of sentence.

The passage introduces BALLAST (Bayesian Active Learning with Lookahead Amendment for Sea-drifter Trajectories), an active-learning method for sequentially placing Lagrangian ocean-current observers. Existing drifter deployments generally use space-filling designs, ad hoc expert choices, or hand-crafted criteria rather than active learning. BALLAST uses a spatio-temporal vector-output Gaussian process surrogate with a temporal Helmholtz kernel, hypothetical observer trajectories, and an expected-information-gain utility to select placement locations at predetermined times. Its contributions include applying active learning to Lagrangian observer placement, accounting for Lagrangian observations through surrogate samples, and combining standard GP regression with an SPDE approach for efficient posterior sampling and utility computation. Numerical results indicate noticeable benefits over other deployment policies in synthetic and high-fidelity ocean-current models.

A cross-sectional substudy of the Kailuan cohort analyzed 1,284 participants to assess long-term visit-to-visit blood pressure variability from 2006–2022 against MRI-defined cerebral small vessel disease (cSVD). High systolic BP variability was associated with moderate cSVD burden and perivascular spaces; high diastolic variability with lacunae; and high pulse-pressure variability with moderate/severe cSVD, lacunae, and perivascular spaces. Associations differed by age and hypertension status: among participants under 60, high pulse-pressure variability was associated with severe cSVD, lacunae, and perivascular spaces, while significant systolic and pulse-pressure effects on cSVD burden occurred only among participants with hypertension. No independent associations were found for white matter hyperintensities or cerebral microbleeds. The authors concluded that long-term BP variability is an independent risk factor for cSVD, particularly with hypertension, and that pulse-pressure variability warrants attention in younger adults. Limitations include possible reverse causation from one-time MRI and selection bias. The preprint was not peer reviewed.

Gary Gensler’s MIT OpenCourseWare lecture “Payments, Part 2” marks Bitcoin’s tenth anniversary with statistics and class predictions. Gensler cites a price near $6,300, a market capitalization of about $110 billion, 17.3 million mined coins, roughly 250,000 daily transactions, more than 500,000 addresses, about 10,000 nodes, nearly one-third of 1% of global electricity use, and $28 billion raised through initial coin offerings. He expects most ICOs and many of the more than 1,600 coins to fail.

The class identifies payment-system problems including excessive intermediaries and parallel ledgers, high costs, delayed merchant settlement, financial exclusion, slow cross-border currency conversion, chargebacks and limited transaction finality, fraud and error resolution, privacy concerns, cyberattacks, and identity theft. Estimated payment costs range from 0.5% to 1% of global GDP, or $400 billion to $800 billion annually, while U.S. card rails cost about 2.75%. The discussion highlights tension between merchants’ need for finality and consumers’ need to dispute charges, as well as the role of delayed settlement in catching errors and fraud.

Blockchain may lower networking and verification costs, and its shared, append-only ledger may suit payment systems requiring multiple parties to read from and write to a common record. However, it introduces scalability, speed, transaction-cost, interoperability, error-resolution, governance, anti-money-laundering, and liquidity challenges. Immutability can conflict with chargebacks, while smart contracts enable programmable payments but present trust, escrow, and functionality limitations.

Participants debate whether blockchain is necessary. A Mastercard representative argued that existing payment systems can provide blockchain’s promised functions, while cryptocurrency transactions and the difficulty of achieving acceptance and scale make replacement impractical. Others emphasized benefits where legal infrastructure is weak or people are unbanked, including self-sovereign wallets and censorship resistance. India’s UPI and payment-bank initiatives were presented as a non-blockchain route to financial inclusion. Gensler suggested blockchain might instead catalyze legacy-system modernization, comparing that possibility with BitTorrent’s industry impact and Ripple’s influence on Swift.

Payment examples included BitPay’s 1% merchant conversion service, cryptocurrency donation processors, institutional projects such as R3, Ripple, Quorum, and Bakkt, Visa’s B2B Connect service, and MIT’s QR-code vending machine accepting Bitcoin, Litecoin, and a stablecoin. Stripe discontinued its Bitcoin support, partly because of limited adoption.

Finally, the class considered cryptocurrency as a bridge between fiat currencies for cross-border payments. This approach could reduce correspondent-bank intermediaries, accelerate settlement, and lower costs for small remittances, but would add exchange spreads, volatility, reserve and liquidity requirements, arbitrage exposure, and weekend-closing frictions. Gensler concluded that its business case depends on the value gained through faster settlement and broader access. The next session will address central bank digital currencies.

The article examines whether ChatGPT can create and backtest a Bollinger Bands trading strategy. Bollinger Bands use a 20-period simple moving average with upper and lower bands set two standard deviations above and below it by default, though these settings can be customized. ChatGPT proposed mean-reversion and squeeze strategies. The tested squeeze strategy defines a squeeze as Bollinger Bands contracting inside Keltner Channels, whose bounds use twice the stock’s average true range. It buys and holds when the lower Bollinger Band is above the Keltner lower band and the upper Bollinger Band is below the Keltner upper band, selling when either condition fails. A Python backtest using unadjusted SPY data from 1993 produced low, erratic returns and a sizable drawdown. Adjusting for time in the market modestly improved results and reduced drawdown. The strategy was not profitable, but ChatGPT coded and backtested it correctly.

Business Insider ranks Taylor Swift’s 20 best breakup songs from 1 to 20, highlighting her range of heartbreak—regret, anger, despair, yearning, bewilderment and relief—and noting three tracks from “The Tortured Poets Department” as recent additions.

1. **“Should’ve Said No”** — An upbeat, triumphant song about betrayal, ideal for post-breakup karaoke.
2. **“Better Man”** — Originally offered to Little Big Town, whose recording won major awards, before Swift recorded a new version with Aaron Dessner.
3. **“How Did It End?”** — A “lovers’ autopsy” combining resignation about a failed relationship with anger, humor and frustration over friends’ curiosity.
4. **“You’re Losing Me”** — A vault track chronicling the long-term demise of a relationship through Swift’s indecision and her lover’s apathy.
5. **“Forever & Always”** — Captures youthful rejection and anger, balancing petulance with vulnerability and uncertainty.
6. **“The Story of Us”** — Turns a brief, painful encounter with an ex into an emotional rupture.
7. **“Hits Different”** — Uses romantic-comedy imagery and remembered artifacts to portray an entertaining but increasingly painful downward spiral.
8. **“Last Kiss”** — A six-minute ballad about intimacy, lingering grief and feeling abandoned by a former partner.
9. **“Loml”** — Expresses bewilderment over a once-vital relationship’s transformation through phantoms, empty graves and a seemingly corrupted timeline.
10. **“Is It Over Now?”** — Combines pop synths, accusations and self-destructive confessions to portray an obsessive romance resistant to closure.
11. **“Picture to Burn”** — A raucous, cathartic song about fury and empty threats against an ex rather than genuine revenge.
12. **“Holy Ground”** — A high-energy, humorous reflection on older heartbreak that benefits from hindsight and perspective.
13. **“The Black Dog”** — Uses aching yet righteous storytelling to examine pain, aftermath and the transformation of a former home into sacred ground.
14. **“Champagne Problems”** — Examines rumors of a woman’s madness, independence, nostalgia and conflict with a domestic future.
15. **“Death by a Thousand Cuts”** — Inspired by “Someone Great,” it portrays a relationship fading after people grow apart, with memories becoming reminders of lost intimacy.
16. **“Right Where You Left Me”** — Centers on acute yearning, as detailed memories intensify loneliness and lead Swift to ask her ex to return.
17. **“Clean”** — Uses synths and metaphors to capture the suffocation of heartbreak and the relief of recovery, with “clean” evoking both rain and sobriety.
18. **“The 1”** — Treats breaking up as a concept, expressing wistful longing for security and certainty that were never truly possessed.
19. **“Dear John”** — A rock-infused takedown whose confrontational force comes from vulnerability and woundedness.
20. **“All Too Well (10 Minute Version)”** — A long-form, detailed account of love’s lasting damage that became widely known after a targeted promotional campaign.

In a New Jersey Superior Court decision (Meola v. Ziman, Nov. 6, 1996), the court held that sick pay and wages paid for personal and family illness days are not collateral sources under N.J.S.A. 2A:15-97 and cannot be credited against a lost wages award. Plaintiff, a passenger injured in an accident caused by the defendant tortfeasor (the car's owner/driver, her husband), lacked income continuation insurance and sought lost wages; defendant sought a collateral source credit. Following Kiss v. Jacob, the court stated the statute's purpose of preventing duplicate benefits and noted that social security and insurance proceeds fall within it. Lacking New Jersey precedent, the court relied on Minnesota's Bruwelheide v. Garvey, other out-of-state cases, and American Jurisprudence § 576: such benefits are earned as part of compensation before injury and must be surrendered because of the defendant's negligence. Since plaintiff exhausted her accumulated sick leave and personal and family illness days, which she can no longer use for future illness or cash out at retirement, recovery would not be duplicative.

The paper examines how Ontario’s special education system excludes and marginalizes disabled, racialized, and other marginalized students despite policies presented as inclusive. It argues that inclusion requires more than inviting students into classrooms: students must belong, have their needs met, and participate in educational decision-making.

Historically, Canadian special education developed from residential institutions and segregated classes. Ontario established official special classes in 1910, while institutional and separate placements continued for decades. Civil rights movements in the 1960s helped advance integration, although disparities persist. Ontario’s later multicultural and anti-racist policies did not consistently reduce discrimination, and racialized students remain overrepresented in several special education disability categories.

Individual Education Plans involve multidisciplinary assessment and team-based placement decisions. Although disability identification can provide access to services, the paper criticizes its reliance on deficit-based diagnoses and labels. Ontario offers five placements: regular classes with indirect support, resource assistance, withdrawal assistance, special education with partial integration, and full-day special education classes. The paper also rejects the “empty vessel” model of teaching, arguing that knowledge emerges through interaction and must account for students’ goals, settings, and circumstances.

Major barriers include inadequate planning, insufficient teacher preparation, limited funding, large classes, unclear policy implementation, and policies whose stated commitments are not reflected in practice. Ontario’s 2018 Policy on Accessible Education for Students with Disabilities guarantees equal treatment and accommodations, with undue hardship assessed through cost, available funding, and health and safety requirements. However, educators receive limited guidance for implementing the policy. The paper also notes that disabled educators lack equivalent accessibility policies and face stigma.

Recommendations include involving students and educators in policy development, adopting intersectional, non-ableist, universal-design approaches, improving teacher training and funding, supporting disabled educators, and ensuring inclusive commitments appear in classroom practices. The paper concludes that the current system does not adequately value disabled students as learners, particularly within racialized populations, and that policies must be reformed to address systemic exclusion.

The Texas Instruments documentation for MSPM0C1105 and MSPM0C1106 covers development resources, support, revisions, and ordering information. X prototype devices have a higher expected failure rate and an undefined end-use failure rate, so TI recommends using only qualified production devices in production systems; TI’s standard warranty applies to MSP devices. Device-name suffixes indicate temperature range, package type, and distribution format.

The MSPM0 development ecosystem includes LaunchPad boards with exposed pins, built-in circuitry, software demonstrations, an XDS110 debug probe, BoosterPack modules, drivers, middleware, documentation, tools, and code examples. Browser-based and offline cloud tools support development. TI Resource Explorer provides access to SDKs, SysConfig configures devices and peripherals and generates code, MSP Academy offers training, GUI Composer simplifies evaluation of selected features, and the included TI Arm-Clang compiler supports TI Arm Cortex MCUs.

TI also provides E2E support forums, update notifications, device documentation, and mechanical, packaging, and orderable information. Revision A removed DGS32 package information and updated device, electrical, timing, CPU, and identification details. Package drawings address thermal-pad soldering, optional vias, stencil coverage, solder-mask tolerances, and package dimensions. Ordering footnotes cover lifecycle status, preproduction terms, RoHS, finishes, moisture sensitivity, reflow temperatures, and part marking. TI cautions that integrated circuits can be damaged by electrostatic discharge and provides resources and design data without warranties, placing application design, validation, testing, and compliance responsibilities on users.

George Bush said the Taiwan Relations Act provides an official, adequate basis for U.S.-Taiwan relations and should be enforced without demeaning restrictions on Taiwanese officials. He pledged fair and dignified treatment of Chinese officials, resistance to foreign interference, and consideration of both China and Taiwan’s views while preserving U.S. interests.

Addressing the Commonwealth Club, Bush cited its history of shaping presidential campaigns and criticized the Carter administration’s foreign policy record. He accused administration spokesmen of obscuring America’s weakened global posture and misrepresenting Ronald Reagan’s commitment to peace by portraying him as potentially leading the country into war. Bush called those claims false and irresponsible.

STAT’s Pharmalittle covers several pharmaceutical developments. The FDA approved another generic mifepristone abortion pill, allowing three U.S. companies to produce it despite opposition from anti-abortion groups and Trump-aligned politicians; the approval is unlikely to change access, as mifepristone combined with misoprostol accounts for about two-thirds of U.S. abortions. Amgen reported that its cholesterol-lowering drug Repatha met the primary goals of a 12,000-patient trial, reducing a composite of heart-disease death, heart attack and stroke, which could broaden its market. The newsletter also references delayed action on a Medicare drug-price negotiation loophole, pharmaceutical layoffs, tariffs and other industry issues.

The NHL’s Stanley Cup Final broadcast from Nashville opens with Luke Bryan performing on the roof of Tootsie’s Orchid Lounge. The league highlights the playoff atmosphere, CMA Fest, and hockey–country music crossover. PPG Arena is sold out, and Nashville screens will show the performance and game.

The passage introduces SafeBehavior, a hierarchical defense framework for mitigating jailbreak attacks against large language models. Motivated by humans’ adaptive, multistage reasoning, SafeBehavior operates during inference through three stages: intention inference, which summarizes a query’s underlying intent and screens for obvious harm; self-introspection, which evaluates the generated response for subtle risks and assigns a confidence score for acceptance, refusal, or revision; and self-revision, which rewrites uncertain responses to preserve user intent while reducing safety violations. The approach is designed to maintain normal output behavior on benign inputs, detect diverse attacks, and limit computational overhead. The threat model assumes a powerful adversary using optimization-based, contextual-manipulation, or prompt-based attacks. The method is evaluated against five attack types, including GCG, DeepInception, Papillon, PPPI, and IFSJ, and compared with seven defenses: Paraphrase, PPL Calculator, Intention Analysis, Retokenization, SafeDecoding, Self-Examination, and Self-Reminder. The passage also reviews white-box and black-box jailbreak techniques and prompt-level and model-level defense strategies.

This study develops and validates a concise learning module introducing critical multicultural education (CME) to pre-service English language teachers in Türkiye. It addresses a research gap: existing research largely comes from North America and Western Europe, while Turkish studies have focused mainly on multicultural education rather than its critical dimension.

Using a qualitative design, the researchers created a two-week, six-hour module covering transformative learning, CME, critical consciousness, critical language teaching, educational inequalities, power, privilege, and social justice. Its development followed four stages: researcher brainstorming and expert input; evaluation by a novice English teacher considered a “critical friend”; implementation with 15 pre-service teachers from four Turkish universities; and a revised implementation at Çanakkale Onsekiz Mart University with 86 students, 10 of whom were interviewed. The module included asynchronous pre- and post-study activities, two face-to-face sessions, readings, videos, discussions, reflection, mind mapping, and critical lesson planning. Small-group feedback led to revised topic sequencing, consolidated digital platforms, more visual materials, and clearer task guidance.

Participants reported personal benefits, including more positive attitudes toward diversity, greater understanding of social issues, improved organization of ideas, expanded knowledge, reduced prejudices, and increased confidence in discussing controversial topics. Professional benefits included greater awareness of educational ideologies, goals, power relations, and teachers’ roles; improved critical decision-making and lesson planning; familiarity with CME concepts; access to teaching resources; insights into critical English language teaching; and guidance on integrating CME into materials and classroom practice.

Reported challenges included the module’s short duration, limited time, dense content, teacher-centered delivery, insufficient guidance on taking critical action, and occasional hesitation during discussions. More visuals, videos, and interactive materials improved engagement, while explanatory questions and a more welcoming classroom atmosphere were used to encourage participation.

The study concludes that the introductory module met its aims of raising awareness, stimulating curiosity, and encouraging initial attitude changes toward CME. It recommends extending the module’s duration, distributing content over more time, adding interactivity and research opportunities, and providing more explicit strategies for critical action. Further research should examine diverse participants and contexts, combine quantitative and qualitative methods, and use longitudinal designs to assess long-term effects.

Using a distributive social justice framework, the study examines whether Pakistan’s higher education reforms have achieved equitable access, focusing on region, urban–rural location, gender, and public versus private provision. Following the establishment of the Higher Education Commission in 2002, enrollment rose from 2% in 2003 to 12.6% in 2021 through new campuses, financial aid, and quality initiatives. Nevertheless, growth remained concentrated in affluent urban areas.

Secondary data from HEC, AEPAM, Pakistan Bureau of Statistics, and the Pakistan Poverty Alleviation Fund were analyzed descriptively. Enrollment increased by approximately 500% between 2001–02 and 2020–21, while women’s enrollment share rose from 27% to 46% between 2001–02 and 2014–15. However, overall participation remained limited, and gender disparities persisted in poorer and less-developed regions.

Access varied sharply by poverty and geography. Extreme Poverty Zone 1, representing 5.6% of the population, had only one public university, no private universities, and enrollment below 0.5%. The low-poverty zone, representing 40% of the population, contained 138 universities and degree-awarding institutions. Punjab, Sindh Urban, and Islamabad recorded the largest enrollment shares, while rural Sindh, Baluchistan, AJK, and Gilgit-Baltistan had substantially lower participation and wider gender gaps. Private universities, concentrated in major cities, often charged fees far above public institutions, further restricting access for lower-income students.

The study concludes that reforms have not resolved structural inequalities associated with class, poverty, geography, rurality, and gender. Recommendations include opening adequately funded public universities in rural and high-poverty areas, regulating private universities, expanding targeted scholarships and inclusive admissions, providing affirmative support for disadvantaged students, and developing affordable, high-quality community colleges focused on rural skills training. Further research is needed on micro-level barriers, institutional practices, and vocational education.

On May 11, 2020, Apple Inc. completed a $8.5 billion debt offering comprising $2.0 billion of 0.750% notes due 2023, $2.25 billion of 1.125% notes due 2025, $1.75 billion of 1.650% notes due 2030, and $2.5 billion of 2.650% notes due 2050.
