In *Hill v. Levine*, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court considered whether a deed’s fifty-foot minimum-lot-frontage restriction had expired and encumbered the plaintiff’s title. The court held that the restriction was included among the deed’s “following restrictions,” limited to twenty years from August 20, 1896, and therefore expired on August 20, 1916. It was a personal agreement between grantor and grantee, not part of a scheme benefiting other lots or an equitable easement appurtenant to them, as subsequent deeds and the Land Court decree omitted it while retaining the building restrictions. Because the deed’s construction was not reasonably doubtful and other lot owners had no basis to challenge title, the possibility of future litigation did not justify refusing specific performance. The decree dismissing the plaintiff’s bill was reversed, specific performance was ordered, and the plaintiff was permitted to seek damages in the Superior Court.

President Yameen Abdul Gayoom said he was willing to hold an early presidential election amid growing unrest after the Maldives Supreme Court ordered the release and retrial of opposition political prisoners, including exiled former President Mohammed Nasheed. The court also reinstated 12 opposition lawmakers, costing Yameen’s party its parliamentary majority and prompting the postponement of Parliament’s opening. Police dispersed opposition protests with tear gas and batons, while Yameen dismissed two police chiefs after the department pledged to enforce the ruling. UN Secretary-General António Guterres urged respect for the court and all-party talks. Nasheed, whose abduction conviction was overturned, plans to challenge Yameen in this year’s election.

Manchester United reportedly received the go-ahead to make a £50 million bid for Fulham teenager Ryan Sessegnon, while Fulham prepare for his departure amid interest from United and Tottenham. Jose Mourinho has also discussed extending Marouane Fellaini’s contract, which expires this season.

Marine heatwaves are prolonged periods of unusually warm water at a particular location and can occur in any season. Analysis of more than a century of temperature data found that marine heatwave days increased by 54 per cent from 1925 to 2016, while their frequency rose by 34 per cent and duration by 17 per cent across the periods studied. Rising ocean temperatures are expected to produce more heatwaves globally.

Recent events have caused lasting ecological and economic damage. The 2011 western Australian heatwave destroyed kelp and seagrass, affecting wildlife and carbon storage; the 2012 Gulf of Maine heatwave disrupted the lobster fishery; and “The Blob” in the North Pacific from 2014 to 2016 caused fishery closures, marine-mammal strandings and algal blooms.

Human-caused climate change increased the likelihood of major events, including Great Barrier Reef bleaching in 2016 and an eight-month Tasman Sea heatwave affecting fisheries and aquaculture. Scientists are developing forecasts to help managers anticipate impacts and reduce risks, alongside urgent action to curb greenhouse-gas emissions.

Microsoft plans Windows 10 accessibility updates: reorganized Ease of Access settings, display enlargement and brightness options, improved Narrator controls and vocal text styling, and enhanced eye control. Insider builds offer early access, with more promised later this year.

Scientists used stored sperm from Sudan, the last male northern white rhino, to fertilize southern white rhino eggs, creating two frozen hybrid embryos that could eventually be implanted, though rhino embryo transfer is not yet developed. Researchers hope to produce northern white rhino embryos using eggs from Fatu and Najin, but biological uncertainties remain, and conservationists warn reproductive technology may overshadow other conservation efforts.

Carolina ended the 2016 season with a 17-16 loss to Tampa Bay, finishing 6-10. The Panthers led 7-3 before rallying to within one with 17 seconds left. Their two-point attempt failed when Greg Olsen slipped and Cam Newton’s pass fell incomplete. Newton completed 56% of his passes and threw three interceptions. The defense allowed 300 yards, while Graham Gano missed three field goals despite a broken bone in his plant foot. Young players were among the few positives. Carolina will select eighth in the NFL draft, their first top-10 pick since 2012.

An MIT study found that 3,000 pooled four-person sedans could meet 98% of Manhattan’s ride demand, potentially reducing congestion and pollution, though riders would wait 2.8 minutes and face 3.5-minute delays. Two thousand ten-passenger vans could further limit traffic. The findings depend on ride sharing, which drivers and passengers have resisted, and could displace many taxi and for-hire drivers.

The lecture examines Kerberos as a cryptographic protocol for authenticating users, workstations, and services over an untrusted network. It was designed for distributed systems in which clients access services such as file, mail, and print servers. The network is untrusted, all parties must trust the Key Distribution Center (KDC), and users must trust their own workstations; application servers need not trust one another, and extra trust relationships between them should be avoided.

The KDC stores a shared key for each Kerberos principal, mapping string names for users and services to cryptographic keys. A user’s key, \(K_C\), is derived from their password, while each service has a secret key, \(K_S\). A client initially contacts the Kerberos interface, sends its principal name and a requested service name, and receives a ticket plus a session key. The session key is protected with \(K_C\), allowing the client to discard its password-derived key afterward. The client can then use the Ticket Granting Service (TGS), another interface to the same KDC, to request tickets for other services. This separation limits the damage from disclosure of \(K_C\), though a stolen session ticket can still permit impersonation until it expires.

Kerberos principals may include instances for separate identities, while service principal names support mutual authentication by allowing clients to verify the identity of the server they contact. Kerberos authenticates users but does not perform application-level authorization; servers determine access through access-control lists and other mechanisms. Principal names are difficult to reuse safely because authorization records may retain an old user’s permissions and are not linked to corresponding Kerberos entries.

A service ticket contains the client and service names, client IP address, issue time, expiration time, and a session key encrypted under the service’s secret key. An authenticator contains the client name, IP address, and timestamp, encrypted with the session key. The service decrypts its ticket to identify the client and session key, then decrypts and checks the authenticator. Ticket lifetimes limit the usefulness of stolen tickets, while authenticator timestamps and server caches are intended to detect replay. The authenticator in Kerberos 4, however, is not bound to the specific application request, allowing an attacker to combine a fresh authenticator with an old request. Kerberos 5 addresses this by authenticating the request and authenticator together.

Kerberos 4 contains several weaknesses. It treats successful decryption as proof of authenticity and integrity, allowing encrypted data to be modified; Kerberos 5 adds separate keyed authentication. Its initial response is encrypted with the password-derived key, so an attacker can request it for another principal and test password guesses offline. Proposed defenses include salted, deliberately expensive key derivation, challenge-response authentication with rate limiting, and password-authenticated key exchange protocols such as SRP or PAKE. Kerberos 4 also uses only DES with 56-bit keys, which has become inexpensive to brute-force, whereas Kerberos 5 supports stronger algorithms including AES. IP-address binding is retained in Kerberos 5 but is optional and is not a sound substitute for cryptography.

Using one session key for both directions creates reflection risks: a message returned by a server can be replayed to that server as though it came from the client. A directional header can identify message origin, while Kerberos 5 instead negotiates separate keys for client-to-server and server-to-client traffic.

The KDC is a critical security target. If compromised, an attacker can issue tickets for any principal and impersonate users or services. Existing connections can continue during a KDC outage because data does not pass through it, and replicated, read-only KDC databases can answer authentication and ticket requests while the master is unavailable. Kerberos lacks general ticket revocation. If a service is compromised, its secret key must be changed through a secure, out-of-band administrative process; retaining the old key lets an attacker decrypt traffic and forge tickets for that service.

The kpassword service changes user passwords. It requires a ticket obtained directly through the initial Kerberos interface rather than through TGS, so possession of a stolen session ticket alone is insufficient. Kerberos 4’s password-change exchange can expose a chain of later passwords if an old password is later disclosed. Kerberos 5 instead uses Diffie–Hellman key exchange to establish a new secret that cannot be recovered merely from recorded traffic.

Remote password-based logins also require care: accepting any reply that decrypts with the entered password permits a forged KDC response. Kerberos therefore uses an additional TGS exchange with machines that share a secret key, allowing the machine to authenticate the KDC. Athena workstations can omit this extra step because local access already entails substantial control of the workstation.

Force erase affects only the user area, not the secure area. The card remains locked and retains Temporary and Group Write Protection during erasure; after the entire user area is erased, it becomes unlocked and clears those protections. An erase error classified as “don’t care” does not prevent continued force erase. While locked, the card accepts only specified commands, including CMD11 and CMD40, while other commands are illegal. ACMD6 is rejected when locked, and bus width may be changed only when unlocked. Hosts can identify the lock state through CARD_IS_LOCKED. Lock/unlock behavior varies among Type 1, Type 2, and Type 3 cards according to specification version, and hosts must follow stated cautions involving force erase, permanent write protection, temporary write protection, and COP cards with unknown passwords.

CMD55 causes the next command to be interpreted as an application-specific command. A defined, legal ACMD sets the APP_CMD status bit, while an undefined but legal command is treated as a normal command with the bit cleared. Illegal commands produce an Illegal Command Error, after which the next command is handled normally. ACMD41 is an exception and does not report APP_CMD status.

CMD6 switches or expands card functions in the access mode, command system, driver-strength, and power-limit groups. It is valid in Transfer State and is mandatory for cards compliant with version 1.10 or later. Mode 0 queries supported functions, resulting selections, and maximum current or power; Mode 1 changes functions. Function 0 is the default, 0xF retains the current selection, and busy functions cannot be changed. Selected functions return to their defaults after a power cycle, a reset CMD6, or CMD0. CMD6 returns an R1 response and a 512-bit status block, with a 100 ms timeout; a status CRC error requires a power cycle. Power Limit defaults to 0.72 W and must account for host supply and heat-release capability. In UHS-II mode, the access-mode and driver-strength groups are unused, the command-system group is optional, and the Power Limit group is mandatory.

Optional High-Speed mode uses a 50 MHz clock for a 25 MB/sec interface and is selected through CMD6. Because different timing modes cannot be controlled together, the host must drive only one card. CMD34–37, CMD50, and CMD57 are reserved for command-system extensions; their behavior depends on whether the standard, vendor-specific, or mobile-commerce function is selected.

CMD8 is issued in Idle state before ACMD41 to verify that the card supports the host’s supply voltage. A compatible card returns R7 with the voltage range and check pattern echoed; otherwise, it remains idle and does not respond. CCS from ACMD41 distinguishes SDSC from SDHC/SDXC. SDSC uses byte addresses and a CMD16-selected block length, while SDHC/SDXC use 512-byte block addressing, fixed 512-byte memory-access blocks, and do not support partial or misaligned access or write-protected groups.

The host may lower or stop the bus clock and must provide eight clocks after bus transactions for card completion. During ACMD41, the clock normally runs continuously at 100–400 kHz, with polling at intervals below 50 ms. CRC7 protects commands, most responses, CID, and CSD; CRC16 protects data blocks and is calculated separately on each DAT line in wide-bus mode. A CRC failure prevents command execution and response and sets the corresponding error status. Read, write, and erase operations have defined timeout rules, including a minimum 100 ms read timeout for high-capacity cards, write busy limits generally up to 250 ms but up to 500 ms for specified SDXC cases, and up to one second after a UHS-II data burst.

Commands have a fixed 48-bit format, are protected by CRC7, and are grouped into classes whose support is advertised through CCC and SCR information. Card Status, 512-bit SD Status, and queued Task Status provide command, feature, and task information. ACMD13 retrieves SD Status, while CMD13 can retrieve Card or Task Status.

Speed-class methods are optional and include Speed Classes 2, 4, 6, and 10, UHS Speed Grades 1 and 3, and Video Speed Classes 6, 10, 30, 60, and 90. The user area is divided into Allocation Units, each divided into 16 KB-based Recording Units that cannot cross AU boundaries. SDSC/SDHC definitions cover fragmented-AU write and move performance, random reads, and FAT-update overhead. SDXC performance applies to sequential writes in entirely free AUs, supports no move operation, and includes FAT, bitmap, directory-entry, and Continuous Information updates. Class 10 performance is defined for entirely free AUs, and CMD20 support is optional.

The disclosure describes methods and systems for detecting, processing, and responding to speech commands across multiple networked media devices, such as loudspeakers. Devices detect an activation or “Hot Word” and compute detection scores based on factors including signal power, Hot Word recognizer confidence, estimated user location relative to the device, and audio processing such as beamforming and noise suppression.

In a centralized approach, a group leader receives device scores, mutes playback, selects devices with the highest scores, activates their microphones, and combines their recorded speech data into a request for an external server. The server returns a requested action, which the leader distributes to the group; devices may play an audible confirmation. In a decentralized approach, devices broadcast scores and server-response confidence levels, and devices with leading values upload audio or perform the requested action.

The system may combine different portions of a spoken command from the best-positioned devices using per-segment or per-word scores and signal-to-noise comparisons supported by synchronized clocks. Networked devices may be dynamically assigned Player, Follower, and Renderer roles for synchronized content distribution, with leader selection based on capabilities such as processing power, codec support, and bandwidth or latency. Implementations may use processors, memory, stored instructions, hardware, or software, and may provide user controls over collection and processing of personal information.

Amazon.com, Inc. filed a Form 8-K dated August 15, 2017, reporting the pricing of a previously announced private placement offering of $16.0 billion in aggregate principal amount of senior unsecured notes. The related press release was filed as Exhibit 99.1.

President Trump told the World Economic Forum that the United States was experiencing strong economic growth, record stock-market highs, job gains, falling unemployment, and increased investment. He attributed this to tax cuts—including lowering the corporate rate from 35% to 21%—reduced regulations, expanded energy production, and bureaucratic reform. He also cited employer bonuses, Apple’s planned investment, and proposed trade agreements, including possible negotiations with remaining TPP countries.

Trump advocated fair, reciprocal trade to address intellectual-property theft, subsidies, and state-led economic planning. On security, he described U.S. efforts to pressure North Korea, confront Iran’s support for terrorism, defeat ISIS, strengthen borders and immigration enforcement, and ask allies to meet defense obligations. He also supported replacing extended-family immigration with a merit-based system and emphasized workforce development and reducing dependence.

In a question-and-answer session, Trump defended tax reform as politically difficult, said unexpected employer bonuses were contributing to investment and stock-market gains, and cited further job creation and record-low unemployment. He said his business experience, particularly buying and turning around struggling companies, prepared him for the presidency, and praised his administration’s pro-business policies and team. He closed by urging leaders to use their influence to benefit their citizens and workers.

The United Nations Conference on International Organization met in San Francisco from April 25 to June 26, 1945, to draft a charter for a world security organization. On June 25, delegates from fifty governments unanimously approved the UN Charter, the Statute of the International Court of Justice, and interim arrangements for the Preparatory Commission. The Charter was signed the next day by 153 delegates, with space reserved for Poland.

The U.S. Senate consented to ratification on July 28, President Truman ratified the Charter on August 8, and he signed the UN Participation Act on December 20. The Charter entered into force on October 24.

Based on the Dumbarton Oaks proposals and later government submissions, the Conference used four commissions, twelve technical committees, four general committees, and an International Secretariat. Committee recommendations progressed to commissions and then to the plenary. Conference records were published in a 22-volume bilingual series, with final instruments appearing in Chinese, English, French, Russian, and Spanish.

A year after *Loper Bright* overruled *Chevron* and ended broad judicial deference to agency statutory interpretations, the article identifies three doctrinal shifts: courts are applying independent textualist judgment; lower courts are divided over the declining use of *Skidmore* deference, with some treating consistent agency views as interpretive support; and Justice Kavanaugh has proposed an exception to the major questions doctrine for national security and foreign policy because of presidential Article II powers and congressional delegation in those areas. The major questions doctrine otherwise remains embedded in ordinary statutory meaning, requiring explicit congressional authorization for delegations of vast economic or political significance. The article anticipates that the Supreme Court’s pending tariff case may test Kavanaugh’s proposed exception.

Danica Patrick was booed by fans at Pocono Raceway after qualifying and, instead of "just keep walking," approached and lectured them, saying "I have feelings" and that her job is to drive the car, not sign autographs. The incident began when an adult male fan slipped through a cordon of fans and was physically restrained by a security guard; Patrick kept walking, was booed, and said she did not sign for the man because she felt it wrong to honor someone who disrespected security. While promoting next month's New Hampshire race in Boston, she said she "had a moment." Her comments sparked debate among drivers: Kevin Harvick said signing autographs is part of every driver's job; Ryan Blaney said it is not their job but something they should do, prioritizing kids; Dale Earnhardt Jr. said it paints her in a bad light but she brought it on herself, and noted signing autographs helps him when frustrated.

Live third-quarter updates from the Week 6 SEC matchup show Alabama leading No. 16 Vanderbilt. Scoring plays included a 30-yard Vanderbilt field goal, Ty Simpson touchdown passes to Germie Bernard and Ryan Williams, a Diego Pavia touchdown pass to Sedrick Alexander, and Alexander’s 65-yard rushing touchdown. Both quarterbacks passed and ran, while the game also featured sacks, punts, penalties and interceptions. Pavia fumbled near the goal line, but Alabama recovered.

The preview says Vanderbilt entered 5-0, while No. 10 Alabama rebounded from a loss to unranked Florida State with a road win over Georgia. Vanderbilt had also defeated then-No. 1 Alabama 35-4 in 2024. Pavia ranked among the nation’s top 10 in non-play-action passing statistics, while Simpson entered with 1,200 yards, 11 touchdowns, no interceptions and a 69% completion rate. Key matchups included Vanderbilt’s pass rush against Alabama’s offensive line and a potential Pavia-Simpson quarterback duel.

Scale-in is defined as gradually building up a position size as the market creates more entry opportunities; it is presented as a planned trading strategy within a broader plan, not a reaction aimed at rescuing a losing trade. For retail investors, scaling in means buying more shares as prices fall, assuming the decline is temporary, which can be seen as a mean-reversion method; dollar-cost averaging is a common implementation, involving setting a target price and investing in volumes as the stock drops below it. This approach lowers the average purchase price, minimizes downside and maximizes upside, but requires substantial discipline, since it means trading against the market and carries the risk of holding an incomplete position if the market reverses. For illiquid stocks it also reduces market impact on entry, though exit slippage remains an issue, which is where scale-out — gradually closing portions of a position, locking in profits and moving stops to break even — becomes relevant.

Day traders apply scale-in differently: they test with a small position and add only if the market moves in their favor, using floating profits from the winning position to fund added risk. The main risk is a sudden reversal wiping out those profits. Institutional traders scale in to fill large orders without moving prices or attracting front-runners; hedge funds such as Jim Simons' Medallion Fund are cited as users.

The scale-in strategy is contrasted with double-down and Martingale approaches, which are described as desperate attempts to salvage losing trades by adding larger positions to reach breakeven. For swing traders, the approach depends on strategy: mean-reversion traders add at reversal levels, while trend-following traders add to winning positions (e.g., adding 100 shares at $25 after a purchase at $20, potentially turning $1,000 into $1,500 of profit).

A backtest comparing full-equity entry on the first signal with a scale-in version showed the scale-in variant had a lower CAGR (equity falling from $1.4 million to $1.06 million), but the authors preferred it for more efficient capital use and improved risk-adjusted return, suggesting scaling in may be an alternative for many trading strategies.

This retrospective single-center study evaluated rebleeding risk among 226 adults with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage treated at Rennes University Hospital from 2020 to 2022. Rebleeding occurred in 33 patients (15%), with no significant differences between rebleeding and non-rebleeding groups in previously established risk factors. Each additional hour after symptom onset increased the odds of rebleeding by 0.7%, independently of other variables, while a higher WFNS score was also an independent predictor. Patients whose aneurysms were secured within 24 hours had a 9% rebleeding rate, compared with 21% among those treated after 24 hours. One- and six-month outcomes did not differ significantly between groups, although patients without rebleeding had a higher rate of Glasgow Outcome Scale 5 at six months. Limitations included the retrospective design, few events, and a pragmatic rebleeding definition that could not always definitively exclude other causes of neurological deterioration. The findings support securing aneurysms as early as possible after symptom onset.

This study evaluated the German 17-item Speech, Spatial and Qualities of Hearing Scale (SSQ17) as a measure of hearing-loss-related quality of life in patients with unilateral Ménière’s disease. Ninety-seven consecutive patients were recruited from a multicenter prospective registry and underwent comprehensive vestibular assessment, MRI, pure-tone audiometry, speech audiometry, and the SSQ17.

Most participants had definite Ménière’s disease, the mean age was 56.2 years, 56.7% were female, and 51.6% used hearing aids. Hearing loss was asymmetric: affected ears had mean 4-frequency pure-tone average of 51.9 dB HL versus 19.3 dB HL in unaffected ears, and monosyllable recognition was 33.9% versus 86.6%.

The mean SSQ17 total score was 6.0, with subscale means of 5.3 for speech hearing, 5.1 for spatial hearing, and 7.2 for qualities of hearing. Scores did not differ significantly among diagnostic categories. Only the additional question on listening in quiet showed a ceiling effect.

The SSQ17 demonstrated excellent internal consistency, with Cronbach’s alpha of 0.960 for the total score and 0.904–0.956 for the subscales. Scores correlated negatively with affected-ear pure-tone thresholds and positively with affected-ear speech-recognition scores for several domains. The researchers concluded that the SSQ17 is a viable tool for assessing hearing-related disability in Ménière’s disease and complements clinical audiometric measures, although it does not assess the broader burden of vertigo or overall disease-specific quality of life.

Inflammation is closely associated with depression and may affect neurotransmitter metabolism, neuroplasticity, dopamine production, and mood. This paper reviews animal evidence and clinical randomized controlled trials of pharmacological and non-pharmacological anti-inflammatory strategies. The animal literature included 31 studies and identified NLRP3, NF-κB, and P2X7R pathways as potential therapeutic targets. Interventions including empagliflozin, vitamin D analogues, natural extracts, acupuncture, exercise, and photobiomodulation improved depression-like behaviors or neuroinflammation in animal models, although most studies were short-term and small-scale.

The clinical scoping review analyzed 11 articles published from 2008 to 2024, encompassing 907 patients with depression. Treatments varied widely and included fluoxetine, infliximab, ketamine, minocycline, celecoxib, glycopyrrolate, SSRIs, and lacquer tree, with treatment lasting two to 18 weeks. Most inflammatory markers were undetectable, although CRP, hs-CRP, soluble TNF receptors, IL-2, IL-6, and TNF-α were measurable in some studies. Anti-inflammatory adjuncts showed favorable results in selected trials, and higher baseline hs-CRP or CRP/TNF levels were associated with better responses to minocycline or infliximab. However, effects were variable, celecoxib was noninferior to placebo while carrying side-effect risks, and evidence was generally heterogeneous and short-term.

The authors identify major barriers to clinical translation, including the inability of fixed animal models to represent heterogeneous human depression, unclear biomarker selection, limited long-term safety and efficacy data, individual differences, and higher costs from drugs and inflammatory testing. They propose systematic development and validation of inflammatory markers, more individualized and combined treatment strategies, and AI-supported patient monitoring and interpretation of clinical data. A proposed AI-guided microrobot for continuous inflammation monitoring and targeted medication delivery remains prospective. The authors conclude that pharmacological anti-inflammatory strategies currently have limited feasibility and recommend greater emphasis on non-pharmacological approaches, such as exercise and positive thinking, alongside affordable, generalizable research.

The article examines calendar effects in long-term U.S. Treasuries using the TLT ETF, which tracks 20-year bonds, over 2004–August 2021. It explains that bond prices and interest rates move inversely and identifies two recurring patterns: weak performance during the first seven trading days of each month and stronger returns during the rest of the month. A long end-of-month strategy reportedly beat buy-and-hold with relatively low market exposure, while a short strategy based on the weak opening days performed poorly alone. Combining the strategies produced a 10.2% annual return versus 3.8% for buy-and-hold, with a 24% maximum drawdown versus 48%. An improved short strategy, held from the previous month’s close through the seventh trading day’s close, averaged 0.6% per trade, had a 5.5% CAGR, and a profit factor of 2. The article also provides Python code for its strategies.

On November 29, 2001, Enron was poised to file what was expected to be the largest corporate bankruptcy reorganization in history after Dynegy abandoned its proposed $23 billion acquisition, citing Enron’s severe operational deterioration. Enron had more than $15 billion in publicly held debt, more than $61 billion in assets, less than $2 billion in cash, and was due to pay lenders $690 million by mid-December. PricewaterhouseCoopers was appointed administrator for Enron’s European holding company and certain operating companies. Enron’s unraveling followed an October disclosure that partnership accounting had reduced shareholder equity by $1.2 billion, prompted lawsuits and an SEC investigation, and led Enron to restate nearly five years of earnings.

The collapse disrupted trading, credit and financial markets worldwide. NYMEX required written authorization for members to accept Enron orders and raised futures margins. Enron reopened EnronOnline solely to close outstanding positions, while rival ICE reported a 65% increase in November trading and a 30% increase in users. Enron had roughly $18.7 billion in derivatives liabilities as of September 30, prompting dealers to prepare for a historically large unwind. European exchanges suspended or restricted Enron’s trading, and the company reportedly guaranteed European electricity deliveries only through Friday. U.S. gas and power trading remained generally orderly, while British prompt power prices fell sharply and German prices were volatile. Enron’s overseas assets, including holdings across Latin America, India and Europe, were expected to complicate any bankruptcy, and Brazil said it could seek to seize Enron’s local assets.

Credit concerns spread to lenders and investors. Credit Suisse First Boston estimated roughly $500 million each in direct Enron loan exposure for Bank of America, Citigroup and J.P. Morgan Chase, with additional exposure at Bank One and Wachovia. German banks also reported sizable but potentially recoverable exposure. Reliant Resources said its approximately $80 million exposure was manageable, while Williams estimated its net exposure below $100 million. Many European energy companies and funds reported limited exposure or had sold Enron holdings earlier, although four Japanese money-management funds fell below par value because of Enron bond losses and faced heavy redemptions.

Enron shares fell to $0.41, were removed from the S&P 500 and were expected to leave shareholders with no recovery in bankruptcy. Its distressed bonds traded around 22 cents on the dollar, with market pricing indicating an imminent filing and little expectation of further interest payments. Treasury yields fell as investors sought safety, bank bond spreads widened, and Enron’s troubles added to concerns about the dollar and U.S. corporate credit.

Enron’s metals unit attracted possible buyers, while its 44%-owned NewPower said it had enough cash and credit through the second quarter and expected a possible Enron bankruptcy would not affect its earnings. The crisis also delayed a $108 million Houston office project because Enron’s expected departure from its headquarters space could increase vacancies and lower rents. Senate Majority Leader Tom Daschle called for Congress to investigate Enron’s collapse and assess whether it exposed broader problems in the energy industry.

Digital laggards often set high-level goals without clearly linking them to strategy, causing employees to deprioritize poorly understood objectives and become misaligned. A “culture of genius” can worsen this problem by encouraging individuals to pursue what they believe is best, even when it conflicts with broader goals.

A data-driven culture supports vertical and horizontal alignment: shared metrics connect individuals and teams to company goals, while common data models and transparent access improve collaboration. Digital leaders emphasize learning, transparent data access, clear progress metrics, and consistency among leadership beliefs, stated values, and daily behavior. Laggards recognize data culture’s importance, but entrenched habits, limited skills, and insufficient top-down focus impede change.

Technologically mature firms tend to combine learning, risk-taking, transparency, and measurement with values-aligned practices. Organizations fall into four patterns: data novices, insight-ready organizations, tech-enabled organizations, and data-reliant organizations that may over-rely on data at the expense of critical thinking. Each can target actions based on its strengths.

A Seattle Public Utilities study found that extreme, long-lasting rainstorms have become more common and severe, while typical showers and drizzle have changed little. Using updated modeling, SPU estimates rainfall once expected every 100 years—4 inches in 24 hours and 1.86 inches in six hours—can now be expected every 25 years; the new 24-hour extreme threshold exceeds 5 inches. SPU will use the data to design drainage, sewage and flood-control projects because existing infrastructure was built for a less intense climate. A storage tunnel under the Lake Washington Ship Canal is intended to keep nearly 60 million gallons of polluted water from entering the canal annually. Officials linked the trend to climate change and said Western Washington needs improved flood preparedness.

NVIDIA’s RTX Blackwell architecture introduces major advances in ray tracing, neural rendering, GPU scheduling, media processing, display connectivity, and power efficiency.

- **Mega Geometry** treats clusters of up to 256 triangles as first-class primitives. Spatially compact batches are built into Cluster-level Acceleration Structures (CLAS), which are then used to construct final BVHs. Because each CLAS contains roughly 100 triangles, subsequent BVH processing is reportedly 100 times less expensive than classic triangle-based methods. CLAS can be generated on demand and cached. All APIs are fully batched and driven from GPU memory, allowing LOD selection, animation, and culling to run on the GPU with minimal CPU communication.
- A **Partitioned Top-Level Acceleration Structure (PTLAS)** supports large scenes by persisting a top-level hierarchy and updating only changed partitions. Static scene regions can remain unchanged while dynamic objects are rebuilt each frame.
- Mega Geometry can map subdivision-surface tessellation directly to cluster generation, enabling fast BVH construction for animated, displaced subdivision surfaces. Support is listed for DirectX 12 through NVAPI, Vulkan vendor extensions, and OptiX 9.0, across RTX GPUs from Turing onward.
- Blackwell’s fourth-generation RT Cores include cluster engines for geometry and BVH compression, deliver up to twice the ray-triangle intersection rate of third-generation RT Cores, and can reduce VRAM use by hundreds of megabytes in typical scenes.
- **Linear Swept Spheres (LSS)** provide hardware-based ray intersection for strand-like geometry. Their spherical radii may vary along each segment, and the hardware also supports ordinary spheres. Rendering human hair with LSS is stated to be about twice as fast as with DOTS while using roughly one-fifth the VRAM.

- **Shader Execution Reordering 2.0** improves GPU thread reordering for divergent ray-tracing and neural workloads. Blackwell’s reorder logic is twice as efficient and more precise, while its application-controlled API provides additional shader-invocation flexibility. Existing applications using SER benefit from the enhancements without code changes.
- The programmable **AI Management Processor (AMP)** uses a dedicated RISC-V processor to schedule GPU contexts on the GPU rather than the system CPU. It aligns with Windows HAGS, reduces CPU dependency and scheduling latency, and coordinates AI, graphics, and other workloads more predictably.

- Blackwell adds hardware encode and decode support for **4:2:2 chroma-sampled H.264 and HEVC**. The format retains full luminance and half the original chrominance information, requiring two-thirds the uncompressed 4:4:4 data while providing twice the color resolution of compressed 4:2:0.
- The ninth-generation **NVENC** encoder improves AV1 and HEVC quality by 5% in BD-BR PSNR and adds 4:2:2 encoding. Its AV1 Ultra High Quality mode adds a further 5% improvement, with combined gains of up to 15%. The RTX 5090 supports three encoders and two decoders, providing more than 50% generation-over-generation export-speed improvement and four times the speed of an RTX 3090. A sixth-generation NVDEC decoder provides twice-as-fast H.264 decoding and 4:2:2 support.
- **DisplayPort 2.1b** supports up to 80 Gbps through UHBR 20, including 8K at 165 Hz and 4K at 480 Hz with DSC.

- Blackwell’s **Max-Q power improvements** include fine-grained clock, power, and voltage-rail gating; a complete GDDR7 memory clock tree that can be switched off; and separate rails for GPU cores and memory. Clocks can respond to workload changes 1,000 times faster than on earlier architectures, while the deepest sleep state is entered ten times faster than on Ada. One small-language-model inference example reports power savings of up to 50%.

- **DLSS 4 Multi Frame Generation** can create up to three additional frames for each traditionally rendered frame. Its AI model is 40% faster and uses 30% less VRAM than the previous method, while an AI optical-flow model replaces hardware optical flow. Enhanced Flip Metering moves pacing to the display engine for more consistent frame timing.
- DLSS 4 replaces the earlier CNN-based models with transformer models for Super Resolution, Ray Reconstruction, and Deep Learning Anti-Aliasing. The transformers can use twice as many parameters and better recognize long-range patterns. Reported benefits include greater temporal stability, less ghosting, improved detail in motion, stronger anti-aliasing, and reduced ray-tracing denoiser artifacts.

- Blackwell supports **neural shaders** through the Cooperative Vectors API for DirectX 12 and Vulkan and differentiable shading features in Slang. Proposed applications include neural texture compression, with stated compression of up to seven-to-one over block-compressed formats.
- **RTX Neural Materials** uses neural approximations of complex layered materials for real-time ray tracing. **Neural Texture Compression** reduces material-data requirements; one demonstration falls from 1,110 MB to 333 MB while improving visual quality. **Stochastic Texture Filtering** reduces aliasing and moiré patterns and benefits from Blackwell’s doubled point-sampled texture-filtering rate.
- The **Neural Radiance Cache** sends path-traced rays after one bounce to a neural model trained on live game data, allowing it to infer final lighting across many additional bounces. **RTX Skin** brings film-style subsurface scattering to real-time game rendering. **RTX Neural Faces** uses a TensorRT-optimized generative model to infer natural faces from a rasterized face and 3D pose data.

- The Blackwell GPU family includes **GB202**, with 92.2 billion transistors, 24,576 CUDA cores, 192 RT Cores, 768 Tensor Cores, and a 512-bit memory interface; it powers the GeForce RTX 5090. **GB203** has 45.6 billion transistors, 10,752 CUDA cores, 84 RT Cores, 336 Tensor Cores, and a 256-bit interface; it powers the RTX 5080 and RTX 5070 Ti. **GB205** has 31 billion transistors, 6,400 CUDA cores, 50 RT Cores, 200 Tensor Cores, and a 192-bit interface; it powers the RTX 5070. The 1942 *Foreign Relations* series comprises six volumes covering general, regional, Near Eastern, African, and American topics, plus a previously published unnumbered volume on China. NVIDIA Corporation reported second-quarter fiscal 2016 revenue of $1.153 billion, up 5% from $1.103 billion a year earlier. Gross profit was $634 million, operating income was $76 million, and net income was $26 million, or $0.05 per diluted share, compared with $619 million, $163 million, and $128 million, or $0.22 per diluted share, respectively. For the first six months, revenue rose 4% to $2.304 billion, while net income declined to $160 million, or $0.28 per diluted share, from $265 million, or $0.46. The effective tax rate rose to 64.0% for the quarter and 34.3% for the half, primarily reflecting an Icera-related deferred tax asset write-down.

GPU revenue increased 9% to $959 million for the quarter, driven by higher sales of high-end GeForce gaming products, while GPU operating income rose to $273 million. Tegra Processor revenue fell 19% to $128 million and operating loss widened to $41 million, as declines in OEM smartphone and tablet sales were partly offset by higher automotive sales. Six-month GPU revenue rose 7%, while Tegra revenue declined 8%.

At July 26, 2015, NVIDIA held $435 million of cash and cash equivalents and $4.070 billion of marketable securities. Total assets were $6.979 billion, long-term debt was $1.399 billion, and shareholders’ equity was $4.185 billion. Six-month operating cash flow was $409 million, investing activities provided $12 million, and financing activities used $483 million.

NVIDIA recorded $89 million of restructuring and other charges for the wind-down of Icera modem operations and expects an additional $15 million to $25 million during the remainder of fiscal 2016. The activities affect about 5% of the global workforce. The company also announced a recall of SHIELD 8-inch tablets sold from July 2014 to July 2015 because of battery overheating risks, recording $21 million of related costs in the first six months, including $15 million in the second quarter.

During the quarter, NVIDIA entered a $400 million accelerated share repurchase agreement and initially received 14 million shares. It also paid $52 million in dividends, returning $452 million of capital to shareholders in total. The company had $1.60 billion of remaining repurchase authorization as of quarter-end.

NVIDIA continued patent litigation involving Qualcomm and Samsung while defending against Samsung’s patent and false-advertising claims; no loss accrual was recorded because potential liabilities were not considered probable or reasonably estimable. It also began an off-balance-sheet build-to-suit lease arrangement for a new Santa Clara headquarters, with banks committing to fund up to $380 million of construction costs. Product developments included the GeForce GTX 980 Ti, cuDNN 3.0, the Pascal architecture roadmap, the SHIELD Android TV, and the DRIVE PX autonomous-driving platform.

The application describes a vehicle driving-assistance and vision system using exterior cameras and optional radar, lidar, LADAR, ultrasonic, and other sensors to detect surrounding objects, lane conditions, and faster vehicles approaching from behind. A processor uses sensor data to determine rearward vehicles’ speed, direction, lane, distance, and available space. It may alert the driver visually, audibly, or haptically and/or automatically accelerate the ego vehicle to match a rearward vehicle’s speed and/or change lanes to mitigate or avoid a rear-end collision. Maneuvers may be driver-triggered, suggested to the driver, or autonomous under assisted, supervised, or higher automation modes. After passing, the ego vehicle may return to its original lane and speed. Decision logic can account for relative speeds and distances, gaps, adjacent-lane space, other traffic, exits, speed limits, lane-change discomfort or delay, safety, and emergency vehicles. The system also supports adaptive cruise-control limits based on the driver, vehicle, trailer, and license type; object detection with display overlays; rear-vehicle detection on curved or occluded roads; and vehicle-to-vehicle and vehicle-to-infrastructure communication.

Mapbox announced partnerships with Microsoft, ARM and Intel’s Mobileye to expand its autonomous-driving mapping tools. Its software will integrate with Microsoft Azure to process camera data and improve navigation algorithms, work with ARM to accelerate feature recognition, and use Mobileye’s cloud data to provide maps about 200 meters ahead as a backup to onboard sensors.

The Seventh Circuit reversed and remanded a case challenging Illinois county jail bail fees imposed in addition to posted bail under state law authorizing counties to charge at least a $1 fee. Six former detainees alleged monetary injury from fees of $11 in Kane County and $15 in DuPage County and asserted Eighth and Fourteenth Amendment claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983.

The court held that the named plaintiffs stated viable individual claims and satisfied Article III standing because their payment of the fees was a concrete injury traceable to each county’s jail policy and redressable through litigation. The district court’s dismissal of the entire action was therefore improper; at minimum, the individual cases against Kane and DuPage Counties had to proceed.

The court also reversed dismissal of the proposed classes against Kane and DuPage Counties, leaving certification and the effects of related actions in Coleman and Ringswald for the district court on remand. Although no named plaintiffs sued the other 17 counties, the common state statute created a “juridical link” that could permit one class action if the plaintiffs satisfied Rule 23’s certification requirements, including typicality, numerosity, commonality, and adequate representation. The court did not itself certify the class and noted that the district court had not undertaken the necessary analysis.

The study demonstrates solid-state near-infrared-to-visible photon upconversion using a DIB-SQ:PCBM bulk-heterojunction sensitizer integrated with a rubrene annihilator and photoemitter, optionally doped with DBP. DIB-SQ acts as the NIR-absorbing electron donor and PCBM as the electron acceptor. Tuning the DIB-SQ:PCBM ratio identified 1:3 as optimal for overall upconverted emission; PCBM loading reduced squaraine aggregation and enabled charge-transfer-mediated population of rubrene triplets. Devices with neat DIB-SQ or PCBM showed little or no upconversion, whereas the blend emitted visible light under low-intensity incoherent 690 nm excitation.

Transient absorption and time-resolved measurements showed that photoexcited donor or acceptor singlets undergo charge separation and form singlet and triplet charge-transfer states. These states transfer energy directly or through molecular triplets in PCBM to populate rubrene triplets. Two rubrene triplets then undergo triplet-triplet annihilation, regenerating a rubrene singlet that emits at 550–650 nm. Charge-transfer states depopulated within approximately 100 ps, while the rubrene triplet population rose over about 5.2 ns and decayed over approximately 1.4 μs.

Doping rubrene with 0.5 vol.% DBP shifted the upconverted emission peak from 562 to 605 nm and increased the emitter’s photoluminescence quantum yield. The DIB-SQ:PCBM (1:3)/rubrene:DBP device reached a saturated upconversion quantum yield of 1.36% above 69.7 mW/cm². Its excitation-intensity response changed from a slope of 1.66 to a linear slope of 1.01 at a threshold of 60.5 mW/cm², reported as among the lowest for solid-state upconversion systems.

A magnetic-field-induced reduction of nearly 10% in upconverted emission at 300 mT, contrasted with increased direct-excitation photoluminescence, further supported triplet-triplet annihilation. The work concludes that fullerene charge-transfer states, often treated as photogeneration losses, can instead serve as intermediates that transfer triplet energy to rubrene and enable NIR-driven upconversion in solid-state optoelectronic devices.

The £1,100 Marin Nail Trail 6 is a trail hardtail with a hydroformed 6061 aluminium frame, offered in four sizes with 27.5- or 29-inch wheels. It features a 120mm RockShox Recon fork, 68-degree head angle, internally routed dropper post, SRAM GX 1×11 drivetrain with an 11–42 Sunrace cassette, Shimano Deore hydraulic brakes, Formula hubs, and Schwalbe tyres. San Diego Unified School District rescinded a resolution inviting newly confirmed Education Secretary Betsy DeVos after objections from the teachers’ union, parents, and community partners. The resolution, sponsored by board president Richard Barrera and Trustee John Lee Evans, aimed to showcase district public schools; Barrera withdrew his support. After protesters blocked DeVos from entering a Washington, D.C., school, American Federation of Teachers President Randi Weingarten condemned the action but invited her to visit public schools. The Court denied the plaintiffs’ motion to dismiss the defendants’ devolutive appeal. Filing three transcripts under the same docket number substantially complied with the law because, together, they contained all proceedings, evidence, and documents from the lower court; requiring a new complete transcript would have been unduly burdensome.

Appellants were not required to name every appellee in their appeal petition; requesting citation of the parties shown by the record was sufficient, with issuance of citations being the clerk’s duty. Omitting the heirs of deceased defendant M. B. Miller did not prejudice the appellants because the record did not establish that they knew of his death when filing, and counsel stated that his heirs had acquiesced in the judgment. Acquiescence by four appellants likewise did not affect the other appellants’ right to appeal, though the Court could decline to adjudicate against those who formally established acquiescence. Because the devolutive appeal was filed before the permitted delay expired, the motion was denied with costs.

Victor Wembanyama’s unusual offseason was shaped by a serious, potentially life-threatening shoulder condition that he said deeply affected him and motivated physical and mental growth. He trained with Hakeem Olajuwon, studied with Kevin Garnett, played soccer in Costa Rica and Tokyo, and spent 10 days at a Shaolin temple in China studying Kung Fu and Chan meditation, while also visiting NASA and organizing a chess and basketball tournament in France.

Olajuwon and Wembanyama completed four 2½-hour workouts focused on maximizing his size, perimeter skills and energy efficiency. Wembanyama developed variations of the “Dream Shake,” added spin moves and kept a jump hook under wraps, while Olajuwon envisioned him as a “big guard” capable of playing all five positions.

Wembanyama also sought to strengthen his connection with San Antonio by holding fan-supporter tryouts, designing a fan atmosphere and leading chants, and bringing the Spurs to a Texas high school for a community workout shortly after devastating floods. Teammates and coaches described him as stronger, more controlled, curious and motivated, and Wembanyama said he was ready to return to basketball.

Case summaries cover bankruptcy, civil rights, constitutional law, criminal law, employment and labor law, family law, insurance, litigation, municipal law, negligence and intentional tort, and real property. In *In re Hood*, the Sixth Circuit held that the Tennessee Student Assistance Corporation lacked sovereign immunity in an educational-loan dischargeability action and affirmed the bankruptcy court’s denial of its motion to dismiss. In *Thakur v. Department of Corrections*, the court found no evidence refuting the department’s nondiscriminatory reason for not interviewing the plaintiff and affirmed summary disposition for defendants. In *People v. Bridgewater*, omission of a negligent-homicide instruction was found to have been waived, with no ineffective assistance or prejudice; convictions were affirmed. In *People v. Byars*, dismissal with prejudice for delayed discovery was held to be an abuse of discretion, and the case was reversed and remanded. *People v. Ferguson*, *People v. Knott*, *People v. Minge*, and *People v. Williams* respectively addressed counsel’s performance, destruction of a videotape, suppression of evidence, and joint representation; all results were affirmed. In *Slawick v. Detroit Newspaper Agency*, the former employee’s defamation claim was not preempted by federal labor law, evidence supported actual malice, and the damages awards were affirmed.

Three parental-rights termination decisions—*In re Guy*, *In re Jones*, and *In re Pittao*—were affirmed on clear and convincing evidence. In *Van Reken v. Michigan Basic Property Insurance Ass’n*, the loss-payable clause was held to be ordinary, leaving the landowners with no greater recovery rights than the insured vendors; the court reversed and remanded for summary disposition for the defendant. In *Moton v. Oakwood Healthcare, Inc.*, the court affirmed striking a supplemental witness list because the defendant did not timely conduct discovery or adequately explain the delay. In *Domine v. Township of Grosse Ile*, the appellate court reinstated the zoning board’s denial of a variance because substantial evidence supported its decision and the hardship was self-created. In *Berry v. John Carlo, Inc.*, the fireman’s rule barred the injured police officer’s claim; in *Garrison v. Mount Clemens General Hospital*, the evidence did not establish hospital negligence; and in *Girard v. Dearborn Cinemas*, the ladder danger was open and obvious. All three decisions were affirmed.

The passage describes the device’s power management, reset, clocking, interrupt, timing, and peripheral-interface behavior. Core Logic Voltage Domains support independently selectable operating performance points that pair maximum module frequencies with voltage ranges; lower-frequency points use lower voltages, and operating points can change in real time through DVFS. Only specified combinations are supported, DDR access must stop before changing DDR frequency, and CVDD domains must remain within 150 mV of one another. Adaptive Voltage Scaling is described but marked unsupported. Switchable SRAM enters shutdown when its power domain turns off, losing its contents, while selected always-on SRAM can be shut down separately.

Power-up and power-down sequences must follow specified ordering and ramping requirements; 3.3-V supplies must not exceed the 1.8-V supplies by more than 2 V. PLL and analog supplies require filtering, and power pins require nearby decoupling and bulk capacitance. Low-power standby turns off switchable domains, runs the Cortex-A8 at its lowest frequency, and clock-gates unused blocks.

System resets include power-on, external, emulation, watchdog, software global warm and cold, test, and local resets. Their effects differ in which logic and peripherals are reset. POR resets the full chip, while warm resets generally preserve test, emulation, and optionally EMAC Switch logic. PCIe and EMAC Switch reset isolation can preserve selected functions and traffic. Reset behavior affects pin states, BTMODE latching, RSTOUT_WD_OUT, power-domain state, and Boot ROM execution. When resets coincide, the highest-priority request is processed.

Clocking supports DEV and AUX references from crystals or 1.8-V LVCMOS sources, a differential SERDES reference, optional audio and 32.768-kHz inputs, selectable clock outputs, and multiple PLLs. PLLs start in bypass mode and must meet specified reference, DCO, output, SYSCLK, and module-frequency limits; PLL_USB must be programmed to 960 MHz when USB is used.

The Cortex-A8 interrupt controller handles up to 128 programmable-priority requests, while the C674x controller combines 128 events into 12 prioritized interrupts and supports multiplexed sources. Peripheral sections cover DCAN, EDMA, Advanced Event Triggering, trace, JTAG, the three-port gigabit EMAC switch and MDIO, GPIO, and GPMC/ELM memory and error-location functions. Electrical tables provide interface timing requirements, and board-routing analysis should account for PCB delays and IBIS models.

The HDMI transmitter supports HDMI 1.3a video and audio, including CEC, DDC, and multiple color-depth and resolution modes. PCB guidance requires controlled TMDS impedance, paired vias, suitable trace geometry, DDC pullups, and an ESD-protection device with no more than 5 pF of capacitance.

In *Ángel Bracero v. S. Ramírez & Co., Inc.* (No. 4453, decided July 24, 1930), the Supreme Court of Puerto Rico reversed a District Court of San Juan judgment awarding damages to plaintiff Ángel Bracero for injuries sustained when bags of rice fell on him in the defendant's shop in Ponce.

The majority (Justice Wolf) noted that the trial court found Bracero to be an independent contractor rather than a workman covered by the Workmen's Compensation Act, so his claim was not barred on that ground, and that the evidence supported the finding that the defendant maintained a branch in Ponce. The court then reached the case on other grounds, criticizing appellant's brief for lacking the "concise" statement of the case required by Rule 42 (assignment of errors should appear early, with argument following), and noting that the appellee had not discussed the doctrine of *res ipsa loquitur* as applied to the facts.

The majority held *res ipsa loquitur* inapplicable: the plaintiff and other workmen were removing sacks from the pile, so the situation was not one in which the defendant had exclusive control, and the plaintiff bore the burden of showing that the intervention of others was harmless. The court found no reason to apply the doctrine and questioned whether it could be invoked for the first time in that court. Agreeing with the appellant that the record showed no negligence attributable to the defendant at the time of the accident, the court reversed the judgment.

Chief Justice Del Toro, dissenting (Justice Hutchison concurring), would have affirmed. He recounted the trial court's findings: on July 8, 1922, Bracero was carting rice for the defendant's Ponce branch; a pile twenty bags high collapsed without his touching it, pinning him; he sustained fractures of his right thigh and hip, a shortened leg, a 15–20 percent loss of use of the leg, partial incapacity for work, and physical and mental pain, and was hospitalized two months. Witness Miguel Muñoz testified he warned the defendant's agents the pile was badly formed and might fall, and that the defendant instead propped it up. Del Toro found the defendant's conduct grossly negligent, the evidence fully supported the trial court's findings, and no passion, prejudice, bias, or manifest error requiring reversal.

In 2011, Akamai was the world’s largest content delivery network, operating more than 100,000 servers across 1,976 networks in 78 countries. It delivered streaming video, website content, cloud infrastructure, security, networking, and related services to major global customers, including Apple, Amazon, Microsoft, Samsung, Netflix, and government agencies.

As vice president of engineering for Akamai’s intelligent platform and international support and services, Charley Dublin identified “Akamai’s localization challenge.” Akamai’s market share declined with distance from the United States as local competitors gained ground, multinational customers developed their own services, and local CDNs offered simpler, cheaper products. Dublin argued that Akamai needed to orient its metrics toward local markets to preserve its global position.

Akamai distinguished itself through a decentralized network of servers placed close to end users, often at Internet service providers. This “edge” approach enabled faster delivery and benefited ISPs by allowing requests to remain within their networks, but required substantially more infrastructure than competing CDNs.

The market included large standalone providers such as Limelight and CDNetworks, an emerging telecom federation called OCX, and in-house capabilities built by Amazon, Microsoft, and other large technology companies. It also included numerous local CDNs focused on locally produced content and competing on price. Meanwhile, Akamai expanded internationally from 2000, generating 29% of its 2011 revenue outside the United States.

Akamai developed products centrally in Cambridge and set global prices, which were generally localized only through currency conversion. Sales targets were also established centrally and often failed to reflect local working hours, customer needs, relationships, or competitive conditions. Headquarters lacked systematic methods for evaluating products and markets before expansion. For example, Akamai acquired U.S.-based Velocitude and imposed sales targets in Japan, where comparable technology had existed since 2002 and local managers rejected the product. Tests in South Korea also revealed that CDNetworks offered locally relevant performance at much lower prices, while Akamai had only a 10% market share compared with CDNetworks’ roughly 70%. Akamai’s brand was also little known in some markets, including China.

In 2011, Akamai reorganized into three product business units and three geographic theaters to improve efficiency, coordination, and customer accountability. Field managers could resolve issues more locally, but decisions involving products and pricing remained centralized, and escalation to headquarters continued to slow resolution.

Dublin’s localization proposal therefore had to determine where, how quickly, and to what extent Akamai should become local while deciding which products, pricing, support, and operational processes should remain global. The central challenge was balancing investment in local capabilities and customer support against potential revenue while preserving a global core and responding to large customers that were becoming competitors.

The paper introduces a two-timescale evolutionary hypergame framework for a voluntary-participation prisoner’s dilemma with cooperation (C), defection (D), and opting out or “loning” (L). Players possess heterogeneous subsets of these strategies, reflecting differences in knowledge, experience, and accessible choices. On the fast timescale, players update their chosen strategies through introspection dynamics: a randomly selected player considers an available alternative and adopts it with a Fermi-function probability determined by the payoff difference and introspection strength \(w\). On the slow timescale, strategy-set frequencies evolve according to replicator dynamics based on relative success.

Pairwise interactions are modeled as a Markov chain, allowing stationary distributions and average payoffs to be derived. Tournament results show that weak introspection favors defection or loning, while greater introspection and larger cooperation benefits favor the strategy set \(\{C,L\}\). Theoretical analysis shows that higher introspection strengthens reciprocal cooperation between \(\{C,L\}\) players and improves their ability to avoid exploitation by defectors. Sufficiently high introspection makes \(\{C,L\}\) outperform both \(\{D\}\) and \(\{D,L\}\), with the required threshold depending on payoff parameters.

In well-mixed populations with the sets \(\{C,L\}\), \(\{D,L\}\), and \(\{C,D\}\), weak introspection leads to low-payoff dominance by \(\{D,L\}\), whereas strong introspection produces high-payoff dominance by \(\{C,L\}\). With all seven nonempty strategy sets, weak introspection favors \(\{L\}\), while stronger introspection shifts dominance toward cooperative sets.

Structured-population simulations on a two-dimensional lattice show similar transitions: weak introspection favors \(\{D,L\}\) or \(\{L\}\), intermediate levels permit coexistence or dominance by \(\{C\}\), and the strongest levels yield complete dominance by \(\{C,L\}\). Overall, the framework shows that heterogeneity and introspection jointly shape evolutionary outcomes and that allowing strategy sets to co-evolve can explain the emergence and stabilization of cooperation in asymmetric populations.

Gold prices are near record highs after rising more than 50% over the past year, with further gains forecast through next year. Recession fears, economic and political uncertainty, expected U.S. rate cuts, a weaker dollar and central-bank buying are driving demand. UBS expects gold inflows of 830 metric tons this year, nearly double its initial forecast, while about 95% of central banks expect global holdings to rise. One forecast cited projects gold will reach $4,000 per troy ounce by mid-2026.

Rising costs are pressuring jewelry companies, especially those selling lower-priced products. Mejuri raised prices and is developing 10-karat gold products, while BaubleBar and Alexis Bittar emphasize gold-plated alternatives. Between July 2019 and June 2024, researchers assessed ex vivo susceptibility of Ugandan Plasmodium falciparum to nine antimalarial drugs at sites in eastern and northern Uganda. Susceptibility was measured using 72-hour growth-inhibition assays, with ring-stage survival assays performed on a subset. They genotyped 1,070 isolates across 80 candidate resistance genes and analyzed additional samples collected since 2016.

Most drugs remained active at low nanomolar concentrations, although quinine was less potent and pyrimethamine had very high IC50 values. From 2016 to 2024, chloroquine susceptibility increased, while susceptibility to dihydroartemisinin, lumefantrine, and mefloquine decreased. Decreases in dihydroartemisinin and lumefantrine susceptibility were modest, and their clinical implications remain uncertain. Many isolates exceeded established ring-stage survival thresholds, although the temporal increase was significant only in eastern Uganda under the study’s criterion.

PfCRT K76T and PfMDR1 N86Y mutations became uncommon. PfK13 C469Y and A675V, more prevalent in northern Uganda but increasing in eastern Uganda, were associated with reduced dihydroartemisinin and lumefantrine activity but not survival-assay results. Strong associations also involved PfCARL D611N with lumefantrine susceptibility and PfMDR1 Y500N with dihydroartemisinin susceptibility. PfDHFR and PfDHPS mutations associated with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine resistance remained prevalent, and PfDHFR C59R and I164L were associated with progressively poorer pyrimethamine activity. No pfmdr1 or plasmepsin 2/3 amplification was detected.

Overall, parasites remained mostly sensitive to commonly used drugs, but changing susceptibilities and genotypes raised concern about artemether-lumefantrine efficacy, supporting continued parasitological and genomic surveillance and policies to limit resistance selection and treatment failure.

The passage introduces InVirtuoGen, a continuous-time discrete flow model for fragment-based drug discovery that operates directly on fragmented SMILES. Unlike autoregressive and masked-diffusion methods that complete tokens sequentially or leave unmasked tokens fixed, InVirtuoGen refines all sequence positions simultaneously, decoupling sampling steps from sequence length and enabling coordinated, bidirectional molecular updates.

Its representation extends SAFE by decomposing molecules with revised BRICS, marking attachment points, separating fragments with spaces, and randomly shuffling fragments to remove ordering bias. The resulting atomic-level vocabulary contains 204 tokens. A diffusion transformer with bidirectional attention parameterizes the model, which is trained with a time-weighted discrete-flow objective and can sample either through the formal Markov update or directly from predicted token distributions.

The model was pretrained on ZINC and UniChem, totaling roughly one billion molecules, and evaluated on de novo generation, fragment-constrained design, PMO property optimization, and lead optimization. For de novo generation, smaller time steps improved quality and diversity, and InVirtuoGen produced a superior quality–diversity Pareto frontier over SAFE-GPT and GenMol. It achieved competitive average results across five fragment-constrained tasks, although preserving prompted fragments required overwriting their positions at every step, effectively reducing the method to masked completion and limiting validity.

For property optimization, the authors combine a genetic algorithm that recombines high-scoring molecules by swapping fragments with PPO reinforcement learning adapted to discrete flows through Monte Carlo sequence log-probability estimates. They report state-of-the-art PMO benchmark performance and improved lead optimization over prior baselines.

Blackwell expands real-time ray tracing through fourth-generation RT Cores that accelerate BVH traversal and ray-geometry intersections, double ray-triangle testing throughput versus third-generation cores, and add an Opacity Micromap Engine, a Triangle Cluster Intersection Engine, and hardware support for Linear Swept Spheres. Mega Geometry enables full-fidelity ray tracing of Nanite-style geometry without low-resolution proxies by treating triangle clusters as first-class primitives. Cluster-level acceleration structures of up to 256 triangles reduce subsequent BVH-build processing by two orders of magnitude, while GPU-driven, fully batched APIs minimize CPU overhead. Partitioned Top-Level Acceleration Structures update only changed scene partitions, supporting large static and dynamic worlds. Mega Geometry also enables rapid BVH construction for animated, displaced subdivision surfaces. Support spans DirectX 12 through NVAPI, Vulkan vendor extensions, and OptiX 9.0, and is available on RTX GPUs from Turing onward.

Linear Swept Spheres provide hardware-accelerated ray intersections for curves such as hair, fur, and grass, support varying radii and direct spheres, and render common hair cases about twice as fast as DOTS while using roughly one-fifth the VRAM. Shader Execution Reordering 2.0 improves GPU utilization in divergent ray-tracing workloads and routes coherent neural work to Tensor Cores; Blackwell’s reorder logic is twice as efficient and more precise than Ada’s. The programmable AI Management Processor uses a dedicated RISC-V processor to schedule GPU contexts on the GPU, reducing CPU dependency and latency while coordinating AI and graphics workloads under Windows Hardware-Accelerated GPU Scheduling.

Blackwell adds hardware encode and decode support for 4:2:2 chroma sampling in H.264 and HEVC. Its ninth-generation NVENC improves AV1 and HEVC quality by 5% BD-BR PSNR, adds 4:2:2 encoding, and provides an AV1 Ultra High Quality mode with a further 5% improvement. The RTX 5090 supports three encoders and two decoders, increasing export speeds by more than 50% generation over generation and fourfold over a single-encoder RTX 3090. Its sixth-generation NVDEC provides twice-faster H.264 decoding and 4:2:2 support. Blackwell also supports DisplayPort 2.1b at up to 80 Gbps, including 8K at 165 Hz and 4K at 480 Hz with DSC.

Max-Q efficiency improvements include advanced clock, power, and voltage-rail gating; separate control of GPU-core and memory power; accelerated frequency switching up to 1,000 times faster than previous architectures; and sleep states entered ten times faster than Ada. In a small-language-model inference example, these changes produced power savings of up to 50%.

DLSS 4 introduces Multi Frame Generation, which can produce up to three additional frames for every traditionally rendered frame. Its frame-generation model is 40% faster and uses 30% less VRAM than the preceding method, while AI-based optical flow and display-engine flip metering improve frame pacing. DLSS 4 also replaces CNN-based models with transformer models for Super Resolution, Ray Reconstruction, and Deep Learning Anti-Aliasing. The transformers process twice as many parameters and improve temporal stability, motion detail, lighting detail, and ray-traced image quality.

Blackwell is presented as a foundation for neural shaders that learn approximations of complex rendering algorithms, decompress textures, infer indirect lighting, and approximate subsurface scattering. Cooperative Vectors for DirectX 12 and Vulkan, together with Slang features, exposes Tensor Cores to pixel and ray-tracing shaders. Applications include RTX Neural Materials, Neural Texture Compression, Stochastic Texture Filtering, Neural Radiance Cache, RTX Skin, and RTX Neural Faces. Neural Texture Compression can provide up to seven-to-one compression over block-compressed formats; in one Neural Materials demo, memory use fell from 1,110 MB to 333 MB. Neural Radiance Cache infers multiple lighting bounces from limited traced rays and trains on live game data. RTX Skin provides real-time ray-traced subsurface scattering, while Neural Faces uses a TensorRT-optimized generative model to produce natural faces from rasterized geometry and 3D pose data.

The Blackwell family includes GB202, with 192 SMs, 24,576 CUDA Cores, 192 RT Cores, and 768 Tensor Cores, used by the GeForce RTX 5090; GB203, with 84 SMs, 10,752 CUDA Cores, 84 RT Cores, and 336 Tensor Cores, used by the RTX 5080 and 5070 Ti; and GB205, with 50 SMs, 6,400 CUDA Cores, 50 RT Cores, and 200 Tensor Cores, used by the RTX 5070. The author argues that Nigeria’s political problems require deeper understanding of its ethnic history rather than reactions based on superficial analysis or passion. He intends to explain Nigeria’s ethnic configuration, its historical effects, and the need for a broad, knowledge-based opposition to the government, built across parties and sectors rather than confined to the PDP.

Nigeria, according to the author, is a nation of distinct ethnicities, and the idea of a monolithic “North” and “South” arose from colonial protectorates. The North historically contained numerous cultures and was unified largely through Islam following Usman Dan Fodio’s conquests, while the South consisted of varied peoples, including the Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa-speaking communities. Colonial rule left the South more administratively integrated and associated with common law, while the North retained emirates, feudal authority and Sharia.

The author presents Ahmadu Bello, Nnamdi Azikiwe and Obafemi Awolowo as foundational leaders with different views of Nigeria. He characterizes Bello as favoring strong regions and a confederal arrangement, Azikiwe as favoring a strong central government and a new national identity that transcended ethnicity, and Awolowo as favoring federalism, with equal regional and central authority and room for each ethnicity to flourish. He says Azikiwe and Bello captured their difference in the exchange, “Let us ignore our differences” and “Let us understand our differences.” Bello’s alliances with traditional rulers are portrayed as partly political, although his position also reflected his lineage and determination to preserve Northern unity.

The passage traces how colonial and postcolonial alliances shaped national politics. Azikiwe’s relationships with Igbo politicians, his attempt to gain the Western Region, and later alliance with the Northern Peoples Congress helped lead to his becoming governor-general with Balewa as prime minister. The author also identifies Harold Dappa-Biriye as an architect of an alliance between the Niger Delta Congress and the Northern Peoples Congress. Following the 1966 coup, which killed Bello and Balewa, many Northerners interpreted the killings through an ethnic lens, deepening insecurity and increasing the importance of control over power.

Four broad Northern political strands are identified: a conservative Ahmadu Bello oligarchy, Ahmadu Bello nationalists, Aminu Kano radicals or nationalists, and Middle Belt nationalists seeking a separate identity. The passage mentions J. S. Tarka and the Ilorin Talaka Parapo movement, and notes Awolowo’s support for recognizing regional minorities. Although the creation of the Midwest Region addressed some concerns, later fragmentation into states produced further demands for separate ethnic identities.

The author says the National Party of Nigeria demonstrated the nationalist potential associated with Bello’s tradition during the Second Republic, but that Northern elites opposed equality and overthrew Shagari in 1983, installing Buhari. After 16 years of military rule, the PDP emerged. Northern leaders within the ANPP later opposed Obasanjo’s second-term bid, used Sharia to mobilize opposition, and promoted northern candidates; at the ANPP convention, southern aspirants were displaced and Buhari became the party’s candidate. The author stresses that this northern oligarchy persisted but did not represent all Northerners.

A diverse opposition is therefore presented as necessary for defeating Buhari without harming national ideals. The author points to northern allies such as Sule Lamido and the late Ado Bayero, whose support for the PDP was met with attacks on their homes or offices. He rejects the idea of a unified “South” that can determine elections alone and insists that opposition must be national. He also questions northern political aspirants’ past decisions, including Bafarawa’s role in bringing Buhari into politics in 2003, Kwankwaso’s move from PDP to APC, and Atiku’s shifting alliances and acceptance of a northern candidacy in 2011. The conclusion warns against treating all Northerners as part of the oligarchy or all Igbos or Yorubas as politically uniform, and condemns calls for unity that ignore Nigeria’s diversity.
