A study led by Thomas Evans detected water-molecule spectral signatures in WASP-121b’s atmosphere, showing that temperature rises with altitude in its upper atmosphere and decreases with altitude in the troposphere. The nearly twice-Jupiter-sized hot Jupiter orbits its star every 1.3 days and reaches about 4,500–4,600°F in its upper atmosphere. Researchers used Hubble infrared transit spectroscopy and found the clearest evidence to date of a stratosphere on an exoplanet. The result allows comparisons of atmospheric processes within and beyond the solar system and is a step toward studying smaller, Earth-like planets and possible biosignatures. Current technology mainly enables study of large, hot gas giants, but future observatories could expand research capabilities. The study was published online in Nature.

Winthrop University will receive $1.1 million from a competitive $20 million National Science Foundation award shared by 10 South Carolina institutions over five years. Funding will support 36 summer research experiences, $330,000 for equipment and upgrades, faculty research, student travel, and two-week teacher workshops for regional high schools. Under the statewide MADE in SC initiative, researchers will study optical, magnetic, electronic, polymeric, biomaterial, and stimuli-responsive materials, combining synthesis with computational modeling for applications in lasers, water treatment, regenerative medicine, clean energy, and biofabrication. Maria Gelabert will direct the project, alongside Fatima Amir, Clifton Harris, Jason Hurlbert, and Robin Lammi.

The NHS Constitution, sometimes called the Patient Charter, sets out patients' legal rights, the NHS's pledges beyond the legal minimum, and patients' own responsibilities, reflecting the founding principle that healthcare should be free at the point of use and based on need rather than ability to pay.

Rights include: access to care (free at the point of use, with exceptions such as prescriptions in England, dentistry and eye care), treatment meeting your needs and preferences, equal access regardless of age, race, disability or other characteristics, and waiting-time standards with alternatives if unmet; quality and safety, including qualified staff, clean premises, nutritious hospital food and continuous improvement, measured by bodies such as the Care Quality Commission; access to NICE-recommended medicines and routine vaccinations, with local funding decisions to be rational, evidence-based and explained; consent, clear information on risks and benefits, and privacy of information; choice of GP practice, involvement in treatment decisions including end-of-life care, and being told openly if things go wrong; and the right to complain, escalate to the Ombudsman, seek judicial review, and receive compensation for negligence.

Responsibilities include looking after your own health, respecting staff and other patients, following treatment plans, and taking part in vaccination and screening. The Charter therefore frames the NHS as a partnership, offering patients empowerment and staff a framework for fairness amid long waiting lists, staff shortages and financial pressures.

The interviewee described the seven-game Chicago series as emotional and exhausting, with three overtimes, overnight travel, media duties and an abnormal practice schedule, hoping rest would help. He noted that roster changes and several players in their first Stanley Cup Final required adjustments, while praising the teams’ resilience and Kyle’s energy and role. He said teams play better when not chasing leads and that Mike Richards accepts whatever role is needed to win. Jonathan was described as focused and highly engaged despite fatigue. A young penalty killer was said to have room to improve through better ice-time management, shot selection, penalty killing, scouting opponents, practice habits and nutrition. The interviewee also praised the supportive Kings atmosphere in Manhattan Beach and Madison Square Garden’s distinctive character. On defense, he said personnel differed from the prior year and that, after a first-period slump, they tried to manage Kopitar’s game.

The passage explains how to calculate and backtest a 14-day Average True Range (ATR) volatility strategy in Python using SPY. ATR, developed by J. Welles Wilder Jr., is typically used for stop-loss placement, position sizing, and identifying potential breakouts rather than generating signals directly. Historical SPY data from Yahoo Finance is processed with pandas_ta to calculate ATR, then tested with a strategy that holds SPY during high volatility and sells during low volatility. The backtest, which did not adjust for dividends and splits, produced modest results: risk-adjusted performance was better, while drawdown was nearly identical to buy and hold. Combining ATR with other indicators may improve results.

A University of Bristol-led study found that chloroplasts diverged from their closest cyanobacterial ancestors more than 2.1 billion years ago in low-salinity habitats, followed about 200 million years later by an intimate symbiotic relationship with eukaryotic hosts. Marine algae diversified around 800–750 million years ago, suggesting complex organisms first evolved in freshwater before colonizing marine environments. The findings may improve understanding of early life and Earth’s carbon cycle.

The neo-Nazi website Daily Stormer, founded in 2013 by Andrew Anglin, was first dropped by GoDaddy and then by Google after the site published an article mocking Heather Heyer, the woman killed when a white supremacist drove into a crowd of counterprotesters at the Unite The Right rally in Charlottesville on Aug. 12. GoDaddy said the article could incite additional violence; Google said it was cancelling the site's registration for violating its terms of service. Neither company hosts the site, which is masked by Cloudflare; ProPublica reported that Cloudflare shared complainants' personal information with Anglin, who targeted them for harassment. Cloudflare said it finds some site content "repugnant" and cooperates with law enforcement but makes no policy change. The Daily Stormer had recently attacked Google for firing engineer James Damore, and the crowdfunding site WeSearchr raised over $46,000 for him. A post claiming Anonymous had hacked the site and would release Anglin's location appeared, but Anglin soon said he regained control. Anglin is being sued by the Southern Poverty Law Center over a harassment campaign against the family of Tanya Gersh; he has avoided court, claims to be in Lagos, Nigeria, and Reveal found he falsified information in that claim. His whereabouts are unknown, and if the suit succeeds his assets could be seized, potentially shutting down the site.

NASA will livestream a six-hour ISS spacewalk on August 17, beginning around 10:45 a.m. EDT. Expedition 52 cosmonauts Fyodor Yurchikhin and Sergey Ryazanskiy will deploy five nanosatellites, collect exterior residue samples, and install handrails and struts. It is the expedition’s only planned spacewalk and among the year’s longest.

A retrospective records-based cohort study at Mulago National Referral Hospital in Kampala assessed outcomes and healthcare-system costs for children admitted with clinical measles in 2018. From 570 admissions, 553 charts were retrieved and 267 were selected by systematic sampling. Data covered demographics, vaccination, comorbidities, complications, treatments, investigations, hospital stay, discharge status, and costs. Direct healthcare costs included tests, radiology, treatment, and supplies, while overheads included staff salaries, maintenance, and utilities.

The sampled children had a median age of one year and median hospital stay of four days. Of 267 patients, 185 developed multiple complications; severe pneumonia was most common, followed by gastroenteritis and conjunctivitis. Thirty children died, giving an in-hospital mortality of 11.3%. Among those who died, 17 were male, 21 were aged zero to one year, and 13 were unvaccinated.

Average direct healthcare cost was US$33.13 per patient, including US$11.73 for blood tests, US$3.48 for radiology, and US$21.98 for treatment. Average overhead cost was US$81.37, mainly human-resource costs, producing a combined estimated cost of US$114.50 per case. Direct costs were significantly higher among males, children with comorbidities, patients hospitalized longer than 15 days, and those who died.

The authors noted that these costs greatly exceeded the estimated cost of measles vaccination and emphasized improved immunization uptake. Limitations included reliance on a public referral hospital, retrospective data, inability to estimate family or societal costs, use of clinical rather than laboratory-confirmed diagnoses, and uncertainty over whether all recorded treatments and investigations were received.

Ten people were killed and 15 injured when a van struck pedestrians on Yonge Street at about 1:30 p.m. Monday. Anne-Marie D’Amico was identified as one victim. Police arrested 25-year-old Alex Minassian, who is accused of renting the van and driving into the crowd; his motive remains unknown. Police continue seeking witnesses and identifying victims.

This disclosure is a continuation of PCT/CN2019/128475 and Chinese Patent Application No. 201811653380.3, whose disclosures are incorporated by reference. It concerns big-data recommendation model training and related methods and apparatuses.

The disclosed method screens initial sample sets for groups containing positive samples. Samples include user features, object features, and labels determined by user operations, such as downloads or purchases indicating positive samples and lack of interaction indicating negative samples. Positive samples are added to a training set, while negative samples are selected according to calculated sampling probabilities. A preset pairwise algorithm may use one or more of three factors: estimated-score differences between positive and negative samples, feature-vector distances between them, and changes in ranking indicators after exchanging their rankings. These factors assign greater sampling probability to negative samples that are more informative for model training. Negative samples may be selected by probability ranking, random comparison, or normalization against the maximum probability.

The resulting training set is used to train a recommendation model with algorithms such as FTRL, logistic regression, or FFM. Model-generated estimated scores can feed subsequent sampling rounds, allowing training and sampling to iteratively influence each other. During recommendation, user and/or candidate-object features are used to calculate estimated scores, candidates are ranked in descending score order, and the first M candidates are recommended to a target user.

The disclosure also describes a sampling and training apparatus, processor-and-memory implementations, a recommendation apparatus, computer-readable storage media, and computer program products. A system architecture includes data collection, model training, model execution, storage, and client devices.

Tests using a HUAWEI APPGALLERY dataset and NDCG@5, NDCG@10, P@5, and P@10 showed better results than no sampling, random sampling, dynamic negative sampling, and optimized logistic-regression sampling. For NDCG@5, reported improvements were 0.0026 over no sampling, 0.0015 over random sampling, 0.044 over dynamic negative sampling, and 0.0026 over optimized logistic-regression sampling.

The NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU uses the Ampere architecture and TSMC’s 7nm N7 process to accelerate AI and HPC workloads. The A100 implementation of GA100 has 108 streaming multiprocessors, 6,912 FP32 CUDA cores, 432 third-generation Tensor Cores, and 40 GB of HBM2 memory. Third-generation Tensor Cores support FP16, BF16, TF32, FP64, INT8, INT4, and binary data, with further throughput gains from 2:4 fine-grained structured sparsity. Compared with Tesla V100, A100 provides 2.5 times the mixed-precision FP16/FP32 performance, up to 20 times the FP32 throughput, 2.5 times the FP64 performance, and up to 20 times the INT8 performance with sparsity. Its 108 SMs deliver up to 312 TFLOPS of dense mixed-precision performance.

A100’s 2:4 sparsity format permits two nonzero values in every four-entry vector. Sparse Tensor Core instructions skip zero entries, doubling computation throughput, while compressed weights reduce storage and bandwidth requirements. NVIDIA’s training-and-pruning recipe reportedly produces virtually no inference-accuracy loss across numerous evaluated networks.

Each SM includes 192 KB of combined L1 cache and shared memory, separate FP32 and INT32 cores for simultaneous full-throughput execution, and hardware-accelerated asynchronous copy and barrier instructions. These features reduce register-file traffic, support overlapped memory transfers and computation, and enable producer-consumer models and finer-grained thread synchronization.

The memory subsystem includes 40 GB of HBM2 delivering 1,555 GB/s, a 40 MB L2 cache with 2.3 times V100’s L2 bandwidth, ECC protection, cache-residency controls, and data compression. A100 supports PCIe Gen 4 with SR-IOV, allowing a PCIe-connected GPU to be virtualized and shared among processes or virtual machines.

Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) can divide an A100 into as many as seven isolated GPU Instances with dedicated compute, cache, and memory resources. GPU Instances can be subdivided into Compute Instances, support Volta-style MPS, and can be migrated between compatible instances or GPUs. MIG provides predictable quality of service, fault isolation, and security for multi-tenant environments.

Third-generation NVLink provides 12 links and 600 GB/s of aggregate GPU-to-GPU bandwidth, along with improved error detection, recovery, and fault attribution. A100 also includes NVJPG hardware JPEG decoding, an optical-flow accelerator, improved global-memory atomics, five NVDEC units, and enhanced error, fault, and containment mechanisms.

CUDA 11 adds support for CUDA Graphs, MIG, Tensor Core sparsity, L2 residency controls, asynchronous copies, and asynchronous barriers. Task graphs reduce launch overhead and accelerate dependency handling, while L2 persistence controls can reserve portions of cache for repeatedly accessed data. Cooperative Groups adds group-wide asynchronous copies and hardware-accelerated reductions.

DGX A100 systems contain eight A100 GPUs connected through NVSwitch, deliver up to 5 PFLOPS of AI performance, and can provide as many as 56 isolated accelerators through MIG. The platform also includes ConnectX-6 InfiniBand networking, the Magnum IO SDK, CUDA 11, GPU-optimized containers, and NGC software for AI, analytics, and HPC deployment.

- The passage defines the SEV-ES/SEV-SNP Guest-Hypervisor Communication Block (GHCB) and its MSR and VMGEXIT protocols. MSR requests include CPUID retrieval, AP reset hold, preferred and registered GHCB GPA selection, page state changes, running at a requested VMPL, GHCB GPA unregistration, hypervisor feature discovery, and termination. CPUID requests return one register value per invocation, do not support nonzero sub-leaves, and exclude function 0x0000000d because it requires XCR0.

- SEV-SNP guests must register a GHCB GPA before first using it. A guest may request the hypervisor’s preferred GPA or supply a GFN to register. The hypervisor must accept the supplied GFN or report rejection; registration replaces any previously registered GPA. A mismatch with the currently registered GPA requires guest termination. Each VMPL may register its own GPA when SEV-SNP Multi-VMPL is advertised. Guests may later unregister the current GPA. Preferred and registered GHCB pages must be hypervisor-owned shared pages for SEV-SNP guests.

- During negotiation, the hypervisor initially supplies GHCB information through VMCB offset 0x00a0. An SEV-ES guest obtains protocol versions and the encryption-bit position through intercepted CPUID processing, configures page tables, allocates and shares the GHCB page, and writes its GPA to MSR 0xc0010130 before issuing VMGEXIT. An SEV-SNP guest additionally verifies SNP status, obtains protocol information through the MSR protocol, registers the GHCB GPA, and then writes the GPA to the GHCB MSR. The guest should use the firmware-validated CPUID page to determine the encryption-bit position.

- The SEV-SNP secrets page reserves bytes 0x00a0–0x00ff for guest use. This area includes per-VMPL guest-message sequence numbers, an AP jump-table physical address, and a guest usage area. The format was updated for 64-bit message sequence numbers. Firmware may also pass secrets and CPUID pages to an EFI guest through the SEV-SNP Confidential Computing Blob EFI configuration table.

- Non-automatic exit (NAE) events other than architectural events generate a #VC exception for SEV-ES guests. The guest examines the VMEXIT code, copies required state into the GHCB, invokes VMGEXIT, and resumes after the VMGEXIT, using an unintercepted IRET to return from the #VC handler. Guests and hypervisors clear and set the GHCB VALID_BITMAP for each request and response. The minimum guest fields are SW_EXITCODE, SW_EXITINFO1, and SW_EXITINFO2; the hypervisor returns SW_EXITINFO1 and SW_EXITINFO2. A nonzero SW_EXITINFO1 value represents an error and may request that the hypervisor inject an exception.

- Supported NAE operations include protected I/O and MSR handling, MMIO reads and writes, page state changes, SNP guest and extended guest requests, AP creation, restricted-injection doorbell management, sending IPIs, emulated APIC timers, APIC ID discovery, running at a VMPL, SEV-TIO requests, Secure AVIC backing-page management, and termination. MMIO and page state operations use a shared, decrypted buffer and may require multiple VMGEXIT calls. Page state changes update progress in shared memory so processing can resume. SNP guest requests use separate shared request and response pages, require sequence-safe retries, and may be rate-limited. Extended requests can return GUID-indexed certificates. AP creation can add, update, or remove a vCPU and its VMSA.

- SMP application-processor startup requires special handling because measured vCPU registers cannot be modified normally. Initial resets use the originally measured state; subsequent resets use AP reset-hold requests to communicate with the hypervisor before returning to real mode at the requested reset vector. UEFI can pass an AP jump table to the OS so the next environment can supply the destination. SEV-SNP AP Creation provides an alternative that allows vCPU hotplug.

- For NMI handling, the hypervisor must not intercept IRET but must intercept #DB; the guest sends an “NMI Complete” message when it can safely accept another NMI. Hardware debug-register virtualization is supported when advertised; otherwise DR7 accesses are intercepted and emulated. SMM and nested virtualization are not supported.

- With Restricted Injection, host notifications use a shared #HV doorbell page containing PendingEvent and NoEoiRequired fields. PendingEvent identifies a maskable interrupt vector, NMI, #MC, and whether further signals are prohibited; NoEoiRequired indicates whether an explicit end-of-interrupt is unnecessary. The host emulates APIC ready, acknowledgment, in-service, and EOI behavior, while the guest must atomically clear and retrieve pending information and validate observed vectors. To avoid missed or premature interrupts, the guest executes HLT with interrupts disabled, and the host immediately re-enters the guest if events remain pending.

The sellers will retain NVIDIA’s $1.25 billion prepayment, while NVIDIA will retain its 20-year Arm license. NVIDIA intends to record a $1.36 billion charge in the first quarter of fiscal 2023, including the prepayment.

The High/Low zone offense combines a three-player outside passing attack with an inside high/low rotation and can be initiated from many alignments or entries. Its continuity relies on interior players rolling, posting, flashing to the middle, moving to the short corner, and reversing the ball. Constant interior movement creates matchup problems, while defensive collapses open spot-up shots. Sharp ball movement and a quick weakside attack force zones to defend sideline to sideline.

Post-roll and high-post-flash options feed interior players or kick out to shooters. Common entries include Dribble Clear, 1-4 Slice, Mid Screen, and Horns, which use back cuts, slices, screens, reversals, and high/low actions. Quick-hitting special plays include Pin Down, which uses down screens; Weakside Double, combining a back-cut layup opportunity with a double screen; and Vegas, using a wing entry, high-post roll, double screen, and cross-court skip passes. These sets can be run late in the shot or game clock and after timeouts.

Charlie Tillett explains how entrepreneurs should build business-plan financials for investors. He emphasizes that financial projections are a company’s scorecard, clarify key assumptions and business drivers, and help founders determine cash needs. Founders need not be accountants, but they should understand and discuss core financial metrics. His downloadable Excel template includes detailed revenue, cost, staffing, and cash-flow projections and is available through MIT OpenCourseWare.

Tillet recounts developing the model while participating in MIT’s $10K Contest and later using similar spreadsheets at NetScout Systems and Reveal Imaging, where he helped raise more than $125 million across over ten transactions. At Reveal, financial planning enabled milestone-based financing, while equipment financing provided additional runway while another round was pending.

Venture capitalists generally seek three-to-five-times absolute returns over five to seven years and expect significant ownership. Equity percentage is calculated as the investment divided by pre-money valuation plus the investment. New financing dilutes existing shareholders, and successive rounds should not be treated as simple subtractions. Investors commonly also receive preferred-stock protections, anti-dilution provisions, and board representation. A mismatch between capital raised and the size of the market opportunity creates tension because investors expect large returns.

Tillet recommends evaluating a business through its income statement: revenue, cost of goods sold, sales and marketing, research and development, general and administrative expenses, and operating profit or EBITDA. He suggests leaving depreciation out of initial plans and retaining G&A costs in G&A rather than allocating them elsewhere. Plans should be developed quarterly, beginning with staffing and near-term expenses, then projecting later years as the company reaches critical mass.

Business models should be compared with peer companies using revenue, margins, departmental spending, operating profit, and revenue per employee. These comparisons can reveal unrealistic assumptions. Product pricing should leave customers enough savings to justify switching while allowing the company to capture sufficient value. Distribution choices can materially affect revenue and sales and marketing costs. For technology companies, he gives broad targets of 10–20% for R&D, 5–15% for G&A, and staffing costs representing roughly 50–66% of expenses; unusually high projected operating margins should prompt review.

Sales projections should be built bottom-up from sales capacity, productivity, conversion rates, and purchase quantities rather than from broad market-share claims. Tillett advises constructing the model directly rather than relying on software that generates plans automatically, because the main benefit is understanding assumptions and formulas. He recommends presenting one best estimate rather than separate best- and worst-case models.

Cash flow is critical but error-prone. Cumulative operating losses plus capital expenditures can serve as a practical proxy for funding needs. His sample model accounts for customers paying 60–90 days late while payroll and other expenses are paid in the current period, allowing founders to identify when additional financing is required.

Employee equity should incentivize future work, and Tillett recommends three- or four-year vesting for founders and staff. He illustrates dilution from employee option pools, angel investments, and successive venture rounds, while stressing that angels may negotiate as firmly as institutional venture capitalists. By the time a company takes its first venture investment, he recommends obtaining experienced financial leadership, even if initially through a part-time CFO, advisor, or controller arrangement, because anticipating financing needs can prevent unnecessary dilution.

The paper presents a proof-of-concept for analyzing instant-messaging data in criminal investigations. It combines a Neo4j property graph for chats, participants, messages, and metadata; Whisper speech-to-text for transcribing audio; and a named-entity recognition and linking pipeline to identify, disambiguate, and cluster entities. Results are accessible through Neo4j visualization and queries and through DAVE, a web application offering keyword and entity-based faceted search, document exploration, and editable annotations.

The approach was developed with investigators using data from two investigations involving fraud and corruption. Whisper Large performed best in an evaluation of 500 noisy Italian recordings, scoring 0.908 BERT F1 and 0.282 word error rate. The entity pipeline processed 1,296 of 1,442 chats in the second investigation, enriching the graph with “mentioned in” relationships. Audio transcripts contained, on average, four times more entities than text messages.

Initial NER results were weak—28.8 F1 for exact span-and-type matches and 47.0 for partial matches—indicating a need for larger gold standards and in-domain fine-tuning, particularly for informal names, abbreviations, and inconsistent capitalization. Investigators nevertheless found graph visualizations, combined textual and relational search, transcription, and DAVE’s entity-based browsing useful, while suggesting direct audio playback.

The tool is designed to support rather than replace human judgment through editable annotations, syntactic search, and verification against original data. Limitations include Neo4j’s query complexity and the need for more advanced interfaces. Future work includes improving entity extraction, developing additional interfaces, and extending enrichment to images and videos. Data are stored locally with restricted access, and external APIs are avoided to protect private information.

The lecture reviews coding for bandwidth-limited additive white Gaussian noise channels. Unlike power-limited channels, where binary codes and Hamming distance are nearly optimal, these channels require multilevel constellations and Euclidean-distance metrics. For lattice constellations, a union-bound approximation expresses error probability through nearest neighbors, lattice coding gain, and shaping gain. With SNR normalized by spectral efficiency, this expression is independent of rate and, in the high-SNR approximation, constellation size. Integer lattices shaped by n-cubes yield a universal baseline for PAM, QAM, and their Cartesian products: four times \(Q(\sqrt{3\,\mathrm{SNR}_{norm}})\). At an error probability near \(10^{-5}\), this baseline is roughly 9 dB from the Shannon limit.

Shaping and coding gains are separable. The optimal shaping region minimizes normalized second moment and is spherical. Its maximum shaping gain is \(\pi e/6\), or about 1.53 dB, approached as dimension increases. Two-dimensional shaping provides roughly 0.2 dB, 16-dimensional shaping about 1 dB, and 32-dimensional shaping about 1.2 dB. Shell mapping in the V.34 modem achieved about 0.8 dB, while trellis shaping was described as an elegant alternative. Uniform high-dimensional spherical shaping also produces Gaussian-like distributions when projected onto one or two dimensions.

Densest known lattices include the two-dimensional hexagonal lattice \(A_2\), with about 0.6 dB coding gain; \(D_4\), with 1.5 dB; \(E_8\), with roughly 2–3 dB; and the 16-dimensional Barnes–Wall lattice, with 4.5 dB. Although nominal coding gains continue increasing with dimension, large numbers of nearest neighbors reduce effective gains. For example, the 24-dimensional Leech lattice has about 6 dB nominal gain and roughly 195,560 near neighbors, leaving effective gain near or below 4 dB.

Barnes–Wall lattices are constructed by recursively partitioning lattice points into translated sublattices, analogous to Reed–Muller codes. Each partitioning step can double the minimum squared distance, producing nested \(D_4\), \(E_8\), Barnes–Wall, and related lattices with increasing nominal gain. The Leech lattice is also related to the Golay code and has exceptional symmetries associated with the classification of finite groups.

Trellis-coded modulation applies the same set-partitioning idea to enlarged constellations. Uncoded bits select a point within a coded subset, while a convolutional code selects the subset sequence. A four-state, two-dimensional trellis code achieves minimum squared distance 4, four nearest neighbors per two dimensions, and about 3 dB coding gain; decoding first selects the nearest point within each subset and then performs Viterbi decoding over subset paths. An eight-way partition permits minimum squared distance 8 and nominal gains up to about 6 dB. Ungerboeck’s codes extended to 256 or 512 states, with low error coefficients, provided effective gains close to 6 dB but required substantial decoder complexity.

Lee-Fang Wei’s four-dimensional eight-way partitioning reduced redundancy to half a bit per two dimensions. Its 16-state implementation achieved about 4.2 dB and was adopted in V.34 and ADSL; higher-state versions added only small gains. The lecture concludes that reasonable trellis codes can provide roughly 5–6 dB of coding gain and, with shaping, about 6 dB effective gain, leaving them approximately 2–3 dB from the Shannon limit.

Higher-performance methods include turbo codes, which can approach within about 1 dB of the limit, and sequential decoding, within about 1.5 dB. Multilevel coding treats each partition level as a separate binary channel; their capacities add to the aggregate channel capacity. Capacity-approaching codes are needed mainly on the first, hardest level, while high-rate algebraic or Reed–Solomon codes can handle later levels. Bit-interleaved coded modulation provides a practical alternative by interleaving coded bits across levels and reusing binary-channel chips; it is commonly used on wireless cellular channels.

The professor characterizes conventional AWGN-channel coding as mature and already close to the Shannon limit. Remaining theoretical questions concern iterative-decoding convergence, statistical physics and inference connections, graph-theoretic properties, and algebraic construction of capacity-approaching codes. Practically important coding research has shifted toward networks and multi-user systems, while understanding AWGN coding remains necessary for wireless-system mutual-information calculations.

The lecturer presents the fourth and final course case study, based on ongoing thesis research into manufacturing microfluidic devices from polymers. Polymers are attractive because they are inexpensive, transparent for observing biological samples, and mechanically tough, while hot embossing offers a potentially fast, low-cost fabrication method.

In hot embossing, a microfabricated stamp is pressed into a heated thermoplastic workpiece. The polymer is heated above its glass-transition temperature, loaded so that it flows into stamp cavities, cooled below the transition while under load to freeze the shape, and then unloaded. Important variables include material, pattern geometry, substrate thickness, temperature, load, loading and hold times, and demolding conditions. Differential thermal contraction creates substantial demolding challenges, including ridges, shearing, and stamp damage. Thermal nanoimprint lithography is a related process using submicrometer polymer films on hard substrates to transfer submicrometer features; uniform residual-layer thickness is critical for subsequent etching.

Stamp fabrication methods discussed include deep reactive-ion etching of silicon, nickel electroplating, and electron-beam lithography for nanoscale features. Silicon stamps can be vulnerable during demolding, while nickel and metallic glasses offer greater toughness. Electron-beam lithography provides high resolution but is slow and expensive, whereas an expensive stamp can subsequently produce many imprints rapidly.

The research seeks computationally efficient design and modeling tools that minimize time, energy, and cost while producing desired microstructures. It considers nonuniformity at the substrate scale, such as nonparallel plates and pressure variation; the device scale, including interactions among differently packed features; and the individual-feature scale, where very narrow cavities are difficult to fill. Carefully designed test stamps containing channels and holes are used to measure penetration and pattern-density effects.

Because detailed nonlinear finite-element polymer simulations are computationally expensive, the work develops simplified models. A one-dimensional viscoelastic model of PMMA shows that cooling below the glass transition preserves deformation while unloading at elevated temperature permits substantial recovery. A faster linear-elastic, rubbery-state approximation, combined with a point-load response function and fast Fourier transforms, predicts cavity penetration and pattern interactions using a fitted temperature-dependent Young’s modulus. Experiments with patterned silicon stamps showed close agreement between this model and measured topographies. The model can also estimate elastic modulus from embossing tests.

Longer holds introduce plastic flow. Adding a linear dashpot and scaling deformation with hold time captured much of this behavior, although narrow features filled faster than predicted. Yield-stress and strain-rate effects remain areas for model improvement. Results were also obtained for ZEONOR and TOPAS polymers. A fractional-factorial TOPAS study varied temperature, force, hold time, and loading time; analysis indicated that temperature, force, and hold time were significant, while loading time was uncertain. TOPAS also exhibited strong orientation-dependent anisotropy.

Process selection involves tradeoffs. Lower temperatures reduce thermal contraction and stamp risks but increase sensitivity to temperature-control errors; higher temperatures improve filling but can increase damage and deformation. Mold lubricants and coatings can reduce friction and mechanical locking but do not eliminate forces caused by modulus and thermal expansion. Precise demolding temperatures can substantially improve feature quality, although high-temperature demolding may cause bowing and requires rapid cooling.

In closing questions, the lecturer said IEEE papers are typically six to eight pages, recommended weighting competing objectives in a combined optimization function, and described one-factor-at-a-time optimization as exploring parameter corners and then randomly selecting the next corner, allowing comparison with response-surface optimization.

The gold/silver ratio measures the relationship between gold and silver prices by dividing gold’s price by silver’s price using the same currency and weight. It shows how many ounces of silver equal the value of one ounce of gold.

Traders commonly use the ratio in a contrarian or mean-reversion strategy. When the ratio is high, indicating gold is relatively expensive and silver cheap, traders may buy silver and short gold. When it is low, indicating gold is relatively cheap and silver expensive, they may buy gold and short silver. The ratio can be traded through futures, options, or related ETFs.

Historically, governments fixed the ratio for monetary stability, including 12:1 in the Roman Empire and 15:1 in the United States under the Coinage Act of 1792. Fixed ratios ended as countries abandoned bimetallic standards and, eventually, the gold standard. The 20th-century average was 47:1; the 21st-century ratio generally ranged between 50:1 and 70:1, peaking at 114.77 in 2020 and reaching a low of 35:1 in 2011. Traders often treat 35 as low and values above 80 as high, though the 2018–2020 spike showed that these thresholds may vary.

Backtests did not produce robust results. A simple strength-buying strategy had positive expectancy but an erratic, untradable equity curve on GLD. A pair strategy buying GLD and shorting SLV when the five-day RSI exceeded 75, and exiting below 50, developed flat. The authors also found no meaningful profitable strategy using the ratio as a stock-market risk gauge and noted that most commodity strategies fail to remain robust and profitable over time.

SFS attestation data should be requested by the OS or platform-management software through side-band/SPDM or in-band/DPE interfaces, with SFS providing measurements to attestation managers. Some schemes prevent updates to certain AMD firmware components, which AMD will not modify.

Each update package requires the correct prerequisite firmware versions to be present before application. Packages must not be applied unless all portions can be fully applied, avoiding forced resets; AMD and customer testing verify that resets are unnecessary. Packages do not persist across warm or cold reboots, so patches may be applied during OS boot, immediately afterward, or during system operation, including sequentially from a filesystem location. SFS commands require a 2MB-aligned TEE_EXT_CMD_BUFFER, specified output and package placement, and a customer deployment agent that assembles the package and optional customer co-signing data in DRAM, sends the command through the TEE mailbox, and passes the buffer’s physical address through additional mailboxes.

The ASP protects the buffer from x86 access, verifies customer and AMD signatures when applicable, loads and runs the patch, updates patch-level data, and returns status. GET_SFS_VERSION_INFO retrieves base firmware and patch-level information using two contiguous pages with specified initialization and SNP page requirements. UPDATE_FW validates the complete package before applying updates. Packages are binary objects aligned to AGESA releases, named `fam_<family>-<AGESA-Release>-SFS-<n>.pkg`, and must match the system’s specific firmware and patch-level combination. Updates run in parallel with x86 and DMA traffic and are designed to minimize performance impact. Some operations require brief quiescence; notably, SEV virtual machines may need to stop and restart for SEV firmware updates, while SEV/SNP virtual machines can continue operating.

The passage introduces a conditional denoising diffusion framework, EqDiff-CT, for synthesizing CT-like images from cone-beam CT (CBCT) to support image-guided and adaptive radiotherapy. CBCT provides daily volumetric imaging but has artifacts, scatter, truncated projections, and unreliable Hounsfield units, whereas planning CT offers better soft-tissue contrast and calibrated HU values but does not capture daily anatomical changes. Synthetic CT may improve dose calculation, segmentation, treatment adaptation, workflow efficiency, and patient comfort.

Earlier approaches include deformable registration with analytical intensity correction, GANs such as CycleGAN, CNN and transformer architectures, and hybrid models. Registration-based methods require prior CT and cannot recover high-frequency structures, while GANs can suffer from unstable training, mode collapse, hallucination, and limited interpretability. Diffusion models offer greater stability but remain computationally costly, with limited investigation of generalization across anatomical sites.

EqDiff-CT performs conditional 2D axial-slice synthesis using a time-conditioned, C4 rotation-equivariant U-Net denoiser implemented with e2cnn. Self-attention captures long-range spatial dependencies, and CBCT slices are concatenated with noisy CT inputs at each timestep to support orientation-consistent reconstruction. Training uses a non-adversarial denoising objective combining MSE and SSIM losses on predicted noise, followed by variance-corrected reverse diffusion. A HU-preserving preprocessing and postprocessing pipeline is also included.

Evaluation uses the SynthRAD2025 Head & Neck dataset with an 80/20 patient-wise split and slice-wise and volume-wise metrics. Experiments showed that the attention-enhanced model outperformed a diffusion model without attention and a CycleGAN baseline in SSIM, PSNR, MSE, and MAE, while preserving the mandible, airway, and cervical spine. The described forward diffusion progressively corrupts reference CT with Gaussian noise, while the trained model learns to reconstruct it conditioned on the paired CBCT.

The passage describes a study developing a model to identify potential sources of influenza A H5 RNA in wastewater. Background: 3–11% of the US population is infected with influenza annually, IAV causing most infections, and wastewater concentrations of total IAV RNA track closely with community infections. The HPAI H5N1 outbreak began in US birds in February 2022, killing millions of poultry and wild fowls; in March 2024 unexplained cattle illness was identified as H5N1, with 865 infected dairy herds and 61 human cases reported in 16 states through December 19, 2024, with no human-to-human transmission reported or suspected. H5 RNA was detected in wastewater at multiple US sites beginning March 2024. Plausible sources include cow's milk (H5N1 is shed in milk, detected in raw and pasteurized retail milk; 12% of milk is wasted at retailers, 20% by consumers, 45% at kindergarten/pre-K lunches, 13% by high school students, entering sewers), poultry feces, wildfowl feces (via combined sewers or open-air settling tanks), and human contributions.

Objectives: (1) identify the timing of the first H5 detection in the sewershed during a period of circulating human influenza, and (2) develop and implement a model of theoretical H5 sources to contextualize findings.

Methods: H1 and H3 assays were designed from NCBI (Jan 2023; Dec 2022) and GISAID (April 2024) sequences using Primer3Plus primers/probes targeting the hemagglutinin gene, verified in silico via NCBI BLAST and tested in vitro against respiratory pathogen panels using ddRT-PCR; H5 and M gene assays were previously described, with M gene indicating total IAV. Biobanked nucleic-acid extracts from 110 wastewater solids samples (grab samples of primary clarifier settled solids) collected September 1, 2023–May 13, 2024 at the Southeast San Francisco POTW (750,000 people; combined stormwater/sanitary sewers), stored 1–10 months at −80°C, were analyzed. Extraction used the Chemagic Viral DNA/RNA 300 Kit H96 plus Zymo OneStep PCR Inhibitor Removal Kit within 24 hours; 0.5–1 g solids dried at 110°C for dry weight. Multiplex dd-RT-PCR (AutoDG, Mastercycler Pro, QX600) used 10 replicates per sample, all exceeding 10,000 droplets, with synthetic/custom gene block positive controls, NTCs, BCoV spike-in and PMMoV endogenous controls; QuantaSoft Analysis Pro thresholding required ≥3 positive droplets (500–1000 copies/g), reported as gene copies/dry g.

The model used a mass balance equation where daily H5 flux equals summed contributions from humans, poultry, wild birds, and milk. Liquid-phase H5 concentrations were calculated with the Freundlich isotherm using a partitioning coefficient; total daily flux combined H5 in solids and liquids, using POTW daily flow rate and total suspended solids.

The study developed two hydrogen-bonded metal inorganic–organic complex (MIOC) crystals and glasses through ligand tuning of ZIF-4 and ZIF-7: monoclinic ZnCl₂(HIm)₂ (MIOC-4) and triclinic ZnCl₂(HbIm)₂ (MIOC-7). Slow evaporation synthesis produced supramolecular networks stabilized mainly by N–H···Cl hydrogen bonds, with additional π–π interactions in MIOC-7. Melt quenching yielded large, amorphous glasses with melting points of 440 and 508 K and glass-transition temperatures of 282 and 359 K for MIOC-4 and MIOC-7, respectively.

In situ XRD showed that melting begins with slippage and distortion of strongly hydrogen-bonded chains, followed by hydrogen-bond rupture and complete disorder. Stacked MIOC-4 chains readily slip, whereas interdigitated MIOC-7 structures dissociate progressively and have greater thermal stability. Hydrogen-bond rupture creates free volume for molecular mobility while allowing coordination bonds to remain intact and avoiding ligand decomposition. During vitrification, stronger N–H···Cl bonds reform, weaker C–H···Cl interactions diminish, and medium- and long-range intermolecular order disappears. Zn–N, Zn–Cl, Zn–C, and ligand correlations remain but exhibit short-range disorder, as shown by FT-IR, Raman, NMR, and synchrotron XRD.

Mixed-ligand synthesis produced physical mixtures of MIOC-4 and MIOC-7 with lower melting points and continuously tunable glass-transition temperatures. The minimum melting point was 415 K for ZnCl₂(HbIm)₀.₄₉₈(HIm)₁.₅₀₂, while Tg increased from 282 to 360 K as HIm was replaced by sterically larger HbIm. Extending the strategy to Co and Cu nodes and SCN⁻ anions yielded additional MIOC crystals and glasses. Hydrogen-bond strength and network topology were identified as the principal determinants of thermal behavior, with smaller effects from metal-node changes.

MIOC-7 glass displayed enhanced, excitation-dependent photoluminescence. Its broad emissions shifted from blue toward yellow with increasing excitation wavelength, attributed to slow molecular relaxation and excitation of frozen conformers with distinct energies. At 370 nm excitation, its internal photoluminescence quantum yield was 3.4%, compared with 1.2% for MIOC-7 crystal. Photoluminescence intensity decreased with rising temperature, and the enhanced visible emission indicates potential anti-counterfeiting applications.

- GDDR6X’s Error Detection and Replay feature identifies failed memory transactions and retries them. Performance plateaus as overclocking produces additional errors, giving users an indication to stop increasing memory clocks.
