Royal Rumble 2017 at the Alamodome is expected to be WWE’s largest, with Goldberg, Brock Lesnar and John Cena confirmed; The Undertaker is expected and Shawn Michaels is rumoured in a non-wrestling role. The card features AJ Styles defending the WWE Championship against Cena, Kevin Owens defending the Universal Championship against Roman Reigns with Chris Jericho suspended in a shark cage, and a 30-man Royal Rumble match. Possible entrants include Braun Strowman and Finn Bálor.

Bath Rugby supporters remained stranded after their team’s 24-20 Champions Cup defeat by Toulon, as snow, ice and wind caused cancellations and disruption across southern England and northern Europe. Flights from Marseille, Nice and Amsterdam were cancelled or diverted, while Heathrow and other London airports were affected. Fans attempted alternative routes through European cities or by train, encountering further delays, cancelled services, mis-booked flights and confusing cancellation messages. The Bath team’s chartered flight returned to Bristol, but many supporters were delayed, missed work, made special childcare arrangements or were unlikely to reach the funeral of a popular season-ticket holder. Some eventually reached London or other UK airports, while others remained in France awaiting later flights. Despite the disruption, several fans described their weekend positively and made the most of the extra time in Toulon and Nice.

China tightened rare-earth export restrictions, requiring licenses for products containing rare earths worth at least 0.1% and companies using Chinese extraction, refining or magnet-recycling technology. Shares of U.S. rare-earth and critical-mineral miners surged amid speculation of further White House investment in domestic supply chains, following administration equity stakes in several miners, including MP Materials. The move preceded an expected Xi Jinping–Donald Trump meeting at the APEC summit in Seoul.

The case examines the causes and aftermath of two Boeing 737 MAX 8 crashes. Lion Air Flight 610 crashed into the Java Sea on October 29, 2018, killing all 189 people aboard. Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 crashed near Addis Ababa on March 10, 2019, killing all 157 aboard. The crashes raised competing explanations involving pilot error, MCAS, Boeing’s design and management processes, and FAA oversight.

The MAX program was launched in 2011 as Boeing’s rapid response to Airbus’s A320neo and the possible loss of a major American Airlines order. Tight schedules and budgets compressed development, while employees reported sloppy work, inadequate review of design issues, and a culture that did not reward people challenging managers. These concerns were part of a broader shift from Boeing’s historically engineering-centered culture following its 1997 acquisition of McDonnell Douglas, including a move toward shareholder-value priorities, outsourcing, layoffs, and what some employees described as contradictory signals demanding openness while punishing dissent.

MCAS was developed to counter a tendency toward nose-up pitching caused by the MAX’s larger engines, which were moved forward and mounted higher under the wings. Testing later showed that the pitch-up condition could occur at low speeds as well as during high-speed maneuvers. MCAS was therefore changed from moving the horizontal stabilizer 0.6 degrees over ten seconds to 2.5 degrees, the high-G-force activation condition was removed, and the system could repeatedly command a nose-down movement while a high angle of attack persisted.

The revised MCAS relied on data from only one of two angle-of-attack sensors, creating a single point of failure. A cockpit indicator and disagree alert could identify inconsistent sensor readings, but they were optional equipment that several airlines, including Lion Air, Ethiopian Airlines, and Southwest Airlines, did not purchase. An Indonesian investigation found that Lion Air had installed a miscalibrated replacement sensor that supplied erroneous data to MCAS.

Boeing sought certification for the MAX as a minor derivative of earlier 737 models and initially gave the FAA limited information about MCAS. The FAA focused on other changes, while Boeing did not formally submit certification documents describing major MCAS modifications. Boeing’s safety analysis did not classify the system-level risk as catastrophic and therefore did not require redundant sensor inputs. Boeing also promoted a “Level B” training plan that avoided flight-simulator training and did not include pilots’ response to unexpected MCAS activation. Investigations concluded that inadequate manuals and training made it harder for crews to respond to the system.

Boeing initially emphasized Lion Air’s maintenance practices and pilot performance after the first crash, then issued an operator bulletin and made an FAA emergency airworthiness directive follow. After the Ethiopian crash, scrutiny focused on whether Boeing had concealed potentially dangerous software, whether its compressed development schedule and corporate culture undermined safety, and whether FAA certification failures and industry pressure contributed. A U.S. transportation inspector general’s report cited communication gaps, management and oversight weaknesses, and insufficient independence within the FAA. A later survey of FAA personnel found reports of strong external pressure from industry.

Following public, governmental, and industry pressure, President Donald Trump grounded all MAX aircraft on March 13, 2019. Review boards examined the crashes while airlines canceled orders and Boeing removed or canceled 1,043 MAX orders by the end of October 2020. The aircraft remained grounded for 21 months and was permitted to return to commercial service on November 18, 2020.

After the crashes, Boeing’s board created a safety committee and recommended clearer engineering authority, an independent safety group, and a permanent board safety committee. Boeing eventually recommended simulator training and the FAA required ground and flight-simulator training. Boeing fired Commercial Airplanes CEO Kevin McAllister and CEO Dennis Muilenburg, while FAA safety official Ali Bahrami later retired.

The case concludes that the disasters exposed unresolved questions about Boeing’s culture, employee ability to raise safety concerns, the adequacy of FAA independence and oversight, and the ability of manufacturers and regulators to prioritize safety over schedule and financial pressure. Estimated direct costs exceeded $21 billion, with estimated lost aircraft sales of $67 billion, while the families of the 346 victims continued to face the consequences.

After seven months out of action, a hockey player sought to return to competitive hockey. He said three weeks of training with the junior Whalers while representing Russia at the Olympics helped restore his focus. North Carolina later made an offer, giving Detroit seven days to match. Although existing financial terms made matching difficult, he hoped to stay because Detroit had long been his “second home” and the team where he defected from Russia to play.

Detroit matched the offer, and he returned, met teammates, addressed concerns surrounding Sergei Fedorov’s contract, and played on Friday night despite exhaustion and jet lag. He said the experience reinforced his desire to remain in Detroit. After coach Scotty Bowman delivered an inspirational speech about keeping things normal, teammate Vladi appeared in the building and on the ice. The player spoke with Vladi in Russian for several minutes, was pleased by his smile and readiness, and said the team’s thoughts were with him.

The paper addresses the modeling bottleneck in Constraint Programming (CP) and the problem of over-fitting in Constraint Acquisition (CA), where global constraints such as AllDifferent, Sum, and Count learned from few examples capture coincidental patterns rather than true problem rules. It extends earlier hybrid CA work into a three-phase framework, "Hybrid CA with Refinement" (HCAR), guided by two research questions: how to systematically evaluate and refine over-fitted candidate global constraints, and which interactive strategies (query generation, confidence management, resource allocation) most efficiently minimize oracle interaction cost.

Phase 1 (passive candidate generation and bias refinement) analyzes a small set of positive examples. It detects structural patterns in grid/matrix or list-like structures, optionally incorporates domain knowledge, matches patterns against a library of global constraint types, instantiates scopes, infers parameters, and requires consistency with all positive examples to form the candidate global set Bglobals. Concurrently, a large fixed-arity bias Bfixed is pruned by removing constraints violated by any example. Because examples are few, both sets may retain spurious constraints; for example, learning a 4×4 Sudoku from two examples could produce an AllDifferent over the main diagonal and unary equality constraints.

Phase 2 (query-driven interactive refinement) is the core contribution. Each candidate receives a confidence score P(c) initialized from priors of an offline-trained machine learning classifier using structural and statistical features, then updated via Bayesian aggregation of oracle evidence. A loop investigates the lowest-confidence candidate, generating informative queries that satisfy already-accepted constraints while targeting the investigated one; a "Valid" oracle response refutes the constraint. Crossing acceptance (θmax) or rejection (θmin) thresholds causes the constraint to be accepted into C′G or rejected, respectively. Rejected globals trigger subset exploration, which generates sub-constraints by removing first, middle, or last variables while preserving type and parameters, up to a depth limit, recovering valid substructures and preventing information loss. An adaptive query budget is initially allocated uniformly; unused budget from accepted constraints is pooled and redistributed, while rejected constraints pass remaining budget to their subsets.

Phase 3 applies an established active learning algorithm (MQuAcq-2), initialized with the refined globals and pruned fixed-arity bias, to learn remaining constraints and complete the model.

Background covers CSPs and global constraints; related work reviews passive methods (ConAcq, ModelSeeker, COUNT-CP, CLASSACQ, MINEACQ) prone to over-fitting, active methods (ConAcq.2, QuAcq, MultiAcq, MQuAcq, projection-based and probabilistic query generation) facing scalability issues with globals, LLM-driven bias-free acquisition (ACQNOGOODS, LLMACQ), and hybrid methods lacking over-fitting correction mechanisms. Empirical validation on diverse benchmarks showed high accuracy and target model coverage from limited examples with manageable query complexity.

This study examined U.S. mathematics education faculty members’ perceptions of research expectations for tenure and promotion. Prior research indicated that expectations vary by institution type, department type, and proportion of time devoted to research, and that expectations may be documented incompletely or left implicit. The study therefore measured both activities faculty viewed as necessary and those they viewed as valuable.

Participants were identified through publications in 55 mathematics education journals from 2015–2017 and several edited book series and practitioner journals. After screening survey responses, 404 members of the target population remained. The survey collected demographic information, expected annual publication numbers, and perceived tenure value of research articles, books, chapters, textbooks, conference papers, practitioner articles, external funding, presentations, professional development, and authorship. Responses were analyzed by institution type, department, and research commitment using descriptive comparisons and multinomial logistic regression.

Overall, respondents typically devoted 20–40% of their time to research and expected about 1.64 publications annually. Research journal articles were consistently valued most, while books, book chapters, practitioner articles, and conference papers generally counted somewhat. There was no clear consensus on textbooks. Presentations were commonly expected, and pursuing external funding was also common, even when funding was not obtained. Professional development was neither generally required nor highly valued. First authorship was considered important.

Expectations differed by institution. R1 faculty typically devoted 40% of their time to research and expected about 2.25 papers annually; R2 faculty expected 1.5, and faculty at other institutions expected one. R2 faculty were more likely than others to have expected publication numbers stated in writing. R1 faculty placed relatively greater value on sole authorship, presentations, and obtaining funding, while faculty at other institutions more often reported no expectation to pursue or obtain funding.

Each 10-percentage-point increase in research commitment was associated with 0.184 additional expected papers. Faculty with higher research commitments placed less value on books, chapters, and practitioner articles, and were more likely to value sole and lead authorship. Mathematics department faculty expected 0.309 fewer papers than education department faculty, held constant, but placed greater value on conference proceedings and pursuing or obtaining funding. They were less likely than education faculty to value professional development, presentations, and first authorship.

The authors concluded that clearer written expectations and open discussion could help faculty, programs, and the broader mathematics education field clarify publication requirements, valued scholarly activities, and whether specific activities are required.

The study examines the orbital and spin Edelstein effects in electron- and hole-doped monolayer transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) subjected to a perpendicular gate field. The field breaks horizontal mirror symmetry, changing the point group from D3h to gyrotropic C3v and inducing momentum-dependent chiral spin and orbital textures. When an in-plane electric field shifts the nonequilibrium Fermi surface, these textures generate net planar orbital and spin moments through the orbital and spin Edelstein effects.

A minimal 5×5 tight-binding Hamiltonian in the metal d-orbital subspace was constructed by Löwdin downfolding a model containing metal and chalcogen orbitals. Its parameters, including electric-field and spin-orbit coupling terms, were fitted to DFT bands calculated using PAW, VASP, and GGA. Near the band edges, the model reduces to an effective Hamiltonian combining Ising and Rashba terms. Intrinsic orbital moments were calculated using the atom-centered approximation, and Edelstein susceptibilities were obtained through Fermi-surface integrals in the relaxation-time approximation.

For hole-doped MoS2, holes first occupy the K/K′ pockets and then the Γ pocket, which dominates the response because γ1 is much larger than γ2. The orbital contributions from the two spin-split bands add, whereas their spin contributions largely cancel. Population of the Γ pocket therefore produces a pronounced orbital Edelstein effect and an initially enhanced spin response that later declines as both Rashba-split bands fill. Small compressive strain shifts the Γ valence band above K/K′ and can substantially increase both responses; about 1% strain is sufficient for MoS2.

For electron-doped systems, conduction electrons occupy the K/K′ valleys. The orbital Edelstein susceptibility grows linearly with electron density and is several times larger than the spin susceptibility. Unlike the hole case, the orbital moments of the two conduction bands have unequal prefactors and therefore do not cancel, while the opposite spin chiralities strongly suppress the spin response. These electron-doping results apply to small concentrations, roughly no more than 0.02 electrons per unit cell, because the minimal model does not reproduce the higher-doping K–Γ conduction-band dip.

Both responses scale linearly with gate field for weak fields and are generally of order 10⁻⁸–10⁻⁷ μB V⁻¹m, one or two orders of magnitude larger than values reported for two other material systems discussed. MoTe2 shows particularly large orbital susceptibilities. The results identify gated, doped monolayer TMDs as promising platforms for studying and potentially using the orbital Edelstein effect in spintronics.

The Keltner Channel, also called Keltner Bands, is a volatility-based technical analysis tool developed by commodity trader Chester W. Keltner in the 1960s. It consists of a central moving average—commonly a 20-period exponential moving average—and upper and lower bands set a specified multiple of the Average True Range (ATR) above and below it. The bands expand during high volatility and contract during low volatility. Traders use them to assess trends, volatility, support and resistance, overbought or oversold conditions, breakouts, and potential entry and exit points. Price moving outside the channels may indicate a reversal, overextension, or possible trend continuation.

Settings vary by market and trading style and should be backtested. A common configuration uses a 20-period EMA and an ATR multiplier of 2. The article also gives a 15-period calculation based on the moving average of high, low, and close prices, with bands two ATRs away.

Keltner Channels can support mean-reversion or momentum strategies. Mean-reversion approaches buy below the lower band or sell above the upper band, while momentum approaches trade breakouts in the direction of movement and may exit near the opposite band. They are also used in scalping and swing trading. Position sizing should account for volatility, account size, and risk tolerance, supplemented by stops or other risk controls.

Compared with Bollinger Bands, Keltner Channels use ATR rather than standard deviation and are described as generally less responsive to price changes. A Bollinger squeeze within the Keltner Channel indicates contraction and consolidation, potentially preceding a directional move.

In the passage’s tests, a Keltner strategy on SPY produced 288 trades, a 77% win rate, 6.3% CAGR, 15% market exposure, and a profit factor of 2, with slightly better results on QQQ. A momentum version using 30 days and an ATR of 1.3 produced 143 trades and 3.6% CAGR. GLD generated about 1% per trade but had a low win rate, with a few large winners offsetting many losses.

The passage advises combining Keltner Channels with other technical and fundamental analysis, considering broader market conditions, and applying risk management because signals and profitability vary.

On December 12, 2016, NVIDIA Corporation entered into a Termination Agreement with Goldman, Sachs & Co. terminating certain outstanding warrants to purchase NVIDIA common stock issued under letter agreements dated November 25 and November 26, 2013. In aggregate, 63,259,180.62 warrants will be terminated. As consideration, NVIDIA will deliver shares of common stock to Goldman, with the amount determined daily based on the volume-weighted average price of the common stock during an observation period from December 13, 2016 to January 31, 2017. The shares are issued in reliance on the Section 4(a)(2) exemption from registration. The agreement is filed as Exhibit 10.1, and the report was signed by Colette M. Kress, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer.

Past government shutdowns have had little lasting effect on markets or growth because workers are typically rehired and losses recovered. This shutdown could differ if President Donald Trump makes furloughs permanent, worsening already precarious employment and adding economic uncertainty. A prolonged shutdown could halt much Labor Department activity, delaying payroll and inflation data, reducing data quality, affecting Social Security cost-of-living adjustments, and forcing the Federal Reserve to rely more on private data. Economists still expect the overall impact to be relatively mild, but furloughed federal employees and contractors could face immediate financial hardship, with Washington, D.C., particularly exposed.

The article reviews Netflix’s documentary “Unknown Number: The High School Catfish,” about Beal City, Michigan, students Lauryn Licari and Owen McKenny after an unknown number sends escalating hateful, sexually graphic messages and death threats. Local authorities investigated for 18 months before the FBI received 720 pages of messages and requested a forensic “dump” of Owen’s phone. The author says the documentary reveals an unexpected perpetrator but provides too little detail about cellphone forensics.

The article also examines how widespread cellphone access can facilitate cybercrime, harm students and complicate investigations. It highlights Oklahoma’s one-year “bell to bell” policy for 2025–26, restricting phones, smartwatches and other internet-capable devices in schools amid parental and student opposition.

The Bank of England allotted £5.085 billion through its six-month indexed long-term repo operation, the highest since March 2020 and more than double the £2.352 billion allocated the previous week. The secured facility offers six-month funding backed by high-quality collateral, typically without surcharges. The allocation reflects rising demand for central-bank liquidity as the BoE unwinds quantitative easing and shifts banks away from relying on abundant reserves. Demand for longer-term repos remains modest compared with the record £87.149 billion allotted through its seven-day facility. Future policy will depend on sustained repo demand and balancing liquidity provision with stable gilt markets.

The Fabian Market Timing Model is a rule-based, long-term trend-following strategy for the S&P 500, developed by Richard Fabian in the 1960s. It uses the S&P 500’s 39-week moving average, with signals confirmed by the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the utilities sector’s 39-week moving averages to reduce false signals. Buy and sell decisions are mechanical and executed weekly. A backtest starting after the dot-com bubble peak produced returns closer to buy-and-hold, with notably low volatility and maximum drawdown. The model’s key value is disciplined adherence to its signals through favorable and unfavorable periods.

A South Carolina House panel advanced a pension proposal that would raise employee contributions from 8.66% to 9% and employer contributions from 11.56% to 18.56% by 2023 to address a $24 billion retirement funding gap, drawing local-government opposition. A bill allowing recognition of concealed-carry permits from all 50 states also advanced. The Senate passed Coastal Carolina University championship license plates, with proceeds supporting scholarships.

Chelsea will face Barcelona in the Champions League last 16 after finishing second in Group C behind Roma. Barcelona topped Group D with 14 points. The first leg is scheduled for February 13/14 or 20/21, with the second on March 6/7 or 13/14. Chelsea beat Barcelona 3-2 on aggregate in the 2012 semifinal before progressing to the final as eventual champions. Lionel Messi will be Barcelona’s focus.

Lorna Gibson reviews bone structure, osteoporosis modeling, metal foams, and the evolutionary use of trabecular architecture. She describes using two- and three-dimensional Voronoi honeycombs with finite-element analysis to model porous bone. Finite-element elastic moduli closely match analytical predictions, while the random structure has less effect on stiffness than on compressive strength. Voronoi strengths are about 0.6–0.8 times those of periodic hexagonal honeycombs because their varied strut lengths and orientations create a wider stress and strain distribution. Failure shifts from elastic buckling to plastic yielding as density increases, with a transition near 3.5% relative density and a strength minimum near 5%.

Models comparing strut thinning with strut removal show that thinning gradually reduces stiffness and strength, whereas removing struts causes much larger losses. Connectivity reaches a percolation threshold after roughly 30–35% density reduction in two dimensions and 50% in three dimensions, when stiffness and strength fall to zero. Perturbed Voronoi models matched the orientation of vertebral trabeculae and reproduced the tested bone’s stress-strain behavior, including localized deformation bands.

The lecture also examines porous metal foams as implant coatings that permit bone ingrowth and as possible materials for vertebral procedures. Titanium and tantalum foams can be produced through replica methods, fugitive-phase processing, foaming agents, argon expansion, freeze casting, and laser sintering. Their measured properties vary considerably, but generally follow foam-like trends.

Finally, Gibson discusses the evolution of mineralized tissues, noting that bone is collagen with calcium phosphate and appears in vertebrates around 450 million years ago, while many earlier mineralized organisms used calcium carbonate or silica. Because trabecular density reflects stress magnitude and strut orientation reflects principal stress directions, fossil architecture can help infer locomotion. Comparisons of the ilium of the roughly eight-million-year-old Oreopithecus with human and non-human primate ilia found more human-like features, suggesting at least some bipedal behavior. Bone quality, including age-related microcracks, can further weaken bone beyond the effects of thinning or losing struts.

Tesla, Inc. filed an unaudited Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2021, reporting results under two operating segments: automotive and energy generation and storage. As of October 21, 2021, 1,004,264,852 common shares were outstanding.

Third-quarter revenue was $13.757 billion, compared with $8.771 billion a year earlier, including automotive revenue of $12.057 billion, energy generation and storage revenue of $806 million, and services and other revenue of $894 million. Gross profit was $3.660 billion, operating income was $2.004 billion, and net income attributable to common stockholders was $1.618 billion, or $1.44 per diluted share. For the first nine months, revenue was $36.104 billion, net income attributable to common stockholders was $3.198 billion, and diluted earnings per share were $2.84.

At September 30, 2021, Tesla reported $57.834 billion of assets, $29.340 billion of liabilities, and $27.053 billion of stockholders’ equity. Cash and cash equivalents were $16.065 billion, inventory was $5.199 billion, property, plant and equipment was $17.298 billion, and digital assets were $1.260 billion. During the first nine months, operating activities generated $6.912 billion of cash; investing used $5.952 billion, including $1.500 billion for digital-asset purchases, and financing used $3.946 billion.

Tesla purchased $1.50 billion of bitcoin during the nine-month period, recorded $101 million of impairment losses and realized a $128 million gain. The September 30 carrying value was $1.26 billion, while reported fair value was $1.83 billion. Digital assets were accounted for as indefinite-lived intangible assets, with fair value based on quoted exchange prices and impairment recognized in restructuring and other expenses.

The company adopted ASU 2020-06 on convertible instruments using the modified retrospective method, resulting in a $263 million cumulative adjustment to opening equity. The change reduced nine-month net interest expense by $196 million and required the if-converted method for diluted EPS.

Debt and finance leases totaled $8.154 billion, down from $11.688 billion at year-end 2020. Convertible notes were converted and settled during the period; the $1.80 billion 2025 senior notes were fully repaid with a $60 million extinguishment charge. Tesla issued $1.08 billion and $904 million of automotive asset-backed notes in March and September 2021, respectively, and repaid or terminated several loan facilities. Subsequent to quarter-end, it prepaid $321 million of solar asset-backed notes and $53 million of solar loan-backed notes.

The filing described COVID-19-related port congestion, supplier delays, semiconductor shortages, temporary manufacturing closures and other disruptions. Construction in progress primarily covered Gigafactory Berlin and Texas and the expansion of Gigafactory Shanghai. Tesla also maintained a long-term Buffalo, New York lease and development agreement requiring $5 billion of combined spending and employment commitments over ten years, with potential annual payments of $41 million for unmet requirements.

Rinholm, Heiberg Solem, and Ulleberg investigate how dialogic principles can be concretized in classroom practice through cases from pre-service music teacher education and upper-primary mathematics education. Against the backdrop of global crises, UNESCO’s call for justice and global solidarity, and Norwegian requirements for critical, participatory, democratic citizenship, the study asks which theoretical concepts can explain dialogic teaching, how teachers promote participation, and how epistemological and ontological dialogue appear and interact.

The interdisciplinary qualitative study uses a deductive, hermeneutic narrative approach, combining theoretical concepts with two contrasting cases. The music case concerns a four-week choir project involving 40 pre-service teachers and includes a teacher’s decision to connect a student-chosen song with her personal experience of losing her brother to AIDS. The mathematics case uses selected transcripts from a 45-minute lesson with 27 seventh-grade students exploring fractions between rational numbers. Students proposed a pattern based on adding numerators and denominators, developed further hypotheses, and tested them with additional examples while the teacher acknowledged uncertainty.

The framework distinguishes epistemological dialogue, concerned with subject knowledge, qualification, and socialization, from ontological dialogue, which addresses students’ lives, self-understanding, subjectivity, and whole-person engagement. Both are related to Bildung, understood as the cultivation of humanity, critical judgment, autonomy, and Mündigkeit. The authors also discuss dialogism, dialogic pedagogy, musicking, mathematizing, and the classroom’s implicit or explicit didactic contract. Genuine dialogue requires more than spoken exchange: teachers must listen, engage as persons and learners, value students’ consciousnesses, negotiate knowledge, ask genuine questions, and recognize that silence and tacit responses may also be meaningful.

Analysis shows that the music teacher combined subject instruction with student ownership of song choices and an emotionally and existentially significant disclosure. The resulting performance expressed joy, love, friendship, sexuality, illness, death, and remembrance simultaneously. Musicking highlighted the social and relational meanings created through musical participation, while also revealing the teacher’s hesitation, doubt, and shame. The case also illustrates the need to balance personal disclosure with students’ emotional safety.

In the mathematics lesson, students shared ideas, explained reasoning, questioned conclusions, formed hypotheses, and pursued counterexamples. These processes constituted mathematizing because participants expressed, tested, and revised their thinking through communicative activity rather than merely receiving knowledge. The teacher’s fallibility, curiosity, openness to student initiatives, and acknowledgment that he did not know the outcome introduced ontological qualities. The episode also showed how students could use their voices, listen, investigate, and participate as responsible learners.

Across both cases, teachers listened carefully, took up students’ contributions, allowed them to shape the activity, retained subject expertise, and accepted pedagogical uncertainty. They showed vulnerability and took risks, making Bildung possible through encounters that transformed students’ relationships to music, mathematics, themselves, and others. The findings suggest that epistemological and ontological dialogue coexist and interact, and that teachers should combine subject leadership with open-ended questioning, reflection time, diverse responses, and genuine interest in students’ ways of understanding.

The authors identify persistent paradoxes: efforts to promote autonomy or student voice may preserve teacher authority or become monologic; ontological engagement may invade students’ privacy, standardize preferred forms of Bildung, or reflect culturally narrow assumptions about emotional and social skills. They conclude that dialogic teaching may support democratic capacities but does not guarantee them, because educational outcomes and causal relationships cannot be fully predicted or controlled.

The speaker urges the council to consider the United States’ role in establishing a durable international peace after the war, asserting that Americans have a duty to help guarantee peace and justice. He argues that any settlement must create terms worthy of preservation and acceptable to mankind, rather than merely serve the immediate interests of belligerents. Before committing to a peace league, the U.S. government should state the conditions justifying such participation. A lasting peace requires an organized force greater than any nation or existing alliance, as well as a covenant including the peoples of the New World. Rejecting both imposed victory and a new balance of power, he advocates “peace without victory”: a community of power and an organized common peace among equals, based on equal participation and shared benefits.

British Transport Police said a 19-year-old woman was sexually assaulted by a man from a group on a train in Weston-super-Mare. Other passengers intervened, and police appealed for information about the April 8 incident.

The lecture reviews linearized general relativity around flat spacetime. Of the ten metric perturbation degrees of freedom, six are gauge invariant and four are gauge artifacts. The radiative, transverse-traceless component \(h^{TT}_{ij}\) contains two physical degrees of freedom, corresponding to gravitational-wave polarizations. For a wave traveling in the \(z\)-direction, \(h_{xx}=-h_{yy}\) and \(h_{xy}=h_{yx}\).

A single freely falling body appears stationary in coordinates that follow it, so gravitational-wave effects must be described through coordinate-independent observables such as the separation of nearby bodies. The relative motion of two nearby free-falling bodies is governed by geodesic deviation and the Riemann curvature tensor. Their separation changes as one wave stretches space along one direction while squeezing it along another. The \(h_{xx}\) component produces the “plus” polarization, while \(h_{xy}\) produces the “cross” polarization. Light bounced between separated bodies also acquires arrival-time shifts, providing the basis for interferometric detection. LIGO measures these effects by timing laser light reflected between mirrors and comparing returning light through interference.

The lecture then derives how to calculate the radiation field. One may solve the linearized Einstein equations in any convenient gauge and extract the gauge-invariant \(h^{TT}_{ij}\), since individual metric components in gauges such as Lorentz gauge can misleadingly appear radiative. Using the retarded solution in Lorentz gauge, a far-field approximation, and the tensor virial theorem, the radiative field is expressed in terms of the second time derivatives of the source’s quadrupole moment. Projecting this result onto the plane transverse to the propagation direction and removing its trace yields the quadrupole formula for gravitational waves. The field scales with Newton’s constant, inverse source distance, and the second derivative of the quadrupole moment. The lecture concludes by noting that a following lecture will derive the related energy-content version of the quadrupole formula.

Researchers identified TRPM8 and TRPP3 as potential therapeutic targets for increasing brown adipose tissue. In human precursor-cell cultures, both channels were highly expressed in differentiated brown fat but not progenitor cells. Activating TRPM8 promoted browning, while inhibiting it impeded browning; genetically disabling TRPP3 prevented brown-fat formation but not white-fat formation. The findings may support drugs or functional foods that modulate energy consumption and blood sugar, with implications for obesity and diabetes.

The Predictors 3 study externally validated the longitudinal Grade of Membership (L-GoM) model in a community-dwelling, multiethnic cohort of 273 older adults in North Manhattan: 123 had mild cognitive impairment (MCI; 83 nonconverters and 40 converters), and 150 had Alzheimer’s dementia (118 nonreverters and 32 reverters to a non-dementia diagnosis). Baseline data covering 11 clinical domains were used to generate individual L-GoM subtype scores and predict survival and need for full-time care over 7.5 years. Predictions were compared with observed Kaplan–Meier survival and full-time-care prevalence curves using simultaneous 95% confidence bands.

Initial L-GoM scores differed significantly between MCI and AD, with MCI cases having higher subtype 1 scores and AD cases higher subtype 3 and 4 scores. AD reverters had higher subtype 1 scores, whereas nonreverters had higher subtype 4 scores. Scores also differed by sex, ethnicity, and ApoE status.

Overall survival predictions closely fit observed data, although two points fell outside or immediately adjacent to the confidence bands. Predictions fit well for AD nonreverters, MCI participants, and the cohort after excluding AD reverters. AD reverters survived substantially longer and needed full-time care less often than predicted, so the model did not fit this subgroup. The authors concluded that these cases likely had premature or incorrect AD diagnoses, noting that 29 of 32 reversions occurred within two to three years.

Full-time-care predictions were generally close after excluding AD reverters. They were excellent for AD nonreverters during the first 36 months and for MCI cases after approximately 48 months, with some early overprediction. Median predicted survival was 76.4 months for MCI cases and 56.7 months for AD nonreverters.

The validation also supports the L-GoM web-based calculator. Initial subtype scores were highly informative for individual prognosis, and combining predicted survival with conditional full-time-care probabilities estimates residual years of life with or without care. Validation extended the model beyond the clinic-based, high-SES, non-Hispanic population used previously, including application to MCI and diverse community participants. Limitations include the small non-Hispanic nonwhite subgroup, the predominantly Caribbean and Dominican composition of the Hispanic sample, and the need for further validation in other minority groups and longitudinal settings.

Fibonacci trading uses ratios and tools to identify potential support and resistance, plan entries and exits, and set stops or profit targets. Common tools include retracement, expansion, fan, and channel tools. Retracements mark levels such as 23.6%, 38.2%, 50%, 61.8%, and 78.6% of a prior price swing; expansion tools estimate the next trend swing, while fans project potential dynamic support and resistance.

There is no universally best timeframe: day traders may use intraday charts, swing traders may use four-hour or daily charts, and suitability should be determined through backtesting. Market volatility affects retracement levels, although many traders favor 50%–61.8%.

Despite its popularity, the passage says Fibonacci trading lacks convincing scientific evidence and is rarely backtested. A cited study of Vanguard ETFs found that passive buy-and-hold outperformed an active Fibonacci strategy, though Fibonacci retracements remained useful for identifying support, resistance, and profit targets. The authors recommend caution, combining Fibonacci with other indicators, and using backtested strategies. Its effectiveness for crypto or day trading is not established.

Day trading involves opening and closing positions within the same trading day to profit from short-term price movements. It requires rapid decisions, constant market attention, substantial capital, discipline, and careful risk management, and can produce significant profits or losses.

The passage presents 21 strategies: momentum, range, scalping, breakout, pullback, reversal, gap, news, pattern, seasonal, dark pool, statistical arbitrage, pairs, order flow, market making, short squeeze, statistical volatility, market profile, regime switching, volatility targeting, and phase analysis. These approaches respectively seek to exploit trends, sideways price ranges, small rapid moves, breaks from established ranges, temporary price dips, trend reversals, chart gaps, market-moving news, chart patterns, recurring seasonal behavior, private order flow, pricing inefficiencies, correlated securities, order imbalances, bid-ask spreads, forced short covering, volatility patterns, market structure, changing conditions, portfolio risk, and market cycles.

Each strategy has distinct requirements and risks. Momentum and breakout strategies can involve strong price moves but substantial losses. Range trading depends on recognizing stable, bounded markets, while scalping demands speed and composure; the passage states that almost all scalpers lose money. Pullback and reversal trading require distinguishing temporary moves from longer-term trend changes. News and gap trading require interpretation of events and market psychology. Seasonal strategies require flexibility because historical patterns can change. Dark pool trading offers privacy but less transparency, while statistical arbitrage, order flow, market profile, and volatility strategies require advanced analytical skills. Market making provides liquidity but exposes traders to inventory and other significant risks. Leverage can magnify both profits and losses.

Day trading differs from swing trading because day traders settle positions by the end of each session, while swing traders may hold positions for days or weeks and therefore face overnight and weekend risks. Day-trading strategies can be adapted to stocks, forex, futures, and cryptocurrencies, but market-specific characteristics require adjustments to analysis, risk controls, and trading hours.

Technical analysis is widely used to identify trends, support and resistance, and entry and exit points, but it is not infallible. The passage recommends converting ideas into quantified rules and backtesting them with historical data. Backtesting can reveal past performance and guide improvements, but it cannot guarantee future results because market conditions change and strategies may deteriorate over time.

Psychology affects trading through emotion, bias, fear of missing out, and impulsive decisions. Suggested controls include detailed trading plans, predefined entries and exits, regular breaks, mindfulness, accepting losses, and learning from mistakes. Discipline and logical analysis are presented as central to controlling risk and avoiding costly errors.

Most trading activity is concentrated around the market opening and closing, when volume and volatility are typically higher; midday volatility and opportunities often decline. Holidays generally reduce participation and liquidity while increasing volatility, and seasonal changes can affect volume and price behavior through earnings, economic events, and investor sentiment. Astrology may be used by some traders, but its effectiveness is described as scientifically unproven and controversial.

Capital needs vary, and the passage cites FINRA’s $25,000 minimum for U.S. pattern day traders, while noting commissions and leverage can require more. The article says consistent daily returns of 1% are unrealistic, while a $10,000 account might potentially earn $200–$300 daily through a 2%–3% return. It also states that as few as 10% of day traders make money.

A backtested SPY example using daily bars from 1993 onward produced 165 trades, a 0.51% average gain per trade, a 60% win rate, a 9% maximum drawdown, and 2.5% annual returns while invested about 2% of the time. The passage also describes the “11 a.m. rule”: a trending security reaching a new high between 11:15 and 11:30 a.m. EST reportedly has about a 75% chance of ending within 1% of its high of the day.

A Yale-Brookings analysis using Bureau of Labor Statistics data finds targeted job losses but no economy-wide disruption from generative AI. Younger workers face a “low-hire, low-fire” market, while long-term unemployment has also risen. AI exposure does not necessarily mean displacement: radiologists, coders, and writers may retain jobs whose work changes. Knowledge-intensive cities are more exposed than industrial areas, with outcomes depending on whether AI supports or replaces workers. Because firms are only beginning to redesign workflows and integrate AI into enterprise systems, researchers expect meaningful systemic effects to take years; displacement is more likely to emerge from organizational redesign than casual chatbot use.

The policy brief compares two school-choice turning points: the 1993 expansion of charter-school authorization and the 2023 emergence of universal Education Savings Accounts (ESAs). Charter schools spread rapidly after Minnesota and California authorized them in 1991 and 1992, while universal ESAs followed earlier Arizona and West Virginia programs. By March 2025, 11 states had universal ESAs, with near-universal New Hampshire bringing the total to 12. Unlike the mostly blue “class of 1993,” the brief describes the “class of 2023” and subsequent adopters as Republican-led.

ESAs give parents publicly funded accounts that can cover private-school tuition, homeschooling, pods, and educational goods and services. They have fewer regulatory requirements than charter schools and generally do not require certified teachers, state curricula, testing, or graduation reporting. The brief traces the model to Milton Friedman’s proposals for tuition vouchers and “divisible vouchers,” arguing that its advocates view ESAs as a means of reducing government’s role and saving public funds. Unlike some European systems, U.S. allocations are substantially below public-school per-pupil spending, requiring families to supplement them to afford more expensive schools.

The brief identifies weak spending and educational accountability as major concerns. Arizona’s universal program inherited more than 170,000 unapproved purchase orders, while Florida’s approved purchases have included recreational equipment, theme-park tickets, televisions, and other items of questionable educational value. It also cites religious schools in which academic and religious instruction are intertwined and notes that ESA students may receive no guarantee of learning scientific reasoning or other essential knowledge.

Financial effects include private-school tuition increases, such as those following Iowa’s adoption of ESAs, and rapidly rising state expenditures. From fiscal years 2013 to 2025, reported voucher spending rose from $77 million to $1.018 billion in Arizona, $376 million to $3.722 billion in Florida, and $150 million to $1.032 billion in Ohio. The brief attributes short-term costs to subsidies for private-school students, including middle- and upper-income families already paying private tuition. Although it acknowledges intended long-term public savings from serving students at lower per-pupil costs, it argues that inadequate funding may impose broader long-term costs by limiting educational quality.

Charter-school fiscal studies cited by the brief show that districts losing students to other schools do not receive proportionate savings because fixed costs remain, requiring reductions to teachers, support staff, books, and other resources. ESAs could intensify these effects in rural communities, where small schools may close or consolidate and where schools serve as civic centers. The brief also describes risks of discrimination against students with disabilities, religious minorities, LGBTQ+ students, and low-achieving students, including the sorting of difficult students into already struggling public schools. Religious private schools accepting ESA funds may similarly discriminate in admissions or employment, with limited legal protections for LGBTQ+ workers and students.

The brief anticipates further expansion through parent advocacy and the proposed federal Educational Choice for Children Act, while noting constraints such as lower private-school teacher salaries and limited numbers of families able to homeschool or operate pods. It recommends repealing ESA programs where possible. Otherwise, it urges lawmakers to halt expansion, impose spending limits, strengthen purchase monitoring, require curriculum audits, certified teachers, annual assessments, and compliance with civil-rights laws, and subject new programs to public hearings or referenda. State education agencies should improve expenditure tracking and publish participating schools, graduation rates, and accessibility to students with disabilities, while local officials should document harms to communities and inform residents.

A Ukrainian startup, Dropla, is using AI to counter Russian ambush drones that are blowing up supply trucks on roads behind Ukraine's "zero line." Founder V'yacheslav Shvaydak said his software, Blue Eyes, processes real-time thermal and optical video from cheap quadcopters flying over supply routes, highlighting landmines and idling enemy quadcopters. Speed is critical: a 30-minute delay, he said, is too late for convoys already on the road. The team, more than two dozen engineers in Ukraine, trained the model for months on over 170 explosive threat types, and recently added ambush drone detection. Detected threats' coordinates are sent to Ukraine's battle management system, letting commanders route around mines while ambush drones typically must be destroyed.

Researcher Federico Borsari of the Center for European Policy Analysis said ambush drones combined with remote mines can disrupt an area's entire logistical chain, requiring constant situational awareness for about 50 kilometers behind the front line, and that Ukraine needs a cost-effective alternative to large sensor networks. The basic Blue Eyes unit is a 2.1-kilogram box connecting to Ukrainian command-and-control stations, handling up to 130 frames per second, though drones currently fly slower than half a truck's speed. Shvaydak declined to disclose costs or effectiveness, said several frontline units have tested it since early summer, and hopes to expand deployments fivefold. Western firms like Anduril and Saab offer similar sensor-integration software, and Ukraine is integrating systems such as DELTA.

The Side Screen Offense is a two-player screen-and-roll isolation used across NBA playbooks. It can be initiated quickly by a post stepping out to set an on-ball screen, making it useful as a late-shot-clock action or after a broken-down play. Right-handed players generally use it on the left and left-handed players on the right, enabling penetration toward the vulnerable middle with their stronger hand. Basic options include driving over the screen, pulling up when the defense goes under, passing back to the post after a switch, and kicking out when a weakside defender helps.

Success depends on the ballhandler and screener functioning as one unit through proper footwork, timing, nonverbal communication, and experience. Defensive reads and counters include turning the corner against a chase, dropping to the post when the baseline defender helps, kicking out when the wing defender sags, pulling up when the defender goes under, driving opposite when the defender cheats over, changing direction when the defender fights through, and using a screener pop when the defense shows and recovers. Against switches, the ballhandler can feed the screener rolling or posting a smaller defender, or clear the screener for isolation against a slower defender. If the defense anticipates the switch, the screener may slip to the basket; if the screen is denied, the screener can backcut for a lob. Against a trap, the ballhandler should back out and move the ball with sharp passes as the screener pops out and teammates form a 2-1-2 alignment.

Common entries include High Post Rub, Power/Motion, and Horns sets, with a Boston variation involving a back screen for a rolling screener. Side Screen action can also flow into Flex, Triangle Game, single or double motion, weakside double-screen, and baseline down-screen continuities. These actions preserve spacing, offensive rebounding position, and options for late-clock shots.

Implementation should include individual fundamental work and whole-part-whole teaching through combination-screen drills and scrimmages. Coaches should scout opponents, teach anticipated defensive reads and counters, vary alignments and entries, attack weaker defenders, and use organized Side Screen action as the shot or game clock expires. The defense must also understand how to disrupt one of the game’s most frequently used offenses.

This continuation application presents an alternative high-pressure fluid end for hydraulic fracturing and incorporates the listed provisional patent applications by reference.

Traditional fluid ends use a single alloy-steel housing with intersecting vertical and horizontal bores, packing seals, stuffing boxes, plugs, valves, and plungers driven by a power end. Operating pressures commonly range from 8,000 to 15,000 psi and may reach 22,500 psi. Corrosion, fatigue cracking at highly stressed chamber corners and the flange neck, and erosion from proppants can cause leakage and failure within several hundred operating hours.

The disclosed fluid end instead comprises multiple side-by-side sections, preferably five, each with a single horizontal bore and no intersecting internal chamber. This permits individual sections to be replaced, reduces manufacturing time and cost, removes traditional stress points, and may allow the use of less costly materials. Each section attaches to a connect plate secured by stay rods, studs, nuts, washers, and alignment pins. Upper and lower intake manifolds allow different fluid and proppant concentrations to be supplied to different sections, while discharge conduits connect the sections to a discharge manifold.

Each section further includes a detachable stuffing box, retainer, plunger packing, packing nut, lubrication passages, fluid-routing plug, and alternating suction and discharge valves. The routing plug uses angled, offset fluid passages and beveled sealing surfaces to reduce stress. Housing seals occupy nearly all of their grooves to limit erosion, while small gaps permit plug expansion, installation clearance, and debris collection. The discharge bore and conduit are positioned to allow gas to escape and are readily replaceable. Overall, the configuration is intended to reduce stress, wear, leakage, and premature fluid-end failure.

A prospective cohort study found that more than 99% of people who experienced a first heart attack, stroke, or heart failure had at least one “suboptimal” cardiovascular risk factor—high blood pressure, cholesterol or blood glucose, or current or former smoking. In two national cohorts followed for 20 years, including more than 9.3 million people, over 93% had multiple risk factors; among women under 60, over 95% had at least one before heart failure or stroke. Researchers said the contrast with cases apparently lacking risk factors partly reflects differences between optimal health levels and clinical treatment thresholds. The study reported that 90% to 95% of affected people had a clinically elevated risk factor, usually blood pressure. Experts said even modest, common abnormalities may contribute to cardiovascular events and could be prevented through treatment, while highlighting inadequate emphasis on prevention in U.S. health care.

MIG securely partitions an A100 Tensor Core GPU into up to seven isolated instances, providing predictable performance, QoS, and security for multi-tenant clients while increasing hardware utilization.

This continuation application addresses power-saving scheduling in 5G NR, where entering a power-saving state can change K timing, RRC parameters, and default uplink beam behavior, potentially causing incorrect HARQ information. A UE receives a base-station power-saving signal containing a minimum applicable K (K0min), determines an application delay, and thereafter enforces the minimum PDCCH–PDSCH scheduling-offset restriction. During the delay, the UE may apply another RRC-configured offset. The power-saving signal may be carried in DCI, and the UE may compare a later DCI’s applicable K with K0min to determine which scheduling offset to apply.

Implementations also provide HARQ-ACK-only or HARQ-ACK/NACK feedback for power-saving signals, with configurable timing and rules for including, positioning, multiplexing, or separating feedback bits in HARQ codebooks. DCI- and reference-signal-based power-saving indicators are described, including CSI reporting for CSI-RS-based indicators.

The disclosure further enhances default beam selection in power-saving mode to avoid deactivated antenna panels or SRS resource sets by considering valid spatial-relation and QCL information, using the scheduling CORESET’s spatial filter, or receiving an SRS resource indicator. Example base-station, UE, and wireless-node architectures are also described.

The Triangle & Two defense places three defenders in a triangle zone and two chasers applying aggressive pass denial. It can contain two primary scorers, provide a change of pace, or help a team hold the ball late. The zone supports chasers against back cuts and dribble penetration, creates doubles in the post and on drives, and can be inverted against two-guard fronts. Chasers’ denial is key to disrupting opponents’ sets.

Ryan Walters resigned as Oklahoma’s state superintendent after 2½ years to lead the national anti-union Teacher Freedom Alliance. Observers described his tenure as a preview of the Trump administration’s top-down education overhaul, with culture-war priorities eclipsing school improvement. His administration opened board meetings with Christian prayer, promoted Bible instruction, pursued anti-LGBTQ and anti-equity policies, revised social studies standards, supported immigration enforcement in schools, and imposed requirements on teachers from New York and California seeking Oklahoma jobs. Walters also welcomed conservative organizations’ involvement in education policy and called Oklahoma a testing ground for Project 2025. He gained support among Christian nationalists and parental-rights advocates but faced criticism from educators, legal advocates, and religious groups; courts blocked parts of his agenda. Although he strongly supported Trump and sought greater national influence, he did not secure a Trump administration position. After Charlie Kirk’s assassination, Walters joined the anti-union organization, citing the need to combat teacher unions, and announced school observances and Turning Point USA clubs. Observers said his national appeal was narrower than Kirk’s.

Ohio State off-ball linebacker Arvell Reese has emerged as a viable first-round pick and potential top-10 selection in the 2026 NFL Draft. At 6-foot-3 and 243 pounds, Reese offers elite speed, burst, strong tackling, leverage and power across multiple front-seven roles. He excels against the run, pursuing plays downhill and occasionally making unassigned plays. His athleticism also suits him as a quarterback spy, while his change of direction and foot speed provide coverage upside. Uncertainties remain regarding his limited coverage reps, processing in zone, ball production and pass-rushing ability. He sometimes tries to make too many plays and must prove his run strength against larger NFL linemen. The longest woolly rhino horn ever found, preserved in Siberian permafrost along a tributary of Russia's Kolyma River, is providing new insights into the extinct animals' biology. Carbon dating of frozen lemmings near the remains placed them at about 19,600 years old. The horn exceeded that of modern rhino species and belonged to a proportionally small adult skull, likely a female, since males typically have thicker horns and longer horns may occur in females, as in African rhinos. Counting alternating light and dark keratin growth bands, like tree rings, showed the rhino lived at least 40 years — the oldest woolly rhino yet found, and older than the maximum age of modern wild rhinos. Researchers also note wear on the horn's front extended nearly half the breadth of its base, suggesting the flattened, saberlike horn may have been used to brush away snow while feeding. The study was published online September 12, 2025, in the Journal of Zoology.

The lecture presents static fusion trees, introduced by Fredman and Willard, as a word-RAM solution to predecessor and successor queries. Using \(w\)-bit words with \(w \ge \log n\), fusion trees achieve \(O(\log_w n)\) query time with linear space, although preprocessing takes polynomial time. They are presented as a B-tree-like structure with branching factor \(w^{1/5}\), whose height is \(\Theta(\log_w n)\).

The central techniques are sketching, parallel comparison, and constant-time most-significant-set-bit computation. A perfect sketch extracts the bit positions where sorted keys diverge in a binary trie, preserving their order. Because an arbitrary query may diverge at an unrecorded position, “de-sketchification” finds the first divergence using a longest-common-prefix computation and performs a second sketch search with a corrected query to recover the correct rank.

Approximate sketches are implemented with masking and integer multiplication. A specially constructed multiplier avoids collisions, preserves the order of important bits, and compresses them into an \(O(r^4)\)-bit span. With \(r < k = O(w^{1/5})\), all key sketches fit together in \(O(w)\) bits. Parallel comparison packs these sketches into fields, uses subtraction to generate comparison bits, and applies multiplication to count the bits and locate the query’s rank.

To find the most significant set bit in constant time, the word is divided into \(\sqrt w\) clusters of \(\sqrt w\) bits. Masks and subtraction identify nonempty clusters, sketching compresses their summary, and parallel comparison identifies the first nonempty cluster and then its highest set bit.

The lecture also mentions AC\(^0\)-RAM and dynamic variants, including exponential search trees and a hashing-based structure with expected \(\log_w n\) update time, but focuses on static fusion trees.

The SCOTUSblog “Relist Watch” column surveys 17 cases the Supreme Court relisted for a second conference, indicating possible interest in petitions involving parental rights and gender identity, religious accommodation, online-platform liability, jury trials, prison litigation, arbitration, appeal waivers, confrontation, public trials, Jan. 6 prosecutions, FDA regulation, unclaimed property, qualified immunity, evidentiary disclosure, military-service tort claims, and racial juror strikes.

The relisted disputes ask whether schools may keep children’s gender identities secret from parents; whether conflicting state vaccine rules can justify denying religious accommodations under Title VII; whether Section 230 shields apps from liability over design flaws, geolocation, recommendations, age verification, and sex trafficking; and whether the Seventh Amendment’s jury-trial right applies to states. Other cases concern the burden for ending prospective jail-relief orders in New Orleans, whether local bread distributors qualify for an interstate-commerce arbitration exemption, which exceptions to criminal appeal waivers are permissible, whether a child witness may testify behind a screen without an individualized trauma finding, and whether streamed trials must include alternatives to courtroom closure. Further petitions involve dismissal of a Jan. 6 case after a blanket pardon, FDA authority over stem-cell procedures, California’s unclaimed-property practices, police qualified immunity, Maryland’s disclosure of forensic evidence, limits on military-related tort claims, and challenges to Black jurors’ removal.

Relisting can suggest a justice’s interest, but the absence of a respondent’s brief generally points toward denial. Two California cases involving stem-cell treatment and unclaimed property were nevertheless relisted without responses.

A Pan Finance financial-news page lists numerous headlines on markets and finance (including Fifth Third's $10.9B Comerica acquisition, OPEC+ output increases, AMD's OpenAI chip deal, and the Bifrost subsea cable) alongside its main article. A confirmed mass-market vehicle would advance Elon Musk's goal of a globally affordable EV and could reshape Tesla's growth trajectory.

The lecture explains life cycle assessment (LCA) as a framework for quantifying products’ or services’ environmental impacts by compiling inventories of environmental inputs and outputs, assessing potential impacts, and interpreting results relative to a study’s objectives. Product-level LCA can support internal supply-chain decisions as well as external comparisons, labeling, and environmental claims. Unlike organizational carbon accounting, product LCA evaluates systems from raw-material extraction through end of life, although ownership of individual supply-chain stages is generally irrelevant.

Using a Dyson-commissioned hand-drying study as an example, the lecturer discusses the four LCA stages: goal and scope definition, inventory analysis, impact assessment, and interpretation. The study compares Dyson Airblade models, an Xlerator dryer, and conventional and recycled paper towels using “one pair of dried hands” as the functional unit. Scope decisions include defining the cradle-to-grave system boundary, excluding capital goods, applying cutoff rules, allocating impacts among coproducts, and handling open-loop recycling of paper towels. Attributional LCA describes a system’s current, static impacts, while consequential LCA models the direct and indirect changes caused by system shifts.

Inventory analysis maps processes, supply chains, bills of materials, and production activities to quantified inputs and outputs. The hand-drying study matched Dyson-supplied bills of materials and activities with ecoinvent data, used proxy data where materials were unavailable, and estimated manufacturing losses and scrap. Impact assessment classifies inventory results by environmental category and characterizes them through indicators including global warming potential, water use, cumulative energy demand, and IMPACT 2002+, which combines midpoint indicators into human-health, ecosystem-quality, resource, and overall eco-point measures. Such aggregation embeds value judgments about trade-offs among impacts.

Interpretation examined how assumptions affected results through one-factor-at-a-time sensitivity analysis, 20,000-run Monte Carlo scenario analysis, and uncertainty analysis of inventory activities. Important variables included hand-drying time, paper-towel quantity and mass, electricity mix, manufacturing location, product lifetime, and supply-chain assumptions. Although many inputs came from company-supplied or prior studies and required assumptions, the study generally found the Dyson Airblade had the lowest impact, particularly for global warming potential, and ranked better than the Xlerator in about 98% of modeled scenarios. Participants questioned standardized manufacturing assumptions, missing and outdated data, and potential bias because Dyson commissioned the study and supplied internal information unavailable to competitors, while Xlerator’s drying-time data came from a Dyson-reported test.

A Children’s Rights Alliance report, based on research with teachers, principals and homeless parents in greater Dublin, found that emergency accommodation and homelessness severely disrupt children’s education. With almost 4,000 homeless children, some attend school hungry and in dirty clothes, face long journeys, sleep in class and frequently miss school because of poor diet, rest and living conditions. Parents sometimes sacrifice food to cover travel costs or vice versa. The report recommends free school travel, funding for meals, psychological assessments and homework clubs, and suitable accommodation near schools, limiting emergency or temporary housing to six months.

This study assessed malaria and other risk factors for malnutrition and evaluated whether intermittent preventive therapy (IPTsc) improved the nutritional status of school-age children in Muheza, northeastern Tanzania. Secondary data from a cross-sectional baseline survey and a three-arm, randomized, open-label trial were analyzed. The trial assigned 1,566 children aged 5–15 years to dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine, artesunate-amodiaquine, or standard care for 12 months, followed by eight additional months of observation. Nutritional status was assessed using weight-for-age, height-for-age, and BMI-for-age Z-scores.

At baseline, 27% of tested children had malaria. Among children aged 5–10 years, 23% were underweight; 21% of all participants were stunted, and 28% were thin or severely thin. Malaria was associated with higher adjusted odds of stunting (AOR 1.78; 95% CI 1.36–2.33), while low socioeconomic status was associated with underweight (AOR 1.50; 95% CI 1.13–2.01). Recent malaria was associated with thinness (AOR 1.37; 95% CI 1.10–1.71), and male sex was associated with stunting.

Malaria prevalence after 12 months was lower in both preventive-treatment groups than in standard care, but changes in weight, height, and BMI over time did not differ significantly between DP or ASAQ and control groups. No treatment-related growth differences remained eight months after treatment ended. The authors concluded that malaria prevention did not necessarily improve nutritional status and recommended integrated malaria-control and nutrition programs, including community collaboration to ensure food availability at schools and provide sustainable nutritional education.

Limitations included incomplete collection of known nutritional risk factors, exclusion of pupils in grades 6 and 7, inability to account for household clustering, and inability to establish a causal effect of malaria on stunting from a single baseline parasitemia measurement.

NVIDIA’s Tesla T4 is presented as a hyperscale inference accelerator for data centers, enterprise systems, and edge devices. It contains 2,560 CUDA Cores and 320 Tensor Cores, supports up to 130 INT8 TOPS and 260 INT4 TOPS, and is claimed to deliver up to 40 times the inference performance and more than 50 times the energy efficiency of CPU-based inference, as well as up to twice the energy efficiency of the preceding Tesla P4. It includes 16 GB of memory and 320 GB/s bandwidth, along with enhanced video decoding, Multi-Process Service support, and improved virtual-desktop density.

The Turing architecture introduces GDDR6 memory, larger L2 caches, improved memory compression, dedicated RT Cores, and Tensor Cores. GDDR6 signaling reaches 14 Gbps with claimed power-efficiency improvements, while compression and bandwidth increases produce roughly 50% greater effective bandwidth than Pascal. The architecture also adds DisplayPort 1.4a support for 8K output, HDR processing, improved HEVC and VP9 decoding, enhanced NVENC encoding, USB-C VirtualLink connectivity, and second-generation NVLink for two-way SLI configurations.

Turing RT Cores accelerate bounding-volume-hierarchy traversal and ray-triangle intersection testing, enabling real-time ray tracing through a hybrid model combining rasterization, ray tracing, denoising, and AI. The passage describes ray-traced shadows, ambient occlusion, and reflections as providing more physically accurate results than traditional shadow maps, screen-space ambient occlusion, and screen-space reflections.

NVIDIA NGX applies deep neural networks through Turing Tensor Cores to graphics and client applications. Its features include Deep Learning Super-Sampling (DLSS), which uses trained models to produce quality comparable to temporal anti-aliasing with roughly half the shading work; DLSS 2X, which approaches 64-times-supersampled quality; and NGX Inpainting, AI Slow-Mo, and AI Super Rez. These services require a Turing GPU and are managed through GeForce Experience or Quadro Experience.

Turing also adds mesh shading, variable-rate shading, texture-space shading, and multi-view rendering. Task and mesh shaders remove CPU draw-call bottlenecks and support very large object counts. Variable-rate shading can set different rates for each 16-by-16 region and supports content-adaptive, motion-adaptive, and foveated rendering. Texture-space shading separates visibility and appearance sampling, reuses shaded texels, and can improve stereo VR efficiency. Multi-view rendering supports four views per hardware pass and up to 32 views through the API.

The document identifies TU102, TU104, and TU106 as Turing GPU implementations. TU104 contains 3,072 CUDA Cores, 368 Tensor Cores, and 48 RT Cores, while the Tesla T4 uses a reduced configuration with 2,560 CUDA Cores and 320 Tensor Cores. TU106 contains 2,304 CUDA Cores, 288 Tensor Cores, and 36 RT Cores but does not support NVLink or SLI. NVIDIA also introduces RTX-OPS, a workload-weighted metric that factors tensor, FP32, ray-tracing, and integer operations according to their expected use in hybrid rendering.
