Coach Vigneault said his team must bring an “A” game against a disciplined, skilled and physical opponent that executes its plan and is difficult to exploit. He praised the first period but said the third-period effort was inadequate against a strong push, adding that the team will make adjustments and focus on the next game. He emphasized compete level, execution, sticking to the plan and playing to the team’s strengths, including speed. Vigneault described Johnny as a consistent, puck-moving defenseman and said his left-handed shot may simplify defenseman-to-defenseman passing, while noting Rafa’s strong play. Rick was praised for his competitiveness, physicality, defense and offensive chances. Vigneault also said Philadelphia, Pittsburgh and Montreal were three distinct previous opponents, while the current opponent combines structure, skill and physical play.

An MIT professor surveys nuclear proliferation, deterrence, and possible pathways to nuclear war, contrasting the gradual, near-certain consequences of climate change with the lower-probability but potentially catastrophic risk of nuclear conflict. He argues that fear and distrust drove the U.S.–Soviet nuclear buildup to tens of thousands of weapons and sustain hair-trigger alert systems. Deterrence has helped prevent nuclear use, but it has not reliably coerced other states and can encourage brinkmanship, instability, and reliance on rational decision-making.

He identifies accidental U.S.–Russian launch, escalation from conventional conflict between India and Pakistan, and North Korean use as major risks. Warning-system malfunctions and cyberattacks could trigger retaliation, while Pakistan’s aggressive posture, delegated authority, and growing arsenal create a danger of escalation or rogue action. He also discusses debates over the 1945 atomic bombings and whether deterrence, nuclear taboo, or other factors explain the absence of nuclear war since 1945.

The professor considers the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty partly effective because fewer countries possess nuclear weapons than predicted in the early 1960s. Its credibility is weakened by tension over disarmament: nuclear-armed states have not fulfilled Article VI’s obligation to give up their weapons, while non-nuclear states seek timetables for doing so. India, Pakistan, Israel, and North Korea remain outside the treaty, and Iran’s enrichment program and interim negotiations are a major focus. He favors continuing the interim agreement, citing Iran’s stated opposition to weapons and acceptance of intensive IAEA inspections.

Although abolition would remove deterrence and is considered difficult to achieve, he maintains that it remains desirable and that policy should compare and minimize relative risks rather than seek a risk-free world. He assesses Obama’s record as mixed, citing the Prague speech, New START, and security improvements alongside limited follow-through, continued hair-trigger deployments, and continued weapon modernization. He regards New START inspections as more important than numerical limits, sees the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty’s monitoring and public opposition to nuclear weapons as reasons for cautious optimism, and suggests conventional precision strike capabilities may eventually replace nuclear deterrence. Overall, he concludes that the current situation is stable only partly because of luck.

The passage urges Congress to create a Cabinet-level Department of Commerce to address labor and capital issues and supervise interstate corporations. It advocates reciprocity with Cuba, trade agreements with Newfoundland, international arbitration through The Hague Tribunal, and settlement of Hawaiian fire claims. It also supports building an isthmian canal in Panama as a continuing, nonpartisan national project, noting that title can be acquired and negotiations with Colombia are underway.

CPRE Bedfordshire says Central Bedfordshire Council’s proposed 44,000–55,000 homes over 20 years is unsustainable, with 60% intended for newcomers and inadequate road and rail capacity. A 2017 assessment found a need for 32,000 homes in 2015–35, with 41% serving existing residents; the council added 7,400 homes for Luton and up to 20% contingency. CBC says government policy requires the figures, based on migration, natural change and affordability.

President Andrew Johnson submitted to the House of Representatives his February 1868 correspondence with General Ulysses S. Grant concerning Grant’s departure from the War Office. Johnson accused Grant of accepting the post of interim Secretary of War with the secret intention of defeating President Johnson’s effort to keep Edwin Stanton suspended, misleading Johnson about his intentions, and defying presidential orders concerning War Department orders issued in the President’s name. He maintained that the President was Grant’s official superior as Commander in Chief and that Grant could have resigned without violating a statute.

Five Cabinet members who attended the January 14 conversation with Grant—Gideon Welles, Hugh McCulloch, Alexander Randall, O. H. Browning, and William H. Seward—responded to Johnson. Their accounts generally supported his recollection of Grant’s assurances and later change of position, although they varied in detail and characterization of Grant’s responses.

Grant replied that he had not intended to disobey any distinct legal presidential order. He said he had interpreted an ambiguous instruction as applying only to orders issued by Stanton as the President’s agent and cited correspondence showing that other departments recognized Stanton’s authority. The enclosed documents included Stanton’s request for an escort to transport public funds from Brownsville to New Orleans, a Post Office request for information about a Texas defense commission and mail-route change, and a Treasury request for military protection of funds in transit.

Vicki Travnicek and Nicole Bruder recommend limiting holiday events, making exit plans, expressing emotions and memories, treating yourself kindly, and creating new traditions while preserving old ones. The Surviving Suicide Grief Support Group, led by people touched by suicide, meets at Smith-Leroy on the first and third Tuesdays, 7–8:30 p.m., and resumes in January; register at 519-537-3611. “Understanding Your Grief” starts April 4 in Woodstock. An eight-week “Healing Journey Through Grief” program runs in Ingersoll Feb. 1–March 22; register at 519-485-1802.

Microsoft Corporation filed a Form 8-K on October 20, 2016, announcing financial results for the fiscal quarter ended September 30, 2016. The press release was furnished as Exhibit 99.1 and was not deemed filed under Section 18 or incorporated by reference absent specific reference.

Medical students face academic, clinical, psychological, and financial stressors that increase their risk of distress, anxiety, depression, burnout, and reduced help-seeking. Resilience is presented as an adaptable, learnable capacity that supports healthy coping, self-directed learning, and adaptation to medical training, particularly during crises such as COVID-19. Although some North American medical programs include resilience-building curricula, such proactive programs remain limited in the Middle East and North Africa.

This qualitative phenomenological study examined medical students’ perceptions and experiences of a resilience course at Mohammed Bin Rashid University of Medicine and Health Sciences in Dubai. The six-hour, pass-or-fail course was delivered during Year 4 of the MBBS program and aligned with constructivist experiential learning and Kolb’s learning cycle. It covered stress and burnout, resilience, cognitive behavioral therapy, healthy coping, mindfulness, meditation, emotional intelligence, mental toughness, gratitude, self-awareness, self-efficacy, and emotional self-regulation. Learning activities included reflection, journaling, mentor feedback, and experimentation between sessions. Assessment involved attendance, an OSCE, and a 500-word reflective essay.

Reflective essays from 37 consenting students were analyzed inductively by two researchers using a six-step thematic approach in NVivo. The analysis identified three interconnected themes: Awareness, Application, and Appraisal. Students understood resilience as an ongoing, intentional process involving adaptability, self-awareness, emotional regulation, reflection, mindfulness, social support, planning, and healthy coping. They applied it through meditation, breathing and sensory exercises, yoga, reflection, reframing, physical activity, prayer, gratitude, time management, self-care, and social relationships. Barriers included limited time, competing priorities, skepticism, habit resistance, discomfort, self-doubt, and the effort required to sustain practice.

Students valued the course for improving awareness, confidence, coping, stress management, emotional regulation, empathy, sleep, concentration, academic engagement, and clinical preparedness. Assignments supported behavior change, while group sessions fostered connection and validation. The findings support curriculum-based, self-directed resilience education for medical students, although conclusions are limited by the single institution and cohort, qualitative methodology, possible social-desirability bias, and the absence of validated pre- and post-intervention mental-health measurements.

North Carolina’s 38-10 loss to Clemson left the Tar Heels 0-3 against Power Four teams and outscored 120-33 overall. Bill Belichick rejected early structural or personnel changes, blaming execution, concentration and coaching, while acknowledging the program is being rebuilt for recruits. GM Mike Lombardi cited talent losses from previous recruiting classes, but player Shipp said his focus was winning rather than rebuilding. UNC prepares to face Cal.

The article presents advocacy as foundational to special education and argues that pre-service teachers need explicit preparation in advocacy skills. It describes a five-credit, 10-week undergraduate course, “All Means All: Inclusive Teaching for Students with Disabilities,” in which advocacy functions as a consistent theme across content, learning goals, assignments, and course structure.

The course combines inclusive special education content with scaffolded practice in argumentative writing, persuasion, policy analysis, and debate. Activities include weekly TED Talk analyses, low-stakes reflections, a jigsaw activity examining major special education cases, an in-class debate on full inclusion, and instruction on disability advocacy history and legislative processes. Students analyze evidence and arguments, take positions opposing their own views, and reflect on disability rights from varied stakeholder perspectives. These assignments lead to a final TED Talk-style presentation and corresponding paper advocating a position on inclusive education. Rubrics, instructor feedback, peer feedback, and recurring assignments allow students to revise and develop their work throughout the term.

The article presents the course as a model for integrating advocacy into special education preparation. It emphasizes that interactive, supportive assignments can help students develop teacher agency, critical thinking, communication, and policy knowledge while preparing them to address inequities and advocate for students in schools, communities, and broader policy systems. Following Madison’s experience as a teacher, the article also highlights the importance of professional networks, collaboration with other special educators, and resources from organizations such as the Council for Exceptional Children. It concludes that advocacy should be woven throughout every course in special education preparation programs rather than treated as a standalone topic.

Urgent youth mental-health needs require support beyond families and schools. Community-based and out-of-school programs—including camps, mentoring, sports leagues and after-school clubs—build trusted relationships and provide spaces where young people feel safe and connected. The authors argue that these organizations should not become clinics but should offer basic support that enables staff to recognize distress, respond appropriately and refer youth to professionals when needed.

This requires sustained investment in staff training, mental-health protocols, resource directories, provider partnerships, warm referrals and support for frontline workers experiencing burnout. Funders can help youth-serving organizations create strategic mental-health plans and strengthen collaboration across schools, families, community organizations and mental-health providers. Citing APA research, the passage notes that more than 80% of young people recommend expanding counseling in schools and community-based organizations.

The lecture surveys contemporary industrial organization and focuses on regulating dominant digital platforms. It identifies new cooperation issues—including intellectual-property pools, standard setting, data pools, collective bargaining, common ownership, and algorithmic collusion—but concentrates on “too little cooperation.” Platforms are modeled as two-sided markets connecting consumers with in-house and third-party apps or merchants. Potential concerns include behavioral manipulation, biased or commission-based recommendations, self-preferencing, exclusion, difficulty of entry, unequal access, and unfair compensation.

European regulation discussed includes the P2B Regulation, Artificial Intelligence Act, Digital Services Act, and Digital Market Act (DMA), while the United States is also moving toward platform obligations. The lecture focuses mainly on contestability and fairness. A traditional Chicago School argument holds that a platform has incentives to maintain a rich ecosystem because it can compensate for discrimination against third parties by charging consumers more. The professor rejects this argument for three reasons: platforms may be unable or unwilling to raise consumer prices; discrimination can protect the platform’s core segment by driving third parties out and deterring entry; and zero lower bounds in both consumer and app markets can produce supranormal profits.

Digital platforms resemble public utilities because they have high fixed costs, low marginal costs, and network effects, but they differ because they are global, change products and market segments rapidly, and do not have stable natural divisions suitable for breakup. The DMA therefore designates large platforms, imposes obligations concerning contestability and treatment of third parties, and relies partly on self-execution because regulators have limited resources. Unresolved issues include which agency will enforce the rules, how interoperability and APIs should be governed, and how fines will be applied.

On contestability, the lecture notes that multihoming, data portability, interoperability, anti-steering measures, and most-favored-nation clauses may facilitate entry. It also discusses the Baumol-Panzar-Willig theory that entry threats can discipline monopoly pricing at Ramsey prices, but emphasizes problems involving investment delays, price reactions, network stickiness, and incompatible networks. Acquisitions by dominant platforms are raised as another possible means of preventing competition.

Traditional access regulation is reviewed through the efficient component pricing rule, which caps an access charge by the incumbent’s loss when a customer switches to a downstream rival. The rule is incomplete because it links access and retail prices without determining either, motivating broader global price caps and Ramsey-based access pricing.

The lecture’s central model distinguishes a platform’s consumer-access price, an in-house app price, a more efficient third-party app price, an access charge, and ancillary benefits from advertising, merchant fees, data, and repeat use. Negative marginal costs create separate zero lower bounds for the core service and apps. If neither binds, the Chicago School argument largely holds. If the app zero lower bound binds, however, the third-party app earns excess profits and the platform has an incentive to foreclose it. Very low access charges can therefore create an incentive for non-price foreclosure, including exclusion from the platform or unfavorable placement. Very high access charges instead squeeze third-party apps as consumer access falls to zero, eventually producing price foreclosure. The lecture states that an access charge equal to the app’s ancillary benefit can be optimal when additional considerations are included.

Because regulators cannot readily observe ancillary benefits, the professor proposes eliciting them from prospective entrants through a masking game. He describes this as a potentially Pigouvian approach but stresses that it remains risky and operationally unfinished. Credit-card regulation’s “tourist test” is presented as a limited precedent. The lecture concludes that effective regulation requires simple, workable rules suitable for authorities with limited staffing.

Avoyelles Parish was projected to spend $8,123 per student in 2017-18, below Louisiana’s $9,015 average, with 25.85% from local revenue and 74.15% from the state. Louisiana’s Minimum Foundation Program starts at $3,961 per student, adjusts for local tax capacity and student needs, and includes flood and small-district adjustments. Funding has no clear link to actual operating costs, prompting a Senate request for a task-force report by Feb. 1, 2018.

Following congressional investigations of CIA activities, President Ford’s EO 11905 (1976) replaced the 40 Committee with the Operations Advisory Group (OAG), which developed covert-action recommendations for the President and periodically reviewed approved operations. It barred U.S. government employees from involvement in political assassinations and domestic intelligence, while the DCI retained responsibility for planning and implementing covert operations. Hughes-Ryan approval and oversight rules continued into the Carter administration.

Carter retained the NSC to guide foreign intelligence and replaced the OAG with the Special Coordination Committee, later called SCC-Intelligence (SCC-I). EOs 11985 (1977) and 12036 (1978) formalized the change; EO 12036 made the Attorney General and OMB director full members rather than observers. SCC-I created the Special Activities Working Group (SAWG), chaired by David Aaron, to review covert-action proposals and ongoing operations, but it gradually fell out of use. Carter also developed “world-wide” presidential findings for lower-risk activities, supported by CIA- and State-drafted “Perspectives” documents specifying policy themes. Riskier operations required separate findings or Memorandums of Notification; from 1978, worldwide actions were added as line items to existing findings.

The lecture introduces 18.100A Real Analysis, whose goals are to develop proof-writing and proof-reading skills and to prove statements about real numbers, functions, and limits. The instructor emphasizes that rigorous definitions establish the objects studied, while theorems express the facts to be proved.

Initial lessons review sets. A set is a collection of objects called elements or members; the empty set contains no elements. The lecture introduces membership, subset, proper subset, and equality notation, along with logical symbols for “in,” “not in,” “for all,” “there exists,” implication, and equivalence. Two sets are equal when each is a subset of the other.

The natural numbers, integers, rational numbers, and real numbers are presented as nested sets:
\(\mathbb N \subseteq \mathbb Z \subseteq \mathbb Q \subseteq \mathbb R\).
Their historical motivation is illustrated through equations not solvable in earlier number systems. A primary course goal is to give a rigorous set-based description of the real numbers.

Set operations are defined: union, intersection, set difference, complement relative to a universe, and disjointness. De Morgan’s laws state that the complement of a union is the intersection of the complements, while the complement of an intersection is the union of the complements. The instructor proves the first law by showing both set inclusions through element-chasing. This illustrates the general structure of a proof: begin with hypotheses, use definitions, logic, and calculations, and derive the desired conclusion. Proof by contradiction is introduced as assuming the negation of a claim and deriving a contradiction.

The lecture then presents mathematical induction. The well-ordering property is taken as an axiom: every nonempty subset of the natural numbers has a least element. Pascal’s principle of induction states that if a statement \(P(n)\) holds for \(n=1\) and \(P(m)\) implies \(P(m+1)\), then it holds for every natural number. The instructor proves this by contradiction, defining the set of counterexamples and using its least element to derive that the same number both belongs and does not belong to that set.

Two induction examples are developed. The first proves, for \(c\neq1\), the geometric-series identity
\[
1+c+\cdots+c^n=\frac{1-c^{n+1}}{1-c}.
\]
The second proves that if \(c\geq-1\), then \(1+c^n\geq1+nc\) for every natural number \(n\). The lecture concludes by explaining that induction requires a base case and an inductive step.

A news roundup covers Democratic calls for an independent Russia investigation after Michael Flynn’s exit; possible U.S. policy changes during Netanyahu’s White House visit; Malaysia’s arrest of a Vietnamese woman over Kim Jong Nam’s killing; NATO talks on military spending, terrorism and Russia; cracks at California’s Oroville Dam; risky driving across age groups; a Boeing union vote in South Carolina; high-tech produce labeling in Sweden; Kate Upton’s third Sports Illustrated swimsuit cover; and Rumor’s Westminster best-in-show comeback.

The study developed and externally validated three machine-learning models—logistic regression, random forest, and boosted trees—to predict lung restriction from spirometric, anthropometric, and demographic data. Development and validation datasets contained 42,462 and 24,524 pulmonary function tests, respectively, from two academic health systems, and used race-neutral reference equations.

The random forest model had the best external-validation performance. Its negative predictive value (NPV) for excluding restriction was 88.3%, compared with 72.7% for the forced vital capacity lower limit of normal (FVC LLN). It had higher sensitivity (83.3% vs. 46.0%) but lower specificity (82.9% vs. 94.4%) and excluded the need for static lung-volume measurement in fewer tests (56.7% vs. 78.4%). It had excellent discrimination but poor calibration, and performance declined during external validation.

All machine-learning models were more accurate and more equitable than the FVC LLN. For the random forest model, NPV was 74.6% among non-Hispanic Black patients and 90.9% among non-Hispanic White patients, versus 49.5% and 79.6% for the FVC LLN. The ratio of Black-to-White NPV was higher for the random forest model, although substantial racial inequity remained. Decision-curve analysis favored the random forest model across most thresholds.

Limitations included possible overestimation of restriction in community populations, poor external calibration, potential ascertainment bias, limited racial and ethnic diversity, and no input from patients or providers. Overall, machine-learning models improved the accuracy and equity of excluding restriction from spirometry compared with the FVC LLN.

The court dismissed Cox’s petition for certiorari challenging District Judge Burnham’s authority to issue a pharmacist’s liquor permit after hearing the application at a later term. Cox and eight other Benton County citizens had remonstrated against the application, citing an existing permit and the town’s small population.

The court held that statutory provisions requiring liquor-permit applications to be heard promptly or at the first term were not mandatory and did not restrict the court’s control over its calendar. When an application could not be heard during a term and no vacation hearing was set, the application would ordinarily stand continued to the next term with other unresolved matters. An adjournment therefore did not automatically dismiss the application or eliminate the court’s jurisdiction. Sections governing filing and notice did not require dismissal when a hearing occurred later. In the absence of evidence to the contrary, cause for a continuance was presumed. The proceedings appeared regular and free of abuse of discretion, and the remonstrants could not complain because they did not appear and request a hearing.

Tesla, Inc.’s Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2018 identifies the company as a Delaware corporation headquartered in Palo Alto, California, with common stock listed on NASDAQ. Tesla reported $46.57 billion in non-affiliate market value as of June 30, 2018, and 172,721,487 shares outstanding as of February 12, 2019.

The filing describes Tesla as a vertically integrated sustainable-energy company operating automotive and energy generation and storage segments. Its vehicles include the Model S, Model X, and Model 3, with future plans for Model Y, the Tesla Semi, a pickup truck, and a new Roadster. The article describes a January 2017 screening process for high-quality “CCC” stocks. It begins with the 342 highest-scoring companies among 684 on David Fish’s “All CCC” list, excluding REITs and MLPs, and applies the Dugan Stock Scoring System plus filters for a minimum 2.25% yield, $5 billion market capitalization, relative Graham number and payout ratio no higher than 70, dividend and EPS growth of at least 5%, debt-to-equity ratio no higher than 1, and Dugan Score of at least 50. The scoring system evaluates risk, value, and past and expected future performance to provide a balanced assessment of a stock’s current condition and prospects. Broker sector recommendations can add or subtract one point. These criteria produced 21 qualifying companies. The article includes an educational-purpose disclaimer and discloses long positions in PRU, AIZ, MGA, BBY, HBAN, DOW, ADM, CSCO, and RAI.

Following a March inspection, the Care Quality Commission rated East of England Ambulance Service NHS Trust as requiring improvement overall, while rating its care as outstanding. Improvements were noted in safeguarding, understanding of the Mental Capacity Act and incident reporting, but the trust failed to meet national ambulance response standards, and winter delays led to serious incidents. Inspectors also identified low staff morale, late shift finishes and disengagement from senior management, alongside praise for caring, dedicated staff and positive feedback from service users. Required improvements include faster emergency responses, consistent application of procedures, reviewed risk registers and better mentoring and support for staff. The trust is working to strengthen local leadership and teams, received £11.5 million in additional funding, and remains monitored by the CQC, which will reinspect its progress.

New Jersey Devils coach Paul DeBoer addressed the press ahead of Game 2 of the Stanley Cup Final against the Los Angeles Kings. He said the team, like earlier series against the Rangers and Philadelphia, can string together consecutive wins after getting its first victory, and rejected calls for lineup changes, saying the club reviews tape after each game and changes only to improve the team. DeBoer noted several good scoring chances in Game 1 (Zajac, Kovalchuk, Elias), credited LA's goaltender for making saves, and said the Devils need to score more than one goal. He expressed confidence because the club has faced similar situations, such as being shut out by Lundqvist and needing to adjust against Florida's power play. On schedule, the team flew in, practiced, had a late dinner, and tried to keep players awake to adjust to LA time; he said the absence of pregame skating is the biggest difference from the regular season. DeBoer praised the officiating and disciplined five-on-five play, said the team battled to the final buzzer and will do the same Wednesday, and criticized a momentum-changing penalty call, arguing the whistle should blow whenever a player loses sight of the puck.

Apple Inc.’s Form 10-Q for the fiscal quarter ended March 30, 2019 reported quarterly net sales of $58.015 billion, down 5% from $61.137 billion a year earlier, primarily because of lower iPhone sales, partly offset by higher Services and Wearables, Home and Accessories sales; foreign-currency weakness also reduced sales. Gross margin fell to $21.821 billion from $23.422 billion, operating income to $13.415 billion from $15.894 billion, and net income to $11.561 billion from $13.822 billion. Diluted earnings per share were $2.46, versus $2.73. For the six months, net sales were $142.325 billion, net income was $31.526 billion, and diluted earnings per share were $6.66.

Second-quarter net sales by category were $31.051 billion for iPhone, $5.513 billion for Mac, $4.872 billion for iPad, $5.129 billion for Wearables, Home and Accessories, and $11.450 billion for Services. Geographic net sales were $25.596 billion in the Americas, $13.054 billion in Europe, $10.218 billion in Greater China, $5.532 billion in Japan, and $3.615 billion in the rest of Asia Pacific.

At March 30, 2019, Apple reported $341.998 billion of assets, $236.138 billion of liabilities, and $105.860 billion of shareholders’ equity. Cash and cash equivalents totaled $37.988 billion, while short- and long-term marketable securities totaled $42.104 billion and $145.319 billion. Six-month operating cash flow was $37.845 billion, investing activities provided $19.192 billion, and financing activities used $43.133 billion. Capital expenditures were $5.718 billion.

Apple adopted several accounting standards, including Topic 606 on revenue recognition, ASU 2016-01 on financial instruments, ASU 2016-16 on intra-entity asset transfers, and ASU 2016-18 on restricted cash. Marketable debt securities were classified as available for sale, with unrealized gains and losses recorded in comprehensive income; no such securities were considered other-than-temporarily impaired. Total cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities included $19.3 billion restricted from general use. Commercial paper outstanding was $11.9 billion, and term debt principal was $101.2 billion.

During the six months, Apple repurchased 164.7 million shares for $32.2 billion and paid $7.011 billion in dividends and dividend equivalents. On April 30, 2019, the board increased the repurchase authorization from $100 billion to $175 billion.

The European Commission’s State Aid Decision required Ireland to recover €13.1 billion plus €1.2 billion of interest from Apple. Apple and Ireland appealed, and the full amount was held in restricted escrow. Israel and Canada signed a modernized free trade agreement in Montreal, replacing their 1997 pact. The revision eliminates duties on thousands of additional products and adds chapters on labor, the environment, trade, gender and small and medium-sized enterprises, along with corporate social responsibility and improved dispute-settlement provisions. Officials said it would expand market access, boost both economies and help double bilateral trade. The agreement takes effect after ratification by both countries’ parliaments.

NVIDIA’s Turing architecture enables real-time ray tracing on single GPUs using dedicated RT Cores, RTX software, and filtering for physically accurate shadows, reflections, and refractions. With Microsoft’s DirectML and DirectX Raytracing APIs, developers can rapidly deploy game AI and ray tracing. Turing also adds advanced shading and inherits CUDA enhancements from Volta.

This study conducts a PRISMA-guided meta-analysis of 13 studies from eight countries (Taiwan, Australia, Turkey, China, Iran, the Netherlands, Spain, and Switzerland; samples of 20–794 participants) examining the effectiveness of AI-related technologies in education. Literature was searched in Google Scholar, ERIC, and Scopus for English-language peer-reviewed studies published from January 2015 to July 2024.

The overall effect of AI technologies was large and statistically significant (effect size 0.86, 95% CI [0.45, 1.27], p < 0.0001; random effects model; I² = 86.15%, with publication bias present). Subgroup analyses found chatbots and generative AI had the strongest effect (1.02, 95% CI [0.45, 1.59], p < 0.0001); online learning and virtual reality showed a positive but non-significant effect (0.79, 95% CI [-0.04, 1.62], p < 0.07); and learning management systems and AI platforms showed a significant positive effect (0.62, 95% CI [0.03, 1.21], p < 0.05).

Three additional algorithmic approaches were applied to the data: Naive Bayes-based algorithms, which indicated a positive result (P(Positive|x) = -13.74 vs. P(Negative|x) = -35.71); TF-IDF/BM25 variants producing an effect of 0.86 (95% CI [0.45, 1.28]); and BERT-based search algorithms producing 0.84 (95% CI [0.39, 1.29]). A hybrid model weighting random and fixed effects equally yielded 0.88 (95% CI [0.48, 1.29], p < 0.0001).

High heterogeneity (I² from 54.03% to 93.23%) was attributed to educational level and subject matter, implementation approaches, and student characteristics. The authors recommend careful context-sensitive implementation, particularly of chatbots and generative AI, larger and more diverse future studies, further validation of the new algorithms, cautious interpretation given publication bias, and policymaking that accounts for varied effects across contexts.

Good nutrition, alongside rest and hydration, supports energy, immune function, and recovery from infections. Fruit and vegetables are especially beneficial because their vitamins, minerals, micronutrients, and prebiotics support immunity; variety and eating a range of colours are encouraged. Vitamins A and C, magnesium, and zinc are highlighted, along with carrots and other orange, yellow, or red vegetables as sources of vitamin A.

Protein is essential for growth, repair, energy, digestion, hormone regulation, and immune defences, while insufficient protein can weaken recovery. Ginger, turmeric, coriander, mint, and basil are noted for their antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, or antibacterial properties. Probiotics, found in foods such as yoghurt, support beneficial gut bacteria, digestion, nutrient absorption, and immune regulation. Nuts and seeds provide minerals, fatty acids, and vitamin E for cell repair. Overall, a varied, balanced diet can help protect health and strengthen defences against infections.

A Danish study of 4,741 mothers found that older mothers’ children had fewer behavioural, social and emotional difficulties at ages seven and 11, but no advantage by 15. Older mothers worried less, had more positive parenting attitudes and greater “psychological maturity,” and scolded or physically disciplined their children less. These benefits should be weighed against increased risks of miscarriage, premature birth and deformities.

Fredrik underwent X-rays, with a report expected by the end of the day, and returned to finish the game despite missing several shifts. Detroit started poorly and was hindered by poor passing and numerous turnovers, particularly in the first half, which limited its offense. Carolina’s defensive line had been productive, strong, and difficult to play against, blocking shots and forcing quick plays and better shot selection. Although ice conditions were mentioned, turnovers were identified as a major problem.

Comparisons to Montreal’s earlier success were rejected, with emphasis placed on the next game and evening the series. Detroit may adjust its line combinations and special-teams deployment because Carolina’s wingers performed well and the Fedorov-Yzerman-Shanahan line’s extended penalty-kill and power-play minutes left other effective players with limited ice time. Carolina also moved the puck out of its zone quickly, while Detroit’s forechecking was ineffective. The team needed better entries, greater puck depth, and fewer low-quality shots that allowed Carolina to counterattack.

Scientists fused human skin cells with empty eggs and coaxed them through meiosis, producing functional eggs capable of forming early embryos. This proof-of-concept could eventually help infertile people have children.
