Adding exposure when the four-day RSI crossed specified levels produced an undesirable result despite retaining the same average trade gain. The passage does not recommend the Martingale method and instead suggests spreading equity across many uncorrelated, data-driven strategies, while distinguishing it from planned scale-in entries.

A New York Times survey found widespread dissatisfaction among federal judges with the Supreme Court’s emergency docket in Trump-related cases. Of 65 respondents, 12 said the Court used it appropriately, 12 said lower courts received sufficient guidance, and two of 54 said it improved public perceptions of the judiciary. Some judges described the orders as opaque, demoralizing and harmful to district courts; one Trump appointee defended them but warned they could appear secret or arbitrary. At least seven of roughly 20 orders lacked reasoning, and nearly all benefited the Trump administration, according to the Times. The survey covered judges from districts handling major Trump-policy cases, but the Times cautioned that respondents may not represent the judiciary. The Volokh Conspiracy criticized the survey for potentially oversampling judges predisposed to disagree with the orders.

The article examines how dance education can function as social studies education and support holistic, inclusive learning despite standardized testing systems that privilege separate disciplines. A literature review and survey of 91 U.S. dance-education graduates found that all major social studies concepts appeared in some dance curricula. The strongest emphases were individual development and identity (97%) and people, places, and environments (94%); power and governance and civic ideals and practices were least emphasized (44% each). Open responses showed social studies content being taught both literally and implicitly through classroom practices, with especially inconsistent understandings of culture. Dance educators often integrated these concepts with little guidance, while prescriptive curricula and unclear relationships between curriculum and pedagogy sometimes obscured them. The article recommends less prescriptive dance curricula, stronger professional development, interdisciplinary education policy, and consideration of UNESCO’s Framework for Culture and Arts Education. Limitations include the small, nonrandom U.S.-only sample, mostly yes/no survey questions, lack of follow-up, and absence of social studies educators’ perspectives.

Colorado’s Prescription Drug Affordability Board voted to cap payments for Amgen’s Enbrel at $600 per unit, establishing a ceiling for government agencies and commercial health plans serving state residents. The limit, also scheduled for Medicare in January, equates to about $30,350 annually per person, compared with roughly $53,000 paid by the average state insurance plan in 2023. The first-in-the-nation move may encourage other states to pursue similar prescription-drug spending controls.

Turkey’s government extended the state of emergency for three months from April 19, citing continued terror threats and the failed July 15, 2016 coup. The measure followed National Security Council advice and parliamentary approval.

The Dolphins earned their first win of the season over the Jets on Monday night, but Tyreek Hill’s early-third-quarter dislocation of his left knee overshadowed the victory. Hill was taken to a hospital and is expected to miss the remainder of the season, leaving Miami’s offense without its primary playmaker. Darren Waller caught two touchdown passes in his first game action since January 2024, and the Dolphins rallied with consecutive scoring drives.

The Jets committed three turnovers and 12 penalties, including six pre-snap flags, and lost three fumbles for the first time since 2023. They managed 65 passing yards through three quarters, while their quarterback rushed for 73 yards and scored on a 43-yard run. New York also surrendered 197 rushing yards, with one Jets runner gaining 81 yards. Coach Aaron Glenn became the third Jets coach to begin his tenure 0-4; no Jets coach has started 0-5.

A proposed method for finding extraterrestrial civilizations avoids the synchronicity required to detect radio signals or lasers. Astronomer Hector Socas-Navarro suggests searching existing exoplanet data for artificial satellite swarms around distant planets. During transits, a large swarm—especially viewed edge-on—could slightly dim starlight before and after the planet crosses its star. The method requires no new telescopes or experiments and could detect long-lasting artifacts even if their creators no longer exist, though its chances of success may be limited.

China will expand its trade-weighted yuan basket from 13 to 24 currencies in 2017, reducing the U.S. dollar’s weighting from 26.4% to 22.4%. The adjustment follows the yuan’s 7% decline against the dollar in 2016 and aims to shift attention away from the bilateral rate. Chinese officials maintain that the yuan is stable and attribute its weakness to the strong dollar.

IMI plc has a consensus “Hold” rating from 18 brokers (two sell, 12 hold and four buy), with an average 12-month target of GBX 1,027.29 ($12.84). BNP Paribas raised its target to GBX 1,400 with an “outperform” rating. Barclays reaffirmed “overweight” at GBX 1,190; Goldman Sachs, Credit Suisse and J.P. Morgan reaffirmed “neutral” with targets of GBX 1,000, GBX 1,020 and GBX 990, respectively. The firm has a GBX 3.29 billion market capitalization and a 52-week range of GBX 751–1,223. IMI is a UK engineering company focused on fluid-control products across critical, precision and hydronic engineering.

Apple Inc. filed a Form 8-K dated July 28, 2022. Under Item 2.02 (Results of Operations and Financial Condition), Apple announced via press release its financial results for the third fiscal quarter ended June 25, 2022, attached as Exhibit 99.1; the information is not deemed "filed" for Section 18 purposes nor incorporated by reference into other filings. Item 9.01 lists the press release (Exhibit 99.1) and Inline XBRL cover page data (Exhibit 104). The report, listing Apple's common stock and nine series of notes registered on Nasdaq, was signed by Luca Maestri, Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer.

The lecture concludes a discussion of Krylov methods, reviewing Arnoldi and introducing conjugate gradients. Arnoldi is presented as a Gram–Schmidt-like procedure that constructs an orthogonal basis for a Krylov subspace. For a symmetric matrix, the associated Hessenberg matrix becomes symmetric and tridiagonal. Stopping Arnoldi partway produces a smaller symmetric tridiagonal matrix whose eigenvalues, called Ritz values, often approximate the low eigenvalues of the original large matrix; ARPACK is mentioned as a suitable software package.

Conjugate gradients apply to symmetric positive-definite systems. Its recursive cycle constructs iterates in Krylov subspaces while producing orthogonal residuals and search directions that are conjugate under the inner product \(\langle x,y\rangle_A=x^TAy\). Each iteration requires one multiplication by \(A\), two inner products, and several vector updates; the cost of the matrix multiplication depends on the number of nonzero entries in \(A\). Its convergence rate depends on the matrix’s condition number.

The method is also interpreted as minimizing the quadratic energy
\[
E(x)=\tfrac12x^TAx-b^Tx.
\]
Its gradient is \(Ax-b\), and positive definiteness ensures that minimizing this energy is equivalent to solving \(Ax=b\). Unlike steepest descent, which follows changing gradient directions and may progress slowly across elongated contours, conjugate gradients chooses mutually conjugate directions that are orthogonal in the \(A\)-inner product. The same direction idea can also be extended to nonlinear optimization.

For symmetric systems that are not positive definite, where conjugate-gradient denominators may vanish, the lecture introduces MINRES. MINRES uses Arnoldi’s orthogonal Krylov basis to minimize the residual norm through a least-squares problem. It is safer but more expensive because the tridiagonal structure is lost and additional Hessenberg coefficients must be computed. The lecture closes by noting that Krylov methods offer efficient recursive orthogonality, while choosing between iterative methods and direct methods such as elimination requires numerical comparison.

Police and Crimestoppers are warning shoppers and cash-handling businesses to guard against counterfeit banknotes during the festive season, when fraudsters target busy shops and temporary staff. In the first half of 2017, 237,000 fake notes with a nominal value of £4.88 million were removed from UK circulation. Crimestoppers and the Bank of England launched the Banknote Checking Scheme to train businesses and reduce acceptance of counterfeits, and are seeking anonymous information about those making, buying or selling them.

STAT’s Pharmalittle highlights two major drug-industry developments. GSK named chief commercial officer Luke Miels as CEO effective Jan. 1, succeeding Emma Walmsley, who led the company since 2017 and oversaw the Haleon spinoff and a shift toward specialty drugs and vaccines. Investors have questioned GSK’s strategy amid HIV patent losses, vaccine challenges, and flat shares. AstraZeneca plans to add a New York Stock Exchange listing while retaining its London and Stockholm listings, giving U.S. investors easier access to ordinary shares amid tariffs and drug-pricing scrutiny. The newsletter also notes that AstraZeneca and Novartis have opened direct-to-consumer sales channels in the U.S.

Zimbabwe’s Livestock and Veterinary Services Department says inconsistent FMD vaccine supplies have allowed infections to spread, with active cases in Chipinge South, Mwenezi, Chivi and Chiredzi and no FMD-free zones. Weak staffing, logistics, funding, technical capacity, movement controls, animal identification, boundary fences and wildlife cooperation compound the problem. Loss of control zones has enlarged the vaccination population, requiring repeated four-monthly doses after outbreaks.

VentureWire, a daily private-company business newsletter published by Technologic Partners, is dated Tuesday, September 19, 2000. Its top stories: Pseudo.com ceased operations and laid off all 175 employees after efforts to raise funding or find a buyer failed; Broadbase Software agreed to acquire Servicesoft in a deal worth about $645 million; Enfrastructure launched with over $100 million from investors including Arthur Andersen, Avaya, IBM and Microsoft; Mary Coleman, formerly chairman and CEO of Baan, was named CEO of RightWorks, succeeding founder Vani Kola; U.K.-based Interregnum opened a GBP 75 million ($105 million) IT fund; and Q9 Networks raised $26.5 million in Series A funding.

An extensive "New Money" section reports dozens of funding rounds, including Darwin Networks ($91 million Series B), IPG Photonics ($75 million), Wheelhouse ($52 million), Everdream ($50 million), Nishan Systems ($50 million), CosmoCom ($40 million), MobileSys ($36 million), StorageWay ($36 million), Skulogix ($31 million), Internet Machines ($30 million) and iPass ($30 million), plus numerous smaller first, seed and early rounds, frequently with new investors joining boards.

Other sections cover new products and name changes (inOvate Communications Group launching with three portfolio firms; Onyx Japan; J3 Technology becoming Impact Innovations Group; BGV PCS Acquisition becoming MainStream PCS; ASPSecure becoming TrustData Solutions); three acquisitions (Optical Solutions/Ziga Systems, Symposium/WeFusion.com, ConsumerSearch.com/Product ReviewNet); six new directors; two new CEOs (CityReach's Sanjaya Addanki and RewardsPlus' M. Gordon Gaddy); the launch of Israeli fund East West Ventures; two venture personnel moves; and three corrections. Advertisements promote a Bessemer Venture Partners career fair, a Harvard Business School private-equity course, and The Wall Street Journal Technology Summit.

Cheltenham Town face a second consecutive summer fight to retain Harry Pell, with a League Two club interested after earlier bids from Blackpool and Chesterfield. The 26-year-old midfielder is contracted until 2019, has scored three goals in five games, and missed the latest match after having two wisdom teeth removed.

Four 2017 Nebraska reports covered agricultural research, local history, education and tourism. The University of Nebraska-Lincoln expanded agricultural and natural-resources facilities and promoted interdisciplinary research, including a $20 million, five-year National Science Foundation project on root and soil microbes and the INFEWS initiative. The Buffalo County Historical Society opened a climate-controlled Family History Center to preserve artifacts and documents, display collections and expand the Trails & Rails Museum; another $660,000 is sought for a west wing. Lincoln Public Schools, which has the lowest student-teacher ratios among Nebraska’s 10 largest districts, is seeking to preserve small classes as its proposed budget draws controversy. In Alliance, Carhenge—a copy of England’s Stonehenge made from junked cars—was preparing to attract eclipse visitors through concerts, tournaments, a powwow and other events, with its history of zoning disputes adding to its notoriety.

Stone tools discovered at India’s Attirampakkam site and dated to 385,000–172,000 years ago suggest humans may have migrated from Africa earlier than previously thought, raising questions about their makers and cultural influences.

AMR is described as a major global threat associated with limited treatment options for infectious diseases. In India, unrestricted antibiotic access, weak regulation, low awareness, inappropriate prescribing and self-medication, inadequate hygiene and infrastructure, and agricultural antibiotic use contribute to resistance.

A cross-sectional study at ACS Medical College and Hospital in Chennai enrolled 346 participants from November 2023 to May 2024. Urine, blood, sputum, wound/pus, and other swabs were cultured using Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion and CLSI guidelines; tissue samples and participants previously receiving antimicrobial therapy were excluded. Older adults comprised 56.6% of participants, females 52.3%, and urine was the most common sample type (42.4%).

Of 346 samples, 264 (76.3%) showed positive growth. Gram-negative organisms accounted for 75.4% of positive cultures. The leading isolates were E. coli (28.8%), Klebsiella spp. (26.9%), Staphylococcus spp. (13.2%), and Pseudomonas spp. (9.5%). E. coli predominated in urine, Klebsiella in sputum and urine, Staphylococcus in wounds, and Pseudomonas in wounds and sputum.

Among E. coli, resistance was highest to polymyxin B (98.7%), cefoperazone/sulbactam and chloramphenicol (97.4%), cefuroxime (93.4%), and cefotaxime (92.1%). Amikacin and gentamicin had the highest reported sensitivities, at 71.1% and 63.2%, respectively. The findings support local antimicrobial-stewardship measures, including multidisciplinary oversight, resistance surveillance, provider education, locally based guidelines, diagnostic testing, restrictions on non-prescription antibiotic sales and self-medication, clinical decision-support tools, accountability, and ongoing evaluation.

Limitations include the short duration, small and context-specific sample, cross-sectional design, rapidly changing AMR patterns, urban focus, missing clinical outcome and comorbidity data, and lack of emphasis on hospital-acquired infections.

This continuation describes a cloud-based industrial data services platform for registering industrial assets, their hierarchical asset models, and available data service applications. Asset owners can select applications through client devices, while gateway devices collect industrial data from referenced tags and analytic components process the data according to the selected application.

Industrial devices support configurable basic information data types (BIDTs), including State, Rate, Odometer, and Event types. BIDTs contain current values and user-defined metadata describing asset names, states, limits, units, data sources, rollover or interval rules, triggering tags, and update rates. Industrial devices expose these BIDTs for discovery by gateway devices.

Gateway devices retrieve BIDT data and metadata, organize them according to user-defined hierarchical asset models, and generate contextualized presentations. Such models can represent plants, production lines, machines, equipment, devices, and different operational or engineering views. An on-premises or cloud-based application server can aggregate asset models from multiple gateways into a plant model, display BIDT data through type-specific widgets and historical trends, retain event and trend history, and customize presentations by user role. A gateway registry can authenticate registered devices and issue time-limited certificates for secure data transfer to customer cloud platforms.

The study used finite-element growth-and-remodeling simulations to generate synthetic thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAAs) caused by combined, spatially varying impairment of elastic-fiber integrity and cellular mechanosensing. The model was parameterized using a mouse Marfan syndrome ascending aorta, and 500 dilatation–distensibility map pairs were created with closely matched maximum dilatations of approximately 1.5-fold. CNN-DeepONet, FNN-DeepONet, UNet, and Laplace Neural Operator architectures were trained using dilatation alone or both dilatation and distensibility, represented as grayscale or heat maps.

Most networks predicted the two initiating insult profiles with roughly 10% or less relative L2 error. Adding distensibility reduced errors by about half across all architectures and substantially improved distinction between combined disease mechanisms. UNet achieved the best overall accuracy, particularly with both inputs, while LNO performed poorly with dilatation alone but became competitive when distensibility was included. With dilatation alone, CNN-DeepONet and UNet were the strongest options. UNet and LNO also delineated insult-region boundaries more accurately than the DeepONet models. Grayscale versus heat-map format had little effect for most networks.

The simulations showed that elastic-fiber and mechanosensing impairments produced different mechanical patterns despite similar dilatation: elastic-fiber-dominated insults produced lower distensibility, whereas mechanosensing-dominated insults generated higher circumferential and axial stresses. Thus, full-field measurements may help assess aneurysm mechanical stability beyond maximum aortic size.

Limitations included a single initial geometry and material parameter set, cylindrical rather than curved anatomy, only stable aneurysm growth, and the omission of other contributors such as impaired collagen cross-linking and altered matrix mechanoregulation. Incorporating variable and human image-based data, unstable growth, dissection or rupture, and longitudinal information was identified as future work.

Joe Hadzima provides an educational, issue-spotting overview of legal concerns for startups, emphasizing that law is fact-specific and that founders should consult legal advisers. He organizes the discussion around intellectual property, business form, people, and financing.

- **Intellectual property:** Founders must determine who owns startup IP and how to protect it before seeking outside financing. IP can be a valuable business asset and may correlate with success; in his study of roughly 9,000 venture-backed companies, 86% of successful companies scored highly in patent strategy. Trademarks identify the source of goods or services and arise through use, with registration providing additional benefits. Copyright arises automatically and protects expression rather than function; ownership generally belongs to the author, so companies need written assignments from contractors and must comply with open-source licenses. Trade secrets provide protection until disclosure and can be maintained through nondisclosure agreements. Patents provide costly but stronger, limited rights to exclude others. Requirements include novelty, utility, patentable subject matter, non-obviousness, and an enabling disclosure. In the United States, public disclosure or sale generally starts a one-year filing period, while disclosure before filing can affect rights abroad. Under the first-to-file system, provisional applications can cheaply establish an early filing date and provide 12 months to decide whether to pursue a full application. Patent applications disclose an invention in detail, but claims determine the enforceable scope and require legal drafting. The speaker discusses patent-landscape mapping and the importance of securing assignments from inventors.

- **University licensing:** The Bayh-Dole Act placed administration of federally sponsored research at universities. MIT’s Technology Licensing Office handles technology transfer, revenue generation, patent prosecution, and licensing. MIT may own inventions produced by employees or researchers under sponsored research or with significant use of MIT resources. Startups commonly seek a six- to twelve-month option before licensing technology and bearing some prosecution costs. Typical arrangements may involve issue and maintenance fees, royalties, patent costs, and single-digit equity instead of some cash payments. Revenue is generally divided among TLO expenses, patent costs, inventors, the relevant department, and MIT.

- **Business form:** Technology companies seeking financing commonly use a Delaware corporation because of its flexible and predictable corporate law. Incorporation provides limited liability for shareholders, although founders remain responsible for their own acts. Early incorporation can reduce exposure to partnership liability. An S-corporation election can avoid corporate-level tax when ownership and shareholder eligibility requirements are met, but typical venture financing may terminate that status. Under Section 83, receiving stock for services can create taxable ordinary income based on its fair market value minus the amount paid. Issuing stock before investment and making a timely Section 83(b) election can help manage this issue.

- **Founders and employees:** Founders should address governance, fiduciary duties, board composition, founder equity, intellectual-property ownership, and transfer restrictions early, potentially using a founders’ memo. Equity divisions have no single formula and may reflect past and future contributions, sacrifice, outside opportunities, and internal equity. Employee equity may motivate some workers, but its effect should not be assumed. In his experience, a first venture round commonly reserves about 12%–18% of equity for employees. Common instruments include restricted stock, incentive stock options, and nonqualified options, with different tax treatment. Common vesting is a one-year cliff, 25% vesting after that year, and monthly or quarterly vesting over the following three years. Equity plans should address repurchase rights, forfeiture, confidentiality or noncompetition violations, acceleration after a change of control, and independent directors.

- **Financing and securities law:** Offers of securities generally require SEC registration unless an exemption applies, and noncompliance can create criminal and personal liability. Business plans and promotional documents should not state or imply offers to sell company interests. Convertible notes can provide quick, relatively inexpensive bridge financing while postponing valuation disputes. Capital structures may include common stock and other senior instruments with different rights. Angel and venture term sheets commonly address liquidation preferences, investor priority over founders, anti-dilution protection, management, and exit arrangements. Straight preferred stock lets investors choose repayment or conversion, while participating preferred may provide additional participation that can disadvantage founders. Anti-dilution protection may use either a severe full-ratchet adjustment or the more typical weighted-average formula.

The author approves legislation establishing a constitutional process for resolving disputed presidential electoral votes, explaining that the election’s outcome depends on contested returns from several states. The bill assigns decisions on single returns to Congress and on double returns to a tribunal whose rulings stand unless both chambers agree otherwise. The author argues that one candidate must have been elected and that legal, orderly resolution will restore public confidence, harmony, and economic activity. Although favoring permanent general legislation for future disputes, the author signs the bill as adequate for the present emergency.

The Sansa Fuze manual describes a portable audio/video player with a 1.9-inch color screen, internal memory, microSD/SDHC expansion, an integrated FM tuner where applicable, and a built-in microphone. It supports MP3, WAV, WMA, secure WMA, audiobooks, podcasts, photos, and converted video formats. Its nonreplaceable rechargeable battery provides up to 24 hours of audio or five hours of video playback and can be charged via USB or optional AC and car adapters.

Instructions cover power, reset, hold-lock, navigation, USB connection, charging, firmware updates, formatting, and file transfer using drag-and-drop, Windows Media Player, Audible Manager, or Sansa Media Converter. Playback controls include repeat, shuffle, MusicEQ, ratings, Go Lists, bookmarks, chapter and speed options for audiobooks, and slideshow settings for photos. The FM radio supports manual and automatic preset scanning, up to 30 presets, regional and mono/stereo settings, and station recordings. The built-in microphone records voice and other audio, while content can also be deleted directly or through a computer.

System settings include wallpaper, list artwork, backlight, power saver, language, date and time, brightness, factory reset, device information, USB mode, formatting, and press-and-hold behavior. The manual also provides troubleshooting guidance, SanDisk support and firmware resources, a one-year limited hardware warranty, and a software license restricting use, modification, redistribution, reverse engineering, and other activities.

The paper examines how digital transformation relates to sustainable development and how national cultural characteristics relate to digitalization. It reviews industrial and digital revolutions, distinguishes digitization, digitalization, and digital transformation, and frames sustainable development around economic growth, social equity, environmental protection, and culture, with macromarketing identified as a mechanism supporting societal acceptance of technological change.

Using 2014–2017 data for 28 EU countries, the study compares the Digital Economy and Society Index (DESI) with measures of competitiveness, innovation, GDP, entrepreneurship, country contribution to humanity, Sustainable Development Goals, and Sustainable Society Index components. It also tests correlations between DESI and Hofstede’s six cultural dimensions.

Digitalization was significantly positively correlated with competitiveness, innovation, entrepreneurship, GDP, and Sustainable Development Goal performance. Social components, including culture, human wellbeing, world order, prosperity, and equality, generally showed positive relationships with DESI. Environmental results were weaker: Planet and Climate was not significantly related to DESI, while environmental wellbeing had a significant negative correlation with digitalization.

Cultural analysis found negative correlations between digitalization and power distance and uncertainty avoidance, while individualism and indulgence were positively correlated. Masculinity was not significant, and long-term orientation showed no relationship with digitalization. The results indicate that digitalization is associated with stronger economic and social performance but not environmental improvement, and that cultural differences are important to digitalization levels.

Limitations include the EU-only sample, the incomplete development of sustainability measurement methods, DESI’s limited scope, and the inability of correlations to establish causation. Further research is proposed to expand country coverage, refine sustainability measures, examine additional cultural frameworks, and develop culturally tailored macromarketing tools for technological change.

Ari Ne’eman recounts President John F. Kennedy’s 1963 dispatch of the President’s Panel on Mental Retardation to the Soviet Union to study intellectual disability and encourage scientific exchange during the Cold War. Soviet officials barred intelligence testing and genetic explanations and denied that socioeconomic deprivation existed in the USSR, pressuring researchers to identify organic causes, including minor brain injuries found through EEG testing. Although Soviet special-education classes resembled American counterparts, official prevalence estimates differed sharply. The delegation attributed much of the gap to diagnostic practices rather than substantially lower impairment.

Ne’eman connects this episode to Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s claims linking autism to vaccines and acetaminophen. He argues that rising autism diagnoses reflect broadened criteria, diagnostic substitution from intellectual-disability categories, and improved access to diagnosis, rather than a new autism epidemic. He also highlights the Kennedy family’s disability-policy legacy, including the 1970 Developmental Disabilities Act, and criticizes the Trump administration’s proposed removal of parts of that law following Medicaid cuts, warning that it would weaken services for autistic people and others with disabilities.

The Sixth Circuit held that the trial court properly addressed the inconsistency between interrogatory No. 4 and the general verdict, and substantial evidence supported the jury’s verdict. The judgment was affirmed.

The Houston Astros defeated the Chicago White Sox 7-1 on Sunday, extending their winning streak to six games and completing a three-game sweep in which they outscored Chicago 27-2. José Altuve’s go-ahead single sparked a five-run seventh inning, and Evan Gattis hit his first home run of the season. Lance McCullers Jr. allowed one run and eight hits over six innings. Chicago fell to 4-14 after losing seven straight games and 12 of 13. Reliever Danny Farquhar remained in critical but stable condition after collapsing in the dugout, and his No. 43 jersey was displayed in the bullpen. The Astros next face the Los Angeles Angels, starting with Gerrit Cole on Monday.

This excerpt from the SD Physical Layer Simplified Specification Version 6.00 defines SD Memory Card command behavior in several areas.

**Card Ownership Protection (COP) and Lock/Unlock:** For COP Cards, an accepted COP Unlock (CMD42[1Fh]) places the card in CMD42 ver. 2.0 mode and enables other CMD42 operations; while FEP is set, only "Set FEP" is supported and the "Set PWD" command requires the COP bit to be 0. Setting FEP stores the new password in the FEP/FEP_LEN registers, disables "Force Erase" and "Reset PWD" (CLR_PWD), and does not change the current lock state. A wrong old password leaves the password unchanged and sets LOCK_UNLOCK_FAILED; clearing FEP requires the correct password and re-enables Force Erase and CLR_PWD. Force Erase (ERASE bit only) on a locked card erases all card content including PWD/PWD_LEN and unlocks the card; it fails on an unlocked card and is prevented while FEP is set. FEP Force Erase uses ERASE with COP and the FEP password, matches only if the password equals FEP, and leaves FEP/FEP_LEN unchanged. Force erase does not erase the secure area, keeps the card locked during erase and write protection until user area erasure completes. CMD42 errors set LOCK_UNLOCK_FAILED (Bit24), and CARD_IS_LOCKED (Bit25) reflects state changes. Tables cover non-COP cards, COP PWD-related functions, and COP-specific functions. ACMD6 is rejected while the card is locked, and bus width can change only when unlocked. Locked cards accept only listed commands (including CMD11 and CMD40); all others are illegal. Three lock/unlock card types exist: Type 1, Type 2, and Type 3 (COP).

**APP_CMD/ACMD and Switch Function:** CMD55 causes the next command to be interpreted as an ACMD, with defined/undefined and legal/illegal combinations handled as described; ACMD41 responses carry no APP_CMD status, and ACMD6, 13, 17–26, 38–49, and 51 are reserved for proprietary use. CMD6 defines six function groups (Access Mode, Command System, Driver Strength, Power Limit, and two reserved groups), each supporting sixteen functions with Function 0 as default. Mode 0 (Check Function) queries supported functions, current selections, and maximum current/power consumption; Mode 1 (Set Function) switches functionality, returning 0xF and making no change if a selection is invalid. The 512-bit status block contains function selections, support bits, maximum current/power, and busy status; Data Structure Version 01h enables busy-status indication, and mode 1 may only be applied to ready functions. Power Limit defaults to 0.72 W, with 1.44 W and 1.80 W settings, and is mandatory in UHS-II mode.

**Other sections:** High-Speed mode (25 MB/sec via 50 MHz) is optional; the Command System group defines CMD34–37, CMD50, and CMD57; CMD8 checks the host supply voltage in Idle state with an R7 response; SDSC uses byte addressing while SDHC/SDXC use block addressing with fixed 512-byte block length; CMD42 is not a memory access command and allows block lengths up to 512 bytes. The host may stop the bus clock but must supply 8 clocks after transactions, with ACMD41 exempted. CRC7 protects commands, responses (except R3), CID and CSD; CRC16 protects data blocks. Read, write, and erase timeouts are specified, including busy limits of 250 ms (up to 500 ms for SDXC) and UHS-II Data Burst timing. Command classes (CCC), command tables, UHS-II command differences, state transitions, and response types R1/R1b, R2, R3, R6, and R7 are defined, along with Card Status, SD Status, and Task Status fields. Finally, Speed Class methods (Speed Class 2/4/6/10, UHS Speed Grade, Video Speed Class) define Allocation Units, Recording Units, write/move/read performance metrics, performance curves, and the FAT update cycle for real-time recording.

Toronto home values surged as strong demand and limited supply fueled bidding wars, with the average Greater Toronto Area sale rising 33.2% year over year to $916,567. Some owners, including Sarah Blakely, sold renovated homes for large profits and moved to cheaper areas or downsized to become mortgage-free. As officials prepare affordability measures, agents say the market is beginning to cool: buyers are delaying purchases, sellers are receiving lower bids, and recent gains may not be repeatable.

Sellers are also leaving Toronto for smaller communities, contributing to price jumps in Hamilton-Burlington and renewed interest in Nova Scotia. Vancouver has seen similar shifts, though its foreign-buyer tax cooled demand for high-end west-side homes. Agents advise Toronto sellers to consider cashing out before a correction, while warning that sellers may not be able to afford to rebuy if prices fall; one agent also calls for action against speculators.

More than 50 patients and attendants narrowly escaped a Lucknow hospital fire without injuries. Over 24 ICU patients were transferred, and a probe was ordered into the hospital’s fire-safety equipment and procedures.

India and Bangladesh meet in the Champions Trophy cricket semi-final at Edgbaston on 15 June, with coverage starting at 3 p.m. IST on Star Sports and Hotstar. India, led by Virat Kohli, aim to continue their strong group form and dominate Bangladesh, whose win over New Zealand featured a record partnership between Shakib Al Hasan and Mahmadullah.

LeBron James, a four-time NBA champion, four-time MVP and 19-time All-Star, has an estimated net worth of $1 billion. He earned $479.5 million over 21 NBA seasons and signed a two-year, $97 million Lakers extension that brought his guaranteed career earnings to $532 million. In 2022, his on- and off-court earnings totaled $126.9 million, including $90 million from endorsements.

James’s major sponsors include Nike, AT&T, Walmart, Intel, Kia and Beats by Dre. His longtime “limitless” Nike agreement has included a dedicated innovation center, while sponsored Instagram posts reportedly earn him about $428,000 each. He also generates income through investments in Blaze Pizza, Lobos 1707 tequila, Liverpool FC, Fenway Sports Group, Canyon Bicycles and a Manhattan office building. His businesses Uninterrupted and SpringHill raised outside investment, and SpringHill produced “Space Jam: A New Legacy.”

James has owned several notable homes, including a $9 million Miami property that he sold for a $4 million profit, a 30,000-square-foot Akron compound and a $23 million Los Angeles mansion. His car collection has included Porsches, a Rolls-Royce Phantom and Ferraris, including a Testarossa for Savannah, although he says he drives a Kia.

Despite being described by former teammate Dwyane Wade as cheap, James spends heavily on his health, including personal trainers, recovery specialists, chefs and masseuses. He has also bought his mother a Porsche and given Savannah a $300,000 engagement ring.

Through the I Promise School, LeBron James Family Foundation and More Than a Vote campaign, James has supported Akron students, pledged about $41 million to send more than 1,000 students to college and encouraged voting. James, 41, has hinted at retirement but has not announced his departure; a widely anticipated “Decision” announcement turned out to be a Hennessy advertisement.

The passage examines the 2018 Baku Declaration of the Non-Aligned Movement and the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting communiqué, assessing their significance for India and the Global South. Both documents opposed protectionism, supported a fair, rules-based multilateral trading system, and backed renewed efforts to resolve the Doha Development Round. They also addressed South-South cooperation, financial inclusion, debt, development financing, trade facilitation, migration, refugees, intolerance, and Palestinian rights.

The Baku Declaration stressed policy autonomy and non-alignment but, according to the author, largely reaffirmed existing economic arrangements without confronting structural inequalities in global economic governance. It strongly supported Palestinian self-determination, condemned Israeli settlement expansion and the occupation of the Syrian Golan, and called for tolerance and respect for diversity.

The CHOGM communiqué aimed to expand intra-Commonwealth investment and trade to US$2 trillion by 2030 while recognizing the vulnerabilities of small states, including debt, limited finance, climate disasters, and exclusion through “de-risking.” It supported the Rohingya, praised Bangladesh’s shelter efforts, and called for safe, dignified returns under UNHCR oversight.

For India, the author identifies tensions between these commitments and government policies, citing India’s previous absence from a NAM summit, criticism of its treatment of minorities and Dalits, and its opposition to Rohingya deportation despite hosting approximately 40,000 Rohingya refugees. The passage concludes that the documents contain welcome commitments but leave unresolved broader questions of trade, technology transfer, market access, policy autonomy, and global economic governance.

The Federal Circuit reversed the district court’s denial of Hilite International’s motion for judgment as a matter of law. Melchior had alleged that two Hilite cam phasers infringed the ’017, ’506, and ’254 patents by varying camshaft phase in reaction to torque reversals. The majority held that Danckert anticipated the asserted ’017 claims because it disclosed every claim limitation, and Melchior’s “direct transfer in a closed line” distinction was not part of the claim construction. The ’506 and ’254 claims were obvious over Danckert in view of Shirai, and Melchior had challenged only anticipation, not obviousness. Judge Newman concurred in the judgment of no liability, disagreeing with the anticipation holding but finding no substantial evidence of infringement because the parties stipulated that no infringement occurred while the external oil pump operated and the record did not establish torque-reversal-only operation.

The study examines students’ perceptions of flipped learning (FL) in Norwegian physical education teacher education (PETE), amid limited research on digital technology in PE. A qualitative, constructivist grounded-theory approach was used. Twenty-two PETE students, evenly divided by gender and with an average age of 24.2, participated in interviews after completing two FL-based units: a practical dance unit and a theoretical motor-learning unit. The intervention included 11 preparation videos of 10–20 minutes and more active, student-centered campus sessions; six traditionally taught units served as comparisons.

Five empirical themes emerged. First, students perceived expectations from teachers and peers to watch videos and participate in classroom discussions, with peer pressure increasing preparation and motivation. Second, videos were viewed as concise, accessible, timesaving, and motivating preparation that extracted the most relevant information. Third, FL supported deeper learning by allowing students to preview concepts, revisit videos, work at their own pace, and apply ideas through peer discussion. Fourth, advance preparation created a supportive learning environment, reduced uncertainty, increased self-efficacy, and allowed students to practice practical movements before class. Fifth, challenges included the inability to ask questions during video preparation, technical problems accessing videos, and the perception that FL sometimes required more time.

Overall, students viewed FL as an engaging and useful approach that improved their understanding of PE teaching, motivation, participation, and learning across both theoretical and practical modules. They also regarded digitally enriched learning as a tool they could apply in their future teaching. Reported advantages outweighed challenges. Limitations included the initial focus on motivation and learning and data collection from a single institution; future research should examine digital-technology implementation and teachers’ technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge in PETE and school PE.

St. Jude researchers used the data-driven NetBID algorithm to identify the kinases Mst1 and Mst2 as key regulators of distinct dendritic-cell functions in mice. Their Nature study found that Mst1/2 and Hippo signaling regulate metabolic differences between CD8α+ and CD8α− dendritic cells, cytokine signaling and T-cell priming. CD8α+ cells were more metabolically active, while Mst1/2 promoted interleukin-12 production through an unconventional NF-κB pathway that supports CD8 T-cell responses. Manipulating metabolism affected CD8α+ cell function and T-cell priming. The findings may inform cancer or immune-disorder treatments by modulating dendritic cells, and NetBID may help identify hidden drivers in other datasets.

Roman pottery found on Chapel St Leonards' beach near Skegness may mark a lost Roman settlement, experts say. It is the third Roman artefact found there since December, when a coin and part of a brooch were unearthed. The site, previously thought to be in Skegness, may lie closer to Chapel St Leonards. Lincolnshire County Council urges residents to report finds, which have also included medieval and Iron Age items.

The Alabama Supreme Court answered the Eleventh Circuit’s certified question in the negative. A provision defining an “insured” as an employee acting within the scope of employment duties does not conflict with coverage for constitutional or civil-rights violations and therefore does not create ambiguity that must be construed against the insurer.

The dispute arose from claims by Janice Shrader and Debra Lynn Livingston against City of Attalla employees Fletcher Mallard and Barnie Gilliland, who allegedly sexually abused them after their arrests. Employers Mutual Casualty Company’s linebacker policy covered civil-rights violations but limited coverage to employees acting within the scope of their duties. The district court found the policy unambiguous and the alleged conduct outside the officers’ duties.

The court distinguished the Titan decisions. Titan I involved a separate conflict between provisions covering unintended injuries and intentional acts; its ambiguity ruling did not address a scope-of-duties limitation. Titan II relied on law of the case rather than independently rejecting that limitation.

Rejecting the argument that the coverage was illusory, the court explained that conduct “under color of state law” under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and conduct within the scope of employment substantially overlap. Thus, civil-rights coverage can apply when both conditions are met. Because the provisions do not contradict each other and the scope-of-duties language is not inherently ambiguous, the court held that the policy must be enforced as written. All justices concurred.

This preprint examines whether short-term outdoor temperature drops worsen COVID-19 during the 2022 Omicron wave in Tomsk, Russia. Based on a “compromised airway epithelium” hypothesis, the authors propose that cold exposure may weaken airway defenses, reduce antiviral responses, inhibit mucociliary clearance, and increase symptoms and disease severity.

Daily official temperature data and COVID-19 hospitalization data from January 1 to March 31, 2022, were analyzed using an adapted case-crossover design in which cases served as their own controls. Hospitalizations and pneumonia were used as proxies for severity. The analysis identified 17 hospitalization surges. Fourteen followed temperature drops exceeding 3°C, typically with a lag of one to two days; eight were classified as primarily triggered by temperature and six as additionally influenced by other factors. Three surges occurred without temperature changes and were attributed to other causes.

The authors conclude that temperature forecasts may help anticipate hospitalization increases and prepare healthcare systems, but note limitations including the single-city scope, lack of a direct severity index, interacting weather variables, and the complexity of separating temperature and humidity effects. They recommend further mechanistic and mathematical investigation of temperature, humidity, supersaturation, and air pollution.

Peter Joseph Saville, a dentist who served Worthing for more than four decades, died peacefully at home on June 27, aged 90. Born in Ilford in 1928, he trained at Guy’s Hospital and served as an Army dental surgeon in Cyprus and Egypt before marrying Josephine in 1954. After joining a Lancing practice, he established his own in West Park Lane.

He was a prominent sportsman, playing cricket, hockey, golf, tennis and squash. He founded The Manor Sports Club’s squash section and served in leadership roles within several local organisations. A devoted Catholic, he was a Eucharistic minister, a long-standing Catenian Association member and a supporter of local charities. He also enjoyed classical music, touring holidays and monthly music nights with friends.

Known as kind and selfless, he was survived by his wife of 64 years, six children and eight grandchildren. His funeral mass was scheduled for July 12 at Saint Mary of the Angels, followed by burial at Durrington Cemetery.

Call to the Pen highlighted the first full week of minor league baseball. Braves right-hander Mike Soroka, 19, opened the season by jumping from low-A Rome to AA and went 2-0 with 11⅔ innings, a 0.77 ERA, 0.43 WHIP, no walks and a 34.15% strikeout rate. Standouts included Kyle Tucker with seven RBI, José Medina with three home runs, Dane Dunning with eight shutout innings and 13 strikeouts, and Josh Staumont with six shutout innings and 12 strikeouts. Visalia and Kane County combined for no-hitters. Leaders included Ian Happ with six home runs, Jorge Mateo with nine stolen bases and Mike Clevinger with 25 strikeouts. The week also featured notable defensive plays and minor league manager Phillip Wellman’s 1,000th managerial win with AA San Antonio.

The passage reports that U.S. stocks have generally performed reasonably during wars and geopolitical conflicts, often with lower volatility than in quieter periods. Initial selloffs, such as the nearly 20% decline after Pearl Harbor and the reaction to Iraq’s 1990 invasion of Kuwait, were temporary. During World War II, the Dow Jones rose more than 60% before the war ended. Researchers studying 1890–2017 associate higher government defense spending with lower stock-market volatility, possibly because military spending supports activity and reduces uncertainty about corporate profitability.

These findings mainly concern wars fought outside the U.S.; conflicts on home soil can cause severe economic and market damage. Germany’s market reopened in 1945 roughly 90% lower, while Russia’s market remained closed following its 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Gold often rises during uncertainty and may also reflect anticipated money printing, making it a long-standing inflation hedge. Oil and other commodities frequently increase when wars disrupt business and supply chains, but commodities have had poor long-term returns compared with stocks.

Nobel Prize-winning biochemist Peter Agre will deliver a free public lecture at 12:30 p.m. May 9 in Gheens Science Hall and Rauch Planetarium. The Johns Hopkins professor and Malaria Research Institute director will discuss science diplomacy, human rights, disease eradication, and international collaboration.

Gold prices edged higher as investors awaited Fed Chair Janet Yellen’s congressional testimony for clues on rate hikes. Spot gold was nearly unchanged at $1,225.06 per ounce, while the dollar was flat and SPDR Gold Trust holdings rose 0.49%. Rising U.S. inflation expectations and Dallas Fed President Robert Kaplan’s call for sooner rate increases reinforced expectations of further hikes; Venezuela’s gold holdings fell 23% in 2016.

The study demonstrates a chirality-selective nanoscale thermal switch formed by combining ferromagnetic [Co/Pt] multilayers with left- or right-handed α-SiO2. Ultrafast demagnetization of the ferromagnet transfers spin angular momentum into lattice-generated chiral phonons whose angular-momentum sign follows the magnetization direction. Time-resolved magneto-optic Kerr effect measurements showed that reversing magnetization changes the apparent thermal conductivity of chiral α-SiO2 by about 0.7 ± 0.1 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, or 7%, while non-chiral amorphous SiO₂ shows negligible dependence. The effect reverses between the two α-SiO₂ handednesses, and the thermal on/off ratio is approximately 1.07 at room temperature and 1.2 at 50 K. Molecular dynamics and first-principles calculations show that heat transfer depends on phonon angular momentum, group velocity, and density of states; efficient transfer occurs when phonon and crystal chirality align. Reduced phonon-phonon scattering at low temperature strengthens the switch. The experiments were supported by DFT-derived machine-learning force fields and classical molecular dynamics, indicating a possible route to electrically insulated spin- and phonon-controlled thermal diodes and switches for nanoscale heat management.

Local college students received honors for academic achievement, leadership, research and service. At Misericordia, Molly Noon was inducted into Pi Theta Epsilon, earned dean’s list honors every semester and participated in campus clubs and projects. Immaculata’s Abigail Kauffman received the senior leadership award.

Three Geisinger CMS 2017 graduates received residency assignments in obstetrics-gynecology, pediatrics and psychiatry. At King’s College, Hayley Hammer entered Psi Chi, Lyle Luckenbill was elected student government treasurer, and Molly McMullen completed a marketing and communications internship while holding several campus roles. Kutztown’s Gregory Schuettler was inducted into Alpha Epsilon Lambda. At Susquehanna, Ashley Machamer presented research at the Eastern Psychological Association meeting, and Kelsey Miller was selected Kappa Delta president. University of Sciences occupational therapy master’s student Shelby Weikel participated in the 2017 pinning ceremony.

Wilkes students Rachael Krell and Shana Noon completed alternative spring breaks. Krell worked on trail and infrastructure cleanup and animal rehabilitation in Costa Rica; Noon taught English in the Dominican Republic. The trips combine community service with cultural experiences and leadership, teamwork and critical-thinking development.

The Debrief, a digital media site launched in 2014 for women in their twenties, is closing after stating it could not “see a viable future,” despite recent British Media Awards success. Many writers are likely to move to Grazia. The site investigated contraceptive-related mental health and campaigned on letting agency fees; readers reacted with heartbroken messages.

Successful school-based mental health programs share strong school-family-community partnerships, keep existing school staff central, and encourage teachers to identify concerns, make referrals, and connect with mental health providers. Programs must also be visible, integrated into school culture, and adapted to local needs.

Minnesota’s nationally recognized model employs community-based clinicians in schools, funds their broader school work through insurance and state support, and gives them protected time to collaborate with teachers. The approach grew through local leadership and bipartisan legislative support; most public-school students now have access to care.

Baltimore’s program reflects this model. To address low referral follow-up and barriers such as transportation, childcare, and stigma, the University of Maryland helped expand mental health services in school-based health centers using credentialed community providers. Providers actively publicize their availability through classroom presentations, social media, events, and direct outreach, helping students and families recognize them as part of the school community.

The model originated in Maryland in the late 1980s and has been adapted in states including Colorado, Wisconsin, and Minnesota. Its central principle is bringing care into schools, where clinicians can work closely with educators, families, and students while reducing access barriers and stigma.

Entering Week 5 of the 2025 NFL season, the Steelers are alone atop the AFC North after its only Week 4 win. The Bengals, Ravens and Browns are struggling or depleted, giving Pittsburgh the strongest position despite its bye. Detroit hosts Cincinnati, while Minnesota hosts Cleveland.

A federal class-action lawsuit alleges the U.S. Army issued less-than-honorable discharges to potentially thousands of veterans without properly considering PTSD and other mental-health conditions. Filed by two Connecticut veterans and Yale’s Veterans Legal Services Clinic, it challenges inconsistent review-board practices and denial of benefits reserved for honorably discharged veterans.

Business Insider summarizes The Economist's "Carrie Bradshaw index," ranking 10 best and 10 worst US cities for living alone by studio affordability. The index divides each city's median wages by the salary needed to keep studio rent under 30% of gross income; 59 cities scored above one, meaning most people can afford a studio, down from 62 last year. Data came from the Bureau of Labour Statistics and Zumper. Coastal cities ranked least affordable, and New York remained most unaffordable for a third year.

A review praises Jaime Smith’s how-to book for prospective college transfer students as clearly written, logically organized, and useful, especially for community college students seeking vertical transfer. It recommends retaining course syllabi and textbook details, choosing a W over an F when necessary, prioritizing institutional fit over prestige, considering housing and living costs, and recognizing that admission to a major may have separate requirements. The reviewer advises consulting local transfer counselors about articulation agreements, credit limits, scholarships, and destination-specific course requirements, which websites may not explain fully. The main criticism is Smith’s vague treatment of completing an associate degree, despite many statewide agreements requiring it and the degree’s potential to prevent credit loss and protect transfer progress. Overall, the book is considered accessible and practical aside from this issue.

This study analyzed cross-sectional data from four Rakai Community Cohort Survey rounds conducted between 2013 and 2020 to assess early sex resumption (ESR), defined as resuming sex within 42 days of voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC), among circumcised men aged 15–49 in Rakai, Uganda.

ESR prevalence declined substantially over the study period, from 45.1% in 2013–2015 to 21.8% in 2015–2016, approximately 21% in 2016–2018, and 14.9% in 2018–2020. In the pooled adjusted analysis, ESR was more common among currently married men (aPR 2.01), previously married men (aPR 1.41), men reporting multiple sexual partners (aPR 1.36), and men whose highest education was primary level (aPR 1.29). Men aged 25–34 and 35–44 also had higher adjusted prevalence than those aged 15–19. HIV status and occupation were not associated with ESR across all survey rounds.

The authors noted that the decline may be related to strengthened post-circumcision counseling beginning in 2016, but stated that ESR remained above the recommended WHO target and posed risks of complications and HIV acquisition or transmission. They recommended involving wives in counseling, targeting older men and men with multiple partners, and providing focused education to men with less education. Limitations included reliance on self-reported sexual resumption, likely underreporting due to social desirability, and inability to determine whether participants were HIV-positive when receiving VMMC.

The author projects net-income growth of 2.5%–6.2% annually through 2023 and concludes that the market has overreacted to CVS’s 2016 setbacks.

This preprint reports a Phase 1/2, outpatient, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-subject crossover human laboratory study (Brown University, 2014–2021; NCT02243709) translating preclinical findings on mifepristone, a glucocorticoid receptor antagonist. Prior work showed mifepristone reduced yohimbine-induced reinstatement of alcohol-seeking in alcohol-dependent Long Evans and Wistar rats, while being less efficacious in genetically selected msP rats; mifepristone is FDA-approved for Cushing syndrome–related hyperglycemia and early pregnancy termination.

**Design:** 32 randomized individuals with AUD, not seeking treatment, received 7 days of oral mifepristone 600 mg/day or placebo, followed by a 3-week washout and crossover. Laboratory procedures paired oral yohimbine (32.4 mg) with cue-reactivity, a priming alcohol dose, and open-bar self-administration. Primary outcome was safety/tolerability; secondary outcomes were craving (ACQ-SF-R), urge (AUQ), cue-elicited salivary output, and alcohol consumption. Cortisol was tested as mediator and family history density of alcoholism (FHDA, median-split) as moderator.

**Results:** No serious adverse events occurred; three non-serious AEs occurred, all on placebo (10% vs 0% on mifepristone). Diastolic blood pressure was lower with mifepristone; mifepristone did not alter alcohol pharmacokinetics or subjective stimulation/sedation. Mifepristone reduced cue-elicited salivary output in both alcohol trials, and reduced craving and urge at alcohol trial 1. Cortisol was higher with mifepristone (supporting compliance and HPA activation), but cortisol did not mediate craving, urge, or salivation. FHDA moderated outcomes: high-FHDA participants had greater craving, urge, and salivation; mifepristone reduced craving and urge only in the low-FHDA group, while reducing salivary output in both groups. Alcohol consumption in the laboratory and outpatient settings did not differ between conditions.

**Conclusions:** Mifepristone with yohimbine and alcohol was safe and attenuated stress/cue-induced alcohol craving independently of cortisol increases, with effects limited to low-FHDA individuals. Limitations included no yohimbine placebo control, no mifepristone blood levels, few females, and potential placebo effects; higher-dose studies are proposed. Funding: NIAAA; study drug provided by Corcept Therapeutics, which had no role in the study.

Ronald E. Gabler was convicted of aggravated assault after a jury found that he followed his estranged wife to Thomas R. Duff’s home, assaulted Duff with his fists, and kicked and strangled him, causing hospitalization. The trial court denied his motion for a new trial.

On appeal, Gabler claimed ineffective assistance of counsel because trial counsel did not investigate Duff’s medical records or physicians and did not object to testimony that Gabler had previously beaten his wife. Applying Strickland v. Washington, the court found no deficient performance or resulting prejudice. Counsel’s decision not to pursue medical evidence was reasonable trial strategy, the records contained damaging information, and ample evidence supported the conviction. Gabler’s own character evidence also placed his character at issue, and the record showed no prejudice. The judgment was affirmed.

The lecture moves beyond tree-level QED diagrams to loop corrections. Tree-level diagrams contain no loops, and their internal momenta are fixed by external momenta, so no momentum integration is required. Loops introduce unconstrained internal momenta that must be integrated over and can be interpreted as quantum fluctuations of the vacuum involving virtual particles.

These integrations generally produce divergences. The divergences arise from extrapolating QED to arbitrarily high energies and arbitrarily short distances, beyond experimentally accessible scales, rather than from perturbative expansion itself. Because these divergences involve complicated expressions, they cannot be removed by the simple subtractions or cancellations used for divergent quantities at tree level. A cutoff could restrict calculations to accessible energies, but no justified cutoff scale was known.

In the late 1940s, Schwinger, Feynman, and Tomonaga developed methods that nevertheless produced physically meaningful results by removing loop divergences, a program known as renormalization. Dyson subsequently simplified and spread these techniques, while Wilson’s later renormalization-group work supplied a deeper physical understanding.

Loop calculations also show that Lagrangian parameters are not generally identical to measurable quantities. The bare mass, charge, electron field, and photon field must be related nontrivially to the physical mass, charge, and fields because interactions alter propagation and particle creation. This parameter adjustment is a second sense of “renormalization,” distinct from removing divergences.

Three basic one-loop processes are discussed. Electron self-energy corrections shift the electron’s physical mass from its bare value and introduce a field-renormalization factor. Photon vacuum-polarization corrections do not generate a photon mass, thereby preserving gauge symmetry, but they do renormalize the photon field. Vertex corrections renormalize the electric charge and generate an anomalous magnetic moment. The opposite renormalization of bare charge and photon field ensures that \(e_B A_B^\mu=eA^\mu\), preserving the structure required by gauge invariance.

The lecture also derives the electron’s tree-level \(g=2\) magnetic moment by taking the nonrelativistic limit of the Dirac equation coupled to the electromagnetic field. The resulting Pauli term contains a spin coupling to the magnetic field with \(g=2\). Schwinger calculated the first loop correction to this value in 1948, obtaining a correction of \(\alpha/(2\pi)\) to the electron anomalous magnetic moment. Its agreement with experiment was an early triumph of renormalization and QED.

Higher-order corrections were computed using increasingly large numbers of diagrams: seven at the next order, 72 at a further order, and 891 for another proposed QED calculation. The anomalous magnetic moment can be measured experimentally with precision around \(10^{-12}\), enabling extremely stringent tests of QED. Despite differences between theory and measurement precision, their very close agreement demonstrates that QED describes nature extremely well.

RNA sequencing of 38 granulomatous myositis (GM) muscle biopsies, compared with other inflammatory myopathies, disease controls, and healthy controls, identified a distinct GM transcriptomic profile. GM showed prominent IFN-γ signaling, elevated immune-cell markers—especially macrophages, CD4 T cells, B cells, and plasma cells—increased HLA class II expression, and reduced muscle-fiber, structural, and mitochondrial markers. Proinflammatory pathways involving IL1B, TNF, TGFB1, additional interleukins, chemokines, TNF-family molecules, and their receptors were also upregulated.

Intersection analysis identified 1,293 genes specifically upregulated and 256 specifically downregulated in GM. The upregulated genes were predominantly associated with highly active macrophages within granulomas, and they correlated strongly with transcriptomic markers of disease activity. Spatial transcriptomics localized key signals, including CD4 T cells, immunoglobulin-producing plasma cells, IFN-γ activity, IL1B, TNF, and TGFB1, to non-caseating granulomas. CHIT1 was the most significantly upregulated gene and showed increased protein expression in granulomas and giant cells.

Machine-learning models based on the GM-specific gene sets performed strongly; support vector machine classification achieved a 99.6% AUC and 98.6% accuracy with cross-validation. The findings support potential transcriptomic approaches for GM diagnosis and disease-activity monitoring. GM pathways overlap with those affected in sarcoidosis, suggesting possible therapeutic relevance that requires further study. Limitations include the exclusion of infectious or genetic granulomatous muscle diseases and RNA-only validation of markers other than CHIT1.

This medRxiv preprint compared REM sleep microstructure in 20 patients with isolated REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD), 20 patients with Parkinson’s disease and RBD (PD+RBD), and 20 controls using video-polysomnography. iRBD patients had a higher phasic REM sleep ratio than controls and PD+RBD patients. PD+RBD patients showed reduced REM sleep duration and proportion, longer REM latency, shorter REM bouts, and lower sawtooth-wave (STW) density and duration than the other groups. Both patient groups had altered STW spectral profiles, with a reduced predominance of lower frequencies and a shift toward higher frequencies. NREM-to-REM transition duration increased progressively from controls (119 seconds) to iRBD (212 seconds) to PD+RBD (376 seconds). Atonia onset usually preceded STW and rapid eye movements in controls, whereas STW usually occurred first in the patient groups. The authors concluded that RBD-related REM abnormalities extend beyond loss of muscle atonia and dream enactment. Limitations included small samples, no Parkinson’s disease group without RBD, medication effects, cohort heterogeneity, limited EEG channels, and the laborious manual analysis of STW. Longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether these markers predict phenoconversion.

The lecture reviews methods for controlling the double-integrator system \(\ddot q=u\). Linear feedback \(u=-Kx\), designed through pole placement or root-locus analysis, reshapes the system’s phase portrait toward the origin. With bounded control, minimum-time optimization produces a nonlinear bang-bang policy with switching surfaces: the control switches between extreme values and follows the switching surface to the goal.

The minimum-time problem minimizes the elapsed time subject to the system dynamics, control bounds, and the requirement that the final state be the origin. Pontryagin’s minimum principle is presented as a constrained-optimization method using an augmented cost, Lagrange multipliers, and stationarity conditions along trajectories. The bounded-control constraint is handled by restricting admissible variations to the allowed control range.

Dynamic programming is then developed first for discrete-time systems with additive costs. The policy cost and optimal cost satisfy recursive equations based on the principle of optimality: at each state, the optimal action minimizes the immediate cost plus the optimal future cost. Backward recursion therefore yields an optimal policy.

Taking the continuous-time limit of this recursion and using a Taylor expansion produces the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation:
\[
0=\min_u\left[g(x,u)+\nabla_xJ^\ast(x,t)^\top f(x,u)+\partial_tJ^\ast(x,t)\right].
\]
Here, \(J^\ast(x,t)\) is the cost-to-go function, or cost landscape. A sufficiency theorem states that a policy minimizing the HJB expression is optimal.

For linear dynamics \(x=Ax+Bu\) with quadratic cost
\[
\int_0^T(x^\top Qx+u^\top Ru)\,dt,
\]
the HJB equation leads to a quadratic value function \(J^\ast(x,t)=x^\top S(t)x\). The minimizing control is linear,
\[
u^\ast=-R^{-1}B^\top S(t)x,
\]
and \(S(t)\) satisfies the Riccati differential equation with terminal condition \(S(T)=Q_f\). For an infinite horizon, the solution approaches a steady state, yielding a time-invariant linear feedback controller; MATLAB’s `lqr` computes this solution.

Applied to \(\ddot q=u\) with \(Q=I\) and \(R=1\), the infinite-horizon solution has
\[
S=\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt2&1\\1&\sqrt2\end{bmatrix},
\]
and the resulting closed-loop response converges to the origin while oscillating.

The lecture contrasts the two analytical methods. Pontryagin’s principle gives necessary local conditions along trajectories and can handle nonsmooth bang-bang solutions; the HJB sufficiency theorem is stronger but requires a differentiable value function. LQR is particularly useful for complex linear systems and linearizations, including airplane landing and inverted-pendulum stabilization. For nonlinear systems, most of these analytical tools no longer apply directly, motivating later algorithmic approaches based on Pontryagin’s principle and dynamic programming.

**Summary**

A hedge fund is an investment pool funded by a limited number of private investors and run by a professional manager to maximize returns and minimize risk. It usually requires a high minimum investment or net worth, so it is aimed at accredited investors and institutions. Hedge funds trade relatively liquid assets and use complex techniques — short selling, leverage, derivatives — distinguishing them from mutual funds and ETFs. Unlike private equity funds, they are generally open-ended, allowing periodic investment and withdrawal based on net asset value. Their aim is to hold both long and short positions so they can profit regardless of market direction.

Most hedge funds use quantified (systematic) or discretionary strategies, or a mix; some are diversified across strategies and managers, while others concentrate. Niche strategies focus on small markets such as real estate (housing, hotels, commercial properties), insurance-linked instruments (life/longevity, natural catastrophes, industry loss, with little correlation to capital markets), and cryptocurrency (buy and hold, ICOs, shorting, futures, relative value). Two examples given are long/short equity, buying undervalued and shorting overvalued stocks, and merger arbitrage, taking opposing positions in two merging companies (e.g., buying at $25 and selling at $30 after a merger for about $5 per share).

The article advises retail traders to think like a "one-man hedge fund": treat trading professionally, keep plans and a trade journal, hold a sizable account, and invest rather than trade if capital is too small for meaningful diversification. It stresses that complementary, low-correlation strategies matter more than individual performance; uncorrelated "mediocre" strategies add value. A chart comparing Brummer & Partners' multi-strategy fund with the MSCI World Index illustrates that a smoother return path is preferred over higher returns with heavy drawdowns. The blog, operating since 2012, offers a compilation of over 160 strategies with plain-English logic.

FAQs note that common strategies include long/short equity, event-driven, global macro, relative value and fixed income arbitrage; advantages include potential higher returns, diversification, professional managers and unique investments; minimum investments typically run $100,000–$500,000; hedge funds are private, for accredited investors only, more aggressive and higher-fee than mutual funds; risks include liquidity, leverage, counterparty and strategy-failure risk; performance is reported quarterly; and tax implications exist, so investors should consult a tax advisor.

Enron also faced lawsuits, document-preservation orders, restructuring issues, and scrutiny of reported losses and accounting practices. Congressional and SEC officials proposed possible reforms to derivatives regulation, accounting oversight, and investor protections.

Canadian researchers combined two university studies involving 145 and 314 students, linking facial width-to-height ratio with sex drive and attitudes toward infidelity. Men with wider, shorter faces were perceived as having greater sex drives and a greater propensity for infidelity, while both men and women with high ratios tended to take relationship bonds less seriously. However, the studies found only a correlation, drew on a small, unusual sample of young students living away from home, and do not establish that facial shape causes unfaithfulness.

Femtosecond laser irradiation was used to create laser-induced periodic surface structures (LIPSS) in approximately 190-nm-thick niobium films. By varying the 343-nm laser pulse energy, the study followed surface evolution from slight roughness through homogeneous ripples with a periodicity of 260 ± 5 nm to film perforation. SEM, TEM, XRD, resistivity, SQUID magnetometry, magneto-optical imaging, and time-dependent Ginzburg–Landau simulations were used to characterize the resulting microstructure and superconducting behavior.

Progressive LIPSS formation reduced film thickness, increased grain size near ripple peaks, and decreased the Nb lattice parameter by approximately 1.05% for fully patterned films. These changes were accompanied by moderate, orientation-independent reductions in intrinsic superconducting properties: the critical temperature fell from 8.93 to 8.53 K, while the upper-critical-field curve shifted downward by about 50 mT.

Laser patterning strongly altered flux pinning and made critical current density anisotropic. Transport and magneto-optical measurements showed that current flowing along the ripples generally supported a higher critical current than current flowing across them, with anisotropy tending toward isotropy as the applied field approached the upper critical field. Optimally treated films exhibited higher critical current densities than pristine films around 6–8 K and below approximately 100 mT, whereas pinning was often reduced under other conditions. Simulations indicated that thickness undulations promote vortex localization in grooves and can increase the critical current along the channels by roughly a factor of two, with a nonmonotonic field dependence associated with transitions from collective vortex motion to individual vortex hopping.

The study introduces PHIVE, an unsupervised, physics-informed variational deep-learning framework for rapid spectral fitting and metabolite quantification in high-resolution whole-brain MRSI. A convolutional encoder maps input spectra to a low-dimensional probabilistic latent space, while a physics-informed decoder reconstructs signals using amplitude, frequency, phase, damping, and a spline baseline. The variational model supports uncertainty estimation, and an ensemble of five independently trained PHIVE models separates aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty; CRLB maps are also generated. A conditional baseline allows different baseline stiffness levels and knot counts to be evaluated with one network.

The experiments used 7T MRSI data from 12 healthy volunteers: eight subjects for training (122,473 spectra) and four for testing (39,051 spectra). Compared with LCModel, PHIVE processed a whole-brain dataset in 6 milliseconds rather than approximately two hours, a six-order-of-magnitude reduction. PHIVE produced metabolite maps broadly similar to LCModel and strong positive correlations across six metabolite ratios, with reported maximum R² values of 0.86 for Glx/tCr and 0.70 for tNAA/tCr. It generally achieved lower coefficients of variation, particularly for Glx and mIns. PHIVE estimated significantly higher mIns concentrations than LCModel, while differences for tNAA, Glx, tCho, Tau, and GSH were not statistically significant. Fits remained coherent at low SNR, although residuals increased, and uncertainty was greatest in low-SNR peripheral and ventricular regions.

Limitations include the absence of a true in vivo ground standard, the small cohort, no dedicated frequency-correction preprocessing, weaker agreement for tCho and mIns, limited interpretability, and no longitudinal validation. The optimal baseline stiffness also remains unresolved. The work is presented as a medRxiv preprint that has not been peer reviewed.
