A February 6, 2002 Enron public-relations email compiled news reports and commentary on the company’s collapse, congressional investigations, off-balance-sheet partnerships, financing difficulties and related legal and financial issues.

Rep. Billy Tauzin expected former CEO Jeffrey Skilling to testify before the House Energy and Commerce Committee on Thursday, with questions focused on an internal report calling Enron’s financial deals “very suspicious,” Skilling’s response to internal warnings and his failure to sign approval sheets for questionable transactions. Former CFO Andrew Fastow was also scheduled to testify. The Senate Commerce Committee and House Financial Services Committee subpoenaed former chairman and CEO Kenneth Lay after he canceled a voluntary Senate appearance; the House set his hearing for February 14, and lawmakers predicted he might invoke the Fifth Amendment. Labor Secretary Elaine Chao was scheduled to discuss retirement-account protections, while the Justice Department, Securities and Exchange Commission and numerous congressional panels investigated Enron. The Justice Department rejected calls for a special prosecutor, while President Bush said any wrongdoing would be pursued.

William Powers, the Enron director who led the board’s internal investigation, testified that key executives knew the partnerships hid liabilities and losses, used Enron assets to enrich themselves and failed to enforce controls. He declined to characterize the conduct as fraud, but said Enron knew in March 2001 that partnerships were causing a $500 million loss and subsequently gave Raptor another $800 million in Enron shares. He testified that the partnerships inflated earnings by $1 billion from the third quarter of 2000 through the third quarter of 2001 and that more than 70 percent of earnings during that period were false.

Powers said Lay had clear warning signs, while Skilling knew about significant Raptor transactions, attended a board meeting approving them and failed to respond to concerns and requests that he formally approve the deals. Fastow, who managed and invested in the LJM partnerships and received about $30 million over two years, could not independently oversee them. Powers also said former executive Michael Kopper made at least $10 million from an unauthorized investment and that documents related to Raptor stock swaps were backdated. Committee investigators said some employees were threatened with dismissal or loss of bonuses for challenging the partnerships.

Arthur Andersen chairman Joseph Berardino testified that his firm did not cause Enron to fail and that information had been withheld from its auditors. The internal investigation found that Andersen actively participated in establishing partnerships and received $5.7 million for related advice. Lawmakers sharply criticized Andersen and its handling of document destruction; Enron lead auditor David Duncan was fired and accused of organizing the destruction of Enron documents.

Hearings also examined the retirement losses of employees and investors. One former employee testified that she lost $40,000, while lawmakers reviewed a roughly three-week lockout on Enron stock in employee retirement accounts during a period of falling share prices. Sherron Watkins had warned Lay that Enron might “implode in a wave of accounting scandals,” prompting the internal review. Fastow was also discussing possible immunity with Justice Department officials, and articles portrayed him as a central figure in the partnerships and an increasing target of investigators.

Enron’s debtor-in-possession financing was reduced from an expected $1.5 billion to between $250 million and $500 million as banks resisted syndicating the loan. A final hearing was postponed until March 6, although Enron cited stronger-than-expected cash and a possible sale of Wessex Water for up to $1.2 billion. Pending sales also included Enron’s energy-trading business to UBS Warburg.

In other corporate matters, Enron Broadband Services owed about $440,000 in back taxes, and Spain’s energy regulator planned to investigate Enron’s Spanish distribution operations. The Houston Astros sought to terminate the 30-year, $100 million naming-rights agreement that created “Enron Field”; Enron said the contract remained valuable and planned to challenge the team’s motion.

Commentary linked Enron to wider investor distrust of creative accounting, with corporate bond spreads widening as investors searched for other companies burdened by hidden liabilities and accounting concerns. Other articles discussed conflicts of interest among auditors and advisers, the possible career consequences of whistleblowers, and the broader effects of Enron on employee trust and corporate reporting. Satirical commentary mocked Enron’s financial structures, Wall Street analysts, Kenneth Lay and the political fallout from the scandal.

The study examined whether role-taking and literacy interventions could reduce reliance on demographic and appearance cues in social-engineering decisions. An online 4×2 mixed factorial experiment recruited 139 adults from Arab countries or with Middle Eastern ethnicity and Arabic as their first language. Participants were assigned to role-taking groups acting as persuaders or persuadees, a literacy group receiving educational material, or a control group.

Before and one week after the intervention, participants evaluated 16 personas representing age, gender, ethnic similarity, and formal or casual attire in a scenario involving a stranger’s mobile hotspot. Role-taking participants completed three scenario-based sessions involving financial advisors and letting agents, while literacy participants completed two sessions challenging stereotypes. Outcomes included trust, willingness to accept the hotspot, word of mouth, and issue involvement. Fifteen repeated-measures ANOVA models, supported by Bayes factors, tested pre-to-post changes.

Neither intervention significantly altered trust or risk-taking across persona characteristics, and word-of-mouth responses also remained stable. Bayes factors generally supported the absence of an intervention effect. Issue involvement decreased significantly overall, although post-hoc comparisons did not identify a specific group as responsible. Adjusting for self-esteem, self-efficacy, and age produced one significant interaction involving self-esteem and attire-related trust, but otherwise no significant effects.

Participants described the intervention as engaging, informative, and thought-provoking, and some reported reconsidering everyday decisions. However, the study found no measurable behavioral debiasing. Limitations included hypothetical scenarios, possible social-desirability and demand effects, static comic-based simulations, and the intervention’s short duration. The authors recommend longer-term, more immersive approaches, including gamified or virtual-reality simulations, to address entrenched biases.

The passage frames the “Berlin-Bagdad” problem as Germany’s effort to organize Central Europe under its political and military influence, with the Poles, Czechs, South Slavs, and Bulgaria as key political issues. U.S. policy should oppose not economic or cultural unification, but the use of that unity by imperialistic groups in Berlin, Vienna, and Budapest to advance selfish foreign policy. The existing order is sustained by shared domination of subject peoples, German control of Austria-Hungary, German-Magyar ascendancy, Bulgaria’s grievance-based alliance, Turkey’s reliance on Germany for nominal imperial integrity, and postwar debts to Germany.

Economic exclusion of Germany from raw materials, markets, and communication routes is identified as the strongest U.S. weapon, useful for bargaining, threats, and inducements after the peace conference. In Austria-Hungary, Czech and South Slav nationalism—and the possible re-emergence of Poland—could weaken the German-Austrian coalition. The proposed strategy is to stir nationalist unrest while rejecting demands to dismember Austria-Hungary, thereby encouraging its rulers to seek security through a league of nations and greater foreign-policy independence from Berlin.

Texas’s HB 8 will replace STAAR with three shorter tests at the beginning, middle and end of the school year, beginning in 2027-28. Schools may select from TEA-approved national assessments for the first two tests, while the agency will develop the third. The law bans practice and benchmark tests, requires scores within about two days and directs the TEA to study how testing could carry less weight in school accountability ratings.

Supporters say the changes will reduce testing time and preparation, allow schools to monitor progress throughout the year and make first and second tests part of instruction. Critics worry that three exams will increase stress, particularly if all follow STAAR’s security and scheduling protocols. They also note that the end-of-year test will continue to dominate accountability ratings because a new progress metric will not be ready when the system launches. An accountability report is due in 2029-30, but implementing its findings is not required.

Parents and educators also want less restrictive testing-day procedures and greater teacher input in developing the final exam. Some districts already use the less stressful, adaptive MAP assessment three times annually.

The passage introduces LAPIS, an extensible, performance-portable compiler framework for computational science and engineering (CSE) and AI/ML, built on the MLIR infrastructure within LLVM.

Motivation. Traditional HPC codes rely on C++/Fortran with programming models such as MPI, OpenMP and OpenACC and frameworks such as Kokkos, Legion and RAJA, with libraries (Kokkos Kernels, Ginkgo, Trilinos, PETSc) providing abstraction layers for sparse/dense and distributed-memory linear algebra. Widely used frameworks like Kokkos emphasize performance and portability over productivity. AI/ML frameworks such as PyTorch, JAX and TensorFlow emphasize productivity and portability but require manual interfacing to optimized libraries such as cuBLAS/rocBLAS; extending them to new architectures is tedious, producing a "hardware/software lottery" that narrows co-evolution of algorithms, libraries and hardware. Physics-informed AI/ML is increasingly applied to demanding simulations (biology, mechanics, DFT, molecular dynamics, chemistry), yet large-scale simulations are written in C++ while ML surrogates are built in Python, requiring significant boilerplate to interoperate. The authors hypothesize that an extensible compiler framework supporting performance, portability and productivity can bridge these gaps, and they address two challenges: such a compiler framework, and interfacing CSE code with Python-based ML code at near-native C++ performance.

Approach. Rather than calling low-level ML framework functions from C++, developers write ML-related functions in Python and LAPIS compiles them automatically to Kokkos-based C++ source that integrates directly into scientific applications.

Contributions. LAPIS provides (i) a custom Kokkos dialect using portable execution and memory abstractions, with range_parallel, team_parallel and thread_parallel operations plus attributes for nesting levels, and single/team_barrier synchronization operations, and Kokkos Kernels operations such as gemm and gemv; (ii) mapping of Kokkos Kernels linear algebra to sparse and dense tensors; (iii) lowering passes, including linalg-to-kokkoskernels, dense-linalg-to-parallel-loops, kokkos-loop-mapping and kokkos-dualview-management; (iv) a Kokkos-inspired memory model with DualView support; and (v) a Kokkos emitter that raises mid-level IR directly to parallel C++ source. Inputs conform to the linalg-on-tensors dialects, with torch-mlir and MPACT frontends.

Mapping details. Loop nesting depth determines the Kokkos form: one level uses range_parallel, two levels use thread_parallel with an inner ThreadVector range_parallel, and three or more use team_parallel with TeamThread- and ThreadVector-level ranges, keeping the innermost loop parallel for GPU memory coalescing. Parallelism is estimated from iteration bounds, e.g., for CSR/CSC traversal the average entries per row ⌈k/N⌉, with vector lengths clamped to backend limits (warp size 32 on CUDA) and defaults of 0 when no hint exists. Side-effecting operations are wrapped in single, and team_barrier is inserted after non-reduction TeamThread loops.

Results. LAPIS lowers one sparse and two dense linear algebra operations and couples CSE and AI/ML use cases (SciML and image processing), matching hand-optimized performance on AMD MI300A and NVIDIA H100 GPUs and Intel Granite Rapids CPUs. Related work (TACO, COMET, MPACT, Triton, DaCe, DISTAL, SpDistal, LegateSparse) is described as generally lacking performance portability or requiring substantial compiler developer effort for new accelerators.

The paper proves that strong pseudorandom unitaries exist in the quantum Haar random oracle model (QHROM), where parties access Haar-random unitaries and their inverses. Its construction is
\(G_U(1^\lambda,k)=X_{k_3}UX_{k_2}UX_{k_1}\),
using a key \(k=k_1\|k_2\|k_3\) of three \(\lambda\)-bit strings. It makes only two oracle queries and samples \(O(\log^{1+\epsilon}(n))\) random bits, while remaining secure against polynomial-query adversaries with forward and inverse access.

The security proof builds on the Ma–Huang path-recording framework. Haar-random oracles are replaced by path-recording isometries, followed by modified operators with independent left and right databases. A query-by-query analysis establishes that an approximate isometry \(S\), which merges two databases and simulates the keys, closely maps the real experiment to two independent Haar-random oracles. The proof uses hybrid arguments, Haar-measure invariance, operator-norm bounds, and negligible statistical distance.

The paper situates this result among prior work on pseudorandom states and unitaries, QHROM and inverseless QHROM constructions, and related idealized quantum models.

Chipotle’s Sept. 12 queso launch drew complaints over its $2.95 price, $3.95 small and $6.25 large orders, and perceived taste. Despite criticism, 63% of test-market tasters said it would encourage more visits, and the company has no plans to lower the price because it uses whole ingredients.

The State Bar of Michigan e-Journal for May 23, 2001, provides case summaries across bankruptcy, civil rights, constitutional law, criminal law, employment and labor law, family law, insurance, litigation, municipal law, negligence and intentional tort, and real property. It also includes editorial and event information, field-of-practice attorney listings, classified advertisements, news and moves, archived issues, and subscriber contacts.

In *In re Hood*, the Sixth Circuit held that Tennessee Student Assistance Corporation was not immune from a student’s educational-loan dischargeability action because states ceded sovereignty over bankruptcy discharge; the bankruptcy court’s denial of TSAC’s motion to dismiss was affirmed. In *Thakur v. Department of Corrections*, the court found no proof that the Department gave a false, nondiscriminatory reason for not interviewing the plaintiff and that statistical racial evidence did not establish disparate impact; summary disposition for the defendants was affirmed.

The criminal cases included *Bridgewater*, where failure to give a negligent-homicide instruction was waived and convictions were affirmed; *Byars*, where dismissal with prejudice for a discovery violation was reversed because a continuance could have remedied any prejudice; *Ferguson*, where the defendant did not establish ineffective assistance concerning his decision not to testify; *Knott*, where routine videotape destruction did not justify dismissal; *Minge*, where facts supporting suspected drug activity justified the vehicle stop; and *Williams*, where an informed waiver of joint representation foreclosed an ineffective-assistance claim. *Slawick v. Detroit Newspaper Agency* involved a former employee’s defamation claim, which was not preempted by federal labor law, and the court upheld findings of actual malice and damages of $106,000.

Three parental-rights cases were affirmed: *In re Guy*, *In re Jones*, and *In re Pittao*. In *Van Reken*, the court held that an ordinary loss-payable clause limited vendors’ rights to those of insured land-contract purchasers, requiring reversal for summary disposition for the insurer. In *Moton*, the court upheld the striking of a supplemental witness list. In *Domine*, it held that the circuit court erred in overturning a zoning board’s denial of a variance and reinstated that decision.

In *Berry*, the fireman’s rule barred the police officer’s negligence claim; in *Garrison*, no evidence showed the hospital was negligent or responsible for the injuries; and in *Girard*, the ladder danger was open and obvious because the plaintiff knew of its defective condition. All three decisions were affirmed. The issue also advertises legal services, expert witnesses, document destruction, lawsuit financing, office space, employment positions, and typing services.

Peggy Mahoney forwarded an August 25, 2000 Energy Central Deregulation Public Forum update. The new question asks whether policy should encourage natural gas exploration and production on federal lands and the continental shelf. Natural gas supplies 25% of current U.S. electricity generation but is expected to fuel nearly 95% of planned power plants; reduced exploration and drilling restrictions may lead to record winter gas prices. Responses were requested by September 15, 2000.

The previous forum asked whether generators manipulated California’s wholesale market and whether price caps should protect San Diego Gas & Electric customers. Selected responses disagreed: some attributed price spikes to supply shortages, high fuel costs, weather, constrained transmission, market design, or generator withholding and collusion, while others denied manipulation. Opponents of price caps said they would discourage investment, supply development, conservation, and market signals. Supporters favored caps or cost-based regulation, while several respondents recommended adding generation and transmission capacity, encouraging competition and demand response, or re-regulating the market.

The case examines CEMEX’s globalization strategy, particularly its “CEMEX Way” for integrating acquisitions. Under CEO Lorenzo Zambrano, who took office in 1985, CEMEX prepared for international competition as Mexico opened its economy, joined NAFTA and entered GATT. It divested non-core businesses, explored exports, invested in the CEMEXNET satellite communications system, and introduced an Executive Information System that allowed managers to share operating data and enabled virtual factory inspections.

After acquiring Tolteca in 1989, CEMEX became Mexico’s second-largest cement producer and a top-ten global producer. Faced with Holcim’s expansion in Mexico and U.S. trade duties, CEMEX acquired majority stakes in Spanish producers Valenciana and Sanson in 1992 for $1.8 billion, gaining a 28% market share. Spain offered growth opportunities, cultural and linguistic ties, and access to lower-cost capital. Transferring Mexican operating practices to Spain produced annual benefits of $120 million and raised operating margins from 7% to 24%. The acquisition also prompted CEMEX to formalize its post-merger integration process and prompted broader use of petroleum coke as an energy-efficient fuel.

CEMEX subsequently expanded through acquisitions in Venezuela, Colombia, the Caribbean, the Philippines, Indonesia, Egypt, Chile, Costa Rica, and other markets. Its initial attempt to impose Mexican management systems in Colombia caused local talent to leave. Consequently, CEMEX developed the CEMEX Way, combining corporate standards with practices learned from acquired companies. Its guidelines called for managing global knowledge, identifying and disseminating best practices, standardizing processes, implementing information and Internet-based technologies, and fostering innovation.

During integration, multinational functional teams cataloged acquired-company practices, benchmarked them against internal and external practices, and promoted superior practices to enterprise standards. Estimates indicated that 70% of CEMEX’s practices came from earlier acquisitions. The integration period fell from 25 months for the Spanish acquisitions to less than five months for Southdown. Middle managers were central to teaching standardized practices, identifying useful local capabilities, and advocating enterprise-wide changes.

Following CFO Gustavo Caballero’s death in 1996, CEMEX applied its integration process to Mexico itself. Forty employees in ten teams spent two to three months identifying $85 million in savings and reinforced the importance of learning and continuous improvement. CEMEX also developed branded bagged cement for Mexican consumers and used cement trading across Caribbean markets to pool demand and increase plant utilization.

In the late 1990s, CEMEX redefined large markets as regions and shifted acquisition analysis from margins to return on investment. These changes led to the 2000 acquisition of Southdown and the $5.8 billion purchase of UK-based ready-mix leader RMC in 2005. The RMC price included a 39% premium and initially depressed CEMEX’s share price, but the deal expanded CEMEX’s geographic presence and diversified its product mix. Despite RMC’s financial difficulties and decentralized culture, CEMEX delivered more than $200 million in synergy savings within one year and expected more than $380 million in 2007. CEMEX acquired control of Rinker in 2007 for $15.3 billion, becoming one of the world’s largest building-materials suppliers. By 2007, it had 65,000 employees, operations in 50 countries, and $21.7 billion in annual revenue. Its share price then fell sharply in 2008 because of the global downturn, credit crisis, and leverage from the Rinker acquisition.

The appendix describes the heavy building-materials industry as a $63 billion EBITDA market comprising cement, aggregates, ready-mix concrete, concrete products, and distribution. Cement and aggregates had high entry barriers and long payback periods; ready-mix and asphalt had fewer barriers and greater product differentiation. Cement generated the highest return on sales, while ready-mix concrete generated the lowest. Because cement had a low value-to-weight ratio and was expensive to transport long distances, the industry remained highly localized and was not export-driven.

By 2004, the six largest cement companies held 42% of global capacity outside China, up from 9% in 1988. China produced more than 40% of global cement, followed by India at 6% and the United States at nearly 5%. Asia represented 56% of consumption, while developing countries accounted for 69% and were projected to reach 85% by 2020. Cement demand varied with GDP per capita, infrastructure and housing needs, weather, population, and urban density. Developing markets generally purchased bagged cement from individual builders, whereas developed markets were dominated by large construction companies buying bulk cement, making branding, logistics, delivery reliability, and adaptation to local preferences important sources of competitiveness.

Paul Clement is expected to become Swansea manager after Bayern Munich granted him permission to speak to the club. The 44-year-old is the preferred choice to replace Bob Bradley, with a potential deal at the Liberty Stadium and a £30 million transfer budget. Relegation looms for the 19th-placed Swans, but owners Jason Levien and Steve Kaplan are willing to invest.

After the Communist Party, led by Mátyás Rákosi, consolidated its power in Hungary, economic failure and widespread discontent intensified following Stalin’s death. Soviet de-Stalinization, events in Poland, and the dismissal of Rákosi encouraged Hungarian opposition. On 22 October 1956, a student rally led to a manifesto demanding national communism; the following day, violence after Rákosi’s radio speech prompted revolutionary councils across Hungary advocating nationalism, neutrality, and Soviet withdrawal.

The Soviet leadership regarded Hungary as strategically essential and initially attempted political concessions, reinstalling Imre Nagy and replacing Ernő Gero with János Kádár. Soviet tanks entered Budapest on 24 October and withdrew on 29 October, but these actions masked preparations for a larger invasion. Attention was diverted by the Suez crisis, enabling the Soviet Union to mass around 250,000 troops and 2,500 armored vehicles around Budapest.

Hungarian fighters resisted the Soviet assault, which began on 3–4 November, but were gradually defeated. Resistance ended by 30 November. Approximately 25,000 Hungarians and 7,000 Soviet soldiers were killed.

A federal judge dismissed Drake’s defamation lawsuit over Kendrick Lamar’s 2024 song “Not Like Us,” calling the “certified pedophile” lyric hyperbolic, nonactionable opinion expressed during a heated rap battle. The judge also dismissed claims alleging Universal Music Group used a “defamation-for-profit strategy” by promoting the song and arranging Lamar’s 2025 Super Bowl performance. Drake plans to appeal.

Springfield police officer Conrad Lariviere faces disciplinary review for a Facebook comment responding to Heather Heyer’s death at a white nationalist rally in Charlottesville. He apologized, denied racism and said he opposed the protesters’ actions. Police launched an internal investigation, while Mayor Domenic Sarno condemned the comments.

The DAWN-plasma study is a phase 2, randomized, open-label, multicenter trial comparing standard of care (SOC) alone with SOC plus convalescent plasma in hospitalized adults with COVID-19. Participants are allocated 2:1, with the primary objective of assessing clinical efficacy and safety. The primary endpoint is the percentage of patients alive without mechanical ventilation at Day 15. Secondary endpoints include clinical status, time to sustained improvement or discharge, mechanical ventilation or death, thromboembolism, transfusion reactions, antibody-titer correlations, safety, quality of life, adverse events, laboratory data, and vital signs.

Eligible participants are consenting adults with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection and radiographic infiltrates or clinical evidence of pneumonia with SpO₂ ≤94%. Exclusions include mechanical ventilation before randomization, unacceptable safety risks, prior grade 3 allergic reactions to plasma, treatment restrictions precluding intubation, and recent anti-CD20 therapy.

Convalescent plasma is administered in four doses totaling 800–1,000 mL, beginning within 12 hours of randomization. Plasma must have neutralizing antibody titers of at least 1/160. The first two units are followed by two more units 24–36 hours after completion of the initial infusion.

The protocol and consent documentation were approved by independent ethics committees, and the study follows the Declaration of Helsinki and ICH Good Clinical Practice guidelines. Five patients withdrew before intervention and one was a screen failure; all were replaced by six newly randomized participants. No patients were lost to follow-up after intervention.

Williams & Connolly confirmed that hackers used a zero-day attack to access a small number of attorney email accounts. The firm reported no evidence that confidential client data was extracted from other systems, including client-file databases, or that unauthorized traffic continues, and said it blocked the threat actor. It believed the hackers were affiliated with a nation-state actor. A Mandiant warning said Chinese-government-linked hackers targeted firms for information on U.S. national security and international trade.

Digital video-output pins carry eight MSBs of green/Y, blue/Cb, or R/CR data depending on RGB, YUV444, Y/C, or BT.656 mode. BT.656 multiplexes luma/chroma and leaves the blue/Cb pins unused. The passage also defines pin-state abbreviations, operating I/O supply voltage, and internal pullup/pulldown defaults.

Coppin State University, a historically Black university in Maryland, says its Expand Eagle Nation program has increased enrollment and recognition. The program offers in-state tuition to residents of the 41 states and territories without an HBCU, as well as the District of Columbia. Qualifying-state enrollment rose from 81 to 195 in the program’s first year, and 416 of this fall’s 1,000 incoming students came from eligible states. Overall enrollment is up 26%.

Coppin has promoted the program through high school visits, transit and billboard advertising, community-college transfer partnerships, and outreach to college-search organizations. Its in-state annual cost of attendance is $27,410, compared with $34,474 for out-of-state students.

The university has prepared for growth by adding courses and faculty, constructing a dorm set to open next fall, and using six off-campus apartment complexes with resident assistants and campus shuttles. However, some prospective students distrust the tuition offer.

Enrollment growth comes as colleges seek students amid a projected decline in high school graduates, although Maryland projects an 11% increase through 2031. Coppin is also benefiting from renewed interest in HBCUs, lower costs, and the sense of belonging they offer Black students.

The TPS7H500x-SP series comprises fixed-frequency, peak-current-mode PWM controllers for space-grade DC-DC converters. The controllers operate from 4 V to 14 V, support switching frequencies from 100 kHz to 2 MHz, require external gate drivers, and can be used with buck, flyback, forward, active-clamp forward, push-pull, and full-bridge topologies.

Device startup can be controlled through EN using VLDO, an external or PGOOD signal, or a resistor divider that programs the VIN startup threshold. EN hysteresis provides undervoltage shutdown. The recommended UVLO threshold is approximately 75% or less of the input voltage. Each device uses an internal 1.23-V bandgap reference, divided to 0.613 V for the error-amplifier reference, and requires a 470-nF REFCAP capacitor. Output voltage is programmed with a VOUT-to-VSENSE resistor divider, with 1%-or-better resistors recommended. A soft-start capacitor controls the gradual output-voltage ramp; synchronous-rectifier outputs become active when the SS voltage exceeds 1 V.

Switching frequency can be set through three modes. In internal oscillator mode, a required RT resistor sets the frequency, while SYNC outputs a clock at twice the switching frequency. In external synchronization mode, RT is left floating and an external clock at twice the desired switching frequency is applied to SYNC. Primary-secondary mode synchronizes two controllers by feeding the primary controller’s SYNC output to the secondary controller; it supports independent synchronized converters or parallel, interleaved operation with additional shared control connections.

Primary and synchronous-rectifier outputs have roughly 150-mA peak capability, making external gate-drive solutions necessary. OUTB is available on the TPS7H5001-SP and TPS7H5004-SP, while SRB is available only on the TPS7H5001-SP. These secondary outputs require a 50% duty-cycle setting. The TPS7H5003-SP has fixed 50-ns dead time and leading-edge blank time, whereas the other devices allow programmable dead times through PS and SP resistors and programmable leading-edge blank time through LEB. Pulse skipping is used to address minimum-on-time issues at high frequencies.

The DCL pin configures maximum duty cycle: 100% when connected to VLDO, 75% when floating, and 50% when connected to AVSS. The TPS7H5004-SP supports only 50%. Peak-current control senses primary current at CS_ILIM, compares it against COMP/2 with a 150-mV offset, and uses a sense resistor for PWM operation and overcurrent protection. Exceeding the nominal 1.05-V current-sense threshold initiates hiccup operation, which uses the CHICC capacitor to control cycle-by-cycle limiting and restart timing. The FAULT pin supports external fault protection and shuts down operation when its threshold is exceeded. Programmable slope compensation is available through RSC to mitigate subharmonic oscillation. Type 2A or Type 2B frequency compensation may be used, with Type 2A adding CHF for high-frequency noise attenuation. Thermal shutdown stops switching above 175°C and permits restart below 160°C.

A 500-kHz synchronous push-pull design example using the TPS7H5001-SP and GaN FETs targets a 5-V output. Selected values include a 205-kΩ RT resistor, 10-kΩ and 1.4-kΩ feedback resistors, 20.5-kΩ dead-time resistors, a 49.9-kΩ LEB resistor, a 33-nF soft-start capacitor, a 2.5 transformer turns ratio, a 0.47-µH output inductor, a 7.5-Ω current-sense resistor, and a 3.3-nF hiccup capacitor. The design uses approximately 2.3 mF of output capacitance, Type 2A compensation with a 10-kHz crossover, and a 102-kΩ slope-compensation resistor. Cycle-by-cycle limiting is designed to begin near 35 A, providing about 45% margin over the 24.25-A peak inductor current.

Layout guidance emphasizes separating feedback and control traces from magnetics and switching nodes, minimizing switch-node copper and high-frequency loop area, connecting analog and power grounds at one point, using short and wide current traces, placing filtering and bypass capacitors near the relevant pins, and routing high-dv/dt gate-drive traces away from sensitive control signals.

The passage interprets the transfer of government to the Democratic Party as more than an electoral victory, calling instead for national reflection, reform, and restoration. Americans should recognize the nation’s material prosperity, moral strength, and achievements in liberty while confronting waste, industrial exploitation, loss of natural resources, human suffering, and government used for private interests. Necessary reforms include revising the tariff, banking and currency systems, industrial organization, agricultural practices, and resource conservation; improving public health, food safety, and working conditions; and protecting property and individual rights. Reform should proceed from evidence and experience, seeking justice rather than partisan advantage, and should correct social evils without destroying the good already achieved. The new era requires a sober, nonpartisan, morally serious dedication to serving the people, with honest and patriotic citizens called to counsel and support the effort.

Indianapolis Public Schools is seeking feedback on a proposal to close three high schools by the 2018-2019 school year. A task force report cites enrollment declining from 109,000 in 1967 to 30,000, leaving all seven high schools under capacity. Meetings continue through May, with closure recommendations expected in June and a board vote in September.

The paper proposes LG-CD, a language-guided multimodal model for detecting changes between bi-temporal remote sensing images. It addresses limitations of traditional methods, which are affected by seasonal, lighting, and shadow variations, as well as CNN-based methods, which have limited long-range contextual modeling. It also aims to overcome scarce annotations, costly data preparation, and incomplete use of multimodal semantics. LG-CD uses a pre-trained SAM2 encoder to extract multi-scale visual features, refined through lightweight convolutional adapters at each scale. CLIP encodes natural-language prompts into word-level and global semantic embeddings. A Text Fusion Attention module uses multi-head cross-attention, with visual features as queries and word embeddings as key-value pairs, to align textual guidance with visual features and emphasize relevant changing regions. A visual-semantic fusion decoder then combines visual and semantic information through cross-attention to produce change-detection masks. The method is presented to improve semantic understanding, detection accuracy, robustness, and generalization across complex scenes and target types.

After ABC canceled Roseanne Barr’s sitcom over a racist tweet, the White House said it was not defending her comments but accused the media of bias against President Trump. Trump sought an apology from Disney CEO Bob Iger, while Sarah Sanders cited perceived double standards and said Trump was focused on other issues.

At Wednesday’s final mandatory minicamp practice before July training camp, Kyle Shanahan said the offense and defense were closely matched, with the offense edging out the defense; both improved but still had areas to clean up. Shanahan’s father, though not part of his staff, informally watches film and offers ideas, providing a trusted outside perspective. Shanahan described his first-year head coaching workload as moving at “1,000 miles an hour” and planned an extended, work-free family vacation after the season. He called play-action vital to his offense because it can force defenses to stop the run, create bootleg and explosive-play opportunities, reduce pressure on the offensive line and quarterback, and keep defenses honest.

Will Ma outlines postflop poker strategy using hand examples and range-based reasoning. He explains that players in the blinds often check to the preflop aggressor because the raiser’s range is generally stronger, then discusses betting roughly 50%–100% of the pot, increasing the fraction on later streets. A minimum bet after being checked to is generally inferior to checking because it gives the opponent a free opportunity to check-raise.

His “Fundamental Theorem of Poker” is that strong hands should be bet for value, weak hands should be bluffed, and middle-strength hands should generally be checked. He contrasts this with preflop play, where selecting the strongest range of playable hands is preferable to mixing very strong and very weak hands. He advises against bluffing highly connected, same-suit flops, where opponents have many flush and straight possibilities, and against weak continuation bets against many players.

When facing postflop bets, Ma says most hands should be folded to a half-pot bet unless the bet is unusually small. He illustrates folding hands with no pair or draw, weak overcards, poor gutshots, small pairs that failed to improve, and hands vulnerable to flushes or straights. Calls become appropriate with stronger holdings such as bottom or second pair on safer boards, while raising generally requires two pair using both hole cards or better at approximately 40 big blinds or deeper. Position, stack depth, and the opponent’s range are crucial: earlier-position opponents have stronger ranges, and shorter stacks make it more appropriate to commit with top pair or an overpair. Ma also notes that strong but invulnerable hands can sometimes be called as a trap, while hands vulnerable to a flush should usually be raised.

Leading the flop is presented as an advanced, potentially unnecessary strategy. It is most defensible when the board strongly favors the player’s range over the opponent’s, often in shallow pots. Such leads require careful balancing because frequent leading changes how an opponent interprets checks, and both strong and weak hands must be mixed to avoid exploitable patterns.

Ma distinguishes implied odds from reverse implied odds. When calling puts the player all in, only equity matters; he calculates that a weak hand can call a three-big-blind raise if it has enough immediate equity. With deeper stacks, however, the same equity may be insufficient because difficult postflop decisions and substantial money remain in the pot, making weak hands such as 7-2 or ace-2 poor calls. Suited connected hands can justify calling because they play well postflop and can generate additional winnings. Set mining is explained as theoretically attractive when a player is deeply stacked, in position, and can win an opponent’s entire stack by hitting a set, though he notes it has become less effective in practice.

Draws can provide both implied odds and bluffing value. Ma explains that the relevant consideration when bluffing is not merely the bluff’s current strength but how many outs it has against the hands likely to call. Open-ended straight draws and flush draws can therefore support profitable check-raises. By contrast, a bluff with no possibility of improvement is poor because it surrenders the pot whenever called. He further advises analyzing what strong hands the bluff represents and whether the board supports that representation; a missed draw can still make a flop bluff credible when it completes a different draw. A bluff should be abandoned when the turn neither improves its equity nor supports the represented range, especially when the opponent’s range is stronger.

Ma closes by summarizing the lecture’s subjects: continuation betting, respecting the preflop aggressor, value betting and bluffing, hand and flop analysis, when to lead, implied and reverse implied odds, set mining, bluffing with draws, and the two bluffing insights: count outs and consider what your betting range represents.

A July 18, 2001 email compiled news coverage of California’s electricity crisis. California lawmakers considered competing plans to prevent Southern California Edison from bankruptcy, including buying its transmission lines for $2.76 billion or $2.4 billion, relying on large users to repay debt, imposing a ratepayer bailout, or giving the state a five-year option to purchase the lines for about $1.2 billion. Consumer advocates warned that business contributions and future fees could ultimately increase consumer costs.

PG&E sued California for compensation over long-term power contracts seized by Gov. Gray Davis in January. PG&E sought millions in damages, while the state acknowledged it owed compensation but said a judge should determine the contracts’ value amid declining electricity prices. California’s consumer advocate also criticized a proposed $1 billion state purchase of San Diego Gas & Electric’s transmission lines as excessive.

Other reports said the state sold surplus electricity at a loss after cooler weather reduced demand, while daily power costs fell sharply and no blackout occurred for two months. Additional coverage addressed June consumer inflation, Contra Costa County’s $1.7 million energy-efficiency project, solar-power incentives, opposition to a power line crossing Pechanga tribal land, and Duke Energy’s 27 percent quarterly profit increase.

Prof. Cyril Dim describes cervical cancer as a malignant cancer of the cervix, caused in almost all cases by high-risk, sexually transmitted human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly types 16 and 18. Precancerous lesions are usually symptomless and can be detected through Pap smears and treated to prevent invasive cancer. Symptoms may include bleeding after sex, foul-smelling vaginal discharge, abnormal vaginal bleeding and pelvic pain; advanced disease can cause weight loss, weakness, anaemia and loss of bladder or bowel control. Diagnosis requires cervical tissue biopsy and histological confirmation, while imaging may help determine the stage. Treatment depends on stage: early cancer may be cured with surgery or radiotherapy, whereas late-stage cancer is managed with radiotherapy and sometimes chemotherapy to prolong life. HPV vaccination and regular screening are important preventive measures. The absence of structured screening programmes contributes to late presentation and a high disease burden in Nigeria, where about 15,000 new cases and 10,000 deaths are estimated annually. Pregnancy remains possible in early-stage disease when symptoms have not developed.

A federal judge dismissed Spencer Elden’s 2021 lawsuit alleging Nirvana’s 1991 *Nevermind* cover constituted child pornography. Judge Fernando Olguin found that the image of a naked baby floating underwater toward money lacked sexual suggestiveness or intent, comparing it to a family photo of a nude child bathing.
Purity and higher-order moments of m-qubit states underpin Rényi entropies, entanglement and coherence measures, and randomness certification.

The coach said Ottawa has a better hockey team than it showed in the first two games but must prove it, with no guarantees in a playoff series. He praised the visitors’ discipline, forechecking, positioning and defense, noting that they outpositioned and outdefended Ottawa and capitalized on its mistakes. The young goaltender played well and gave Ottawa chances to win, but Ottawa did not test him enough, particularly in the second game.

He identified center play, puck possession, forechecking support, fewer turnovers and greater speed as areas needing improvement. Ottawa should be more patient, attack with speed, avoid risky passes and force the visitors to adjust. He believed home ice, fan support and a stronger fourth line could provide energy. Pahlsson’s line contributed physically, won faceoffs, established low puck position and protected the puck, while Rob Niedermayer was described as an important player on a key line.

Chris Neil was given the day off because his wife was expected to give birth. The coach expected a large, emotional home crowd, cautioned players not to be overly hyper at the start, and planned to use the fourth line more than in the previous game.

The position paper examines how artificial intelligence is transforming higher education and identifies four affected areas: teaching and learning, research, organizational management, and relationships with external entities. It argues that AI should develop 21st-century human capabilities through learning, self-correction, and reasoning, while acknowledging differences between traditional institutions and AI-oriented ones in governance, training models, and personalized learning.

A document review using the B-ON and SCILIT databases, combined with the authors’ reflexivity as experienced university teachers, supports the analysis. Potential applications include adaptive learning, automated grading, data analysis, translation, personalized tutoring, plagiarism detection, predictive analytics, learning recommendations, speech recognition, student support, text analysis, chatbots, and virtual reality. AI may also facilitate research tasks, streamline administrative processes, provide rapid feedback, improve accessibility, and help prepare students for a technology-intensive labor market.

However, integration presents challenges involving equitable access, inclusion, bias, diversity, privacy, data security, ethics, teacher training, student differences, cost, organizational conservatism, policy, and the limitations of AI itself. Adoption may require participatory institutional change and reshaping traditional teaching, research, and governance structures.

The paper therefore advocates AI literacy among all stakeholders so they can critically evaluate and effectively use AI. Teachers require additional competencies in understanding AI’s educational applications, supporting research and data analysis, managing AI resources, and assessing its use critically. Researchers, students, and institutions are encouraged to engage in discussion, action research, and problem-solving to determine appropriate uses of AI, preserve academic freedom, and guide future research.

A player describes being surprised and grateful to return to the lineup after two weeks away. He credits his teammates, calls the team’s three Cups in nine years special, and praises coach Pat’s no-nonsense, focused leadership and tough style.

An analysis by Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller found that attorneys and staff at the 100 highest-grossing firms and 50 larger plaintiffs-side firms directed 92.45% of their 2023–2024 campaign contributions to Democrats—about $52 million versus $4 million to Republicans. The roughly 12-to-1 Democratic advantage increased from 6-to-1 in an earlier analysis covering 2017–2020. Cleary Gottlieb had the highest Democratic contribution rate among top-grossing firms at 99.7%, while Nelson Mullins had the lowest at 66.4%.

The lecture reviews quantum discrete symmetries—parity, time reversal, and charge conjugation—in complex scalar and Dirac field theories. Classical parity reverses spatial coordinates, time reversal reverses time, and charge conjugation maps a scalar field to its complex conjugate. Quantum symmetries are implemented by unitary operators, except time reversal, which must be antiunitary. This anti-linearity is required for a time-reversal operator to transform the Schrödinger equation into its time-reversed form, and it also changes the definition of the operator’s adjoint.

For a complex scalar field, the action is invariant under parity, time reversal, and charge conjugation, each with an arbitrary phase. Requiring repeated transformations to reproduce the original field constrains each phase to \(+1\) or \(-1\); under parity, these cases are conventionally called scalar and pseudoscalar. In creation and annihilation operators, parity and time reversal reverse momentum, while charge conjugation exchanges particles and antiparticles.

For Dirac fields, parity and the other discrete symmetries require matrices acting on spinor space. Parity requires a matrix \(D\) that commutes with \(\gamma^0\) and anticommutes with the spatial gamma matrices, making it proportional to \(\gamma^0\), up to a phase. A charge-conjugation matrix exists because the transposed gamma matrices satisfy the same Clifford algebra as the original matrices. The fermionic time-reversal matrix is related to the charge-conjugation matrix and \(\gamma^5\). These discrete transformations are independent of continuous Lorentz transformations.

The lecture then introduces fermionic path integrals. Because fermionic fields anticommute, their path-integral variables are Grassmann variables, following Berezin’s prescription. Grassmann variables anticommute with one another and square to zero, so functions of them are finite polynomials. Left and right derivatives can differ by signs, and the lecturer adopts left differentiation by convention. Berezin integration is linear, assigns zero to integrals of total derivatives, and is normalized by \(\int d\theta\,\theta=1\), yielding \(\int d\theta\,f(\theta)=f_1\) for \(f(\theta)=f_0+f_1\theta\). Multivariable integration and changes of variables require additional sign care.

U.S. stock index futures rose Thursday as strong early earnings and a rebound in oil prices offset caution over U.S.-North Korea tensions and France’s close presidential election. Of 57 reporting S&P 500 companies, 75.4% beat earnings expectations; first-quarter profits were estimated up 10.8%. Oil recovered on signals OPEC supply cuts may extend beyond midyear, though inventories remained high. Qualcomm rose after beating estimates, while eBay fell after weak profit guidance.

This continuation application describes systems, devices, and methods for spatially and temporally synchronizing a rotating LIDAR sensor with one or more cameras. Active sensors emit signals and detect reflections to scan an environment, while passive sensors such as CMOS-based cameras detect external light. LIDAR data can provide distance and related environmental information, while camera data can provide image, color, and intensity information.

In the disclosed embodiments, a rotating LIDAR emits light beams or pulses and detects their reflections. Cameras provide adjacent rows of sensing elements oriented parallel to the LIDAR’s rotation axis and may operate in a rolling-shutter mode to produce image pixel rows with row-specific exposure periods. A controller can select the order of pixel rows and individual pixels, adjust exposure delays and camera start times, and determine camera operation based on the LIDAR’s beam order, pointing direction, field of view, rotation rate, and rotation direction. The LIDAR’s beam sequence or rotation characteristics may also be adjusted to correspond with the camera sequence.

A camera ring may position multiple cameras around the rotation axis, with overlapping fields of view and optional curved image-sensor surfaces, to reduce blind spots and improve correspondence between captured pixels and LIDAR reflections. The system may also include a power supply, stationary and rotating platforms, a rotary link, actuators, optical elements, a housing, and an optional display.

The controller can associate image pixels with LIDAR data according to capture times, exposure periods, pointing directions, and viewing directions. It may then map pixels to LIDAR points and combine camera color or intensity data with LIDAR distance, depth, texture, reflectivity, and related information to generate depth-annotated images, colored point clouds, or other three-dimensional representations of the environment.

Quantbot Technologies LP increased its Zoe’s Kitchen position 114.5% in Q2 to 17,056 shares worth $203,000. Massachusetts Financial Services added 219,288 shares in Q1 to own 766,158; CalPERS raised its stake 193.3%, and FMR established a new $8.984 million position. Director A. Alexander Taylor II bought 3,100 shares for $39,897, increasing his direct holdings to 7,508. ZOES opened at $12.39 and had a $242.04 million market capitalization, a 12-month range of $10.77–$27.41, and 50- and 200-day averages of $12.85 and $14.30. The Appellate Division affirmed Bradford Washington’s convictions and sentences for murder in the second degree and related offenses under indictment No. 999/05 and his guilty-plea conviction for murder in the second degree under indictment No. 1000/05. His challenges to the detective’s testimony, the consciousness-of-guilt instruction, and the prosecutor’s summation were unpreserved or meritless. He raised no independent challenge to the second indictment.

Darren Osborne was sentenced to life imprisonment at Woolwich Crown Court, with a minimum term of 43 years, for driving a van into worshippers outside Finsbury Park mosque in London in June. The attack killed Makram Ali and injured nine people. Osborne was convicted of murder and attempted murder after reportedly shouting “I want to kill all Muslims.” The prosecutor said he had been “brainwashed” into Islamophobia. Ali’s family welcomed the verdict and described him as peaceful and innocent. Police said the community’s response showed Osborne had failed to create division and hate.

Several hedge funds trimmed healthcare holdings in the second quarter as S&P 500 healthcare stocks rose 6.7%, outperforming the broad index’s 2.6% gain. Jana Partners exited nine healthcare companies, while Third Point cut its Humana and Baxter positions. A delayed Senate vote and failed scaled-down Affordable Care Act replacement plan followed. Hedge funds gained 1%, while several sold energy holdings after the sector fell 7% amid declining oil prices. Quarterly 13F filings may not reflect current positions.
Facebook is adding a Trending News section to its iOS and Android apps, aggregating stories and ranking them by how many publications share them.

The patent discloses a coil-less, wickless atomizer for electronic cigarettes and similar vaporizing devices. An electronic smoking device includes a housing, power source, control electronics, liquid supply, and atomizer. The atomizer uses one or more hollow woven fiber tubes whose ends contact the liquid supply. The tubes transport liquid toward a heating section by capillary action through their hollow interiors and through their porous walls.

The woven fiber tubes may be conductive throughout, or only the heating section may be conductive. A higher-resistance section between lower-resistance conductive sections, electrical leads, or surface contacts generates heat when current is applied, vaporizing liquid to form aerosol. The tubes may be C-, L-, or U-shaped and can vary in diameter. Multiple tubes may be arranged parallel or in contact, allowing liquid transfer between tubes and staged aerosol delivery. A larger tube may contain the heating section while smaller adjacent tubes supply liquid.

Suitable materials include carbon fiber and composites combining resistive and capillary materials, such as nickel-chromium with silicon dioxide, carbon fiber with Dacron, or ceramic fibers with stainless steel. Electrical resistance may be controlled through fiber selection, weave pattern, geometry, coatings, plating, sputtering, or other surface modification. Illustrative embodiments use masked areas and sputter coating to create distinct conductive and heating regions.

During use, a sensor or manual switch activates the heater, and airflow carries the resulting aerosol toward the inhalation port. The disclosed atomizer combines heating and liquid transport in one component, potentially enabling compact atomizers and controlled resistance, wicking, and aerosol production.

The U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Massachusetts denied Randall Fincke’s motion to reconsider his liability under Massachusetts securities law § 410(a)(2) for falsely stating in Access Cardiosystems’ October 2002 Business Plan that patent counsel had advised that its defibrillator did not infringe known patents. The court found that no such advice, formal or informal, had been given and that the statement was objectively false and material.

The court ruled that damages under § 410(a)(2) require a causal nexus between the misrepresentation and a specific securities sale, although proof of reliance and loss causation is unnecessary. It found the investors’ testimony that every investment relied on the Business Plan to be not credible. The April 2003 investments arose from a new company overview, financial negotiations, and restructuring needs, while post-April 2003 advances were loans rather than stock purchases. Only Joseph Zimmel’s $1 million October and $500,000 November 2002 stock purchases were made “by means of” the Business Plan.

The court entered judgment for Zimmel of $1.5 million plus 6 percent annual interest from May 25, 2007, costs, and postjudgment interest. It also entered judgment for Access of $281,534.62 for Fincke’s fiduciary-duty breaches, plus 12 percent annual interest from July 6, 2004, costs, and postjudgment interest. The request for attorneys’ fees was waived because no evidence was presented.

The BIRDS workshop aims to connect digital-library domain experts with computational researchers to develop practical, innovative research systems for digital libraries. It seeks to address shared challenges, including limited resources, varied user access needs, and restrictions on sending material to services such as ChatGPT. Planned outcomes include establishing a continuing workshop series, discussing early-stage ideas at TPDL, and producing a SIGIR Forum report.

The full-day, in-person event includes introductions, a keynote on successful practitioner–researcher collaboration, scientific speed-dating, a moderated panel, and breakout discussions. Topics may include LLM use and limitations, OCR practices, interface evaluation, and effective access paths. Participants will summarize discussions in plenary and may co-author the report. The primary audience is practitioners and researchers interested in digital-library systems, especially students and library representatives, with approximately 25 participants expected. The workshop is organized by Christin Katharina Kreutz and Hermann Kroll.

The Ohio Supreme Court upheld the one-year residency requirement for divorce and annulment under R.C. 3105.03, which exempts alimony-only actions. Applying Shapiro and Dunn, the court held that the requirement did not penalize the constitutional right to interstate travel because divorce is not a basic necessity and Ohio has a compelling interest in regulating marriage and its dissolution. The requirement was the least restrictive means of ensuring that Ohio’s divorce laws were not applied to nonresidents, because residency requires proof of an intent to make Ohio a permanent home. The statute does not bar newcomers from obtaining divorces and may encourage reconsideration or reconciliation of marital problems. Although the appellant had not met the residency requirement when she filed, she did by the appeal, so the constitutional issue was not moot. The judgment was affirmed.

On August 17, 2022, Apple Inc.’s Compensation Committee approved the Apple Inc. Executive Cash Incentive Plan, allowing eligible executives and designated employees to receive cash awards based on performance goals, with payment levels set by the Committee. Awards are generally forfeited if a participant leaves before payment unless the Committee decides otherwise. Apple’s Board also adopted amended and restated bylaws permitting shorter notice for special Board meetings, expanding shareholder nomination and proposal disclosure requirements, updating special-meeting and written-consent procedures, requiring non-white proxy cards, and allowing reduced procedures during emergencies. The bylaws also included ministerial, clarifying and conforming changes. The amended bylaws and incentive plan were filed as Exhibits 3.2 and 10.1, respectively.

In a 30th-anniversary retrospective, the passage argues that Oliver Stone’s *Wall Street* has remained supreme among later finance films because it combines a rags-to-riches story, a hero’s journey, and a fairy tale. Its vivid depiction of 1980s culture, financial excess, fashion, and technology captures the era, while Bud Fox’s rise and Gordon Gekko’s influence blur the line between aspiration and wrongdoing. Michael Douglas’s portrayal of Gekko—modeled partly on Ivan Boesky, Michael Milken, and Carl Icahn—created an enduring symbol of financial success and greed and earned Douglas an Oscar. Although ostensibly the antagonist, Gekko is charismatic, targets corporations rather than everyday investors, and gives the film balance beyond a simple “money is bad” message. The story’s cautionary foundation, period detail, and memorable lines have made the film a lasting cultural touchstone.

Amazon.com, Inc.’s Form 10-K covers the fiscal year ended December 31, 2016. The company was incorporated in Washington in 1994, reincorporated in Delaware in 1996, completed its IPO in May 1997, and trades on NASDAQ under “AMZN.” It operates through North America, International, and Amazon Web Services (AWS), serving consumers, sellers, developers, enterprises, and content creators. Consumer operations include retail websites, electronic devices, digital media, and Amazon Prime; seller programs generate commissions and other fees; AWS provides compute, storage, database, and related services; and Kindle Direct Publishing offers authors and publishers a 70% royalty option. The company also generates advertising and co-branded credit card revenue.

Amazon reported approximately 341,400 employees at year-end 2016. Jeffrey P. Bezos was president, CEO, and chairman, while Andrew R. Jassy led AWS and Jeffrey A. Wilke led Worldwide Consumer. The filing identifies major risks from intense competition, rapid expansion, new products and geographic markets, international operations, foreign exchange rates, fulfillment and data-center capacity, seasonality and inventory, commercial relationships, acquisitions, key personnel, cybersecurity and system interruptions, intellectual property, stock-price volatility, taxation, government regulation, suppliers, product liability, payments, and seller conduct. It specifically notes regulatory risks affecting Amazon’s operations in China and India.

As of December 31, 2016, Amazon reported 172.158 million leased square feet of facilities and 7.187 million owned square feet, primarily in North America, Europe, and Asia. There were no unresolved SEC staff comments, and mine-safety disclosures were not applicable. The company had 2,448 shareholders of record as of January 25, 2017, had never paid cash dividends, and reported 477,170,618 shares outstanding as of that date.

Net sales rose from $61.093 billion in 2012 to $135.987 billion in 2016. Operating income was $4.186 billion in 2016, compared with $2.233 billion in 2015 and $178 million in 2014. Net income was $2.371 billion in 2016, and operating cash flow was $16.443 billion. Total assets reached $83.402 billion, and long-term obligations totaled $20.301 billion.

In 2016, North America generated $79.785 billion in sales and $2.361 billion in operating income; International generated $43.983 billion in sales and a $1.283 billion operating loss; and AWS generated $12.219 billion in sales and $3.108 billion in operating income. Consolidated sales increased 27%, with growth of 25% in North America, 24% internationally, and 55% in AWS.

Cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities totaled $26.0 billion at year-end 2016. The company generated $16.4 billion of operating cash flow, used $9.9 billion in investing activities and $2.9 billion in financing activities, and spent $6.7 billion in cash on capital expenditures, primarily for fulfillment capacity and technology infrastructure supporting AWS. Management stated that operating cash flows, marketable securities, and available borrowing were expected to meet anticipated operating cash needs for at least the following 12 months, subject to uncertainty.

Critical accounting judgments included inventory valuation and income taxes. Inventories were valued using first-in, first-out and the lower of cost or market; each additional 1% of valuation allowance would have increased 2016 cost of sales by approximately $130 million. Tax uncertainties included IRS transfer-pricing disputes concerning 2005–2006 transactions and a European Commission investigation into Luxembourg tax treatment.

A modified Google Camera app enables HDR+ on Android phones with Snapdragon 820, 821 or 835 processors, though results may not perfectly match Pixel quality. Amazon is offering refunds for dubious solar-eclipse glasses. HBO refuses to pay hackers who have leaked episodes and emails, including upcoming “Curb Your Enthusiasm” episodes. Excerpts from retired Justice Anthony Kennedy’s memoir highlight his emphasis on judicial humility, integrity, good-faith reasoning, and clarity, especially in close cases. Kennedy rejects labeling himself an originalist or pragmatist but believes constitutional interpretation can improve over time without changing the Constitution. He discusses controversial rulings in Citizens United, same-sex marriage, the 2000 presidential election, and flag burning, stressing adherence to legal issues over personal or political preferences. He also recounts the personal fallout and eventual reconciliation with Justice Antonin Scalia following the same-sex marriage decision.

Kennedy describes his opposition to cameras in the courtroom, fearing they could disrupt candid judicial discussions. On abortion, he states that although he personally considers it wrong, moral objections do not determine legal rulings, and he remained on the Court to uphold his constitutional oath. He says presidents must interpret the Constitution in good faith while deferring to Supreme Court rulings, recounts a chilling meeting with Vladimir Putin, and describes the vandalism of his family’s home after he declined to reduce the bail of a Manson family member. The excerpts close with Kennedy’s humorous recollection that his family regarded the Rolling Stones, Tom Petty, Blondie, AC/DC, and Lynyrd Skynyrd as avant-garde.

The Simons Observatory’s Large Aperture Telescope uses SMuRF microwave-frequency multiplexing to read out nearly 31,000 transition-edge sensor detectors. Because its warm coaxial transmission lines are exposed to diurnal temperature swings in the receiver cabin, changes in cable length and dielectric properties can cause systematic phase drift that may mimic detector signals.

The study used untracked off-resonance “pilot” tones to measure this drift. Measurements from 290 tones generated by 30 AMCs over 22.6 hours showed that time delays correlated with ambient temperature, with total shifts of a few picoseconds over one day-night cycle. The delays clustered by individual RF transmission-line circuits, with some spread due to their 2 GHz frequency range.

The measured phase drift was converted into an inferred TES noise-equivalent current using calibrated resonator offsets and SQUID-curve measurements. For one UFM, the median post-calibration resonator offset was −3.31 × 10⁴ Hz, while the median SQUID frequency response was 5.71 × 10⁻² Hz pA⁻¹. During a 40-minute constant-elevation scan, the resulting phase-drift noise was not a significant contributor to overall on-sky detector noise and remained within the readout-noise budget. The authors therefore do not expect this effect to affect the telescope’s mapping speed.

Tesla, Inc.’s fiscal 2022 Form 10-K describes a company focused on accelerating the transition to sustainable energy through electric vehicles and energy generation and storage products. Its two reportable segments are automotive and energy generation and storage. Automotive includes Models 3, Y, S and X, early Tesla Semi production, regulatory credits and related services; energy includes Powerwall, Megapack, Solar Roof and solar systems.

Tesla emphasizes direct sales, company-owned service and Supercharger networks, financing, leasing and insurance, along continued development of battery, powertrain, software, Full Self-Driving and AI technologies. It manufactures vehicles and energy products at facilities in the U.S., China and Germany, relies on extensive global supply chains and reported 127,855 full-time employees at year-end 2022. The filing also discusses competition, government incentives, safety and other regulations, intellectual property, sustainability and human-capital practices.

Identified risks include macroeconomic and COVID-19 effects, component and raw-material shortages, battery-cell dependence, manufacturing delays and costs, demand uncertainty, stronger competition, international operations, product defects and liability, financing and residual-value exposure, obligations concerning Gigafactory New York, reliance on key personnel including CEO Elon Musk, and cybersecurity incidents.

Evelyn Montiel helped her family run an ice cream truck and fruit stand in East Oakland while excelling in high school. With support from Students Rising Above (SRA), she transferred to USC, graduated, and completed a pre-MBA program at Stanford. When the recession left her unable to find work, SRA connected her with an investment-firm interview. She became a finance broker at a Silicon Valley startup and credits SRA with shaping her success.

NVIDIA Corporation’s Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended January 29, 2017 describes a Delaware corporation headquartered in Santa Clara, California, with common stock traded on the NASDAQ Global Select Market under “NVDA.” The non-affiliate market value of its voting stock was approximately $28.98 billion as of July 29, 2016, and 589 million shares were outstanding as of February 24, 2017.

Founded in 1993, NVIDIA invented the GPU and expanded from PC graphics into artificial intelligence. Its two reportable segments, GPU and Tegra Processor, share a common architecture and serve gaming, professional visualization, datacenter, and automotive markets. Product brands include GeForce, GeForce NOW, Quadro, Tesla, DGX, GRID, Tegra, DRIVE PX, SHIELD, and Jetson. NVIDIA combines processors, system software, algorithms, libraries, systems, and services through vertical integration. Its AI platform includes GPUs, the CUDA programming language, cuDNN, NVLink, and DGX systems for deep-learning training and inference. The company reports that GPUs can accelerate parallel workloads by 10–75 times versus CPUs and sped up deep-neural-network training by as much as 12 times during the prior year.

NVIDIA sells primarily through a network of OEMs, ODMs, AIB manufacturers, system builders, distributors, retailers, and other industry partners. ASUSTeK represented 12% of fiscal 2017 revenue. Sales generally use standard purchase orders with short lead times, and only a small, insignificant portion of backlog is noncancelable. Most revenue comes from consumer products, which have historically been stronger in the second half of the fiscal year.

NVIDIA uses a fabless manufacturing strategy. TSMC and Samsung manufacture wafers, while independent subcontractors perform assembly, testing, and packaging. This reduces fixed manufacturing costs and risks but creates dependence on third parties for supply, capacity, quality, yields, and delivery. At fiscal year-end, cash and marketable securities had risen 35% to $6.80 billion, which management believed sufficient for at least 12 months of operating requirements. NVIDIA had 10,299 employees, including 7,282 in research and development, and spent $1.46 billion on R&D in fiscal 2017, following $1.33 billion in 2016 and $1.36 billion in 2015.

Key risks include intense competition, failure to anticipate market needs, low manufacturing yields, cybersecurity and privacy incidents, product defects, dependence on external manufacturers and software tools, supply constraints, and difficulty winning customer designs. Additional risks include customer concentration, inaccurate demand forecasts, excess inventory, international operations, natural disasters, acquisitions, intellectual-property litigation, volatility in operating results, privacy regulation, headquarters construction and lease-financing obligations, indebtedness, convertible-note dilution, and provisions that may impede a change in control. Revenue from customers outside the United States and Other Americas represented 80% of fiscal 2017 revenue. Intel’s final $200 million licensing payment was received in January 2016, with related revenue recognized through the first quarter of fiscal 2018.

NVIDIA’s headquarters complex includes eight leased commercial buildings totaling 896,565 square feet and six owned commercial buildings on 36 acres. It also owns a research and development building in Hyderabad, India, leases other domestic and international facilities, and targeted completion of a new Santa Clara headquarters for the fourth quarter of fiscal 2018. Unresolved staff comments and mine-safety disclosures were not applicable; legal-proceedings information was incorporated from the financial-statement notes.

The quarterly dividend was increased to $0.14 per share, or $0.56 annually, in November 2016. NVIDIA paid $261 million in cash dividends in fiscal 2017. Its repurchase authorization was increased by $2 billion through December 2020; 245 million shares had been repurchased for $4.59 billion, with $2.73 billion of authorization remaining. The company intended to return $1.25 billion to shareholders through dividends and repurchases in fiscal 2018. Convertible-note settlements and remaining warrants could dilute per-share earnings and existing shareholders’ ownership.
