Gunmen attacked U.N. peacekeeping facilities in Timbuktu and Douentza, Mali, killing seven people in Timbuktu and a Malian soldier and U.N. peacekeeper in Douentza. MINUSMA reported eight attackers killed and dispatched a quick reaction force and helicopters to Timbuktu. The U.N. is investigating possible links between the attacks.

A Treasury Department report ordered by President Trump recommends rolling back parts of Obama-era Wall Street regulations, including repealing Dodd-Frank’s CEO pay-gap disclosure requirement. It also proposes easing IPO rules so companies can privately test investor interest, raising the annual crowdfunding limit for small private firms from $1 million to $5 million, and having the SEC and CFTC harmonize derivatives oversight. Republicans and business groups framed the changes as ways to boost capital markets, job creation, and economic growth. Democrats and consumer advocates warned that reducing post-crisis safeguards could expose taxpayers to another bailout. The recommendations require some congressional action but could largely be implemented by regulators, though related legislation stalled in the Senate.

Arizona ammunition dealer Douglas Haig was charged with manufacturing armor-piercing bullets without a license after his fingerprints were found on unused bullets in Stephen Paddock’s Mandalay Bay hotel room. Haig sold Paddock 720 tracer rounds before the Oct. 1 Las Vegas shooting, but records do not establish whether that ammunition was used. Haig said the sale appeared ordinary and he had no way to know Paddock would carry out the attack that killed 58. His lawyer said he held a press conference to protect his reputation after his identity was inadvertently disclosed in court documents. Haig has closed his ammunition business and received death threats since his name became public.

LLMs are increasingly used as synthetic respondents and agents to simulate demographics, attitudes, behaviors, survey responses, and experimental outcomes. Their apparent predictive success stems largely from pattern matching learned from massive training datasets, scaling, prompt conditioning, and sometimes fine-tuning or alignment. These capabilities make LLMs useful for narrow, explicitly conditioned prediction, but their outputs should not be interpreted as draws from human populations or as principled Bayesian beliefs. LLM sampling reflects learned token probabilities rather than a posterior updated with new evidence, and repeated prompts can exhibit order dependence, unstable predictions, and reduced or distorted response variance.

The paper identifies several methodological risks. Models may reproduce familiar main effects while failing on interactions, novel stimuli, identity-sensitive interventions, or out-of-domain tasks. Fine-tuning can improve specialized performance while encouraging overfitting, circular replication, and weak generalizability; evidence cited also suggests that heavily instruction-tuned models may perform worse on statistical-coherence tests. Such findings raise concerns about whether synthetic agents model human behavior generally or merely imitate training material.

Researchers are therefore advised to treat LLM agents as high-capacity conditional predictors rather than calibrated population samples. They should measure and report calibration, subgroup validity, response dispersion, and human-baseline accuracy; account for distribution shift and model bias; avoid posterior-style inference from overly homogeneous synthetic samples; and use confidence sets, adaptive sample sizes, and augmentation rather than replacement of human data. Agents should be grounded in individual human data or specific tasks where possible, while limiting claims to validated domains.

Sampling protocols should prevent self-conditioning, randomize item order, fix decoding settings, test independence and order invariance, and document position or self-preference effects. Stress tests should vary prompts, contexts, stimuli, and experimental setups, with failures and extrapolative limits openly reported. Full reproducibility requires releasing prompts, model versions, decoding parameters, seeds, aggregation procedures, and relevant uncertainty estimates.

The paper concludes that LLMs have substantial near-term potential as domain-specific tools for social prediction, instrument pretesting, counterfactual exploration, and research design. Their responsible use requires transparent limitations, rigorous validation, continued human data as the inference standard, and a multitude of specialized agents rather than a universal model of human behavior.

NIST’s revised guidance recommends simple, long, memorable passwords, including phrases, lowercase letters, and common English words, instead of special characters, mixed case, or expiration. The study evaluates the quality of early childhood education in 71 Anganwadi centers across 25 villages in Nuh Block, Mewat district, Haryana, to support school readiness and equity in preschool education. Using a mixed-methods design, researchers assessed centers’ infrastructure, physical learning environments, sanitation, learning resources, administration, and Anganwadi workers’ qualifications, knowledge, attitudes, and pedagogical practices. Data were collected from August to September 2021 through checklists, observations, photographs, and interviews.

Most centers lacked adequate safety and learning conditions. Although 41 had boundary walls and 39 had gates, only 23 had safe building structures and 14 had leveled floors. Thirty-five provided space for children to sit comfortably, but none had mats or desks and chairs; only three had lights or fans, and one had outdoor play equipment. Only three centers had clean drinking water, functional toilets, and safe kitchens. Basic learning materials were largely absent, and no center had a preschool timetable, while most lacked preschool registers and parent-meeting records.

All workers had more than six years of experience, but most had not completed matriculation. None was fully familiar with the five developmental domains or their importance, and 69 of 71 did not recognize their strengths or areas for professional development. Frequent training was lacking, parent involvement was limited, and many record-keeping duties were not fulfilled. In teaching, 63% mainly used repetition and memorization, while 37% used activity-based methods.

The discussion identifies broader rural challenges involving inadequate infrastructure and resources, insufficiently trained educators, poverty, limited parental engagement, linguistic and cultural barriers, and weak monitoring and evaluation. It highlights NEP 2020’s emphasis on holistic, play-based education for children aged three to six, qualified educators, inclusive curricula, parental and community participation, and regular assessment.

Recommendations include establishing standardized infrastructure and learning resources with a defined implementation timeline; training Anganwadi workers in child development, appropriate curricula, classroom management, and related skills; raising parental awareness; and strengthening monitoring and accountability. State governments are encouraged to work with parents, communities, NGOs, and businesses to improve Anganwadi-based preschool education.

The AMD Geode CS5535 Revision A3 specification update catalogs hardware deviations and associated workarounds. Indexed limitations include ATAC SSMI during DMA, GLIU clock-domain wake failures, ACPI PM1 byte-access hangs, PMC register-write corruption, KEL status errors, PCI back-to-back read failures, UART clock gating in CEIR mode, PCI timing violations, nonsynchronous SSMI, IDE PIO during UDMA, ACPI S3 wake failures, LPC I/O during legacy DMA, USB clock gating, CD-ROM command failures, incorrect UDMA timing, unaligned PRD hangs, LPC synchronous-transfer aborts, SMB NEGACK behavior, GLPCI retry counting, post-suspend GPIO writes, missing LOWBAT_FLAG, and delayed Sleep_X deassertion.

PIT deviations include failing to cancel an incomplete counter-latch command during read-back and immediately loading a new count in mode 3. Software should complete latch operations before read-back and avoid relying on mode-3 count replacement. XPIC AEOI handling can send two interrupts instead of one because the IRR bit is cleared too late; AEOI should be used only when nested multilevel interrupts are unnecessary. Legacy DMA rotating priority may not rotate channel priorities as expected, although transfers still complete.

The GLIU debug port can hang and its data-pattern detection feature does not operate; the debug port should not be used, and affected detection registers should remain at their defaults. GLIU unexpected-address errors also fail to set the expected error flag and response exception, though this has no functional impact outside debugging.

A thermal alarm causes Faulted Standby, but the PMC cannot recover autonomously because the alarm signal is blocked in the Work domain. Power cycling repeats until the alarm clears. PMC Sleep_Clock controls must be enabled in the appropriate PMC register even when disabled through GPIO, or Sleep_Clock-dependent options may not operate as expected.

UART accesses during 8237 block- or demand-mode DMA are discarded or return all ones; software should wait for terminal count or use single-byte transfer mode. A diagnostic LPC-to-memory software-DMA combination completes without writing data and should be avoided. PCI I/O addresses of 10000h or higher hang because the CS5535 claims them; such cycles and illegal ATAC or Diverse Device LBAR values must not be generated. The CS5535 also fails USB over-voltage protection requirements, requiring external protection circuits.

PIC edge inputs can miss interrupts and hang the system when automatic Local-bus clock gating turns off while the source remains high; automatic clock gating should not be enabled in this situation.

ATAC and ACC prefetch settings can expose part of the next PRD when tables are not 8-byte aligned. PRD entries should be defined before transfers, and audio PRD changes should be at least two tables ahead. A UDMA write following a host-terminated UDMA read may continue an incorrect CRC after device termination; host terminations should be prevented using ATAC Error MSR bit 8. During IDE master DMA, ATAC fails to block PIO when IDE_PIO_SSMI_EN is set, although the SSMI and flag are generated; the feature is intended only for debugging and workarounds.

Future LLM benchmarks should dynamically generate samples to reduce contamination, vary task difficulty, and assess individual capabilities rather than only aggregate scores, while adapting psychometrics to AI. Toll purchased a Denver residence from Mrs. McKenzie, believing he had merchantable title. The property had originally been purchased by her late husband, Charles D. McKenzie, from Owens. An unrecorded deed and a recorded trust deed securing an $8,000 loan from George W. Casey were found after McKenzie’s death. His will left everything to his widow and left two minor daughters as heirs.

Casey, acting to protect the minors’ interests, arranged for a replacement deed from Owens directly to Mrs. McKenzie and destroyed the original deed. Mrs. McKenzie then sold the property to Toll for $11,000, warranting merchantable title. After learning that the minors owned an undivided one-half interest, Toll entered a contract with Mrs. McKenzie and Casey requiring probate and guardianship proceedings, a sale of the minors’ interest to Toll, and payment of costs and attorney’s fees to perfect his title.

The will was probated, and Mrs. McKenzie as executrix obtained an order approving the sale. She also qualified as guardian and receipted for the minors’ share of the proceeds. Toll later repudiated the transaction and sought to set aside the proceedings. The probate court sustained a demurrer to his reply, and Toll then sought to enjoin foreclosure of Casey’s trust deed.

The court held that the transaction constituted constructive fraud because it was intended to deceive, but there was no intent to injure the minors. The probate and guardianship proceedings adequately disclosed the facts, and the sale effectively conveyed the minors’ interests despite technical deviations from their contract. Toll had already paid the money due the minors, so no further cash payment was necessary. Casey, however, had principally caused the defective title and could not benefit from his own wrongdoing. The judgments were affirmed as modified: Toll was to pay the remaining encumbrance and interest, reduced by Casey’s contractual obligations, and Casey was then to release the trust deed. Costs were allocated between the parties, and the case was remanded on rehearing to effect the modified judgment.

Micro E-mini Nasdaq 100 futures (MNQ) are electronically traded on CME Globex and offer exposure to the Nasdaq-100 Index at one-tenth the size of E-mini contracts. One contract equals the index value multiplied by $2. The minimum price fluctuation is 0.25 index points, or $0.50 per contract, for outright trading and 0.05 points, or $0.10, for calendar spreads. Contracts are listed quarterly for five consecutive quarters and cash-settled using the index’s special opening quotations on the third Friday of the contract month, when trading ends at 9:30 a.m. ET. They have no block-trade eligibility.

Globex trading runs Sunday at 6:00 p.m. to Friday at 5:00 p.m. ET, with a daily break. Some brokers also offer CFDs, which permit continuous trading without expiry or rollover and involve swapping the difference between opening and closing prices. Trading requires a futures-broker account and sufficient margin.

Leveraged ETFs use debt and financial derivatives to amplify the daily returns of an underlying index, commonly at 2:1 or 3:1 ratios; inverse ETFs profit when the index falls. They magnify losses as well as gains and are generally unsuitable for long-term investment because of high costs, volatility decay, daily rebalancing, and the limited long-term suitability of their derivatives.

The recommended use is short-term trading—preferably day trading, or swing trading for no more than a few days—to speculate on an index’s short-term momentum. Risk can be managed through stop-loss orders, diversification across markets and leveraged, inverse, and traditional ETFs, fundamental analysis of tracked indices, attention to liquidity, and monitoring volatility and market conditions to rebalance.

Performance can be evaluated with measures such as the Sharpe ratio, Jensen’s alpha, and appraisal ratio, although Treynor’s ratio may not adequately capture leveraged ETF risk. Maximum drawdown and maximum adverse excursion are also important, particularly during losses or crises.

Reported backtests showed one strategy averaging 1.25% per trade, with 7.6% annual returns and an 18% maximum drawdown over 100 trades while invested only 9% of the time. A QLD version averaged 2.25% per trade and returned 13.6% annually over 98 trades, close to QQQ’s 14.2% buy-and-hold return, with the gap attributed partly to QLD’s time decay. The QLD strategy nevertheless lost more than 35% during the 2008–09 crisis, while a less robust strategy produced a QLD maximum drawdown above 55%.

For US citizens and residents, ETF profits are taxed like stock profits: short-term gains at short-term capital-gain rates and long-term gains at long-term rates, with net gains taxed after capital losses can offset them. Tax treatment depends on domicile. Overall, leverage can produce substantial gains but can also cause severe losses and force traders to exit near market bottoms.

The TLV322x uses a sinking-only open-drain output that can be pulled up externally from 0 V to 5.5 V independent of the comparator supply. This supports wired logic ORing and logic-level translation. TI recommends pull-up current of 100 µA to 1 mA; resistor selection affects rise time, output low voltage, and power dissipation. Pull-up resistance above 1 MΩ produces a slower exponential rising edge. A series current-limiting resistor is recommended if output shorts are possible. Unused outputs may remain floating or connect to V−.

Internal ESD protection clamps inputs 0.2 V beyond the supply rails. Series input resistors are recommended for low-impedance sources, with clamp current limited to 10 mA or less. During power-on reset, which activates for up to 32 µs after the 1.65 V threshold is crossed, the output remains low. After reset and once the minimum supply voltage is reached, the output reflects the differential input state.

The comparator output is determined by the relationship between VIN and VREF, and swapping the inputs inverts the logic. Propagation delay varies by transition direction and increases as overdrive decreases, particularly below 100 mV. External hysteresis can prevent output chatter caused by slow input crossings or noise near the offset voltage; it supplements the TLV321x’s 1.8 mV internal hysteresis. Inverting configurations use a three-resistor network, while non-inverting configurations use two resistors and a voltage reference to define upper and lower switching thresholds.

A low-side current-sensing example uses an amplified shunt-voltage signal to trigger a high-speed comparator. Recommended layout includes a 0.1 µF ceramic bypass capacitor at the supply pin, a stable low-noise supply, minimal input/output coupling, close placement of input resistors, and optional output damping below 100 Ω for long traces.

Within seven days of vaccination, injection-site reactions after BNT162b1 or BNT162b2 were well tolerated, resolved quickly, and were mostly mild or moderate; injection-site pain was most common. Systemic events, including fever, tiredness, headache, chills, vomiting, diarrhea, and new muscle or joint pain, were also well tolerated, temporary, and mostly mild or moderate, with tiredness and headache most common. Reactions and systemic events in Phase 2 and Phase 3 booster groups were similar to those in the broader Phase 2/3 population.

In Phase 1, 10-, 20-, and 30-µg doses of BNT162b1 and BNT162b2 were well tolerated, while the 100-µg BNT162b1 dose was stopped after Dose 1 because of injection-site reactions or systemic events. The 30-µg BNT162b2 dose was selected for Phase 2/3. No Phase 1 participant left the study because of medical problems, and no single medical problem occurred in more than two participants in any dose group.

In Phase 2/3, 30 µg BNT162b2 was well tolerated. Fewer than 1% left the blinded study because of medical problems: 32 of 21,926 BNT162b2 recipients and 36 of 21,921 placebo recipients. Most medical problems were mild or moderate, and most problems in the BNT162b2 group involved injection-site reactions or systemic events. No single medical problem occurred in more than 1% of participants aged 12–15 years. Among participants aged 16 and older, nausea occurred in 1% of BNT162b2 recipients and less than 1% of placebo recipients.

Serious medical problems were uncommon. In Phase 1, two were reported and were not believed vaccine-related. In Phase 2/3, no single serious problem occurred in at least 1% of any group. Researchers considered a small number potentially vaccine-related, including temporary arm or leg numbness or tingling, a portal-vein blood clot, and a mini stroke or temporary blood-flow blockage; no serious problem related to the vaccine was reported among participants aged 12–15. Among 324 BNT162b2SA recipients, four had serious problems, none considered vaccine-related. Few serious problems followed Phase 3 or Phase 2/3 booster doses, and researchers generally did not consider them vaccine-related, although two participants aged 16 or older had problems considered potentially related.

No participant died in Phase 1. During Phase 2/3, deaths occurred in 85 of 23,141 initial BNT162b2 recipients, 62 of 21,371 initial placebo recipients who later received BNT162b2, and 23 of 23,141 placebo-only recipients. The deaths had varied causes and were not believed to have been caused by BNT162b2. No participant died in Phase 3 among those receiving BNT162b2SA without prior BNT162b2.

The Franklin County Court of Appeals held that Technology Education Corporation (TEC) could not be held liable for breach-of-contract claims brought by Gail Erdy, Tamara Wolford, and Monica Jones. TEC purchased the school’s assets from Educational Leadership Corporation (ELC) after the plaintiffs had completed their courses.

Although successor corporations generally are not liable for a predecessor’s obligations, the court found no express or implied assumption of liability because the incorporated asset purchase agreement excluded liabilities arising before the sale, including student-contract claims. TEC’s knowledge of pending litigation did not establish implicit assumption, and no bona fide purchaser requirement applied. The record also did not show that TEC was a mere continuation of ELC because it had separate directors and stockholders. Further, because this was a contract claim rather than a strict products-liability action, the plaintiffs still had to prove their claims. The court reversed the judgment and remanded for further proceedings.

The application discloses endpoint-agent techniques for preventing ransomware from encrypting files on target machines across Windows, macOS, iOS, and Linux environments. An endpoint agent monitors file-system activity, including file opens, metadata changes, writes, deletions, renames, and directory enumeration, through mechanisms such as a mini-filter driver. It detects unauthorized interaction with forged honeypot files or directories and applies configurable security policies that may block the operation, terminate the associated process, alert the user, and monitor or log activity.

To reduce storage use and avoid file residue, the agent can use a mini-filter driver to inject falsified file entries into directory-query results, including at the beginning and end of enumerations. Attempts to access these virtual entries are redirected to a small number of physical honeypot files stored in one directory. Their names, types, sizes, dates, and contents can be configured to resemble files ransomware commonly targets. Virtual honeypot directories can similarly redirect ransomware to real directories containing attractive files. Entries may be positioned to increase the likelihood that ransomware encounters them before genuine files, potentially preventing encryption before it begins. Legitimate shell-based enumeration can be recognized and excluded to reduce false positives.

Protected volumes and directories may be specified by paths or patterns, while process exceptions can be based on executable paths, binary attributes, signing, or configured process lists. The agent can receive notifications of newly mounted volumes and apply protections to them. Its components include file-system monitoring, protected-directory and exception configuration, virtual-content storage, policy management, response services, and an interface for configuration, alerts, and logs. A Windows GUI permits rules to select activation, prevention or notification actions, user alerts, and applicable processes; default settings enable activation, prevention, and alerts for all processes except configured exceptions. Security events may report the malicious process and hash, attempted files or folders, blocked operation and paths, agent and content versions, and other details, with critical-severity SIEM events.

The Chande Momentum Oscillator (CMO), introduced by Tushar Chande in his 1994 book *The New Technical Trader*, measures momentum by comparing recent higher and lower closes. It is calculated as 100 × (sum of higher closes − sum of lower closes) ÷ (sum of higher closes + sum of lower closes) and ranges from −100 to +100.

Readings above zero indicate strength and below zero indicate weakness, but interpretation depends on the prevailing trend. Values above +50 are considered overbought, while values below −50 are oversold; these signals are less reliable in strong trends because they can persist. Divergence between price and CMO swings may signal potential reversals: bullish divergence pairs a lower price low with a higher CMO low, while bearish divergence pairs a higher price high with a lower CMO high. Traders may also use a nine-period moving average of the CMO as a signal line.

CMO measures momentum rather than identifying the main trend. It is most useful when combined with trend indicators, price action, or trendlines to identify pullbacks ending within the direction of the broader trend. In sideways markets, it can support mean-reversion trades by signaling long entries near support through oversold readings or bullish divergence and short entries near resistance through overbought readings or bearish divergence.

The passage reports a Python backtest of a nine-day CMO strategy on the dividend-adjusted SPY ETF using a five-day maximum holding period. The strategy produced an attractive risk-adjusted return, lower drawdown than buy-and-hold, and declining returns when holding periods were extended to 10, 15, or 30 days. Optimal settings and timeframes depend on the strategy and asset and should be determined through backtesting. Short-term traders may use 15-, 30-minute, or hourly charts, while swing traders may use four-hour or daily charts.

Compared with RSI, CMO uses the difference between higher and lower closes relative to total price movement, while RSI uses the ratio of higher to lower closes. The stochastic compares the latest close with the period’s price range. CMO can perform poorly in volatile, directionless markets but may remain overbought or oversold for extended periods during strongly trending markets. It can be added to supported trading platforms directly or through a custom indicator.

This bibliometric study maps the intellectual structure and emerging trends in primary science education research. Using VOSviewer, the authors analyzed 2,295 English-language, peer-reviewed articles from the Web of Science Core Collection spanning 1997 through December 2024 through bibliographic coupling and co-word analyses.

The coupling analysis identified five thematic clusters: augmented and virtual reality with ICT integration; equity, engagement, and teacher competence; cognitive and metacognitive supports for conceptual understanding; dialogic teaching, interdisciplinary integration, and teacher beliefs; and artificial intelligence, computer science, and computational thinking. Co-word analysis identified four related themes: dialogic argumentation, discourse, and scientific literacy; teacher beliefs, pedagogical knowledge, and professional development; achievement, engagement, and conceptual change; and computational thinking and technology integration in STEM education.

The findings indicate a shift from content transmission toward student-centered, inquiry-based, digitally supported, dialogic, and equity-oriented pedagogy. Digital tools show potential for improving engagement, motivation, and conceptual understanding, but their effectiveness depends on infrastructure, access, teacher competence, and meaningful pedagogical integration. Persistent barriers include inadequate teacher preparation, limited resources, rigid curricula, unequal digital access, and gaps in culturally responsive computational thinking and understanding teacher identity during reforms.

Based on these findings, the study proposes the DIG-EDU-QUEST framework, integrating culturally responsive inquiry, pedagogical practices, technological affordances, and sociocultural equity. It recommends sustained teacher development, inclusive and culturally responsive digital integration, interdisciplinary curricula, adaptive instructional models, supportive policies, and scalable interventions for resource-limited settings. Future research should incorporate qualitative and mixed methods, include non-English publications and regional databases, and examine underexplored topics such as longitudinal argumentation development, teacher learning trajectories, culturally responsive pedagogy, and equitable implementation of computational thinking.

The human microbiota, once regarded as freeloaders, is now recognized as essential to health and involved in digestion, metabolism, immune responses, and inflammation. Disruption of gut microbes may contribute to conditions including childhood asthma, obesity, colitis, and colon cancer. Researchers estimate that a typical body contains about 39 trillion bacteria alongside 30 trillion human cells.

Microbial communities, collectively called the microbiome, vary in composition and activity throughout the day. Their daily rhythms may help explain how factors such as late-night eating and exposure to electric light after dark affect health. Mouse studies show that microbial metabolites circulating in the blood alter gene activity in the liver, affecting its circadian physiology. Antibiotics and altered feeding times changed these patterns, while gut microbes also influenced the liver’s response to acetaminophen, which was least toxic at dawn and most toxic at dusk. Researchers suggest that circadian variation in drug metabolism, potentially including chemotherapy, could affect treatment effectiveness and side effects, though this has not been established in humans.

Advances in DNA sequencing, statistical analysis, and computing have made it possible to study these vast, interdependent microbial communities. Humans, especially long-term antibiotic users and night or shift workers, may experience metabolic changes through microbiome pathways that could increase risks of obesity and metabolic syndrome.

Analysts viewed Article 50 as largely symbolic; sterling was expected to depend on the EU’s response, economic conditions and exit terms. It remained nearly 20% below its June Brexit-vote level. Retail buyers of euros were nervous, while companies increased hedging. Potential renewed Scottish independence voting added uncertainty.

Multi-organ research is a key frontier for understanding human aging and disease, and integrating AI with multi-organ imaging genetics promises to advance precision medicine while introducing quantitative intermediate endophenotypes. Three catalysts have advanced genetics: consolidation of large multi-omics datasets (UK Biobank, FinnGen), open-science efforts making GWAS summary statistics publicly available (FinnGen, PGC, GWAS Catalog, OpenGWAS, GWAS ATLAS, and brain imaging genetics portals such as BIG, BIG-KP, BRIDGEPORT, and MEDICINE), and computational genomics methods relying on GWAS summary statistics and linkage disequilibrium information (e.g., LDSC for SNP-based heritability and genetic correlations; Mendelian randomization for causal relationships), which depend on sensitive model assumptions. Despite these advances, the genetic foundation of AI endophenotypes for pleiotropic disease endpoints in multi-organ systems remains largely uncharted. The authors previously derived 2024 multi-organ AI endophenotypes (MAE), including 2,003 multi-scale brain structural covariance networks, 9 dimensional neuroimaging endophenotypes across four brain diseases, and 12 biological age gap measures across nine organ systems, and publicly released UKBB GWAS summary statistics via the MEDICINE portal. FinnGen released GWAS data for 2,269 binary and 3 quantitative disease endpoints from 377,277 individuals and 20,175,454 variants, and PGC made neurological disorder GWAS results public. This study uses these resources and advanced computational methods to characterize the genetic architecture of the 2024 MAEs and 525 disease endpoints (>5,000 cases), including 521 FinnGen endpoints and four PGC brain endpoints (Alzheimer's disease, ADHD, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia), systematically benchmarking genetic analyses and comparing statistical methodologies.

A man spent more than four hours on the roof of the Cambridge Mill restaurant before surrendering to negotiators. During the standoff, officers closed nearby roads and asked onlookers to let negotiators work. Two acquaintances told media the man was distressed over a recent breakup and had recently been restricted from the Bridges homeless shelter. The man, wearing a black fur-trimmed winter coat and camouflage pants, smoked, read a book, and tossed items to the ground, including clothing; a digital device found in the parking lot and along the Grand River is being investigated as stolen. After becoming agitated, he climbed down, paced the roof, appeared to survey escape options, slid down the far side of the peak, and then walked toward negotiators and surrendered. He was taken to Cambridge Memorial Hospital for a mental health assessment, with charges pending. General manager Alex Kastner said staff began assessing damage, theft, and how the man entered, and that the alarm system responded almost immediately, suggesting he was inside only three or four minutes before police were dispatched. The crowd in the street applauded the ending, and the company expressed gratitude to emergency services.

The passage specifies SD Memory Card physical interfaces, operating modes, initialization, commands, data transfer, erase operations, and write protection.

UHS-II standard-size cards use dedicated UHS-II contacts in addition to the SD bus interface, with SD bus contacts 7 and 8 assigned to RCLK. Cards must not drive unused SD lines in UHS-II mode, and hosts must keep those lines at defined levels. DAT[2] may be used as an interrupt line for UHS-II SDIO cards. Unused lines must be set low before VDD1 is turned off during hibernation. ROM cards are permanently or temporarily read-only cards; write-protected writable cards are excluded. ROM cards treat specified write and erase commands as unsupported, may optionally support CMD42 and security commands, and have no write-protect switch.

UHS-I supports DS at up to 25 MHz and 3.3 V, HS at up to 50 MHz and 3.3 V, SDR50, SDR104 at up to 208 MHz and 1.8 V, and DDR50 at up to 50 MHz and 1.8 V. Maximum throughput of 104 MB/s requires both host and card to support SDR104; otherwise performance is limited to 50 MB/s. UHS-I applies to SDHC and SDXC cards, and DDR50 is mandatory for microSD and optional for standard-size cards. Initialization uses CMD0, ACMD41, and CMD11 to switch to 1.8 V signaling when supported. UHS-I operates in 4-bit mode except for CMD42, uses CMD6 to select bus speed, driver strength, and power limits, and uses CMD19 for sampling-point tuning when required.

UHS-II adds the SD bus modes DS, HS, optional SDR104, and optional DDR50, along with FD156, optional HD312, FD312, and FD624 interface modes. Their stated maximum rates range from 156 MB/s to 624 MB/s. HD312 cannot be used in ring topology. A UHS-II host must support both the legacy SD bus and UHS-II interfaces. During initialization, the host supplies RCLK and STB.L and starts UHS-II initialization when STB.L is detected on the second lane; otherwise, after a 200-microsecond timeout, it may initialize the card through the SD bus interface. UHS-II initialization comprises PHY, device, enumeration, configuration, and SD-TRAN initialization.

The specification defines Application Performance Class minimums, including 500 write and 1,500 read IOPS with 10 MB/s sustained sequential write, or 2,000 write and 4,000 read IOPS using Command Queue and Cache. Cache can lose unflushed data at power-off. Self Maintenance performs internal background data management, while Command Queue allows command submission during data transfer in voluntary or sequential modes. A Low Voltage Interface permits initialization using 1.8 V I/O. The enhanced FD624 mode is also designated UHS-III; UHS-II cards support Ranges A and B, while UHS-III cards support Ranges A through D.

The host controls all communication through broadcast and addressed commands. Card identification mode uses only the command line and covers reset, voltage validation, card identification, and RCA publication; data transfer mode uses point-to-point communication with a selected card. CMD0 resets cards, and CMD8 verifies the supplied operating voltage and check pattern. CMD8 must precede the first ACMD41 when initializing SDHC or SDXC cards. ACMD41 must follow CMD55, uses the OCR voltage window and HCS field, and is repeated until the card becomes ready or the host’s timeout expires. An OCR value of zero permits a voltage-range query without starting initialization. CMD2 obtains the CID, CMD3 assigns the RCA, and SDXC initialization follows the SDHC process.

Data transfer includes card selection through CMD7, CSD retrieval through CMD9, optional DSR configuration through CMD4, and bus-width selection through ACMD6. Read commands include CMD17 and CMD18, while CMD12 can abort reads and writes. Blocks use CRC protection. Block-read units have a maximum size of 512 bytes, and CMD16 may select block lengths up to 512 bytes. CMD24 and CMD25 perform block writes, and the card may buffer data while indicating busy status on DAT0. Reads and parameter-setting commands are not accepted while programming. CMD32 and CMD33 followed by CMD38 identify and erase ranges. DISCARD may deallocate selected blocks, leaves their contents undefined, and is limited to SDHC and SDXC cards outside SPI mode. FULE logically erases the entire user area, also applies only to SDHC and SDXC cards outside SPI mode, and has a one-second busy timeout.

Write protection may be implemented mechanically, internally by the card, or through password locking. Password data is stored in PWD/PWD_LEN registers, while optional Card Ownership Protection uses an FEP/FEP_LEN password. CMD42 provides password set, change, clear, lock, unlock, Force Erase, and COP functions, with errors reported through LOCK_UNLOCK_FAILED. When FEP is set, COP Unlock using CMD42[1Fh] is required after reset before other CMD42 functions are available. Force Erase is disabled when FEP is set; FEP Force Erase requires the correct FEP and leaves the FEP registers unchanged. Locked cards accept basic commands, ACMD41, CMD16, and the lock-card command class, while other commands are illegal.

CMD55 marks the next command as an application-specific command. ACMD41 is a defined exception whose response does not carry the APP_CMD status. CMD56 provides a general command extension. CMD6 switches or expands card functions through four groups: access mode, command system, driver strength, and power limit. It is mandatory for cards compliant with Physical Layer Specification Version 1.10 or later, is valid in the Transfer State, and requires checking the card’s specification version or CSD support bits before use.

The passage argues that employers’ liability laws should place the full cost of workplace accidents and deaths on employers, who could incorporate those costs into production prices and pass them to consumers. It also urges coverage for employees in navy yards, arsenals, and similar facilities.

It supports compulsory government investigation of disputes between employers and employees, using the anthracite coal commission as a model, to promote conciliation and prevent strikes and lockouts. From 1881 to 1900, strikes affected 117,509 establishments and displaced 6,105,694 workers, while 1,005 lockouts affected nearly 10,000 establishments and displaced more than one million people. A national conciliation and arbitration commission could hear both sides impartially, resolve misunderstandings, and encourage settlements without legally binding the parties.

Quest Diagnostics grew from a New York pathology laboratory into the largest U.S. diagnostic-testing company by revenue, reaching $7.4 billion in 2014 through acquisitions and a network of more than 2,000 patient service centers. Its core laboratory business weakened beginning in 2008, including the loss of UnitedHealthcare to LabCorp. CEO Steve Rusckowski, hired in 2012, introduced a turnaround strategy centered on operational excellence, growth, organizational simplification, and “Everyday Excellence.” Jim Davis and Scott Jeffers began standardizing processes through the Quest Management System while focusing attention on employee turnover, which cost Quest an estimated $50 million to $70 million annually.

Quest consolidated 20 regional customer service centers into two National Customer Service centers in Lenexa, Kansas, and Tampa, Florida, supported by approximately 250 work-at-home representatives. The centers operated continuously, averaging 55,000 calls daily, with 70% being inbound requests for test results. Consolidation difficulties, high labor costs, 60% first-year representative turnover, more than two-minute wait times, low first-call resolution, inconsistent regional systems, and frequent transfers contributed to customer losses. Davis and Jeffers prioritized quickly answering calls and having representatives resolve questions on the first attempt.

The NCS employed regional “pods” for physicians and hospitals and national pods for patients. Representatives handled technical and administrative questions, often requiring specialized knowledge of tests, specimen handling, and company policies. New representatives received six weeks of classroom training and were supposed to shadow experienced colleagues, but understaffing frequently prevented this. It took about 90 days to become productive, while roughly 80% of training time went to onboarding. Compensation and performance standards emphasized speed to answer, calls completed per hour, and attendance. Regional differences complicated workforce routing, while unplanned absenteeism, supervisor overload, and escalating calls contributed to unstable operations.

Quest’s customer service offering included laboratory results and support through online portals, Care360, QuestConnect, and MyQuest. Representatives also handled test orders, complaints, billing questions, and routing for physicians, patients, and employees. The NCS served throughout the specimen lifecycle, from collection and transportation through testing, result delivery, and billing.

In 2015, managers identified four immediate priorities: implementing step-based pay tied to skills, creating career paths, improving supervisor development, and developing a workforce-planning strategy. MaryAnn Camacho joined as Executive Director of National Customer Service in July 2015, observed frontline work and listened to calls, and recognized that broader operational changes were needed to reduce wait times, improve first-call resolution, and make NCS a more attractive workplace.

After ratifying a reciprocity treaty with Hawaii, the king sent a commissioner to Japan to negotiate a commercial treaty; the U.S. minister at Honolulu opposed it as diverting trade from the United States and fostering British competition. In December 1868, President Johnson argued that reciprocity would protect Hawaii from foreign control and preserve stability until its people voluntarily sought union with the United States. Annexation sentiment persisted, but Seward deferred action because of Reconstruction. U.S. intervention against the coolie trade failed to curb it. In 1871, Minister Henry A. Pierce urged renewed consideration of annexation, and President Grant sent his dispatch confidentially to the Senate for its views. Pierce’s abstract called annexation the islands’ perceived political destiny and cited Hawaiian consent after the king’s death, native depopulation, foreign settlement, Palmerston’s opinions, and Hawaiian history.

The Money Flow Index (MFI) is a momentum oscillator from 0 to 100 that combines price and volume data to measure money flowing into and out of a security, identify overbought and oversold conditions, and signal potential reversals. It resembles a volume-weighted RSI and differs from Chaikin Money Flow, which relies on price and exponential moving averages without volume. MFI also generates bullish and bearish divergence signals, which can be identified with trendlines on price and the indicator.

The article cites readings above 80 as overbought and generally describes readings at or below 20 as oversold, although its strategy section uses 30; it states that 80/20 is the common threshold. Extreme signals work best in range-bound markets, while traders are advised to follow strong trends rather than trade countertrend. The default lookback is 14 periods; longer periods produce fewer, potentially more reliable signals, while shorter periods produce more, often false, signals. Optimal settings should be backtested for the market and strategy.

The proposed strategy combines MFI extremes with bearish engulfing patterns for short trades and bullish engulfing patterns for long trades. Reported tests showed a 10.4% annual return for Pepsi versus 9.8% for buy-and-hold, a 10.6% CAGR for SPY versus 9.7%, and a 15% CAGR for a combined PEP/SPY portfolio. Performance on GLD was poor, attributed to mean reversion not working well for commodities. The passage concludes that MFI can aid trade timing, but profitability depends on proper use and backtesting.

This descriptive bibliometric and content-analysis study reviewed 273 modern physics education studies conducted in Turkey between 2000 and 2023. Studies were purposively selected from national and international databases using specified Turkish and English keywords. A Modern Physics Education Publication Classification Form was developed, reviewed by five experts, pilot-tested on 12 studies, and applied by two coders with 91% coding reliability. Data were coded in Excel and analyzed in SPSS.

Most studies were articles published in Turkish, with publication activity concentrated between 2010 and 2020, peaking in 2019, 2015, and 2016 before declining. The most frequently studied topics were atoms, the photoelectric effect, relativity, nuclear energy, the Compton effect, and Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle. Common objectives included evaluating instructional methods and materials, assessing students’ cognitive and affective characteristics, and reviewing curricula, textbooks, and measurement instruments.

Quantitative studies commonly used quasi-experimental designs and descriptive surveys, while qualitative research most often used case studies. Samples generally involved education-faculty undergraduates, high-school or middle-school students, and teachers; the most common sample size was 31–100. Many studies did not report their sampling method or intervention duration, and long-term interventions were uncommon. Interviews, tests, questionnaires, and scales were the most used data-collection tools, while frequency/percentage, t-tests, item analysis, content analysis, and descriptive analysis dominated data analysis. Validity and reliability practices varied, with reporting often insufficient.

Reported outcomes included improved achievement, concretized knowledge, problem-solving and higher-order thinking, and more positive attitudes, alongside persistent classical-physics interpretations, conceptual misconceptions, and negative emotions. Textbooks and curricula were frequently criticized for unclear or age-inappropriate content, limited visual support, and inadequate reflection of modern physics. Although most discussions cited supporting literature, explanations were often insufficient or absent.

Recommendations included larger and more varied samples, especially among secondary-school students; greater use of qualitative and mixed-method designs; longer interventions; simulations, interactive experiments, visual materials, and individualized instruction; incorporation of modern physics philosophy, history, and interdisciplinary links; development of a dedicated curriculum; and improved textbook and validity/reliability reporting.

This disclosure (a continuation application claiming priority from U.S. Provisional Application No. 62/354,059 filed Jun. 23, 2016) relates to computer vision and to machine recognition and identification of objects appearing in video or image content.

Background: Video and image content contains many objects that humans readily perceive but machines struggle to recognize and identify. Because objects in an image stream constantly move, appear, and disappear, automated recognition in continuous video requires substantial computation, which is challenging for resource-limited devices such as smart TVs, computers, and phones. Viewers also lack information about depicted products (maker, year, price, brand, where to purchase, local inventory), and current content delivery systems such as Netflix, Apple TV, and Amazon Prime provide no product recognition, while brands and merchants cannot reach such viewers. The same shortcomings exist for images in digital photo galleries on social media sites and other web pages.

Disclosed embodiments provide systems, methods, and non-transitory storage media for automated recognition of objects in video/image content. A system has a memory and a processor configured to: receive a video stream of video frames; select at least one frame according to a frame selection rate; partition the selected frame into a first plurality of image blocks; recognize a second plurality of image blocks comprising an image of an object based on an image recognition parameter determined by a machine-learning algorithm; determine that at least one of those blocks corresponds to the object based on a likelihood metric derived at least from the frame selection rate; and display information identifying the object.

Detailed embodiments: A system includes a media device, content database, product database, merchant database, media server, and network. The media device (tablet, smartphone, computer, set-top box, game console, etc.) includes a recognition engine with frame selection, partition, analysis, and accuracy modules plus display, communication, and data interfaces and a shopping cart module. The frame selection rate (e.g., every frame, every other frame, one of three) controls how often frames are analyzed; higher rates yield higher likelihood metrics but greater processing cost, and rates may be changed by viewer input or automatically by the accuracy module. The partition module divides frames into pixel blocks (e.g., 16×16, 32×32) or leaves the frame whole. The analysis module applies machine-learning algorithms (including deep learning with layered neural networks) using weighted parameter sets, optionally informed by product-database data and exchanged with other devices/servers, detecting edges, colors, shapes, features, and text; it identifies a first region via feature metrics/thresholds, then iteratively narrows to sections, comparing likelihood metrics to predetermined thresholds until a product is accurately recognized, optionally using image matching and audio/speech analysis. Title profiles store products recognized per content title to populate carts without re-analysis.

The shopping cart module populates a digital cart (in real time, delayed, or pre-populated) with recognized products, aggregates product and merchant data (price, brand, description, availability, vendors, reviews), personalizes carts and recommendations using viewer transaction, browsing, social media, and messaging data, prioritizes items by interest level, allows purchase in real time or later, links to merchants (including preferred merchants based on revenue/referral agreements, inventory, and price), and may display advertisements. User interfaces show a content region alongside an overlay or side shopping-cart or widget region that is transparent or opaque, may fade in/out, appear at intervals, or be user-prompted, displaying product descriptions, recommendations, and checkout/clear controls, with widgets moving automatically to product-free areas and revealing carts or merchant links on selection. The media device and/or media server include memory, processors, storage, operating systems, and communication software.

Using group theory and first-principles DFT, the study identifies and quantifies higher-order atomic magnetic multipoles in altermagnets by projecting real-space spin density onto tesseral harmonics. In MnF₂, a d-wave altermagnet, an octupole and a 32-pole are in phase, producing a macroscopic multipole despite canceled dipoles. In CrSb, a g-wave altermagnet, octupoles cancel while an in-phase 32-pole remains.

The noncollinear spin density is much smaller than the collinear component but more clearly reveals the symmetry and relative phase of altermagnetic multipoles. Without spin-orbit coupling (SOC), noncollinear components vanish. Finite SOC induces symmetry-allowed noncollinear octupoles and 32-poles linearly in SOC strength, while modifying collinear multipoles only slightly and quadratically.

In KMnF₃, antiferromagnetic order and fluorine-octahedral rotations break anti-translation symmetry and induce altermagnetism. An in-phase 32-pole grows linearly with the rotation angle. These multipoles connect to macroscopic response tensors, including piezomagnetism, second-order magnetoelectric effects, and strain-induced magnetization. The results emphasize the importance of higher-order multipoles, noncollinear spin density, SOC, and structural symmetry in real altermagnets.

The study examines the relationship between open and vocational education, two systems that support adult and lifelong learning and help learners gain professional qualifications, knowledge, skills, and ethics. Chinese policies have promoted their development, flexible learning, open educational resources, and recognition of learning achievements. Both domestic and international research supports their integration, although China has focused more directly on coordinated development, while foreign research emphasizes adult education and online learning.

Using CiteSpace 6.2.R2, the study analyzed literature published from 2012 to 2023 through keyword co-occurrence, research-hotspot timelines, and citation-burst analysis. Chinese literature came from CNKI, while foreign literature came from Web of Science and was refined with additional search terms related to open, adult, and vocational education.

In China, major research hotspots included open and vocational education, higher vocational education, open universities, distance education, and integrated development. Research before 2016 primarily examined the separate development models of the two sectors; afterward, it increasingly addressed their integration through teaching models, curricula, online education, credit systems, professional and course integration, evaluation, and learning outcomes. Citation bursts from 2014 to 2015 included teaching processes, credit recognition, higher vocational education, open educational resources, and integrated school management. Since 2018, integrated and coordinated development have received strong attention.

Research outside China primarily focused on vocational education, adult education, vocational training, online learning, professional development, and lifelong learning. Since 2013, attention has centered on adult vocational education and skills, and since 2018, online learning for adult learners has become increasingly prominent. Citation bursts since 2020 include online learning, vocational education and training, adult and blended learning, young adults, technology, and personality, with online learning and vocational training showing the strongest bursts.

The findings indicate a divergence between China’s emphasis on integrating the two education systems and other countries’ emphasis on adult skills and online learning. The 1-3-1 zone is presented as a versatile defense built around overplaying passing lanes, spreading the offense, and creating interception and deflection opportunities. It emphasizes active, coordinated movement, reading the passer’s eyes and motions, and personnel assignments favoring a strong left-wing rebounder, an agile baseline defender, and a tall player at the top against small guards. Ball-location shifts for all five defensive positions are detailed, along with adjustments for skip passes, baseline closeouts, middle penetration, and weak-side rebounding. The “Three in a Line” variation keeps a big defender near the basket while wings cover the corners and maintain help defense. Trapping is a central feature, especially near the corners and out-of-bounds lines. Traps can be hard or soft; defenders should pressure without fouling or reaching, force lob or bounce passes, deny escape lanes, and capitalize on deflections and interceptions. Specific trap alignments and role exchanges after skip passes are also described. The zone can extend into half-court or full-court pressure.

The invention provides a system and method for multiple-factor verification of vision-based interactions using two or more complementary monitoring systems. Each system generates an evaluation, and a verification system combines the evaluations to determine monitoring alignment, including agreement, discrepancies, confidence levels, and updated interaction models. A preferred implementation uses computer vision, potentially with multiple cameras, alongside an independent system having different attack vectors, capabilities, and limitations.

Monitoring systems may include computer vision, RFID or other radio-frequency tags, smart infrastructure sensors and scales, user applications, smart carts, point-of-sale systems, profile prediction systems, and security-tag barriers. The invention is described primarily for retail, including checkout-free and expedited checkout using virtual carts, but it also applies to security monitoring, rentals, healthcare, manufacturing, autonomous vehicles, and other computer-vision-driven activities.

The method executes at least two monitoring systems, determines their alignment, and triggers actions such as enabling or halting checkout, directing worker inspections, scoring customer profiles, generating operational recommendations, updating or retraining monitoring systems, and triggering security alarms. The combined approach may improve accuracy, reduce false positives, limit manual inspections, mitigate adversarial manipulation, support system training, and increase user trust.

The report defines a lipid profile as total cholesterol (TC), HDL cholesterol (HDL-c), triglycerides (TG), and LDL cholesterol (LDL-c). It notes that HIV/AIDS remains a major global health burden, while ART reduces HIV-related morbidity and mortality but may alter lipid levels and increase cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk. Because CVD risk among people living with HIV receiving ART in Rwanda was not well characterized, the study assessed their lipid profiles, cardiovascular risk, and associations with ART regimens at University Teaching Hospital of Butare (CHUB).

This cross-sectional study was conducted from January to February 2021. It included 199 participants: 150 HIV-positive ART recipients and 49 HIV-negative controls. Participants were selected systematically, and those with hepatitis B/C, thyroid abnormalities, pregnancy, hypertension, kidney disease, diabetes, alcoholism, or obesity were excluded. Serum lipid levels were measured spectrophotometrically using Cypress kits and a Humalyzer 3500, and data were analyzed in Excel and SPSS, with P-values of ≤0.05 considered significant.

Among the ART group, 66% were female, the mean age was 49.4 years, and 72% received first-line treatment. Lipid abnormalities included hypertriglyceridemia in 32%, high LDL-c in 8%, low HDL-c in 19.3%, and hypercholesterolemia in 15.3%; TC was borderline high in 24% and normal in 60.6%. Compared with controls, ART recipients had significantly different triglyceride (P=0.046), LDL-c (P=0.039), HDL-c (P=0.021), and TC (P=0.045) distributions. The authors attributed differences between studies to factors such as population, setting, treatment duration, and participant exclusions.

The study concludes that ART recipients exhibited significant lipid-profile changes associated with potential CVD risk. It recommends routine lipid-profile testing in people living with HIV, additional cardiovascular tests such as troponin, creatine kinase-MB, CRP, and electrolytes, broader studies across health institutions, and use of the findings to inform CVD prevention and management policies.

This continuation application describes screen-display methods, apparatus, electronic devices, storage media, and program products for managing multiple application interfaces. To reduce obstruction, an electronic device can automatically minimize one interface when the user operates another. In one embodiment, a first application is displayed full screen while a second application appears as a floating window; operation on the first interface minimizes the floating window and displays it as a floating ball, application icon, contact avatar, or video pop-up. Edit-box focus events can trigger minimization, focus loss can restore the floating window, and the minimized representation can be positioned away from the cursor. Operating a floating window can maximize it while minimizing the full-screen interface, including when multiple floating windows are present.

In a split-screen embodiment, two non-overlapping application interfaces are displayed side by side. Operating one interface displays it full screen and minimizes the other within it. Focus loss or interaction with the minimized interface can restore the side-by-side display, and a maximization option can initiate the transition.

The embodiments also describe configurable floating-window sizes, shapes, and locations, transparency, and scaled interface elements. The detailed description outlines the device’s processor, memory, display, communications, audio, camera, sensors, and a layered Android software architecture in which a window manager adjusts interface parameters. These methods are embodied in screen-display apparatus, electronic devices, computer storage media, and computer program products.

Random numbers support Monte Carlo simulations, modeling, cryptography, and games. Cryptography requires unpredictable, robust randomness for key generation and encryption/decryption. Software PRNGs use deterministic mathematical models and seeds; if the seed and model are known, attackers can predict later values, making them unsuitable for cryptography. Hardware RNGs derive randomness from physical sources and are more suitable for cryptographic use. AMD’s Zen architecture includes a cryptographic coprocessor for generating secure random numbers, exposed by the Secure RNG library through an easy-to-use software API.

The passage surveys single-node and distributed container patterns. For sharded backends, routing can be handled by a stateless load balancer inside the service or by a client-side ambassador proxy. The ambassador exposes a single localhost endpoint, selects the appropriate storage shard, and separates application code from sharding logic. Kubernetes examples use Redis or Memcached shards with DNS-based services and twemproxy. Ambassadors can also broker environment-specific service connections and split traffic between production and experimental implementations; nginx can consistently route 10% of requests to an experiment through IP hashing.

The adapter pattern converts an application’s interface to a predefined standard through a separate, reusable container. It can adapt monitoring interfaces for Prometheus, normalize logs with Fluentd, capture Redis slow queries and Apache Storm events, and expose rich MySQL health checks. This avoids modifying heterogeneous or third-party application images and isolates failures while supporting reuse and independent updates.

Microservices divide an application into components running in separate processes and communicating through APIs. Compared with monoliths, this supports small autonomous teams, stable contracts, independent releases, and service-specific scaling, but complicates debugging, design, and failure diagnosis. Distributed patterns can reduce these difficulties by providing reusable designs.

Replicated load-balanced services use identical stateless replicas behind a load balancer. Multiple replicas provide redundancy and rolling-update resilience, while readiness probes distinguish running containers from those ready to serve requests. Session tracking may use IP hashing, cookies, or consistent hashing to minimize remapping when replicas change. A separate caching tier can improve latency and throughput, rate limiting can protect against excessive traffic, and a distinct nginx tier can terminate SSL using certificates separate from internal services.

Sharded services divide requests or state among shards, with a root selecting the appropriate shard. Sharding allows data to exceed one machine’s capacity and uses memory more efficiently than replicated caches. Sharding functions commonly apply deterministic, uniform hashing and modulo; keys must distinguish requests with different responses while grouping equivalent requests. Consistent hashing limits remapping during resizing. Replicating individual shards improves fault tolerance, upgrade safety, and scaling of overloaded “hot” shards.

Scatter/gather sends a request simultaneously to all leaves, combines their partial results, and improves latency through parallel processing. It can also use sharded data when the dataset exceeds one machine. However, coordination overhead and straggler nodes can limit gains, especially at high percentiles and with many leaves, so each leaf shard should be replicated for reliability.

Function-as-a-service provides rapid deployment, automatic scaling and restarts, and stateless modular functions, but complicates dependency tracing and debugging. It is poorly suited to long-running background work, large in-memory datasets, and sustained high request volumes because of execution limits, startup latency, and per-request pricing.

An open-blinded, cross-sectional study evaluated the urinary protein-to-creatinine (P/C) ratio in adults with symptomatic, drug-naïve urinary tract infections (UTIs) at Padmashree Diagnostics in Bangalore, India, from August 2017 to June 2018. Of 80 recruited participants, 27 were excluded for urinary creatinine below 20 mg/dL and seven for absent proteinuria, leaving 46 participants with a mean age of 38.11 ± 7.3 years; 67% were female and 33% male.

Urine specimens underwent microscopic assessment for pyuria, culture and sensitivity testing, reagent-strip protein screening, sulfosalicylic acid protein quantification, and spectrophotometric Jaffé creatinine measurement. Participants were classified by KDIGO-based P/C ratio as Stage I, below 15 mg/mM creatinine (12 participants); Stage II, 15–50 mg/mM (16); or Stage III, above 50 mg/mM (18).

Urinary creatinine was significantly reduced at all stages compared with the reference interval of 168 ± 132 mg/dL (p<0.001), although creatinine levels did not significantly differ among the three UTI stages. Mean urinary protein increased from 2.6 ± 1.7 mg/dL in Stage I to 8.0 ± 4.6 in Stage II and 48.5 ± 46.0 in Stage III; Stage III was significantly elevated versus the normal reference (p<0.001). Mean P/C ratios were 9.0 ± 3.6, 30.4 ± 8.0, and 180.6 ± 142.9 mg/mM creatinine, respectively, with a statistically significant increase across stages.

The authors concluded that proteinuria was associated with UTIs and that combining urinary protein and creatinine measurements improved assessment of renal involvement, with the P/C ratio serving as a useful marker of UTI-associated kidney impairment and disease severity. Longitudinal studies were recommended to evaluate prognostic significance and therapeutic outcomes.

TSLA options are derivatives that give holders the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell a set number of shares at a predetermined price by a specified date. They offer leverage, hedging, and speculation but also complexity and the potential for substantial or total losses. Buyers cannot lose more than the premium paid, while sellers face significant risk.

Strategies include long calls, long puts, covered calls, and spreads. Long calls and puts are directional bets, while covered calls and spreads can reduce risk; selling puts may generate income but carries substantial risk. Strategy selection should reflect risk tolerance, investment goals, and market outlook.

Potential returns depend on the option, strike price, and the underlying price at expiration. Common orders are limit, market, and stop orders. Options with shorter expirations and higher volume are generally more liquid. Fees vary by broker and may include commissions, platform, regulatory, and margin charges, while tax treatment depends on the trades and country.

The passage emphasizes backtesting, quantified analysis of past price patterns, a defined trading plan, and risk management such as stop losses and taking profits. Traders should avoid overtrading and entering positions without understanding returns and risks. Market sentiment may be useful, but decisions should be based on backtests rather than discretionary judgment. Profits cannot be protected from overnight market movements, although a clear plan can support automation and reduce unnecessary monitoring.

The message argues that the Constitution grants Congress no general power to undertake a system of “internal improvements,” including roads, canals, railroads, rivers, and harbors. Neither the Constitution’s preamble nor its general-welfare clause supplies such authority, and the phrase “internal improvements” is too undefined to establish a constitutional power. Enumerated powers authorize only specific works necessary to exercise them, such as roads, harbors, or canals required for military, naval, or commercial functions; using them to support a comprehensive federal program would improperly enlarge federal power, displace state and private enterprise, and burden the national treasury.

The message reviews congressional acceptance of lighthouses, beacons, buoys, and piers, followed later by appropriations for river and harbor improvement. Statutes from 1789 and 1845, upheld by the Supreme Court, identified public navigable waters as salt or fresh waters navigable by vessels of specified tonnage and used in foreign or interstate commerce. Nevertheless, no fixed constitutional line divides permissible federal projects from local ones, requiring caution, especially when spending primarily promotes revenue rather than military or naval needs.

The message recommends that permanent federal harbor works receive ceded land and jurisdiction, that each project be considered in a separate bill, and that federal appropriations be limited to works necessary to exercise unquestionably constitutional powers. Other improvements should be undertaken by states or private interests and funded locally.

The passage describes a continuation patent application (Ser. No. 16/003,543, filed Jun. 8, 2018) claiming priority to U.S. Pat. No. 10,019,011 and Provisional Ser. No. 62/569,718 (filed Oct. 9, 2017), directed to autonomous vehicle technology featuring a machine-learned yield model.

Described embodiments include a computing system controlling an autonomous vehicle, the autonomous vehicle itself, and a computer-implemented method: each obtains feature data descriptive of a first object perceived by the vehicle, inputs it into a machine-learned yield model, receives a yield decision describing yield behavior relative to that object, and (for the method) generates a motion plan executing that behavior and controls the vehicle's motion accordingly.

In the detailed description, an autonomy computing system includes a perception system (receiving LIDAR, RADAR, camera, and positioning sensor data plus map data, and determining object state data such as position, velocity, acceleration, heading, orientation, footprint, and class), a prediction system (predicting future object locations), and a motion planning system with a trajectory generator, an optimization planner (e.g., iterative linear quadratic regulator), cost/reward functions, and scenario controllers such as a yield controller, pass/ignore/queue controller, lane change controller, and speed regressor.

Features used by the yield model may describe an object's location relative to travel ways and the vehicle, its relationship to the vehicle's travel route, required deceleration or acceleration (optionally compared with jerk limits), traffic signal transition timing and last transition time, stop line, cross traffic line, and exit point locations, and gap data (temporal gap start/end, predicted red light time, distances to enter/exit, required acceleration, intersection type). The model may output a yield or no-yield decision, score gaps for selection, and generate gap penalties using push and stop fences. Gridlock-prevention analysis may use lead vehicle and following vehicle position, velocity, acceleration, distance to rear bumper, distance to crossing line, available queueing space, and traffic signal characteristics, either overwriting gap-based decisions or serving as an input to them. The motion planning system then generates cost-optimized trajectories complying with the yield decision.

Training may be supervised using log data annotated with yield labels, simulated yield behaviors, hand labeling, or automatic scoring functions with thresholds, including pairwise labeling of yield versus no-yield outcomes and a gap labeling scheme comparing gap plan scores to a stop plan score. Stated benefits include replacing hand-crafted rules, lower memory and faster decisions, on-board operation avoiding remote latency, improved safety and comfort, scalability across locations, and easier retraining.

Studies over more than 20 years involving 4,979 children, along with international research, suggest that close work—including reading and screen use—is not an important driver of childhood myopia, while outdoor light exposure can reduce its development. Myopia typically begins in early elementary school and causes distant vision to blur because the eye grows too long; glasses or contact lenses are generally needed lifelong because the eye cannot shrink.

Having two nearsighted parents raises a child’s risk to about 60% when outdoor time is low. About 14 hours outdoors per week can lower that risk to roughly 20%, comparable to children without nearsighted parents. Outdoor time, however, has little or no effect on prescription changes in children already nearsighted.

The leading proposed mechanism is that brighter outdoor light triggers retinal dopamine release, signaling slower, normal eye growth. Other possibilities include exercise and vitamin D, but more research is needed. Regular childhood eye examinations are important because children may not recognize blurred vision as abnormal. Sun protection and sunglasses are advisable because ultraviolet exposure can create other skin and eye problems.
