The passage explains the offensive guard position in football as an under-appreciated but vital offensive-line role, sharing responsibilities with centers and tackles while requiring both strength and athleticism. Guards use intelligence, tenacity, and quickness to block for the run and pass, often facing powerful defensive tackles and blitzing linebackers alone; allowing A or B gap penetration pressures quarterbacks and disrupts timing, unlike tackles who can let quarterbacks step up or slide. Football IQ, awareness, communication, and handling stunts, twists, blitzes, and simulated pressures are essential. In running, guards combine toughness and technique to win matchups, form double teams, enable runs up the gut for 4+ yards, pull to second and third levels, and kick out defensive ends to create lanes. Guards line up in the interior between tackles and center; the origin of the term is unclear. Abbreviations include G, LG, and RG, with nicknames like Hogs, Bruisers, Bulldozers, Big Uglies, and Monsters. Required skills include functional strength, footwork, agility, speed, hand placement, and blocking technique; a typical build is 6'3"–6'5", 300–320 pounds, sturdy and compact. Notable guards cited are Larry Allen (11 Pro Bowls, one Super Bowl) and John Hannah (7-time All-Pro, Hall of Fame).

KPMG reports that U.S. organizations deploying AI agents quadrupled from 11% to 42% in six months, while employee resistance fell from 47% to 21%. A KPMG principal said direct experience shifted workplace sentiment from fear to “cognitive fatigue,” but AI remains immature for most enterprise uses and still requires human oversight. Although technology departments lead adoption, leaders increasingly view AI as an enabler that calls for critical thinking, questioning and adaptability rather than worker replacement. Traditional KPIs miss much of AI’s value, according to 78% of leaders, who are tracking productivity, profitability and quality. AI is also reshaping entry-level work, with 56% of leaders expecting recruitment changes within a year.

The passage outlines a three-phase early offense system. Phase 1, the Early Push, advances the ball before the defense can organize, creating mismatches and forcing defenders to react. Getting the ball into the offensive operating area within two to four seconds may produce an open one-on-one opportunity. Coaches are urged to teach how to attack outnumbered situations: breakaways should prioritize passing ahead, scoring, and preventing transition opportunities; 2-on-1 and 3-on-1 situations should aim for layups, often by creating another numerical advantage; 3-on-2 situations should produce open jump shots and putbacks; and 3-on-3 situations should create a 3-on-2 advantage. Players should use few dribbles, finish strongly while staying inbounds, box out for rebounds, and avoid charges. After careless inbounds following an opponent’s missed layup, the shooter may attempt a solo press steal. Missed layups in practice are not tolerated and result in automatic push-ups. Proven fast breaks rely on quick, wide lane releases involving wing, middle, trailer, and push lanes.

Phase 2, Early Flow, begins when the initial push does not create a good shot or advantage. The offense should flow directly into action without bringing the ball back out, preventing the defense from setting and allowing offenses to exploit isolations and two- or three-man opportunities. These flow actions function as half-court offenses and include a collection of 64 sets organized by go-to player, screen action, isolation type, and other categories. Successful execution depends on spacing and player strengths and weaknesses.

Phase 3, Continuity, continues attacking without hesitation as the shot clock declines, preventing defensive organization and rushed shots while maintaining court balance, rebounding position, and second efforts. Flex Continuity uses baseline and down screens in a “pick the picker” action, with multiple passing, posting, reversal, lob, and back-cut options. Passing Game Continuity favors quick, athletic players, continuous movement, open lanes, and individual freedom, requiring strong offensive-rebounding practice. Mid Screen Continuity centers action around an on-ball screen for penetration, pull-up shooting, rolling, or kick-out passes. Side Screen Continuity is a simple but versatile late-clock action offering drives, jump shots, rolls, and outlets when trapped. Inside Triangle Game uses strong interior screeners, wing spacing, reversals, post options, back screens, and skip passes to create scoring opportunities and defensive mismatches.

SanDisk’s EULA grants users a limited, nonexclusive, non-sublicensable, transferable, royalty-free license to use bundled software solely for personal use on SanDisk products and services on one computer or hardware device at a time. Users may not modify, translate, reverse engineer, disassemble, decompile, rent, lease, disclose proprietary information, separate components, or embed the software into other products. SanDisk and its licensors retain ownership. The software is provided “as is” and “as available” without warranties, and users assume the risk and costs of defects. Liability for damages is excluded, and total liability cannot exceed the amount paid for the software. Government use is subject to restricted-rights provisions. SanDisk may terminate the license for violations, requiring users to delete or destroy all copies. The software is not intended for hazardous or other high-risk activities requiring fail-safe performance. California and U.S. federal law govern, with exclusive venue in Santa Clara County, California, and export-law restrictions apply. The device must not be disposed of with unsorted household waste; users should consult local waste authorities for return and collection systems.

Costco sells gold, silver, and platinum bars and coins to members online and at certain warehouses. Inventory and transaction limits vary, and products priced near commodity spot prices can sell out quickly. Online orders typically arrive within 3–5 days. In stores, shoppers can call ahead or check displays, complete a merchandise pickup slip, and pay at the front office. Precious metals are excluded from Costco’s return policy and price adjustments. The article advises against financing purchases with credit-card debt and warns that selling metals may require advance planning and involve unexpected costs.

The passage reviews literature on STEM education, project-based learning (PBL), design processes, architectural studio education, technical drawing, and visual communication. STEM education emphasizes problem-solving, collaboration, critical thinking, creativity, and real-life contexts, while PBL is described as learner-centered, teacher-supported, constructivist learning that crosses subject boundaries and involves research, experimentation, knowledge construction, and reflection. Design is characterized as a cyclical, feedback-driven process rather than a linear search for one perfect solution. Architectural education centers on studio-based learning, where students address open-ended design problems, learn by doing, communicate visually, and develop their work through repeated critique. Its historical roots include the French Academy of Architecture and the Bauhaus, and criticism is presented as central to developing spatial thinking, professional knowledge, creativity, and reflection in action. Technical drawing and graphics are important communication tools that also support spatial thinking.

The study’s purpose is to identify prominent elements of first-year architectural design education at BUU Faculty of Architecture and use analogical reasoning to identify possible implications for STEM education. The researchers addressed the lack of literature connecting these disciplines and selected an ethnographic method to examine how students learn design. The researcher observed a first-semester architectural design class for four weeks, recording student presentations, teacher critiques, students’ responses, and their use of visual communication without participating in class discussions. The class contained 30 students working in six groups on different plots. Observation reports were transcribed, coded, and analyzed thematically, while interviews with eight volunteer students were used to check consistency and strengthen validity. The findings were also compared with relevant literature, and theoretical triangulation was employed.

Students researched design solutions, prepared drawings and models, and presented their developing work through sketches, concept sheets, storyboards, plans, scale models, and other visual techniques. They received critique twice weekly and presented increasingly developed projects over several weeks. Four themes emerged: confronting open-ended problems; gaining experience in portfolio-file preparation; developing presentation techniques; and meeting a culture of criticism. Instruction encouraged students to think beyond familiar approaches, investigate problems thoroughly, consult prior work, examine sites and community needs, justify design decisions, and consider spatial, structural, functional, environmental, safety, cost, and construction issues. Teachers challenged assumptions and errors, while students defended, revised, and improved their proposals. Interviews indicated that students regarded the course as developing conceptual and abstract thinking, but identified difficulties involving models, hand drawing, presentations, time, motivation, perfectionism, and repeated design revisions.

The discussion offers six analogical implications for STEM education: all grade levels should receive sustained opportunities to solve open-ended problems independently through experimentation and learning from mistakes; project work should be strengthened and, at upper-secondary and undergraduate levels, potentially serve as a graduation requirement, while lower grades should focus on problem situations; STEM problems should be authentic, connected to students’ lives, and meaningful in terms of sustainability and economic value; younger students should physically encounter relevant materials, tools, and equipment even when they are not expected to produce concrete products; technical drawing and graphics courses should be included in general high-school programs; and undergraduate instruction should move beyond technical rationality toward reflection in action while adopting studio-style critique and jury-based assessment. These STEM conclusions are presented as analogical inferences rather than as effects directly tested by the study.
The court denied Atkins’s coram nobis application, finding he failed to establish ineffective assistance of appellate counsel.

The American Red Cross reports its blood supply is still recovering from severe March winter storms, which canceled more than 270 blood drives nationwide, leaving over 9,500 donations uncollected; Connecticut lost 39 drives and 1,287 donations. Donors are urged to give blood when it's safe.

Acordis, IT provider for the Miami Heat, will sponsor the Jewish Federation of Broward County's "Men's Nite Out" on May 9, 2018, at The Signature Grand in Davie, featuring "Mr. October" Reggie Jackson. Acordis helps firms cut costs via technology; registration starts at 6:00 PM for networking.

Kalai explains that Fiat–Shamir is not automatically sound in the random-oracle model. A cheating prover can query the oracle, guess each verifier challenge, and retry with a different commitment until the guess succeeds; presenting only the successful transcript hides these repeated attempts. Thus a protocol with a \(1/2\) cheating probability remains insecure, and even sequential repetition to make the error \(2^{-\lambda}\) does not prevent the attack.

He proves that Fiat–Shamir is sound in the random-oracle model for a public-coin protocol with a constant number of rounds and negligible soundness error. The reduction converts a polynomial-time cheating prover in the noninteractive version into an interactive prover that succeeds with probability at least its success probability divided by its query bound, minus a negligible amount, yielding a contradiction. For \(c\) verifier messages, the corresponding loss is \(q^c\). Protocols with many rounds may also qualify under round-by-round soundness, as GKR does.

Kilian–Micali has four rounds and can achieve negligible error, so Fiat–Shamir is sound for it in the random-oracle model. The lecture stresses that this model is only a theoretical sanity check: it does not prove security for an explicit hash function, and contrived hash functions can make the protocol insecure.

Sequential repetition preserves zero knowledge, but parallel repetition of the particular three-round Hamiltonian-graph zero-knowledge protocol does not. A 2019 result showed that this protocol is Fiat–Shamir sound; if it were zero knowledge, an efficient simulator could produce an accepted transcript for a no-instance and thereby break Fiat–Shamir soundness. Thus the lecture states that an interactive proof satisfying Fiat–Shamir soundness cannot be zero knowledge. Kalai also notes that practical security failures are more often caused by weak randomness, poor key generation, or implementation flaws than by failures of the cryptographic core.

The paper examines AI’s expanding role in higher education and its effects on teaching, research, administration, student engagement, and workforce preparation. Adoption is accelerating globally, with 86% of surveyed students using AI for academic purposes. Common applications include intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, predictive analytics, automated grading, generative AI, chatbots, real-time translation, and virtual simulations. These tools can personalize instruction, provide immediate feedback, identify students at risk of dropping out, streamline administrative work, accelerate research, and improve course completion and retention.

Institutions are responding through faculty training, interdisciplinary AI curricula, policy frameworks, and collaboration among educators, policymakers, technologists, and students. China’s Squirrel AI and Arizona State University are highlighted as examples of scaled implementation. ChatGPT is presented as useful for writing and brainstorming, Bard for real-time research and data, and Gemini for emotionally responsive learning. AI also supports collaboration, lifelong learning, accessibility for students with disabilities, career preparation, and teaching across the performing arts, sciences, medicine, business, and liberal arts.

Significant barriers remain, including faculty resistance, inadequate infrastructure, limited funding, digital divides, academic dishonesty, algorithmic bias, privacy and consent concerns, lack of transparency, and possible student dependence on AI for emotional support or decision-making. Ethical oversight, robust academic-integrity policies, diverse stakeholder participation, targeted investment, and continuous evaluation are therefore essential.

The paper recommends treating AI as complementary to educators rather than a replacement for human instruction. Institutions should strengthen digital literacy, involve students in AI design and governance, ensure equitable access, align implementation with institutional and public policies, and support interdisciplinary research on AI’s long-term effects on learning, critical thinking, and emotional intelligence. Collaborative and ethically governed adoption is presented as essential to ensuring that AI advances higher education without widening inequalities.

Players kept their game plan, stayed composed while down a goal instead of opening up, and scored, including one goal past Belfour. They called it unfortunate that Dr. McMullen must sell the team, saying they are hockey players, not business people. A goalie said facing the same shooter twice feels odd.

The North Dakota Supreme Court reversed the suppression of evidence obtained after Denise Hahne failed to stop at a temporary sobriety checkpoint and was charged with driving under the influence. The district court had assumed that checkpoints must give motorists a safe and legal opportunity to avoid them, but the court held that avoidance is merely one factor in evaluating the intrusion caused by a checkpoint stop. Checkpoint constitutionality turns on whether the seizure is reasonable under the three-part balancing test addressing public concerns, advancement of the public interest, and interference with individual liberty. Hahne’s first-time argument concerning checkpoint effectiveness was not preserved. The case was remanded to determine whether the checkpoint was constitutionally reasonable.

New Jersey ranked 25th in a 2018 healthcare scorecard, down two spots and below all other Northeast states. It performed well in access to care, children’s coverage and infant mortality, but could improve preventive care, reduce readmissions and control medical costs.

OECD says trade restrictions and high oil prices threaten global growth, while tariffs could hurt confidence, investment and jobs. It cut this year’s world growth forecast to 3.8%, with 3.9% expected next year.

Alan A. Brister sued the United States for a refund of 1989–1992 tax overpayments that the IRS offset against tax liabilities created by reversing purported 1985 and 1986 withholding credits. Brister had claimed $10,435.50 and $5,231.42 in withholding from his employer, Solar Roofing, Inc., although those amounts were never paid to the Treasury. Brister, the company’s accountant, prepared the false W-2 forms and used the nonexistent withholding to obtain refunds and force Solar Roofing to repay his loans through the IRS.

The IRS made the adjustments in 1993, more than three years after the returns were filed. The Government relied on 26 U.S.C. § 6501(c)(1), which permits unlimited assessment of a false or fraudulent return filed with intent to evade tax. The court found by clear and convincing evidence that both returns were knowingly false. Brister knew the withholding had not been remitted, had not obtained proper employer authorization, and made no effort to ensure payment. The court also found intent to evade tax because the false withholding credits produced a larger refund and used the IRS to collect Brister’s debts, even though his legitimate withholding credits would otherwise have generated refunds. Thus, the 1993 adjustments were timely, and judgment was entered for the United States with costs.

The 13/48 trading strategy uses two exponential moving averages to generate momentum signals. A bullish crossover occurs when the 13-period EMA moves above the 48-period EMA, suggesting a buy; a bearish crossover indicates a sell. The strategy works best in clearly trending markets but is riskier in sideways or choppy markets, where crossovers may be unreliable. Backtesting across markets found it performs best on stocks. For the S&P 500 cash index from 1960 onward, it produced a 5.1% annual return versus 7.2% for buy and hold while invested 66% of the time, though its reported risk-adjusted return was slightly better at 7.8%. Overall, the strategy is lagging and prone to whipsaws, so it is not a guaranteed route to profits.

Rapid advances in information and communication technologies have expanded distance education, a planned and systematic method of teaching and learning through mass-media and digital tools. It allows teachers and learners in different physical locations to interact synchronously or asynchronously, removes time and place limitations, and provides flexibility in learning hours, pace, and location. Reported benefits include lower costs, broader access to learning, lifelong learning, self-learning and self-management skills, and improved access to information and varied content. Limitations include insufficient socialization, weak outcomes for some learners lacking individual learning skills, inadequate practical training, difficulty achieving behavioral or attitudinal change, and possible overuse of digital technologies.

Equality of opportunity in education is described as providing all learners equal, nondiscriminatory access to the means and resources needed for education and development of their competencies. Distance education may reduce educational inequality, especially for people facing social, economic, geographic, or time-related barriers, but digital gaps involving unequal access to internet and communication technologies, differing technical competencies, and unequal ability to use technology effectively can reinforce inequality. Such gaps remain particularly relevant in underdeveloped and developing societies.

The study examines how distance education affects equality and inequality of educational opportunity and develops proposals for reducing inequality. It uses a qualitative case-study design with a descriptive approach, examining participants’ prior experience of distance education. Criterion sampling selected 47 participants: 21 faculty members who had taught through distance education and 26 students who had completed a semester of distance education. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with three open-ended questions addressing the meaning of equality of opportunity, distance education’s impacts on equality and inequality, and suggestions for promoting equality. Content analysis identified codes, categories, and themes. Findings were checked with participants, interpreted by another specialist, and compared with prior studies.

Faculty members identified positive effects of personal learning pace, easy access to information, self-learning opportunities, and freedom from time and space constraints. They also identified negative effects associated with technology-access problems, inadequate internet connections, unsuitable home-learning environments, additional equipment costs, insufficient attention to learners’ competencies and interests, and widening differences in academic success.

Students similarly regarded flexibility, freedom from time limitations, the availability of free courses and materials, and access to varied online sources as contributions to equality. They identified unequal financial capacity and internet-access problems as major causes of inequality. These concerns were consistent with faculty members’ reports and with literature cited by the authors concerning digital infrastructure and unequal educational outcomes.

Recommended measures include identifying learners’ characteristics, competencies, and interests at the beginning of study; improving learners’ digital literacy; ensuring equitable access to necessary technology; resolving internet-infrastructure problems; providing official funding and assistance for technology access; and offering teacher consultation and support. The authors recommend that governments update relevant policies and budgets, support families and students facing access barriers, and that teachers focus on learners’ needs and digital competence in addition to academic achievement.

The lecture defines an entangled state as one that cannot be written as a product of two subsystem states. For entanglement to be a usable resource, the subsystems must also be physically distinct and separately addressable, manipulable, and measurable. Thus, a single-photon superposition with vacuum and the inseparable electron singlet in helium do not count as resource entanglement, whereas separated photons can. Examples include polarization-entangled photons and the dual-rail Bell state \(|01\rangle+|10\rangle\).

Entangled states exhibit nonlocal correlations and are fragile against environment-induced decoherence. Weakly entangled states offer little benefit for teleportation or improved measurement precision. One proposed solution is purification: using identical copies of \(a|00\rangle+b|11\rangle\), Alice and Bob apply local controlled-NOT operations and measure their target qubits. The outcome \(1,1\), occurring with probability \(2|a|^2|b|^2\), projects the remaining photons into a maximally entangled Bell state; unsuccessful copies are discarded. Weaker entanglement therefore requires more attempts. Producing many copies independently does not violate no-cloning.

The lecture measures entanglement for pure states by taking the partial trace of the joint density matrix and calculating the von Neumann entropy of the reduced subsystem. Greater randomness in the reduced state indicates greater entanglement. Each Bell state has entropy one bit, while a factorized product of pure states has zero entropy. The Schmidt number provides another measure, although different entanglement measures are not necessarily one-to-one related. Characterizing entanglement in general mixed, many-body systems remains difficult.

Entangling atoms is harder than entangling photons because atoms lack optical beam splitters and Kerr media, but atoms can remain stationary much longer than photons in cavities. A suggested molecular approach would photodissociate a dimer of identical atoms to separate a spin singlet into two Bell-state components, though suitable systems are difficult to realize. A practical alternative uses light emitted by two atoms or ions. Photon measurements herald probabilistic entanglement of the atoms, provided the measurement erases which atom emitted which photon.

A balanced beam splitter enables this erasure through Hong–O–Mandel interference: identical photons bunch into one output, while photons with distinguishable states can exit separately. Quarter-wave plates create polarization superpositions, and simultaneous detector clicks identify cross-polarized inputs, allowing the atoms’ ground states to be projected into an entangled Bell state. Identical bosons bunch, identical fermions anti-bunch, and classical particles can take all four output paths equally.

Microsoft Corporation filed a Form 8-K (Item 7.01, Regulation FD) dated August 3, 2017, disclosing that effective July 1, 2017 it early adopted FASB's new revenue recognition and lease standards. Revenue recognition (full retrospective method, prior periods restated) materially impacted consolidated income statements and balance sheets with no impact on cash flows; Windows 10 license revenue is now recognized predominantly at billing and delivery rather than ratably, and certain multi-year commercial subscriptions recognize license revenue at contract execution, while hardware, cloud offerings such as Office 365, and professional services remain substantially unchanged. Leases (modified retrospective approach) materially impacted balance sheets through right-of-use assets and operating lease liabilities, with no material impact on income statements or cash flows; capital leases remain substantially unchanged. Restated fiscal 2017 and 2016 financial information appears in Exhibit 99.1, which was furnished and not deemed filed under Section 18 of the Exchange Act.

In May 2007, Victor Reinoso had 12 hours to recommend a chancellor to lead the Washington, DC Public Schools (DCPS) under Mayor Adrian Fenty’s newly established mayoral control. DCPS had 150 schools, 55,000 students, roughly 4,000 teachers, pervasive patronage, high leadership turnover, and serious academic, management, facilities, special-education, and accountability problems. Although spending ranked third among the 100 largest districts, DCPS spent the most on administration and the least on teachers and instruction.

Reinoso, a business consultant and former DC school board member whom Fenty had appointed deputy mayor for education, became disillusioned with the board’s culture of consensus and slow decision-making. Believing mayoral control offered a more direct reform path, he assembled a flat, 12-person team with education and project-management experience and commissioned the Parthenon Group to assess DCPS. The study found DC last among 11 systems reviewed in fourth- and eighth-grade reading and mathematics achievement, while documenting declining enrollment, short superintendent tenure, and six longstanding “pain points”: weak accountability, insufficient emphasis on teaching, operational inefficiencies, inadequate special-education support, facilities disrepair, and poor community responsiveness.

Reinoso also privately drafted the legislation that placed DCPS under the mayor, transferred daily management to a mayorially appointed chancellor, limited the school board’s policy authority, moved facilities management to a separate authority, and created an interagency commission for children’s services. The DC Council passed the legislation on April 17, 2007, with the takeover scheduled for June 12 and results required within five years.

Seeking a chancellor able to pursue radical rather than incremental reform, Reinoso sought an entrepreneurial, results-oriented leader committed to teaching, learning, accountability, and higher expectations. He considered Rudy Crew, whose aggressive reforms in New York and Miami had produced academic gains and a loyal team, and Michelle Rhee, whose teaching and nonprofit work emphasized teacher quality and student achievement despite her limited administrative experience. He also continued to consider incumbent superintendent Clifford Janey, whose extensive reform plans were constrained by his cautious approach. Shortly before the deadline, however, Reinoso’s search was disrupted by controversy over unattributed material copied from Charlotte-Mecklenburg schools; he apologized, while a senator temporarily held the takeover legislation. The passage ends before Reinoso submits his recommendation.

The paper develops quasi-Monte Carlo methods for efficiently estimating expected clinically relevant quantities from a nonlinear tumor-growth model with uncertain diffusion and proliferation coefficients. The model is a semi-linear parabolic reaction–diffusion PDE combining tumor invasion, logistic proliferation, linear treatment effects, homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions, and an initial tumor fraction in \([0,1]\). Random-field uncertainty is represented by truncating an infinite-dimensional expansion to finitely many terms.

The work establishes well-posedness and explicit a priori bounds for general random-field models, then derives parametric regularity bounds for uniform random fields and rigorous QMC error rates. The non-monotone nonlinearity \(u(1-u)\) requires a new proof using preservation of the solution range \([0,1]\) and a falling-factorial bound. Numerical experiments support the theory and include log-normal random fields on an unstructured domain previously used for glioma models. Spatiotemporal discretization error is left for future work. The paper extends prior QMC analysis, which largely focused on linear PDEs, to nonlinear parabolic equations.

Commissioner.COM’s Nov. 25, 2001 e-report combines promotional offers with a Week 11 fantasy football update. It provides NFL injury and availability news, expected starters and returns, recent performance statistics, and start/bench recommendations across all 32 teams. The report also previews Luccis Losers at Team Chick and lists both teams’ lineups with 0.0 points.

Mesh is a short-to-intermediate offensive concept that creates natural picks and defensive confusion. Against man coverage, it keeps playmakers moving so they can beat one-on-one matchups; against zone, receivers settle into voids for short completions. It works against cover 2, 3, and 4 with solid execution, though it can struggle against zone blitzes or simulated pressure, and is more suited to blitzing teams in man coverage.

Route coaching differs slightly by coverage. Against man, the TE runs a deep drag (4-5 yard landmark) staying on the move, the X receiver runs a shallow drag (3-4 yards), the Z receiver works vertically to 10 yards on a steep angle, the fullback releases to an arrow route, and the tailback releases wide on a flare. Against zone, the TE and X receivers may sit in voids after passing the tackle's alignment.

The quarterback must release five eligible receivers, anticipate blitzes, and throw quickly; he can "throw into pressure" because all areas of the field are worked. Progression remains constant against all looks: flare, shallow drag, deep drag, then fullback arrow. The Z receiver's corner route is a pre-snap decision.

Variations include "mesh rail" (running back primary on the rail, Z receiver on a sit route, X receiver speed out) and adding a sit route over the football at 8-10 yards, an answer against zone that also creates picks against man. Bruce Eien demonstrates mesh as a smash concept variation in his single-wing offense.

Culp reported fiscal 2017 net sales of $309.5 million, down 1.1%, and record pretax income of $29.7 million. Net income was $22.3 million, or $1.78 per diluted share, while adjusted EBITDA rose 7% to $40.1 million and represented 13% of sales. Return on capital was 32%. Fourth-quarter sales were unchanged at $77.4 million, while pretax income declined 2.3% to $7 million and net income increased to $6.2 million, or $0.49 per diluted share.

Mattress fabrics delivered record annual sales of $190.8 million, up 2.4%, and record operating income of $29.4 million, up 11%. Capital investments and lower input costs supported results despite production-facility changes. Upholstery fabrics recorded annual sales of $118.7 million, down 6% because of weak residential furniture retail, and operating income of $11.1 million versus $11.3 million previously. Hospitality and performance fabrics, favorable China currency effects and a broader product mix supported profitability.

Culp ended fiscal 2017 with $54.2 million of cash and investments, no credit-line borrowings, $33 million of operating cash flow and $18 million of free cash flow. It spent $14 million on capital expenditures and $6.3 million on dividends. The board approved a $0.21-per-share special dividend, Culp’s fifth in six years.

Mattress-fabric investments included North Carolina distribution and knit-fabric consolidation, Canadian expansion, relocation of mattress-cover production to Highpoint, North Carolina, and a Haitian joint-venture facility expected to begin operations by the end of the fiscal second quarter. The changes were expected to generate about $1 million of annual savings, primarily in fiscal 2018’s second half.

Upholstery sales and operating income increased slightly in the fourth quarter. Hospitality represented about 10% of upholstery revenue and carried gross margins 50% to 75% above residential margins. Management was cautiously optimistic about completing one, and potentially two, low-risk bolt-on hospitality acquisitions during fiscal 2018.

For fiscal first-quarter 2018, Culp expected overall sales comparable to the prior year, mattress-fabric sales and operating income slightly lower, and upholstery sales and operating income slightly higher. Expected pretax income was $7.8 million to $8.4 million, including about $300,000 of relocation expenses. Fiscal 2018 capital expenditures were expected to remain comparable with fiscal 2017, with another year of solid free cash flow anticipated. Management expected operating results to improve as relocation activity subsided and savings began, while short-term mattress-industry demand remained uncertain. Raw-material costs were described as stable, and the projected fiscal 2018 GAAP tax rate was 35% to 37%.

Chris Lattner, the engineer who created Apple’s Swift programming language, has joined Google to work on Google Brain’s artificial intelligence efforts. He previously led Swift at Apple and Tesla’s troubled Autopilot program, leaving Tesla after about six months due to reported conflict with Elon Musk.

The passage defines the SEV-ES and SEV-SNP Guest-Hypervisor Communication Block (GHCB) specification. SEV-ES and SEV-SNP encrypt guest register state during world switches, preventing direct hypervisor access. Automatic Exits expose no guest registers, while Non-Automatic Exits (NAEs) allow guests to control which register state is shared with the hypervisor through the GHCB.

The GHCB is a 4 KB, page-aligned decrypted region whose format mirrors the SEV-ES VMCB save-state area, though only fields required for VMGEXIT processing are specified. The GHCB MSR protocol uses the lower 12 bits for requests and the remaining bits for guest-physical addressing, version negotiation, CPUID requests, AP reset hold, GHCB registration, page-state changes, VMPL selection, termination, and other operations. SEV-SNP guests must register their GHCB GPA before first use. Version 2 adds a 52-bit hypervisor feature bitmap through which optional capabilities are advertised.

Guests handle NAEs through a #VC exception and VMGEXIT, using SW_EXITCODE, SW_EXITINFO1, SW_EXITINFO2, and VALID_BITMAP to exchange required state and hypervisor errors. Defined events include I/O and MSR protection, VMMCALL, nested-page MMIO access, page-state changes, SNP guest and extended guest requests, AP creation, restricted-injection doorbell and timer operations, APIC ID retrieval, VMPL changes, SEV-TIO requests, Secure AVIC backing-page management, and termination requests. SNP guest requests can return certificates, while TIO requests support trusted-device measurements, certificates, and attestation reports.

Additional sections define the SNP secrets page’s guest-reserved area, including 64-bit guest request sequence numbers; the EFI SNP Confidential Computing Blob protocol; SEV-ES identification through CPUID; and SMP boot procedures using AP reset hold, jump tables, or SNP AP Creation and VMSA pages. Restricted Injection uses a shared doorbell page with PendingEvent and NoEoiRequired fields to emulate APIC interrupt delivery, while the host emulates interrupt acknowledgment, in-service, and EOI behavior. NMI handling requires the hypervisor to intercept #DB rather than IRET. Hardware debug-register virtualization is supported through the SEV_FEATURES DebugVirtualization bit, with DR7 interception and caching as the fallback. SMM and nested virtualization are not supported.
Scott must decide how much time to devote to coaching versus family. He is expected back next year and is praised for his exceptional energy and passion for hockey.

Channel 4 chief Alex Mahon called its 28.6% gender pay gap “unacceptable” and aims for equal numbers of men and women in the broadcaster’s 100 highest-paid roles by 2023. Although women comprise 59% of staff, they hold only 34 of those posts. Channel 4’s gap exceeds the 17.4% national average, while ITN’s is 19.6% and the BBC’s 10.7%. A PwC review found no evidence of gender bias in BBC pay decisions but criticised limited transparency; BBC Women rejected it, and former China editor Carrie Gracie resigned over inequalities.

The disclosure addresses sealing in high-pressure valves and hydraulic fracturing fluid ends exposed to corrosive or abrasive fluids, where conventional seals mounted on mating components abrade against the device body, causing body erosion, leakage, and costly weld repairs. The disclosed construction instead mounts seals in recesses or endless grooves formed in the body, with the seals extending against sealing surfaces of the mating components. This transfers erosion from the body to components that are less complex and less expensive to repair or replace, extending operating life and reducing downtime and costs.

In the illustrated plug valves, body-mounted seals engage the valve insert and retaining nut, while alternative spring arrangements engage the insert. The rotating plug remains selectively alignable with the inlet and outlet to open or close the flow passage. Inserts may be resurfaced or replaced, and disposable liners may be used as sacrificial wear members. Various seal types, including elastomeric, metal, spring, axial, radial, and crush seals, are contemplated.

In the illustrated fluid ends, a reciprocating plunger pressurizes fluid within intersecting housing conduits. Body grooves hold seals that engage discharge and suction plugs, valve seats, a stuffing-box sleeve, and a suction manifold. Other embodiments use a recessed corner overlying the stuffing-box sleeve to form a crush seal, or a breather opening to vent pressure trapped in the sleeve clearance. Erosion-resistant treatments for plugs include HVOF treatment, tungsten carbide coatings, and carburizing.

Claimed embodiments include fluid-end assemblies with intersecting conduits, concentric endless grooves, plungers, annular seals, recessed corner sections, and stuffing-box sleeves overlying those corners, as well as a method for manufacturing such an assembly. The disclosed principles may also apply to other high-pressure flow devices.

CTPNet is a multivariate long-term time-series forecasting framework designed to jointly learn inter-channel, intra-subsequence, and inter-subsequence dependencies. Its channel-wise representation module uses temporal-query multi-head attention, combining periodically reused learnable queries with input-derived keys and values to capture cross-variable interactions while reducing the effects of noise and missing values. After a residual connection with the original input, the series is downsampled according to its inherent period, and each subsequence is encoded into a higher-dimensional latent space. Trend-wise representation learning uses efficient attention to model local trend variations within subsequences, while periodic-wise representation learning applies the same network to transposed encoded features to capture dependencies across subsequences. A decoder and inverse downsampling reconstruct the forecast. Experiments across ETTH1, ETTH2, ETTM1, ETTM2, ECL, SOLAR, TRAFFIC, and WEATHER benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance, with 54 first-place results.

The paper examines how generative AI could enhance and reshape higher-education assessment while addressing academic integrity, authenticity, and AI literacy. Traditional exams, short-answer questions, and essays are criticized for being uniform, time-intensive, focused on memorization, and insufficiently representative of professional tasks. Generative AI can perform strongly on written and multiple-choice assessments, while AI-detection tools remain unreliable, may produce false positives, and risk disadvantaging students whose first language is not English.

Two broad assessment strategies are proposed: minimizing AI’s influence through authentic, real-time, practical, or invigilated assessments; and incorporating AI as a defined component of learning and assessment. The latter includes using AI to draft outlines, generate questions or materials, conduct research, produce ideas, and critically evaluate AI output. Because AI capabilities may rapidly advance, assessments based on tasks current models cannot perform may soon become obsolete. AI-generated feedback can provide rapid, personalized support, but its accuracy, contextual understanding, bias, and alignment with curricula remain concerns.

A case study at a UK university redesigned a 2,000-word immunology essay within a postgraduate MSc program. Students received instruction on ChatGPT, prompt engineering, academic integrity, and assessment requirements; generated an initial outline with ChatGPT; critiqued peers’ outlines; and then improved their outline and wrote the final essay without further AI assistance. Survey results from 20 students found that 57.9% had previously used generative AI, but only 5% were very confident using it. Students valued AI for planning, drafting, research, revision, and generating ideas, while identifying accuracy, outdated information, superficial responses, and unverifiable sources as limitations. They found the generated outlines useful starting points but often generic, and welcomed the opportunity to learn about AI’s capabilities and limitations.

The paper concludes that universities should combine AI-supported and traditional assessment rather than simply replace established methods. Institutions should provide equitable training for students and educators, embed AI literacy in curricula, clarify ethical use and referencing, maintain human judgment, and develop robust assessment frameworks that emphasize higher-order skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, evaluation, and creativity.

The Louisiana Supreme Court affirmed Ray Jones Jr.’s conviction and sentence for first-degree murder of his two-and-one-half-month-old son. Jones had been found guilty by a jury, which recommended life imprisonment without probation, parole, or suspension of sentence.

Jones challenged the admission of three statements in which he described attacking the child’s mother, striking the baby, and throwing him into the backyard. The court held that his hospital statement to his psychiatrist was voluntary and unsolicited, and that his later hospital statement to hospital personnel was likewise voluntary and not the product of police interrogation. Miranda warnings were therefore unnecessary for both statements.

The Supreme Court also upheld the admission of Jones’s police-station confession. Although Jones initially invoked his right to have counsel present, he subsequently said he wanted to tell the officers what happened. A detective’s religious comments did not constitute interrogation because they were not reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response; Jones then voluntarily confessed. Alternatively, any error in admitting the confession was harmless beyond a reasonable doubt because the two hospital statements and other trial evidence overwhelmingly established his guilt.

The Court also found no abuse of discretion in the trial judge’s restriction of defense counsel’s cross-examination of the psychiatrist about hypothetical “bad information” from family members, because no evidence showed that such information had been provided and only Jones’s mental condition at the time of his statements was relevant.

The passage describes systems and methods for active ground-terrain mapping to control mobile work machines, particularly agricultural combines and sprayers. A triggered pose detection sensor measures geographic position and orientation. Using machine dimensions and sensor placement, the system estimates ground-contact points and identifies a machine ground plane. A configurable virtual point cloud is positioned coplanar with that plane, with adjustable resolution, width, length, and offset, and moves with the machine over a field.

At each pose measurement, estimated ground elevations are generated for the point-cloud locations. Confidence weights decrease as distance from the sensor increases, and values are aggregated by georeferenced map cell using weighted averaging or other methods. Map layers can retain elevation, confidence, sample count, and variance. The system can map an entire field, estimate elevations on the fly for a region of interest, merge data with existing maps, store data locally or remotely, and communicate it to other systems.

The elevation data can control propulsion, steering, sprayer-boom height, harvester-header height or orientation, crop-volume estimation, communications, and operator interfaces. The described implementations may use hardware, software, remote servers, cloud services, and mobile devices.

The study examines the potential for micro-credentials in Mauritian higher education, focusing on education and industry leaders’ familiarity with them, their compatibility with academic credits, their perceived value, and the regulatory environment needed for adoption. Micro-credentials are presented as records of assessed learning and competencies that can support upskilling, reskilling, lifelong learning, employability, and the transition from traditional education to technology-driven work. Although their benefits are widely recognised, barriers include limited stakeholder understanding, uncertain reliability, weak recognition, resource constraints, technical infrastructure needs, and difficulties mapping or stacking them within formal qualifications.

A qualitative study used semi-structured interviews with 10 educational leaders from six public and four private higher education institutions and four industry champions and potential employers in ICT, finance, and related sectors in Mauritius. Participants were purposively selected, and interview data were analysed thematically.

Respondents were generally familiar with micro-credentials but described them inconsistently, ranging from short, competency-assessed courses and certificates of attendance to mini qualifications that can complement diplomas or degrees. Badges were less familiar, generally seen as unofficial recognition tools, and were sometimes treated as equivalent to micro-credentials.

Most participants favoured a flexible or hybrid model that would minimise disruption to existing credit systems while allowing micro-credentials to convert into, and accumulate towards, academic credit. They also valued self-paced and personalised learning pathways that respond quickly to industry needs. However, micro-credentials were regarded as potentially disruptive, supporting a phased approach involving experimentation, prototyping, and initial use in professional development before fuller integration into degrees.

Recognition depended on credible assessment, quality standards, trusted awarding bodies, verifiability, and employer confidence. Employers valued micro-credentials as accessible, affordable evidence of skills, but retained concerns about their practical use and reliability; they also needed to shift job requirements from conventional qualifications toward competency profiles. Formal recognition required an adapted National Qualifications Framework capable of accommodating different fields, levels, and granularities of learning, including informal learning, and defining pathways through which accumulated micro-credits contribute to recognised qualifications.

The study concludes that Mauritius needs a unified framework integrating micro-credentials into institutional credit systems and the National Qualifications Framework. Such integration could improve academic and industry recognition, formalise varied learning, support lifelong learning, and help address skills shortages.

A Phase 2 randomized trial found that adding 16 weeks of omalizumab to oral immunotherapy (OIT) improved outcomes for children aged 4–15 allergic to multiple foods. At week 36, 30 of 36 children (83%) receiving omalizumab could safely eat at least two grams of two or more allergenic foods, compared with 4 of 12 (33%) receiving placebo. Oomalizumab-treated participants also had fewer adverse events during weeks 8–16. Larger studies are needed to confirm the results.

The excavation uncovered roof fragments, including one with a bullet hole, 1930s milk bottles and other debris. The passage catalogs non-verbal communications used by soccer players and coaches. Hand signals include calling for set pieces, indicating openness for a pass, directing runs, requesting passes, signaling for substitutions, organizing defensive walls, directing teammates forward, identifying opponents to cover, indicating through-ball or throw-in delivery, and communicating set-piece types. The goalkeeper uses additional signals to organize defenders and announce long punts or drop-kicks.

Other signals include nodding to start play or reposition a teammate, tapping the chest or head to request a throw-in, smacking or raising the ball to begin a throw-in, running over or bouncing the ball to begin a set piece or identify a corner, and using made-up signals for an offside trap. Players request substitutions by raising a hand overhead and circling their forearms. Coaches may establish agreed signals with players, especially when crowd noise prevents oral communication. The document also notes Pelé’s unseen hand signal directing a teammate to bounce a throw-in off his back.

The passage specifies SD Memory Card operation, initialization, data transfer, protection, and bus-speed behavior for UHS-I, UHS-II, and UHS-III interfaces.

- **UHS-I:** After power cycling, a card starts in 3.3V signaling mode. CMD0 selects SD or SPI mode, while 1.8V signaling is available only in SD mode. Once switched to 1.8V, the card remains in that signaling mode until power cycling and cannot switch to SPI. ACMD41 negotiates operating conditions and 1.8V support through S18R and S18A; CMD11 performs the voltage switch, after which SDR12 is the default timing. UHS-I normally uses a 4-bit bus. CMD6 selects bus speed, driver strength, and power limit, while CMD19 supplies tuning blocks for sampling-point adjustment. UHS104 requires tuning, whereas UHS50 makes it optional.
- **UHS-II and UHS-III:** UHS-II supports legacy SD modes and the UHS-II interfaces FD156, HD312, FD312, and FD624, with optional half-duplex operation and specified speed ranges. A host detects UHS-II initialization through STB.L on the D1 lane, with a 200-microsecond card-defined detection timeout before falling back to the SD bus interface. Initialization covers PHY, device, enumeration, configuration, and SD-TRAN stages. UHS-III adds FD624, supporting up to 624 MB/s.
- **Card initialization:** The host is the master and uses broadcast and addressed commands. Identification begins with CMD0, CMD8, and ACMD41. CMD8 verifies voltage and communication conditions; ACMD41, preceded by CMD55, checks operating voltage and host capacity support and is repeated until initialization completes. CMD2 obtains the CID, CMD3 assigns the RCA, and CMD7 selects a card for data transfer. CMD9 retrieves card-specific data and CMD4 optionally configures driver strength.
- **Data transfer:** Read and write commands can be stopped with CMD12. Successful writes move the card to the programming state, while failed writes return it to the transfer state. Block writes may be buffered, and ACMD23 can pre-erase blocks. Erase sequences use CMD32, CMD33, and CMD38. DISCARD treats discarded contents as indeterminate, while FULE logically erases the full user area. CRC protection detects transfer errors, and cards report address, block-length, write-protection, and erase-sequence errors.
- **Bus width:** The default bus is 1-bit. ACMD6 selects 4-bit operation, but a locked card must first be unlocked with CMD42.
- **Write protection and locking:** Cards support mechanical, internal, and password-based protection. Password and ownership information is retained in nonvolatile PWD and FEP registers. CMD42 sets, replaces, clears, locks, or unlocks passwords and supports force erase. Card Ownership Protection adds COP-specific modes, FEP management, and restricted access until COP Unlock is issued. Locked cards accept only specified commands.
- **Application-specific and switch commands:** CMD55 causes the following command to be interpreted as an ACMD when defined. CMD6 checks or changes functions in access mode, command system, driver strength, and power-limit groups, returning supported functions, selected values, and power consumption.
- **Additional features:** Application Performance Class specifies minimum random and sequential performance. Cache can improve performance but may lose data if not flushed before power-off. Self Maintenance permits background data management. Command Queue supports ordered or host-triggered execution of submitted tasks. Low Voltage Interface enables initialization in 1.8V rather than 3.3V I/O mode.

Blackwell’s AI Management Processor (AMP) is a dedicated, programmable RISC-V-based GPU scheduler that offloads GPU-context management from the CPU. It aligns with Windows’ HAGS model, reducing CPU-GPU communication, latency, and scheduling bottlenecks while coordinating AI and graphics workloads for smoother frame rates, faster LLM responses, and improved multitasking.

Blackwell adds H.264 and HEVC hardware encoding and decoding for YUV 4:2:2 video. Compared with uncompressed 4:4:4, 4:2:0 uses half the frame data while 4:2:2 uses two-thirds, retains twice the color resolution of 4:2:0, and is suited to cameras and professional color workflows. The ninth-generation NVENC encoder improves AV1 and HEVC quality by 5% BD-BR PSNR, supports 4:2:2, and adds an AV1 Ultra High Quality mode offering another 5% improvement and up to 15% combined BD-BR PSNR gains. The sixth-generation NVDEC doubles H.264 decoding speed and adds 4:2:2 support. The RTX 5090 supports three encoders and two decoders, increasing export speeds by more than 50% generation over generation and fourfold over a single encoder in the RTX 3090. Blackwell also supports DisplayPort 2.1b at up to 80 Gbps, including 8K at 165Hz and 4K at 480Hz with DSC.

Blackwell’s Max-Q design improves efficiency through faster power-state transitions, fine-grained clock and unit gating, GDDR7 memory-clock gating, and separate voltage rails for GPU cores and memory. Frequency switching responds to workload changes up to 1,000 times faster than prior architectures, allowing higher clocks during active periods and power savings during short idle intervals. Entry into the deepest sleep state is 10 times faster than on Ada, and one small-language-model inference example achieved power savings of up to 50%.

DLSS 4 adds Multi Frame Generation, which uses fifth-generation Tensor Cores and AI-based optical flow to generate up to three additional frames per traditionally rendered frame. Its generation model runs 40% faster than the previous method, uses 30% less VRAM, and runs once per rendered frame. Enhanced Flip Metering moves pacing to the display engine, whose doubled pixel-processing capacity supports higher resolutions and refresh rates.

DLSS 4 also replaces convolutional neural networks in Super Resolution, Ray Reconstruction, and Deep Learning Anti-Aliasing with transformer-based models. Transformers use self-attention to identify long-range patterns, support twice as many parameters, and improve temporal stability, ghosting, motion detail, ray-traced lighting, and image quality.

Blackwell advances neural shaders by exposing Tensor Cores to graphics shaders through Microsoft’s Cooperative Vectors API for DX12 and Vulkan and Slang language features. Potential applications include RTX Neural Materials, which approximates complex multilayer materials; Neural Texture Compression, which can provide up to 7:1 VRAM compression; Neural Radiance Cache, which infers indirect lighting from limited ray tracing and trains on live game data; RTX Skin, which brings ray-traced subsurface scattering to games; and RTX Neural Faces, which uses generative AI to infer realistic faces from rasterized images and 3D pose data. Neural texture compression reduced one demonstration’s material memory use from 1,110 MB to 333 MB while providing higher visual quality, while Blackwell’s improved point-sampled filtering rate accelerates stochastic texture filtering.

The Blackwell GPU family includes the flagship GB202 with 92.2 billion transistors, 192 streaming multiprocessors, 24,576 CUDA cores, 192 RT cores, and 768 Tensor cores, used in the RTX 5090. **Summary**

This medRxiv preprint (not peer reviewed) reports a Phase 2/3, observer-blind, randomized, controlled trial of SII-NVX-CoV2373 (Covovax, manufactured by Serum Institute of India) in Indian children and adolescents aged 2–17 years. A total of 920 participants were enrolled (460 aged 12–17 years; 460 aged 2–11 years) and randomized 3:1 to two doses of vaccine or saline placebo on days 1 and 22, with follow-up visits on days 22, 36, 85 and 180 and telephone contact on day 120. Recruitment proceeded stepwise with safety reviews by an independent Data Safety Monitoring Board and Indian regulators.

The primary objectives were to assess non-inferiority of vaccine responses versus adults who had received the same vaccine (using anti-spike IgG and neutralizing antibody geometric means at day 36, with a lower 95% confidence limit of >0.67 for non-inferiority) and to compare safety against placebo.

Results: After dose two, anti-S IgG rose 101.9-fold (12–17 years) and 169.2-fold (2–11 years) with seroconversion of 98.8% and 99.1%; neutralizing antibody GMTs rose 84.9-fold and 115.3-fold with over 98% seroconversion. Non-inferiority versus adults was met in both cohorts for both assays (lower 95% CI limits 1.08 and 1.38 for anti-S IgG; 1.17 and 1.70 for neutralizing antibodies), with pediatric titers exceeding adult titers. Immune responses, including hACE2 inhibition activity, were also demonstrated against Delta, Omicron BA.1 and BA.5, at levels slightly lower than against the ancestral Wuhan strain. Titers declined by day 180 but remained well above baseline and above placebo.

Safety: Two serious adverse events occurred in vaccinated adolescents (viral infection, gastroenteritis), both deemed unrelated to vaccination; no adverse events of special interest and no SAEs were reported in the 2–11 year group. Solicited adverse events were more frequent in vaccine than placebo recipients, most commonly injection site pain, tenderness, headache, fatigue and fever; nearly all were mild and resolved without sequelae.

The authors note that efficacy was not assessed in this study, that previously infected participants were excluded, and that a safety profile without myocarditis signals may support pediatric use, concluding the vaccine is safe, well tolerated and highly immunogenic and may be used in pediatric COVID-19 vaccination. The study was funded by Serum Institute of India; several authors are SIIPL or Novavax employees.

Mud Bay, a Pacific Northwest natural pet retailer, pursued a “Good Jobs Vision” to improve employee and customer experience while strengthening the company. The U.S. pet-store market was growing, but brick-and-mortar stores faced competition from grocers, mass retailers, and online sellers. PetSmart’s revenue declined from 2013 to 2018, while Petco grew modestly and expanded through acquisitions and partnerships.

Mud Bay began in 1988 when Elsa Wulff purchased a small farm store near Olympia, Washington. After initially selling miscellaneous products, the business focused on healthy dog and cat food, employee education, and customer guidance. It acquired eight failing Bosley stores in 2000, converted them to its natural-food model, and returned to profitability before expanding into Washington and Oregon. By 2014, Mud Bay operated 27 stores, generated $38.4 million in revenue, and emphasized consultative selling, highly trained staff, quality products, and everyday low prices. Employees received open-book management, profit sharing, flexible scheduling, and opportunities for advancement, but the company’s low margins constrained wages and contributed to 48% staff turnover.

In 2014, managers and home-office employees participated in discussions that led to a 20-person strategic planning group, “The Twenty.” It established five strategies: invest in staff; offer fewer products at everyday low prices; standardize processes and empower continuous improvement; improve efficiency through cross-training and slack; and partner with animal-welfare organizations.

From 2015 through 2017, Mud Bay increased wages and benefits, expanded medical-insurance eligibility, introduced an Employee Stock Ownership Plan and Employee Assistance Program, and launched leadership, harassment, and diversity training. It reduced active SKUs from 3,750 to 3,180, created store-based category expert teams, and lowered prices. Delivery and some store processes were standardized, while unified lead roles and shared-store staffing increased flexibility. Mud Bay also expanded animal-welfare partnerships, adoption events, donations, and outreach. Progress was uneven: hiring practices remained inconsistent, inventory adjustments did not improve, no formal idea system was established, and task-based staffing and systematic slack were not achieved.

By 2018, Mud Bay averaged prices about 7% below PetSmart and Petco and roughly matched Amazon and Chewy. Customer ratings on Yelp, Google, and Facebook averaged 4.8–4.9. Between 2014 and 2017, sales grew 70%, sales per labor hour rose from $116.86 to $132.07, full-time employment increased, average hourly earnings rose, and store-staff turnover declined from 48% to 31%. Employees collectively owned 4.8% of the company. These gains came with reduced profitability as lower prices, higher labor and benefit costs, and home-office growth compressed net margins from 2.18% in 2014 to 1.99% in 2017.

With insufficient profit blocking completion of the 2018 budget, COO Tracy Yamane renewed her proposal to close stores at 8:00 p.m. rather than 9:00 p.m. Monday through Saturday. The change would save labor, reduce “clopenings” and unpopular midday shifts, and let employees leave earlier. Co-CEO Marisa Wulff supported it; co-CEO Lars Wulff feared lost revenue and reduced customer convenience. An analysis covering nearly all stores across six weeks in three seasons compared sales near opening and closing with average half-hour sales. The passage ends as the annual planning team reviews the analysis and prepares to decide.

The study examined education students’ and lecturers’ experiences of the effectiveness of Physical Education teacher training in distance mode at North-West University in South Africa. Practical workplace experience and skills are essential components of teacher qualifications, yet limited research had addressed distance Physical Education training. The qualitative study used open-ended questionnaires with 17 third-year distance students and semi-structured interviews with four lecturers. Participants were purposefully selected, while expert review, participant confirmation and independent transcript validation supported data credibility. Inductively identified themes were student–lecturer interaction, lecturer competence and enthusiasm, distance-learning obstacles, practical training experiences, and the influence of course content on perceptions of Physical Education.

Students regarded lecturers as accessible, responsive, professional, caring and knowledgeable, although the absence of physical contact was a disadvantage. Students’ confidence, competence and subject knowledge increased, while lecturers reported strong passion for Physical Education and a commitment to providing high-quality training. Major obstacles were limited foundational knowledge, inadequate technological skills or internet access, and inefficient assignment administration, including delayed submission and feedback.

Videos generally supported the development of practical skills and understanding of movements, and students valued the ability to replay them. However, insufficient practical videos and long delays in receiving feedback prevented students from correcting their performance immediately. Despite anticipated difficulties, most students found the course content interesting and reported a more positive view of Physical Education’s value and compulsory status.

Recommendations include greater face-to-face contact, additional technological training, improved use of videos and other media, stronger learner-interaction functions, and more effective university management and administrative systems.

Rieva Lesonsky explains that poor document management wastes time and money, limits access, risks exposing sensitive information, and harms customer service. She cites a Xerox survey finding that 40% of business processes remain document-driven, while 81% of surveyed businesses plan to improve document management. Recommended steps include tracking print costs, scanning documents to cloud services through Xerox ConnectKey-enabled printers, creating customized digital workflows, enabling mobile access, restricting printing with PINs and color controls, and monitoring toner supplies.

Passports legally attest U.S. citizenship and may be issued only to U.S. citizens; the Secretary of State and diplomatic or consular officers issue them under presidential rules. Although law-abiding citizens who comply generally receive passports, issuance is discretionary. Applicants must establish citizenship, U.S. domicile, and intent to return and perform citizenship duties. Expatriation—abandoning allegiance with intent to become permanently resident or a citizen abroad—bars issuance and is determined case by case, as no legislative definition exists. Temporary foreign residence does not necessarily constitute expatriation, but permanent foreign domicile and withdrawal from U.S. ties may create a presumption of expatriation; permanent foreign residents cannot receive passports even when expatriation is not established. A contradicted sworn intent to return creates doubts about an applicant’s purposes. Relevant factors include severed U.S. family, property, and business ties, weighed against retained connections, health or financial barriers to returning, and especially representation of legitimate American enterprises abroad. Citizens residing where the United States exercises extraterritorial jurisdiction may remain abroad indefinitely for safety and generally receive passports when their pursuits are legitimate and do not prejudice foreign relations. The Department has also recognized inherited citizenship rights for some descendants in American communities in Turkey under Turkey’s extraterritorial regime.
