The article explains the 200-day moving average (200DMA), a trend-following indicator that averages an asset’s closing prices over 200 trading days to smooth short-term fluctuations. A close above the average generally signals an uptrend, while a close below signals a downtrend. The article focuses on a simple crossover strategy using the SMA: buy when the price closes above the 200DMA and sell when it closes below.

The strategy’s primary strength is defensive. It helped exit before major bear markets, including the S&P 500 declines of 2000–03 and 2007–09 and the 2020 oil-price crash. The Mt. Lucas Management Index also used a comparable long-term rule to hold commodities long or short. Paul Tudor Jones cited the 200DMA as a way to assess sentiment, avoid catastrophic losses, and “play defense.”

The strategy is not a guaranteed solution. In markets without significant recessions or prolonged declines, repeated whipsaws, false signals, commissions, slippage, and missed opportunities can cause it to underperform buy-and-hold. A backtest from March 2009 produced an 8.5% CAGR versus 12.8% for buy-and-hold, though its maximum drawdown was lower at 19% versus 34%. A longer S&P 500 test nearly kept pace with buy-and-hold while substantially reducing drawdowns, but could create tax liabilities.

Since 1960, the S&P 500 crossed above its 200DMA 187 times, yet only 28% of the resulting trades were winners; the strategy also had a maximum of nine consecutive losing trades. Jeremy Siegel’s variation, requiring a 1% move above or below the average, performed slightly better than the original rule but still had lower absolute returns than buy-and-hold in his cited research. Adding a 200DMA filter to another strategy reduced total return and trading frequency but improved drawdown and win rate.

Daily bars are the most frequently used timeframe, though only backtesting can determine the best setup. SMA and EMA results were similar, with the article favoring the SMA for simplicity. A stock below its 200DMA is considered to be in a bearish trend but may still be tradable. Overall, the 200DMA is presented as a simple, broadly useful tool for filtering noise and avoiding bear markets, not as a “silver bullet” for consistently outperforming buy-and-hold.

The NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU architecture introduces major memory, partitioning, interconnect, reliability, and programmability improvements.

- A100 features a five-site HBM2 subsystem with 1,555 GB/s bandwidth, 2.3× V100’s L2 read bandwidth, and a 40 MB L2 cache nearly seven times larger than V100’s. Cache-management and residency controls improve reuse, reduce writebacks and redundant DRAM traffic, and support persistent caching. Compute Data Compression can save up to 4× DRAM read/write bandwidth and up to 4× L2 read bandwidth.
- Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) can divide an A100 into as many as seven isolated GPU Instances, each with dedicated compute resources, L2 cache allocations, memory controllers, and DRAM bandwidth. GPU Instances can contain multiple Compute Instances, enabling independent contexts and Volta-style MPS support. MIG provides quality-of-service guarantees, fault isolation, and vGPU migration, although it is compute-only and disables L2 set-aside functionality.
- Third-generation NVLink provides 12 links, 600 GB/s aggregate bandwidth, peer-memory access, improved error recovery, and non-posted writes. A100 also supports PCIe Gen 4 with 31.5 GB/s per direction on x16 links and SR-IOV GPU sharing and virtualization.
- New fault-handling technologies improve error attribution, isolation, and containment within multi-GPU and MIG environments. NVLink-connected systems also return remote page-fault information to the source GPU.
- Additional hardware includes a five-core NVJPG JPEG decoder, an optical-flow accelerator supporting optical flow and stereo disparity, five NVDEC units, and improved atomics—11× higher FP16 and 2.7× higher FP32 throughput than V100.
- CUDA 11 adds task graphs for define-once, repeatedly executed workflows; A100-specific launch and dependency optimizations; asynchronous global-to-shared-memory copies; hardware asynchronous barriers for arbitrary thread subsets; and L2 persistence controls configurable in 2.5 MB increments. Cooperative Groups adds group-wide asynchronous copies and hardware-accelerated reductions.
- DGX A100 combines eight A100 GPUs and NVSwitch connectivity, delivering up to 5 PFLOPS in a 6U system and supporting as many as 56 isolated MIG accelerators. Its software stack includes CUDA 11, NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and GPU-accelerated containers for deep learning, analytics, inference, and HPC.
- The appendix explains neural-network pruning and sparsity. A100 supports fine-grained structured sparsity, including 2:4 sparsity, to balance workloads and improve utilization while maintaining accuracy in evaluated networks.

The lecture surveys hinged dissections, including animated examples and books by Greg Frederickson. The lecturer identifies a general software tool for animating them as a possible project, alongside implementing slender-adorned chains, designing dissections with fewer or more elegant pieces, and developing an alphabet-based family that converts the numeral six into a square, eight, four, or nine.

A universality proof shows that fixed-size polyominoes, polyhexes, polyiamonds, and polyabolos can be hinged-dissected. The proof uses induction on the shape’s dual graph: base pieces are divided into two parts and hinged, a spanning tree provides leaves, and each removed leaf is reattached by aligning and reconnecting hinges. Similar constructions work for triangles and tetrahedra. The resulting chains are often slender, and subdivision into slender pieces can enable continuous motion, though the number of pieces may increase by roughly a factor of three.

Other discussions cover chain-based mechanisms that can continuously fold into arbitrary shapes, DNA origami as a related technology, and reconfigurable robots. Unlike robots whose modules detach and reconnect, chain-folding robots remain connected throughout motion. Hardware examples include small and large MIT robots and a salt-triggered device that folds from a square into an equilateral triangle.

The “piece-lie” or superposition technique produces dissections between rectangles of different dimensions and between a square and an equilateral triangle. It has inspired proposed reconfigurable tables and other furniture, including a four-piece Dudeney cabinet and a conceptual reconfigurable house.

The standard hinged-dissection construction can require exponentially many pieces as it corrects hinges one at a time. A proposed pseudopolynomial construction for grid-aligned polygons instead uses equal-area triangulations, slender triangle chains, localized hinge relocation, rectangle conversions, and “pseudocuts” to overlay transformations while keeping recursion depth bounded.

In three dimensions, matching volume alone does not guarantee a dissection. The Dehn invariant, computed from edge lengths and dihedral angles, must also match. Equal volume and equal Dehn invariant are sufficient in three and four dimensions, while the general conditions for five or more dimensions remain unknown. Efficient algorithms for comparing invariants and constructing three-dimensional dissections also remain open, as does a formal account of converting three-dimensional dissections into hinged ones.

Researchers at the Universities of York and St Andrews found that New Caledonian crows and kea parrots selected the correct tools more successfully after exploring objects during play. The birds incidentally learned object properties through this “latent learning,” but showed no evidence of deliberately seeking tool information. Separately, World Animal Protection reported a 292% rise in wildlife selfies since 2014 and warned that social-media attention contributes to cruel treatment of iconic Amazon species.

The passage defines the SEV-ES and SEV-SNP Guest-Hypervisor Communication Block (GHCB) protocol for non-automatic exit (NAE) events. An NAE is an exit that is not an automatic event. In SEV-ES, it causes a hardware #VC exception whose error code matches the event’s VMEXIT code. The guest inspects the code, copies required state into the GHCB, and executes VMGEXIT. After the hypervisor runs the guest again, it resumes after VMGEXIT and can return results through the GHCB. The #VC handler exits with IRET, which should not be intercepted except during NMI handling.

Protocol versions define supported NAE events and their minimum guest and hypervisor state. Hypervisors need not intercept every instruction that generates a listed NAE, but must handle VMGEXIT requests for those events. Guests must handle their #VC exceptions but may instead paravirtualize the affected instructions. Both parties reset the VALID_BITMAP before setting valid fields. Guests normally mark SW_EXITCODE, SW_EXITINFO1, and SW_EXITINFO2, while hypervisors mark SW_EXITINFO1 and SW_EXITINFO2. Additional state is optional and cannot be relied upon. Software must protect VMGEXIT activity on the issuing vCPU by disabling interrupts and preemption while accessing the GHCB. A nonzero SW_EXITINFO1 value reports an error; the value 1 requests exception injection, with the EVENTINJ value in SW_EXITINFO2. Unsupported NAEs use the Unsupported Event exit code.

Event-specific processing includes decoding or paravirtualizing IOIO_PROT, MSR_PROT, and MMIO faults. MMIO and string operations may use the GHCB shared buffer and decrypted buffers and can require multiple VMGEXIT calls. Page State Change events use a shared Page State Change structure to request private or shared pages and to issue PSMASH or UNSMASH hints, with progress recorded so processing can resume. SNP Guest Request events communicate synchronously with SNP firmware through shared request and response pages, preserve the message sequence number, return firmware status, and should be retried when requested. Extended Guest Requests can also return VCEK or VLEK certificate data.

Other NAEs support SNP AP creation and removal, #HV doorbell-page management, restricted-injection IPIs and virtual APIC timers, APIC ID discovery, running a vCPU at another VMPL, SEV-TIO trusted-device requests, Secure AVIC backing-page registration, and guest termination. AP creation requires RMPADJUST for the VM Save Area and permits SNP vCPU hotplug. Guests identify SEV-ES support through hypervisor-provided CPUID properties.

SEV-ES and SEV-SNP application-processor startup requires special handling because initially measured registers cannot later be changed. The first reset uses the original register values; subsequent boots can use reset-hold requests and an AP jump table. SNP AP Creation provides an alternative and is required when Restricted Injection prevents INIT-SIPI use. SEV-ES does not support vCPU hotplug, while SNP AP Creation can support it.

For NMI delivery, the hypervisor must not intercept IRET but must intercept #DB; the guest sends an NMI Complete message when it can safely accept another NMI. Hardware debug-register virtualization is used when supported; otherwise DR7 accesses are intercepted and the written value is cached. SMM and nested virtualization are not supported.

Restricted Injection uses an #HV doorbell page for common host notifications. PendingEvent occupies bytes 0–1 and identifies pending maskable and non-maskable events, including NMI, #MC, and an interrupt vector; NoEoiRequired occupies byte 2. The page is host-owned and shared, and guest accesses use C=0. The host emulates APIC ready, acknowledgment, in-service, and EOI behavior and signals #HV as needed. Guests must atomically retrieve pending events before acting, use implicit or explicit EOI handling, and validate observed vectors. For HLT, guests execute with interrupts disabled, and the host immediately re-enters the guest if events are pending. Doorbell configuration is performed through VMGEXIT actions for obtaining a preferred address, setting a page, and querying its assignment.

The passage describes a continuation patent application concerning address obfuscation for memory, including systems, memory devices, mapping components, and methods. Address obfuscation complements wear-leveling, which extends memory lifetime by moving data among physical memory cells so that individual cells are not accessed excessively. Logical addresses remain fixed during such movements, while physical locations change.

The disclosed technology maps logical addresses to physical memory addresses using configurable mapping functions that can vary by device, die, memory array, or time. This makes a predictable wear-leveling pattern harder to reverse-engineer and limits the usefulness of information obtained from one memory entity against others or the same entity later. In examples where a failed cell exposes a wear-leveling pattern, different initial address mappings produce different failure sequences despite identical physical data movement.

A selection component selects among supported mapping functions, while a mapping component and its subcomponents derive physical-address bits from logical-address bits. For each bit, selectable operations may include pass-through, inversion, XOR, XNOR, address swapping, and other Boolean functions, including operations using multiple logical-address bits. This permits a very large number of possible mappings.

Mapping functions may be fixed during manufacture using hardwiring, trim parameters, fuses, or anti-fuses, or selected dynamically. Selection can depend on random-number generation, unique identifiers for a device, die, or array, a schedule, or triggers such as boot, reboot, host commands, access-count thresholds, or detection of row-hammer or other malicious activity. Examples also describe randomization using shift registers, asynchronous oscillators, and counters, with selections potentially changing at power-up in volatile memory.

When a host issues an access command containing a logical address, the memory device uses the selected mapping function to determine a physical address and accesses the corresponding data. The physical-address space may be larger than the logical-address space to accommodate scratch cells used during wear-leveling. Example three-bit mappings illustrate pass-through and inversion configurations as well as more complex XOR/XNOR mappings.

The described system can include an external memory controller, a device memory controller, one or more memory dice, local controllers, and 2D or 3D memory arrays. It may also include a processor, BIOS, peripherals, and an I/O controller, with command/address, clock, and data channels connecting the host and memory. A memory die includes programmable cells, word and digit lines, row and column decoders, and sensing circuitry used for read, write, and refresh operations. Control functions may be distributed among the external, device, and local controllers or implemented by the processor.

The disclosed methods and apparatus select a mapping function, optionally select a logic operation for each logical-address bit, route address bits through mapping subcomponents, receive an access command, determine a physical address, and access the corresponding data. Additional features include random-number-based selection, identifier-based selection, scheduled or event-triggered changes, use of multiple mapping functions, security-key-controlled selection, and wear-leveling data transfers. A security key may enable direct, pass-through addressing for manufacturer testing and debugging, with that mode disabled before shipment. Drawings and tables illustrate system architecture, mapping components, memory arrays, address mappings, wear-leveling sequences, and operational flowcharts.

This passage is the user manual for the SanDisk Sansa Fuze MP3 player, covering safety, features, operation, and support.

**Safety and cleaning:** Read the full manual before use; do not wear headphones while driving, cycling, or operating motorized vehicles, and avoid high volumes, which can cause noise-induced hearing loss (sounds below 80 decibels are unlikely to cause damage). Keep the player away from moisture, clean it with a soft lint-free cloth, supervise young children, never force connectors, and never disassemble, crush, short-circuit, or incinerate the battery. Dispose of the device through local waste systems and comply with copyright law for home/personal use.

**Features and overview:** The player has a 1.9" color screen, FM radio (where applicable), built-in microphone for voice recording, and a microSDHC expansion slot. It supports MP3, WAV, WMA, secure WMA, Audible and audiobooks, MPEG4 video, and JPEG photos. The non-replaceable internal rechargeable battery lasts up to 24 hours of audio or 5 hours of video.

**Controls and connection:** The power switch turns the player on/off and resets it (hold ~10 seconds); the Hold switch on the right locks all buttons while music continues playing; the thumbwheel navigates menus and adjusts volume. The player charges via the Sansa cable and a computer's USB port (or an optional AC/car adapter), and can be connected for file transfer, firmware updates, or formatting, which erases all content.

**Transferring content:** Music can be dragged and dropped into the MUSIC folder or transferred using Windows Media Player (adding files to the library, creating playlists, synchronizing), while Audible files require Audible Manager. Photos and videos are converted and transferred using Sansa Media Converter, which supports cropping, rotating, and resizing.

**Playback features:** Music options include Repeat, Shuffle, MusicEQ, adding/removing songs from the Go List, and deleting songs. Audiobooks offer chapter mode and playback speed. Video playback includes bookmarks, rating, brightness, and deletion. Photos support slideshows with shuffle, looping, slide duration, slideshow music, a Photo Go List, and deletion. The FM radio allows manual tuning, up to 30 presets, auto preset, viewing presets, and recording stations; region (USA/Japan) and mono/stereo mode can be set.

**Recording, deletion, and settings:** Voice recordings are made with the built-in microphone. Content can be deleted on the device or via computer. System settings cover wallpaper color, album art display, backlight, power saver, language, date/time, brightness, factory reset, device info, USB mode (Auto Detect/MTP/MSC), formatting, and press-and-hold behavior.

**Support and warranty:** The manual provides troubleshooting answers, directs users to SanDisk's support site and technical support number, and states a one-year limited warranty plus an end user license agreement for accompanying software.
12,000-year-old camel engravings at Jebel Misma suggest early human presence in the once-verdant Nefud.

The author argues that K–12 education’s emphasis on broad “skills,” metacognition, critical thinking, and a “portrait of the graduate” has displaced substantive knowledge of geography, history, science, math, languages, literature, and the arts. Such goals are often vague or depend on content: students cannot think critically about unfamiliar subjects, as examples involving cricket terminology and string theory illustrate. The passage also challenges equating knowledge with memorization and dismissing it as obsolete because information can be looked up, noting that experts retain extensive information and that background knowledge is essential to strong reading.

The author identifies declining standards, including rising high-school GPAs, reduced graduation-testing requirements, and uneven use of knowledge-rich curricula. Fifteen states are described as joining an initiative promoting high-quality instructional materials, though even approved English curricula may lack sequential knowledge, and AI can be misused to weaken curricula. Ultimately, the piece contends that knowledge is necessary for complex and critical thought and that schools should provide children with substantive content rather than prioritize fashionable skill lists.

Malaria remains a major global health burden, with 247 million cases and 619,000 deaths reported in 2021. Nigeria accounted for nearly 27% of global cases, with an estimated 68 million cases and 194,000 deaths. Insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) are a cost-effective malaria-control intervention, particularly for children under five and pregnant women.

This secondary analysis used the 2021 Nigeria Malaria Indicator Survey, covering 13,727 households and 14,476 women aged 15–49. Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals were used to examine ITN ownership and use.

In 56% of households, at least one ITN was available, averaging 1.3 nets per household; 25% had enough nets to cover all members if each net were shared by two people. Ownership was higher in rural than urban households, in the North West and North East, and among lower wealth quintiles.

About 41% of children under five slept under an ITN. Use was significantly associated with age, residence, geopolitical zone, and household wealth, but not sex. Younger children, rural residents, children in the North West or North East, and children in lower wealth quintiles were more likely to use ITNs.

About half of pregnant women used an ITN. Use varied significantly by geopolitical zone and wealth quintile. Women in the North East and North West and those in lower wealth groups had higher odds of using an ITN. Women with no or primary education also had higher odds of use than those with more than secondary education.

The authors concluded that ITN coverage and utilization remained below the National Malaria Strategic Plan target of 80%, despite progress linked to mass distribution, antenatal-care, and community-based interventions. They recommended expanded distribution, improved healthcare access, stronger health education, and continued monitoring to address regional and socioeconomic disparities.

NVIDIA Corporation’s unaudited Form 10-Q for the quarter ended May 1, 2022 reported revenue of $8.29 billion, up 46% year over year and 8% sequentially. Gross profit was $5.43 billion and gross margin was 65.5%, compared with 64.1% a year earlier. Operating income was $1.87 billion, down 4% year over year, while net income was $1.62 billion, down 15%, and diluted earnings per share were $0.64, down 16%. Operating expenses increased 113% year over year, largely because NVIDIA recorded a $1.35 billion acquisition termination charge after NVIDIA and SoftBank ended the proposed Arm acquisition because of significant regulatory challenges.

Graphics segment revenue was $4.62 billion, up 34%, with operating income of $2.48 billion. Compute & Networking revenue was $3.67 billion, up 66%, with operating income of $1.61 billion. By market, Gaming revenue rose 31% to $3.62 billion, Data Center revenue rose 83% to $3.75 billion, Professional Visualization revenue rose 67% to $622 million, Automotive revenue fell 10% to $138 million, and OEM and Other revenue fell 52% to $158 million. Revenue was billed to Taiwan at $2.78 billion, China including Hong Kong at $2.08 billion, and the United States at $1.93 billion. No customer accounted for at least 10% of quarterly revenue.

As of May 1, 2022, NVIDIA reported $45.21 billion of assets, $18.89 billion of liabilities, and $26.32 billion of shareholders’ equity. Cash and cash equivalents totaled $3.89 billion, marketable securities totaled $16.45 billion, inventories totaled $3.16 billion, and long-term debt totaled $10.95 billion. The company generated $1.73 billion of operating cash flow, received $2.61 billion from investing activities, and used $2.45 billion in financing activities. NVIDIA repurchased 8.6 million shares for $2.00 billion and paid $100 million in dividends during the quarter. On May 23, 2022, its board expanded and extended the repurchase authorization to $15 billion through December 2023.

Stock-based compensation expense was $578 million, and $4.95 billion of unearned stock-based compensation remained. The present value of operating lease obligations was $899 million, future unconditional purchase commitments totaled $11.44 billion, and long-term debt consisted of unsecured senior notes maturing between 2023 and 2060. NVIDIA had not issued commercial paper under its $575 million program.

In May 2022, NVIDIA settled with the SEC over cryptocurrency-mining-related disclosures in fiscal 2018 Form 10-Q filings, agreeing to cease-and-desist from violating certain securities laws and pay a $5.5 million civil penalty without admitting or denying the SEC’s findings. Related securities and derivative lawsuits remained pending or stayed; NVIDIA recorded no accrual for the described contingencies because potential liabilities were not considered probable.

Demand remained difficult to forecast because of cryptocurrency-market volatility, product transitions, channel decisions, pandemic-related behavior, and long manufacturing lead times. China lockdowns, the war in Ukraine, and supply-chain constraints affected demand and production; NVIDIA paused direct sales to Russia. Management reported effective disclosure controls, no material changes in internal control over financial reporting, no material changes in significant accounting policies or critical accounting estimates, and no material climate-related impact on operations to date.

Chef Mario Batali took a leave from his businesses and was removed from ABC’s “The Chew” amid sexual misconduct allegations. He apologized, took responsibility for past behavior and said the reported conduct matched his.

HMD Global opened the Nokia 8’s Android 8.1 beta but had not shared the promised kernel source 136 days later. Its CPO said the bootloader would remain locked for security, though kernel modifications would be released. Critics called the delay a GPLv2 violation harming goodwill, despite limited value for custom ROMs.

Researchers analyzed 39 Ediacaran seafloor fossils from Newfoundland, about 560 million years old, and identified a spongelike organism previously classified as decomposed organic matter. Its pores and upward-projecting tubes suggest it was a filter feeder that lived atop other organisms and could reach 53 centimeters long. The creature resembles a sponge and may be an ancestor of modern sponges. Its spiky appearance inspired a name honoring punk rocker John Lydon, or Johnny Rotten, and the Beothuk fruit jiggamint, now called gooseberry.

A University of Queensland study found that Black, Western Green and Jamesons mamba venoms have two neurological effects: postsynaptic neurotoxicity causes limp paralysis that current antivenoms treat, while presynaptic toxicity can then cause painful, uncontrolled muscle spasms. This explains why patients may initially improve after antivenom before spasms develop. The researchers also found geographic differences in Black Mamba venom, particularly between Kenyan and South African populations, complicating treatment. The findings support developing specialized antivenoms and improving evidence-based snakebite care.

This systematic review examines AI applications in higher-education assessment, grading, and feedback, guided by the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework. It assesses AI’s effectiveness in automating and standardizing assessment, its accuracy and fairness relative to traditional grading, and its capacity to provide personalized feedback. Literature was searched in five academic databases, screened by two reviewers, assessed for quality, synthesized thematically, and reported using PRISMA 2020.

Twenty studies were included. Findings indicate that AI can improve efficiency, scalability, consistency, and rapid feedback, particularly for objective assessments in STEM. It can reduce educators’ workload, monitor student progress, tailor learning pathways, and provide timely individualized feedback, supporting engagement, self-regulated learning, and diverse student needs. Students generally welcomed AI’s convenience and personalized feedback. In African universities, including Zambia’s nascent initiatives, AI may help address large classes, limited resources, and inconsistent grading.

Challenges remain, including algorithmic bias, privacy and data security, transparency, inadequate infrastructure and training, digital inequality, academic integrity, and limited adoption. AI is generally more reliable for objective work than for assessing creativity, critical thinking, communication, and other subjective qualities. The review concludes that AI should complement rather than replace human judgment and calls for validation across diverse settings, longitudinal research, ethical governance, professional development, and collaboration among educators, technologists, and policymakers.

Birmingham City’s top ten away days of the previous decade are ranked, highlighting dramatic victories, promotion and survival moments, and strong travelling support. An MIT Sloan case examines the April 2010 Deepwater Horizon disaster, BP’s organizational and safety culture, the decisions preceding the Macondo well blowout, and the resulting human, environmental, and economic consequences.

On April 20, 2010, two explosions aboard Transocean’s Deepwater Horizon rig forced 126 workers to abandon the rig. Eleven people died and 17 were injured. The rig burned for 36 hours and sank on April 22, taking the well’s top pipe and blowout-preventer components with it. After the well was capped on July 15, nearly five million barrels of oil had spilled into the Gulf of Mexico, making it the largest marine oil spill in U.S. waters. High gas levels had been present, but alarms had been disabled because of false alarms; a warning over the public-address system preceded the explosion.

BP’s history included a period of state ownership, privatization, financial decline, and extensive cost cutting. From the mid-1990s, it pursued growth through mergers, including Amoco and ARCO, and presented itself as environmentally conscious through “Beyond Petroleum” and alternative-energy investments. CEO Tony Hayward pledged greater safety focus and reduced risk aversion while cutting management layers and reducing the workforce. Earlier decentralization had shifted authority and performance-based compensation to autonomous site managers under an “asset federation” model, but this arrangement reduced information sharing on risk practices and centralized oversight of performance targets.

BP had a significant prior safety record. The 2005 Texas City refinery explosion killed 15 people, injured 180, and caused losses exceeding $1.5 billion. A Baker Report found reduced maintenance and safety spending, senior-management responsibility, and weak corporate communication about process safety. In 2006, more than 200,000 gallons of oil leaked into Alaska’s Prudhoe Bay from corroded pipeline, despite regulatory warnings since 2001. BP subsequently implemented leadership, auditing, maintenance, and process-safety initiatives, yet between June 2007 and February 2010, 97% of willful OSHA refinery safety violations went to two BP-owned refineries.

BP acquired the Macondo rights in March 2009 and held a 65% interest, with Anadarko holding 25% and MOEX Offshore 10%. Drilling resumed on February 3, 2010, after Hurricane Ida delayed the project. The 51-day, $96 million drilling estimate had become an 80-day project that exceeded its budget. Transocean charged roughly $500,000 per day plus similar contractor fees. A 2009 safety audit had identified 390 urgent repairs, while the drilling-control computers frequently froze and the rig had not visited dry dock for nine years. Many BP decision-makers had recently assumed their roles.

The case focuses on three disputed decisions to close the exploratory well:

1. **Casing design:** BP chose long-string casing, which provided two barriers against gas flow and could be installed faster, over liner-tieback casing, which provided four barriers but required more time and an estimated additional $7–10 million. An initial plan review recommended against long-string casing, although a revised review made it the primary option.

2. **Centralizers:** Halliburton’s OptiCem model found a significant risk of gas-flow problems with the planned six centralizers and recommended at least 21. BP personnel questioned the model and decided against additional centralizers. A later Halliburton report classified the well as having a “SEVERE gas flow problem,” but its covering email did not mention the hazard, and key BP managers said they had not read the relevant page.

3. **Cement-bond log and mud circulation:** BP performed only a partial mud circulation—about 30 minutes rather than the estimated six to 12 hours—and chose not to conduct a cement-bond log despite Halliburton’s channeling warnings and the loss of 3,000 barrels of drilling mud. BP’s decision tree did not detect this failure mode, while a bond log was the only accurate diagnostic cited. A Congressional inquiry also questioned the failure to install a lockdown sleeve.

The spill affected 25 national wildlife refuges, reached all five Gulf states, and damaged wetlands during the breeding season of numerous species. Louisiana’s affected shoreline grew from 287 miles in July to 320 miles by late November. Economic consequences included Transocean’s $560 million loss, $374 million in lost oil, potential fines of up to $3.5 billion, falling BP share prices, and criticism of BP’s public relations. A U.S. deepwater-drilling moratorium contributed to an estimated 250,000 Gulf-region job losses across energy, fishing, and tourism. BP created a $20 billion claims fund, which by February 2011 had received more than 500,000 claims and paid over $3.6 billion to 170,000 claimants.

As of early 2011, investigations were continuing and participants disputed responsibility. The case concluded that the three principal decisions, BP’s organizational culture, contractor relationships, incentive systems, and handling of safety warnings may have contributed to the disaster, with several decisions favoring cost reduction and expediency over caution.

Lecture 14 examines limited attention as part of economic decision-making. Experiments on change blindness, the gorilla test, and dichotic listening show that people can direct attention but have limited capacity to process simultaneous information. Attention may also be affected by distractions, environmental conditions, worries, sleep, poverty, and temptations, and may improve through practice.

High-stakes examples illustrate costly inattention. EntreMed’s stock rose sharply when an already-reported cancer-treatment result received front-page coverage, while traders initially paid little attention to the original publication and later replication failure. Confusion between similarly named companies and stock tickers provides another example.

Chetty and coauthors study inattention to sales taxes using a model in which consumers fully perceive salient information but process opaque information only in proportion to \(1-\theta\), where \(\theta\) measures inattention. In a California grocery-store experiment, displaying sales-tax-inclusive prices reduced demand for treated goods by 2.2 units, or 8.8 percent relative to baseline. Using the tax rate and an estimated price elasticity of 1.59, the authors inferred that consumers reacted to sales-tax changes only about one-quarter as much as to other price changes. Nonexperimental evidence similarly found strong responses to salient excise taxes embedded in prices but almost no response to less transparent sales taxes.

Tax design may intentionally use salience: ordinary taxes are easier to collect when consumers do not alter behavior, whereas taxes on goods involving externalities or internalities are more salient because governments want consumption to decline. Heterogeneous attention can also mean that some consumers distort their choices substantially even when average responses appear small.

The lecture then considers whether inattention can have large welfare consequences. People may fail to encode relevant information when their existing beliefs do not suggest that it matters. For example, seaweed farmers in Indonesia knew their line-spacing practices but neglected pod size. Participating in an experiment alone had little effect, while receiving summarized results and recommendations led to substantial improvements. This supports the idea that inaccurate beliefs can prevent people from noticing information that could correct them, producing persistent errors and potentially large welfare losses.

In this inaugural address, President Roosevelt pledges candor and resolves that "the only thing we have to fear is fear itself," insisting that the nation will endure, revive, and prosper. He acknowledges severe material distress—shrinking values, rising taxes, frozen trade, idle enterprise, lost savings, and unemployment—but argues the crisis stems not from a lack of substance but from the failure of those who manage the exchange of goods, whose "unscrupulous" practices he indicts before the court of public opinion. Lacking vision, they responded to the failure of credit only by lending more money and pleading for restored confidence. He calls for restoring the temple of civilization to ancient truths, judging success by social values rather than monetary profit, holding that happiness lies in the joy of creative achievement, and rejecting the belief that public office should be valued for pride of place and personal profit. Confidence, he says, thrives only on honesty, honor, and unselfish performance, and restoration demands action now, not merely ethics.

His greatest task is putting people to work, achievable through direct government recruiting on a wartime footing combined with needed public projects, alongside redistributing population from industrial centers to the land, raising agricultural values, preventing foreclosures of homes and farms, drastically reducing the cost of government, unifying scattered relief efforts, and nationally planning transportation, communications, and utilities—acting quickly rather than merely talking.

Two safeguards against the old evils are required: strict supervision of banking, credit, and investments to end speculation with other people's money, and an adequate but sound currency. He will urge a new Congress in special session for detailed measures and seek state assistance, prioritizing the domestic economy over international trade, though he will still work to restore world trade through international readjustment. Guided by the interdependence of all regions of the United States, he dedicates the nation to the "good neighbor" policy, and urges that Americans cannot merely take but must give, submitting to a common discipline as a sacred obligation binding them as in armed strife.

Taking unhesitating leadership, he holds that the constitutional system can meet extraordinary needs through changes in emphasis without losing essential form, but warns that unprecedented need may require a temporary departure from the normal balance of executive and legislative authority. Should Congress fail to act, he will request broad executive power to wage a war against the emergency. Facing arduous days, he expresses confidence in essential democracy, accepts the people's mandate for direct, vigorous action, and asks God's blessing.

The U.S. Department disapproved of Consul-General Allen’s request that Shanghai authorities surrender Kim Ok-kiun’s Korean murderer, since U.S. consular jurisdiction did not extend beyond American citizens. U.S. Minister Sill reported that rebels defeated government troops near Chon-ju, captured the city and seized weapons, while the government lacked adequate military capacity. He urged Admiral Skerrett to send a ship to Chemulpo to protect Americans, noting that most of the squadron was assigned to the Bering Sea and that British, French, Chinese, and Japanese vessels had already been sent. Sill requested immediate assistance only if required to safeguard American interests. Chinese Chargé Denby reported that, following the Korean king’s appeal, China had dispatched 1,500 troops to Korea, planned to increase the force to 2,225, and ordered three warships to Chemulpo. Li Hung-chang assured Japan and Russia that the troops would be withdrawn when hostilities ended.

A Jan. 19, 2001 email circulated a collection of Enron-related news reports, dominated by coverage of California’s electricity crisis. Pacific Gas & Electric and Southern California Edison were near bankruptcy after power costs surged while retail rates remained capped under 1996 deregulation law. The utilities had accumulated more than $11.5 billion in power-related debt and suffered additional defaults and credit-rating downgrades. Rolling blackouts occurred amid tight supply, high demand, aging generating facilities, low hydroelectric output and sharply higher natural-gas prices.

California approved $400 million for the state to buy power for the utilities and regulators prevented the utilities from unilaterally cutting customer service. Gov. Gray Davis also proposed purchasing as much as $3.5 billion annually under multyear contracts at $55 per megawatt hour, compared with an average customer rate of roughly $72. Federal officials issued temporary orders requiring electricity and natural-gas suppliers to continue serving California, while proposed wholesale price caps drew opposition from Ken Lay and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. Gas pipeline disruptions also threatened fuel supplies and refinery operations.

Reuters reported that the crisis had made utilities a more heterogeneous and risky investment, with major losses for shareholders and bondholders and potential credit exposure for power producers such as Reliant Energy, Duke Energy and Southern Energy. Pennsylvania’s Public Utility Commission separately rejected GPU Energy’s comparison to California, attributing GPU’s problems to its own decisions to divest generation and avoid sufficient long-term supply contracts.

Other reports said Dow Jones’s bandwidth price table expanded from two to ten city-pair routes, with Aquila Broadband becoming the third bandwidth market maker; Enron was making markets for Los Angeles-San Jose rather than Los Angeles-San Francisco. EOTT Energy Partners, an Enron subsidiary, declared a fourth-quarter 2000 distribution of $0.475 per common unit, payable Feb. 14. Enron Energy Services also signed a ten-year energy-management agreement with Owens-Illinois covering 53 manufacturing facilities in 20 states and projected energy purchases exceeding $2 billion.

MACD and RSI are momentum indicators that can be combined to analyze trends and price swings. MACD, based on 12- and 26-period exponential moving averages with a 9-period signal line, is mainly used to identify trend direction and momentum. RSI, which ranges from 0 to 100, is primarily used to identify overbought conditions above 70 and oversold conditions below 30, though it can also signal divergences and failure swings.

Traders may use MACD to define the overall trend and RSI to identify swings, or use one indicator to confirm signals from the other. Possible rules include buying when MACD rises above its signal line and RSI rises after reaching oversold territory, and shorting under the opposite conditions. Because both indicators measure momentum, combining them may be redundant, and their relative accuracy depends on the parameters, asset, and market tested.

A backtested strategy used MACD, RSI, and a third mean-reversion filter, buying when all three conditions aligned and selling when the filter reversed. On SMH from 2001 onward, it recorded 235 trades, a 73% win rate, and an average gain of 0.88% per trade, including 0.03% commissions and slippage per trade. The strategy performed best on semiconductors and did not suit every asset, underscoring the need for clear rules, testing, and asset-specific evaluation.

The flexbone is a run-heavy offense evolved from the wishbone, emphasizing option plays and misdirection. It is often associated with the triple option and can be viewed as an original spread offense because multiple backs create running threats across the formation.

Personnel requirements include a decisive quarterback who can run, make reads, and adequately threaten defenses with play-action passing. The fullback must be powerful and athletic for inside runs and blocking, while the slotbacks need to block, run, catch, and play receiver. Wide receivers must block and occasionally threaten defenses deep, and offensive linemen must excel at cut and combination blocks while adjusting to defensive fronts.

The flexbone’s unusual structure can force defenses to spend more time preparing for its options and creates assignment confusion among several potential ball carriers. It supports strong ball control, long possession, and physical wear on opponents, particularly against weaker tacklers. Its weaknesses include limited passing volume, difficulty mounting late comebacks or moving quickly in two-minute situations, and significant practice demands that leave less time for pass development. Its mesh reads, pitches, and timing requirements can also cause problems in poor weather.

Common formations include the double slot, with two A-backs positioned behind and outside the tackles; one A-back often goes in motion, sometimes reversing direction at the snap. The trips formation moves an A-back across the formation as a receiver, while the receivers-over formation places an extra receiver across from the line to block, though he is ineligible to catch a pass.

The primary running play is the triple option, featuring a fullback dive, quarterback keeper, or pitch to a trailing A-back. The quarterback reads the defensive end to determine the dive, then may read an unblocked linebacker or safety for the pitch. The midline option attacks the middle through a quarterback-fullback mesh; the quarterback reads the unblocked three-technique defensive tackle and either gives to the fullback or replaces the defender. The rocket toss is a quick outside run in which the quarterback spins away and tosses to a moving A-back, often with the fullback going opposite the toss to occupy defenders.

Common passing plays include the play-action post wheel, which disguises a pass as a running action; the toss boot, which uses fake toss action before the quarterback rolls away to find a backfield receiver or crossing route; and four verticals, which often use comeback routes when defenders play softly over outside receivers. Four verticals is especially useful against one-high defenses or when receivers face single coverage.

The flexbone has historically been used by Navy, Army, and Air Force. Paul Johnson ran variants at Georgia Southern, Navy, and Georgia Tech, whose 2009 team won the ACC Championship. Harding won the Division II national championship in 2023, and the offense remains widely used at many high schools, particularly where strong passing quarterbacks are less common.

As Germany marked 500 years since Luther's Reformation, the Protestant church, facing dwindling attendance, turned to social media to reach people with little time for in-person worship. In Magdeburg, Pastor Ralf Peter Reimann launched an experimental Twitter service at the Walloon Reformed Church of St. Augustine, where about 40 parishioners tweeted during evening prayers and a screen displayed a hashtagged feed of messages from across Germany. Reimann argued social media could help retain and attract followers in a secular society, citing Luther's "priesthood of all believers" and the idea that Christians, not only pastors, should communicate with one another. Historian Ulrike Zitzlsperger drew a parallel with Luther's 16th-century pamphlets, cheap and widely distributed, which spread debate so rapidly that the Catholic Church could not suppress them. Responses were mixed: some users shared prayers and encouragement, others found it hectic, and 86-year-old Ingeborg Brunner, without a smartphone, preferred singing hymns. NVIDIA’s A100 Tensor Core GPU introduces the Ampere architecture with third-generation Tensor Cores for HPC and deep learning. TF32 Tensor Cores require no script changes and provide up to 8× the FP32 throughput of A100 and 10× that of V100, while FP16/BF16 mixed precision provides up to 2× the throughput of TF32, 16× that of FP32 on A100, and 20× on V100. FP64 acceleration reaches 19.5 TFLOPS, 2.5× Tesla V100 performance. In cuSOLVER’s TCAIRS iterative-refinement solver, TF32 was the fastest and most robust Tensor Core format, achieving a 2.0× geometric-mean speedup over the FP64 solver and up to 4× on large complex matrices.

A100 supports 2:4 fine-grained structured sparsity, allowing two nonzero values in every four-entry vector. Sparse Tensor Cores skip zero-valued operands, doubling math throughput, while compressed weights reduce storage and bandwidth requirements by 2×. NVIDIA’s dense-training, pruning, and fine-tuning recipe produced virtually no inference-accuracy loss across numerous vision, detection, segmentation, language, and translation networks; training acceleration without accuracy loss remains an active research area.

The GPU’s compute and memory hierarchy includes separate FP32 and INT32 cores, 192 KB per SM of combined L1 cache and shared memory, 40 GB of HBM2 memory delivering 1,555 GB/s, and a 40 MB L2 cache that is 6.7× larger than V100’s. L2 bandwidth is 2.3× higher, and compute data compression can improve DRAM and L2 bandwidth by up to 4× and L2 capacity by up to 2×. ECC protects HBM2, L2, L1 caches, and register files. Tensor Core improvements include sharing data across 32 warp threads rather than eight, larger matrix operations, 8× fewer issued instructions, and 2.9× fewer register-file accesses for matrix multiplication.

The Multi-Instance GPU feature can partition an A100 into as many as seven isolated GPU Instances with dedicated compute, cache, and memory resources. Compute Instances support simultaneous contexts and Volta-style MPS, while MIG migration can move virtual GPUs between matching instances and physical GPUs. This provides quality-of-service and fault isolation for multi-tenant workloads and can deliver up to seven times as many GPU Instances.

Third-generation NVLink provides twelve links per A100, 600 GB/s aggregate bandwidth, peer-memory access, and improved error recovery. A100 also supports PCIe Gen 4 at 31.5 GB/s per direction for x16 links and SR-IOV virtualization. Additional hardware includes a five-core NVJPG JPEG decoder, an optical-flow and stereo-disparity accelerator, five NVDEC units, and FP16 and FP32 atomic operations reported as 11× and 2.7× faster than V100.

CUDA 11 adds support for A100’s Tensor Core formats, sparsity, CUDA Graphs, MIG, and L2 residency controls. New programming capabilities include task-graph launch and dependency optimizations, asynchronous global-to-shared-memory copies, hardware asynchronous barriers, and Cooperative Groups reductions. L2 persistent-cache allocation can be set in 2.5 MB increments, although it is disabled in MIG mode. A100 has compute capability 8.0 and omits display connectors, RT Cores, and NVENC.

DGX A100 combines eight A100 GPUs with six NVSwitches, providing 4.8 TB/s aggregate bidirectional bandwidth, up to 5 PFLOPS of AI performance, and up to 56 isolated accelerators through MIG. It supports large-scale InfiniBand and Ethernet fabrics, NVIDIA’s Magnum IO and DeepOps software, and GPU-optimized containers, models, and SDKs delivered through the NGC Private Registry.

The Larry Swedroe Portfolio is an evidence-based, diversified strategy designed for long-term growth with reduced volatility and drawdowns. Its standard allocation is 30% stocks and 70% bonds: 15% U.S. small-cap value, 7.5% international small-cap value, 7.5% emerging markets, and 70% intermediate bonds. Implementation generally favors low-cost, passively managed index funds or ETFs, with allocations adjusted for risk tolerance and investment horizon.

Swedroe recommends bottom-up value investing, focusing on companies with strong balance sheets, consistent earnings, and good management while avoiding overpayment. He favors small-cap value stocks for their historical outperformance, greater growth potential, market inefficiencies, and lower correlation with the broader market, although they carry greater volatility and loss risk. His approach also emphasizes diversification across asset classes and regions, avoiding active management and market timing, and periodic rebalancing—annually or when allocations deviate by a specified threshold, such as 5%.

A backtest using VIOV as the U.S. small-cap value proxy and data from 2012 with daily rebalancing produced an annual return of 3.71%. Because of its large bond allocation, the strategy is expected to trail stocks over long periods and may be better suited to risk-averse investors or pensioners. The passage also cites a presumed 30-year compound annual return of 6.28%, while noting the benefit of consistently lower interest rates.

In his 2011 shareholder letter, Warren Buffett said Berkshire Hathaway should repurchase shares below estimated intrinsic value to benefit continuing shareholders. The Florida District Court of Appeal reversed summary judgment for The Personal Service Insurance Company and George Johnson, Jr. Langston was injured in Florida while riding in a vehicle owned by George Johnson, Jr. and operated by Fred Johnson. Under Florida tort law, an owner entrusting a vehicle to another may be personally liable for the operator’s negligence. The court applied Ohio law to interpret Personal Service’s surety bond. Although the bond’s terms limited the surety’s liability, Ohio statutory language created a lien for holders of final judgments against the principal for damages arising from motor-vehicle ownership or use. The court distinguished Kerr because the present accident occurred in Florida, where George Johnson could be liable, and found Thornton did not address contractual liability under the bond. Because Personal Service would be liable for a judgment obtained against George Johnson, the court reversed and remanded for further proceedings.

This theoretical paper examines how an Australian university developed an “Arts Specialism” to address insufficient arts-education competencies among pre-service primary teachers, particularly amid limited curriculum time and education-policy restructuring. Using Ball’s three contexts of policy-making—policy influence, policy-text production and policy practice—and critical discourse analysis, it examines the specialism’s curriculum text, supporting documents and implementation.

The literature identifies the educational and cultural value of arts while documenting barriers including inadequate teacher preparation, insufficient time, limited resources and a mismatch between policy intentions and classroom implementation. By the early 2000s, the university had reduced arts education to one of 32 primary programme courses, despite the Australian Curriculum requiring sequential learning in dance, drama, media arts, music and visual arts.

Supported by university leaders, arts organisations, policymakers and community stakeholders, the university developed four specialism courses following a compulsory foundation course. Standards developed with the National Advocates for Arts Education emphasised expert content knowledge, pedagogical knowledge and effective classroom teaching. The courses address all five arts through contemporary and traditional practices, digital technologies, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander arts, school-based projects, performances, presentations and displays. Each course lasted 12 weeks, with the four-course suite reported as providing 600 hours of arts education.

Implementation required negotiation over staffing, costs and timetabling. COVID-19 prompted a shift to online delivery and the development of external, community-based arts projects. School partnerships and a children’s arts festival provided practical teaching experience. Phased implementation, collaboration among arts staff and support from arts and education organisations helped build PST capacity. PST feedback reported increased confidence, arts content and pedagogical knowledge, culturally responsive teaching and a stronger understanding of the arts’ value in education.

Persistent constraints included insufficient time, staffing and resources, the need to balance arts courses with other programme requirements, and industrial-relations issues affecting casual staff. The paper identifies opportunities to expand the specialism, strengthen policy support and arts-industry collaboration, and conduct mixed-methods research on graduates’ professional journeys and nationwide school-based curriculum implementation. Research followed ethical standards, with consent obtained for anonymised PST comments.

Centuries of stories describe children reportedly raised by wolves, apes, or sheep, though many are considered hoaxes. A nineteenth-century Texas legend told of a “Wolf Girl” who was reportedly seen with wolves, captured, escaped during a wolf-induced panic, and later appeared with two pups before disappearing. For NMI injection, the hypervisor must not intercept IRET but must intercept #DB and use the guest’s “NMI Complete” message to determine when another NMI can be injected. Intercepting #DB allows the guest to choose when to send that message, provided it does so only when another NMI can safely be handled. In the example, the NMI handler sets a per-CPU variable, sets TF using PUSHF/POPF immediately before IRET, and makes IRET the next instruction. The resulting #VC with error code 0x41 invokes a handler that checks the scenario, clears the variable, and issues “NMI Complete” via VMGEXIT.

On SEV-ES hardware supporting DebugVirtualization, hardware debug-register virtualization is enabled through the VMSA SEV_FEATURES field; hardware saves and restores debug state, and the hypervisor clears all related intercepts. Otherwise, the hypervisor intercepts DR7 reads and writes, caching writes without changing the actual DR7 and returning the cached value on reads. SMM is unsupported, as is nested virtualization under SEV-ES and SEV-SNP.

SNP RestrictInjection limits host notifications to a #HV doorbell. Its common format targets OS-level notifications while leaving driver-specific data separate. The doorbell is APIC-aligned: PendingEvent occupies bytes 0–1, NoEoiRequired occupies byte 2, and bytes 3–63 are reserved. The backing page must be host-owned rather than RMPUPDATE-assigned, and guest accesses must use C=0. PendingEvent bit 15 is NoFurtherSignal, bits 14–10 are reserved, bit 9 indicates a virtual #MC, bit 8 an NMI, and bits 7–0 hold an interrupt vector. An acknowledged vector enters service and later requires EOI. A nonzero NoEoiRequired means an explicit EOI is unnecessary; guests attempt to clear it atomically and, if that fails, request an X2APIC EOI MSR write via VMGEXIT.

Because #HV ignores interrupt shadows, a guest entering HLT must not inspect pending interrupts or enable interrupts. If an HLT intercept finds pending work, the host must immediately re-enter the guest, which then examines interrupt state as after receiving #HV. Doorbell configuration uses GHCB VMGEXIT SW_EXITCODE 0x8000_0014: guests can request a preferred address, must SET one under Restricted Injection, and may QUERY whether one exists. Accepted pages may be RMPUPDATEd by the host after the guest PVALIDATEs them; reused old addresses require page assignment first.

The host must emulate APIC presentation, acknowledgment, in-service, and EOI semantics. It writes ready vectors to PendingEvent while the vCPU is stopped, schedules #HV for a newly pending vector when NoFurtherSignal is clear, and may replace an unacknowledged vector with a higher-priority one without another #HV. Nonmaskable events set their bit and NoFurtherSignal. The host tracks vectors and EOI-assist state, treats vector clearing as acknowledgment and in-service entry, and treats NoEoiRequired clearing as EOI. Explicit APIC EOI writes and assisted EOI are treated identically.

Guests must atomically exchange PendingEvent with zero before acting on a vector because the host may replace it without another #HV. They may acknowledge immediately or defer until EFLAGS.IF permits. For EOI, guests atomically clear NoEoiRequired; if it was already zero, they must explicitly write the X2APIC EOI MSR via VMGEXIT. With EFLAGS.IF=0, guests must still handle nonmaskable events, clearing their flags and NoFurtherSignal while leaving an unacknowledged vector unchanged if they dispatch only those events. Guests must validate vectors against expected interrupts. Noncooperative hosts may cause denial of service; under normal operation, receipt of #HV while NoFurtherSignal is nonzero is grounds for a system panic.

The passage argues that iPhone’s closed ecosystem offers stronger security than open Android devices, though iOS is not immune to malware. For iOS 10.3.1, it highlights encryption via passcode, PIN, or fingerprint; two-factor authentication prompts; automatic erasure after ten failed login attempts; and secure iCloud backups. iPhones also include built-in anti-malware protections, regular updates, and an exclusive app store. Find My iPhone lets users locate, lock, or erase a stolen device through iCloud. The passage says iOS more tightly controls app permissions than Android, citing 375 publicly disclosed iOS vulnerabilities in 2015 versus 130 for Android. It attributes Android’s weaker security partly to manufacturer-specific customization, fragmented updates, and Apple’s exclusive control of iPhone hardware and software.

U.S. builder sentiment slipped as the NAHB/Wells Fargo index fell to 68 in April from 71 in March, below analysts’ forecast of 70.
