Last-shot basketball situations require preparation, composure, conditioning, and practiced execution because a single possession can determine the outcome. Teams should get the ball to their best shooter, exploit defensive overplays, keep plays simple, and have nonshooters attack the offensive boards, since many games are decided by putbacks. Holding for the final shot can create a 12-point swing based on the teams’ combined final and opening possessions of consecutive periods.

The basic guideline is to hold for the last shot with fewer than 30 seconds remaining when leading or trailing by fewer than eight points. A suggested sequence places players in position with 10 seconds left, initiates play at eight seconds, takes the shot and prepares for a second effort at three to five seconds, and gives opponents little time to advance after a rebound.

Teams should practice skip and baseball passes, half-court shots, tipping, offensive rebounding, and intentionally missed free throws, including the requirement that the ball hit the rim. Coaches should save at least two timeouts, take one with only one to three seconds remaining, and preferably inbound at half court with fewer than four seconds left. Other strategies include pushing after an opponent scores, shooting in line with the basket, counting down the clock with the bench, and using a designated, skilled inbounds passer. Preset plays should account for the time, court location, and whether the situation involves a rebound, free throw, field goal, or jump ball. Maximum recommended dribbles are one with three seconds remaining, three with five seconds, and five with seven seconds.

As tensions rise on the Korean Peninsula, Canadians debate Canada’s limited influence and inconsistent engagement with North Korea. Despite strong Asian ties and its Korean War legacy, veterans and experts argue for sustained security diplomacy and humanitarian action amid nuclear tests, missile launches, and fears of renewed conflict.

The passage defines SD memory card write, erase, protection, command, and error-handling behavior. Block writes append CRC bits, which the card verifies before programming; invalid block lengths, addresses, alignment, or protected areas cause errors, while valid writes may use partial blocks. Busy status is indicated on DAT0, and hosts can poll status, deselect cards, or interleave operations. ACMD23 pre-erases blocks to accelerate multiple-block writes, and ACMD22 reports the number successfully written.

Erase operations use CMD32 and CMD33 to define ranges before CMD38. DISCARD deallocates blocks whose contents become indeterminate, while FULE logically erases the entire user area; both are limited to SDHC and SDXC cards and have specified busy timeouts. Write protection can be mechanical, internal, or password-based.

CMD42 manages password locking, unlocking, password replacement, clearing, and force erase. Card Ownership Protection extends these functions with a Force Erase Password, COP Unlock, and restricted CMD42 operation when FEP is set.

CMD55 introduces application-specific commands. CMD6 checks or changes functions in six groups, including bus access mode, command system, driver strength, and power limit. The passage also covers 25 MB/s high-speed mode, CMD8 voltage checking, SDSC versus SDHC/SDXC addressing, CRC7 and CRC16, command classes and formats, bus-clock control, and read, write, and erase timeout requirements.

October 2025’s night sky features a supermoon on October 6, when the full moon may appear 30% brighter and up to 14% larger because it coincides with perigee, its closest approach to Earth. October 4 marks International Observe the Moon Night. The Draconid meteor shower, produced by debris from comet 21P Giacobini-Zinner, peaks around October 8 and can produce up to 10 meteors per hour, though supermoon brightness may hinder viewing. The Orionid shower, caused by Halley’s Comet debris, peaks October 21 at about 20 meteors per hour. Its best viewing period is from midnight until around 2 a.m., when the new moon leaves the sky dark.

The lecturer addresses a corrected typo in homework 1, emphasizing that the revision makes the intended problem easier and supports learning. He then previews the remaining linear algebra topics: eigenvalue decomposition and, in the next lecture, singular value decomposition.

Matrix reordering is introduced through permutation matrices. Multiplication on the left swaps rows, while multiplication by the transpose on the right swaps columns. Permutation matrices are unitary because \(PP^T=I\). Reordering equations and unknowns is presented as a form of preconditioning: it can reduce numerical error through pivoting and reduce fill-in, making large systems tractable by Gaussian elimination.

A sparse diffusion example uses a Plinko board, where a chip moves left or right with equal probability. A sparse matrix with two off-diagonals of \(1/2\) propagates the probability distribution, eventually producing a roughly binomial or Gaussian spread. Repeated multiplication tends toward a uniform distribution, and certain distributions are eigenvectors of powers of the matrix.

The lecture then defines eigenvectors as vectors whose direction is preserved under multiplication by a matrix, though their length may change by an eigenvalue. Eigenvectors are determined only up to scale, while each eigenvalue represents the associated stretch factor. Eigenvalues are obtained by solving
\[
(A-\lambda I)w=0.
\]
Nontrivial solutions exist when \(A-\lambda I\) is singular, so its determinant must be zero. The resulting degree-\(N\) characteristic polynomial has roots that are the matrix’s eigenvalues. Diagonal and triangular matrices have their diagonal entries as eigenvalues. A real matrix has at most \(N\) distinct eigenvalues, which may be real or complex; complex eigenvalues occur in conjugate pairs. The determinant equals the product of eigenvalues, while the trace equals their sum.

Chemical-reaction rate matrices illustrate the physical interpretation of eigenvalues. Their eigenvalues have units of rate, a zero eigenvalue represents a steady-state process, and other eigenvalues describe transformations among chemical species. Corresponding eigenvectors can be found through Gaussian elimination of \((A-\lambda I)w=0\), with free variables reflecting nonuniqueness.

Algebraic multiplicity is the number of times an eigenvalue occurs as a root of the characteristic polynomial. Geometric multiplicity is the dimension of its null space and the number of linearly independent associated eigenvectors. Geometric multiplicity cannot exceed algebraic multiplicity. A matrix with a complete set of eigenvectors can be diagonalized; otherwise, some directions cannot be decoupled and alternative forms such as Jordan normal form or Schur decomposition are needed.

For a complete eigenvector set, the eigenvectors form the columns of \(W\), the eigenvalues form the diagonal matrix \(\Lambda\), and
\[
AW=W\Lambda,\qquad A=W\Lambda W^{-1}.
\]
This diagonalization simplifies systems of equations and linear ordinary differential equations. For symmetric matrices, normalized eigenvectors are orthogonal, allowing \(W^{-1}=W^T\). In differential-equation applications, diagonalization separates the system into independent scalar equations whose solutions are exponentials controlled by the eigenvalues. The lecture concludes by noting that eigendecomposition will be practiced in the next two homework assignments.

Taylor Swift has broken numerous music records since 2006. At 17, she became the youngest artist to write and perform a No. 1 country song with “Our Song.” She was the youngest CMA Entertainer of the Year winner in 2009 and the youngest Grammy Album of the Year winner in 2010 for “Fearless,” a record later surpassed by Billie Eilish. Swift became the first woman to win the Grammy twice for “1989,” three times for “Folklore,” and the first artist to win four times for “Midnights.”

She holds records for the most American Music Awards, with 40; 29 No. 1 hits on Billboard’s US Digital Song Sales chart; the most Grammy Song of the Year nominations, reaching eight with “Fortnight”; and the longest No. 1 hit, “All Too Well (10 Minute Version).” “Red (Taylor’s Version)” spent a record 99 weeks atop Billboard’s Top Country Albums chart, while “Fortnight” extended her Video of the Year record.

Swift is the only artist to occupy all 10 top positions on the Billboard Hot 100 in one week, a feat she repeated with “The Tortured Poets Department.” Her releases also set Spotify single-day streaming records: “The Life of a Showgirl” became the most-streamed album in one day, and “The Fate of Ophelia” became the most-streamed song in one day. The latter was also Apple Music’s biggest song of 2025.

Her Eras Tour earned a record $2 billion, making it the highest-grossing tour ever. Swift’s estimated net worth reached $1.6 billion, making her the world’s richest female musician.

The exponential moving average (EMA), also called the exponentially weighted moving average, gives greater weight to recent prices than the simple moving average (SMA), making it more responsive to current market conditions. It is calculated as EMA = (K × (C − P)) + P, where C is the current price, P is the previous period’s EMA, and K is 2/(n + 1). EMAs smooth price data, help identify trends and changes in direction, and may also indicate support or resistance. However, they remain lagging indicators, cannot identify exact price turning points, and may generate false signals when overly responsive.

Backtests using SPY closing prices evaluated four EMA strategies. Short-term mean-reversion strategies—buying when price crosses below a short EMA and selling when it crosses above—performed best with a 5-day EMA, producing a 7.41% CAGR and a 30.54% maximum drawdown. Long-term trend-following strategies—buying above and selling below a longer EMA—performed best with a 200-day EMA, returning 7.84% with a 26% maximum drawdown, compared with 56% for buy and hold. A strategy that bought below the 50-day EMA and exited after 200 days produced 10.17% per trade. Results excluded reinvested dividends.

Traders can use EMAs through crossovers, directional filtering, or trend-aligned entries and exits, and can combine them with indicators such as the MACD and RSI. Shorter periods may produce more false signals, while longer periods lag more. Backtesting is needed to determine the appropriate EMA period for an asset class; no EMA period is universally best. The article concludes that EMA strategies work best with either short periods for mean reversion or long periods for trend following.

A systematic literature review examined papers published from 2000–2017 in selected leading Information Systems journals using the terms “digital business strategy,” “digital transformation,” and “business digitalization.” The search produced 292 articles; title, abstract, and keyword screening reduced this to 54, and full-text review yielded 28 articles. Following Wolifswinkel’s guidelines, open, axial, and selective coding identified 12 dimensions of digital transformation, six of digital business strategy, and ten of organizational capability.

Publication activity began increasing in 2009 and rose substantially in 2016. Research concentrated on automotive, banking, telecommunications, healthcare, oil and gas, and manufacturing, primarily in the United States and Europe, with less activity in Asia, the Middle East, Latin America, and Africa.

The review identified shared dimensions among the three concepts. All three include external collaboration through digital platform ecosystems. Digital transformation and digital business strategy share technology use and structural changes, while digital transformation and organizational capability share digital leadership, agile and scalable operations, digitally enabled customer service, and digital artefacts. Digital business strategy and organizational capability share dynamic capabilities.

The resulting framework presents digital transformation as digital business strategy in action, with digital business strategy serving as its blueprint and organizational capabilities enabling its implementation. It concludes that organizations require continuously developed and reconfigured capabilities and suitable digital strategy initiatives to achieve digital transformation and improve performance, offering guidance for senior managers and information systems researchers.

April the giraffe’s YouTube livestream ranked second in company history, behind Riot Games’ League of Legends channel, with over 232 million views. Viewership peaked when she delivered a male calf, drawing 1.2 million simultaneous viewers.

The editors of the Foreign Relations series had complete access to retired Department of State records from 1981–1989, including central files, decentralized "lot files," Executive Secretariat files, and overseas diplomatic post files. Central files stored in electronic and microfilm formats, and decentralized files judged worthy of permanent preservation, will eventually be transferred to the National Archives and made accessible after declassification and processing. Research was conducted through special access to restricted documents at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library and other agencies; although all material printed in the volume was declassified, some was drawn from still-classified documents that Reagan Library staff were processing and which might not be available in full at publication. Presidential papers include significant foreign-affairs documentation from White House offices, the Department of State, and agencies such as the National Security Council, CIA, Defense Department, and Joint Chiefs of Staff. Some research came from records scanned for the National Archives' Remote Archives Capture project, which coordinated declassification of classified presidential library records; because not all records were scanned, editors sometimes could not confirm whether attachments belonged to a document and noted them as "Not found attached."

Documents appear chronologically by time in Washington, D.C., with memoranda of conversation placed by conversation date rather than drafting date. Editorial treatment follows Office style guidelines supplemented by guidance from the General Editor and the Chiefs of the Declassification and Publishing Divisions. Originals are reproduced as exactly as possible, including marginalia, which is described in footnotes; texts are transcribed according to conventions for publishing historical documents within the limits of modern typography. Editors supply a heading for each document. Spelling, capitalization, and punctuation are retained except that obvious typographical errors are silently corrected; other mistakes and omissions are corrected by bracketed insertions, with corrections in italics and additions in roman type, and original underlining is printed in italics. Abbreviations and contractions are preserved, with a list of abbreviations and terms in the front matter of each volume. In telegrams, the telegram number, including special designations such as Secto, is printed at the start of the text.

Bracketed insertions also indicate omitted text on unrelated subjects (roman type) or text remaining classified after declassification review (italics). The amount and, where possible, nature of non-declassified material is noted by the number of lines or pages omitted. Entire withheld documents are listed in chronological order with headings, source notes, and the number of pages not declassified. All brackets in the original text are identified in footnotes, and all ellipses are original.

The paper studies multi-period allocation of a fixed resource supply under stochastic, nonnegative demand to maximize expected revenue. A static formulation determines all allocations at the outset. It is a convex problem based only on marginal demand distributions and can be solved efficiently by bisection on its dual variable, though it ignores temporal correlations and sequentially revealed information.

The proposed alternative is a sequential shrinking-horizon policy. At each period, it allocates only the current period’s resources, then re-solves the remaining allocation problem after observing that period’s demand and updating future demand distributions through conditioning. The policy requires conditional quantile functions, applies to arbitrary demand models, and is heuristic rather than guaranteed globally optimal. When demands are independent, it reduces to the static solution.

Simulations use jointly log-normal synthetic demands and compare the sequential and static policies with a roll-forward baseline and a noncausal oracle allocation. Under correlated demands, the sequential policy consistently earns the highest revenue among causal methods, approaches oracle performance, and generally has the lowest revenue variance. Future work will integrate the policy with online learning of demand distributions.

The paper argues that cultural change is among the hardest elements of digital transformation. Research surveying more than 150 firms found that technological maturity correlates with stronger three-year revenue and enterprise-value growth, with digital leaders outperforming laggards. Interviews with leaders and laggards identified four cultural themes distinguishing digitally mature organizations:

- A growth mindset that encourages sensible risk-taking, experimentation, continuous learning, employee development, and the use of data for feedback.
- Transparent data sharing that creates shared context, supports collaborative and informed decisions, and discourages data hoarding, while appropriate governance protects data.
- Employee empowerment to examine relevant data, set realistic goals, and measure performance through meaningful metrics.
- Shared, objectively measured targets that align teams with organizational strategy while allowing autonomy and creative execution.

Digital leaders actively embed these practices into daily operations. They view unsuccessful experiments as sources of learning, prioritize critical-thinking skills over narrow job training, and use data broadly for decision-making. Digital laggards instead emphasize short-term results, existing processes, risk aversion, restrictive data access, and individually made or poorly grounded decisions. They often set aspirational objectives without sufficient data, rely on qualitative evidence of effort, and keep goals weakly connected to strategy.

Case studies illustrate how a pharmaceutical company created a controlled environment for responsible experimentation in a regulated industry and how a retailer implemented real-time sales reporting to improve operational decisions. Even digital leaders face tensions, including excessive analysis, difficulty balancing experimentation with failure, inconsistent data access, and the need for cultural change over time.

The paper concludes that strong data cultures align beliefs, values, and daily behavior, producing both vertical and horizontal organizational alignment. Organizations may begin in one of four patterns: data novice, insight ready, tech enabled, or data reliant. Each can build on existing strengths through targeted cultural and technical actions.

The article examines how anti-critical race theory (CRT) bans affect Native content instruction in teacher education at predominantly white public institutions in Idaho, Utah, and Arizona. Drawing on IRB-approved stories, interviews, and observations from a decade of research, as well as their experiences as educators and scholars, the authors use Tribal Critical Race Theory (TribalCrit) and ethnographic methods to analyze how bans perpetuate “colonial unknowing,” or sanctioned ignorance of Native peoples, histories, cultures, and sovereignty. One author is a Navajo citizen; the other identifies as a white settler-scholar.

The authors describe anti-CRT legislation in Idaho, Utah, and Arizona as attempts to codify histories of colonization and race as un-American. At the time of writing, 42 states had introduced or passed such legislation. Cited research indicates that these laws chill educators and embolden white supremacist ideologies. Arizona enacted restrictions in 2021 that were later ruled unconstitutional, while a proposed 2022 constitutional amendment was not placed on the ballot. Utah adopted a resolution directing the state education board to recommend how teachers should discuss racism. Idaho’s HB 377 restricts discussion of race and gender and defines prohibited CRT tenets; a state task force found no consistent evidence of indoctrination, and proposed legislation would have allowed private lawsuits against districts violating the law.

Teacher education has also lacked adequate preparation for Native-centered instruction. Public-school teachers were overwhelmingly white in the three states and nationally, and research cited by the authors indicates that fear, discomfort, and limited knowledge of Native peoples constrain teaching about race and Native histories. Professional development on Native-centered pedagogy is scarce. Although state standards increasingly require instruction about Native histories, ways of knowing, and tribal sovereignty, few provide funding or competency requirements, and some omit direct collaboration with tribes as equal partners.

Using TribalCrit, the authors emphasize that colonization is endemic and that educational policies toward Native peoples have historically supported assimilation. They describe whitewashed settler narratives as representing whiteness as normal, objective, and privileged while rendering Native knowledge and presence illegitimate or invisible. Their analysis identifies three effects of anti-CRT bans: continued silencing of Native perspectives and content, the perpetuation of Native invisibility in public education, and refusal to learn culturally sustaining pedagogies.

Stories from schools and teacher-education programs illustrate these effects. A district serving a 70 percent Native population stopped culturally responsive and tribal-history training after Idaho’s HB 377 was enacted. In Arizona, laws mandating Native-history instruction were narrowed by legislators to exclude tribal sovereignty and later went unimplemented despite Albert Hale’s advocacy for teaching Native history to foster mutual respect. Teacher candidates’ reflections revealed persistent stereotypes and invisibility of neighboring Native communities, while a white child speaking near a reservation stated that she believed all Indians were dead. Arizona social-studies standards focused heavily on pre-1860 history and societies portrayed as extinct. In other cases, students and faculty resisted instruction on sovereignty, Native erasure, colorblindness, meritocracy, and the history of forced child removal and Christianized boarding schools.

The authors conclude that teacher preparation and schools continue the logic of settler colonialism even after explicit federal policies of Native erasure ended. They call for Native history and content at all levels of education and for critical democratic education that recognizes Native nationhood and sovereignty as essential to preparing all students to support democracy and tribal sovereignty.

Five-year-old Lyla Carreyn returned home after receiving a kidney from her 4K teacher, Beth Battista. Despite post-surgery complications, including an infection, she needs more than 15 daily medications, thrice-weekly lab tests, and readmission if infection or rejection appears.

Tesla, Inc. reported that on September 4, 2020, it completed the sale of $5.0 billion before commissions of common stock through its previously disclosed “at-the-market” offering program. Final settlement was expected by September 9, 2020.

The study characterized county-level face-mask use across the United States from September 2020 to May 2021 using 8,338,877 self-reported responses from the COVID-19 Trends and Impact Survey. “All” or “most of the time” responses were classified as masking and aggregated by county and month. Bayesian binomial regression addressed small local samples, raking adjusted for age, sex, and education, and county-level bias estimates derived from overreported vaccination rates were applied to correct masking estimates, assuming similar bias in both behaviors.

Bias-corrected masking was strongly spatially heterogeneous, ranging from 0.11 to 0.96 and varying substantially within states. Masking was more common in urban counties, with median fitted proportions above 0.8 in urban counties and below 0.6 in the most rural counties. Masking peaked in January 2021 and was lowest in May 2021; the decline coincided with rising vaccination, declining infections and reported worry, changing CDC guidance, and mask-mandate removals, but the study did not establish causation. Community-reported masking closely approximated bias-corrected self-reported estimates, with differences ranging from −6 to 5 percentage points.

The findings indicate that statewide or national aggregation obscures meaningful local variation and support geographically targeted public-health policies and disease models that account for local behavior. Limitations included unmeasured response biases, reliance on Facebook users, recall and dishonest reporting, small samples, and the untested assumption that vaccination and masking responses have biases of equal magnitude and direction.

The lecture applies optimal-control tools to walking robots, identifying periodic motion and impact-driven hybrid dynamics as the main technical challenges. The Van der Pol oscillator illustrates stable limit cycles: trajectories approach the same periodic orbit without synchronizing in phase, so standard trajectory-convergence and Lyapunov arguments do not directly apply. Poincaré sections and maps convert continuous-time limit-cycle stability into discrete-time fixed-point stability; local stability requires a multiplier with magnitude below one.

The lecture reviews the history of legged-locomotion research: Eadweard Muybridge documented animal gaits, McMahon modeled human walking as ballistic motion with a passive swing phase and a stiff stance leg, and McGeer built passive dynamic walkers that descended ramps without motors or controllers using gravity and inertia.

A rimless-wheel model captures the essential dynamics of passive walking. It assumes a pinned stance foot, instantaneous transfer of support, and inelastic impulsive collisions. Its motion settles into a stable limit cycle when energy gained descending the slope balances energy dissipated at impact; insufficient energy produces standing, while excessive energy can lead to backward motion. The analytical Poincaré map identifies stable rolling and standing fixed points, their basins of attraction, and exceptional trajectories associated with a homoclinic orbit. Collision velocity follows a simple mapping involving \(\cos(2\alpha)\), and impact loss is presented as the dominant source of walking energy loss.

More articulated models extend these ideas: a compass gait adds a swing leg and hip joint, while a kneed walker adds legs with knees and additional collisions. Both can exhibit stable limit cycles under suitable conditions, though their basins of attraction are smaller. Future topics include applying optimization and gradient methods to hybrid walking dynamics and reviewing current walking-control approaches.

At the second taking of the presidential oath, the speaker says an extended address is less necessary because four years of public declarations and known military progress have made the situation clear. The nation had feared civil war, with one side seeking to dissolve the Union without fighting and the other determined to preserve it even through war; war nevertheless occurred. Enslaved people, concentrated in the South, constituted the central interest behind the conflict: insurgents sought to strengthen and extend slavery, while the government sought only to limit its expansion. Both sides expected a shorter, easier victory, invoked the same God, and prayed for victory, though neither prayer was fully answered. The speaker frames slavery as an offense whose removal may require prolonged suffering and trusts that God’s judgment is righteous. The passage presents a simple gold trend-following strategy based on a 12-month (250-day) simple moving average and backtests it with monthly prices from 1971 onward. The strategy holds gold when its price is above the average and moves to cash when below. It generated 26 trades, grew an initial 100,000 to 10 million, and substantially outperformed buy-and-hold, which reached 4 million; slippage and commissions were excluded. The strongest results occurred around a 12-month moving average, plus or minus a few months, or roughly 200–250 days. Its main benefit is avoiding major drawdowns, including after the 1980 and 2012 peaks.

Gold’s tendency to move sharply after long inactive periods is favorable for trend following. Unlike stocks, however, gold produces no cash flows or tangible value and requires storage and insurance, although it has historically been an inflation hedge; the passage argues that stocks may be a better hedge. Investors can generally gain exposure through the GLD ETF or gold futures, though futures results may differ from the spot-price tests. Past success does not guarantee future performance.

**Summary**

This preprint study evaluates the Disk Potentiation Test (DPT) for rapid identification of Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase (KPC) and metallo-beta-lactamase (MBL) in clinical isolates. Carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae pose a global threat because of limited antibiotic options, and their carbapenemase genes spread horizontally via plasmids, transposons, and integrons, producing multidrug resistance. Existing detection methods (Modified Hodge Test, Carba NP, mCIM, antibody- and PCR-based assays) either lack specificity for enzyme type, cannot distinguish carbapenem-resistant from carbapenem-susceptible isolates, or are costly and less accessible locally.

Between January and June 2020, 147 imipenem-resistant gram-negative isolates were collected from outpatient, inpatient, and ICU units of Evercare Hospital (formerly Apollo Hospital), Dhaka, Bangladesh. Carbapenem non-susceptibility was defined by VITEK® 2 MIC values (≥1 µg/ml for Enterobacteriaceae; ≥2 µg/ml for *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* and *Acinetobacter baumannii*). KPC was detected using phenylboronic acid disks (zone difference >5 mm), and MBL using 0.5 M EDTA (zone enlargement >7 mm); data were analyzed in SPSS v27.0. Ethical approval and oral informed consent were obtained.

All 147 isolates showed 100% imipenem resistance, with the highest prevalence in the >60 age group, in male patients (78.2% vs. 21.8%), and in the ICU. Most resistant isolates had MICs ≥16 µg/ml. Of the isolates, 24.49% (36) produced both KPC and MBL, 53.06% (78) produced neither, 2.04% (3) KPC only, and 20.40% (30) MBL only; *A. baumannii* was the most frequent producer of both enzymes. KPC positivity was 26.53% (ICU 23/69, IPD 14/62, OPD 2/16) and MBL positivity 44.89% (ICU 33/69, IPD 28/62, OPD 5/16). Tracheal aspirates yielded the most dual-enzyme samples, followed by suction tips, blood, wound swabs, urine, endotracheal tube tips, sputum, and pus.

The authors conclude that high resistance levels and enzyme prevalence, especially in ICU and *A. baumannii*, underscore the need for antimicrobial stewardship, surveillance, strict infection control, and accessible detection methods.

The excerpt covers electrical characteristics and detailed architecture for MSPM0G3519, MSPM0G3518, MSPM0G1519, and MSPM0G1518 microcontrollers. Internal or external voltage references can supply the ADCs; internal-reference configurations map REFN and REFP to VREF− and VREF+, require a decoupling capacitor, and prohibit external connections on those reference pins. ADC linearity is evaluated using TUE = √(EI² + |EO|² + EG²), and temperature measurements use a factory calibration value with specified ADC, VREF, and sampling-time settings.

The CPU subsystem includes a 32-bit ARM Cortex-M0+ operating from 32 kHz to 80 MHz, an instruction prefetch cache, SysTick, an MPU, and an NVIC. Five power modes—RUN, SLEEP, STOP, STANDBY, and SHUTDOWN—optimize consumption through configurable policies and two power domains. The PMU provides regulated core supplies, brownout monitoring, and protected trims. Clock sources include internal and external LF/HF oscillators, a 32–80 MHz SYSPLL, and clocks distributed to the CPU, peripherals, ADC, and low-power subsystem.

Twelve DMA channels support multiple transfer widths, repeated or single transfers, interrupts, cascading, stride mode, and transfers up to 64K elements. The event fabric routes peripheral interrupts, DMA triggers, and direct inter-peripheral events. Memory includes dual-bank flash with ECC, data flash, bank swapping for OTA updates, and up to 128 KB of SRAM divided into protected and unprotected banks with configurable read-write/read-execute partitions. The devices provide up to 93 GPIO pins and programmable IOMUX functions.

Two 12-bit ADCs support simultaneous sampling, 4 Msps operation with greater than 11 ENOB, hardware averaging for 14-bit effective resolution at 250 ksps, internal temperature and supply channels, and internal or external references. Other analog peripherals include a linear temperature sensor, selectable 1.4 V or 2.5 V VREF, comparators with reference DACs and wake/fault-handling support, and a buffered 8/12-bit DAC with self-calibration, FIFO, DMA, and event-trigger support.

Security and processing features include AES-128/256 acceleration, firewalls, a four-key secure keystore, TRNG, CRC-16/CRC-32, and a 32-bit math accelerator. Communication peripherals include UART with LIN support, I²C with SMBus and DMA, SPI up to 32 Mbit/s, and CAN-FD up to 5 Mbit/s in G351x devices. Low-frequency peripherals include RTC_B, IWDT, WWDT, and general-purpose and advanced timers with capture/compare, PWM, fault handling, cross-triggering, and ADC-trigger capabilities.

SWD supports debugging, while the password-protected BSL supports UART/I²C programming and multiple invocation methods. Factory constants provide device identification and trim data. Recommended layout includes VDD/VSS ceramic decoupling, an NRST pullup/pulldown circuit, an optional SYSOSC frequency-correction resistor, a VCORE capacitor, and pullups for open-drain I/O. The document also provides development-tool information, April 2025 revision details, package drawings, orderable information, and mechanical and lead-free documentation.

Kenneth Kaylor appeals a final judgment dissolving his marriage to Sharon Kaylor, arguing the rehabilitative alimony award exceeded his ability to pay. The Second District Court of Appeal agreed and reversed only the financial aspects of the judgment, remanding to fashion an award consistent with appellee's needs and appellant's ability to pay; all other aspects were affirmed.

The parties married in 1973 with two children. Appellee, permanently employed as a real estate salesperson, earned $745 monthly gross and claimed she needed $1,200 more monthly. Appellant earned $600 weekly gross ($462 net) and owned a 20% interest in his insurance agency, estimated at $100,000 but not readily marketable. The trial court awarded appellee custody, the marital home, $4,800 yearly alimony for two years, $7,800 yearly child support, $4,230 yearly house expenses, an automobile, children's medical expenses, and life insurance. The award reduced appellant's net income of about $2,000 monthly by $1,395, leaving $600, and exceeded appellee's testified expenses by $175 monthly, effectively causing financial hardship.

The passage documents stackless, register-based AGESA host services for x86-64 and AARCH64. AMD_ENABLE_STACK initializes the processor/cache system and a pre-memory stack region, divides the region among cores, maps it globally, configures MTRRs, and creates a UEFI_SEC_PEI_HAND_OFF. It must run on every core. Protected mode leaves SS unchanged and requires a zero-based GDT descriptor; real mode uses a 16-bit SS:ESP format. It reports allocation success, stack reentry with reset, or an unknown processor family. AARCH64 systems with PSP rely on PSP DRAM initialization and do not use the stack or early macros.

AMD_DISABLE_STACK, invoked only by the BSP after memory becomes available, disables CAR without changing MTRRs, flushes and invalidates all cache lines without writeback, and leaves processor cache enabled.

AmdCreateStruct allocates and initializes AGESA structure storage using PreMemHeap, PostMemDram, or host-provided memory, copies StdHeader, and returns a pointer. The host must ensure sufficient capacity for host-provided storage; successful initialization overlays the parameter block, while insufficient space returns an error and preserves it. It requires a stack and should be paired with AmdReleaseStruct.

Other services return a DIMM read/write data-eye bitmap, a socket/core APIC address and presence, and pre-memory executable-cache capacity for the current core. The latter two apply to x86-64. These services require an established stack, and the data-eye service also requires coherent HyperTransport links.

This study examines the scope, importance, role, and barriers of curriculum literacy in education. Curriculum literacy involves understanding educational programs’ purposes, structure, and content; evaluating methods, materials, and outcomes; adapting programs to learners’ needs; and using materials and technologies effectively. These skills can help teachers and administrators provide flexible, inclusive instruction, improve professional practice, and support student learning. Barriers include inadequate training, time constraints, bureaucratic obstacles, and rapidly changing curricula.

Using thematic content analysis, the researchers searched Scopus for “curriculum literacy” and reviewed titles, keywords, abstracts, and conclusions. Twenty-nine accessible, peer-reviewed journal studies were included after six unrelated studies were excluded. The analysis found increasing scholarly attention, particularly after 2020. Earlier research emphasized social studies education, followed by activity theory and cultural contexts, while recent studies focus on digitalization, artificial intelligence, dyslexia, diagnosis, and learner empowerment. Research is concentrated in social sciences and in Australia, the United States, and Türkiye, with limited geographical and disciplinary coverage.

The findings connect curriculum literacy with effective use of materials and technology, pedagogical development, culturally responsive and inclusive teaching, critical curriculum evaluation, student participation, and improved learning experiences. A positive but weak relationship between teachers’ digital literacy and curriculum literacy indicates a need for greater digital-skills development.

The study recommends training for educators in digital platforms, contemporary teaching methods, and curriculum evaluation; expanded resources and supportive policies; alignment of curricula with technology; interdisciplinary research; and equitable programs responsive to individual and cultural needs. It concludes that strengthening curriculum literacy can improve teaching, support digital transformation, and enhance education quality.

**Purpose and scope.** The paper offers a snapshot of the state and potential of digitalization in Vietnamese higher education (HE) and proposes recommendations to support institutional digital transformation.

**System overview.** Vietnam's national education system has four levels, with HE the highest, offering Bachelor's, Master's and doctoral degrees. MOET governs the system except three-year-program colleges and vocational training (under the Ministry of Labor, War Invalids and Social Affairs). There are 237 universities (172 public, 67 private, including two national universities), but only 119 are directly managed by MOET; others fall to line ministries, local government or foreign organizations. The system is relatively centralized, with MOET regulating management, curriculum design, enrollment and program operation. A 2018 World Bank report ranked Vietnam's education as "Above-Average Performing."

**Policy framework.** The 2020 National Digital Transformation Program (toward 2025, vision 2030) sets dual goals — transforming the nation around digital government, economy and society, and building world-famous digital technology companies — with education among eight priority areas and seven HEI targets, including IT human resources, embedding digital technologies in programs, open mass online courses, universalized online exams, recognized online certificates, data warehouses for teaching resources, and technology for individualized learning. The 2022–2025 Project adds two objectives: drastically innovating educational organization (online access for 50% of students and teachers, domestic platforms used by over 50% of students, over 50% of HEI offering online degree programs, 20% of classes online) and innovating management through technology and databases (all HEI using digital management platforms, a national education database, paperless student services).

**Pre-COVID conditions.** Digitalization before 2020 was slow and uneven: some universities integrated digital technologies, while many lacked foundational infrastructure and ICT; the HE system is considered underfunded. Infrastructure in private universities (Vinschool, FPT Education, Phenikaa) was often better funded. Barriers included low digital skills among staff and students, slow adaptation among older staff, fragmented oversight across agencies and inconsistent bylaws. Vietnam's 2021 Digital Evolution Index was 46.79 (below Thailand, Malaysia and Singapore) and it ranked 96th in the 2020 Global Talent Competitiveness Index. Most HEI had adopted learning management systems (LMS), but distance learning platforms were uncommon — over half of HEI avoided distance teaching, and full-time programs remained largely face-to-face; digital materials and data warehouses were limited to a few institutions.

**Post-COVID developments.** The pandemic drove a massive increase in online teaching and e-learning, and MOET's amended 2021 regulations allow up to 30% online volume in regular/full-time Bachelor programs, 20% in joint Master and PhD programs, and online testing up to 50% of course assessment. LMS use is now widespread in public HEI with government, donor and technology-company support, enabling paperless procedures (enrollment, records, tuition), and management tasks such as academic records and payroll are being digitized, though duplicated or unsynchronized databases remain a concern. The unified HEMIS system links DoET units and roughly 53,000 institutions, covering some 1.4 million students, and supports entrance selection and enrollment for more than 300 universities. The Vietnamese Knowledge System contains nearly 5,000 e-lectures, about 7,000 theses, over 31,000 multiple-choice questions and 200 e-books; private data warehouses (Viettel, VNPT, MISA, Topica, FPT, VTC Intercom) and MOOCs, including VMOOCs with 50+ free courses developed by Hanoi and HCMC Open Universities, are also in use.

**Recommendations.** MOET should provide clear guidance, criteria and evaluation frameworks and disseminate policies through training and webinars; increase investment, special funding for digitalization projects, infrastructure (high-speed internet, hardware, software, cybersecurity) and partnerships with companies and international organizations, and train institutional leaders' digital literacy. HEIs should build lecturer capacity in five areas — intellectual property, copyright and cybersecurity; pedagogical practice; digital skills; personalized learning models; and digital mentorship for senior lecturers — and support students through digital skills training and fully online administrative procedures including thesis, enrolment, tuition and scholarship processes.

**Conclusion.** Post-COVID, government and institutions have committed to digitalization at national and institutional levels despite uneven progress; HEIs have built platforms for distance learning and applied digital technology to management, teaching and learning, and increasing numbers are developing digitalized materials and shared resource data warehouses.

Both groups had comparable baseline characteristics. Subjects had a median age of 74, were 59.9% male, and had mean BMI 28.7 kg/m² and MMSE 28.3; 93.6% had normal baseline examinations, while hypertension and atrial fibrillation were common.

The Nasdaq 100 E-mini futures contract (NQ) is an electronically traded derivative based on the Nasdaq 100, an index of the 100 largest non-financial companies listed on Nasdaq and heavily weighted toward technology stocks. It debuted on June 21, 1999, is one-fifth the size of the full Nasdaq futures contract, and expires quarterly in March, June, September, and December.

Trading strategies typically combine fundamental and technical analysis with entry and exit rules, position sizing, risk management, and market psychology. The passage describes a paywalled volatility strategy, strategy #1 (F101), with three buy variables and one sell variable. A backtest using Norgate’s continuous, back-adjusted CME data, daily bars, and trades at the close from contract inception to the present applied no stop-loss or other risk controls. Historical seasonality suggests the futures tend to perform better in spring and fall than in winter and summer.

One NQ contract equals the Nasdaq 100 index value multiplied by $20, with prices quoted in dollars and cents per index point. Trading occurs on CME Globex from 6:00 p.m. ET Sunday to 5:00 p.m. ET Friday, with a daily break from 5:00 to 6:00 p.m. Contracts are cash-settled using special opening quotations of the index, normally on the third Friday of the contract month at 9:30 a.m. ET. The minimum price fluctuation is 0.25 index points for outright Globex trading and 0.05 for BTIC, TACO, and calendar spreads; corresponding tick values are $5 and $1.

Traders access the contract through a funded futures broker account. The contract is leveraged, creating potentially large losses from price movements. Price influences include Federal Reserve decisions, component-stock prices, economic news, and the U.S. Dollar Index.

Based on TradingView, the contract’s all-time high was 16,676.50 in November 2021, while its low was 797.50 on October 3, 2002. It traded at 11,615.75 on December 6, 2022.

Unlike futures, broker-provided CFDs do not require contract expiry or rollover and can be held indefinitely, although not all CFDs track the futures contract precisely.

A bear trap is a bullish trading pattern in which a sharp price decline during an uptrend tricks sellers into expecting a reversal or continuing downtrend. Price then rebounds, often triggering their stop-loss orders, and resumes the prior trend. The passage links these traps to fear of missing out, impulsive trading, market manipulation, and cascading stop-loss orders.

Potential bear traps may be identified through breaks of support or trendlines, bullish divergence between price and indicators such as RSI or MACD, and positive fundamental developments. No single indicator is reliable; traders should combine technical and fundamental analysis and backtest their strategies.

Retail traders can reduce risk by avoiding decisions based solely on price, considering company fundamentals and broader market conditions, not blindly following the crowd, and maintaining disciplined execution. The passage also presents a strategy that buys on breakdowns and sells on strength, reporting strong historical results and moderate drawdowns for QQQ and leveraged QLD, while warning that leverage can magnify losses.

NVIDIA’s Turing GPU architecture combines improved memory and display systems, hardware-accelerated real-time ray tracing, AI-based graphics, and new rendering techniques. Lossless memory compression and GDDR6 bandwidth increases raise effective bandwidth by approximately 50% over Pascal, with comparable gains reported for the TU102-based RTX 2080 Ti versus the GP102-based GTX 1080 Ti. Turing’s display engine supports DisplayPort 1.4a, DSC 1.2, 8K output at 60 Hz, HDR, and BT.2100 tone mapping. Its NVENC and NVDEC units add H.265 8K encoding, bitrate reductions, and support for additional HEVC and VP9 formats.

Turing supports USB-C and the VirtualLink standard, allowing VR headsets to receive power, display data, and tracking data through one connector. For multi-GPU configurations, TU102 and TU104 use second-generation NVLink rather than Pascal’s SLI Bridge, supporting two-way SLI and new display configurations.

Real-time ray tracing is enabled by RT Cores in TU102, TU104, and TU106. RT Cores accelerate bounding-volume hierarchy traversal and ray-triangle intersection tests, offloading work from streaming multiprocessors. Combined with denoising and hybrid rendering, which uses rasterization where effective and ray tracing for effects such as reflections, refractions, and shadows, this makes physically based ray tracing practical on a single GPU. Turing is described as delivering over 10 gigarays per second and roughly ten times Pascal’s software-based ray-tracing performance. Ray-traced shadows, ambient occlusion, and reflections provide more accurate results than conventional shadow maps, screen-space ambient occlusion, and screen-space or probe-based reflections.

NVIDIA NGX uses deep neural networks and Turing Tensor Cores to accelerate AI-based graphics features. Deep Learning Super-Sampling (DLSS) reconstructs high-resolution images from lower-resolution rendering, offering quality similar to temporal antialiasing with substantially less shading work; a larger DLSS 2X network processes target-resolution input to approach 64-times supersampled quality. Other NGX services include AI Inpainting, AI Slow-Mo, and AI Super Rez.

Turing also introduces mesh shading, with cooperative task and mesh shaders that reduce CPU draw-call bottlenecks and support dynamic level-of-detail selection. Variable Rate Shading independently controls shading frequency for each 16-by-16-pixel region and supports content-adaptive, motion-adaptive, and foveated rendering. Texture Space Shading decouples visibility from appearance sampling, stores shading results in texture space, and reuses them across pixels, frames, views, and other computations. Multi-View Rendering processes up to four hardware-supported views per pass and supports up to 32 views through the API, enabling efficient stereo, shadow, and multi-instance rendering. Turing also extends DirectX 12 resource binding with bindless constant-buffer and unordered-access views and supports Tier 2 resource heaps.

TU104 includes 48 streaming multiprocessors, 3,072 CUDA Cores, 368 Tensor Cores, and 48 RT Cores, while TU106 includes 36 multiprocessors, 2,304 CUDA Cores, 288 Tensor Cores, and 36 RT Cores; TU106 does not support NVLink or SLI. The document also introduces RTX-OPS, a workload-based metric that weights tensor, FP32, ray-tracing, and integer operations according to their measured use in hybrid-rendering workloads.

The UC1825B-SP supports standard converter topologies including push-pull, forward, half-bridge, and full-bridge designs. PCB layout should minimize EMI by using a low-EMI ferrite closed-core inductor, keeping feedback traces direct, thick, and away from the inductor and noisy power traces, and placing ceramic input, optional feed-forward, and compensation capacitors close to the IC.

High-current traces should be short, direct, and thick, with at least 15 mils per ampere. The inductor, output capacitors, and output diode should be close together, while component grounds should connect directly to a ground plane. Multilayer boards can use separate power and signal planes, with approximately one standard via per 200 mA for significant interplane current. Switching current loops should be arranged in the same direction during both operating states to reduce radiated EMI.

Each output driver supports 2-A peak current. A dedicated power-ground section should serve PGND, MOSFET sources, input return, and the bulk input capacitor. VCC must be bypassed directly with a high-frequency capacitor, and the output clamped with a high-current Schottky diode to VCC and PGND. VREF and analog circuitry should be bypassed to signal ground; TI recommends low-ESR/ESL ceramic 1-mF capacitors for VCC and VREF. The IC requires appropriate ESD handling precautions. Remaining sections cover TI support resources, glossary, packaging and ordering information, disclaimers, and legal terms.

The MSPM0C1105/6 data sheet covers pin attributes, electrical characteristics, device architecture, peripherals, application guidance, documentation, and packaging information for these 32-bit Arm Cortex-M0+ MCUs. The devices operate up to 32 MHz, support 1.62–3.6 V operation and temperatures from −40°C to 125°C, and provide up to 64 KB of flash and 8 KB of SRAM.

Each digital I/O maps to a PINCMx register whose PF bits select the pin function. IOMUX supports one IOMUX-managed digital function per pin, although non-IOMUX-managed signals can coexist with it if no contention exists. PINCM.PF and PINCM.PC are recommended as zero when using non-IOMUX functions. Standard-with-Wake I/O can wake the device from SHUTDOWN, while all I/O can wake it from higher low-power modes. Unused pins should be configured as GPIO and terminated as outputs low or inputs with internal pullups. The active-low NRST pin must be pulled high for startup.

Electrical specifications address recommended and absolute-maximum conditions, supply current, thermal characteristics, power-on and brown-out reset, flash endurance and timing, clock behavior, digital I/O, ADC, temperature sensor, voltage reference, comparator, and communication-interface timing. Flash supports in-circuit programming and erasing, 1 KB minimum erase sectors, and up to 100,000 program/erase cycles on selected sectors.

The devices provide DMA and event-management systems, GPIO and IOMUX, a 12-bit 1.6-MSPS ADC, comparator with an 8-bit DAC, internal 1.4 V or 2.5 V references, temperature sensing, CRC-16, three UARTs, one SPI, two I²C interfaces, real-time clock, independent and windowed watchdogs, general-purpose and advanced timers, and SWD debug support. Five operating modes—RUN, SLEEP, STOP, STANDBY, and SHUTDOWN—use two power domains to balance performance and power consumption.

Recommended application circuitry includes 10 µF and 0.1 µF decoupling capacitors near VDD/VSS, a 47 kΩ NRST pullup with a 1000 pF pulldown, and pullups for 5-V-tolerant open-drain I/O used by I²C or UART. TI also provides development tools, reference documentation, package drawings, ordering information, revision history, and ESD-handling guidance.

The lecture reviews the criterion that a sequence converges to \(x\) exactly when \(|x_n-x|\to0\), along with the squeeze theorem and the limit \(c^n\to0\) for \(|c|<1\). After stating the binomial theorem, the lecturer proves three special limits:
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1{n^p}=0,\qquad
\lim_{n\to\infty}p^{1/n}=1,\qquad
\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{1/n}=1
\]
for appropriate positive \(p\). It also explains that rational and real powers of positive numbers can be defined using roots, completeness, and density of the rationals without first introducing exponentials or logarithms.

The main topic is the limit superior and limit inferior of bounded sequences. For a bounded sequence \((x_n)\), define
\[
a_n=\sup\{x_k:k\ge n\},\qquad b_n=\inf\{x_k:k\ge n\}.
\]
Then \(\limsup x_n=\lim a_n\) and \(\liminf x_n=\lim b_n\). The sequence \((a_n)\) is nonincreasing and bounded below, while \((b_n)\) is nondecreasing and bounded above, so both defining limits exist and satisfy \(\liminf x_n\le\limsup x_n\).

Examples include \((-1)^n\), whose limsup is \(1\) and liminf is \(-1\), and \(1/n\), for which both are \(0\). The lecturer proves that every bounded sequence has a subsequence converging to its limsup and another converging to its liminf. This stronger result immediately yields the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem: every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence.

Finally, the lecture proves that a bounded sequence converges if and only if its limsup and liminf are equal; when they coincide, their common value is the sequence’s limit. The theorem is presented as useful in existence arguments involving extrema and in subjects such as PDEs.

**Background and Aim:** Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) is a major public health burden. Alteplase, approved in 1996, improves outcomes but has only moderate fibrin specificity, residual intracranial hemorrhage risk, a 4–5 minute half-life, and complex administration (bolus plus one-hour infusion). Alternatives (rhPro-UK, ancrod, desmoteplase) showed no significant functional advantage. Tenecteplase, a DNA variant of alteplase, has enhanced fibrin specificity, greater resistance to PAI-1, a longer half-life, and can be given as a 5–10 second intravenous injection. This retrospective study aimed to evaluate tenecteplase's time-management advantages and clinical benefits in routine practice, supporting the rationale for its off-label use.

**Methods:** Patients at the First Affiliated Hospital of Ningbo University received alteplase (January 2022–February 2023) or tenecteplase (March–November 2023) within 4.5 hours of onset; dosages were 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg) and 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg), respectively, with ethics approvals obtained. Collected data included baseline characteristics, NIHSS and mRS scores, 24-hour NIHSS, imaging, hospital stay, onset-to-treatment (OTT), door-to-needle (DNT), and door-to-puncture (DPT) times; workflow endpoints were DNT ≤45 min and DPT ≤120 min; safety endpoints were symptomatic ICH (sICH) and any ICH. SPSS 23.0 univariate tests and binary logistic regression were used (P<0.05 significant).

**Results:** After exclusions, 120 tenecteplase and 144 alteplase patients were analyzed; groups were largely comparable (hyperlipidemia and atrial fibrillation differed; baseline NIHSS, mRS, and thrombectomy rates did not). Tenecteplase significantly reduced OTT (133 vs 163.72), DNT (36.5 vs 50), and DPT (117 vs 193) and increased DNT ≤45 min (65.83% vs 40.44%) and DPT ≤120 min (59.09% vs 13.79%); tenecteplase independently predicted both targets (OR 2.951 and 7.867). NIHSS improvement at 24 hours was higher (64.17% vs 50%; OR 1.715), hospital stay shorter (6 vs 8 days), and sICH (3.33% vs 4.86%) and ICH (13.3% vs 15.28%) were not significantly different. Baseline NIHSS predicted sICH and ICH; atrial fibrillation predicted ICH.

**Conclusion:** Tenecteplase was feasible, associated with earlier neurological improvement, better workflow efficiency, and shorter hospitalization, with safety comparable to alteplase. Limitations include single-center, non-randomized/unblinded design, early-stage outcomes, and predominantly mild-to-moderate strokes; larger multicenter studies and longer follow-up are needed.

The Sandwich Islands’ strategic Pacific position made their future important to the United States. The government requested information on Hawaii’s population, trade, resources, debt, and condition while cautiously exploring annexation sentiment without committing to policy. In 1874, unrest following King Lunalilo’s death led U.S. forces to land at Hawaiian authorities’ request; British forces occupied the barracks for eight days before withdrawing. King David Kalakaua later visited the United States to promote reciprocity negotiations, despite opposition from the British and French commissioners.

This study examines digitalization in education, specifically within private-sector education departments, where prior literature is limited. The introduction frames digitalization as part of the broader digital transformation and Industry 4.0, noting that COVID-19 accelerated remote working and online education, and that companies must adapt their working models and human resources practices accordingly. The literature review links digitalization in education with Education 4.0, flipped classrooms, digital cooperative learning, gamification, augmented and virtual reality, personalized learning, and technology-enhanced learning, while emphasizing the role of human resources in developing employees' digital skills and addressing cybersecurity, the digital gap, and unequal access.

The research uses a qualitative design with 20 expert-managers working in private-sector education. Data were gathered through a researcher-developed semi-structured interview form of five questions, distributed by email during the pandemic, with five participants interviewed via Zoom for 30 minutes. Analysis used inductive content analysis through coding, with codes, categories, and themes organized into four stages.

Results show most participants worked in national companies (95%), had 15 or more years of experience (85%), and worked in organizations with 300+ employees (60%). Reported challenges fell under company-side issues (63%): technological problems, limited financial resources, content unsuited to digitalization, difficulty explaining benefits and ensuring participation, lack of applications and digital training materials, reduced efficiency, original content creation, and trainers' shift to an informing role. Participant-side issues (37%) included resistance and fear, inability to use body language, attending training while working, slow adaptation, unfamiliarity with learning technologies, distraction, unequal opportunity, and low digital literacy. Adaptations included online and hybrid training, digital education systems, online academies, training videos (65%), updating content and organizing workshops and projects (40%), and using digital platforms and tools (20%). Positive effects included time, cost, and location-independent savings (70%), equal opportunity and increased motivation (65%), and improved accessibility and gamification (60%). Negative effects included participant indifference and concentration problems and lack of trained workforce (70%), reduced interactive face-to-face education, decreased efficiency, and cyberbullying (60%), and being less effective than face-to-face training, measurement problems, and cheating tendencies (25%). When defining digitalization, 60% cited technological possibilities and 40% cited easy access.

The discussion notes that digitalization and Industry 4.0 are intertwined, that AI and robots replace some professions, that teachers need digital literacy, and that risks include digital inequality, screen time, addiction, health problems, cyberattacks, and loss of social identity. The conclusion reports effects similar to earlier studies, highlighting participants' fears, scarcity of original content, and low digital literacy, alongside private-sector use of online platforms, edited content and videos, and virtual reality applications, as well as access independent of time and place. Recommendations state that educational institutions must adapt, that full digitalization is premature since face-to-face education will persist, and that technological content, virtual reality materials, and gamification should be expanded, with private-sector practices informing national and higher education institutions.

The study presents an end-to-end workflow for inverse-designing superconductors using a guided diffusion model, computational screening, and experimental validation. A DiffCSP foundation model was pretrained on more than two million Alexandria crystal structures to learn plausible crystal formation without property conditioning. It was then fine-tuned on 7,183 labeled superconducting samples using an adapter that conditions generation on target critical temperatures, \(T_c\), while preserving the pretrained structural prior. Classifier-free guidance with weight \(w=2\) generated 200,000 candidate structures.

Tests on 1,000 generated structures showed that, without guidance, predicted \(T_c\) values followed the fine-tuning distribution. Conditioning on 10 K shifted the distribution toward the target, whereas an out-of-distribution target of 110 K produced predominantly low-\(T_c\) structures, indicating that the learned structural prior constrains extreme extrapolation.

Multistage filtering combined machine learning and DFT calculations to assess metallicity, formation energy, thermodynamic and dynamical stability, and \(T_c\). From 200,000 candidates, 34,027 unique structures remained after initial relaxation and deduplication; 20,994 were metallic, 10,877 had BEE-NET-predicted \(T_c>5\) K, 9,167 passed machine-learning convex-hull screening, and 1,818 were dynamically stable. Refined phonon-based predictions identified 1,365 candidates with predicted \(T_c>5\) K, of which 773 had DFT-calculated \(T_c>5\) K and \(E_{\text{hull}}<200\) meV/atom, with \(T_c\) values extending to about 35 K. The candidates comprised 133 binaries, 455 ternaries, 178 quaternaries, and 7 pentanaries. The pipeline produced a 2.3% hit rate, compared with 0.017% for an element-substitution baseline and 0.83% in a prior generative study.

Eighteen structurally diverse candidates were selected for arc-melt synthesis using composition, vapor-pressure, stability, A15-variant, and structural-clustering filters. Nine showed evidence of superconductivity above 4.2 K, generally at temperatures below predictions. X-ray diffraction indicated that the predicted ordered structures usually did not form; samples were predominantly disordered BCC solid solutions, multiphase mixtures, or known binary phases.

The study attributes these outcomes partly to sparse reference data and incomplete convex hulls, which can make unstable or unrealizable candidates appear viable. Of 28 candidates identified as on or near the hull, AFLOW comparison found eight matching known prototypes, five representing new arrangements of known symmetry frameworks, and 15 with no known prototype or isopointal match; these formed seven structural families, including a nine-member A15-derived family. Proposed improvements include alternative guidance and generative backbones, discrete diffusion for compositions, local DFT convex-hull refinement, disorder-aware screening, multiobjective optimization, and active learning that incorporates experimental non-formation as negative feedback.

This bibliometric study examined the development, structure, themes, and collaboration networks of research on mathematics and mathematics education in special education. Most publications appeared in special education journals, particularly the *Journal of Special Education* and *Remedial and Special Education*. The authors linked the field’s recent growth to inclusive education, STEM research, educational reforms, and pandemic-related learning losses. **Summary**

SynDoc is a proposed hybrid framework for domain-specific Visually Rich Document Understanding (VRDU) that combines a discriminative model and a generative Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM). It addresses limitations of prior approaches: VLPMs depend on costly curated fine-tuning data, while MLLMs lack domain-specific knowledge and produce unreliable outputs.

SynDoc has four components. The Synthetic Data Generator extracts structure and text via off-the-shelf OCR and PDF parsing tools, then uses MLLMs for multi-task inquiry generation (semantic QA pairs and spatial-aware QA pairs) and multi-aspect quality verification (meaningfulness and question–answer consistency). The Discriminative "Warmer" uses a VLPM backbone (LayoutLMv3 in experiments) with an entity-retrieval head, a span-based QA head, and a grid matching head. Adaptive Warmer Tuning proceeds in stages: structural adaptation aligns queries with document grids, followed by semantic adaptation combining fine-grained span and coarse-grained entity losses. Recursive inference cross-feeds outputs between warmer and MLLM, updating prompts with retrieved entities over iterations until predictions stabilise.

Experiments used four KIE datasets — FormNLU (printed and handwritten), CORD, Ephoie, and FUNSD — with ANLS as the primary metric, comparing against Idefics2, InternVL2, Qwen2-VL, GPT-4o, and Gemini 1.5. Proprietary models generally outperformed open-source ones, and Qwen2-VL was the strongest open-source model. Adding warmer knowledge to Gemini improved results (e.g., FormNLU printed 76.09→81.91 with top-K recursive hints; CORD 84.35→85.19), while FUNSD could introduce noise. Analyses showed meaningfulness verification consistently helped, consistency verification sometimes hurt (likely due to OCR errors), prior MLLM outputs and structural adaptation improved the warmer, and Top-3 retrieval beat Top-1 with Top-5 adding marginal gains. Multimodal backbones generally outperformed text-only RoBERTa, though not always. Recursive inference improved both warmer and generator, with OCR-challenging datasets benefiting from more iterations. Case studies showed corrections of hallucinated values and near-correct predictions from iterative refinement. The authors note further work is needed for cross-domain generalisability.

The lecture shifts from cosmology to constructing the spacetime of a compact, static, spherically symmetric body with a vacuum exterior. The most general static spherical metric is diagonal; coordinate transformations remove the time-radius cross-term. Schwarzschild coordinates use areal radius, so nested spheres have area \(4\pi r^2\), while isotropic coordinates treat all spatial directions equally and were used in the earlier weak-field solution.

The exterior is solved by setting the Ricci tensor equal to zero. Combining equations gives \(\phi=-\lambda\), and integration yields
\[
\phi=\frac12\ln(1+a/r).
\]
Matching radial free fall in the weak-field, large-\(r\) limit to Newtonian gravity requires \(a=-2GM\), producing the Schwarzschild metric. Carl Schwarzschild derived this exact vacuum solution in 1916 while ill and serving in the German Army.

Birkhoff’s theorem shows that any spherically symmetric vacuum exterior is described by the Schwarzschild metric, even if the source changes over time while preserving spherical symmetry. Such changes cannot produce gravitational waves, and the exterior geometry depends on the source’s mass rather than its radial distribution. Allowing time-dependent metric functions and imposing the vacuum equations demonstrates that a time-like Killing vector can be recovered, enabling conserved energy for objects in the exterior.

The body’s interior is modeled as a static perfect fluid with spherically symmetric density and pressure. Einstein’s equations are used to define a mass function,
\[
m(r)=\int_0^r4\pi\rho(r')r'^2\,dr',
\]
and to relate the metric to the fluid’s pressure and density. This gravitational mass differs from the proper-volume-integrated baryonic mass because gravitational binding lowers the combined energy of the fluid.

Together with pressure-gradient conservation, these relations yield the coupled Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff equations for the metric function, mass function, density, and pressure. A stellar model is constructed by choosing a central density and an equation of state, integrating the equations, and matching the interior solution to the Schwarzschild exterior at the body’s surface.
