The passage describes NVIDIA’s Turing GPU architecture, which combines rasterization, real-time ray tracing, AI, and simulation. Its display engine supports higher resolutions, faster refresh rates, native HDR processing, and BT.2100 tone mapping. DisplayPort 1.4a with DSC 1.2 supports 8K at 60 Hz, including two 8K displays with one cable each, while 8K can also be transmitted over USB-C.

Turing improves video encoding and decoding. Its enhanced NVENC encoder supports H.265/HEVC 8K encoding at 30 fps and offers up to 25% bitrate savings for HEVC and 15% for H.264. The updated NVDEC supports HEVC 4:4:4 8-, 10-, and 12-bit streams and VP9 10- and 12-bit HDR. The passage reports that Turing’s encoder provides better quality than fast x264 software encoding with much lower CPU use and makes 4K streaming practical on typical systems.

VirtualLink, an open USB-C standard led by NVIDIA, Oculus, Valve, Microsoft, and AMD, allows a VR headset’s power, display, and tracking data to use one connector by combining four HBR3 DisplayPort lanes with SuperSpeed USB 3. Turing also replaces the Pascal-era MIO and PCIe interfaces for SLI transfers with second-generation NVLink. TU102 has two x8 links and TU104 one, providing 25 GB/s per direction per link. Turing supports two-way SLI with these GPUs but not three- or four-way configurations, and NVLink enables additional display topologies.

Turing adds RT Cores to each streaming multiprocessor for real-time ray tracing of reflections, refractions, shadows, and indirect lighting. RT Cores handle BVH traversal, bounding-box tests, and ray-triangle intersection testing, offloading work from shader multiprocessors. The passage reports performance above 10 billion rays per second and roughly tenfold improvement over software ray tracing on Pascal. Support is provided through NVIDIA RTX technology and libraries, OptiX, Microsoft DXR, and the forthcoming Vulkan ray-tracing API.

Turing’s recommended rendering model is hybrid rendering: rasterization handles visibility and work for which it remains effective, while ray tracing supplies effects where it offers greater visual value. Developers may instead use ray tracing throughout a workload when image fidelity is the priority. Denoising reduces the number of rays required, and RT Cores accelerate the underlying BVH operations. The passage describes ray-traced shadows as replacements for shadow maps, ray-traced ambient occlusion as more detailed than screen-space occlusion, and ray-traced reflections as avoiding the holes and artifacts common to screen-space and cubemap methods.

NVIDIA NGX is a deep-learning technology stack within RTX that uses DNNs, neural services, and Turing Tensor Cores to accelerate AI-based graphics and client applications. NGX exposes pretrained features through an API and is managed through GeForce Experience or Quadro Experience. Its models can use CUDA 10, DirectX, Vulkan, and TensorRT.

Deep Learning Super-Sampling (DLSS) is trained using 64× supersampled reference images and matching lower-quality inputs. It produces results comparable to temporal anti-aliasing with roughly half the shading work by allowing rendering at a lower sample count. The passage claims that this helps the RTX 2080 Ti reach twice the performance of the GTX 1080 Ti. DLSS 2X uses a larger network to transform final-resolution input into an image approaching 64× supersampling quality and handles some moving, transparent, and disoccluded content more clearly than TAA.

Other NGX features include Inpainting, which synthesizes replacement content for removed image areas using trained real-world imagery; AI Slow-Mo, which analyzes motion and inserts interpolated frames to create smoother slow motion; and AI Super Rez, which generates new pixels to enlarge images or video by 2×, 4×, or 8× while preserving detail and depth of field.

Mesh Shading introduces task and mesh shader stages using cooperative thread models. Task shaders dynamically process object lists, launch mesh shaders, and select appropriate levels of detail, while mesh shaders generate triangles for rasterization. This reduces CPU draw-call bottlenecks and can increase the number of real-time objects by more than an order of magnitude. Mesh and task shaders can also perform dynamic geometry cutaways for CAD-style applications.

Variable Rate Shading (VRS) permits independent shading rates for each 16×16-pixel region. Developers can spatially or per-primitive vary rates, decouple shading from visibility, and combine shading results across multiple pixels or non-square footprints. Content Adaptive Shading lowers rates in areas with little color change, Motion Adaptive Shading reduces rates for moving objects, and Foveated Rendering lowers peripheral rates according to eye focus. VRS can also raise rates above one sample per pixel when used with multisample anti-aliasing.

Texture Space Shading (TSS) stores shading results as texels and reuses them across requests, frames, or stereo views. It decouples visibility sampling from appearance shading, permits different sampling grids and rates, and improves temporal stability and VR performance by avoiding repeated shading of unchanged data.

Multi-View Rendering processes multiple viewpoints or character instances in one pass. Turing hardware supports four views per pass, while the API supports up to 32. Geometry is fetched and shaded once, with view IDs controlling view-dependent attributes and shared attributes computed only once. Turing extends Pascal’s simultaneous multi-projection support and is useful for stereo and wide-field-of-view VR, cascaded shadow maps, and multiple character instances.

Turing also supports bindless constant-buffer and unordered-access views, resource co-location in shared heaps, and Tier 2 resource heaps. For VR, VirtualLink reduces cabling, MVR supports additional projections for immersive headsets, VRS enables foveated rendering, and RT Cores accelerate ray-traced audio in VRWorks Audio.

TU104 contains 48 SMs, 3,072 CUDA Cores, 368 Tensor Cores, 48 RT Cores, a 256-bit memory interface, and one x8 NVLink link. It is used in products including the GeForce RTX 2080, Tesla T4, and Quadro RTX 5000. The Tesla T4 version has 40 SMs, 2,560 CUDA Cores, 320 Tensor Cores, and 320 GB/s of memory bandwidth and targets inference workloads. TU106, used in the GeForce RTX 2070, has 36 SMs, 2,304 CUDA Cores, 288 Tensor Cores, and 36 RT Cores but supports neither NVLink nor SLI.

RTX-OPS is presented as a workload-based metric that derates tensor, FP32, RT, and integer throughput by their expected utilization. The stated example assumes tensor operations at 20%, CUDA cores at 80%, RT cores at 40%, and INT32 pipelines at 28%, yielding an RTX 2080 Ti value of 78.

**Summary of Lecture 7 (Part 1), 6.5630 F23 — Yael Kalai**

**Administration.** Kalai noted a small issue with problem set problem 2B (a required assumption is posted on the course website), mentioned Thanksgiving and that he will be away the week after giving a keynote on BARGs (batch arguments) by a three-author work whose results will be presented by one of the authors (Jain, Jin, Choudhuri). The final class will wrap up the semester's results.

**Recap and today's plan.** Previous classes covered interactive protocols, GKR for bounded-depth computations, PCPs, and the Kilian–Micali protocol, giving four-message computationally sound proofs for all of NP with proofs whose length is proportional to the security parameter. The goal now is to reduce four messages to one. Last class introduced the Fiat–Shamir paradigm, which eliminates interaction by replacing the verifier with a hash function. It was proven sound in the random oracle model (treating the hash as a random function), but soundness with an explicit circuit remained a long-standing open problem, important because Fiat–Shamir is used widely in practice. Random oracle security has been a very good proxy in practice, though contrived counterexamples exist — notably Kilian–Micali itself, which is secure in the random oracle model but not with certain collision-resistant hash functions.

**The zero-knowledge detour (recap).** A three-message zero-knowledge proof for Hamiltonian cycle: the prover picks a random permutation π, commits to π(G)'s adjacency matrix (1 for edges, 0 for non-edges); if b = 0 it opens the cycle positions (which must be 1s forming a cycle); if b = 1 it reveals π and opens only the non-edges (which must be 0s). It is zero knowledge but only half-sound, since a cheating prover can guess b. Repeating the protocol in parallel with a security parameter number of copies, each with a fresh permutation, restores security in the random oracle model (by a general result on protocols with negligible soundness). Parallel repetition does not preserve zero knowledge, which resolves the apparent tension with Fiat–Shamir (previously stated as: a zero-knowledge protocol cannot be Fiat–Shamir secure).

**Goal for today.** Show the parallel-repeated Hamiltonian-cycle protocol is Fiat–Shamir secure in the standard model, for a particular commitment scheme and an explicitly constructed hash function, assuming fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) — and, for the presentation's simplicity, circular-secure FHE, with a follow-up result removing the circular security requirement via lattice techniques (an instantiation based on circular-secure LWE is believed but unproven).

**Motivation.** Applying Fiat–Shamir to this protocol yields a noninteractive zero-knowledge (NIZK) proof, resolving the long-standing open problem of lattice-based NIZK (Canetti, Lombardi, and Wichs, 2019). The technique is far more general: it also yields security for the GKR protocol (under LWE/FHE) and leads to SNARGs and to batch arguments for NP (to be presented after Thanksgiving).

**Deriving the hash function.** For a fixed statement outside the language, each first message α admits essentially one "bad" challenge β on which a cheating prover can succeed, so the hash must avoid that β for every α. The naive choice h(α) = β_bad(α) ⊕ 1 fails because computing β_bad requires opening the commitment, which is hard — that hardness is exactly the source of the protocol's power. If a trapdoor made β_bad computable, the hash would work, but the trapdoor cannot be published (it would break zero knowledge); prior obfuscation-based attempts produced very strong, dubious assumptions.

**Commitment via public-key encryption.** Using encryption as the commitment: a public-key scheme has KeyGen, Enc, Dec with correctness and semantic security (indistinguishability between encryptions of any two fixed messages). Binding requires the public key to be honestly generated, so it is placed in a trusted common reference string (CRS) known to both parties, with no one holding the secret key. The prover opens by revealing the randomness used in encryption. The CRS public key need not be truly random but is indistinguishable from random; using the true key gives statistical soundness with computational zero knowledge, while using an all-zero "fake" key gives computational soundness with statistical zero knowledge.

**Fully homomorphic encryption.** FHE is a public-key encryption scheme with an additional Eval algorithm that takes ciphertexts of bits, a circuit c (additions and multiplications mod 2), and outputs a ciphertext of c evaluated on those bits, with completeness (decryption yields the circuit's output with probability 1 minus negligible).

**The hash function and the soundness proof.** The hash key consists of an FHE public key plus an encryption (under that key) of a function g — in the actual scheme g is an all-zero circuit of a size T — and evaluation computes g(α) under the hood via homomorphic evaluation with a universal circuit, yielding an encryption of g(α). For the analysis, replace g with a special g*: g* computes β_bad from α using the commitment's trapdoor, decrypts that string with the secret key, and XORs in 1, so g*(α) is never equal to β_bad (decryption is deterministic, so equality of ciphertexts would force the decrypted values equal). Soundness then follows: an efficient cheating prover that cheats with non-negligible probability on a graph without a Hamiltonian cycle would, by semantic security and efficiency, also succeed with the hash key encrypting g*, but with g* cheating is information-theoretically impossible — a contradiction. This requires circular security: (public key, encryption of the secret key) must be indistinguishable from (public key, encryption of all zeros), bit by bit. Here T is the number of bits needed to represent g*. Kalai then took a break, with the NIZK portion to follow.

This medRxiv preprint reports a randomized, single-blind, placebo-controlled trial of intranasal SA58 antibody spray as post-exposure prophylaxis for COVID-19. The study enrolled healthy adult workers at 21 Beijing construction sites between November 26 and December 9, 2022, after exposure to a confirmed SARS-CoV-2 case within 72 hours. Of 1,634 randomized participants, 1,222 were included in the safety analysis and 1,123, who were baseline RT-PCR negative, in the efficacy analysis. The study ended early before reaching its planned sample size.

SA58 reduced the risk of laboratory-confirmed symptomatic COVID-19 from 14 cases among 299 placebo recipients to 7 among 824 SA58 recipients, with estimated efficacy of 80.82% (95% CI 52.41%–92.27%). It reduced RT-PCR-confirmed infection by 61.83% (95% CI 37.50%–76.69%). No severe COVID-19 or deaths occurred, and all sequenced infections were the Omicron BF.7 sublineage. Adverse events were mild, with no serious adverse events, adverse events of special interest, withdrawals, or deaths reported.

- **Bandwidth contracts:** After carriers and trading companies spent more than nine months without a standard bandwidth agreement, two master trading agreements were posted on the CompTel website and a third was circulating. Enron and Williams publicly identified themselves, while participation by El Paso, Aquila, Koch, Reliant and others remained unconfirmed. - **Sierra Pacific Resources:** Sierra Pacific canceled its May 1 quarterly dividend of 25 cents per share because of high power costs, and its shares fell 8.3% to $13.29. The Nevada utility said the move would save less than $20 million. A 17% rate increase approved in February was insufficient to cover rising wholesale costs, and the company lost $18.2 million, or 23 cents per share, in the fourth quarter. Its planned $3.1 billion purchase of Enron’s Portland General Electric unit remained delayed by California restrictions on utility asset sales.

- **California electricity trading:** Energy wholesalers’ activities were blamed for rising California power bills, while wholesalers cited higher natural-gas costs and the state’s deregulation and rate-cap policies. Attorneys general in California, Oregon and Washington investigated possible antitrust violations, and lawsuits alleged that generators withheld electricity and fixed prices, although no concrete price-fixing evidence had been assembled. A California grid report found that 98% of trading bids during part of the prior year reflected noncompetitive behavior and that wholesalers collected as much as $6.9 billion in unjustified rates. Energy trading had a blanket CFTC oversight exemption, while FERC planned increased monitoring. Enron reported 2000 operating profit of $1.6 billion, up 160%, and denied benefiting from California prices, attributing its success to market efficiency.

- **Independent power producers:** Williams, Calpine, Dynegy and Mirant were expected to meet or exceed first-quarter earnings forecasts, while Enron and Reliant remained on track. Higher electricity and natural-gas prices and increased trading volumes lifted profits despite concerns over unpaid California utility debts. Reliant reported sharply higher earnings, and Calpine maintained guidance despite receivables from bankrupt PG&E. FERC had ordered 13 producers to justify California charges or issue refunds, including $45.8 million for Dynegy and $29.6 million for Williams, but analysts considered refunds a limited near-term risk. Possible future price caps and state intervention remained threats.

- **Seattle City Light:** Seattle spent a record $92 million on wholesale power in March, exceeding its entire 1999 annual power bill, as drought conditions increased market purchases. Enron supplied $25.5 million, far more than Sempra Energy’s $7.4 million. Although market purchases represented only about 15% of Seattle’s electricity, they accounted for more than 90% of its power costs. City Light stored water, pursued additional hydroelectric and gas-fired power contracts, and passed through a 28% rate increase. Local utilities sometimes charged Seattle more than Enron, and reported market prices reached $450 per megawatt-hour. City officials expected new contracts by October to reduce dependence on the open market, though Bonneville Power Administration rates could rise sharply. This medRxiv preprint reports a retrospective mortality audit at Kitwe Teaching Hospital (KTH), a tertiary hospital serving northern Zambia. Background notes that TB remains the world's leading cause of mortality from a single infectious agent; WHO's 2019 report estimated 10 million incident cases and 1.5 million deaths globally, with incidence of 132 per 100,000 population and 15–21 times higher TB risk among people living with HIV. Zambia ranks among the top 30 high-burden countries (2018 incidence 346 per 100,000). Most Zambian TB patients are managed at primary health facilities, with complicated cases referred to secondary/tertiary hospitals, where most TB deaths are recorded; a prior KTH study found TB caused 21% of all deaths and was the leading cause of death among adult inpatients.

Methods: 74 mortality files attributed to TB (June 2018–June 2019) were reviewed using a standardized form covering demographics, symptoms, HIV serostatus, hospital stay and outcome, diagnoses and comorbidities at death, and laboratory and radiological findings. Thirty files were excluded (deaths within 24 hours of admission or lacking clinical/laboratory confirmation of TB). Data were analysed in SPSS 16.0 and Microsoft Excel.

Results: 67.6% of deaths were male; mean age 39.2 ± 11.6 years; 83.8% were from high-density residential areas; 81.1% were HIV-positive. Commonest symptoms were cough (41.9%), fever (40.5%), diarrhea (29.7%), productive cough (27.0%), headache (21.6%) and shortness of breath (16.2%). Mean arterial pressure was 81.5 ± 17.4 mmHg on admission versus 75.9 ± 19.1 before death, and pulse rate 112.1 ± 29.7 versus 94.1 ± 23.4 per minute. Laboratory abnormalities included hemoglobin below 11.5 g/dL (39.2%), hypoalbuminemia (12.2%), renal dysfunction (10.8%) and raised AST (18.9%); chest X-ray showed miliary changes in 6.8%.

Discussion and conclusion: deaths clustered among younger HIV-positive men residing in crowded areas, with hyperdynamic pulse rates, anemia and multi-organ involvement; limitations include retrospective design and missing data. The authors call for stronger early recognition of clinical instability and recommend a prospective study of mortality predictors, including whether malignancy contributes.

The Amazon’s 2024 fire season was its most destructive in more than two decades, affecting 3.3 million hectares and releasing an estimated 791 million tons of carbon dioxide—roughly Germany’s annual emissions and seven times the previous two-year average. For the first time in the 2022–2024 analysis, fire-driven degradation surpassed deforestation as the Amazon’s main source of emissions. Satellite analysis and Monte Carlo simulations linked the surge to drought, climate change, forest fragmentation, and land-use mismanagement. Brazil recorded its highest forest-degradation emissions, while fires affected over 9% of Bolivia’s remaining intact forest. Researchers warn that degraded forests can retain their canopy while losing biomass and ecological function, potentially escaping existing policies and accounting systems. The passage describes a feedback-controlled, high-voltage nanosecond pulsed electric field (nsPEF) generator and treatment system for therapeutic electrotherapy, particularly tumor treatment. NsPEF pulses have sub-microsecond durations, typically 0.1–1000 nanoseconds, and may be applied periodically at high voltages. The passage states that nsPEF treatment can induce apoptosis in tumor cells, selectively avoid substantial effects on surrounding normal cells because of its non-thermal nature, and stimulate an immune response against tumor cells.

The system includes a controller, power supply, pulse generator, interface, electrodes, and optional sensors. A user can specify pulse amplitude, polarity, duration, rise and fall times, frequency, pulse quantity, tissue-temperature limit, and other treatment parameters. The controller generates separate control signals for the power supply and pulse generator. The power supply provides the voltages used to charge the pulse generator, while the pulse generator produces controllable high-voltage pulses. Feedback signals representing measured pulse, patient, electrode, or environmental characteristics can be used to adjust the supply voltage, pulse width, number of pulses, frequency, duty cycle, or other parameters.

Several pulse-generator architectures are disclosed. In one implementation, capacitors are charged during a charge mode and discharged through serially connected switch stacks during a discharge mode to produce a high-voltage output. Power MOSFETs arranged in Marx-switch stacks allow high output voltages with few stages, high efficiency, low impedance, and variable pulse duration. Multiple circuits can be connected in parallel to increase current and power or in series to increase voltage. Driver circuits use amplifiers, capacitors, transformers, and optional clamp circuits to produce switch-control pulses corresponding to input trigger pulses. Switch elements may include snubber and overcurrent-protection circuits, while lossy transformers can suppress transient coupling and limit output-pulse duration.

The passage also describes seven-needle and two-pole suction electrodes. The seven-needle electrode draws a tumor into a vacuum chamber and applies electrical fields between a center electrode and six outer electrodes. The two-pole electrode places opposing electrodes around a tumor within a suction chamber. Electrode selection depends on tumor shape, size, stiffness, accessibility, and the availability of a path for the electric field to cross the tumor. Needle electrodes may be used percutaneously or through endoscopes or laparoscopes.

Feedback control compares sensed values with desired values and modifies system controls so subsequent measurements more closely approach the desired values. Measurements may include pulse amplitude, width, frequency, current, voltage, pulse shape, power, energy, tissue temperature, conductivity, arcing, and environmental conditions. Control methods include PID control, lookup tables, and fixed-step adjustments. If temperature or delivered energy exceeds a specified maximum or warning threshold, the controller can reduce delivered power by lowering pulse width, frequency, or voltage. Additional methods verify the pulse generator’s charge voltage before generating pulses. Analog-to-digital converters and current monitors can provide voltage, current, and thermal feedback for these control loops.

Wearable or handheld visualization devices present 3D bone and implant models, cutting planes, entry points, axes, depths, and other plan data, with user controls based on gaze, gestures, voice, or manual input. Additional features include simulated range of motion, anatomical-preparation validation, closed-loop tool control, surgical-item identification, deep-neural-network classification and surgery recommendations, smart implants, and patient monitoring. Detailed embodiments focus on shoulder arthroplasty and ankle joint repair.

The "Back Cut" offense is designed to exploit the weaknesses of the Diamond & One defense, which is weak in the corners and middle. It generates open looks, lay-ups, offensive putbacks, and uses single/double baseline screens to free the Star player, forcing opponents out of their Diamond & One alignment. The offense has right- and left-side entry variations, each built around three looks: a back cut (ballhandler drives the gap between two defenders as a post flashes to the middle), a corner cut (ballhandler cuts to the corner, wing passes to a post stepping to the high post, and the post feeds a baseline back cut), and single/double action with base and down screens, including a "fake cross" option when the Star's defender cheats over the screens. Implementation depends on execution, coordination, preparation for double and base screens and strong post ups, defensive recognition, non-verbal communication, timing, and experience. Teaching methods include Whole-Part-Whole learning, drills (1-on-1 low post and high post isolation, half- and full-court scrimmaging), and game strategies such as scouting opponents, anticipating defensive reads and counters, reacting to substitutions and timeouts, varying alignments and entries, and attacking the weakest defenders. The Diamond & One defense itself is described as four defenders in the zone with a fifth in strong pass denial, best used against odd or one-guard front offenses.

The article defines night trading as identical to overnight trading: holding positions from the close of the trading day (16:00 Eastern) until the next open (09:30), rather than trading during after-hours sessions.

According to the statistics presented, since SPY's 1993 inception, all S&P 500 gains have come from holding the index overnight — an average of 0.04% per night, too small on its own to cover slippage and commissions. The same tendency appears in gold (GLD, about 0.03% per night) and is stronger in gold miners (GDX, roughly 30% CAGR compounded from 2007). By contrast, buying the S&P 500 at the open and selling at the close every day has produced zero returns since 1993, and GDX open-to-close holding averaged -0.09% per day (-25% CAGR). The article attributes the overnight drift to inflation and earnings growth over time, with compensation for added overnight risk.

The authors note that exploiting the bias requires solid trading rules, not simply buy and hold, and they list published resources including 200+ free strategies, a 2014 overnight strategy with seven years of out-of-sample performance, and three backtested 24-hour close-to-close strategies (950 trades, 0.33% average gain per trade). They conclude overnight stock strategies are "low-hanging fruit" offering reasonable risk, though not a path to wealth.

Dengue is a mosquito-borne disease caused by four dengue virus serotypes and lacks approved direct-acting antivirals. AT-752 is an oral guanosine nucleotide prodrug that is metabolized to AT-9010, an inhibitor of the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase; AT-273 is a plasma surrogate marker for intracellular AT-9010 exposure.

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 1 study evaluated the safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of ascending single and multiple oral doses of AT-752 in healthy adults. Sixty-five subjects were enrolled: 41 in single-ascending-dose cohorts dosed from 250 to 1,500 mg and 24 in multiple-ascending-dose cohorts receiving 1,000 mg once daily, 750 mg twice daily, or 750 mg three times daily. Food-effect and Asian-ethnic cohorts were also included.

AT-752 was well tolerated, with no serious adverse events, adverse-event discontinuations, or treatment- or dose-related trends in laboratory results, vital signs, or ECGs. Treatment-emergent adverse events were generally mild or moderate and resolved by study end; sporadic gastrointestinal events occurred mainly at higher doses.

After single doses, AT-281 appeared rapidly and was eliminated with a half-life of approximately 0.5 hours, while AT-273 had a longer half-life of approximately 15–25 hours, indicating sustained intracellular active-metabolite exposure. Exposure increased across 250–1,500 mg. A high-fat meal delayed and reduced peak concentrations but had limited effects on total exposure, supporting administration with or without food. Pharmacokinetics were similar between the Asian and predominantly Caucasian cohorts, indicating no apparent ethnic sensitivity. Urinary recovery was low to moderate, with total recovery around 20–30%.

During multiple dosing, AT-281 did not meaningfully accumulate, whereas AT-273 exposure increased with dosing frequency, and steady state was essentially reached by Day 3. Only 750 mg three times daily produced mean trough AT-273 concentrations exceeding the in vitro DENV inhibition EC90 of 0.64 μM during the first day and maintained them throughout treatment. Overall, AT-752 demonstrated favorable safety and pharmacokinetics and supported further clinical dose selection for dengue treatment.

The March 7–8, 2001 articles describe California’s severe electricity crisis. Wholesale prices had risen sharply while retail rates remained constrained by the 1996 deregulation law, and demand growth and insufficient generation contributed to shortages. PG&E and Southern California Edison accumulated roughly $13–14 billion in unpaid power costs, lost supplier credit, and faced possible blackouts and bankruptcy. At least 10 plants closed in two weeks because PG&E had not paid for deliveries.

Gov. Gray Davis’s administration responded by having the Department of Water Resources purchase power on an emergency basis. By March, the department was reportedly buying 95%–99% of California’s daily needs. The state also announced 40 long-term contracts or tentative accords worth about $40 billion, intended to secure power for nine million homes over a decade at an average price of $69 per megawatt-hour, compared with roughly $30–40 before the crisis. Consumer advocates questioned whether above-market terms would be locked in for years, while energy-industry representatives said confidentiality was necessary to preserve competitive advantages.

The state planned to issue about $10 billion in revenue bonds to recover power-purchase costs and was negotiating to buy the transmission grids of PG&E, Edison and San Diego Gas & Electric. PG&E reportedly sought at least $7 billion, possibly $10 billion, for its grid, which the state would upgrade and lease back. Consumer advocates considered the proposed payments excessive, and PG&E warned that selling its network could reduce its customer and revenue base.

Long-term contracts and conservation were expected to cover only part of summer demand. Experts said as much as 43% of daily needs might still have to be purchased in the volatile spot market, where prices averaged $411 per megawatt-hour and had reached as high as $1,500. The state called for at least a 10% reduction in consumption, while the Independent System Operator warned that peak demand could go unmet and forecasts anticipated rotating outages. The state approved a temporary 51-megawatt gas-fired “peaker” plant at San Francisco International Airport expected to serve about 50,000 homes by August, despite local concerns about pollution. Contra Costa County also began searching for possible plant sites amid resident objections, and a proposed 600-megawatt Golden State Power project faced health and environmental concerns.

Regulators were also deciding how the state would repay billions in emergency power costs and who would bear spot-market charges. PG&E and Edison said ratepayer revenues were insufficient to repay the DWR, while consumer groups and regulators considered alternative revenue formulas. The state’s bond plan depended on collecting substantially more from utility customers, raising concerns about rate increases, the state budget and California’s credit rating. Davis favored long-term contracts and conservation to limit immediate rate increases, but Wall Street analysts said the strategy did not resolve the gap between wholesale and retail prices.

Other disputes involved utility finances and service. El Paso Energy shut six cogeneration plants with about 175 megawatts of capacity because PG&E had not paid for December through February deliveries. A bill intended to reduce payments to more than 600 alternative-energy generators stalled amid objections to higher rates for a small group of wind producers. The PUC considered PG&E’s proposal to lay off hundreds of additional workers; a judge recommended restoring 725 previously eliminated positions and blocking 2,125 more cuts because reduced staffing could impair service and outage response. SMUD and other municipal utilities sought exemptions from PG&E-directed rolling blackouts, arguing they had secured supplies and implemented conservation while PG&E’s financial problems were not their responsibility.

Congressional proposals included wholesale price caps and extending daylight-saving time to reduce peak demand, but no consensus emerged. Local disputes also continued over PG&E’s $91 million Tri-Valley transmission project and proposed power-plant sites. A commentary additionally argued that California faced an estimated $90 billion infrastructure gap beyond electricity, emphasizing deferred maintenance, demand management and coordinated regional planning.

Two clinical trials found that oral semaglutide at 25 milligrams and Eli Lilly’s investigational small-molecule orforglipron helped people with obesity lose weight. Oral semaglutide produced an average weight loss of nearly 14% over up to 64 weeks in more than 300 participants, while the highest orforglipron dose produced about 11% loss over up to 72 weeks in more than 3,000 participants. Both pills are taken daily and require no refrigeration or injector, potentially making treatment easier and less expensive to manufacture and distribute. Side effects included nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and constipation, which generally diminished over time; no liver toxicity was observed, though longer-term studies are needed. Pricing and insurance coverage remain unknown, and approval and availability by 2026 are uncertain.

The case examines Nissan’s operational resilience before and after the March 11, 2011 earthquake, tsunami, and Fukushima nuclear emergency in Japan. The disaster caused more than 25,000 deaths, injuries, or missing persons, damaged 125,000 buildings, and was expected to cost ¥16.9 trillion. About 80% of Japanese automotive plants suspended production, while industry production fell nearly 60% in March and April and 9% for 2011. Disruptions to Japanese suppliers affected automakers worldwide, including Nissan, which sustained damage at six facilities and had about 50 critical suppliers impaired.

The case reviews the Japanese automotive industry’s development, including Nissan’s establishment in 1933, post-war dependence on government loans and U.S. military orders, early technology transfers, and Toyota’s development of just-in-time manufacturing and the Toyota Production System. Although these methods reduced inventories and improved efficiency, they also created vulnerability when information or material flows were disrupted.

Nissan used a more flexible, regional, and decentralized supply chain than Toyota’s tightly controlled system, while retaining strong central coordination during global crises. Its corporate leadership included diverse nationalities and overseas experience. Nissan also maintained a simplified product line, using build-to-stock production for a few model variants and build-to-order production for the remainder.

Following Renault’s 1999 rescue of Nissan from near bankruptcy, management retained a “crisis mentality” emphasizing vigilance, rapid response, and clear responsibility. Nissan established a dedicated risk-management function, an executive risk committee, designated risk owners, and regular Board reporting. Divisions were empowered to take preventive action. Its preparedness measures included seismic reinforcement, improved business-continuity planning, disaster simulations, and an earthquake response plan prioritizing human safety, prevention of secondary disasters, rapid recovery and continuity, and support for neighboring communities.

After the 2011 disaster, Nissan convened its Global Disaster Control Headquarters within 15 minutes and created a Recovery Committee. Its response emphasized global information sharing, global allocation of constrained components toward higher-margin vehicles, targeted production slowdowns, use of inventories and alternative sources, and decentralized decision-making. Regions sent representatives to Japan, production was adjusted around anticipated bottlenecks, vacations were rescheduled, and air freight was used to expedite critical parts.

Nissan recovered more effectively than Honda, which also faced supply-chain constraints, by continuing its localization strategy. In 2012 it announced plans to raise localized American production from roughly 70% to 90% by 2015 and reduce components imported from Japan to North America by 50% by the end of fiscal 2013. It also planned to improve component-level continuity planning, identify risks beyond first-tier suppliers, extend continuity planning to second- and third-tier suppliers, and rebuild a more robust supply chain.

Los Angeles subway construction has recovered numerous Ice Age fossils, including remains from rabbits, mammoths, camels, bison and horses. Paleontologist Ashley Leger monitors excavation sites and led the recovery of an intact juvenile mammoth skull during the Metro Purple Line extension. Unearthed after 15 hours, the rare skull retained both tusks and was named Hayden. It is being studied and displayed at the La Brea Tar Pits and Museum.

California environmental rules have required paleontologists at certain construction sites since work on Los Angeles’ first subway line began in the 1990s. Similar urban excavations elsewhere have uncovered fossils, ancient seashells and a wooden boat. Museum officials praised California’s efforts to protect archaeological and paleontological finds during development, while noting that expanding cities are likely to reveal more buried history.

Tesla, Inc. filed a Form 8-K on January 29, 2020, reporting financial results for the quarter and year ended December 31, 2019. Its Fourth Quarter and Full Year 2019 Update was posted online and filed as Exhibit 99.1.

The passage addresses two matters. First, it states that Cuba's provisional government will end once elections are held and a new government inaugurated peacefully and in order; the United States wishes Cuba only to prosper morally and materially and to preserve order so as to keep its independence. If elections become a farce and insurrectionary habits persist, continued independence would be impossible and the United States, having assumed sponsorship of Cuba's national career, would intervene again to secure orderly government, safety of life and property. The speaker urges the Cubans, for whom he expresses sympathy and regard, to weigh their responsibilities so their new government may run smoothly, free of both flagrant denial of right and insurrectionary disturbance.

Second, it reports the Third International Conference of American Republics, held at Rio de Janeiro from July 23 to August 29, as arranged by the Bureau of American Republics following the 1901–2 Mexico conference. The conference discussed trade, communication, and intercourse among American nations, reaching conclusions with substantial unanimity and completing its work within the six weeks allotted, showing greater practical efficiency than earlier conferences. The speaker thanks Brazil and Rio's people for their hospitality, notes that the Secretary of State served as honorary president, and describes his tour of Brazil, Uruguay, Argentina, Chile, Peru, Panama, and Colombia—omitting Paraguay, Bolivia, and Ecuador because of distance—carrying a message of peace and friendship that was warmly received by governments, press, professions, business, and the public.

Stocks fell Tuesday as healthcare companies and banks declined; Goldman Sachs, Johnson & Johnson and Cardinal Health posted sharp losses. Major indexes slipped, and the 10-year Treasury yield fell to 2.21%.

This study demonstrates that simple annealing can improve the thermoelectric performance of n-type Bi2Te3-based alloys by decoupling carrier and phonon transport. Bi2Te2.6Se0.4 was prepared by melting–hot pressing and annealed at 723 K. Te(Se) volatilization formed cation vacancies and other atomic-scale defects, lowering carrier density while increasing mobility and the power factor. These defects also strengthened phonon scattering and substantially reduced lattice thermal conductivity. After 100 h of annealing, carrier mobility reached 295.97 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹, room-temperature lattice thermal conductivity fell to 0.48 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, and the material achieved a peak ZT of 1.06 at 373 K, a room-temperature ZT of 0.78, and an average ZT of 0.99 over 300–423 K. The results position annealing as a scalable post-synthesis route for enhancing n-type Bi2Te3-based thermoelectrics for thermal-management and cooling applications.
NTT Docomo installed smartphone wipes in some Narita Airport restrooms until March 15. The wipes advertised its Wi-Fi service and translation app; studies found phones germier than toilet seats.

The Supreme Court allowed Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook to remain on the Fed’s Board of Governors while it considers whether President Donald Trump had legal cause to remove her over alleged mortgage fraud. The Court deferred Trump’s challenge to an injunction until oral argument in January 2026. Cook denies wrongdoing concerning mortgage applications and has not been charged.

The ruling allows the Fed to continue operating through year-end. Cook will vote at the FOMC’s October and December meetings, when officials have indicated quarter-point rate cuts, and possibly in January. Trump maintains he lawfully removed Cook for cause, while her lawyers say she should remain. The dispute is seen as a potential landmark case over the Fed’s independence from political interference.

The study develops a classification, mathematical model, and evaluation methods for the ISO 25023 “Accessibility” subcharacteristic, with emphasis on users with visual impairments. It addresses the lack of methodologies for determining key parameters and for weighting accessibility metrics.

“Accessibility” comprises “Accessibility for users with disabilities” and “Supported languages adequacy.” Four subproperties are defined: perceptiveness, operability, understandability, and localization. Their respective attributes are alternative text, color contrast, subtitles and audio descriptions; keyboard and structured navigation; clear instructions, input assistance, and correct input support; and availability of state, English, popular European, and other languages. Attribute and subproperty values are calculated through ratios or weighted formulas. Localization weights for a Ukrainian website are 0.6 for Ukrainian, 0.2 for English, 0.08 each for German and French, and 0.04 for other languages.

The proposed methodology was applied to the Vasyl Stefanyk Precarpathian National University website, with image descriptions and color contrast assessed using the Image Alt Checker and WCAG Contrast Checker. Expert analysis supplied weighting coefficients. The overall accessibility value was 0.67916, approximately 0.68, which was classified as “excellent” on a Fibonacci-based quality scale. The main weaknesses were the zero values for subtitles/audio descriptions and input assistance, low alternative-text coverage (0.15), and structured navigation (0.47). Color contrast (0.99), keyboard navigation (1), clear instructions (1), and correct input support (0.83) required little immediate improvement.

The resulting framework enables quantitative assessment and identification of deficient accessibility areas, supporting recommendations for more inclusive and standards-compliant web resources.

This protocol describes a systematic review addressing barriers, facilitators, implementation strategies, and adjunctive interventions for structural interventions supporting HIV evidence-based interventions in the United States. The review responds to persistent HIV disparities, unequal access to PrEP and antiretroviral therapy, and an implementation gap between developing interventions and applying them in practice.

The authors will examine implementation determinants, implementation strategies, and adjunctive interventions; identify literature gaps; and clarify distinctions among these categories. A May–July 2024 search of MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, Web of Science, Sociological Abstracts, Google, ProQuest sources, and a CDC structural-intervention compendium identified 8,098 records before deduplication. Eligible studies will focus on HIV, be at least 50% U.S.-based, use implementation or hybrid implementation-effectiveness designs, and report implementation outcomes or structural interventions addressing social determinants.

Natural-language-processing screening classified 8,092 articles, after which trained reviewers will conduct duplicate title/abstract and full-text screening with independent review and consensus resolution. Data will be extracted in COVIDENCE and coded for determinants, strategies, and adjunctive interventions. Determinants will be coded in MaxQDA using CFIR 2.0 and classified by valence, level, and structural-intervention type. Strategies will be mapped to ERIC, while adjunctive interventions will be mapped to TDF and COM-B. Analyses will quantify and stratify findings by population, setting, intervention, outcomes, study design, equity focus, and specification, supplemented by NLP-based narrative synthesis.

Results will be disseminated through two primary papers, additional population- or intervention-specific manuscripts, conferences, and an HIV implementation-science dashboard. At publication, title/abstract review was underway, with full-text review and extraction planned for January 2025 and analyses for June 2025–June 2026.

The Supreme Court agreed to hear five cases in its 2025–26 term, including a challenge to Hawaii’s 2023 law barring concealed-carry permit holders from bringing handguns onto private property open to the public without the owner’s explicit permission. The Ninth Circuit upheld the law and related bans on guns in “sensitive places.” Challengers argue the Second Amendment applies and that the appeals court improperly relied on post-Reconstruction-era laws; the Trump administration urged the justices to review the case.

The Court also granted cases concerning whether Cuban state-owned entities and cruise lines can be sued over property confiscated by Cuba under the 1996 Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity Act and whether the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act bars those suits. Other cases address a Michigan estate’s claim that a foreclosed home was sold below fair market value in violation of the Fifth and Eighth Amendments, and whether federal motor-carrier law preempts state negligence claims against brokers while preserving states’ safety authority.

Schaeffler created the 1,180-hp 4ePerformance electric Audi RS3 using four Formula E motors, all-wheel drive, torque vectoring and a 64-kWh battery pack. It uses RS3 LMS race-car bodywork and reaches 124 mph in seven seconds. Audi is prioritizing the e-tron SUV and additional electric models as Formula E expands, with Mercedes-Benz, Porsche and Nissan joining or replacing existing entrants.

This cross-sectional study examined relationships among self- and other-oriented mentalization, attachment, and personality pathology within the DSM-5 Alternative Model of Personality Disorders (AMPD). Participants included 109 adults from psychiatric inpatient and community/university samples; 54% met criteria for a personality disorder. Mentalization was assessed separately for self-related uncertainty and four styles of other-oriented mentalizing: correct, hypermentalizing, undermentalizing, and nonmentalizing.

Self-mentalizing deficits were the strongest and most consistent predictors of impaired self- and interpersonal functioning and all five Criterion B traits, including Negative Affectivity, Detachment, Antagonism, Disinhibition, and Psychoticism. Correct other-mentalizing uniquely predicted fewer interpersonal functioning impairments, while other mentalizing styles generally had limited independent predictive effects. The regression models explained 18%–55% of outcome variance.

Attachment anxiety and avoidance were associated with Criterion A impairment, while anxiety was associated with all Criterion B traits and avoidance primarily with Detachment. Correct other-mentalizing weakened the relationship between attachment anxiety and interpersonal impairment, whereas hypermentalizing strengthened it. Self-mentalizing moderated the links between attachment anxiety, Negative Affectivity, and Detachment. For attachment avoidance and Detachment, correct other-mentalizing weakened the relationship, while undermentalizing and nonmentalizing strengthened it.

The findings suggest that strengthening self-mentalizing may be a foundational therapeutic target, while other-mentalizing may be particularly relevant to interpersonal functioning and Detachment. Intervention priorities may therefore vary with attachment style. Limitations include the cross-sectional design, small and heterogeneous sample, unassessed comorbid disorders, differing assessment methods, and limited generalizability, requiring longitudinal and larger-sample replication.

The passage urges that remaining public lands be reserved for actual settlers and home builders, while ending large-scale acquisition and illegal fencing of public domain. The paper characterizes the thermal performance of Mod-Cam, the commissioning receiver and single-module precursor for the FYST Prime-Cam instrument, which will use large arrays of superconducting microwave kinetic inductance detectors (KIDs). Measurements focused on the 280 GHz module’s aluminum (Al) and titanium-nitride (TiN) arrays. In the cold-load configuration, the detector stage was held at 100 mK for eight hours, yielding an RMS temperature fluctuation of \(3.2\times10^{-5}\) K. Thermal responsivity was measured by sweeping the bath temperature from 96 to 105 mK and tracking resonator frequency shifts. Median responsivities were \(1.995\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}\) for 2,409 Al detectors and \(-6.081\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}\) for 1,886 TiN detectors. TiN showed the larger responsivity magnitude and opposite sign to Al, consistent with their differing kinetic-inductance fractions, superconducting gap energies, and defect effects.

Using measured optical responsivities and assumed FYST background loads of 5–9 pW, thermally induced equivalent optical power fluctuations were 0.20–0.27 fW for Al and 0.11–0.13 fW for TiN. At 5 pW, these correspond to fractional contributions of only 0.0040% and 0.0023%, respectively. The results validate Mod-Cam’s cryogenic design and thermal-control system and indicate that thermal fluctuations will not limit FYST sensitivity. Future work will repeat the characterization under direct optical loading from a cryogenic blackbody source.

Erik Demaine introduces MIT 6.851 Advanced Data Structures, covering temporal data structures, geometry, dynamic optimality, memory hierarchies, hashing, integer structures, dynamic graphs, strings, and succinct data structures. Course requirements include weekly problem sets and lecture scribing, with optional open-problem sessions.

The lecture uses a pointer-machine model: data resides in nodes with a constant number of fields, operations create and access nodes, and pointers are followed from a fixed root. Persistence means preserving all versions of a data structure while updates produce new versions. Four levels are described: partial persistence allows only the latest version to be updated; full persistence allows any version to be updated, forming a version tree; confluent persistence allows versions to be combined, forming a DAG; and functional data structures prohibit modifying existing nodes, providing the strongest form of persistence.

Any pointer-machine structure with constant numbers of incoming and outgoing pointers per node can be transformed into a partially or fully persistent structure with constant multiplicative time overhead and constant additional space per modification, amortized over operations. For partial persistence, each node stores modification records identifying the version, field, and new value. Reads inspect these records. When a node’s modification capacity is exhausted, a replacement node is created and current pointers are redirected recursively. Back pointers are maintained only for the latest version. A potential function based on modification counts establishes constant amortized costs. This result can be deamortized to give a constant worst-case slowdown for partial persistence; the corresponding worst-case result for full persistence was described as open.

Full persistence additionally represents versions as a tree, which is linearized using an order-maintenance data structure. Each version has beginning and ending markers, allowing ancestor relationships to be tested in constant time. Back pointers must be maintained across all versions. When a node overflows, its modification tree is split into roughly balanced parts, modifications are applied to the resulting nodes, and pointers are redirected recursively. A potential function based on unused modification slots again yields constant amortized overhead.

Confluent persistence is harder because version DAGs cannot be linearized as easily as trees and combining versions can double a structure’s size, potentially producing exponential growth after \(u\) operations. A general result introduces a version’s “effective depth” and gives logarithmic time and space overhead, which can still be linear in the number of updates when effective depth is large. Corresponding lower bounds tie required space and update time to effective depth. Under a restriction that combined versions share no nodes, logarithmic overhead is possible; the discussion uses link-cut trees and fractional cascading. Whether constant overhead is possible for general confluent persistence remains an open question.

Functional structures use path copying rather than modifying existing nodes. Balanced search trees can support updates in \(O(\log n)\) time, functional deques support constant-time operations and concatenation, and tries can provide \(O(\log n)\) search using constant-time deque operations. Constant-time functional split and concatenation remains an open problem. Versioned trees used in systems such as Subversion can represent confluent version DAGs with bounds logarithmic in node degree, and improved to logarithmic-logarithmic degree bounds using additional techniques. The best known separation between fully functional and ordinary data structures is a factor of \(O(\log n)\).

The Missouri Supreme Court will weigh whether the Missouri Human Rights Act prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, terms absent from the statute; lower courts are split.

In R.M.A v. Blue Springs R-IV School District, a transgender teen sued after his district barred him from the boys' locker room, claiming sex discrimination. His lawyers argued gender identity is a protected gender-related trait; the district said the statute omits it and that school districts aren't "people" under the Act. Dismissed in 2016, the case was affirmed on appeal in July 2017.

In Lampley and Frost v. Missouri Commission on Human Rights, gay employee Harold Lampley alleged mistreatment for failing to appear stereotypically masculine, and colleague Rene Frost alleged discrimination and retaliation over their friendship. The commission denied both claims, an appeals court disagreed in October 2017, and the state appealed, arguing the claim concerns sexual orientation, not sex.

Finder.com's annual America's Biggest Money Mistakes survey found 78.3% of Americans have made a financial mistake in their lifetime. The most common error was overspending on fun activities such as shopping, vacations and dining out (64%), reported more often by women (66.2%) than men (58%). Men more frequently regretted bad investments (24.5% vs. 11.4% of women) and excessive gambling (14.7% vs. 6.3%), while women more often regretted letting a partner control family finances. Dropping out of college was the second-most cited regret for both sexes (about 20%); Bureau of Labor Statistics data show dropouts earn a median $774 weekly versus $907 for all workers and $1,173 for bachelor's degree holders, with higher unemployment (4.0% vs. 2.5%). Generationally, millennials and Gen X-ers admitted mistakes at similar rates (78.9% vs. 79.1%), baby boomers lowest (74.1%); millennials overspent most (70.8%) while boomers most regretted bad investments (26.6%). Other regrets included overpaying for weddings, online scams, and having children (over $233,000 to raise per USDA estimates).
Six-year-olds worked harder and focused more on repetitive tasks when pretending to be Batman or Dora the Explorer; those focused on themselves took frequent breaks.

Denmark’s Systemic Risk Council urged tighter mortgage rules for highly indebted households, especially in Copenhagen and Aarhus, to protect financial stability. It recommended restricting most interest-only or variable-rate loans when debt exceeds 400% of pretax income, with exemptions limited to about 15% of loans. The government must respond within three months and explain any refusal. Established after the 2008 crisis, the council noted that booming urban property markets and rising household debt warrant action; Denmark’s covered bond market is worth about 2.8 trillion Danish crowns ($402 billion).

The paper proposes an active-learning queue-prioritization algorithm for scientific workflows in which generative AI produces many novel but potentially nonsensical candidates. An XGBoost surrogate model predicts expensive simulation scores and uncertainty; a custom acquisition function combines these predictions with cheaper criteria to reorder candidates before evaluation. The surrogate is retrained as simulation results accumulate. This filtering reduces wasted computation and prevents unstable candidates from being reused to fine-tune the generative model, thereby mitigating model decay.

The method is demonstrated on 1,000 candidate metal-organic frameworks for carbon capture. A fine-tuned DiffLinker model generates organic linkers for zinc-based cubic MOFs. Candidate viability is assessed using molecular-dynamics-simulated internal strain, SAScore-based synthesizability, and similarity to HMOF linkers. With active learning, the workflow produced an average of 604 high-performing candidates versus 281 without prioritization, with less than 1% added computational overhead.

Reordering experiments found that exploitation prioritized stable MOFs quickly but produced less accurate stability predictions, while exploration improved model accuracy but identified fewer stable MOFs. A weak exploration–exploitation balance achieved both low prediction error and a high number of stable structures. Active learning also mitigated degradation caused by fine-tuning DiffLinker on overly broad sets of top-ranked linkers. Multi-objective acquisition functions showed that prioritizing synthesizability alone slightly improved that metric while sharply reducing stable discoveries, whereas prioritizing HMOF similarity increased stability without ensuring experimental viability. Overall, combining generative models with active-learning prioritization improves the efficiency, diversity, stability, and predictive modeling of MOF discovery.

Professor Noelle Selin discusses mercury as a global environmental and supply-chain issue, focusing on the 2013 Minamata Convention. Atmospheric mercury travels across national borders, mixes globally, and deposits into ecosystems, where it converts into neurotoxic methylmercury and accumulates in food chains. The resulting neurological and cardiovascular risks affect pregnant women, children, and the general population, while artisanal and small-scale gold mining exposes miners and nearby communities. Major sources include coal combustion, gold mining, industrial processes, product use, waste, and cremation.

Selin explains that the 2002 UN global mercury assessment called for international action. The United States initially favored voluntary programs, while the European Union promoted a binding treaty. Changing national policies, increased support from developing countries, and the Obama administration’s renewed U.S. mercury regulation enabled negotiations to begin in 2009. Following five negotiating sessions, countries signed the Minamata Convention in October 2013. Strong U.S. and EU domestic laws influenced the agreement, which reflects a lowest-common-denominator approach that may require less-expensive controls than those imposed in Europe or the United States.

The convention addresses mercury across its full life cycle, including emissions, products, international trade, and waste. Regulated products and processes include thermometers, electrical switches, batteries, fluorescent lamps, dental amalgam, chlor-alkali production, and vinyl chloride production. Negotiators considered a blanket product ban with exceptions but instead developed lists of products to be phased out or phased down, along with exemptions. Many decisions resulted from negotiation among countries rather than detailed product-by-product scientific analysis. Exemptions included mercury preservatives in vaccines because they allow vaccines to be used where refrigeration is unavailable. Dental amalgam was designated for phase-down without a fixed deadline, while 2020 became a compromise date for several product phaseouts.

Mercury trade is restricted to exempted uses, and mercury waste is addressed partly through coordination with the Basel Convention. Because mercury is an element that cannot be destroyed, contaminated materials are encapsulated and isolated rather than converted into harmless substances.

Artisanal and small-scale gold mining illustrates the treaty’s supply-chain challenges. Mercury may enter informal markets through dental practices and dealers, then be used to form gold amalgams. Mercury-bearing waste is often discharged locally, and amalgam is burned to recover gold, releasing mercury unless safer methods such as retorts are used. The convention does not prohibit artisanal mining because it supports many livelihoods; instead, it promotes regulation, formalization, safer technologies, and capacity building.

Selin also describes links with the Stockholm, Rotterdam, and Basel conventions, the Global Environment Facility, the World Health Organization, the International Labour Organization, and the Food and Agriculture Organization. International environmental treaties have limited enforcement, relying instead on reporting, diplomatic pressure, funding, and capacity-building assistance.

For companies, participation in negotiations was generally limited to observer status, advocacy, and informal lobbying. Firms promoted mercury-free technologies, protected product interests, and exchanged information about best practices. Selin argues that European chemical regulations increasingly set emerging global standards, while many developing countries adopt them because of limited technical capacity and access to equipment. The treaty is expected mainly to stabilize mercury levels unless later negotiations strengthen emissions controls, although its legal and political signal may already influence corporate behavior. The lecture concludes with course planning for project reviews, strategy discussions, and company case studies.

Jim Cramer reversed his bullish view on Snap, citing the unpopular app redesign, celebrity backlash and risk that user engagement and advertising could decline. He considers the stock too expensive and recommends waiting, though he would buy at an attractive price. Snap reports first-quarter results May 1.

Researchers led by Dr. Shinichi Furuya of the NeuroPiano Institute and Sony Computer Science Laboratories scientifically demonstrated that pianists can alter piano timbre through precise touch and key movements. Their non-contact Hackkey system measured all 88 keys at 1,000 frames per second and 0.01-millimeter spatial resolution while 20 renowned pianists produced contrasting timbres. In a listening experiment, 40 participants—including pianists and people without musical experience—consistently perceived the intended timbral differences, even when volume and tempo were controlled; pianist listeners showed greater sensitivity.

A linear mixed-effects model identified specific movement features associated with timbral variation, including acceleration during escapement and deviations in hand synchronization. Experiments varying only these features produced distinguishable timbres, providing causal evidence linking key movement to sound. Published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the findings establish touch-based timbre manipulation as a trainable motor skill rather than a metaphor. The research may support evidence-based music instruction, recommendation systems for learners, and further study of sensory-motor integration, with potential applications in neuroscience, rehabilitation, skill transfer, and human-interface design.

The passage surveys container and distributed-system patterns, emphasizing modularity, separation of concerns, portability, reliability, and independent scaling. Ambassadors isolate applications from environment-specific service discovery, connection brokering, and request splitting, while adapters normalize heterogeneous monitoring, logging, and health-check interfaces without modifying third-party containers. Examples use nginx for traffic experiments, Prometheus exporters for monitoring, Fluentd plugins for log normalization, and adapter containers for database health checks.

Microservices divide applications into independently developed and scaled components connected through APIs, improving agility and scalability but complicating debugging and architecture. Replicated load-balanced services provide redundancy and availability; readiness probes identify prepared instances, session tracking uses IP or application-level hashing, caching layers improve latency and capacity, rate limiting limits abuse, and nginx provides SSL termination. Kubernetes Deployments and Services implement these layers.

Sharded services partition data among shards selected by deterministic, uniform hashing. Appropriate shard keys improve cache reuse, while consistent hashing limits remapping during resizing. Replicating individual shards improves resilience, permits rolling upgrades, and allows hot shards to scale independently. Ambassadors and shared routing services offer different complexity, latency, and bandwidth trade-offs.

Scatter/gather distributes computation across all leaves for parallel processing, with the root combining partial results. Sharded leaves extend data capacity, but coordination overhead and stragglers can reduce latency and availability gains; replicated shards mitigate failures.

Function-as-a-service provides event-driven, stateless, automatically scaled execution with simplified deployment but introduces operational complexity, unsuitable fit for some long-running or memory-intensive workloads, and unfavorable sustained-request economics. A FaaS decorator pattern can transform requests or responses, including adding defaults before API processing.

KaviKrishna describes a participatory action research program combining an Indigenous Knowledge System (IKS), community-based participatory research (CBPR), telemedicine, clinical care, and laboratory research for tuberculosis in rural Assam, India. Its Indigenous Kamarupa Information Network uses local temple complexes, community volunteers, home visits, focused discussions, nutrition support, and patient monitoring for screening, contact tracing, follow-up, and relapse or multidrug-resistant TB detection. Since 2010, this network screened 300 pulmonary TB cases and 500 suspected cases; a supplementary dataset contains follow-up information for 210 patients.

Clinical cohorts included treated Idu-Mishmi patients studied for TB dormancy and 250 patients recruited across northeast India, including MDR-TB cases. Sputum, blood, and bone-marrow samples undergo BSL-3 culture, drug-susceptibility testing, PCR, MIRU-VNTR/spoligotyping, and pilot whole-genome sequencing with bioinformatics analysis. The laboratory identified non-tuberculous mycobacteria in some samples initially suspected of pulmonary TB and detected Beijing, CAS/CAS1-Delhi, and orphan lineages. Preliminary sequencing identified rpoB and rpoC mutations in material recovered from circulating or bone-marrow mesenchymal stem cells in some sputum-negative, post-treatment relapsed cases, suggesting a possible stem-cell niche role in MDR evolution.

The stem-cell studies use immunomagnetic cell sorting, quantitative PCR, and a nonreplicating MTB mouse model. The researchers report viable dormant MTB in mesenchymal stem-cell populations from the lungs and bone marrow, granuloma formation after transfer of infected cells, and MTB reactivation following coronavirus-induced oxidative stress, enhanced stemness, HIF-2α elevation, and p53 suppression. Clinical and animal findings are described as supporting further investigation of dormant MTB and host-pathogen interactions.

Additional assays include an Alamar Blue microplate method for minimum inhibitory concentrations, a most-probable-number minimum-duration-of-killing assay, a modified MPN assay for viable but nonculturable MTB, and bacterial live/dead staining. Reported MDK99.99 values were 4 µg/mL for two days with rifampicin and 15 µg/mL for four days with ursolic acid against H37Ra. The authors propose that combining community participation, traditional communication networks, clinical monitoring, molecular surveillance, and laboratory research could support locally tailored TB control, patient-specific treatment, and epidemiological monitoring. Whole-genome sequencing data are available through NCBI accession PRJNA1054003.

This final session of MIT OpenCourseWare course 23 (Digital ID), led by Gary Gensler, was the last "use case day," with students presenting papers on trade finance, supply chain management, and identity and access management. Gensler praised the papers, noted that some leaned "minimalist" while others leaned "maximalist," and observed that blockchain technology may have genuine use cases alongside hype, with more viable applications than tokens.

On supply chain management, a student with four to five years in supply chain sustainability described the push for traceability and transparency (referencing De Beers), driven by concerns about conflict minerals and water stress. Most companies rely on annual supplier self-assessments that cannot be verified, so customers take supplier claims — such as no child labor — at face value; blockchain was presented as a way to make such claims verifiable. Gensler pressed her on whether she had moved past "rock bottom minimalist" thinking, and she said only marginally.

Much of the session addressed what identity is. Participants described it as contextual (date of birth, nationality, face), as inherent and unique to the individual, and as something society constructs and verifies. Gensler noted that attributes can be shared (identical twins) while identity remains unique, and recounted anecdotes about face recognition unlocking an iPhone, identical twin cousins opening each other's phones, and Facebook tagging his twin brother. One student proposed a practical definition: hash each person to produce a unique number (such as via iris or retina scan), the hash being collision-resistant and usable for KYC, credit cards, and detecting new customers. Limitations were noted, including replicable biometrics, cloned identities, and the dependence of hashing on biometric attributes.

Gensler organized identity into attribute (retina, age, address, citizenship), claim (name, age, citizenship, bank account), credential (driver's license, ID card, passport), and attestation (third-party verification). He traced credential history (16th-century English passports; permitting systems 100–150 years old, paper-based, with photographs only from the early 20th century) and distinguished authentication (proving a claim) from authorization (permitting an action), using the bar-age-check example. The ecosystem includes users, service providers, and identity providers (such as states issuing birth and marriage certificates), plus attribute authorities and certificate authorities.

A student described man-in-the-middle attacks against fake websites and how certificate authorities signing website public keys, combined with digital signatures over content (the New York Times example), protect passwords. Gensler noted that public-key cryptography predates Bitcoin by roughly 12 years and secured the internet via TLS/SSL, that there are more than 100 certificate authorities, and that one is involved roughly 100 billion times a day; the browser performs this at the protocol level, as indicated by the lock icon. Consensus, not hashing, was identified as the core obstacle to decentralizing public key infrastructure: everyone must agree which key belongs to Facebook.

Pain points discussed included privacy and security, identity theft, forged credentials, keeping identity attributes updated, and protecting personally identifiable information under laws such as GDPR. Gensler reported about 20% of the room had replaced a credit card in 2018 due to compromise; fraud runs roughly 15–18 basis points against Visa's ~270-plus basis point interchange, of which the issuing bank bears about 200. As chair of Maryland's Financial Consumer Protection Commission, he described credit unions' argument that banks bear the cost of merchants' breaches and the state's live debate over imposing cybersecurity duties on non-financial firms, noting merchant opposition and the commission's advisory role. Major breaches cited included Marriott, Equifax, Facebook (50 million), Wells Fargo (3 million), and India's 1.1 billion Aadhaar IDs.

State identity systems discussed were Estonia's e-identity (since 2002, X-Road software, not blockchain, with e-health records, population ~1.3 million) and India's Aadhaar (12-digit ID with fingerprint and iris biometrics, the fastest system to reach one billion users, optional, with courts in 2018 rejecting mandatory linkage to welfare benefits). Aadhaar's problems included hacks, errors that left people unrecognized and halted assistance, and reported suicides and deaths, prompting public debate over its net benefit.

Self-sovereign identity was defined as people and entities controlling their identities more than currently, direct access without intermediaries, portability of identity attributes, and broad usability and interoperability. Gensler stressed it does not rely on blockchain and echoes a 19th-century practice of entering a store without documents and paying with coins. A student questioned whether it requires a decentralized monetary system, since banks and platforms require waiver of anonymity; Gensler conceded that firms like Facebook and Google might cut off users and noted the concept has not been widely adopted.

Potential blockchain benefits cited were preventing identity theft and impersonation, lowering verification costs and fraud, tracing provenance, resisting censorship, and improving privacy. Challenges included replicating personally identifiable information across all nodes, immutability conflicting with GDPR's right to erasure, changing attributes such as citizenship requiring appended updates (as with Bitcoin ownership), and loss or theft of a private key meaning loss of identity, suggesting multiple biometrics or exception procedures. Gensler judged these challenges surmountable.

Gensler noted ICO-based efforts such as Civic Secure Identity, Existence IC, and Sovrin (none yet operational, with doubts about ICOs), Bitnation's voluntary citizenship and passport (no UN, WTO, or geographic basis), the Decentralized Identity Foundation's decentralized ID program, Rebooting Web-of-Trust events and papers, and W3C digital ID standards work. He identified the U.S. Social Security number — initially a retirement program identifier, now tied to the Patriot Act, KYC/AML, banking, and tax systems — as a public-policy obstacle private systems cannot fix, since changing it would require banks and insurers to change operations. Describing self-sovereign identity platform architectures such as Bits on Blocks, where individuals hold their attributes and choose when to release them, he polled the class: about a quarter planned to receive a blockchain-backed MIT diploma, which he called a novelty. The course concludes Tuesday with a wrap-up on blockchain's business applications and separating hype from reality.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Will Rosenzweig of the Southern District of Florida was fired by email while off work observing Rosh Hashanah, after conservatives published past blog posts attributed to him criticizing President Donald Trump during his first term. Commentator Natalie Winters cited alleged posts from his private "Hosts of Error" blog, including claims that Trump was "mentually unfit" and "an institutional terrorist." Rosenzweig reportedly wrote the posts while an associate at Kobre & Kim and joined the U.S. attorney's office in September 2020, working on complex economic crimes cases; he did not respond to a request for comment. The Miami Herald reported he is the latest of dozens of federal prosecutors fired by Trump's Justice Department who were believed to be at odds with the president or his agenda. Three other Southern District of Florida prosecutors who previously worked with former special counsel Jack Smith — Brooke C. Watson, Michael Thakur and Anne McNamara — have also been fired. In his first public remarks since leaving the DOJ, Smith expressed dismay at the dismissal of career public servants and attacks on the rule of law, warning that political opponents and critics are targeted to silence them. Days after his speech, U.S. Attorney Erik S. Siebert of the Eastern District of Virginia left his position after Trump pressured him to indict New York Attorney General Letitia James and former FBI Director James Comey.

Canadian and U.S. indexes fell Friday. The TSX composite dropped 81.78 points to 15,694.52, and the Canadian dollar rose to 79.70 cents U.S.; the TSX closes Monday Oct. 9 for Thanksgiving. Wall Street declines followed a report that U.S. nonfarm payrolls fell 33,000 in September, a first drop in seven years, as Hurricanes Harvey and Irma slowed hiring. Wages rose 0.5%, lifting the dollar to a 12-week high. The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq all fell, dragged down by Costco, energy and technology losses.
