The paper examines collective academic exile and four higher education projects (HEPs) established or relocated outside Russia following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine and increased repression of academics. It frames these initiatives as “education in emergencies” and explores their self-conceptions, relationship with the homeland, and roles in conflict and post-conflict contexts.

In Russia, monitoring of international academic collaboration, foreign-funding restrictions, “foreign agent” designation, ideological prosecution, censorship, and layoffs drove thousands of academics abroad. Some emigrated individually, while others relocated entire institutions or re-established them with former colleagues. These projects range from autonomous online courses to accredited, host-university-based programs. They share a connection to Russia through Russian-language instruction and participation by Russian students, and they operate as transnational networks sharing faculty across borders.

The study uses phenomenological semi-structured interviews with project leaders and discourse analysis of public materials. Conversational discourse analysis and thematic analysis, triangulated through ATLAS.ti, examine how project leaders construct their missions and identities. Sources are anonymized to protect participants from possible persecution.

The projects conceptualize themselves in three connected ways. First, they serve as “safe havens,” offering fleeing scholars positions, funding, scholarships, visa assistance, continuing Russian-language higher education, intellectual freedom, solidarity, and continuity of professional identities. They also function as diasporic knowledge hubs that help members navigate integration into foreign academic systems.

Second, they seek to preserve and reconceptualize Russian academic heritages, including schools of thought, liberal arts education, critical thinking, research traditions, and the Russian language. International collaboration is used to reassess inherited practices and understand the war. However, the paper finds this reconceptualization limited and inconsistent; hierarchical teaching, inherited assumptions, colonial attitudes, and exclusions remain insufficiently examined.

Third, the projects turn anticipation of return into active, pragmatic “hope-making praxis.” Although return remains uncertain, organizers pursue feasible educational and social transformation in exile and envision a democratic, educated future for Russia. The paper concludes that HEPs combine sanctuary, preservation, and active hope while calling for further research into their inherited biases, international influences, mission-practice gaps, and changing roles over time.

This medRxiv preprint reports a Markov cohort model evaluating whether a RATIONS-style nutritional supplementation program would be cost-effective for reducing tuberculosis (TB) incidence and mortality among household contacts (HHCs) of persons with TB (PWTB) in India. Background: TB caused 10.6 million cases and 1.3 million deaths in 2022; undernutrition is the leading TB risk factor, accounting for at least 2.2 million cases, and undernourished individuals with TB face higher risks of death, treatment failure, and relapse. The RATIONS trial (>10,000 HHCs in eastern India) provided a food basket costing $13/month for 6 months and reported a 40% reduction in TB incidence over two years plus ~35% lower mortality in PWTB who received nutritional support.

Methods: The model, built in TreeAge Pro v22.2.0, followed a cohort of 100,000 HIV-negative HHCs over their lifetimes using 6-month time steps across health states (TB development, cure, post-treatment phases, death). The intervention provided HHCs a daily multi-micronutrient tablet, rice, and lentils (23g protein, 750 kcal/day) for 6 months, and PWTB a supplement (1,200 kcal, 52g protein) during treatment. Parameters came from RATIONS, WHO, and other published sources; outcomes were TB incidence, deaths, DALYs, and costs, discounted at 3%, with government and societal perspectives, an India-specific willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold of US$550 per DALY (23% of per-capita GDP), and deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity analyses.

Results: Per 100,000 HHCs, the intervention produced lower lifetime TB incidence (6,749 vs 7,718; RR 0.87), lower TB mortality (906 vs 1,529; RR 0.59), and 13,775 DALYs averted. Government costs were $3.93 million vs $0.76 million; societal costs $7.76 million vs $5.24 million. ICERs were $229 per DALY averted (healthcare perspective) and $184 (societal), both below the WTP threshold. Results were most sensitive to supplement cost and TB incidence risk ratio; the intervention remained cost-effective for supplement costs under $75 (one-way), under $56/$59 (two-way, government/societal), and was favored in 99.95% and 99.97% of probabilistic simulations at $550.

Discussion: Authors note the intervention was modeled in a high-deprivation setting and that excluding relapse, disengagement, transmission, pre-diagnosis costs, drug-resistant TB, and externalities suggests conservative estimates. They conclude RATIONS-style nutritional support is cost-effective where TB and undernutrition burdens are high and call for operational and economic research alongside implementation.

The speaker says a disputed goal is inconclusive on video and that Toronto’s referees should be trusted, while tough bounces are difficult to control. Despite poor stats in one game, he praises a player’s playoff performance, Milwaukee’s organization, and its treatment of players.

The speaker says his team remains alive in the playoffs and seeks greater offensive success by driving defensemen to the net. They hope to build on a late third-period win, play hard against a Western Conference opponent, and take the playoffs one game at a time.

This MIT OpenCourseWare lecture, given by a professor, introduces the open problem of "dynamic optimality" for binary search trees: whether there is a single binary search tree that performs as well as every other binary search tree on every access sequence. The question dates to the 1980s and remains an active area of research.

**Model.** The binary search tree is treated as a restricted pointer machine: data is stored as keys in the tree; one may follow left, right, and parent pointers in constant time, and may rotate a node with its parent (the child moves above the parent, preserving the BST property). Only searches are considered, assumed successful, with no insertions or deletions. The cost of a BST algorithm is essentially the number of nodes touched during searches.

**Worst case vs. amortized case.** An adversary argument shows that Ω(log n) time is required in the worst case, since a binary tree holding n items must have depth at least log n. Dynamic optimality, however, asks whether every access sequence can be served well — not just the worst one — with the cost determined per sequence. Several bounds are introduced: the *sequential access property* (in-order access in constant amortized time, achievable by some trees, for example by using rotations to simulate a linked list); the *dynamic finger property* (log k amortized per operation when the key distance between consecutive accesses is k, achievable in a BST but difficult; level-linked trees achieve it easily); the *entropy bound* (if a key is accessed a fraction p_k of the time, pay about log(1/p_k) per operation; this is the optimum when rotations are forbidden, i.e., the static optimum); and the *working set property* (pay the log of the number of distinct keys accessed since that key was last accessed, implying the entropy bound). The working set and dynamic finger properties are described as near-duals; dynamic finger implies sequential access. A *unified property*, introduced in 2001, combines dynamic finger and working set, charging the log of the sum of the spatial distance and temporal distance to the nearest recently accessed key; it is achievable by a pointer machine, but it is unknown whether any BST achieves it, the best known BST bound being the unified bound plus log log n.

**Dynamic optimality.** The goal is a BST algorithm whose total (amortized) cost on any sequence is within a constant factor of the offline optimum, where the optimum ranges over all BST algorithms, including ones customized to the sequence. Whether this is possible is open, as are versions restricted to online algorithms or to pointer machines. The lecturer notes that log log n competitiveness is known, and that any balanced BST is log n competitive.

**Splay trees.** Splay trees are introduced as self-adjusting trees: after locating x, x is splayed to the root by repeated two-rotation steps (rotate the parent then x in the "zig-zig" case, x then the parent in the "zig-zag" case). They cost at most log n amortized per operation, while the simpler "move to root" algorithm can cost √n per operation. Splay trees satisfy the sequential access property (Tarjan, 1985), the working set and entropy properties (original paper), and the dynamic finger property (proved over 100 pages in two papers). Whether splay trees satisfy the unified property or are dynamically optimal remains unknown.

**Geometric view.** Accesses are plotted as points, with key order on one axis and time on the other. The nodes touched by a BST execution form a point set that is *arborally satisfied*: every rectangle spanned by two points not on a common horizontal or vertical line must contain another point. The lecturer proves both directions of this characterization. Forward: any BST execution is arborally satisfied, argued via the lowest common ancestor of two accessed keys and the rotations that must occur between two access times. Reverse: from an arborally satisfied point set one can build a BST using treaps — simultaneously a binary search tree on the keys and a min-heap on next access time — by rearranging, via rotations, only the touched nodes (which form a connected subtree containing the root), relying on the fact that any two trees on the same keys are convertible by a linear number of rotations.

**Geometric reformulation and greedy algorithm.** Minimizing the cost of a BST becomes the problem of adding the fewest points to an access point set so that it becomes arborally satisfied. Its complexity is unknown (possibly NP-hard), no constant-factor approximation is known, and the best known is a log log n approximation. A greedy algorithm adds points bottom-up in time order, satisfying unsatisfied rectangles at the current time step. In tree terms this is equivalent to following the search path and rearranging those nodes into a local treap by next access time — apparently the obvious offline optimum, though unproven.

**Online version.** Because the greedy rule only inspects the past, it can be made online. The construction uses *split trees*: BSTs supporting removal of a node to the root together with splitting the remainder into two parts in constant amortized time, achievable with a balanced BST and a parallel search that splits in order log(min(n1, n2)) time, with the halves interleaved into a BST. This yields a tree of split trees that simulates the offline greedy treap via lazy evaluation. The lecture closes by noting that lower bounds, to be covered in the next class, nearly but not quite prove the greedy algorithm optimal.

A premature newborn from a faith-healing church family died from complications of prematurity without immediate medical attention; her twin survived after receiving care. Deputies are investigating, but no one has been charged.

A finite-temperature CFT on flat space is described by a black hole with a planar horizon, while a CFT on a sphere is described by global AdS. On the sphere, the radius \(R\) introduces a scale, so physics depends on the dimensionless product \(RT\); thus low- and high-temperature regimes are distinct.

The spherical theory admits three gravitational saddle points: thermal AdS, a large AdS black hole, and a small AdS black hole. Above a minimum temperature, the two black holes can have the same temperature but different horizon radii and entropies. Their free energies are determined by renormalized Euclidean actions, with the lowest free energy dominating the partition function. The small black hole is never stable because it lacks positive specific heat. Thermal AdS dominates below a critical temperature \(T_c=2\pi R/(d-1)\), while the large black hole dominates above it. This Hawking–Page transition is first order: the free energy is continuous, but its first derivative is discontinuous in the large-\(N\) limit. The high-temperature spherical limit corresponds to the flat-space theory and a planar-horizon black hole.

A field-theory toy model uses two matrices of \(N^2\) harmonic oscillators with an \(SU(N)\)-singlet constraint. Low-energy states have order-one degeneracy, whereas states with energy of order \(N^2\) have exponentially large degeneracy. At high temperature, this entropy overwhelms thermal suppression, causing the same phase transition. The mechanism depends primarily on large-\(N\) degeneracies rather than microscopic details or interactions.

Faviola Dadis alleged that Steven Seagal sexually assaulted her during a 2002 casting session in a Beverly Hills hotel room. The 33-year-old neuroscience doctoral candidate reported the assault to police, and Los Angeles prosecutors are reviewing her case. Seagal’s attorney did not immediately respond.

Dadis said the encounter caused depression, anxiety, PTSD, and difficulty trusting men. She delayed reporting because she feared being blacklisted in entertainment and cited recent misconduct reports and Portia de Rossi’s allegation in coming forward. At the news conference, she appeared with attorney Lisa Bloom and Regina Simons, who alleged Seagal assaulted her in 1995. Jenny McCarthy has also alleged harassment by Seagal. Seagal denied the allegations made by other actresses, and Bloom said no lawsuits were immediately planned.

Top-seeded Bemidji won the Region 10C title after building a 5-0 lead and holding off Crookston. Ben Thoma pitched seven innings for the win, striking out seven and allowing one run, while Thomas Revering pitched two innings of relief. Cody Benson went 3-for-5 as the Blue Ox scored seven runs. Crookston beat Moorhead 3-2 in extra innings to earn runner-up and a state berth. Bemidji received a first-round bye in the 48-team state tournament and will first play Aug. 27 against the winner of Fort Ripley and Blue Earth. The championship is Sept. 4.

Dale Capstick of Coxheath, Nova Scotia, has seen nightly visits by palm-sized giant house spiders since August, with her husband killing about 30. Charles Andrews captured one that died and shrank; Nova Scotia Museum biologist Calum Ewing identified it as Eratigena atrica, a harmless European house spider. Native to western Europe and present in Nova Scotia since the mid-1990s, the species has a 10–18 millimetre body and leg span up to 10 centimetres. Often found in sinks or bathtubs because they cannot climb smooth surfaces, they feed on insects and may leave or starve when prey is gone. Persistent infestations can be addressed by exterminators.

Meizu cut the Pro 7 and Pro 7 Plus prices by 600 yuan to 2,499 and 3,299 yuan, with the series starting at 1,999 yuan from December 12. Both phones have secondary displays, dual 12MP rear cameras, Flyme OS 6, and 3,000mAh or 3,500mAh batteries.

Rushin Shah, Apple’s former head of Natural Language Understanding for Siri, left after five years to join Facebook, citing a desire for a new challenge. Shah helped build Siri’s voice-recognition, intent-interpretation, classification, and conversational “banter” features. His departure comes amid growing competition from Alexa and Google Assistant as Apple expands Siri to Mac, iOS features, and a Siri-based HomePod. Facebook lacks its own voice-activated assistant, and Shah may help develop one or improve “M” in Messenger; his exact role is unspecified. Apple has not named a successor.

The latest Canadian Couch Potato episode examines the balance between cost and simplicity in investing. Guest John Robertson discusses indexing options, robo-advisors, and their differing fee structures; his AutoInvest.ca tool compares all-in costs, while his course Practical Index Investing for Canadians offers account-opening and portfolio-building tutorials. The episode’s Ask the Spud segment reviews Vanguard’s one-fund asset-allocation ETFs, which charge 0.22% but may not suit every investor. Key considerations include portfolio size, automatic contributions, ETF-trading experience, account complexity, and target asset mix. Vanguard’s Balanced and Growth ETFs target 60% and 80% equities, respectively; no equivalent ETF targets 50% or 70% stocks, and the Conservative ETF’s 60% bond allocation may be less attractive, with GICs suggested as an alternative. Switching costs also vary: TD e-Series users would save under $2 monthly per $10,000, while Tangerine users would save about $7.

HPE introduced the Edgeline Services Platform, Edgeline Data Aggregation App, and Edgeline Address Translation App to help customers combine IT and operational technology (OT) and manage expanding IoT deployments. The platform runs IoT applications where equipment resides, while the apps aggregate data from OT devices and distribute network address translations to subnetworks through remotely managed, software-defined configuration. The offerings form part of HPE’s Software Defined OT approach.

ESA inaugurated New Norcia 3, a 35-meter deep-space antenna at its New Norcia station in Western Australia. Scheduled to enter service in 2026, it is the fourth antenna in ESA’s Estrack network and the site’s second, expanding capacity for spacecraft communications and data downloads.

The antenna includes components cooled to about −263°C, enabling detection of extremely weak signals, and a 20-kW radio-frequency amplifier for sending commands to spacecraft millions or billions of kilometers away. It will support current ESA missions including Juice, Solar Orbiter, BepiColombo, Mars Express, Euclid, ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter and Hera, plus future Plato, Envision, Ariel, Ramses and Vigil missions. It can also assist NASA, JAXA, ISRO and commercial missions through cross-support arrangements.

The €62.3 million project was led by European contractors with substantial Australian industry involvement and included a €3 million contribution from the Australian Space Agency. CSIRO locally operates the station, whose location complements ESA’s facilities in Argentina and Spain and enables around-the-clock deep-space coverage.

UCL and Imperial College London researchers revealed that polymyxin antibiotics kill Gram-negative bacteria by forcing cells to rapidly overproduce and shed their protective outer layer, creating gaps that let the drugs enter. High-resolution imaging and biochemical experiments showed that this disruption and bacterial death occur only in active cells; dormant bacteria remain unaffected because they stop producing their outer armor. When sugar was added to wake dormant cells, polymyxin B killed them after a 15-minute delay. The findings may help explain antibiotic persistence and recurrent infections, and suggest strategies involving waking dormant bacteria or stimulating armor production to improve treatment effectiveness.

The passage defines SD Memory Card initialization, identification, data-transfer, erase, security, and function-switching behavior. After bus activation, the host issues CMD8 for Version 2.00 or later cards and repeatedly sends ACMD41 with voltage and HCS settings. The OCR busy bit indicates initialization completion, while CCS identifies SDSC, SDHC, or SDXC cards. The first ACMD41’s arguments control initialization, repeated commands use the same arguments, and the host timeout must exceed one second. The host then uses CMD2 to obtain each card’s CID and CMD3 to assign an RCA. UHS-I initialization can request 1.8 V signaling through S18R and CMD11, while CMD19 supports sampling-point tuning.

Identification operates at fOD, after which data transfer can use fPP. CMD9 retrieves the CSD, CMD4 optionally configures the DSR, and CMD7 selects one card for point-to-point communication. Reads use CMD17 or CMD18; writes and other transfers use commands including CMD24, CMD25, CMD27, CMD42, and CMD56. Data blocks are CRC-protected and generally limited to 512 bytes. CMD12 stops transfers. Misaligned accesses, invalid lengths, and write-protected areas produce errors. Block writes may be buffered, with DAT0 indicating programming status; programming, erase, parameter-set, and read operations have state restrictions. Deselecting a card can release its DAT lines without interrupting programming, while reset may terminate operations and destroy data. ACMD23 can pre-erase blocks for faster writes, and ACMD22 reports the number of successfully written blocks.

Erase operations use CMD32 and CMD33 to define a range and CMD38 to execute it. Protected sectors remain unchanged. DISCARD makes discarded contents “don’t care” and has a 250 ms timeout; FULE logically erases the entire user area and has a one-second timeout. Both are supported only by SDHC and SDXC cards and not through SPI.

Write protection can be mechanical, card-internal, or password-based. CMD42 manages PWD and PWD_LEN and supports setting, replacing, clearing, locking, and unlocking passwords. Locked cards accept only specified commands and reject ACMD6 bus-width changes. Card Ownership Protection adds FEP and FEP_LEN, COP Unlock, additional CMD42 functions, and FEP-protected force erase. Force erase removes all card content and password data, unlocks the card, and does not erase the secure area.

CMD55 causes the following command to be interpreted as an ACMD; the APP_CMD status indicates whether a defined or undefined ACMD was accepted and interpreted accordingly. CMD6 switches functions through six groups, including bus speed, command-system extension, driver strength, and power limit. Mode 0 queries supported functions and maximum power, while Mode 1 changes selected functions. The default power limit is 0.72 W, and inadequate power prevents a function from initializing. Optional High-Speed mode uses a 50 MHz clock for 25 MB/sec and requires separate host-to-card connections because only one differently timed card may be driven.

CMD8 checks whether the card supports the host’s supplied voltage. SDSC uses byte addressing and CMD16-defined block lengths, whereas SDHC and SDXC use block addressing, fixed 512-byte memory-access blocks, and do not permit partial or misaligned access.

The West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals considered whether a private employer violated state public policy by terminating three at-will cleaning-maid employees for refusing to take polygraph tests. The plaintiffs had signed an agreement in January 1981 authorizing polygraph testing, refused testing announced for June 1982, and were discharged on October 12, 1982.

The circuit court ruled that the discharges violated substantial public policy and certified two questions. The Court held that whether substantial public policy exists is a question of law for the court, not the jury. It also held that at-will employees are protected when an employer’s discharge contravenes substantial public policy, relying on West Virginia’s recognition of individual privacy interests and 1983 legislation restricting employer use of polygraph tests. The majority concluded that requiring or requesting polygraph testing as a condition of employment is contrary to West Virginia public policy, although not every such test is prohibited. It affirmed the circuit court’s ruling and remanded for further proceedings.

Justice Miller, joined by Justice Neely, dissented. They argued that no established public policy prohibited polygraph-related discharge when the plaintiffs were terminated in October 1982, because the relevant statute did not become effective until July 1983. They also concluded that the cited privacy cases did not establish an invasion of privacy in this case and that the majority improperly created a new rule after the fact. Justice Neely separately emphasized that the decision was a radical, substantive departure from settled at-will employment law and that prospective application would be more appropriate.

Both teams played well in a fast Game 1 of a three-game Stanley Cup series against Tampa Bay, but the Lightning’s goalie had the upper hand. The speaker’s team scored no goals, needs better chances and a killer instinct, and hopes to get breaks next game. The officials were praised, though some players might benefit from rest.

Bishop Hassan Kukah urged Nigerian politicians to improve governance and respect citizens’ concerns, saying persistent frustration and election-related divisions were testing the military’s patience. He praised the military for sustaining democracy for 16–17 years, warned against hiding misgovernance behind religion, and called on citizens to question leaders’ promises and show greater courage. Kukah also urged tolerance of opposing views and announced a leadership forum where Ghanaian President Nana Akufo-Addo would lecture on sustaining democracy in Africa.

Austin Police Chief Brian Manley appealed to those responsible for three package bombs that killed two people and injured two earlier in the month, asking them to contact authorities before more harm occurs. All victims were Black or Hispanic, and authorities were investigating the attacks as a possible hate crime. Manley said investigators received help from about 500 federal agents, reviewed 735 suspicious-package reports, logged 236 interviews and checked 435 leads. The reward for information was raised to $100,000, in addition to the governor’s $15,000 reward, and police sought more public tips.

The passage combines a frequently repeated roundup of global business headlines with a feature on UK Chancellor Rachel Reeves’s November budget. Topics include instant-payment links between the SNB and ECB, a BRICS bank’s first Indian rupee bond, Trump’s H-1B changes, BBVA’s €17 billion bid for Sabadell, stock-market movements, SharpLink’s Ethereum share tokenization, South Korea’s data-centre recovery, an Iran-Russia nuclear deal, infrastructure investment, OpenAI parental controls, U.S. chip rules, and regulatory actions involving Meta and TikTok.

Reeves declined to rule out tax increases, citing geopolitical instability, U.S. tariffs, rising borrowing costs and the need for fiscal discipline, while noting that avoiding VAT rises remains policy for now. Darren Jones likewise left manifesto tax caps open. With forecasts of a shortfall of up to £30 billion, analysts said Reeves is preserving flexibility, leaving households and businesses uncertain amid tension between investor confidence, spending control and voter expectations.

Microsoft Corporation filed a Form 8-K dated January 29, 2020, furnishing a press release announcing its financial results for the fiscal quarter ended December 31, 2019. The press release was filed as Exhibit 99.1 and was not deemed “filed” under Section 18 of the Exchange Act or incorporated by reference absent specific reference. The report was signed by Frank H. Brod.

Questia Media, an online college library and research service, laid off 139 employees, reducing its workforce from about 280 to 140. Founder Troy Williams said the company was slowing the addition of digitized books because it was struggling to raise additional capital. The service launched in January with roughly 1,000 subscribers but recently exceeded 5,000, prompting the company to expect positive cash flow in about 18 months and seek another funding round.

U.S. markets were mixed ahead of a Federal Reserve meeting. The Dow fell 51.66 points to 10,883.51, while the Nasdaq gained 25.20 points to 2,198.77. A report showing first-quarter worker productivity declined 0.1% raised inflation concerns and pushed the 10-year Treasury yield to 5.24%, while shorter yields fell as investors expected another Fed rate cut. Chip stocks advanced on Cisco’s earnings, but financial stocks weakened, and Enron fell $1.93 to $56.11.

Enron Japan officials said Japan’s deregulated electricity market lacked meaningful competition because of regulatory requirements, transmission-network costs and uncertainty over transmission fees. Non-utility suppliers represented only 0.2% of the market. Enron called for an independent regulator, citing the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry’s historical ties to incumbent utilities, and was relying on a Brattle Group study of the industry to support its case for reform.

Williams began expanding into European gas and power markets with a London operation staffed by 25 traders, initially covering the UK, Germany, Scandinavia and Benelux. The company planned to sell structured trading and risk-management services to utilities rather than acquire power stations, with possible expansion into crude oil and refined products and early attention to Spain and Italy.

Indian reports said families of Enron executives overseeing the 2,184-megawatt Dabhol Power Company project had relocated from Bombay to Singapore as security was tightened. Enron declined to say whether the moves were corporate or personal. The nearly complete, $2.9 billion project faced termination after the Maharashtra State Electricity Board reneged on its commitment to buy the plant’s output and defaulted on payments. DPC’s board authorized management to terminate the power-purchase agreement, while lenders indicated they would support termination if governments did not resolve the crisis. More than 15,000 jobs were reportedly at risk.

MSEB denied that it had underused its own generation capacity to justify buying Dabhol power, stating that most DPC electricity supported grid frequency and that its Uran plant was constrained by inadequate natural gas and expensive furnace oil. MSEB also said India’s federal government had not pressured it to continue the agreement. The dispute moved toward London arbitration, with MSEB appointing a former High Court judge and Enron having appointed its own arbitrator. A government panel was also reviewing the power-purchase agreement. The Swadeshi Jagran Manch demanded a judicial probe into alleged inflated demand projections and continued advocacy for cancellation.

Separately, Prize Petroleum planned to acquire Enron’s 30% interest in the Panna, Mukta and Tapti offshore fields, valuing it at about Rs 600 crore. Prize Petroleum, half-owned by Hindustan Petroleum Corporation, would invest Rs 1,900 crore in the project. Enron had sought to farm out its stake after becoming uncomfortable operating the fields.

The ADS868xW is a fully integrated, fully differential 16-bit SAR ADC data-acquisition device with an integrated analog front end, programmable gain amplifier, ADC driver, and buffered precision reference. It supports single-ended and differential bipolar or unipolar inputs with straight-binary output. The full-scale range equals positive full scale minus negative full scale, and the LSB size is FSR/2¹⁶.

An active-high ALARM/SDO-1/GPO output can be configured for alarm operation. The input alarm monitors the converted input against programmable high and low thresholds with common programmable hysteresis: the high alarm triggers above its threshold and resets at threshold−hysteresis−1, while the low alarm triggers below its threshold and resets at threshold+hysteresis+1. The AVDD alarm monitors the analog supply against fixed typical limits of 4.7 V and 5.3 V. Both alarms are enabled by default and can be disabled through RST_PWRCTL_REG bits. Active and tripped flags are available in ALARM_REG; active flags clear at the end of each conversion, while tripped flags clear after the register is read. Alarm status can be accessed through the pin, internal registers, or appended output flags.

The multiSPI digital interface supports standard SPI and source-synchronous transfers, with configurable control, timing, and single- or dual-SDO output. Supported host connections include standalone configurations and daisy-chained devices sharing CONVST/CS and SCLK. Daisy-chained devices require identical register configurations and an optimal frame of 32×N SCLK edges; output data returns from the last device to the first.

The device has RESET, ACQ, and CONV states. The active-low RST input can trigger either an application reset or a full power-on reset. A rising CONVST/CS edge initiates conversion and causes the device to return to ACQ afterward; the host can detect completion through RVS or wait for the maximum conversion time.

A transfer frame begins with a falling CONVST/CS edge and ends with its rising edge, which starts a conversion. Input and output operations use 32-bit shift registers. A 32-clock frame is optimal and executes a valid command; shorter frames cannot perform writes but can provide valid output bits; in longer frames, the final 32 input bits form the command. Byte and half-word commands support register reads and writes, with half-word commands ignoring the least significant address bit.

Output data for the next frame can be a fixed test pattern, 8- or 16-bit register data, or the latest 16-bit conversion result. DATAOUT_CTL_REG can append device address, input-range, AVDD-alarm, input-alarm, and parity information. Four legacy SPI modes support configuration, while reads can use single-SDO SPI, dual-SDO SPI, or source-synchronous timing. Source-synchronous mode uses RVS as the output clock and permits internal or external clock sourcing.

Nine configuration registers control device identification, reset and power, SDI and SDO protocols, output data, input ranges, alarms, and alarm thresholds. Writes to protected reset/power bits require first writing 69h to address 05h. The data-output register also supports fixed patterns and even-parity bits.

An application example combines an ADS8681W with an eight-channel MUX36D08 differential multiplexer to create an eight-channel industrial input module. It supports software-configured voltage or current channels, including bipolar ±2.5 V, ±5 V, and ±10 V and unipolar 0–5 V, 0–10 V, 4–20 mA, and 0–20 mA ranges. The ADC settles to 1% accuracy in under 5 µs and supports NTC-thermistor temperature monitoring using programmable alarm thresholds and hysteresis to prevent noise-induced false triggers.

The device uses separate AVDD analog and DVDD digital supplies. Application guidance specifies close placement of 1 µF and at least 10 µF supply-decoupling capacitors, separate analog and digital PCB regions, short ground paths, and specified REFCAP and REFIO capacitors. Programmable NAP and power-down modes reduce consumption at lower throughput; power-down retains the interface and registers while powering down analog blocks. The document also provides support resources, ESD guidance, revision information, and mechanical and orderable information.

Mary Carolyn Fine appealed a judgment denying her custody of her son, Edward, and confirming custody in Edward’s father, Edward T. Denny. The court declined to address whether the Nevada divorce court had jurisdiction or whether Fine was estopped from challenging its custody decree. Although both parents had suitable homes and were equally fit, the trial court could consider Edward’s best interests, including continuity and stability of his home life. Because Edward had lived with his father from age two, except for a 14-month interruption, the court found that maintaining custody with the father was not an abuse of discretion despite the statutory preference for mothers of tender children. The judgment was affirmed.

The lecture introduces ordinary differential equation initial value problems (ODE-IVPs), written in standard form as \(dy/dt=f(t,y)\), with all initial conditions specified at the same time. Higher-order equations and physical systems can be converted into systems of first-order equations for use with MATLAB solvers, which generally return time points and corresponding matrices of solution values. Integration may proceed forward or backward from the initial time.

Forward Euler is introduced by truncating a Taylor expansion and repeatedly updating \(y\). Its local error is of order \(\Delta t^2\), while its overall error is approximately of order \(\Delta t\), making it relatively inaccurate and computationally expensive to refine. The method is analogous to the rectangle rule. More accurate rules, such as the trapezoid and midpoint rules, achieve overall errors of order \(\Delta t^2\).

Because an ODE’s derivative depends on the unknown \(y\), directly adapting midpoint and trapezoid formulas is difficult. A higher-order Taylor expansion would require Jacobian evaluations, which are costly. Runge-Kutta methods instead estimate future values using available function evaluations. Second-order Runge-Kutta uses two evaluations, while MATLAB’s ODE45 combines fourth- and fifth-order methods, compares their estimates, and adjusts step size according to specified tolerances.

The lecture emphasizes numerical stability: errors introduced at one step can be amplified by later steps. This amplification is governed by the norm of an iteration matrix involving the derivative of the update formula. Systems with positive eigenvalues in the differential equation’s Jacobian are inherently unstable and can amplify small perturbations. Even stable equations can become numerically unstable if the solver and step size are poorly chosen. For \(dy/dt=-2y\), Forward Euler with \(\Delta t=1\) produces an oscillating sawtooth rather than decay toward zero; a smaller step size behaves more reasonably. Homework requires writing and comparing ODE solvers, and implicit methods will be covered next.

The chapter examines modeling and validation for digital business processes in extended enterprises, where organizations with common goals collaborate across company boundaries. It presents an MDA-based business process model with three components: a static domain model of actors and resources, a workflow model of process activities, and a value model describing exchanges among participants.

Business rules are expressed through controlled natural languages such as Attempto Controlled English and SBVR, then translated into logic-based representations including DRS, OWL DL, RuleML, and SWRL. Automated reasoning requires hybrid approaches because externally sourced information is often incomplete and requires open-world assumptions, while internally controlled information can use closed-world assumptions. The chapter also addresses limitations of current semantic formalisms and the representation of alethic and deontic business rules.

Workflow modeling approaches include BPMN, UML Activity Diagrams, Petri nets, π-calculus, and temporal logic. Declarative representations support consistency checking, data export, and annotation, including checking BPMN structures against static models and runtime logs. Value models use graphical techniques such as REA and e3-value, as well as logic-based representations, to quantify value transfers, dependencies, and collaboration profitability.

Relations among business-rule, value, process, implementation, and log-file models support static, semi-dynamic, and dynamic consistency checks. Monitoring compares actual value exchanges in system logs with forecasts, while process discovery derives process descriptions from logs. Remaining issues include detecting areas requiring model changes and representing stakeholders’ reasons for actions.

The article examines digital storytelling as a tool for modernizing African higher education and teacher training. Digital storytelling combines traditional narrative methods with digital media such as text, images, audio, animation, and video to create personal or group stories. Its educational uses include fostering creativity, digital and media literacy, reflection, critical and higher-order thinking, problem-solving, technological competence, motivation, engagement, and learning autonomy. The process generally involves pre-production planning, production of narration and visuals, and post-production assembly, publication, and audience feedback.

A qualitative document analysis reviewed 15 scientific articles published from 2000 onward on digital storytelling in African higher education and teacher training. Studies from South Africa, Nigeria, Egypt, Tanzania, Uganda, and Kenya primarily used qualitative methods and examined educational, personal, cultural, and social outcomes.

Reported benefits include stronger student engagement, peer learning, interaction with lecturers, improved map-reading and oral proficiency, and greater control over learning. Digital storytelling also supports identity expression and empowerment, especially for marginalized groups, while sometimes reinforcing stereotypes. It can build classroom community, increase cultural understanding, prepare pre-service teachers for multicultural classrooms, preserve oral traditions and indigenous knowledge, support postgraduate research, and enable social activism.

Integration occurs across geography education, language learning, teacher training, assessment, and rural education. Barriers include inadequate equipment and unreliable electricity, insufficient resources, limited technological proficiency, low teacher confidence, rigid curricula, and insufficient time. The article concludes that digital storytelling has potential to enrich culture and promote transformative learning, while emphasizing narrative content rather than technology in assessment and calling for continued research and context-sensitive implementation.

According to court documents, casino mogul Steve Wynn settled in December 2006 with a former employee who later accused him of sexual misconduct. After the Wall Street Journal reported multiple allegations against Wynn, his attorneys alleged that the woman sought public disclosure of the settlement and attempted to extort him. Wynn reported her to the FBI; her attorney denied the extortion claims, while the FBI declined to confirm its investigation. The newly revealed settlement’s terms were not disclosed. The report followed a separate $7.5 million settlement with a former manicurist and came two months after Wynn resigned as Wynn Resorts chairman and CEO. Wynn denied the allegations and blamed his ex-wife, whose attorney denied involvement.

Jeremy Corbyn used a taxpayer-funded, chauffeur-driven Ford Galaxy diesel car while advocating action against air pollution and a phased-out diesel policy. The car waited on double yellow lines outside his Islington home for 40 minutes before taking him to Westminster; the driver was not ticketed, and the vehicle was later liable for a £24 Ultra Low Emission Zone charge from April 2019. The car emitted 189g of CO₂, achieved 36 mpg, and cost £280 annually in vehicle tax. Corbyn said he accepted the driver for security reasons and was advised to give up cycling, despite living near a Tube station. The arrangement drew criticism for hypocrisy and privilege, while Corbyn insisted that any diesel phase-out should not punish people.

The lecturer defines AMO physics through the activities of its research community and its building blocks: atoms, molecules, photons, and electromagnetic fields. He characterizes it as low-energy quantum physics and highlights the hydrogen atom, two-level systems, and harmonic oscillators as paradigmatic systems. The field has evolved from studying individual particles and collisions in gases toward few-body and many-body physics, entanglement, quantum gases, quantum information, and overlap with condensed matter physics.

A major theme is AMO physics’s progression from observing nature to controlling it. Control has progressed from manipulating internal states through optical pumping, to controlling motion through optical forces, laser cooling, and Bose–Einstein condensation, and finally to controlling individual atoms and photons. Current aims include assembling controlled systems into highly entangled, correlated many-body states and exploring previously inaccessible regions of Hilbert space.

These advances have been driven by technology. Large, expensive dye lasers gave way to robust solid-state and diode lasers; ultrashort, high-intensity pulses enabled strong-field atomic physics; frequency combs enabled highly precise frequency control and metrology; and high-finesse cavities enabled single-photon studies. Historically, major milestones included laser spectroscopy, optical traps, Bose–Einstein condensation, studies of ultracold fermions, entanglement, and correlations. Emerging areas include quantum computation, topological states, and micromechanical oscillators cooled to their ground state.

Course 8.422 is the second part of MIT’s graduate AMO sequence and may be taken before or after 8.421. Prerequisites are 8.05 and 8.06, particularly perturbation theory. Planned topics include QED and light–atom interactions, spontaneous emission and open-system methods using density matrices and master equations, optical forces, trapping and cooling, single photons, quantum-information gates, many-body quantum gases, and trapped-ion sideband cooling. Advanced atomic structure, high-energy collisions, and high-intensity short-pulse laser physics are excluded.

An extended example uses atoms in optical lattices. Interfering laser beams create a periodic potential, which the lecturer describes through classical, quantum-optical, and microscopic perspectives. Deep lattices isolate atoms for precision measurements and atomic clocks, while magic wavelengths decouple internal clock transitions from mechanical motion. Shallow lattices allow tunneling, band structure, Bloch states, Bose–Einstein-condensate-to-Mott-insulator transitions, and fermionic metal-to-Mott-insulator crossovers. Pulsed lattices serve as beam splitters in atom interferometers for measuring inertial forces and can probe momentum and energy transfer in interacting many-body systems.

The course includes ten research-derived problem sets, no midterm or final, and a term paper due on the final class day. Classes meet Monday and Wednesday, with occasional Friday makeup sessions.

University of Utah researchers mapped Old Faithful’s near-surface geology and hydrothermal plumbing using 133 portable seismometers, ambient-vibration analysis, and other seismic techniques. The study identified the geyser’s reservoir as a network of cracks and fractures approximately 200 meters in diameter, holding about 300,000 cubic meters of water. Seismic tremors intensified for roughly 60 minutes before each eruption, followed by about 30 minutes of quiet. The tremors were linked to the rapid cooling, collapse, and implosion of hot, pressurized bubbles as the reservoir refilled after an eruption.

The study also examined how seismic waves are altered by underground features and how ambient ground vibrations can reveal shallow geology. Published in Geophysical Research Letters, the research was led by doctoral student Sin-Mei Wu and represented more than a decade of planning by Robert Smith and colleagues. The team conducted another survey in November 2016 and planned further deployments to study temperature effects, earthquake-wave reverberation, and the Norris Geyser Basin.

Commenting on memoranda from other governments, Secretary Stettinius said all should attend the general conference with open minds and as few formal commitments as possible, since formal positions would be harder to change later; he urged a flexible rather than crystallized approach, noting that Dumbarton Oaks proposals had been kept informal because they might require modification. Discussions addressed objections to the name "United Nations" (coined by Roosevelt on December 31, 1941, for the January 1, 1942 joint declaration) and whether Chapter I should enumerate specific principles such as respect for international treaties, juridical equality of nations, and territorial integrity.

Stettinius's diary (December 1, 1944–July 3, 1945) records preparations for the Yalta and Mexico City Foreign Ministers' meetings. On January 10 he urged notifying the six Latin American "associated nations" that they might be excluded from initial participation in the United Nations Conference unless they declared war and thus qualified as United Nations, with missions in Montevideo, Asunción, Lima, and Santiago to inform presidents or foreign ministers. He pressed staff to speed memoranda, including ten points, for Roosevelt's Big-Three meeting and prepared to cable Pasvolsky to begin calling a United Nations Conference, with delegation makeup, date, and place settled in advance. Voting procedure remained the chief outstanding issue: the British would accept a compromise formula, but Roosevelt felt the United States would probably have to yield to the Russian view of unanimity in exchange for Soviet concessions on seventeen votes. Stettinius regarded Yalta as the first chiefs-of-state meeting he attended; he kept his Crimea notes in the vault an extra month for security, and they are missing from Department files.

The First Circuit affirmed the denial of Ronald L. Johnson’s habeas corpus petition and held that his confession was voluntary. Johnson was convicted in 1964 of first-degree murder, armed robbery, and related offenses arising from a liquor-store robbery and the shooting of a Boston police officer. His confession followed approximately eight and one-half hours of custody and was challenged as coerced.

The court independently reviewed the undisputed facts under the “totality of the circumstances” standard and concluded that Johnson’s will had not been overborne. Although Johnson was injured, had limited education and intelligence, lacked sleep, received no Miranda warnings, and never requested counsel, those circumstances were not coercive without evidence of actual threats, improper influence, or police-inflicted injury. He remained alert, resisted police at booking, participated in lineups, and challenged witnesses’ identifications.

The court also relied on Johnson’s prior, often hostile experiences with police, which indicated that he was not likely cowed by police contact. His identification of witnesses in the lineups exposed him to incriminating evidence but did not constitute coercion. The short period before the confession, his refusal to give an incriminating statement, and the absence of evidence that police had abused him outweighed his claimed physical and psychological vulnerabilities. Because the confession was voluntary even under the burden-shifting standard of Lego v. Twomey, the court found it unnecessary to decide whether Lego applied retroactively or whether the trial court had failed to consider all circumstances.

Eighteen scientists, including 13 U.S.-based researchers, received French grants to conduct climate research in France. Camille Parmesan and Benjamin Sanderson said France’s support and worsening U.S. research conditions influenced their decisions. Parmesan will spend five years at an experimental ecology station in the Pyrenees, while Sanderson will work in Toulouse with France’s national meteorological service.

**Summary**

The COVID-19 pandemic required sustained behavior change, restrictions, masking, testing, and vaccination, with compliance shaped by beliefs, risk perception, trust in government, and demographic factors. Mass testing and early diagnosis were key control measures, and understanding how adherence to preventive measures changes over time can guide future outbreak policy.

This study describes tests conducted by the Healthy Davis Together program, launched in September 2020 in Davis, California, and expanded in July 2021 to Yolo County as Healthy Yolo Together. The program combined free high-throughput saliva-based asymptomatic testing, targeted communication campaigns, education to reduce misinformation, personal protective equipment distribution, community partnerships to build trust, and local economic investment. Most tests were PCR saliva tests (98.4%) with 1.6% rapid antigen tests (BinaxNOW for symptomatic individuals).

Among Yolo County residents, 770,165 tests were administered to 89,924 people (53,869 in Davis), reaching about 41.1% of the county and 78.4% of Davis residents. Data were divided into Pre-Delta, Delta, Omicron, and Post-Omicron periods; daily tests per 100,000 were 422, 746, 895, and 435 respectively. Overall, 12,626 tests were positive among 11,545 individuals. Participants were 43.1% female and 37.3% male, with participation of at least 25% across race/ethnicity and age groups under 85. Highest positivity rates were American Indian/Alaska Native (7.6%), Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (5.6%), Latinos (4.5%), and people aged 20–44.

Omicron had the highest daily participation (1,959 average tests; ~895 per 100K), the most positive cases (5,865; 50.8% of all positives), and the most frequent testers (39.7% vs. 31.9%, 28.9%, 31.4%). New participants declined across periods (39,819; 33,814; 13,503; 2,788). Excluding those under 18, 12,591 of 67,083 adults (18.8%) were frequent testers, averaging 6–7 days between tests, with one person tested up to 116 times during Delta. Women, ages 19–44, and White participants were consistently the most frequent testers.

The authors note that women's greater participation aligns with prior literature on greater risk aversion and precautionary behavior, describe Omicron as a turning point with post-Omicron declines attributable to pandemic fatigue, and acknowledge that the data cannot explain the reasons for observed differences or individual behavioral determinants.

Worcester paid city employees over $11 million in overtime in 2017, including $4.4 million for police. Officials attributed police overtime to specialized work, training, protests, events and grants—not understaffing—while public works overtime covered snow removal and water-main breaks. Police also received $9.3 million in detail pay, with several officers earning more from details than regular salary. City Manager Edward Augustus Jr. was the highest-paid employee, and 223 employees earned over $100,000.

Indiana officials reported 278 flu deaths this season, while IU Health said flu season can continue until mid-April. IU Health experts said flu and norovirus can survive on surfaces for days or weeks and infect people who touch their faces. In a lab experiment, a reporter had normal skin bacteria on her hands before and after washing, prompting advice to scrub harder and longer. Her phone contained normal mouth, throat, and skin flora but could carry pathogens to her face. IU Health recommends regular soap, 20–30 seconds of washing, scrubbing hands and fingernails, thorough rinsing, and handwashing at key times to reduce illness and spread.

This study examines how walking can become an aesthetic experience through art-based practices and foster environmental awareness among prospective teachers. Conducted over 10 weeks in an undergraduate fine-arts teaching program in western Türkiye, the qualitative study involved seven participants and took place online following the 2023 earthquake. Participants completed walking routines, maintained visual and textual diaries, photographed and questioned focal points, examined Francis Alÿs’s *The Collector* and other works involving walking, and created individual artworks or designs.

Data included visual diaries, course recordings, participant texts, artworks, and interviews. Thematic analysis used axial coding, triangulation, participant validation, and multiple coders to strengthen credibility. The art-based methodology supported sensory, reflective, and collaborative engagement with place.

Participants progressively expanded their understanding of walking from an ordinary physical activity to a practice associated with freedom, identity, health, memory, social relations, and environmental concerns. Their walks heightened awareness of urban rhythms, sounds, animals, architecture, natural settings, urban isolation, and social problems. Artistic inquiry and visual analysis helped them connect personal experiences with broader social issues and incorporate subjective experience into their work. Participants created performances, collages, digital works, and other art forms, while also identifying difficulties in expressing emotions, choosing subjects, and using materials effectively.

The study demonstrates how daily walking can connect life, art, and education, support multiple perspectives and visual literacy, and become a form of critical inquiry with potential for social change. It also distinguishes this sustained, place-based engagement from the fleeting tourist and flâneur gazes and recommends future research on participatory, community-based approaches.

India’s Supreme Court ordered that political parties can no longer seek votes in the name of religion, caste, creed, community or language. The author criticizes the ruling as politically significant, legally unclear and potentially unimplementable. They argue that identity-based mobilization has helped marginalized groups counter discrimination and gain representation, including through reserved seats. Although acknowledging that communalism, hate speech and orchestrated violence have damaged Indian democracy, the author says these problems require stronger enforcement of the rule of law and political engagement rather than judicial bans. They also note that electoral priorities are changing, with young voters increasingly considering leadership, delivery, infrastructure and public goods alongside identity-based concerns. Concluding that social divisions inevitably shape politics, the author urges the judiciary to allow India’s electoral democracy to evolve without imposing artificial restrictions.

Apple Inc. reported unaudited results for its fiscal 2023 third quarter ended July 1, 2023. The quarter included 53 weeks, compared with 52 weeks in the prior-year period. Third-quarter net sales were $81.797 billion, down 1% from $82.959 billion, while nine-month sales were $293.787 billion, down 3% from $304.182 billion. Third-quarter net income rose to $19.881 billion from $19.442 billion, and diluted EPS was $1.26 versus $1.20. For the nine months, net income was $74.039 billion versus $79.082 billion, and diluted EPS was $4.67 versus $4.82.

Third-quarter gross margin was $36.413 billion, or 44.5%, compared with $35.885 billion, or 43.3%. Operating income was $22.998 billion versus $23.076 billion. Nine-month gross margin was $128.721 billion, or 43.8%, and operating income was $87.332 billion versus $94.543 billion. Third-quarter research and development expense increased to $7.442 billion from $6.797 billion, primarily due to headcount-related expenses, while selling, general and administrative expense was nearly unchanged at $5.973 billion. The effective tax rate declined to 12.5% from 15.7% for the quarter and to 14.6% from 16.3% for nine months.

Third-quarter product sales were led by iPhone at $39.669 billion, down 2%; Mac at $6.840 billion, down 7%; iPad at $5.791 billion, down 20%; and Wearables, Home and Accessories at $8.284 billion, up 2%. Services sales increased 8% to $21.213 billion, primarily because of advertising, cloud services and the App Store. For the nine months, iPhone sales declined 4%, Mac 24%, iPad 1%, Wearables, Home and Accessories 3%, while Services rose 7%.

By segment, third-quarter net sales rose 5% in Europe and 8% in Greater China, while declining 6% in the Americas, 11% in Japan and 8% in the Rest of Asia Pacific. Currency weakness relative to the U.S. dollar negatively affected total sales and several segments. Nine-month segment sales declined 6% in the Americas, 1% in Europe, 2% in Greater China and 8% in Japan, and increased 1% in the Rest of Asia Pacific.

As of July 1, 2023, Apple reported total assets of $335.038 billion, total liabilities of $274.764 billion and shareholders’ equity of $60.274 billion. Cash and cash equivalents were $28.408 billion, current marketable securities were $34.074 billion and non-current marketable securities were $104.061 billion. Nine-month operating cash flow was $88.945 billion, investing activities provided $1.311 billion and financing activities used $85.335 billion, leaving $29.898 billion of cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash at period-end.

Apple repurchased $18.0 billion of stock and paid $3.8 billion of dividends during the third quarter. For the nine months, it repurchased 365 million shares for $56.1 billion, excluding excise tax, and paid $11.267 billion in dividends and dividend equivalents. The quarterly dividend was $0.24 per share, and the company stated that it intended to increase the dividend annually, subject to Board approval. Commercial paper outstanding was $4.0 billion, and fixed-rate notes had a $105.3 billion carrying amount and $95.3 billion fair value. Manufacturing purchase obligations totaled $38.4 billion, with $38.1 billion payable within 12 months.

Apple said its cash, unrestricted marketable securities, operating cash flow and access to debt markets were sufficient to meet cash requirements and capital returns for at least the next 12 months. Deferred revenue was $12.2 billion, with 67% expected to be recognized within one year.

During the quarter, Apple announced a 15-inch MacBook Air with the M2 chip, Mac Studio with M2 Max and M2 Ultra chips, Mac Pro with M2 Ultra, and Apple Vision Pro with visionOS, expected in early calendar 2024. It also announced iOS 17, macOS Sonoma, iPadOS 17, tvOS 17 and watchOS 10.

Regarding legal matters, the European Court of Justice held a hearing in May 2023 on the Commission’s appeal of the annulled European Commission State Aid Decision, with a decision expected in 2024. In the Epic Games litigation, the Ninth Circuit affirmed rulings concerning App Store Review Guidelines, but Apple obtained a stay of the injunction barring anti-steering provisions pending a possible U.S. Supreme Court appeal; Epic appealed that stay. Management stated that other legal matters were not reasonably likely to result in a material loss beyond recorded accruals. Disclosure controls were effective as of July 1, 2023, no material changes occurred in internal control over financial reporting, and there were no material changes in risk factors or critical accounting estimates.

Abraaj, a $13.6 billion private-equity firm focused on developing economies, has been promoted by Kim and Gates as a model for attracting private capital to investments such as hospitals in developing markets. Its $1 billion health care fund raised $545 million to buy hospitals in Nigeria, Pakistan and India. At a September investor meeting, financial statements showed more than $200 million remained uninvested. Investors questioned founder Arif Naqvi and fund manager Khawar Mann, sought bank statements and an independent audit, and requested repayment; Abraaj returned more than $100 million in December while also hiring KPMG.

The IFC invested $100 million in the fund, the Gates Foundation invested $100 million, and the U.S. OPIC had a $150 million loan to Abraaj. A World Bank investigation closed without finding evidence of wrongdoing. The fund invested only about half its capital, while its $145 million purchase of Hyderabad hospital network CARE generated lower-than-expected profits. Naqvi was seeking to raise a $6 billion fund for investments benefiting developing countries.

Amazon.com, Inc.’s Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2018 reported unaudited financial results. Third-quarter net sales increased 29% to $56.6 billion, operating income rose from $347 million to $3.7 billion, and net income increased from $256 million to $2.9 billion. Diluted earnings per share were $5.75, compared with $0.52 in the prior-year quarter. For the first nine months, net sales rose 37% to $160.5 billion, operating income increased to $8.6 billion, net income rose to $7.0 billion, and diluted earnings per share reached $14.10.

Third-quarter segment sales and operating income were $34.3 billion and $2.0 billion for North America, $15.5 billion and a $385 million operating loss for International, and $6.7 billion and $2.1 billion for AWS. Sales grew 35% in North America, 13% internationally, and 46% in AWS. Management attributed North American and International gains to higher unit sales, third-party seller sales, advertising revenue, and slower expense growth, partly offset by fulfillment-network expansion. AWS growth reflected increased customer usage and productivity, partly offset by price reductions and higher infrastructure and payroll spending.

At September 30, 2018, Amazon reported $143.7 billion of assets, $39.1 billion of stockholders’ equity, $20.4 billion of cash and cash equivalents, and $9.3 billion of marketable securities. Operating cash flow was $8.6 billion for the third quarter and $14.2 billion for the first nine months, compared with $3.8 billion and $6.0 billion in the prior-year periods. Investing cash flow was negative $5.6 billion for the quarter and negative $8.8 billion for the nine months, while financing cash flow was negative $2.4 billion and negative $5.9 billion, respectively.

Amazon adopted new revenue-recognition guidance on January 1, 2018, increasing retained earnings by approximately $650 million. During the first nine months, approximately $2.6 billion of Amazon Prime fees were reclassified from product sales to service sales, and advertising reclassification increased service sales by approximately $2.0 billion. The company also adopted guidance on restricted cash and income taxes and planned to recognize operating lease assets and liabilities beginning January 1, 2019.

Amazon acquired Ring for approximately $839 million and PillPack for approximately $753 million, both net of acquired cash, plus other companies for $46 million. The aggregate purchase price allocation included $1.2 billion of goodwill and $671 million of intangible assets. Amazon had $24.3 billion of unsecured senior notes outstanding and $579 million of other long-term debt. It established a $7.0 billion commercial paper program and a $7.0 billion revolving credit agreement, with no commercial paper or revolving-credit borrowings outstanding at quarter-end.

Contractual commitments totaled $124.4 billion, including $40.2 billion for debt principal and interest, $16.1 billion for capital leases, $8.3 billion for finance leases, $24.5 billion for operating leases, and $21.8 billion for purchase obligations. Purchase obligations and open orders totaled $15.7 billion. Amazon reported that operating cash flow, cash and marketable securities, and borrowing arrangements were expected to meet anticipated operating cash needs for at least the following 12 months.

Disclosed contingencies included possible sanctions penalties, indirect-tax claims, a South Carolina assessment concerning third-party seller taxes, and tax contingencies of $3.4 billion. The IRS sought approximately $1.5 billion of additional federal tax in transfer-pricing disputes, while an initial approximately €250 million Luxembourg state-aid recovery was placed in escrow. Critical accounting judgments included inventory valuation and income taxes; each additional 1% of inventory valuation allowance as of quarter-end would have increased cost of sales by approximately $175 million. The filing cautioned that forward-looking results remained subject to economic, competitive, operational, legal, tax, acquisition, and international risks.

The team reviewed video to clarify goals and plans to review more. Facing a world-class playoff goalie, it will focus on reducing blocked shots, getting the puck to the net, using screens, and pursuing rebounds without bumping opponents.

The passage frames #MeToo as a rapidly emerging force in Canadian politics. It cites the resignations of Nova Scotia PC leader Jamie Baillie, Ontario PC leader Patrick Brown, and Liberal cabinet minister Kent Hehr, noting that the allegations against them had not been tested in court. The author rejects the claim that fairness has been overturned and argues that political parties should hold leaders to high standards, including avoiding the appearance of gross impropriety. While recognizing legitimate skepticism and the importance of due process, the passage maintains that fairness requires presuming complainants are truthful until evidence proves otherwise. It attributes the recent wave of allegations to a culture that long silenced women and concludes that #MeToo must be fair to endure.

Indiana is hiring private tutoring companies to improve middle school reading through outcomes-based contracting, a pay-for-performance strategy linking most payments to student improvement, after state officials found no other state's approach successful enough to copy. Education Secretary Katie Jenner said vendors pitched her all summer after middle school reading scores fell; contract structure and whether a formal request for proposals will follow remain undecided, with districts potentially drawing on state dollars and Jenner seeking donations and grants. The Center for Outcomes-Based Contracting, created in 2024 by the Southern Education Foundation, recommends at least 40% of contract value hinge on defined gains; it reports about half of 2025 member-contract goals were met, with vendors earning roughly 68% of possible bonuses. Early results elsewhere have been mixed: Duval County (50% guaranteed pay) reported math growth, Ector County discontinued the model, and Denver results varied. Stanford researchers called findings from eight districts "promising" but noted financial risks for vendors and implementation complexity. Attendance, motivation and imperfect measures complicate the approach, which targets struggling readers.
